Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide is a L4D clone in the clothes of the Warhammer universe and it's pretty damn fun.
The Story:
The Story takes place in the city of Ubersreik, which is overrun with Skaven which are rat like creatures which roam the city streets in hordes. You assume the role of one of five heroes who are trying to contain the situation.
The game is not story driven, the only story segments before every level and that's pretty much all you learn of the story.
The Gameplay:
The gameplay is as stated a pretty much carbon copy of Left 4 Dead. You can play with up to 4 friends and you can pick one of five different characters who play differently. One character is a mage, one is an archer and one wields double shotguns.
Each character has a projectile weapon and a melee weapon. The game focuses more on melee as ammo is harder to come by, but in general you should be able to conserve your ammo until the next ammo box.
The game is set into three acts where you are tasked with different goals, which range from getting to one location and trying to scavenge food, or destroying something.
If you played L4D you pretty much know what you're getting into with Vermintide as even the special enemies are just reskins of the enemies from L4D.
Graphics:
The games visuals are absolutely amazing. It's one of the best looking games visually and atmospherically. When you walk through the streets of Ubersreik and look around you and see these buildings being destroyed by the skaven is absolutely incredible.
Audio:
The games soundtrack and audio are rather bland. The audio sometimes cut out when the characters talk to each other and sometimes the audio completely disappears when you get attacked by the special times. The soundtrack is also really bland.
Closing Remarks:
The game has a few negatives. The level design is rather bad in the later segments where there's too many sections where you can fall of the map and die and have to repeat the entire level again. The game is also rather short clocking in just around 6 to 7 hours long. The game has a few reasons to go back to it, like a horde mode and quests which give you bonus loot, also there's DLC which add a few more missions to the main game. Would I suggest Vermintide ? Yes, it's a really fun game with it's flaws, but I highly suggest waiting till a sale until you bite the bullet with this one.
Final Rating:
7/10
Pros:
+ Fun Gameplay
+ Visuals are amazing
Cons:
- Bad level design in later levels
- Bland soundtrack

Almost the definition of mediocre. It doesn't do anything that hasn't already been done better before.
Shallow, dull characterization and a plot that can't decide if it wants to be serious (and typically luddite "humanoid robots are immoral") or goofy all wrapped in some fairly generic third-person shooter gameplay that cribs thoroughly from other games.
It sure throws in just about everything too in the hopes that a decent game will emerge: you've got the dismemberment mechanic from Dead Space (but without the concept of alternate weak spots that made it interesting), a light RPG system of character customization, selectible companions (with a "loyalty" system that will influence some of the cut-scenes and the ending), some on-rails shooting sections, and most awkwardly of all a speech-recognition system (that never worked for me) for controlling the AI companions and answering occasional questions. Except while they were throwing all of this together they never thought about whether it improved the game or added anything. So it just feels very mashed together.
The levels are deeply linear and the settings aren't anything new or exceptional (slums, factories, sewers, offices, etc.).
The story sort of tries, but again, the mood whiplashes between goofy and overly serious and I found myself sympathizing far more with the "villains" than the dumb, meathead protagonist. The later plot twists range from obvious to ludicrous.
The shooting itself is... decent, but it's unexceptional. If you absolutely have to play a third-person shooter there's nothing technically wrong with it and it will provide about 15 hours of generic gameplay, but you can almost certainly do better.

Easy as pie classic style point and click, but it's still pretty fun to go through it especially if you like silly humor, superheroes, and the references a plenty that go with it.

Supreme League of Patriots is a point-and click superhero parody in which the player controls "The Purple Patriot" and his alter ego, Kyle – a clumsy and not that bright guy whose dream is to win a spot on the newest hit reality TV show, America's Got Superpowers.
The salt and pepper of this game is given by the dialogs, which are supposed to be funny, but in fact they are mostly satiric and witty, and at times bland and annoying. The game is overall slow paced, most of the time is spent on reading the dialogs and the actual puzzle sequences are rather few.  Clicking an object triggers a whole set of dialogues and there is no option to skip them even if you went through them once (you can skip the lines one by one, but not the whole dialogue). Sometimes the player can’t solve the puzzle even if he has the right object in the right place, since it can’t be used until Kyle has spoken to a particular character. Other times Kyle’s character blocks the objects which the player needs to interact with. And sometimes there is no indication about what the player is expected to do, even after exploring all the dialogues.
Overall, I consider that the price is too high for the quality that the game offers, even for one episode, so I would advise to purchase it during a sale. On a positive note, it’s very easy to obtain all the achievements because most of them are story related. There is no need to do 2 playthroughs to get 100% completion since the game comes with a save/load feature which means that you can save the game at key points and reload in order to explore other paths.

Even the horniest teenage boys won't have the patience for Supreme League of Patriots. The humor is painfully juvenile, turning every little thing into a sexual, racist, sexist, or homoerotic innuendo. Many of the jokes center around taking potshots at the dim-witted protagonist, Kyle. These insults are rarely funny, but they're delivered with a British accent, so they've got to be witty. Right? I'd like to sympathize with Kyle, but he is maddeningly slow. I'm not just talking about his intelligence either. The poor buffoon trudges about the game like a brain-dead troll, and talks nearly as fast too. Every attempt this game makes at being quick-witted is sabotaged by the broken dialogue system. A short pause between each line disrupts the conversational flow and makes every interaction tedious. Speaking of things that are broken, the inventory system is completely nonsensical. Belongings are interacted with via the inventory button on the top of the screen, but to equip something you have to use the inventory found by hovering near the bottom of the screen. I was initially attracted to SLOP because of its beautiful screenshots. It is a very pretty game... when it's not in motion. Animations are stiff, and characters who are supposed to be stationary tend to shift about awkwardly, like they'd rather be somewhere else. Hey, I understand. I'd rather be somewhere else too.

This game is one of the hardest recommendations to justify giving.
It's a (mostly) survival-horror game directed by Shinji Mikami (of Resident Evil 1/4 fame), but it is survival in the sense that it really does not care about the user experience being simple in the slightest. Horrific things will happen, none of which I will spoil, and you will be left directionless and without instruction, and if you can't figure it out, you're instantly dead. Bad game design is employed to create a realistic surrealist experience. I admire this.
Does that even make sense? No. None of this does, really. The story actually has some admirable level of depth and is always connected to the environmental and creature design, including some horrific areas and things I daren't spoil. Themes are scattered liberally across the figurative narrative floor and you are left directionless and without instruction. I admire this also.
The tone shifts from tense hide-and-seek to all-out chase, to white-knuckle action without batting an eyelid. Location is temporary, so don't get comfortable, you'll probably be somewhere completely different soon, once again directionless and without any form of instruction other than to survive and a basic objective.
This sounds like a kind of terrible game, a confused one, but it is so far from it long-term. Bosses are almost universally frustrating for sure, with one-hit instadeaths that, while dodgable, feel truly unfair of the game and not skill-driven for the player. Outside of these, Mikami has crafted a shifting series of nightmares for you to go on a whistle-stop tour through, leaving you dazed and confused, the only time to empathise with the protagonist Sebastian. We are confused, he is confused, and there is a series of explanations to be found buried deep (and in some really good Kidman stealth DLC) giving some real food for thought after the credits roll.
Make no mistake, this game is a frustratingly flawed survival horror/thriller masterpiece.

Wartile is a miniature collector's wet dream.
From head to toe this game drips in the perfect aesthetic that the developer was trying to capture. Everything from the maps, textures, movement and characters themselves all feel like they were taken straight from a board game. It's actually kind of insane how good this game looks.
Wartile will no doubt attract a niche audience of collectors and tabletop players due simply to how the game looks. On that basis alone if you are a collector you should probably pick this up when it leaves Steam Early Access.
As far as gameplay goes, this is where the game faulters a little so far. The general combat and movement is servicable at best right now. It uses almost a turn-based system, but movements and abilities are in real time with a cooldown timer on when you can move characters again.
While moving around feels good when exploring the map, it runs into a problem in combat as sometimes you may accidentally move a character to an unintended tile or the game won't snap your character into the correct tile. This can cause you to take a few extra hits which could wind up with you losing the level. There is a lot of focus on moving and flanking enemies in combat both from you and the A.I., so the controls need to be worked on a bit to make sure misclicks are kept to a minimum.
The levels have also seemed a bit cheap to me every now and then, sometimes I run into bad luck and get swarmed by enemies. It's slightly annoying but the levels aren't usually long enough to make it a big deal.
While going through the levels you are looting gold, finding items and buying new miniatures to use in the game. This is where Wartile excells as it takes the best aspect of miniature collecting and improves on it by doing things you can only really do in a video game. Each miniature is customizable in their equipment, which while a very common thing in video games, having that available visibly in a miniature theme looks and feels absolutely fantastic. You even have displays for your characters in the menus of the game.
Overall Wartile is a game that you should keep your eye on if it seems at all interesting. Wait until some of the edges are ironed out through Steam Early Access, then go on a full fledged digital collectathon.

Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide is a L4D clone in the clothes of the Warhammer universe and it's pretty damn fun.
The Story:
The Story takes place in the city of Ubersreik, which is overrun with Skaven which are rat like creatures which roam the city streets in hordes. You assume the role of one of five heroes who are trying to contain the situation.
The game is not story driven, the only story segments before every level and that's pretty much all you learn of the story.
The Gameplay:
The gameplay is as stated a pretty much carbon copy of Left 4 Dead. You can play with up to 4 friends and you can pick one of five different characters who play differently. One character is a mage, one is an archer and one wields double shotguns.
Each character has a projectile weapon and a melee weapon. The game focuses more on melee as ammo is harder to come by, but in general you should be able to conserve your ammo until the next ammo box.
The game is set into three acts where you are tasked with different goals, which range from getting to one location and trying to scavenge food, or destroying something.
If you played L4D you pretty much know what you're getting into with Vermintide as even the special enemies are just reskins of the enemies from L4D.
Graphics:
The games visuals are absolutely amazing. It's one of the best looking games visually and atmospherically. When you walk through the streets of Ubersreik and look around you and see these buildings being destroyed by the skaven is absolutely incredible.
Audio:
The games soundtrack and audio are rather bland. The audio sometimes cut out when the characters talk to each other and sometimes the audio completely disappears when you get attacked by the special times. The soundtrack is also really bland.
Closing Remarks:
The game has a few negatives. The level design is rather bad in the later segments where there's too many sections where you can fall of the map and die and have to repeat the entire level again. The game is also rather short clocking in just around 6 to 7 hours long. The game has a few reasons to go back to it, like a horde mode and quests which give you bonus loot, also there's DLC which add a few more missions to the main game. Would I suggest Vermintide ? Yes, it's a really fun game with it's flaws, but I highly suggest waiting till a sale until you bite the bullet with this one.
Final Rating:
7/10
Pros:
+ Fun Gameplay
+ Visuals are amazing
Cons:
- Bad level design in later levels
- Bland soundtrack

I have mixed feelings about this game.  It's a neat little game that can engross you for a couple days, but I think it lacks longevity after that.
PROS:
-The game is pretty unforgiving at first, which can make for a nice challenge.
-The graphics are fairly nice.  If you enjoy building towns that look pleasing, then you might enjoy this game.
-There are user-made mods for the game, which I haven't tried but I assume they would add replay value.
CONS:
-The UI takes an hour or two to get used to.  Some tooltips are wrong.
-Some elements of the game are clearly incomplete.  There are certain buildings that were obviously intended to do more, but it hasn't been implemented yet.
-Most buildings can't be upgraded, which would seem like an obvious inclusion.
-The game stops growing in complexity after a relatively short time.  Once you figure out how to stock enough food to survive a winter cleanly, you don't really need to do anything else.
Overall, it feels like the game has potential, but it's not there yet.  So many mechanics could have been implemented better.  I was hoping that a town-building/survival game like this would have blossoming complexity, with more things to worry about as you expand, but it's not really like that at all.  There are some things to discover and some things to research, but they're mostly just bigger numbers that don't change the gameplay at all.
I'm happy with my purchase because I got a reasonable amount of game time out of it for a low-ish price, but I think most people would want more than that, which is why I would not be able to recommend this game.

What can I say about Binary Domain?
Let's start with the "not so good" (I wouldn't call it bad, just some things that people may not like about the game but personally I don't mind) The story is cliché and predictable, the characters are so stereotypical and the menu system on PC is a joke (I'll give you a clue... Console port).
Now that I've got that out of the way let's talk about what I absolutely love about this game.
I LOVE the entire game. It's absolutely fantastic. This is a game that the Terminator franchise should have had. I'm not even joking. No matter how cliché the story is, I loved it. It's very easy to think about how it must feel for the hollow children to find out they're androids. The horror of not knowing they are or anything. Absolutely incredible.
The combat in this game is very good, if you're a fan of 3rd person cover based shooters then it shouldn't take you too long to get a hang of the controls for this game. It's fairly easy.
The voice command system is nice, but I feel it's more of a gimmick. Many times I'll find myself telling your companions to charge, so that they get shot at while you pick off all the enemies and for most cases that works. Also I don't know why a "liking" system is in this game, basically something is said in a conversation and you can respond in multiple ways, someone in your group will like what you said and another will dislike you for it. Say enough disliked things to a person and they will ignore your commands in combat, it's a terrible feature. But you can live with it if you know what to say during those prompts.
Now, I mentioned that the menu controls for this game is bad on PC, well they are. It's much easier to play this game with a 360 controller if you have one, it'll make playing a lot easier.
Why did I mention Terminator earlier? Well forgive me for enjoying shooting killer robots hell bent on killing you and  your friends. They're so AUTHENTIC in how they look, the damage system is especially very nice, not to mention they all have glowing red eyes which is awesome. They also do a Terminator crawl when you shoot off their legs. Oh, did I forget to mention you can shoot off their body parts? Yes, the damage system is that advanced. You can ever shoot of their heads and they will proceed to shoot every figure near them, so if you do that when they're near enemies, they will shoot their own robots (don't question the logic of that).
Overall it's a VERY fun game, one that I just love to revisit over and over.

Supreme League of Patriots - Issue 1: A Patriot Is Born is the set-up for a later joke, one that only becomes clear in the dying embers of the first issue, but it does enough to stand on its own through clever writing and strong characters. A string of on-stage injuries leads to Kyle being treated by a gothic nurse whose primary form of medication is euthanasia. Mel has an on-going feud with a judge on the panel (who wears his trousers ludicrously high) about his dependency on insulting put-downs and his inability to come out of the closet. It has a shotgun approach to mockery and snide humor. When you boil it right down, it's actually pretty mean-spirited. Perhaps that’s what drew me in.
Full Review //

There are few things as vapid or as insipid as the Saturday night television lineup. Countless celebrity chat shows and talent(less) competitions litter the schedule, each one an almost identical copy of the other.  You could liken those shows to television junk food – the type that really clogs your arteries up and causes a cardiac event in later life. There’s never anything original on either, like, say, ‘America’s Got Death Defiers’. Our weekend television schedules are positively crying out for some originality! Supreme League of Patriots has the answer and its protagonist, Kyle Keever, has set his eyes on winning the America’s Got Superpowers crown. Kyle’s ultra cynical British pal Mel is also on hand to give some moral support, as well as the occasional intelligence based insult. Over the course of the first episode the pair take the world to task on everything from police brutality to homophobia.
Supreme League of Patriots follows the Telltale formula, splitting its story up into three distinct ‘issues’ as they’d call them in the comic book world. The Telltale comparisons is particularly noteworthy not only because the game is an episodic point and click, but also due to its similarities to the Sam & Max series. Having said that,  Sam & Max always toed the line between adult and kid-friendly humour, whereas Patriots takes a hop, a skip and a jump over that line, so expect adult gags aplenty.
As the inaugural episode of the series you’ll become acquainted with Kyle and Mel, their apartment and their day jobs. Kyle is a professional lay about with a dream of becoming a professional actor, he enjoys pizza, porn and sleeping. He thinks he can get his big break by entering America’s Got Superpowers as “The Purple Patriot”, a hilariously off-colour interpretation of Uncle Sam. His mate Mel is much the same but he also works in the computing department at the local police force.
Kyle’s a bit of an idiot and forgets where his audition is so you start off by around the apartment for the address and then create a map to the television studio. Once you’ve accomplished that you are on your way, and the game’s silly humour really starts to kick in.
The action plays out much like any other point and click game, meaning you’ll have to keep an eye out for points of interest in each location and pick up any items that might come in useful. Kyle isn’t a particularly talented chap, so most of the  puzzles revolve around helping him cheat his way through his audition. Whether it’s helping him feign superhuman strength or the ability to fly, you’ll need to think outside of the box. Failing that, you can always just mouse around the screen until you find something that you missed earlier. If you get really stuck you can also consult Mel, who will see you through some of the harder to decipher puzzles.
Supreme League of Patriots main draw isn’t its bog-standard gameplay, rather it’s the discourse between Kyle, Mel and the other goofballs you’ll meet between the game’s opening and closing scenes. Every location is packed with stand out one-liners, such as Mel’s ex-girlfriend calling her ♥♥♥♥♥♥ “old glory” because she expected it to be treated with reverence. The game also takes a masked swipe at TV talent show judges who bear a striking resemblance to David Hassellhoff and Simon Cowell, painting one as a talentless oaf and the other as a “privately gay” gentleman.  Barring a few duff, borderline homophobic jokes the writing is startlingly on point and self-aware, ridiculing how bland and repetitive point and click games can be at times. There’s a joke in there for pretty much everyone and the humour is spread on so thick that both Yanks and Brits alike will get have a giggle.  The script isn’t a laugh-a-minute by any means, but it kept a crease at the edges of my lips from start to finish.
As I mentioned before, the game bears the usual hallmarks of the point and click genre and does little to shake things up, so chances are you will enjoy Patriots if you are a fan of the genre, and detest it if not. The humour is always the main focus of the game though, and the tasks you’ll complete are simply there to keep the gags rolling in.
Issue one of Supreme League of Patriots ends on a cliffhanger, as all good episodic content does, leaving Kyle, ahem, The Purple Patriot in a precarious situation. Will he make it out alive? Will Mel stop being such a sarcastic knob? Will Simon Cowell ever come out of the closet? All of these questions and more might be answered in issue two, so stay tuned for my review. Oh, and definitely pick up issue one while you are at it!

Cat Quest is a super cute action-adventure game a la Zelda. There's a lot of fun, open-world exploration and just enough hidden stuff to find. The graphics and sound are top-notch -- actually, much, much better than I expected, given its modest price. I completed one whole do-everything-get-all-the-achievements playthrough in about 18.5 hours, which is pretty good value for about ten bucks. And, what can I say, it's an incredibly charming, lighthearted game.
There are extra modes for replaying with more difficulty, if that's your bag (it's not mine), and about half the Steam achievements lie in beating the game on subsequent playthroughs.
The story is pretty light, and it's certainly not an RPG in the sense that there's really no choosing and playing a role. All the quests are pretty much linear, and there's no branching decisions. However, that's not the kind of game that I think it purports to be. What it is instead is good, clean fun, light, long enough to provide great gaming value but which doesn't overstay its welcome.
Also, it never crashed once on my Mac (that's saying something) and the controller support is excellent -- I didn't touch either the keyboard or mouse at all for my entire time with the game.
I have zero complaints about this game, really.

Have 8 hours free? Like to play third-person shooters? Enjoy witty banter and bad voice acting? Boy have I got the game for you. It's called Gears of War. Get Binary Domain if you would rather just shoot robots over and over again until your hands cramp up. Oh, and try the multiplayer. It's GREAT.

A fun third-person futuristic robot/mecha shooter. It has the same game mechanics as to the Gears of War series, but instead you shoot robots! You will be in favor to get it when it's on sale though. I was surprised the game had a good story behind it, but disappointed how short it was. The only flaws to Binary Domain was the amount of cutscenes, and the countless times your clumsy AI teamates bugged you and got in your line of fire. Other than that, I recommend this to anybody who likes Japanese mecha or third-person shooters.

As I write this its $3.75 on Amazon.

As legions of robots walk towards you, like so many ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Terminators and you smack them in the face, you'll thank me.
(Use a controller though)

The momentary joy of shooting robots is far outweighed by stereotyped characters, ultra-derivative plotting, non-functional voice recognition, frustrating and repetitive bosses, dialog that fluctuates (sometimes mid-sentence) between cliched and nonsensical, uninspired art direction, and disorientingly monotonous level design. It has the feel of an ambitious game that wanted to be Gears of War, Uncharted, and Ghost in the Shell all rolled into one but it comes off as soulless, bland, and not very much fun to play.

Solid game play and heavy rpg elements - run and gun. If you enjoyed the Mass Effect series, this plays a lot along the same lines. I really wanted to recomend this game, on the basis it is ultimatley free, very solid foundation and quite alot of fun overall.
But its game that still needs alot of love and Expansion from the developers - but sadly It just doesnt feel like the devlopers care about it all that much.
There are several issue which are dragging down this games great potential.
1) Development progress seems quite half hearted, the Russian faction was a welcome addition, but that was along time ago. Very little content added since. Doesnt feel like the devs are investing very mutch $$ back in to the game. Same old maps and game modes start to feel tired before you grind even 30% up the Ranking tree.
2) Pricing, The In-game purchases are over priced and the grind is punishingly slow, Grinding vs paying to progress is not well balanced like it is in say - WarThunder, it really is bordering on the greedy side of the Free to play model.

3) Faction Balancing as pointed out by many, needs to be addressed fast, as the game is becoming one sided. Most experienced players flock to Axis/Germany and they will win the majority of matches.
4) Im sorry - but Aircraft flight and damage models are just abysmal, (the plane almost feels like its on rails), -that plus you can count the number of avaliable aircraft on one hand.
5) Will they EVER fix the prone bug?
6) Many players complain of the games 'arcadeyness' (e.g number of torso shot to aquire a kill) Nothign really wrong with that, but maybe the devs could consider a more realistic game mode for the hard core players on Steam (of which there are many).

Have you ever played a strategy game where it takes 5+ minutes for a single turn to take place? Apparently that's what a lot of people want... as comment sections are flooded with "this game should have been turn-based garbage!" Which is funny since steam has a wide selection of garbage that you can sift through and find what your looking for. It's like someone who drives a pickup truck being dissapointed when presented with a brand new Hybrid... "It would be so much better if this prius had a hemi in it! Toyota is ignoring an entire demographic!!!" That's all I'm hearing when I read people's complaints that this isn't a turnbased game, move on and allow players who enjoy this type of game to help nurture and grow this game.
That said this is early access... I can see some tweaks with UI and menus and what-not, but overall I'm having a lot of fun just sitting down and playing the game as is.
Seldom does a game change up a given formula this much and gets away with it, the core experience is something new and refreshing, and it's nice to be able to say that. Getting rid of the turn based aspect immediately remedies my frustration with those types of games, and while doing so it opens up an entirely new meta in the game that I'm still coming to terms with. An excellent, unique, action survival-horror experience. The story may not make itself obvious, but tracking down the documents, listening to the narratives, and overall thinking about the predicament you're in reveals all you really need to know about what's going in this title's psychotic world. The Evil Within is kind of like playing a punishing version of Resident Evil 4, but you're on acid, with a hint of Silent Hill tugging your balls. Definitely recommend!

When talking about a game made by a fan-favorite creator of good ol' Resident Evil 4, Shinji Mikami, expectations have arisen. I loved playing RE4 on my Gamecube, and then again on the PC trying to get almost all achievements. Can The Evil Within win my heart as RE4 did so long ago? It did to a degree, but not entirely.
I've just finished Nightmare mode as of writing this, so I have a fair evaluation of the game.
The story revolves around a detective by the name of Sebastian Castellanos who was just called in after just coming off a case. The report was multiple homicides at Beacon Mental Hospital.
After a rather odd noise is heard and nearly driving off the road, the detective and his two companions Joseph and Kidman, walk to the door.
From here, I will not spoil, but the result is a often confusing mess of information that some people will not understand until later. The story gives you bits and pieces no solving it, while not entirely giving it away. Even after the end, I still was scratching my head a little in regards to some of the story. However, I found myself figuring out the main plot rather easily, but just missing some parts at the end. It also didn't completely answer some questions which knocked points off for me.
A person has to pay very close attention to the details and information in the game to properly understand the story in its entirety which I will admire though.
Here is where a few similarities will come into play, but we'll hold off on that.
The gameplay is 3rd-person shooter, with emphasis on action, and some stealth mixed in. Stealth I would like to point out, is crucial in some areas to save ammo, especially on harder difficulties. Over the course of the game, you're given different weapons, craftables, and more besides.
Difficulty is at a good pace. You have Casual for players that aren't as good and who just want to enjoy the story, you have survival which is basically normal mode, Nightmare which can be hard at times but much more fun then survival. Sadly you cannot access it until you beat Survival. Then we have Akumu.....I'll be honest and say that I tried to do this, but then when I realized that I'd have to face certain areas where I'd often get nicked, I did not want to go through that torture. Akumu is basically one-hit-you-dead. (masochist mode)
One thing that people have often complained about is the spikes in difficulty at parts. I'd like to alleviate those fears and say that while they're difficult, it just requires a different approach. Once I figured out an easy way to stop enemies with a certain craftable, I was much more happy.
The creep factor is nicely prominent in the beginning 3-to-5 (depends on the person) chapter areas, but begins to lose ground as you progress and get used to the enemies, and the shock factor just deteriorates. Each new chapter contains several little hidden nooks and cranny's that treasure hunters will sure to love. (seriously some hiding spots are EXTREMELY hard to find if you're not looking carefully)
New Enemies appear at a decent pace which I like, and some will eventually have new things given to them. It's sad that they threw out one of THE most creepy mobs in the game later on which left me kinda sad because they were so unpredictable at times.
Bosses have a good difficulty to them. Not too easy, but not too hard either
The game, sadly, is rather linear. This took some points off for me.
You'll face various things like bombs, traps, and more. You'll play little minigames of defusing a bomb and it's a risk, but the rewards are extra parts to craft items later.

Enemies dodge just like RE4
We got our loving Sadist (not spoiling but you-know-who that refers to in RE4)
Enemies will point at you and react to you just like RE4
Ammo is Scarce like RE4
Only thing that wasn't as prominent: You can move while aiming down sights! You can reload AND run without having to stop and pause in the middle of enemies! BLASPHEMY V
(Just a joke haha)
So has this game lived up to RE4 and rekindled my love? Partially. It has several elements that I liked, but others I didn't.
It's a good game with some flaws that hold it back from being GREAT. Hopefully the upcoming The Evil Within 2 will address some story plot, gameplay, (either get rid of stealth or make it better just choose one dang it!), better level design, and a few other quandaries that I had.

A classic rts. Features a ton of different races for both humans and monster creatures called frytans. Each human civilization has various unique upgrades and gods that can help them win. Humans needs to maintain their towns happiness and taxes. As well as trade amongst other humans and frytans in order to keep up with upkeep of your builinds and units. Frytans on the other hand require attacking and enslaving towns to earn tribute to maintain upkeep. while seeming a bit easier, you are forced to be far more agressive early on otherwise you will lose money.
The AI in the game is pretty difficult. Most of the time you will have to abuse the games stop time mechanic to make several decisions just in order to keep up. The campaign isn't anything to really brag about. It's decent and follows the human group that you pick trying to survive against the frytans and building an empire. Theres really no interesting plot or characters that appear.
I honestly can't speak about the multiplayer as i have yet to play it due to the lack of online players. Your chances of playing against someone is low, but the offline gameplay for this game is interesting enough to keep you entertained.

Devs too busy waving their new DLC around to actually fix the game and had to rely on a random user mod to fix a problem that's been plaguing the basic gameplay for months. Honestly, the lack of support for this title is incredibly disheartening. Instead of fixes we get cheeky replies and promises of patches and then months later we find them releasing DLC to farm shekels and teasing possible VR support when the game is FAR from ready to recieve such a gimmick. Even now the most recent update has many users crashing at start up for no reason and I've yet to see some acknowledgement of this issue.
Honestly all of this vitriol comes from the fact that it is indeed a good game, at least from what I've played of it. It's well put together (aside from the very prominent stuttering issues that not only the devs trivialize, but half the game's community does as well), It's graphics are nice, the atmosphere is amazing, and the potential for a unique and terrifying story is there. Obviously a lot of work and love went into this project, but the that love and work seems to stop when it comes to supporting and making sure this little child of theirs is working properly for all it's users.
Wouldn't recommend in it's current state because of the distinct lack of support.
Update: Having finished the game, would have to say that it is indeed a fantastic game, but, yet again, it has many issues that arise from the game being made in Unity. The issue I mentioned before still remains for some, and now on top of that disappointment I have the pleasure of knowing the game is severely lacking in the optimization department. Also I ran into a very weird camera glitch in one of the final rooms which I'm assuming was due to the scripted camera movements in said room not being coded properly.
Looking at specific objects and events dropped the game below 9 fps for me on medium settings, and this is a rig with GTX 1070, 12 GB DDR3 RAM, and and eight-core processor. That being said, this only plagues a small part of the game, which, although unnacceptable, I could look past due to the amazing story and atmosphere.
I'm definitely much, much closer to giving this game a reccommendation after finishing it. It is, in many ways a masterpiece. A deeply, deeply flawed masterpiece that in all honesty could be fixed if the Devs gave priority to fixing the many issues on the backend, but a masterpiece nonetheless. I haven't been this tense and scared in a game in awhile. But, unfortunately, I still think that the issues and substandard support that plague this game outweigh the asking price. I really hope that changes.
P.S. The Doll sequence was unintentionally hilarious, I laughed my♥♥♥♥♥off for ~10 minutes because of it. May not've been intended, but it was a nice change of pace to break up the spooks.

Decent game but really bad port.
There is only anti-aliasing, shadow quality (the PS3 shadows were pretty bad and jaggy), the SSAO quality, motion blur and vertical sync. What is really annoying is how the game automatically assumes that you will be playing on an xbox controller. It's amazing. As soon as you start the game all of the instructions are given with the xbox buttons. I beat my head against the wall as I tried figuring out which key did what. So I had to quit the game and go into configuration menu to figure out how to play the damn game.
The main pillar of this game is the gameplay. It's pretty fluid but I still find the consolized running slightly sluggish. The first 20 minutes of the game are kind of boring and slow but the game gradually picks up the pace. The plot is convoluted at first but you eventually realize the gravity of the invasion of the dormant sleeper cyborgs which is pretty cool.
Back to the gameplay, there are the usual steps like take cover, shoot, gather the pulse charge, throw the grenade AND.... order your teammates to either cover you, advance or hold the ground. At the very beginning of the game the trust level between you and your team mates is pretty low though so do not expect them to always follow your orders. For instance if you tell them to charge the advancing robots, your partner will basically tell you off.
Well, the story is okay. There are a few good dramatic moments. The story not only focuses on you and your team mates but also on the gangs and the law enforcement. So it is nice to see the game world unfold through different vantage points. You get to interact with your team mates as well as other miscellaneous characters during the game. You can choose different dialogue options the outcome of which will influence your team mates' level of trust towards you.
There are annoyances though. Most of the time your AI team mates will keep saying the same thing over and over again should you venture away from them. They will say things like "Sam, over here!", "Sam, you are going the wrong way", "Sam, what are you doing? Grab that grenade launcher".
So yeah, on one hand there is communication with your team mates, but on the other hand there is a limited amount of one liners to be thrown around.
Another MAJOR annoyance is the inability to turn off music, that's right. The incessant battle rock will keep playing almost every time you are in a major engagement. I was really hoping they would tweak the PC version better and give us the opportunity to get rid of music for maximum immersion. This kind of thing ruins many games for me. I mean it is EASY to implement that option in games.
I felt like some of the checkpoints were not equally balanced. I had to restart my progress way back because the checkpoint was placed way to far. Such examples include the water chase stage and the highway chase stage.
The water looks atrocious, seriously. It's like this horrid looking gray sheet that you cover yourself with every night.
Another annoyance is that even though your character speaks in cut scenes, your character NEVER says anything during in-game dialogue which is kind of sloppy. They could have easily programmed the number of various responses into the dialogue, so I know they just got lazy.
I also didn't like the level design much. I know it is a small thing to gripe about but I just didn't feel that inspiration from visiting the various locations in the game. I mean the skyscraper stages are nice but some of the industrial areas are pretty boring. Some levels are as boring as visiting a box factory. I think what could have helped is the vivid background animation. Just throw in some background activity like running civilians, passing cars, machinery producing somethings, etc. The metropolis just kind of felt empty.
Some smaller flying enemies in re-spawin a couple of times in the game which is a no no in my book. The enemy AI is also not particularly smart. They rely on firepower and numbers more than agility and taking cover.
As you progress through the game, you will meet certain soldiers of different nationalities. You will even meet a peaceful robot. Some of the missions will give you a chance to choose different partners. You can only only have 2 partners at a time. Each friendly AI has a different weapon and specialization. You get to keep 3 health syringes and so do your team mates. When you are down you can either use your syringe or ask them to use theirs to pick you up. There are various weapons in the game
In many ways the game reminded me of Vanquish although that game had a much faster pace. The boss fights are pretty cool but most of the time it is still about finding the vulnerable spots and shooting those. There are also some cool set pieces but the dated animations detracted from having too much fun. I just did not find the graphics all that compelling in general.
For the most part the game holds up. It is fun killing robots, conserving your ammo, working with your teammates and getting out of near impossible situations. As you kill enemies, you accumulate credits which you can use for upgrading weapons. You can beat about half the game and only be able to fully upgrade your basic assault rifle. There are also not as many robot models - around 5-6, not counting the sometimes bigger enemies.
The game also screams for co-op campaign. They could have easily implemented it here since you are never alone during the campaign.

First thing: Do not buy this game at full price, it frequently goes on sale for over %50 off (at the time of the writing of this review it is currently %80 off).
Secondly: There are other Mount and Blade titles... this one is widely considered the best.
This game would best be desribed as a mix of the Total War series, Skyrim (without the magic), and Sid Meiers Pirates! (for the single player campaign).
The Good:
The unique gameplay is what really sells this game, there is no game quite like it (the closest would be Chivarly: Medieval Warfare, but Chivarly is much more simplistic).
This game has some pretty serious depth.
The single player campaign provides hundreds of hours of gameplay; with a great mix of action, strategy, and roleplaying.
The AI isn't terrible.
A huge modding community.
Runs well on older machines (more on that later).
Mostly stable and bug-free (more on that later also).
The Bad:
While the game has depth; it's certainly unpolished and seemingly incomplete in areas (tournaments a big example of this).
The single player campaign can become a bit of a repetitive grind.
The AI could be worse... but it could be a lot better.
The reason it runs well on older machines?  The graphics are dated (this game came out in 2010, it looks like a game made in 2005).
While not terrible in terms of bugs, this isn't the most stable game either.
The Ugly:
All of the women in the single player campaign look the same.
The architecture in despressingly bland.
Not the greatest game ever made; but certainly a great deal.

I had kept my eye on this game for some time after enjoying Banished.  Often, the two are compared and in many ways this game borrows heavily from Banished.  I would not call it a rip off or clone in the same way I wouldn't compare the various RTS games of the early 2000's.
This game is harder than Banished and less polished.  The villager AI could use improvement.  Some buildings were not very effective.  For instance, adjacent to my coop sat a hunting camp.  Bears and boars roamed freely and my hunters where nowhere to be seen while they ransacked my crops and coops.  Other times the villagers would freeze to death or stave with ample food supplies and stove fuel available to them.
The color pallete of the game blends together to a point where it can be hard to distinguish objects and buildings.  I would recommend the developers put a little more color in the game.  I have good vision and I am not colorblind so I don't think the issue is on my end physically or with my computer's hardware/video output.
For those that write off the game altogether, I think that's unfair.  This game has the potential to really shine.  It's not Banished with better graphics in the same way Warcraft II isn't Rise of Nations.  Improvements to the AI, diversified maps, textures and a color scheme will make this game stand on its own.

Is this a rip-off of Banished?

Using that description..Banished stole ideas from the ANNO series... Where to draw the line between "ripping off" & "being inspired/heavily influenced by". So many negative reviews..

Going first person was exciting and made the entire experience better. Reloads, loads.. no issues at all. Not a single crash. Not sure about the negative reviews I did not experience any of these issues. I made it to year 14 without a single hiccup.
In the end this is a very solid game. No known bugs in my gameplay. New and fresh ideas in the genre. Did not feel "incomplete". In my opinion it is far superior to other games I own in this line-up. Look for this type of gameplay? Dont hesitate to buy Life If Fudal:Forest Village.

•	Challenging difficulty – not impossible to beat, but it requires good decisionmaking skills
•	Slow Pace: sometimes you just sit and stare how figures keep hitting each other. The game is real-time, but the cooldowns between attacks feel a bit too much, they do not give the impression of “awesome Viking fights”
•	The game just was not fun to me: positioning matters, skill choice matters, but there are not many skills that you can use at once (it’s also unclear how cooldowns for character spells work). Basically, most of the game you move your figures and then stare how they fight.
•	Tutorial is not nearly enough: it gives a glimpse of basic controls, but it’s entirely possible (and actually probable) to lose the first mission after that: some game mechanic exploration would help, like telling players about block chances, possibility to equip items (after tutorial is over), some tips on tactics (like a lot of strategy games to during loading times), etc.
•	Fonts: I am not sure if the game is made in Unity, but the fonts really give away that “Unity Feel”: they are just not sharp enough and don’t look good. The UI is not terrible, but the fonts make it look that way. The fonts up close (score, gold) could use some anti-aliasing, but the points far could use more sharpness: otherwise signs on board (i.e. options) look blurred.
I really respect the developers for trying out a new idea; As it often happens with Early Access games – the game has great potential, but I think it went into Early Access a bit too early. I don’t necessary mean that the game is bad, It just feels like it's very far from its potential now and I suggest waiting till it's done. I recommend skip this one for now and get back to check it out later, once it’s fully released.

I enjoy Star Trek Online quite a bit. The game is a solid casual F2P MMO that at most times adds to the lore of the original/next generation Star Trek series. I started playing STO, back when it was first released in 2010 with a subscription fee up through the move to F2P off and on. The game has grown nicely and evolved over the past four years, improving the over all presentation and the developers had been listening to the feedback from the player base.
Unfortunately times are beginning to change and head in the unpleasant direction most F2P MMO are going. Signs of "Pay to Win" are starting to appear in the game.
With the release of the new Delta Rising expansion, the price of the new Tier 6 ships has risen to a $30 per ship and there are no free ships given to players past the Upper Admiral rank (3 ranks below cap) which is a major disappointment. Also only ships purchased from store can be upgraded from Tier 5 to Tier 5-U.
While the typical F2P MMO player base complaints that come with change are currently populating the STO forums, there is a valid growing concern by players that Star Trek Online is heading toward the wrong direction.
On the upside, you can experience three different factions (Federation, Klingon and Romulan) with three different career types (Tactical, Science, or Engineering), up to the old level cap of 50 (Vice Admiral rank) with out spending a dime in the game Zen Store and there quite of enjoyable story driven content to be played through. Even with the concerns about the future of the game, I still recommend giving Star Trek Online a try, if you are looking for a fun casual MMO experince set in a active sci-fi universe.

Basically if you are even considering this game, you know approximently what you are getting into at a base level. Moero Chronicle is a fan-service heavy, dungeon crawling RPG. If that sounds good enough already, you probably don't care what else I post, but oh well, I'll sort of break it down some.
Story: So... the story is pretty lack luster. Basically the world is under some sort of corruption and it is up to our hero to save the monster girls around the world and save the day. Honestly, sub-par stories are par for the course for most dungeon crawling RPGs, so I'm not going to harp on this too much, but just be prepared to not have much depth to this story.
Controls: Like a few people in other reviews have mentioned, the controls are sort of awkward at first, though unlike the conclusions they made, its not a deal breaker. Once you get use to them, its pretty easy to adjust. Not ideal, but by no means something that makes the game unplayable. I'd probably recommend a controller if you have one avaliable, as the "bumping scratch" portions seem much more natural with the controller than with mouse/keyboard, at least to me.
Sound: Again, not something that is super memorable, but not bad either. The sound is fairly atmospheric in nature. Some of the clips that play in cutscenes kinda set the mood, but its definitely a weaker part to this game. Not much variation and just could have been done better to be honest. Also, to note. I don't know a ton of Japanese, but I know enough to realize the subtitles are not spectacular as well. Voice acting is fairly good though.
Difficulty: Quiet simply, the lowest two difficulty modes are complete garbage and shouldn't even be included. Even at the 2nd lowest difficulty, the game basically plays itself. I put the game on the highest difficulty almost immediately, and it is a fairly challenging game. I'd heavily recommend it, specifically if you are looking for a challenge. If not, the 2nd highest difficulty is a nice compromise.
Gameplay: Gameplay basically makes up 90% of the appeal of this game. The game is... actually a pretty solid Dungeon Crawling RPG. A few things can be unbalanced, but overall I think the game actually delivers pretty well in this category. There is enough customization to have multiple strategies and builds to the teams you make, and the equiptment varies as well. I won't harp on the... "aesthetics" of the additional job costumes as again, I knew what I was getting into when I got this game, but the game plays actually very solid. Significantly better than I was expecting.
Overall, the game isn't exceptionally memorable in a lot of ways, but it actually is a very enjoyable experience. Nothing will come out to grab you and be super memorable, but if its on sale or you just want to play another dungeon crawler like I did, I'd recommend picking it up , as long as you understand how fan-service heavy it is and are ok with that.

Pros:

- There's 5 different heroes with different weapons. Also the heroes has jokes they sometime says which makes for a good giggle.

Cons:
-The only real problem I have with this game is that it is not very populated. Usually I'm already 30% through the map before anyone joins, and most of the time they leave when that map is over. So it's kinda difficult to have a consistant team for several maps. Luckily good people are more plentiful than toxic people so there's that. If you have friend(s) to play with, then that solves the problem somewhat.
- Can become repetitive for some. Luckily there are different objectives on some maps which helps a little bit, though they all have the same goal, slice through the hoard of rats and get out safely.

Pro and con, depending on personal opinion:

You can highten the chance of getting a rare item with ''colletibles'' you find in the form of tomes, loot dye and grimore in each campaign map, which also are cleverly hidden around the map, easy to find when you know where but if not, good luck finding them. They also give an extra sense of challenge for the reward you get from them. Tome replaces health item and grimore replaces potions (Either strength or speed).

This game sells itself short. Well, it fails to sell itself at all really. Gifted to me by a friend, who was equally unsure of the game, I thought I would give it a try. What an excellent addition to my 2013 collection The Ship turned out to be. Just in the nick of time as well!
To put it simply, you're a predetermined character on a ship and are given a mark. Similarly, another character has been given you as their mark, so you can't just run round willy-nilly. If you ever watched Ace Ventura as a child then you'll catch the game's drift fairly quickly. You're on a hunt - for humans.
Varied weapon choice provides replayability and good humour. There are plenty of bizarre and wonderful weapon to find and take out your mark with, each with a reward. Bat someone with an umbrella in a public place and you'll be well remunerated. Similarly, tipping hats to Cluedo and whacking someone with a candlestick will also get you big bucks.
Considering that the sole goal of the game is to commit murder, The Ship is surprisingly light-hearted and amusing. It's one of those games you can dip in and out of without getting hooked, but get quick jollies from. I've thoroughly enjoyed this somewhat hidden gem and would recommend it highly.

Let me start by saying that the premise for this game is fantastic! A future where robots can look and act just like humans, to the point that the robots themselves actually believe they are alive. Such robots are outlawed, a violation of global law, but someone is producing them, and it‘s your job to find out who it is, stop them, and destroy every robot you find on your way. But how do you know who these robots are? They could be all round you. Who can you trust? Can you even be sure you aren’t one? It’s a setting ripe for suspicion, deep contemplation into the nature of life, and gripping moral choices. And the story and general aesthetic were absolutely brilliant!
That said, the implementation could have been a whole lot better. The game turned out to be VERY linear, which is not necessarily a bad thing (Spec Ops: The Line was very linear, and I consider it to be a masterpiece), but something about this game felt slightly off. Maybe it was because of the unholy amount of inescapable boss fights. Maybe it was that the suspicion of this world didn’t seem as prevalent as it could or should have been. Or maybe it was that any potential tough choices (and there were a lot) were made for you in the cut-scenes, leaving you powerless to the whim and fancy of the game.
The trust mechanic, which could have had so much potential, turned out to be little more than shoot the enemy to gain trust with your squad, and shoot your squad to lose that trust (which was easy to do, since they seem to have a habit of running in front of you in combat). You can also talk to your squad and choosing the right response will net you some more trust, but you are never able to intervene or choose sides when your squad has a argument, so it becomes just a matter of just agreeing with whoever you’re currently talking to, even if it goes against what you‘ve just told another squad-mate. And the more trust you have with your squad, the better an ending you get.
But the absolute biggest problem was the inconsistent characterization. I couldn’t ever really take the protagonist seriously, which is a shame because he had some deep revelations and some truly heart-wrenching moments. But the rest of the time he was making sarcastic and juvenile wise-crack comments in a attempt to...to…I don’t really know why. It did absolutely nothing for the story or the endearment of his character, the only thing it did accomplish was to tear me out of my immersion almost every time he opened his mouth. The other characters were slightly better, but they weren’t immune to the bad writing either, and there were times when they all devolved to nothing more than stereotypes; Big Beefy African-American guy with a machine gun, hot Asian sniper, no-nonsense British agent, etc.
Do I recommend it? That’s a hard one. For most people I would say no, there are tons of better games out there more worthy of you‘re time. But for anyone (like me) that enjoys seeing what the medium potentially could be capable of doing, and wants to play through a game that almost got there, then yes, play it. Because while this review may sound extremely negative, I actually did have some good moments with this game. It was good, it just wasn’t all that it could have been, which is sad, because it could have been incredible!

Binary Domain is an unusual paradox. It is an absolutely gorgeous game - great animation, lighting and textures - that wastes all that artistry on some of the least interesting locales: slums, garages, sewers. It has some fun firefights that inevitably over-stay their welcome. The game has a wide variety of enemy types who still, in the end, fail to distinguish themselves from one another. The story and characters touch a lot of interesting points but are inanely combined in a way that only the Japanese can manage.
Basically, Binary Domain is the closest you can get to an interactive anime movie. It feels very Japanese, which I suppose is a good thing if you are otaku but lacks the solidity and seriousness that Western gamers expect. In fact, the gameplay itself feels as if the developers at Sega intended to create a modern, western-style FPS without quite understanding why people found them so appealing. Thus, too-frequent cut-scenes interrupt the action, enemies are often invulnerable until certain scripted sequences play and there's a disturbing reliance on the old "shoot the glowing orange weak-spot" mechanic that most FPS developers left to rot ten years ago. Its almost worth it for the artistry of its graphics and animations, but the gameplay was forgettable at best.

All of the descriptions of this being a Japanese Gears of War are completely accurate. It's a third-person cover-based shooter, with a quirk in that you can influence how much your team likes you by speaking to them using your headset. You get prompted with yes/no questions pretty often, and they like/dislike you depending on your performance in combat. Shoot a bunch of robots, they think you're great! Shoot them, and they complain. Something I didn't necessarily realize is that the social system affects your ending!
The game looks great. It's super-smooth, with only a bit of slowdown when I'd have like 10 robots exploding at the same time, and that was really rare. There are a ton of boss fights, but none of them are frustrating as they all subscribe to the "shoot the blinking parts" philosophy. The controls work great with mouse and keyboard. The voice acting isn't perfect, but your team is composed of soldiers from different nations. Some of the accents are bad, and some are passable, but what thrilled me is that the Japanese police, who would have no business casually speaking English to each other, actually speak Japanese with subtitles! That tiny attention to detail means a lot to me. When Return to Castle Wolfenstein came out and all the Germans spoke English with German accents, I was totally disappointed.
The story is well written. It's a nice sci-fi, what makes a man yarn. It has a pretty lighthearted tack to it, without being completely cartoonish. It's more like a good action movie that occasionally asks serious questions. It sets up a sequel, which I'm looking forward to, but I don't think we'll see. I don't think Binary Domain sold all that well, and it's a serious departure for its creator who previously made all the Yakuza games. I never played any of them, but they have a rather dedicated following.
Next time Binary Domain goes on sale somewhere (I got it from Amazon, Steam-redeemable), you should get it. Don't be completely turned off by the B grade cover art. It definitely exceeded my expectations.

Layers of Fear is a very interesting, very creepy game!
The thing to note about this game is there is no fighting, there's no inventory, it's a walking simulator, or maybe even a haunted house one, but at the same time there's a deeper story being weaved throughout.
The main gameplay may remind people of such games as Amnesia:The Dark Descent or P.T. (Silent Hill teaser that's now cancelled), and it certainly has that vibe to it, but in its own unique way.
I love the use of art as a way to scare and creep you out, and it's done very well. I believe all the paintings (with a couple exceptions) are actual artwork (I recognized some).
The atmosphere is spot on, with noises and flashes of something waiting for you (or is it?) hidden away. You'll also find notes, drawings, and momentos that open up the story, and based on what you do, how many you find, will alter the ending, in addition to opening up new things on a secondary playthrough, giving the game a nice replay value.
The main game will probably take no more than 3-4 hours, with the DLC coming in around 1-2 hours.
The DLC is quite good, albeit a bit short but offers up some new ideas and should definitely be played after completing the main game.
If you're looking for a nice creepy game that offers up something unique, Layers of Fear will do the job.

I am a huge fan of the original 7K game and have spent countless hours on that game and 7KAA. I knew that this game would simply expand on the graphics and provide a few enhancements in gameplay. Nevertheless, it's a great game still in spite of the dated graphics (and who says dated graphics need to look ugly? It's still a beautiful game in its own way). Why fix something that is not broken in the first place? This is a series that has a focus on the fun aspects of RTS - diplomacy, spying, monster-battling and sheer combat, and not a tedious RTS game where you need to constantly micromanage your economy by routing workers to different resources or keep building walls around your area and still being surprised to find that somehow enemies have slipped through and wreaking havoc on unarmed civilians.
Even after a short time of playing, this game has some good additions to the original 7K game, which only expands the genre and in no way takes away from the fun aspects. The best part is you can customize the difficulty at any level you prefer.
Be warned, this is an addictive genre if you get used to it. Quite inexpensive and well worth the price paid, in spite of its age.

RPG elements, for example units get improved combat stats by fighting/training and equipable items exist. Taking cities of other civilizations gives you the ability to train units of that civ. Units have loyalty and may betray you and many more... The gameplay is a bit hard to grasp, but when you get into it you will love this game.

I remember my first hours playing this game. They were pretty good. Why? Well, cause I really got fast the hang of it. The game itself isn't that complicated as it may seem. The very concept of the game is unusual, that is, being a RTS and a FPS at the same time, but it is pretty simple in its essence. As I have played only the FPS part (didn't reach the required rank for the RTS part) I see myself capable of writing a review about the part which is the first thing new players meet.
You see, this game is kinda like the Battlefield series. There are many similarities between these two: you get to enter vehicles, get to use planes, tanks, capture points, defend, attack points and many more. It's very tactical. One thing that makes the game different from the BF series is that it is F2P and that it has a STORE in which you buy with the credits you earn in battle weapons, mines, pistols, vehicles and etc..., and later modify them and maintain these modificatons. This economic aspect of the game adds the requirment to unlock and to buy things after you unlock them, thus making the player play and earn credits required to obtain them. This very concept can sometimes, and as it is in most cases, for a begginer seem very frustrating. There are many games with this concept out there (WoT, WT, etc.. etc..) and if you have played these you can have an idea of what it will look like. You'll get to a point in game in which the game requires you to put in more time and effort to be able to succeed to the next level or to purchase an item, vehicle, modification and such. Well, this game is no different in that way. So if you're a begginer don't expect to get right into the heat of the battle at the very start. Patience is required for this game.
As a begginer you will be placed in Tier 1 battles. Tier 1 battles are battles in which participate players who haven't yet acquired RANK 5 on their account. In these battles you will be placed among other players who have just begun with the game just like you. The purpose of this is that you get acnkowledged with the  basic game mechanics until you're ready for the real thing; WAR battles.
After you reach RANK 5 (btw. if you're a good player, that is, if you in battles capture points, defend them, destroy tanks, have good KDR) it will need you about 20 hours or so to reach that level. Until than you're forced to play small Skirmish maps which will probably bore you out but at the same time make you capable enough for the WAR battles. During this time, you'll have enough credits and time to unlock few modifications, and even some weapons, which you could try out immediately, but I reccomend you to spare up the credits for the better guns (Tier 2 guns that is). The starting weapons are solid and if you have any FPS skills you can do pretty well with them even in later stages of the game.
After reaching RANK 5, you'll get introduced to Tier 2 players, which are players of any rank above RANK 5 (Majors, Corporals, Generals, players who have been playing the game much more than you and probably who are much better than you). At this stage you will be able to join the real battles, the WAR battles. The results of the WAR and it's battles depend on the outcome of the battles in which you will participate. If your faction loses the battle, the city, for which you have fought, will be lost and the enemy faction will capture it. Also, at this point you will be facing tanks, planes, better weapons, more modifications, mines and a new mode of play; Assault in which one team attacks while the other defends the cap points. This mode is fought on bigger maps and the style of the play changes drastically. Everything you have learned in the previous Skirmish battles in Tier 1 will seem useless. You will probably get killed and you will feel a lot of times underpowered even if you have played like a pro in Tier 1 battles. Every player has felt this on their skin. This is because you need to learn the pace of these battles, the way these battles work, the behaviour of players in these battles, everything will change. I HIGLY RECOMMEND YOU TO NOT PLAY WAR BATTLES IMMEDIATELY AFTER REACHING RANK 5. STICK TO STAGED BATTLES FOR A FEW DAYS UNTIL YOU FEEL READY FOR  THE WAR BATTLES.
This will be your hardest time in game, but remember, that, I repeat, everyone at one time went trough this, so don't quit so easilly, as you will be probably tempted to. After time passes and you play more of these battles, you will learn the mechanics of them and you will notice that you are getting better and better, and the game is getting more interesting to you as you play. You will be able to unlock new weapons and enter tanks, planes, APCs and the game will just surprise you with these features which you haven't been able to adapt to. You will then slowly get the hang of it, and become a decent player which will make the faction and it's generals proud.
Remember also, that this game is currently in its development stage, nothing is final and is prone to change. This also means that the players are able to influence the development of the game and it's mechanics, which is great, because there are FORUMS in which many suggestions are being proposed and reviewed, just like you'll view this, by the developers. The main motto of the company which runs this game (RETO-MOTO) is that the players develop the game, so have this in mind.
As you can see, all the bad reviews are written by players with no more than 10 hours spent on the game. This game needs patience and expecting it to be like a CoD game, you will just waste your time. The ones which wrote the bad reviews are not the type of gamers this game needs, so you'll have to keep that in mind also.
I hope I have helped you to make real expectations of the game before you try it.

Wartile an epic battle of your strategic ability against an AI, one that like the Terminators are out to destroy you mercilessly.
First the bad. There really isn't much "bad" about the game. If we apply the basic "it's early access" mentality to it we can ignore a few of the minor annoyences. In fact, it's been twenty-four hours since the release and they have already patched some critical errors. That being said one major issue I see is that we can in fact just ignore most of the mobs and rush to the objectives. If we complete the final objective we win the battle.
The good. If we ignore the fact that we can just run past the mobs and complete MOST missions and instead focus on playing it to the fullest, we then realize that it's a great game. At times the action moves so quickly as I try to move my pieces up to the enemies that I have to slow it down (Space bar) just to get all the move actions in before the enemies fill my "tank" with arrows.
All things considered and based on this being a review written just after the 24 hour mark, I consider this an amazing game with so much potential to be a game that I won't put down for quite some time (much like Banner Saga - but with the potential of being better. WAY better).
Definitely buy this game. Just do it.

First off understand this is really an early access title. The game lacks a lot in way of polish and some comfort of life things. As the game is right now I would honestly say it is a matter of 'buy to support'. I expect this game to grow into a good game. Right now though it is mediocre.
The graphics of the maps are gorgeous. The same can't be said of UI and main menu screen.
The main core gameloop is solid tactics if a bit fiddly. It's a bit easy to miss the intended tile.
Using the special ability of a unit needs work. No reason really why you have to mark a unit. Also there is no feedback on ability cooldown. Both could be solved with having the cards up all the time with cooldown indicator.
The items and feedback of stats gain/loss if equipping them also needs work. It is usable but only just.
So TL:DR.
A solid tactical miniature simulator with great potential. Right now it is very rough around the edges and lacking in content.
Only recommended if you want to support the future and have some patience. If you expect a full game, stay away for now.
(Haven't tried multiplayer yet. Might come back and edit when and if I do. Personally I hope more for coop to get some love :D)

It's a decent sequel to the original. But it feels strangely more aggravating. There are certain things (like picking up an empty gun even though a loaded one is closer, or dropping a gun instead of throwing it) that I don't remember being as angry about in the original, though I don't know if that's because I forgot about it or because it didn't happen. The plot also makes no sense (reading up on it afterward, it looks like this is both a prequel and a sequel to the original, but the levels are out-of-order and follow at least five different characters), and the 'choose a mask for a special power' concept from the original is there, but strangely disjointed, so you will most often not have access to a favorite. Overall, I got what I wanted out of this game, except I think I bought it on sale.

Today I replayed the first Hotline Miami in one go, so decided to revisit this to see if my opinion on it changed. It hasn't. I want to enjoy Hotline Miami 2 so, so badly, but it just feels like an uninspired imitation of the original. The introduction of new characters means there's more ideas, but much less in the way of options or opportunities to actually use them, and the level design is awful, making the free-flowing, chaotic melee that characterised its predecessor become ridiculous gunfights through windows halfway across the map, shooting blindly and hoping something works for once. I want to enjoy it so badly, but I'm hugely disappointed. Just stick to the first one.

- Somewhat repetitive quests given by NPCs
Pros:
- Simple yet efficient combat system
- Rather intelligent AI
- Takes up next to no disk space
- Runs on almost any computer
- Freedom to do and be almost anything
- Excellent NPC character development and variation
- Looks amazing considering the game's size and engine
My overall thoughts? One of the most fun games I have ever played. I would strongly reccommend for anyone looking for a medieval warfare game.

Moero Chronicles is a First person dungeon crawler that features cute girls, a somewhat silly story, Turn based battles, and panty collecting.
So first of all if you have played other games like stranger of sword city or the New Tokyo legacy you will be right at home as far as dungeon crawling goes.
The party system is a bit odd though as you can have five monster girls on your party and Io the Male lead as an item user/buffer. It all makes a bit more sense when you play it. There are some Monster girls related to the story that you can’t miss but there are many optional that you can recruit as well.
In order to recruit the girl’s story related or not they generally play out as boss fight. In order to try to recruit them you must raise Otton the Seal thingy’s desire bar so he can shower them with money and then Io can use his “POSITIVE DESIRE” all over them. To raise that bar though you either need to hit her weakness or beat up her clothes. I know it sounds weird but nothing makes you come to your senses like being ganged up on and having your clothes beat up and getting your forehead poked.
The Monster girls that do all the fighting for you all have an elemental affinity and weakness. Each girl also has 4 classes kind of or Panties in this games case. You can find them in chests or from special monsters but before the girls will wear them you gotta raise that affection. The classes aren’t explicitly named out but their stats and move sets change depending on what set they are wearing.
The story is pretty silly at its core and never takes itself too seriously. It’s a pretty light hearted affair a boy and his childhood friend get forced into saving the world and have to out all the rampaging monster girls back to their normal selves.
All in all I liked the game. I even went and got all of the Post game monster girls. I didn’t 100% complete the game like getting all the girls to max affection and find all the outfits but I played it to my satisfaction. It’s a solid goofy yet perverted jrpg dungeon crawler.

I've only played this for a short time (at the time of this review), and I'm already addicted.
I played a
of instagib in a Quake engine game (JK2) in the past, and this brought back a ton of nostalgia and even some long-dormant muscle memory.
This game offers everything you would want in a 100% instagib setting. In addition to being well-balanced and fast-paced, enemies are easy to see, the maps are skillfully created, and the gameplay is so much fun.
