What I expected to be a shiny reskin of Left 4 Dead has really impressed me, to put the recommendation simply.
While the surface mechanics and setup are similar to Valve's seminal coop opus, and liking Left 4 Dead definitely makes one more likely to enjoy Vermintide, the latter's razor-sharp focus on the coop experience really sets it apart.  You won't find the deep asymmetrical PvP here that co-exists with L4D's core experience, but what you will find is a much deeper and more variable co-op experience.
Each hero available (5 total) plays in a notably different fashion, from the fast, damage-dealing elf ranger to the tanky dwarf.  On top of that deference to player preference, there is seemingly literal craploads of gear that drops based on mission success and random chance, with each piece tied to a particular hero.
Do you want your Imperial Knight to be a tank in plate with a heavy shield, or a two-handed warhammer berserker headshotting giant rats with abandon?  In addition to a myriad of melee playstyles, there are just as many ranged weapons, from gatling cannons to longbows to repeating crossbows and braces of pistols.  Change up your favorite hero to suit your group or just your mood!  It's damn sweet.
The community has been welcoming and helpful to me, and I really can't overstate how much this game's surpassed my expectations.

A very basic first person dungeon crawler with monster girl catching, and lewd stuff on the side.
It's very fun, but has a few problems. I shouldn't even call them problems, but more of things you will have to get used to. Firstly I want to say that the game ran perfectly for me. Out of the 10hrs I've played so far I haven't had any crashes, glitches, or anything of the sort. Also I never played the Vita version, so no comparisons from me. Just a review of the game itself.
-Story
Nothing special here really. The protagonist Io is useless (I'm not bashing Io they literally send him out for this reason) so they send him on a quest to stop the monster girls from rampaging. He goes with his childhood friend (who is a monster girl) on the quest while recruiting the girls he rescue in his party. Pretty basic story so I have nothing to say about it.
-Capturing
The way to capture the monster girls is to strike their weak points, and then play a rubbing mini-game (or more like tapping button mini-game for us controller users). The game throws a bunch of information at you about it, so it was hard to remember everything. When I first played I couldn't remember how to do anything except tap, but eventually learned them all after a few hours. Then I became a pro monster catcher. So it may be annoying at first, but you'll get used to it.
-Combat
You have a basic attack, special attacks, and the main character buffing/using items on the side. Pretty simple. The combat is very fast paced in the beginning, being able to take down every monster with a normal attack. You can pretty much press the auto button and watch your party do the rest. Later in the game the monsters become WAY more difficult. No more auto for you, unless you want a fast death in the game. I was really happy with the difficulty increase because I was getting bored of autoing through the game.
My only problem with the combat was that I felt like Io is very awkwardly placed. What I mean by that is that you'll be casting spells and using abilities with your party. Your really focused on your girls HP/SP, planning what they'll do next, and what the enemies are doing next. Then Io pops up to throw an item or stock his energy to buff. It just breaks it up and I felt like he really didn't need to be there. Maybe it won't be a problem for anyone else, but I didn't enjoy him being there for combat.
-Monster Girls (Party Members)
I think the greatest part about the game is how every girl has a bunch of jobs they can do. So there is no "best team or party." You can just pick your favorite girls and play through the game. I'd only recommend that you at least keep a healer of course. I've even seen some playthroughs of people using the girls in the first dungeon. They all have interesting designs so have fun with mixing your party up. The girls also have traits about them, each with their own passive. I can't remember off the top of my head, but they are really cool. Like if you put a Leader trait with a Clumsy trait, you'll get an increase in HP. Just another fun way to mix up parties.
-Dungeon Crawling
First person view with encountering enemies during exploration. My only problem with the dungeon crawling was the encounter rate. It's really ridiculous. I remember fighting a battle, taking one step, then another battle happened. Then I took another step and it's an ambush. Then 3 more steps and another battle. I couldn't get any chance to breathe sometimes. I got very annoyed with this so I cut back on exploring. I just went for the goal after the 4th dungeon. Which I really hated to do since I really wanted to collect items, and explore every inch of the maps.
-Final
I recommend this game if you want a first person dungeon crawler with monster girls in it. It's very lewd of course, so there's that to enjoy too. A lot of the things I complained about are more personal. Maybe you'll play the game and have no problems with the encounter rate, or Io's involvement in combat? You can see for yourself if you try it out.

If you don't love dungeon crawlers, you probably shouldn't bother with this one. There isn't much in the way of substance, and the game tries to make up for this with ample amounts of fanservice.
With that said, the game does not take itself seriously. There are several instances of the game making fun of itself, as well as the characters doing the same. The humor provided by these instances makes it more than worthwhile.
I personally enjoy dungeon crawls and am more than accustomed to not having extravagant animations during battle or really anywhere else. However, the character portraits are animated during cutscenes, at least to the degree of a higher-quality visual novel. The game is nice to look at (to say nothing of the lewd scenes), which is always a nice treat in a dungeon crawler.
The music is nothing to write home about, and sometimes even grating. The voice acting is well done however (though bear in mind it is in Japanese), and the VAs adequately portray their characters in any given situation.
Definitely not a game to pick up for thrilling or engaging story, or cutting-edge gameplay, but for the price, it's a great dose of humor and dungeon-crawl/fanservice fun.

Everything about Ratz Instagib is pretty damn awesome:
- FOV that isn't absurdly tiny
- Very customizable
- Decently low system requirements
- Simple to pick up, hard to master gameplay
- Perfect for a lunch break/boredom streak
- Goofy-looking cosmetics that drop every so often
- Intricate maps
- Multiple gametypes
- No major or blatantly apparent bugs
However, Ratz suffers from a particularly annoying problem: a tiny playerbase. For various reasons, people are just not playing Ratz Instagib. Instagib is a gamemode that is pretty easy to burn out of, and when Ratz first came out, that was all that could be done: FFA Instagib. Now there are actual gamemodes but the few that are playing are the hyper-dedicated Quake Live clown arena rejects who excelled at holding their "s" key and firing rails and people like me who just wanted a quick outlet for deathmatch fun. I will say that more competitive players will thumb their noses up at it because Ratz is made on Unity and the physics used for Ratz instagib are pretty funky and annoying, but if you're a casual player who wants to gather some friends for a night of instagib, Ratz is your jam.
It's a shame that the playerbase is so miniscule, but I still recommend Ratz Instagib because while you can install Xonotic, Quake Live, CPMA, or Warsow, Ratz is just that much easier to not only get into (left click shoots your rail, right click is your no-self-damage rocket jump, wasd to move around), but to simply just jump in and play. No need to haunt an IRC channel looking for duels or pray  that the regulars are goofing around on the instagib server, just launch Ratz and go frag.

This is an amazing game, it's an FTP first-person shooter that's set in the European Theater of WWII. You start as a standard infantryman, but as you increase in rank you can unlock new classes (like tank crewman, fighter pilot, recon, and paratrooper). The game also allows you to unlock new weapons and vehicles through both rank and by earning combat ribbons (basically an achievement system). There is also a place to get together with friends of the same class and form a squad so you can all play together (number of friends in you squad is dependent on your class, i.e. infantry can have six, while tanks can have three). You can also have multiple soldiers, so you can have a variety of classes to play with (I have an infantryman, a tank crewman and a fighter pilot).
There is also a place where you can pay to unlock vehicles and weapons early (although for tank crewman, if you buy a heavy armor off the bat you will not be able to use it very often until you get to a rank where there are heavy armor squads).
Another neat feature is you can unlock upgrades for your weapons, like a hair trigger for your guns that will increase ROF but decrease stability. Or for tanks and jeeps you can get infantry support crates (ammo and health, or anti-tank weapons).
All in all, this is a great game and it's only in beta form. It has a great diversity of classes, weapons, and vehicles. If first-person shooters are your thing, then you should definitely try this game, and since it's free, it can't hurt to try it

Update:
After playing this game intensely for a few days, things are not as negative as I painted them at the outset but I would still recommend avoiding the game for the time being.
Forget all the difficulty and struggle; there is a near-exploit that will ensure you never have any real challenge in the game, and that is to build a field to start and have 4 farmers growing potatoes. The first harvest will be phenomenal and you'll never face the dreaded starvation meltdown if you manage things right. So much for this being such a difficult game.
But again, this shows serious balance issues: four farmers right off the bat shouldn't overpower the game, and farm (and orchard) yields should be seriously nerfed. On the other side, fishing and particularly gathering (currently less than worthless) should get a hefty boost; this rebalancing would make the game an actual challenge.
With taters just rolling in and filling your warehouses to bursting, the problems of glacial pacing and slow workers are now rather unimportant and the game becomes a leisurely town builder, as you add more sophisticated production chains and optimize your settlement's layout. Problem here is that once you reach about ten years -- the time when the settlment starts to mature and you can think of building ports and bakeries -- the game becomes buggy and saves are corrupted and soon enough you have a fatal CTD. So save early and save often; you'll need it.
All that said, my review is still negative, mostly because of the fatal flaws of bad code as well as the above-mentioned balance issues, particularly with fields and  those pesky trees, which grow like kudzu and should yield more and grow slower because as it is now they are simply ridiculous.

Seven Kingdoms 2 was really a great game. And still is because it aged well. However, this so-called HD remake is not so great. I have 10 FPS in game on a computer which runs new games pretty well. It doesn't matter if I play in 800x600 or 1920x1080, FPS remains the same. Odd thing is when I scroll the screen, FPS rises to 30 but drops back to 10 when the screen is still. Maybe it's the drivers, but I'm not willing to tamper with older versions when everything is OK in other games.
So, if you want to play Seven Kingdoms 2 - go to GOG and buy their original version.

Don't be discouraged by the outdated graphics and sound. This game is truly a unique gem and easily forgotten but offers so much even today despite it's somewhat dated looks.
In Seven Kingdoms you take control of an human civilization on a typical rts styled map, you can pick between 12 civilizations which all look aesthetically different and have various strengths/weaknesses. Furthermore you can pick a Frythan race, which are mythical and gruesome creatures bent on enslaving everyone. Both factions play very different, where human civilizations are more refined and deep, the Frythans are more about conquering.
The game has some very unique mechanics, basically the player tries to take over towns (either peacefully or with force) to increase your population. Recruiting them as builders or soldiers from a pool. Diplomacy, wafare, research and espionage are of utmost importance and allow you for different playstyles. You can pick between various approaches to conquer your enemies which is certainly a welcome change, it's a lot deeper than your typical rts. It has some major 4x elements so there are a lot of factors that you have to consider. The Frythan faction is more straight forward though with a heavy emphasis on warfare. The campaign is certainly unique and has some Risk elements, don't expect anything amazing but it's still very entertaining. I definitely recommend this game for the multiplayer though, playing with a friend is a blast.
The things that I could critique is the dated graphics and sound assets, but I personally don't mind it that much. It is servicable and still quite good. Also sometimes it can be a bit confusing if there is a lot of activity going on, there are sometimes a lot of factors to manage but luckily the hd edition allows for a larger overview, making it easier to navigate. Which reminds me that this game can be extremely challenging at first, the AI is actually really competent and can easily wipe you out even if you consider yourself an expert at rts games.
Still I definitely recommend this game for anyone who likes a somewhat unique rts with a nice twist. It offers variety from other games and runs on every pc.
One last thing I want to mention is that the developer is really present and communicates intensively with the community in order to fix bugs, balance game and make it overall a better game than it used to. That is very recommendable and helped me with some issues that I previously had with the game.

Binary Domain. Simply put an 8/10 game to the core. Having just finished my first playthrough i can say it's been an amazing ride. The game has many different guns and plenty of teamwork with the AI allies. the voice commands, while can be helpful if you have a mic, does not impede the enjoyment if you don't, with a button that brings up the list of commands at will. The story is fun and twists and turns along the route. While the game may be short in my terms, for an FPS it's a decent length. Completing the game unlocks chapter unlock, allowing you to challenge yourself to go back and pick up any pieces you've left behind. From what it would appear to me, the story changes depending on who you have in your group and how much trust you have with each person. So I can speculate the story and ending that i got for each companion would be different if i had other choices and members along for the ride.
The only negative side i would say is that the game is clearly made for the consoles, the UI has a bit of difficulty naviagating and responding with the mouse, but this is negligable and doesn't distract from the enjoyable parts of the game.

Binary Domain is a really engaging third-person shooter. If you enjoy murdering waves upon waves of robots, then this is the game for you! Some caveats are in order, however: first, the default controls (owing to its console origins) are far less than ideal. You'll probably need to do a bit of fiddling to get it the way you want it to play. Second, this game is very cutscene-heavy. Granted, the story is pretty interesting, but it nevertheless seems to go on and on while you're waiting to shoot robots.
Fortunately, they introduce a lot of varied gameplay and the boss fights are very cool. Not an amazing game, but definitely a good timewaster.

Anyways I would give it a 8/10. Anyone who's a fan of 3rd person action or science fiction in general should give it a crack.

I was going through a rough time in my life. My parents were fighting constantly, I had no friends, and everyone I met hated me because I was fat. I needed something to prevent me from suicide. I could not find anything I really liked. I tried buying toys, but the store clerks always prevented me from buying anything because I was overweight. I tried making a vlog on YouTube about my troubles, but I was banned from youtube for supposedly impersonating Gabriel Iglesias. Google fined me all of my money until I only had $10 left.
The only things I had were things necessary for my survival. I was fed a potato every other day and also given water in a shot glass. Sometimes I forced myself to use the water as a way to bath instead of drinking it. I was locked in my room every day cuz my parents were busy fighting about which console to play on. Well, not entirely.
I had this netbook, one my parents got me for my birthday when I was 12. I used it for school, mostly, until now. I was also lucky enough to have a charger, and all the stuff you need to use the netbook. I decided, maybe give video games a try. No one would judge me there. I was unable to play the f2p games because A. They took too much storage and B. I would be banned whenever I joined a multiplayer game. I remembered the $10 I had left.
I knew I had to find something that gave me a reason to live. I looked through the steam store. Jesus almost nothing was $9.99! I was about to give up and just end my life when I found this game. Ratz Instagib. $9.99, without 10% tax. It took up all the space on my netbook. After waiting for it to download, I opened up the game. Upon opening it up there was a well made launcher with many options. Once I opened up the actual game, I heard a sweet jazz song, and saw some badass looking ratz and a cool map. Was this what I needed to continue living
It was. I am proud to say Ratz Instagib saved my life. The characters were deep, had personality, and I was able to connect with them. The story was unique, suspenseful, and I shed multiple tears. The graphics were revolutionary, and the soundtrack was the first good thing I had heard in awhile. It, in a way, provided everything I needed to live. The characters were my friends. The game was like a good parent. The game was easy to fap to. I could have just played the game for my entire life. It was amazing. It changed me. Here I am, sitting in my room, now infested with bullet ants and bees, starved half to death and with my throat about to dry up. But you know what? I do not care. Because I have Ratz Instagib. And I will always have Ratz Instagib. This game is my life now. I am finally happy. I am finally free. I know now the meaning of life. And only because  Lino Slahuschek games spent their time on this godly game.

Heroes and Generals is a weird combination of Arma 3 and Battlefield 1, but set during WW2, and its free to play. I personally enjoy the game very much but cant say I recommend it for all. The amount of grinding is a little ridiculous, and at times battles can feel extremely unbalanced if one team has a tank or air superiority. As an infantry or paratrooper unit there is litte you can do to take out tanks, and air vehicles are nearly impossible. Tanks wouldn't be an issue if you were allowed to swap loadouts or weapons, but the only way to do this is to have multiple characters and a squad that can hold multiple different kinds of units, and these things involve a lot of grinding and in game currency. At times it feels like a meat grinder: you spawn in and instantly get killed by a tank or someone with the best gun, and in this way the game is unbalanced. I'm guessing that the reason the game is like that is so that people are more tempted to buy the better guns using real money, but still this system is severely broken. The game is not friendly to new players, especially those who come looking for a CoD style WW2 shooter. If you're looking for that, you've come to the wrong place and you will end up frustrated. Patience and planning are key to doing well, and without those things you will be unhappy. Despite its many flaws the game is very fun, especially if you have a friend to play with. 7/10

A really excellent game all around.  There are some jump scares, but they're not cheap--the deep, lovingly cultivated atmosphere puts real weight behind them, and they often manifest in a way you don't expect.  The graphics are outstanding for an indie title, and it really serves to draw you in--which is important, because the main terror in the game revolves around suddenly wishing you *weren't* so immersed.  There's no combat, so the fear comes from seeing things you wish you weren't seeing.  The story and characters are fantastic, but the truly memorable moments come from watching one hellish event after another unfold in front of you, and the helplessness to stop it.
Okay, I mean, you COULD just turn it off.  But you won't.
The game begs to be played in one sitting the first time, so make sure you have the night free, turn down lights (where applicable), and enjoy.
Short, spoiler-free list of things that you may not want to experience (or may sweeten the deal):
--Alcohol abuse
--Unreality
--Rats
--Baby dolls (so many baby dolls)
--Space out of time/Time out of space
--Eyes/scopophobia
--Suggestion that a doggo may be seen that fails to deliver on adorable doggo (a large shortcoming but worth forgiving)
--Paintings
This game gets a big, shiny gold star for no sexualized violence!  Thank you, devs.

A really interesting and under-appreciated experience. I've been playing this game intermittently for 7 years and it still feels a fresh and original experience.
The game is first-person built on the little dated but reliable Source engine. To win you must earn a certain amount of money. Cash can be used to buy food, items, healing etc and to earn it you must find, identify and covertly kill your assigned target while ensuring that you are not yourself killed by the anonymous player assigned to hunt you. More interesting and unique methods of assassination earn you a greater reward. If you are killed by your hunter you will be out of the round and you will be unable to earn anything until the next round.
While doing all this you have to maintain your basic human needs; eating, drinking, sleeping, washing etc which if neglected will disable you and bring about your early demise. This clever little mechanic ensure you can't just camp in a safe place and wait out a battle, and gives your hunter the opportunity to catch you unawares.
You must kill your target covertly; if you are witnessed brandishing a weapon either by security, cameras or multiple witnesses you have your weapons confiscate, be put into prison for a set amount of time, and fined a heavy penalty. Not only does this delay the elimination of your target, it also leaves you in a very vulnerable situation to whoever is hunting you.
The art and level design add significantly to the experience. Set on a variety of 1920's era cruise ships the art style is stylish, lighthearted and a little slapstick.  The level design is fantastic; each map has all kinds of secret locations, stashes and traps that make them a joy to explore. Even after playing for many years I still discover new exciting details.
One thing to remember is that this game is meant to be enjoyed as a multiplayer experience. While the AI passengers can sometimes catch you out, and are suitable for practice, it's broadly speaking pretty dumb and doesn't offer much of a challenge. The AI is most useful for padding out the number of passengers on a cruise, making identification and execution of your human target more of a challenge, indeed doing your best to imitate the sometimes strange behavior of the AI can be an excellent technique to lure you target into a false sense of security.
There are only really two criticism I can make of this game;
The first is a little unfair given its age but worth mentioning. There is a limited population in the online servers which can make finding an enjoyable populated game a little difficult. Luckily buying the game contains 2 additional copies free which gives you some copies to share with friends which is a pretty good deal. Especially considering there is no joy quite like hearing the frustration of a good friend when you catch them out and brutally eliminate their avatar.
Secondly the learning curve can be a little steep. However I believe there are a single player and tutorial package included now although I have yet to try them. On the other hand its pretty easy to pick up with playing with a friendly experience player.
tl;dr a unique multi-player assassination experience that is still worth the asking price despite its age. Best shared with friends.

This is the Multiplayer portion of The Ship. I said I didn't like the singleplayer, but the multiplayer is a totally different story.
Also another little note, at time of writing, the in-game server browser is broken. You can find games through Steam (Steam Window: View > Servers > Change Filters > set game to The Ship).
The Ship seems to be a lesser known, yet highly underrated game about murdering other people without being spotted. It's a true blue stealth game in that you actually have to kill your quarry without being seen by anyone. If you pull out a weapon in front of a guard, security camera, or are seen holding one for too long by other players, you get arrested and penalized. The game also punishes random deathmatching, so players have less incentive to grief. The game is really tense because
while you're hunting your target, someone else is hunting you, and you have no idea who it is until they start looking shifty, make a move on you, or kill you.
It also combines a little bit of The Sims in that you have to manage your needs: hunger, thirst, toilet, cleanliness, boredom, fatigue, socialization... All the while trying to hunt down your quarry. The game also encourages mixing up your murder weapons by increasing the money you get for a kill with a given weapon the longer it goes without being used. Once a weapon is used, it drops to the bottom of the list and only gives you the minimum payout.
The game is a buttload of fun and deserves more love and attention. This game also comes with a bunch of copies that you can give to friends. I highly recommend it, especially if you can pick it up during a sale.

Think "The Sims" crossing over with "Assassin's Creed", you are all random shipmates with individual pseudonyms aboard a variety of different and even exotic vessels for maps.
Your main objective: Kill your designated quarry, whilst watching out for other competing hunters, and tending to  your own basic human needs; hunger, sleep, boredom, hygiene, and using the facilities (Make sure you close the door first!).
And proclaim your prominence as the dominant hunter, with a comedic arsenal of fun assertives such as: A Tommy gun, Blunderbuss', shanks, Wallet-bombs, and even Mannequin Arms. Just don't get caught by the fuzz when commiting your dasterdly deeds!
There's just nothing more amusing than whipping out a full automatic, and eviscerating your best friends while they're busy "passing time on the porcelain throne"... *sighs happily* Good times.
All in all... The perfect party game to play with friends. ^^

This game could have been a nice throwback to old platformers, and I must say that, aesthetically, it looks the part. It looks like some Super Mario Bros clone (and, in fact, the sound for the health items is the one for one up in the original SMB), and that wouldn't be necessarily bad; unfortunately, its mechanics feel somewhat "sloppy". For example, in a few levels there's boxes you need to move, which you can either push or pull. With such a mechanic, one would think there'd be a specific button for grabbing boxes, but no; you need to get close to the box, and then you might be able to pull it (sometimes it doesn't work, and sometimes you want to move away from the box and end up pulling it with you). There's a dash mechanic, but other than in a couple levels, it doesn't really come in handy. You've also got a gun, but most of the time it's quicker to either jump over the enemies to kill them, or avoid them altogether.
The levels are a mixed bag; in all of them, except for the final boss level, you must find a key in order to open the exit door. While some are decent enough, there's a few ones with some really tedious or annoying platforming. In one of them, for example, you're supposed to cross a huge pool of water (your character dies if it touches it), by bouncing over flying enemies. The levels have checkpoints, but one issue with them is that, whenever you die, the enemies get "reset", but your bullet counter does not.
Well, in short, this game isn't very good. I mean, it's not terribly bad, but it's not something I'd recommend.

I had a joke review up previously, but I decided to write a serious one.
Going into this game, I had low expectations. The writing looked awful from the infamous mall scene with Audrey and Kyanna. The gameplay looked pretty boring.
I was legitimately impressed by this game. It takes the classic bejewled style puzzle gameplay and tweaks it just enough that it  feels fresh. The sentiment and passion mechanic makes you plan your moves out ahead. On higher difficulties, you'll fail quite a bit if you're not precise.
There's a waifu for everyone in this game. A small touch, you can play as either a male or female and there's no difference outside of the pronouns used in dialogue and a few changed lines.  It's not  a huge deal, but I really appreciated that there wasn't any pandering to either gender.
The OST is pretty catchy. You'll be humming some of the tracks for days to come.
Oh, and there's a huge amount of time you can sink into the game. Replaying will get you 100 percent completion and new achievements, and there's an infinite time attack mode for masochists.
I highly recommend this game.

Horror in evey sense of the word.  I don't think I've been quite so distubred since System Shock 2.  Dead Space 1 & 2 definitely have their unique body horror, but nothing quite like this.  Inventive in a disturbing way.  The body horror is off the charts and your heart is going to be racing as you try to manage your way through levels, especially the boss encounters.
Gameplay definitely can be described as the traditional "tank" controls with the tight 3rd person camera over the shoulder.  You can shoot and move and you're going to have to.  Lots of options at play to build your character as you see fit.  More stealth in the early game and more shooting in the late game.
If there's a negative to be had, I think the addition of stealth is problematic.  I love stealth games so it's not a huge issue for me.  But this game was designed around it.  If you screw up stealthing, shooting is an option, but limited resources make it punishment if you're not good at doing stealth.  There were points where even I was out of ammo and barely making it through to the end of chapters.  So if you're not into stealth gameplay, you may want to look elsewhere.
Story is solid, but perhaps leaves a bit too much in the dark.  I hear that the DLC expansions add more to it so I work make it a negative.  It's intriguing, but not easy to follow with characters that are interesting but not personal enough to really get to love.  You don't spend enough time with them and their motives (and even your own in certain regards) are not all together clear beyond "let's not die."
All in all, if you're looking for a tense horror game with boss fights ala Resident Evil and Dead Space, this is definitely a game for you to look into.

The quest for an equal to Amnesia: The Dark Descent continues.
However I did find the "game" , if you can even call it that, quite enjoyable. I see a lot of quips about it being a walking simulator. Unfortunately that is not far from the truth. I will start off with where the game succeeds before I will list its failures.
The graphics for a B game are actually very nice. I had a fun time checking out the paintings. They also did a very good job with the atmosphere. It did indeed create a very creepy feeling. I also found the story somewhat enjoyable and intersting enough for me to try and get to the next step which is all you really need. Could it have been better? Definitely, but it was good enough. The music was decent and the jump scares were good (although few).
Now where the game utterly fails is it's description of it being a game at all. There really isn't anything to do as far as puzzles are concerned. There isn't any way to fail really unless you just stop "playing" . There is no tension where you must hurry and do this or that will happen or hurry up and collect this before that happens or hurry up and figure out this or else you will go no where in the story. It also lacked quite a bit of VO which could have made the story a bit more intriguing. I think these are important elements not only to a horror game but to a game in general. I mean, can you really call it a game if there is nothing to figure out? Now before anyone starts to whine I will say that yes, near the end when you collect the last two pieces of the six that there is something that you can sorta say are puzzles but they are so inane that I probably would have put something like that at the very beginning of the game rather than at the end.
So my search continues for a horror game as well put together as Dark Descent. The only one that has come close in the last few years is Outlast. I am not sure if I could say this game is worth $20. I got it for $8 and if you can get it for that then I think it is worth it. I did like the overall effort though, so I will get it a thumbs up although I wish Steam went to a star rating system to be more accurate.

The Worms crew returns, and this time they’ve got balls! The classic Worms™ Pinball sends the cute little pink guys spinning across one of the most realistic pinball tables ever created. Battle with honour through the mystic art of Worms. Kung-Fu or hang at high noon with the grizzliest, pinkest cowboys this side of Texas. Only Worms. Pinball offers an action packed pinball simulation of pure wormage! Worms. Pinball leaves nothing to the imagination. The table sports 3D LED displayed sub-games and parallel objectives, transparent ramps, user-controllable moving gadgets, moving mechanical parts and wild sound effects and music. The table contains over 150 animated parts and thousands of frames of rendered FMV animation for the LED display. It’s got tilt functions, hit combinations as well as drop and dead catches, bounce and flip passes, bang backs, death saves, magnetic fields and countless other exciting features. The depth of gameplay, variety of action and sophisticated table rules ensures that Worms Pinball will have all gamers, not just hard-core pinheads, hooked.
Worms Pinball is a great pinball game with a fun and entertaining table that provides adequate challenge. The pads are responsive, the physics are decent, all the ramps and pits are accessible with just enough practise, and the old-school Worms 1 theme adds the perfect amount of nostalgia factor to make you revisit it from every now and then.
What is atrocious though and makes part of me want to give it a thumbs down, is the price. This one used to be called Addiction Pinball with an additional table (featuring a now-forgotten Team 17 game, ‘World Rally Racing’, an even better table) and cost less on disc at release than this one on Steam now.
If you can grab it in a bundle, do so, but I highly advise against actually purchasing it even at half discount.

As for me, I'm off to play something else.

I got the game since it was real cheap and expected a decent, but not amazing third person shooter. For the most part my assumption was correct, but I was a bit pleased with the cutscenes and story. It certainly borrows heavily from other stories about robots and humans, like Ghost in the Shell, and it is laughably predictable at times. Still, the presentation and voice-over is quite nice, and I found the characters to be mostly likable and even funny. The attention to detail is not always great, but the game is good with mixing up locations and characters to keep the player interested. There's also a jet ski level for some reason.
It tries to do some interesting things with the gameplay with squad-based tactics and upgrades, but these seem a bit like an afterthought and don't do much to make the game more fun. For the most part the gameplay is pretty standard cover-based TPS stuff, but with some crazy boss fights here and there.
Overall, the campaign helped elevate the game from a mediocre shooter to a decent game that I found enjoyable. Not great, but worth a go.

The production values are a bit dated, but don't let that fool you.  There hasn't been an RTS like this since 1999.  It's been praised as sort of a "Thinking Man's Age of Empires," and that is a fair description.  Instead of mining for resources, you must tax your citizens and trade at markets.  Instead of creating units at barracks, you must draft those same citizens at forts and place them under a capable general to train.  Slipping a few spies into enemy ranks can turn the tide later on - imagine your enemy's face when his most trusted general defects to your side with half his men!  And of course there is always the war against the Frythans - spend too much time fighting your human enemies and you'll both be sorry when a horde of monsters comes charging in...
Or you can just play as the Frythans and build an army of gorrillas.
My only criticisms are that at the maximum resoltion the game seriously hurts my eyes.  Maybe it's my moniter or my settings.  Either way, it plays just fine for me at lower resolutions.  Sound and visuals are a bit dated and some of the sound effects in particular are very generic.
Despite all that, it's a worthy addition to anyone's library.  It puts the "Strategy" in Real Time Strategy again and makes you think, scheme, plan, and negotiate your way to victory instead of spamming units or racing to the end of some tech-tree.  Check out the other reviews, and you can see that the game definately has some staying power despite its age.

Binary Domain is an action-packed third person shooter set in the technically highly advanced Tokyo of the year 2080 where intelligent robots are a regular part of everyday's life.
You are Dan Marshall, member of a so-called Rust Crew, which is specialized on enforcing the New Geneva Convention that regulates advancement of robot technology and forbids the creation of 'Hollow Children', robots with a human-like appearance.
The story is futuristic and has that 'I, Robot' kind of touch, which is pretty cool and fairly well done - especially since it comes with a couple twists towards the end of the game. Despite the rather serious story, there are many amusing dialogues and slapstick-ish moments between you and your squad members, which is a nice change for the action-packed fights.
Being a third person shooter, Binary Domain comes with the typical cover-based gameplay mechanics and controls, so nothing new or surprising there. When played with mouse and keyboard, the aiming can act a bit funny at times, but all in all the controls are responsive and get the job done.
To my surprise, the game comes with a couple of tactical elements. You can order commands to your squad members, upgrade your own and your squad members' weapons, equip them with various enhancements to improve their abilities and endurance and during certain key points in the game you even get to swap your squad members entirely.
Additionally, with dialogue choice and ingame actions you alter your squad's morale and either increase or decrease the trust they put in you. Depending on that, your squad members may eventually disobey your orders during a fight, leaving you alone against a hoard of enemies.
While the game doesn't exactly provide you with extensive graphics options, it looks and runs fairly decent. Partially, you encounter some low-resolution textures in the game, but overall there's not much to complain.
A really cool and innovative thing in the game is the SpeechFX feature. If you have a microphone plugged in, you can configure and use it within the game to reply to your squad members or issue orders by directly saying 'Move', 'Hold' and so on.
With around 10 hours of playtime for the story, it provides a decent length without ever really getting tedious or boring. Binary Domain also features a multiplayer mode with various game modes, however, unfortunately it is pretty much dead by now, so don't even bother thinking about buying the DLCs for the game.
All in all, Binary Domain is a surprisingly good third person shooter with funny dialogues, cool tactical elements and a lot of action, so if you're up for some robot♥♥♥♥♥kicking, make sure to check this game out!

I am mixing my personal review with a brief introduction to aspects of the game that are often misjudged or poorly explained in most reviews:
1 - Personal review
2 - Loot/crafting system
3 - The playerbase paradigm
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. I kept this game on my wishlist for months before I went and bought it on sale. I must say, after playing for a few weeks, all my hopes and fears for this game were confirmed. The game is an absolute blast, one of th best co-op experiences ever concieved. The core mechanics are exectuted perfectly, the melee combat is straightforward but very refined with its nuances and overall really satisfying.
There is a tactical and a stratecic depth behind the surface as well, with characters and weapons setups better at single target or trash clearing, better at burst or dps, better at staggering groups or eliminating elites in a crowd etc...
Not only the depth to the combat system is much richer than you could think on a first run but it allows for several different playstyles based on your class and weapons combinations.
The progression via the loot system is what keeps you motivated BUT gear really has a somewhat minor impact on difficulty, the progress trought the difficulty levels of the various missions it's all made by improving at the game and learning all the details of a particular level, it's defendable spots, its fixed ammonition cashes, its most common random encounters etc...
Succeeding at this game is all ACTUAL skills and actual experience.
The control you have over the difficulty also enriches the feeling of progression and the sense of reward you get. Maybe you beat The Horn of Magnuss on Nightmare before, but the first time you do it with also 3 tomes and 2 grimoires it's a fresh feeling of a victory drenched in ratblood. Also every run is unique, I've had lucky runs on nightmare with but a few special encounters and normal runs that went for the worse when the Rat Ogre decided to emerge in the middle of an horde while we were clamped up defending in a corner.
2. Lots of people describe the RNG loot system as the flaw in the game but I do not agree. First of all, the system is not purely based on RNG, at least not anymore. Sure, you cannot decide what rewards to get after each mission, but you have a dedicated crafting system that allows you to salvage or merge what you don't need, roll weapons of a particular kind you need, reroll its talents and then reroll its talents' number rolls. You will never be suffering for that yellow musket for your imperial soldier for too long because you know you will get your hands on it eventually, luck only dictates how quickly and what other stuff you might get in the meantime. If you like to play different characters (wich will be very helpfull if you don't have a dedicated team) you will probably get something somewhat usefull most of the times.
3. The only real flaw I can find to this game is its reliance on a healty playerbase both in terms of quality and quantity.
Quality is mostly an issue at lower difficulty levels so not too tragic for the overall game experience but can dissuade some new players before they get to experience the best the game has to offer. You will happen to run into players that don't know a level well enough to play it on hard and screw your entire team while at times you will get totally carried thought it by someone more experienced.
The quantity will affect your solo player ability to find lobbies and teamates for any mission on any difficulty level. Maybe you want to finish the Wizard's tower on Nightmare but everyone else is just farming Smuggler's run and all you can do is start by yourself and hope someone will fill in for the bots. The fact that there are daily contracts will facilitate you in finding groups since most people will be playing the missions with the contracts on that day.
Now, please take my wards with a grain of salt, I am a solo player and I am still having massive ammounts of fun, I did hit a bit of a wall when transitioning from normal to hard but after a while I became the one carrying noobs trought it no problems. I believe this issues would only affect you if your friends are as bad as mine for not buying this game with me, if they are somewhat decent go buy all together and enjoy the bloodshed like a family.
If you remember this review when you beat your first level on nightmare feel free to add me, I need better friends.

I wanted to write this comment to counter a bit all the negative reviews concerning the copy of Banished.
Banished is a great game and I played a lot of it since the start a long time ago, and while Forest village has similarities in the UI, I cannot say that they copied all from Banished. The UI was great, so why not inspire yourself of it ? I don't see why someone should always reinvent the wheel when it already works well. If not, everything is a copy of everything (iOS, Android, Windows, etc.).
Now concerning the game. It has a huge potential ! I already spent hours on it, and the amazing graphics, buildings and landscapes really do add immersion and fun.
I didn't encounter serious bugs. Only one when choosing another crop when it has already begun doesn't update it.
So, although I really like this game, there are still things I'd like to see. There are not so many buildings and after a point in the game, you have everything, the challenge is gone and the only thing remaining is expansion.
This is although counterbalanced by amazing mods out there, like one that adds a lot of content (new recipes, new advanced production chains, new seeds, etc.). With this mod, the game is a lot more fun and "realistic".
As we see in the game, there are still many buildings that cannot be built yet, so I suppose it's not developped yet, but planned. I'm also very eager to see the viking invasions like they promised to do.
So all in all, it's pretty similar to Banished, without being a copy of it and with specific new things in it, and awesome graphics !

I really wanted to enjoy this game.
I feel like there is a lack of good arena shooters out there right now, and this game really misses the "good" part of that phrase, in all honesty.
For a game that totes around the name RATZ, you'd expect they'd sure as hell know how to make a Rats map, but they've managed to prove even this wrong.
Through many maps you cannot infact access the undersides of tables, chairs, or go through the walls.
These may seem like simple details, but these additional forms of cover can change gameplay entirely, and it doesn't really feel like I'm playing on Rats maps when I play any of this game.
The point of a Rats map isn't that you're supposed to actually be the size of a damned Rat, you're supposed to be small enough to cram yourself between the couch cushions and find the remote.
Another issue I came across was the controls. Or should I say physics? Actually, in this case I'll go with both at the same time, because it seems like this time around the physics and controls got together and decided to get drunk off their♥♥♥♥♥because neither of them act quite right and they become kind of unbearable to be around.
If you manage to jump high enough, or wall climb, it can take a rediculous amount of time to finally get your feet back on the ground.
Now this could be argued back with the point that you have tons of air control, but this is also an issue.
You shouldn't be able to make sharp 180 degree turns while catapulting yourself at breakneck speeds through the air.
At that point, the game essentially becomes a competition to see who can get highest in the air, get the best vantage point, and use the walls to consistently levetate at said altitude.
It breaks the flow and destroys one of the biggest factors of an "ARENA SHOOTER".
I feel like the game should be urging me to thrust myself through the air and be bunny jumping through courses, but I've only found that to lead to death in this game.
In a good arena shooter like Quake, movement is key, and you need it to survive.
But this game taunts you by dangling the gameplay in front of your face, then slapping you when you finally reach to do it.
Overall this game is a good effort, and a good concept, but it's executed so poorly that I feel that it isn't worth the money. Not now, not ever, because this game has sailed so far from the original concept that the search teams went missing.

Before I start this review, I would like to say that I haven't played this game a lot. I bought it 2 days ago, so I'll judge it from my experience as of now.
Alright so, starting off, I would like to mention the fact that this game was made with the Unity engine. It's really good for any kind of games, especially 2D.
Now, the story of this game in a nutshell: A robot has been sent from Earth into a random planet. Then that robot causes problems against Earth, by enslaving the creatures of that planet and you, Mr. Mustache, have to stop this whole situation. The first level of the game seems very good. The textures and the level design are very good and the same counts for the Mustache guy (he has quite a nice style). The music of the game is pretty good, the same counts for most of the sound effects, except from one of them: the 1-up sound from Mario that's being used in this game. I don't really have a problem with it, since it's just a stupid sound, but it was a bit unexpected from a pay to play game. I usually see this sound effect in Mario online games. And now, let me go to (maybe) the most important aspect of the game that dragged me in even more into playing it: the difficulty. The difficulty in this game is actually really good. It's not too easy, but it's also not too hard. The game doesn't have cheap deaths (which are being used in video games sometimes) and the controls are quite smooth (well not the smoothest of all for me, since I mostly play 8-bit games on consoles, but it's pretty smooth).
Overall, it's a game that I totally recommend as of now (I haven't played a lot as I said before). If I finish the game anytime soon, I'll probably change a few aspects of my review. Anyway though, I don't believe that you'll regret it if you buy it, especially right now that the price has dropped (only for 8 more days though). For 50 cents, you get a nice, difficult and fun 8-bit game with a weird guy with a mustache and the 1-up sound effect from Mario!

Life is Feudal: Forest Village sure feels a lot like Banished but it’s very lacking in a general sense. The game just doesn’t feel like it’s been completed. There’s not a lot of building variety and once you’ve played for a certain time there just isn’t much else you can do except build more of the same buildings to make your city larger. At that point it’s just a point-and-click game with not much of a challenge to it.
The terraforming feature is horrible because it shapes the ground with exact 90 or 45 degree angles. It just looks bad. When I played I just avoided ever using it due to that problem. Another feature that’s in the game is the 1st person mode which is, in my opinion, completely pointless and does not fit into the graphical style of Forest Village. Up close everything looks real ugly.
Wildlife AI is very bad and often walks through buildings and citizens. Bears hang out in the town square and people walk around it without a care in the world. It’s a small thing that ruins some of the immersion.
The things that Life is Feudal: Forest Village does well is the real time weather & seasons system. It gives the game atmosphere but without any building variety it’s wasted potential.
The difficulty level is based around how well you can prepare for winter. If you are not stocked for winter your entire village will likely perish and you will have to start over.  I enjoy the concept but it’s very hard to determine exactly how much you need of everything to survive an entire winter since the population size will be different each time and children are born during winter. It’s easy to guess in the start of the game but gets very hard when the village reach a larger population.
I would not suggest this game to anybody in its current state. Not even during a sale. If you think that this game looks good then I strongly suggest that you pick up Banished instead since that game feels more balanced, got better overall atmosphere and building variety. It’s got a lot of the same features without the negatives of this game.

Review Version: 1.0.6266, July 13th, 2017
Despite many many hours played in this game, I have to write a review that ends with a tenative thumbs down until it sees a substantial update.
Forest Village is a single player city building/survival management game in the Life Is Feudal series, which includes a MMORPG and a single player RPG in development. Population management and resource production are key in this game - influenced by mechanics that are sure to see more fine tuning but offer interesting necessities for conservation and control of growth.
Forest Village's time scale is a bit odd - babies become children in a year, a teenager in the next, and an adult in the next. leaving the strange question over the real scale of time in the game and the occasional laugh at the wrongness of some combination of villagers expecting a baby. Winters are brutal times of no growth and cold, meaning you are preparing for the trials of winter all year, every year.
It's addictively challenging at all times due to population growth, which is only controllable by being rather creatively cruel to your settlement, eliminating houses or allowing some to die off and preventing people from having children by reaching a self-imposed cap. Production of food is labor intensive in many ways, and investments in care often mean choosing who goes where and when - a good credit to the game's depth, but needs some work to iron out the weaknesses and brutal strategies required to control things.
The game has much room to grow and mature but has many buildings that do not do anything but serve as placeholder for a future update. While small fixes and hot fixes have been published, it's been a while since the game added anything to fill the big gaps it left for itself. There needs to be more stronger differentiation between resources, more resources, more buildings, more things to upgrade with more mature growth and upgrade mechanics.
For 25 bucks, the game has proven worth the money, but this doesn't change the fact that it's incomplete and contains placeholders. It needs to be completed and it deserves to be completed.
I sincerely hope that the team produces a substantial update within 3 months of the release - doubts are strengthening and communication and transparency are very low. I hope this changes. I'll gladly flip this review to thumbs up once the game sees a subsantial mechanical or content update that completes what was put in it.

Starts great, awesome atmosphere, good looking graphics, a story that degenerates faster than light into a weird zombie-like apocalypse where you will struggle to survive. So what's wrong with this game? It was quite discussed at the release and people loved it or hated it. II ended up hating it as I barely made it to chapter 7 before I refused to go on.
Anyways The Evil Within is directed by Shinji Mikami, and if you wonder why you're supposed to know him it's because he directed the first and the fourth chapter of Resident Evil, Dino Crisis and God's Hand. Is this important? It is, as The entire game (or at least the 7 chapters I've been able to play) has really great dark atmospheres, gruesome locations, splatter scenes and situations filled with suspance and tension typical of horror movies. The story begins in a very straight and simple way. As Detective Sebastian Castellano you're reaching a mass murder crime scene at the Beacon Mental Hospital along with a cop and your two collegues in a police car. Nobody around, abandoned police cars at the main entrance, and piles of corpses inside the hospital. And this is just the very beginning. An incredible beginning, even though it's quite simple it really throws you into an ominous mistery that is about to degenerate... A lot... And really fast. The premise is great, direction is great, and there are situations where the oddities will make me doubt the sanity of the protagonist itself... More than once.
So The Evil Within is undoubtedly good, on the paper, and is well supported by a good graphic engine (which I realize right now is the notorious id Tech 5) and even on my system configuration I've been able to play with mid-high settings with an oscillating range between 20 and 40 FPS, depending on the situation. So what's wrong, what else can be said about this game? Gameplay...
The Evil Within IS a survival Horror. This means you will be constantly on the verge of dying without ammos, and there's nothing wrong with this, a good survival horror must give you this sense of struggle to get past your enemies even against all the odds. The scarce quantity of ammunitions will obviously force you to move cautiosly to avoid the enemies or at least to take them down silently. Very well, I have no problem with stealth games, I've been playing the entire Metal Gear Solid saga, and splinter cell, I don't see the problem here, I can easily approach a stealth game... But not this one.
First things first:
. A third person "sided" camera is not a problem, as long as it's well handled. But here, a stealth survival horror, I NEED to move cautiosly in many places, especially around corners. So am I really supposed to prepare MYSELF the side of the camera EVERY TIME trying to figure out a combination of movements especially in restricted areas where my movements are already limited otherwise I'm dead? Asking for a button or a combination is too much? Fine, then give me a central camera and all troubles are gone. But nope... This is not a serious problem that totally ruins the gameplay experience, I know... But it's the first. Let's move ahead.
. Because there's no specific mechanism to hide behind walls, corners or objects which is essential. It IS essential because otherwise you have to wager on your position hoping the enemy sight has limits, or maybe even considers the fact you're hiding in the dark (HA, yeah, sure...). So you'll end up with borderline situations where you will barely hide behind a pile of hay bales, you will mistakenly push ahead the bales expecting the enemy to spot you instantly, but he (she IN MY CASE) will pass through and spot you with their magic fisheye FOV. Simply magnificent for a game that claims to be stealth...
I guess I shouldn't even consider

That was NOT MY IDEA, the game ITSELF showed me the hint. And since the butcher can't be killed with just a stab in his head (realized later in other situations and with guides as well) I just kept dying. Thank you for explaining something I can do, but not now, not with that enemy and not there because it doesn't have any sense as there's nothing to do right there except for stealing the keys for an exit that is actually the other way...

Having played this game for a while, I've found it to be fairly enjoyable. There's a lot to do, lots of customisation in terms of ships, ship appearance, character appearance, weapons, equipment etc. I have not tried the PvP as I'm not inclined to do so with this sort of game (there are some games I'd rather do the PvE of rather than PvP, and this is one. Not a bad thing though, personal taste is the thing here). Controls are fairly responsive, even when using a laptop trackpad. A couple of glitches here and there, but so far nothing game-breaking. My main issue is the hefty prices put on DLC and premium currency. The total cost for all of the DLC currently available is somewhere around £148, which for three items is ludicrously expensive. When comparing this to another game that has three packs of DLC that I've been playing recently - Dark Souls 2 (but on Xbox 360 as I don't have a PC (I'm on Mac) setup that can run it) - I found that for the far more affordable price of the DLC for that, it makes me wonder why the DLC for Star Trek Online is so expensive. Perhaps it's because it may provide more hours of gameplay in the form of missions, which is a good thing, but is not necessarily a good reason to make it so pricey. But, I digress. Overall, this game is a pretty good game. A few interesting ideas in it that are executed well. Hours and hours of gameplay, even without DLC. Fantastic array of customisation options. My only grip being the high prices set on DLC and premium currency which, in the end, are not necessary to enjoy this game.

The missions generally revolve around you slaughtering rats or running fetch quests (while slaughtering rats).  Slaughtering rats gets old as you see the same 7 or 8 enemy types on every single level, the only difference being the quantity that attack at any one time.  There is an extremely heavy focus on melee combat as ammo drops for ranged weapons are rare.
The game only has 13 levels, all of which can be finished in about 30 minutes or less by a proficient team of adventurers (60 minutes for noobs), unless you die and have to restart the entire mission because there are no checkpoints.  Additional levels can be purchased as DLC but I suppose they won't offer much new.  I don't like that the lack of levels means the game ends before you can really experiment with most of what Vermintide has to offer.  I only crafted and upgraded 1 weapon the entire time, so the full use of the Forge and Shrine still eludes me.  I experimented with each character but ultimately only really played with 1 character the whole time.
So yes, I would recommend this game if you have a group of friends to play with, but I wish the game offered more content rather than trying to force you to replay the same 13 levels over and over again.

This game is frequently described as a "Left 4 Dead clone", which is a fair comparison on one hand, but I believe also doesn't do the game the justice that it deserves.
While the horde mechanics are similar, the Skaven themselves are far more fascinating enemies to fight, having AI that is almost shockingly intelligent at times (e.g. individual skaven sometimes flattening themselves against a wall, hoping you won't notice them), paired with very well done, and frequently amusing, voice acting. Instead of just fighting waves of zombies with the occasional powerful zombie, the Skaven are foes with a personality, making them far more fun to fight and making each individual kill a satisfying act of catharsis.
Not only are the skaven interesting, but the colourful cast of characters are just as unique in individual class mechanics as they are in personality and appearance. Voice acting is convincing and well done, and very frequently entertaining as the characters make sarcastic quips at one another that give them very tangible chemistry. Each character is different to play in their own way, and I personally found that every character is fun to play in their own way (a rarity in games with a class system, in my experience!).
Lastly, rather than the usual hunt for weapons in the Left 4 Dead series, the game instead has a randomized loot system (stay with me, I'll address this!) which rewards our intrepid heroes with weapons and trinkets when they finish a mission. While my distaste for Overwatch's random lootbox system is practically a recurring joke in my group of friends, I find the system used by Vermintide to be much more fair. Not only is it impossible to use real money to get better odds at loot (there are no in-game, pay-to-play purchases, only extra DLC that is unnecessary for an overall fun experience), but the ability to try and increase the odds in your favour plays into mechanics, where the player can loot tomes and grimoires which are hidden across the mission maps in order to get a better chance at better loot, at the price of increased mission difficulty. Furthermore, even if one has miserable luck with the loot system, there is a crafting system to help improve weapons with secondary buffs, and a prayer altar which allows the trading of crafting materials in order to receive more randomized loot, so there are several different ways to pursue the weapons a player desires, and that is excluding the recently implemented Contracts and Bounty board system.
All of these factors create a thoroughly enjoyable gameplay experience, but even the experience outside of gameplay itself is made more enjoyable thanks to the continued development and support from the developers, FatShark, who listen to fan feedback far better than the majority of independent developer and publishers that I've encountered. The game was released in 2015, but brand new content and mechanics have been added to the game ever since, many of which were entirely free or at least had free content attached to them.
Without a doubt, Vermintide is easily one of the best Warhammer lisenced games on the market, and is absolutely worth the full price of admission. Don't miss out, and good luck with your rat slaying! Make Cousin Okri proud!

First of all: I love this game.
The story is superb and as a die-hard Trekkie, I can vouch that the developers' attention to detail when it comes to the Star Trek Universe is marvellous. Even the "title theme" is instantly recognisable as Star Trek, while being something completely new at the same time.
The fact that a lot of known Star Trek actors (Leonard Nimoy - Spock, Tim Russ - Tuvok, Michael Dorn - Worf, etc.) lend their voices to their characters and you get to talk to them and fight alongside them makes my Trekkie heart beat a lot faster (one of the highlights for me was fighting alongside
and traveling to the Mirror Universe).
I have concentrated on the story so far as that is the most important aspect of a game to me. I am no expert in different aspects of gameplay and controls and the like, so I leave that to others. But I do enjoy that you have both ground and space fights. not to mention the
missions, allowing me to engulf myself in RPGing in my favourite fictional universe.
So, if you are a Trekkie such as myself, this game is definitely for you. For everyone else, this is still a superb online game (stunning graphics for FTP) with an intriguing story (although you won't get all the in-jokes and references, don't worry, it's definitely not a game you can only understand after memorising each and every dialogue from all five shows and ten films - but maybe it will pieque your interest in Star Trek). I can definitely recommend it.
EDIT: Oh, if you're wondering why I have spend so little time on this game if I love it so much: I don't always play it through Steam (gaming on Linux can be a tricky thing sometimes). But believe me, I have clocked A LOT of hours on STO.

Short description: Binary Domain (BD) is a third-person shooter best compared to Mass Effect (without the RPG/story-stuff) or Rainbow Six (without Tom Clancy and annoying Patriotism).
Setup: Set in a dystopic near future (2080), in the world of BD the ocean-level has risen and killed about 2/3 of human population. So the 1.world-countries did the only logical thing - build up high and replace the missing work-drones with robot-work-drones, because, what could go wrong? Of course everything goes wrong and you, Dan Marshall, US-soldier and now member of a so called "Rust Crew" are moving in (into japan, that is) to investigate who on earth produces these new human-looking Androids and why they go all shooty-shoot on meatbags. At your side you've got the black guy Big Bo, british back ups (Charlie and Rachael), chinese sniper-love-interest Fei Lee/Faye, and later on, french super-killbot Cain.
But more important are your enemies: The Robots. And lots of 'em.
Your standard 0815-enemy (who looks like Sonny from "I, Robot") has several hit-locations and the great physic-engine takes care that every one of your shots blasts away the exact part hit, which results in robots falling down, crawling around, getting disoriented, loosing their weapons etc.
Anyway, the real fun starts, when you encounter one of the several bosses - ever wanted to destroy a real mega-sized Transformer? Now's your chance!
Pro:
- Mowing down robot-armies and bringing down the bosses is cool and has an old-school ring to it ("Shoot at the glowing orb in his stomach!" - Captain Obvious), but, due to graphics, physics and presentation, still feels pretty "BÄÄÄM!".
- Obligatory chase-scenes are actually fun.
- Smart cover-system
- Your squad-mates are at least sometimes helpful and pretty durable.
- Reputation-System with squaddies adds a liiittle motivation to play efficient to earn their respect (and earn the best end).
- You get as much play-time as from Call of Duty, but for a fraction of the money.
Mixed:
- The story is at best "predictable", at worst "flat".
- Your squad is entirely 1-dimensional and stereotypical.  Now, nobody would criticize that about any Call of Duty, or Rainbow Six (or its clones), but for some reason people seem to think it's a major-flaw of BD. I don't. I think it's wasted potential, nothing more, nothing less.
- You can upgrade the chars with nano-machines (eg. +10% damage, faster regeneration etc.) and upgrade the weapons each char uses. However, most upgrades feel as if they don't have any effect at all. Also: Some do, most don't.
Contra:
- You can "communicate" with your squad, via keys or - brace yourselves - via voice! Only flaw? I don't want to say the voice-option does NEVER work - but it's save to say, that it will work so badly, that you won't want to use it. In fact:
- The whole "communication" is a bad joke, as it occurs like this:
Bo is impressed with your mad headshot-quota and honestly compliments you for your fancy way of killing helpless bots. Now you've got the chance to answer and show what a cool guy you are! Your options:
"Thanks."
"Shut up."
"I love you."
"Sorry."
"F**k you!"
... ... ... you may notice that only one answer seems appropiate, while most seem not even coherent at all. Of course you can answer however you want and just pretend that Dan is a rumbling, raging lunatic, but it still feels pretty weird.
- Also, your reputation with the squaddies has only 2 consequences: Which ending you get, and if your squaddies obey your commands. Which is useless, as giving commands is a pain in the a** and a complete waste of time.
Overall: To enjoy this game, you need to remember what it's all about: A quick and cheap little shooter to take out the trash, filled with bright explosions, giant robots and some fanzy japano-aesthetics. If that sounds fun to you, you should totally go for it.  I'll give it a 80 out of 100.

This game isn't a bad game - it's just definitely not yet finished!
Is this a question about quality of gameplay? No, not yet. Here it's about the quantity of features that are advertised and also represented in-game as buildings but that are actually not yet working. For example there is a building one can build to get general statistics regarding the production and education of the citizens. Banished has  a similar building and its quite useful when one has built larger cities. In Forest Village there is a building for this purpose, too, but it also states in the tooltip that yet the functionality has to come. Also in the menu there is a "Statistics-Button". You can click on buildings to get statistical information, it says. Only problem is, you don't. The button does nothing at all. You get no information.
Same with the research building, for example, that sits there as a 3D model without any function at the moment. Then there is  an upgrade functionality that is not working for all buildings, yet this functionality was planned.
Why did they push out Version 1.0? Its definitely not there yet. This behaviour of the devs is very unsettling, because they obviously try to sell a game that formally looks finished but clearly isn't. Did they abandon it? They say they didn't. But this kind of behaviour doesn't help their credibility.
If you read the comments you also get an idea about the shortcomings of this game regarding quality. In terms of quality, it's not about this game being hard, its about that you can have 30 people and over 3000 potatoes, besides plenty of fish, apples and very centralized small structures and still here and there people may starve to death because they got stuck somewhere near the barn without any reason. You as a player have no influence on something like this and in the later game this can be a real problem. I don't need to elaborate further on this, read the negative reviews and forget anything that was written before, say, 10h of gameplay at least. These are problems that become more obvious in the later game. (Certainly after the famous 2h period...)
To put it into one sentence: Banished doesn't look as good, but at least it works, not to speak of the buckload of functionality Banished provides over Forest Village!
This game doesn't work properly and that's a huge problem, when every small failure can lead to the death of a whole settlement - and that's what this is all about! But we want the faults to be on our side, not on behalf of a half-baked code.
I really hope the devs are pushing the updates more regularly and fix the problems with this game. Some shorcomings are ridiculously easy to fix, like the missing UI sclaing option or the loading screen that has a resolution of 600x400 or something, wtf? Oh no, it's a copy of Banished!
Well... not exactly. It's doing everything that Banished does, but better. In some ways, it's easier than Banished, but only in some ways. Trees grow faster.
Let's see what it does right:
The first person mechanic is what, in my opnion is what this game does best. You can select a villager and do his job for him. More efficiently. For an example, a farmer might want to take a break and eat or something. However, you can take control of the farmer and say "No. No you do not. You finish planting those crops or SO HELP ME GOD..!"
You can also plant trees when in first person. You can literally plant a brand new forest without waiting for it to grow.
Also, there's a view of the insides of the buildings. You can literally walk around the village and look at your kingdom as a citizen. Frankly, it's quite amazing.
Also, are you having trouble with mountains? DIG THEM DOWN! There's terraforming, baby! Admittedly, it needs some work on, sure, but no more taking a 50 mile walk around the mountain! You can dig a ramp instead!
The one thing I wish it did as Banished is to provide a mechanic for planning. That and canceling building roads. Every goddamn time I lose my town because I start working on stone roads too early and the villagers, being stupid, care about the damn things FAR more than survival.
edit: actually, you CAN cancel the goddamn roads. It's just a bit difficult to find. No more problems with villagers being incredibly stupid.

I honestly and whole heartily recommend this game. I've always like this kind of city builders, where it's you against everything else. And in this game it most certainly is everything against you. A chicken coop; Almost every possible animal. Farming; Winter. O, and on the point of winter, we can refer to it as the great killer.
In the first few attempts I played everything according to winter. Desperately trying to survive more the 2 winters, this resulted in a lack of food after a while. Building up population and building up complexity is more difficult in this game than any I played before. Simple because a forester can't collect food, or a weaver can't collect wood or food or anything else that might help you survive.
In the end, you'll be building complexity and only use it every other winter, which is a great step forwards. And after that, you slip up and everyone dies of hunger or hypothermia or fire or ... Whatever other cause of death you could encounter...
I do recommend this game. You'll enjoy ever second of planning a village. And maybe; just maybe, you'll start planning a castle. So buy this game. Wait for a discount or just buy if it you have the funds. You won't regret this. As a city builder this is an amazing game. Well balanced and highly realistic.
