A really interesting, clever and cool consept! It's like Battlefeild, Call of Duty, or as I often compare it with, Team Fortress 2. Think of it as the building ideas from Minecraft. The map is made out of blocks, and it's an online multiplayer FPS game. It has four classes as I know. Them being the Commando, the Marksman, the Engineer and the Miner. The Commando is often equiped with a RPG and a Mini Gun, usefull for raiding a base or defending yourself in Zombie mode. The Marksman is my favourite though, equiped with (Of Course!) a Sniper Rifle, and a pistol. This is great for stealth, especially with you create a base at the top of a large building (Such as Big Ben), and owning everyone before they can even make it to your team mates. It isn't the most usefull in zombie mode though, unless your on a large tower, in that case it's very usefull, but you'll have to act fast or a load of Zombies will tear it down. The Engineer has an assult rifel. But he often would use a jetpack for getting around. But he is not to usefull and will often be found useless due to only really having is weak Assult Rifle. Thought in Zombie mode it shines as getting up tall buildings and protecting it self from Zombies. There have only been about 5 times i've been able to kill a Engineer as a Zombie due to it turning around noticing I'm charging at with full speed, and all he does is shoot at me for 1 second, and he owned me! And last, but not least, the Miner. This is the Zombie survival beast! He'll often be shooting you with his shotgun, and killing you in two or one hits. Or he'll just shoot you with deadly mining gun which is used to dig holes. He'll often be one of the last survivers in the Zombie round, only because he was hiding underground, often with some other person to protect him and wait for everyone two realise he was underground. There are also many different sort of rounds you can play in. Like Team Fortress 2 you got pleanty of different rounds to choose from. Only in Ace of Spades, there different. In Team Fortress 2, the fun in that was killing the others with the different classes. You know, blasting peoples guts out with the Heavy, blowing people up with the Demoman, burning people to crisp with the Pyro, sniping enemies as the Sniper and even backstabbing others as a Spy. As fun as that sounds (depending on your personallity), it doesn't mach up to Ace of Spades, you see in Ace of Spades you'll often be ACCTUALLY be doing your mission. And yes in Team Deathmach your goal is to kill as many players as you can on the other team, which is my favourite type of match. But in other missions such as Diamond Mine, you acctually try to get that diamond and get it back to your base. There are other missions such as Capture The Flag, Occupation, VIP, but the two rounds that stand out the most to me are Team Deathmatch and Zombie Mode. In Team Deathmatch your goal is simple as the title, kill as many as the other players on the enemy team, and the team with the most kills wins. And course the consept of making a structure such as a bridge, a sniping tower or simpily block by block is super usefull. And at the end of a match you get to see a picture of the acctual map, and a picture of what it is when you finnished, and it's fun to see the destruction and objects you placed on the map. On Zombie mode you must build your self protection in only a minute from the zombie, but you may be randomly picked to be a zombie and try and kill all the others, one a human has been killed it turns into a Zombie too, and there is no reversing it. The only way you will survive to the end is get in a group of people and defend yourselves. Zombies also have the power of running fast, very fast. Zombies can destroy up to 10 blocks at a time. The idea of a zombie is that it is a rufless killer who will do anything to get to you. It will smash walls to get to you, so kill Zombies who may be getting close to you fast. In the first 5 minutes of the round you won't often get attacked by a Zombie if your base was cleverly built in a safe place, but then there's more! The more zombies there are the more your going to get noticed, and when you and your team mates are all in the same place, all the other players (as Zombies) with demolish your base until the get there claws on you and you become one as well! That's something you need to think about too. Try and make your base on a large building other than a very thin one all they will thear it down from the bottom, like a chainsaw cutting a tree. In terms of Graphics and gameplay it's in median condition. The gameplay is fun and interesting, but will often be disruped by lagging (at the first 2 minutes of the game), bugs such as randomly not being able to move from a block for about 30 seconds, and just crashing because it lost connection from Steam for some reason. Other than that it's still incredibly fun. In terms of graphics, you get what you see! But the retro style graphics are similar to Minecraft's graphics, and it wouldn't have the same experiance with realistic grapincs.
So overall, I reccomend this to FPS fans, and if your new to MMOs, the this is a good game to start with. This is a game for those people that were playing Call of Duty and thinking 'Man! I could really use a structure here'. Or someone who's playing Minecraft and thinking 'Dude! I wish there were guns in this game and it didn't have such a dull feel to it'.
So I give this game a 7/10
Your more than likely to enjoy it and not getting annoyed by bugs, you'll love it!

You play as either a young Tom Cruise, or a 45 year old balding man, with a beer belly the size of Mars. I like to think you play as the 45 year old man. Within only a few hours, you'll be interesting characters, such as a 21-year old tsundere, with a raging drug and drinking problem, and almost 40 year old cougar, who constantly calls you Daddy! As we all know, you are in an amazing state of mind once you've had multiple drinks. Feel free to try this method out, on your next date!
Do you enjoy a bit more girl-on-girl action? Have no fear! The girls won't even blink as you switch from gender-to-gender, multiple times, giving them horrors directly from Hell, as your body shifts and shapes to fit another gender. It's no problem to them, no! Not in the least.
Do you enjoy puzzles? Maybe you just want to play some puzzles and avoid those (uh-oh) "naughty" pictures. You're probably asking, how to turn those off! Great question!
Moving on, you should remember that this game is basically Bejeweled, but just with more young women.
If you like controlling your mindless harem of young college students, an alien, a cougar, and a neko, buy HuniePop!

Source mod gone full retail. The Ship is a great premise: Find your target among the people on a cruise ship and take them out, while someone else is doing the same to hunt you down. Throw in a Sims style needs system so players can't camp, a weapon bounty system so players need to try out new weapons, and a lovely 1920's style atmosphere, and you *should* have a great game.
However, The Ship does show many problems, mostly when compared to it's mod predecessor. In the mod, there would be many civilians to confuse and work around to get to your target. In The Ship, you rarely see more than one or two civilians in total on these large cruise ships. Because of this, many games just turn into a deathmatch rather than a complex game of stalking and decieving. You can turn up the amount of civvies, but there's still a very small limit on that, and rarely multiplayer servers turn this config on.
The Ship is also very dated. The game hasn't been updated in many years, and the controls show it. Even once you get past that, there's still some very strange workarounds you can find on the levels. It just feels old, rather than classic or "old school". What's worse, the previous devs have been absorbed into Ubisoft, and the current publisher for The Ship, Blazing Griffin, can't secure the rights to modifiy the game's code (even after a failed Kickstarter campaign), so it's stuck like this for the forseeable future.
If you can gather together a group of friends who all understand the little things and problems with The Ship, you can enjoy it for a while, but it won't last forever. Grab it if it's on sale.

In The Ship, you rarely see more than one or two civilians in total on these large cruise ships. Because of this, many games just turn into a deathmatch rather than a complex game of stalking and decieving. You can turn up the amount of civvies, but there's still a very small limit on that, and rarely multiplayer servers turn this config on.
The Ship is also very dated. The game hasn't been updated in many years, and the controls show it. Even once you get past that, there's still some very strange workarounds you can find on the levels. It just feels old, rather than classic or "old school". What's worse, the previous devs have been absorbed into Ubisoft, and the current publisher for The Ship, Blazing Griffin, can't secure the rights to modifiy the game's code (even after a failed Kickstarter campaign), so it's stuck like this for the forseeable future.
If you can gather together a group of friends who all understand the little things and problems with The Ship, you can enjoy it for a while, but it won't last forever. Grab it if it's on sale.

Having finished Binary Domain I have to admit I now sort of get it why it was overlooked and underrated in certain circles. It's a rare example of a game that manages to transcend its, nowadays at least, by-the-numbers TPS approach by infusing with it actual soul and personality that will keep you going throughout. Not to say that interesting boss battles, good pacing with gameplay variation, and story twists don't help, but the final impression was one of genuine care put into the game's creation, even though the voice command system is incredibly lackluster and tacked on. As a sucker for cover shooters, this game had been on my radar for a while. Thanks to an Amazon sale I got to pick this up at a price point I couldn't resist. The verdict? Well this is a cover shooter so the action does get a bit stale at times and some of the QTE events may have well been insta-death since they happen with little warning. Overall great game. Highly recommended.

If you’re a sucker for very Japanese games, the name Yakuza Studio rings a bell. The developer team, associated with SEGA, has created the “Ryu ga Gotoku” series, known as Yakuza in the west.
East & West united: Gundam meets Blade Runner
No need to study an entire Yakuza encyclopedia this time: “Binary Domain” draws heavily from the western SciFi genre (most prominently: cyberpunk classic Blade Runner), making the squad-based shooter a more universally accessible affair. Similar to Ridley Scott’s neon-colored dystopia “Binary Domain” is set in a not-so-distant future. In the late 21st century technology has taken giant leaps, but of course, everything else is straight down the gutter: Global warming, rising sea levels, poverty… you name it, “Binary Domain” has it. With worldwide population significantly decimated, robots had to be used as the main labor force to build new cities, and they also came in handy as domestic servants or kids’ playmates. But the pro-robot-agenda has ceased since Japanese-made “Hollow Children” – almost indistinguishable from humans and potentially violent – kept appearing. The countermeasure? The “New Geneva Convention”: Prohibiting production and distribution of human-like robots. Needless to say, actually being a “Hollow Child” yourself – even without knowing it – hasn’t become the smartest idea since.
Heroes from Hollywood subs’ bench
As Dan Marshall you’re a member of the “Rust Crew”, an international task force that deals with violations of the “New Geneva Convention”. Dan is portrayed as your stereotypical, loudmouthed, hot-headed American as seen in countless Hollywood productions. If this is Team Yakuza’s potshot at one-dimensional American movie protagonists it turned out quite well. While the story touches upon rather serious issues (racism, xenophobia, human greed and megalomania), Dan and his allies don’t hesitate to frequently pull off cheesy one-liners at the most inappropriate time. With that “so-bad-it’s-good”-charm it captures the overall Hollywood (semi-)Blockbuster feel of the game.
Your mission in futuristic Tokyo is to localize and capture scientist Youji Amada, head of the Amada Corporation and persona non grata in terms of illegal production of “Hollow Children”.
Derivatively awesome
Familiar with cover-based action games like “Mass Effect” or “Gears of War”? Then “Binary Domain” does in fact feel like your standard fare. It doesn’t bring anything new to the table, save for the voice input feature. Recognizing six different languages you can use a mic to give your squad members basic commands. It’s nice having it just for the sake of it, but since the possibilities are very limited you’re just as good off sticking with keyboard inputs. Every now and then you’re prompted to react to what your team-mates are saying. We’re not speaking “Mass-Effect”-type consequences here, but depending on your choices your allies will behave more positively or negatively towards you.
Derivative as it might be – with its linear level design and the occasional QTE – “Binary Domain” happens to be an immersive experience. The production values are on par with AAA titles like “Mass Effect” or “Max Payne 3″ and the pacing is so well executed that it just feels like an interactive Hollywood action movie – which, depending on your taste, might be a good or bad thing. But, it’s perfectly evident that Team Yakuza’s ambition to create something huge is there, and that has to be acknowledged, whether you think the core gameplay is fun or not. Essentially you solely clear corridors of foes, watch a cutscene, repeat that process and eventually stumble upon a larger-than-life Mecha boss. But at least it seems that “Binary Domain” is perfectly aware of its limitations. It succeeds in presenting you the little that it has in the most possibly appealing way. Give “Binary Domain” a shot. It was my personal 2012 sleeper hit!

Mechanically, it isn't much more than a competent third-person cover-based shooter. The few unique elements it has don't significantly separate it from its peers, and it's most unique feature is not nearly as cool as the developers probably thought it was and is kind of broken—that feature being the voice integration. I'd recommend just turning it off and using the simpler and also flawed button-based command/response system.
The ideas incorporated into the story aren't particularly original but they're well presented and there there are some good bits of dialog mixed in with the awkward lines. Graphics boundaries aren't pushed, but there's a solid look to everything and some good animation. The boss encounters are neat, although somewhat marred by devolving into prolonged fights where you dump a few hundred thousand rounds of ammunition into their glowing weak spots. Sometimes friendly AI will walk into your line of fire and then get pissy with you about it, which slightly lowers their “trust level” with you.
I doubt anything about Binary Domain will blow your socks off, but the game has an odd charm to it and I definitely enjoyed playing it. If I had paid full price for it ($25 as of writing this) I would have felt content with my purchase, and at a discount it was a steal.

Star Trek Online is a game made by Cryptic Studios and Published by Perfect World Entertainment. The game had a very poor start, and was labelled as a 'dead MMO' a very long time ago. Since those dark days however, Star Trek Online has taken a miraculous turn for the better. It's as if someone got up from their depression in the developpers studio and said 'Let's kick some serious ***, people!'
Well, whatever the case may be? It worked. Star Trek Online is an absolutely 'amazing' game, with everything from brand new graphics, to hourly events, to monthly special events that do not simply throw new content at you, but actually introduces it through an event!
The game also has a huge amount of Roleplay potential, with the ability to enter the bridge of your own ship, and even, if you have Starfleet/Klingon standard ships, go into the rest of the ship, such as crew quarters, etc.
Star Trek Online, at first release, took place in 2409, 30 years after the events of the movie Star Trek: Nemesis. It largely follows the storyline of Star Fleet, but can also include the Klingon Empire(After rank 25 has been achieved). Since Legacy of Romulus has been released, you can also now play as a Romulan.
Gameplay:
Star Trek Online has two gameplay modes. It has ship control, and it has regular person control. Much of the combat used to, in the old terrible days, happen in space, and ground combat was an eye sore. Now, Ground combat is just as viable(albeit a bit harder) than space combat, and features everything from Melee to healing to ranged to ballistic artillery. There are more types of weapons than you care to think about; Rifles, snipers, miniguns, dual wielding pistols, swords, bat'leths, Vulcan lirpas, shotguns, grenades. And for each of those? There's a different style of damage; Phaser, Disruptor, Plasma, Antiproton, each of which look different. The choices in terms of weaponry are literally endless, you couldn't make enough characters to try them all! The same goes for ships, giving you everything from torpedoes to cannons to phasers to custom special weapons unlocked through events.
The gameplay of this game has gone from an F, to an A++.
Character Creator:
Yes, this thing needs its own subsection, deal with it XD
The game features 3 different classes, each of which have some specific strengths and weaknesses, but dont in any way limit you to a certain type of ship etc. Any class, can fly any ship, use any weapon, etc.
Tactical Officer(Red shirt): A strange mixture between DPS and Support, the Tactical officer lends a hand to his allies with buffs to damage and evasion, while also dishing out some impressive damage. They primarily fight ground combat with either melee, ranged, or grenades, and in space, they prefer small, agile escort fighters.
Science Officer(Blue Shirt): The primary source of physical healing and support in the game. They suffer in damage, but do healing and support where others cannot, such as Heal over Time and defense bonuses. They prefer to fly Science Vessels, or Carriers.
Engineering Officer(Yellow Shirt): The primary source of damage and shield healing in the game. They do a little bit of everything, and are profoundly Overpowered in the game at the moment. An engineer can lay down turrets or Mortar gunners, and can absolutely obliterate enemies with orbital strikes, grenades, mortars, sentry turrets, and an impressive affinity for melee weapons. They are also the primary tank of the game, taking impressive agro with their damage and having the strongest Shield healing capabilities in the game, keeping them alive while doing RIDICULOUS amounts of damage. Did I say their damage is crazy? They prefer to fly the large, hulking cruiser ships, nicknamed 'Space whales' due to their slow turn rate, but what they lack in maneuverability, they make up for in brute strength, and survivability.
As for races. There are more races in this game than I care to list. There is pretty much every single species ever to be featured in Star Trek, EVER. And if none of those appeal to you? Heck, MAKE YOUR OWN! Yeah! The character creator lets you custom design your own alien species! Wanna hail from the Gamma Quadrant? Never been seen before by Alpha Quadrant inhabitants? Not a problem! Just design it and write the lore for it!
What kinda ships are there, then? (Let me again repeat that EVERY CLASS above can actually fly ANY ship thrown at them, except they have their 'best choices' all the same.)
Escorts: The most iconic one being the USS Defiant(Deep Space Nine). Small, and very powerful damage dealers. They are the only type of ships that can fit Dual Heavy Cannons, some of the most serious weapons you've ever seen. They're tiny ships that can set a galaxy ablaze, blasting everything in front of them into nothingness. Though they're fragile, and will be easily overpowered if focused by enemy ships.
Science Vessels: The most Iconic being USS Voyager(Voyager). They're not too strong with their weapons, but they have a little ace in their sleeves called 'exotic damage'. Their primary weapon is their deflector dish, and they can conjure up all manner of strange phenomenons in the universe, from rifts to gravitational anomalies that rip ships to pieces. They might be the healers, and supporters in a firefight, but don't corner one and force it to fight back. You'll regret it.
Carriers: The largest of all the ships. These ships are a sort of sub-ship for Science Commanders to choose if their aim is to tank. The ship itself is no longer the primary source of damage, instead its allowed to focus entirely on defenses and shield power. Instead, they leave the damage to their arsenal of fighters. They dispath squadrons of tiny, very hard to hit fighter ships that can, in unison, utterly overwhelm a larger ship. Flying a carrier well takes skill, but once you have the control of the fighters down, you're a force to be reckoned with in a space war.
Cruisers: The most iconic one being USS Enterprise series. these are the massive, floating citadels of the galaxy. They sport crew sizes as big as small cities, and have the largest potential for tanking of any ship. Despite their affinity for survivability, they still have an impressive array of offensive weaponry, and can, if flown right, be a serious problem all by itself for the enemy. Nicknamed Space Whales.
Special Ships: These can only be unlocked by opening lockboxes, which cost real money, OR bought for very high prices in the in-game auction house. Some can also be unlocked by buying them with a special, hard to gain currency called Lobi Crystals.
Graphics: The graphics are a little bit hit or miss. In terms of their fuction, they are adequate, however they are by no means as good as other, new-age titles. Still, the graphics are impressive considering the hardships this game went through, and are still great eyecandy when floating around in space :3
Overall Score:
I'm gonna give this game 9.2/10. It is just doing too many things right to not deserve it. I would have preferred giving it 10/10, but the ONE draw back this game has, the MAJOR archilles heel of this title? It's free to play nature. The game gives you everything for free, that's true, 'except' for special ships, new outfits, and even some specific races, like Federation Klingons, or Caitian/Ferasan(Cat people for the furries <3 ) The game is, largely, a 'lockbox' hell game, and if you are not interested in that, and can ignore it? The game is at least a 9.8/10, ALMOST PERFECT, but not quite.
Do I recommend this game? Honey, there's no MMO out there which I can safely recommend more earnestly, than this one. If you like Star Trek, and MMOs? This is a game you absolutely have to play.

Since STEAM does not feature a "neutral" button for reviews I will have to explain in which circunstances I am recommending this game.
Worms Pinball is, obviously, a pinball simulator but totally themed with the (original) Worms universe. This game was developed in the late 90s, an era where pinball simulators were popular in computers and other game systems as a consequence of the significant computer graphics evolution to bring more "realistic" experiences. I remember to play the demo version of the game back in 1998 and enjoying the short experience.
Of course by being a pinball simulator this means there is nothing else to be expected so the game obeys to its name and purpose. People that are expecting the classical mechanism of Worms' games are being naive as this is a real spin-off.
So without big surprise, Worms Pinball is a game for casual and short gameplay. I can only recommend this game to people that are Worms and/or Pinball fans that are ok to kill around 30 minutes of time entertaining themselves. Because in a real scenario it is a game that you will get bored quickly. And people that are smart enough will NEVER pay full price for a near 20-year old simulator that doesn't offer more than what the name implies. Buy it for the cheapest possible if you are really interested in keeping it.

Cat Quest is a rather casual action/adventure RPG. I ended up completing the whole game, including all of the side quests and getting all of the equipment (though a certain bug required extra time to get a specific item). But even though I did all of that, I would say that the game probably should not be "Overwhelmingly Positive," which owes to Steam's inability to review in ways other than simply "Good or Bad." I do not think that the graphics or game's sense of humor should save itself from its bigger flaws.
The graphics for the game are pretty nice, though I'd say a majority of the world looks pretty similar in style until later on, with a few outskirts being drastically different than the rest, including some funny easter egg areas. The music and sound never gave me any issues (except for the cat "meow"-ing when hit in combat sometimes, which bothered me for some reason).
But I would say that the story and gameplay are the imbalanced parts of the game. The story, as a whole, is a little funny at times, but basically boils down to "Here's some main villain out of nowhere; follow him." And more than half of the side quests redirect to this main villain again, though it's usually towards the end of quest chains going "He is the reason this happened!" There are some places where the main storyline gets a little weird, and makes you think of where it will go... But by the end of the game, it sort of falls away and ends really quickly, like you just ran off of a cliff. Not much is resolved, and the interesting parts of the storyline remain as hidden references. My reaction to the end was "Huh? That's it?"
I would say that the side quests had more fun with their mini-stories than the main storyline itself did. There's a lot of humor in them, of course, with many puns and jokes. Some people might find it off-putting, but I enjoyed that aspect for the most part.
For the gameplay, however, it's a simple system. You gain experience and gold. You level up. You swing weapons, dodge, blast magic, and collect equipment. You run around for quests. (Actually, running back and forth across the map is probably most of your gameplay time until you unlock a new movement ability.) This is pretty much "Any RPG Experience Ever (TM)" in the simplest terms. The gameplay is action-oriented and you get to mostly explore as you want, so you're not forced following certain quests the whole time. You can find higher-leveled side quests and try them earlier on, for instance, like I did, instead of following early quests or the main storyline.
But the mechanics used for exploration and combat are the downside. If you play the game consistently without many breaks, you should probably find that the game is overly easy, becomes repetitive, and lacks repeatability. If you're really bad at dodging the enemies, then you might find it difficult for some reason. There are maybe between 20 to 30 types of enemies in the game, but there's only about 6 ways the enemies can attack you. Each enemy only follows similar attack sets for the most part, with slightly altered ranges and directions. Thus, the combat boils down to "Dodge this way, attack, wait, dodge that way, attack, wait" ad infinitum.
Most of the equipment in the game is unnecessary, and you will probably ignore a lot of what you come across. Even the spells you acquire (while some are useful in certain corridors) for the most part are not needed. In fact, you can probably complete the game with just the Fire spell you unlock near the very beginning. While the quest stories are a little fun, all of them pretty much resolve with clearing out a dungeon or destroying a group of enemies on the overworld, hence repetitive combat is the main key point.
About the only way for the game to change "difficulty" is to buff enemies, debuff equipment, or for you to fight high-level things as a weakling. All of these methods are essentially artificial difficulty and do not require any extra strategy or change in gameplay, for the most part, and only would make the game more grind-like. Ironically, the developers are releasing "Mew Game" as a New Game Plus format that has modifiers to do the above, such as prevent usage of armor or weapons, or limit yourself to Level 1 for the whole game. It's quite ridiculous actually, after I tested around with it a bit. I am unsure why some people would enjoy it, considering all it does is make a battle take longer even though you're still performing the exact same actions you did the first time around.
As said earlier, I think a good amount of positive reviews simply think humor and charm cover for the game's rating, while I think it definitely has some big design issues.

I've played Cat Quest for 15 hours or so and I must say I immensely enjoyed it. Did not expect the game to be as fun as it actually is, I foresaw a shallow indie RPG and got something really fun with a lot of charm! Combat is engaging, progression is quite complex and the story/atomosphere/art style are all amazing.
Some design input:
At the very beginning when I started playing and was about 1 hour into the game, I was utterly immersed and then... I started doing all the side quests. What I found vaguely irritating (less so at the later stages of the game due to certain gameplay mechanics) was that each hub had a questline with progressively higher level requirements. This meant that you could not complete storyline A and then move onto the next hub with a different questline.
From my point of view, this has two major disadvantages: first of all, I'd much rather experience one story as a whole and complete it without initiating another narratives at the same time. It just feels disruptive when you're doing multiple questlines concurrently and sometimes one might actually forget what the quest he/she was on is about. Secondly, you have to constantly move between different hubs which can get quite tedious and boring and also it juts artificially lengthens the game which is not a good thing in my opinion.
I just think that the player experience would be much better if the hubs were designed in a somewhat different manner:
instead of having Hub A with quests for levels 1, 4, 9 > Hub B with 2, 5, 10 > Hub C with 3, 6, 13 the dispersion should look something more like the following: Hub A with 1, 2, 3 > Hub B with 4, 6, 7 > Hub C with 5, 8, 9.
Anomalies in level requirement curve should be much rarer.
​
Of course this is purely subjective and someone might not prefer the latter, just my two cents.
The game is deceptively simple and has a lot of depth behind it which I really love. With that being said, while I really appreciate any types of 'secrets' if you will in all kinds of games (huge fan of zelda and the souls series) and a design philosophy which doesn't give everything to the player on a silver platter, some of the 'secrets' that were put in Cat Quest might be game breaking to a certain degree.
To give you some examples, dungeons such as the founder cave or the hidden level 99 cave can be exploited to easily farm gold and experience with A MUCH HIGHER efficiency than any other method in the game. When you introduce such areas, monsters there should probably not be able to respawn after being killed.
That way discovering these areas will still feel rewarding but consequently players won't be able to exploit them and at the same time will avoid ruining the game for themselves (other content becomes trivial after completing the said dungeons multiple times and farming the same spot repeatedly is really not fun).
The spell/ability system is somewhat luckluster imo or rather the foundation for it is good but the spells themselves need some tweaking/balancing. The very first one you get (the AoE circle) along with +% DMG that you get later on are clearly the best choices and shun other potential fun builds.
Also, Willpower and Faith both need a major nerf since they render all the other much cooler looking equipment useless.  ^^ Lets us assume that you can only get Faith and Willpower at the very end of the game without making other content trivial. These items still outshine all the others though. Even then, that should not be the case in my opinion. I think it's much more interesting if you have a lot of varied gear and every single set is somewhat better in a different area.
The game is quite short which is fine given its pricing but more importantly since I think it could get monotonous if it were a lengthy title. As I have already said, the combat is engaging and fun BUT you're basically doing the same thing over and over again. What this game could use is some additional minor twists in gameplay from time to time, perhaps logical puzzles of some sort that require you to interact with environment in a certain pattern?
Cat Quest has a lot of potential I think and while it is already an amazing game, in my humble opinion it could benefit a lot from replayable 'end game' content. I wonder if the developers thought about future systems to implement? How about something along the lines of greater rifts as seen in Diablo.
I'd suggest adding procedurally generated dungeons with randomized monsters that get progressively harder and scale endlessly. You could call them 'dragonblood challenges', an ancient arena of sorts that the past dragonblood used to test their might. :)
You could even add an in-game leaderboard of some kind that would allow the players to compare their dragonblood challenge scores though I suppose that might be slightly trickier to implement.

An entertaining co-op game, much in the style of the Left 4 Dead series, with common enemies, hordes, and specials that do much the same kind of thing.  But this game is so much more than a L4D clone.  It shifts the emphasis more to melee (for most characters - though all characters can still utilize quite decent ranged attacks), and it delves at least partially into the lore of the Olde Worlde of Warhammer, before whatever they've done to it these days.
The players get a choice of 5 characters, with 4 distinct flavours, (unfortunately the Dwarf and the Soldier play rather similar and have very similar equipment options with nothing being truly unique among them).  And what is great other than the unique style and feel of the characters and the various equipment options you can equip them with - each charcter gets 3+ melee and 3+ ranged options, is the banter and repartee between them.  This dialogue gives genuine touches of humour and characterisation to what otherwise would just be the toon that you play, and it helps to really craft their personalities - yes, again like L4D.
The magic of the Bright Wizard is nice, and whilst powerful, the inbuilt kryptonite of her power is her power itself, and a careless player might soon find that they are taking more damage from their own spells than that of the ratmen.
Friendly fire exists in this game, but only on higher difficulties and only with ranged and AoE attacks.  And whilst you feel it, it is nothing compared to the battering the enemy can deliver to you, allowing for you to sometimes be indiscriminate in the pursuit of achieving victory.  So players that dislike FF shouldn't feel turned off by the fact that it exists, as it is rarely the reason for failure.
There is a loose campaign that ties each of the missions together,  and 2 lots of DLC opening up 3 new maps each.  And kudos to the developers for the way that they've handled the DLC.  If you don't have it, all that stops you doing is hosting a game on one of those maps, and from accepting Contracts from the Bounty Board for those maps.  Indeed, a player without the DLC can still play on those maps if someone who has purchased it, hosts the game and they join.  Each DLC pack also has 2 new weapons.  The Witch Hunter gets 2 and the Elf and Dwarf both get 1.  It would have been nice had the Dwarf's gone to the Wizard as a melee option - but perhaps in the future.
As to the faults of the game, yes it's not perfect.  The Bots are a new kind of stupid.  They make the L4D bots look like intellectuals.  There is no collision detection, so enemies can move through you, attacking as they do, and you have little recourse when you can't see them.  It is easy to get caught up on the smallest obstacle at times also and the game does crash probably more than i'd like - though this has been greatly improved in the last update.  The randomness of the Loot allocation can be frustrating at times, especially early on, though nowadays it's far easier to get good loot and lots of gems to improve them with a very basic "crafting" system, though it still takes some getting used too, and a lot of luck to get the exact item - especially trinkets, that you want.
Overall, it's a very fun game to play - especially with friends, and all the more challenging when you try to carry bots through the missions.
4/5

The Evil Within is the latest from Shinji Mikami, who helped produce, direct & design a few games you might have heard of. Titles like Resident Evil, Dino Crisis, Phoenix Wright and more. The Evil Within is a "survival horror" in the RE vein and it's a doozy. You play a police detective who is dispatched to an asylum only to find himself transported to a surreal world full of creatures, ghosts and traps. Any more than that and I'd be spoiling the story but you start to learn more about everything on the way through journals, newspapers and cutscenes.   One thing The Evil Within gets cold is the atmosphere. There's definitely a good sense of dread (especially early on) here.  The creatures here can be snuck up but if they see you, it's a problem. That problem is made worse that ammunition is not very generous in this game. You will desperately look around searching every nook and cranny for green gel (to help level you up), ammo & matches. I've never played a game where I was happy just to find two bullets. Death will come quickly and offten as well. I haven't died this many times since I played Hotline Miami. Well over 60 deaths in my first (and probably only) playthrough. I will warn you this game is not a very good port. I ran into many crashes and some annoying freezes that came at the worst times possible. Overall though I'd recommend The Evil Within. If you like games like this go for it. $8.49 during the sale for everything is well worth it. If you don't care for difficult games, have much patience or don't like dying over & over this might not be the game for you.

What happens when a self-centred painter obsessed with perfection and beauty loses the ability to create great works after a tragic event? Well, first he neglects his family and goes batsh*t insane. Then, the result is Layers of Fear - a haunting first-person trip through the crumbling mansion and even more crumbling mind of the nameless protagonist artist. He wants to create that perfect painting for reasons you'll have to discover by playing it but many things are holding him back. The final painting's look will be down to you and how you choose to play.
The game is packed full of scares. They want to scare the absolute crap out of you and on occasions, the game does it spectacularly and in ways I have never seen in a video game. That said, the format does become a little predictable and you begin to expect scenery changes, doors appearing/disappearing and paintings altering etc. This neutralises some jump scare events later on but it does not mar the game as a whole though. The scares stay fresh and varied enough to continue catching you out right to the end. To say the whole game is just a long series of jump scares would not be right though because it isn't. The whole thing is a very trippy, atmospheric experience and the story, if you take the time to uncover it all, is very compelling. I always had that shaky feeling of being unsettled pretty much throughout my whole play through. Sometimes having to even stop and freeze through fear of what I might see beyond the next door.
It isn't that long of a game. A careful and thorough first play through should take between 4-5 hours but in that game time, a lot will happen and a lot will scare you. The level of detail is very impressive, I'd like to know if the paintings in the game were created just for the game or if the developers took them from ones that actually exist in the real world. Some of them boast some truly disturbing imagery!
The game also plays on a popular survival horror mechanic. Different endings can be unlocked according to how you play the game. Something seasoned horror gamers should be very familiar with by now. This is always good. It adds replay ability and also gives you more than one possible story.
I like Layers Of Fear and would definitely recommend it as a neat little interim game to play between longer term gaming committments. Play at night though and with headphones. The scares just won't hit home if you're sitting in a sunny room. If you're still unsure, then maybe get it during a Steam sale to save a few pennies.

Binary Domain is a game I honestly stopped playing out of frustration with its controls and the amount of enemies that can stagger and stun lock you, forcing cheap and frustrating deaths.
My girlfriend picked it back up in my stead, and over a couple more nights with it, we finished it up and the both of us had about the same reaction.
"Well...this surely is another one of these!"
The game may as well be the Japanese take on Gears of War, only with a bit more of a lighthearted tone and cheesy anime-style sci-fi setting. The characters were certainly a lot more fun than the chunky Dudebros in Gears, but the story itself is about on par with Bionic Commando 2009's ridiculous plot twists. It may be crazy and totally nuts, but I felt that the game wanted me to take it seriously, rather than looking at these kinds of games and stories in some kinda funhouse mirror.
The high point of the game are its boss encounters, which are charmingly modeled after old-school boss fights in which the goal is to shoot the core. These setpieces (though at times frustrating) are the welcome break between all the unimpressive corridor shooting and extraneous RPG elements.
If you want some decent'ish cover-based shooting and a schlocky and fun set of voiced and written characters, you got it. Binary Domain is competent enough to be entertaining for a bit, but it's designed by folks who still don't quite understand why the more renowned entries in this genre work.

Maybe not a critics choice, but overall a great experience that only people who played and finish it will recommend. It feels like a big theme for games in 2012 was "Let's make the player feel bad for what they do." Spec Ops definitely does it, and a lot of the other games also had various shades of it. In this context, Binary Domain was the perfect refresher. Like Saints Row, this is a game that just wants you to have fun. You're gunna go in, shoot robots to bits for 9 hours, and you aren't going to get guilt tripped into feeling like a horrible person at the end.
I haven't played many of these "Third person cover based shooters" that seem so popular these days, but Binary Domain easily feels the best so far. Getting into cover is a snap, shifting cover is also quick and easy, and the game mixes it up with enough moments where you'll want to run and strafe around slower enemies to keep things fresh. The shooting also feels incredibly satisfying as well, the robots you shoot blow up real nice, and there are various elements like blowing their legs off to send them into a crawl, or decapitating them to cause them to go haywire and shoot at their companions. The level of destruction in this game simply wouldn't work with human enemies, but since you're fighting robots, who cares! Shoot em all!
The game also has a ton of unique boss fights, the occasional vehicle sequence, and fairly interesting story. It keeps these things all in nice balance, moving briskly from one thing to the next. It's too bad this game wasn't called Contra, it would've sold a lot better.
If there's one disappointment I had with the game, it's that the story landed with kind of a thud. It has some pretty heavy moments regarding self-aware robots, and if that counts as life, and then takes a hard line kill-em-all stance, which just felt crazy to me. But maybe that's OK, because I sure didn't want to game to start making me question what I was doing Spec Ops style, but it still felt weird for the game to go there, then back off entirely.

First off, I loved the first game a lot, it was a breath of fresh air, very difficult but still fair (in the sense that you're given a fighting chance), great art style, great soundtrack and a story that was a tad forgettable. I hate to be a sequel hater, but in my opinion Hotline Miami 2, while still a good game, doesn't live up to its predecessor. Here's why:
Difficulty: by far the biggest problem. While both Hotline Miami games are "pull your hair out" difficult, Hotline Miami 2 is the kind of cheap, unfair difficulty that did not plague the first game as much (there were a few instances, but not every level). By far the most common thing (and many reviewers pointed this out) is getting shot from halfway across the map. Part of this problem is that the maps are too big. If the free look had a longer reach (which was a special mask in the first one, but I'll get to that), this wouldn't be a problem, but I can't count the times I knew I didn't clear a level and I got blasted dead by some guy through four windows from the opposite side of the map. Difficult I have no problem with, I know when I messed up and I know what to correct on my next attempt.
Less open, free gameplay: while Hotline Miami had a roster of masks (that weren't all useful, but still), here you have a few characters that each have their own playstyle. In a way, this is good because it forces you to try different things, different ways of causing mayhem, but I think it limits your freedom in how to complete a level by doing so. For example, the Soldier character MUST wield a weapon, and has a non-throwable knife as a sidearm. As someone who relied heavily on melee, this is a nightmare and it would be cool if you had a "vanilla" choice as well. That way, you could remedy some shortcomings of the level design (for example, use the giraffe mask to lengthen the reach of free look).
Story...?: the first game didn't have much of a story, but to be fair, it didn't try to. This game attempts something akin to a story and while some elemenst are amusing, I ended up not caring for it because it lacks any particularly enthralling characters or plot lines, and honestly, it's a bit of a mess. It's not a bad thing, I just think it was a bit tacked on.
Although subjective, I think the soundtrack in this game is still a notch better (more mature, maybe) than the first game's offering (and that was already amazing, so that's saying something).
Overall, if you're not a fan of this series, this one won't win you over. It's a good entry, but it has its fair share of problems; I'd recommend the first game more than this one, but if you bought it in a bundle, it's still worth playing through.

text: Turn Clue into a first-person shooter on 1920's era luxury liners, sprinkle in bits of The Sims, and you've got The Ship. Instead of having to uncover a killer, The Ship makes you the killer. To be more specific and familiar to the gaming audience, The Ship is a very polished and creative take on the Assassin's Creed Multiplayer experience (but also keep in mind that this game came before the Assassin's Creed Multiplayer genre was released)....where the main gameplay mechanic revolves around finding your target, called your quarry, and breaking their face as stealthily as possible. To do so, there are plenty of lethal weapons and objects to wield, and even some environmental traps that you will find yourself potentially avoiding. To add flavor, everyone else on each map has a quarry as well. While pursuing your own target, you'll need to stay alert and attempt to spot the passenger readying a knife for your back. The Sims element of the game, quells upon your daily needs to survive (food, drinks, toilet, sleep, etc). The 'character's needs' element makes for a deeper gameplay experience, as your character is vulnerable to attack while you're downing a bag of chips or snoring on a bed. And it is surely funny when your friend murders you on the toilet. The Ship is one of very few games that brings a large amount of enjoyment to my friends and I. Built on Valve's Souce engine, a majority of gamers can experience a $20 title with basically 4 copies to gift away. A little too much? Ask four of your friends for $4 each, and your all set! Overall, The Ship is a very innovative, satisfying and humorous experience that a bunch of 5 friends can't pass up. "Let us set sail!."

Star Trek Online is a game made by Cryptic Studios and Published by Perfect World Entertainment. The game had a very poor start, and was labelled as a 'dead MMO' a very long time ago. Since those dark days however, Star Trek Online has taken a miraculous turn for the better. It's as if someone got up from their depression in the developpers studio and said 'Let's kick some serious ***, people!'
Well, whatever the case may be? It worked. Star Trek Online is an absolutely 'amazing' game, with everything from brand new graphics, to hourly events, to monthly special events that do not simply throw new content at you, but actually introduces it through an event!
The game also has a huge amount of Roleplay potential, with the ability to enter the bridge of your own ship, and even, if you have Starfleet/Klingon standard ships, go into the rest of the ship, such as crew quarters, etc.
Star Trek Online, at first release, took place in 2409, 30 years after the events of the movie Star Trek: Nemesis. It largely follows the storyline of Star Fleet, but can also include the Klingon Empire(After rank 25 has been achieved). Since Legacy of Romulus has been released, you can also now play as a Romulan.
Gameplay:
Star Trek Online has two gameplay modes. It has ship control, and it has regular person control. Much of the combat used to, in the old terrible days, happen in space, and ground combat was an eye sore. Now, Ground combat is just as viable(albeit a bit harder) than space combat, and features everything from Melee to healing to ranged to ballistic artillery. There are more types of weapons than you care to think about; Rifles, snipers, miniguns, dual wielding pistols, swords, bat'leths, Vulcan lirpas, shotguns, grenades. And for each of those? There's a different style of damage; Phaser, Disruptor, Plasma, Antiproton, each of which look different. The choices in terms of weaponry are literally endless, you couldn't make enough characters to try them all! The same goes for ships, giving you everything from torpedoes to cannons to phasers to custom special weapons unlocked through events.
The gameplay of this game has gone from an F, to an A++.
Character Creator:
Yes, this thing needs its own subsection, deal with it XD
The game features 3 different classes, each of which have some specific strengths and weaknesses, but dont in any way limit you to a certain type of ship etc. Any class, can fly any ship, use any weapon, etc.
Tactical Officer(Red shirt): A strange mixture between DPS and Support, the Tactical officer lends a hand to his allies with buffs to damage and evasion, while also dishing out some impressive damage. They primarily fight ground combat with either melee, ranged, or grenades, and in space, they prefer small, agile escort fighters.
Science Officer(Blue Shirt): The primary source of physical healing and support in the game. They suffer in damage, but do healing and support where others cannot, such as Heal over Time and defense bonuses. They prefer to fly Science Vessels, or Carriers.
Engineering Officer(Yellow Shirt): The primary source of damage and shield healing in the game. They do a little bit of everything, and are profoundly Overpowered in the game at the moment. An engineer can lay down turrets or Mortar gunners, and can absolutely obliterate enemies with orbital strikes, grenades, mortars, sentry turrets, and an impressive affinity for melee weapons. They are also the primary tank of the game, taking impressive agro with their damage and having the strongest Shield healing capabilities in the game, keeping them alive while doing RIDICULOUS amounts of damage. Did I say their damage is crazy? They prefer to fly the large, hulking cruiser ships, nicknamed 'Space whales' due to their slow turn rate, but what they lack in maneuverability, they make up for in brute strength, and survivability.
As for races. There are more races in this game than I care to list. There is pretty much every single species ever to be featured in Star Trek, EVER. And if none of those appeal to you? Heck, MAKE YOUR OWN! Yeah! The character creator lets you custom design your own alien species! Wanna hail from the Gamma Quadrant? Never been seen before by Alpha Quadrant inhabitants? Not a problem! Just design it and write the lore for it!
What kinda ships are there, then? (Let me again repeat that EVERY CLASS above can actually fly ANY ship thrown at them, except they have their 'best choices' all the same.)
Escorts: The most iconic one being the USS Defiant(Deep Space Nine). Small, and very powerful damage dealers. They are the only type of ships that can fit Dual Heavy Cannons, some of the most serious weapons you've ever seen. They're tiny ships that can set a galaxy ablaze, blasting everything in front of them into nothingness. Though they're fragile, and will be easily overpowered if focused by enemy ships.
Science Vessels: The most Iconic being USS Voyager(Voyager). They're not too strong with their weapons, but they have a little ace in their sleeves called 'exotic damage'. Their primary weapon is their deflector dish, and they can conjure up all manner of strange phenomenons in the universe, from rifts to gravitational anomalies that rip ships to pieces. They might be the healers, and supporters in a firefight, but don't corner one and force it to fight back. You'll regret it.
Carriers: The largest of all the ships. These ships are a sort of sub-ship for Science Commanders to choose if their aim is to tank. The ship itself is no longer the primary source of damage, instead its allowed to focus entirely on defenses and shield power. Instead, they leave the damage to their arsenal of fighters. They dispath squadrons of tiny, very hard to hit fighter ships that can, in unison, utterly overwhelm a larger ship. Flying a carrier well takes skill, but once you have the control of the fighters down, you're a force to be reckoned with in a space war.
Cruisers: The most iconic one being USS Enterprise series. these are the massive, floating citadels of the galaxy. They sport crew sizes as big as small cities, and have the largest potential for tanking of any ship. Despite their affinity for survivability, they still have an impressive array of offensive weaponry, and can, if flown right, be a serious problem all by itself for the enemy. Nicknamed Space Whales.
Special Ships: These can only be unlocked by opening lockboxes, which cost real money, OR bought for very high prices in the in-game auction house. Some can also be unlocked by buying them with a special, hard to gain currency called Lobi Crystals.
Graphics: The graphics are a little bit hit or miss. In terms of their fuction, they are adequate, however they are by no means as good as other, new-age titles. Still, the graphics are impressive considering the hardships this game went through, and are still great eyecandy when floating around in space :3
Overall Score:

An entertaining co-op game, much in the style of the Left 4 Dead series, with common enemies, hordes, and specials that do much the same kind of thing.  But this game is so much more than a L4D clone.  It shifts the emphasis more to melee (for most characters - though all characters can still utilize quite decent ranged attacks), and it delves at least partially into the lore of the Olde Worlde of Warhammer, before whatever they've done to it these days.
The players get a choice of 5 characters, with 4 distinct flavours, (unfortunately the Dwarf and the Soldier play rather similar and have very similar equipment options with nothing being truly unique among them).  And what is great other than the unique style and feel of the characters and the various equipment options you can equip them with - each charcter gets 3+ melee and 3+ ranged options, is the banter and repartee between them.  This dialogue gives genuine touches of humour and characterisation to what otherwise would just be the toon that you play, and it helps to really craft their personalities - yes, again like L4D.
The magic of the Bright Wizard is nice, and whilst powerful, the inbuilt kryptonite of her power is her power itself, and a careless player might soon find that they are taking more damage from their own spells than that of the ratmen.
Friendly fire exists in this game, but only on higher difficulties and only with ranged and AoE attacks.  And whilst you feel it, it is nothing compared to the battering the enemy can deliver to you, allowing for you to sometimes be indiscriminate in the pursuit of achieving victory.  So players that dislike FF shouldn't feel turned off by the fact that it exists, as it is rarely the reason for failure.
There is a loose campaign that ties each of the missions together,  and 2 lots of DLC opening up 3 new maps each.  And kudos to the developers for the way that they've handled the DLC.  If you don't have it, all that stops you doing is hosting a game on one of those maps, and from accepting Contracts from the Bounty Board for those maps.  Indeed, a player without the DLC can still play on those maps if someone who has purchased it, hosts the game and they join.  Each DLC pack also has 2 new weapons.  The Witch Hunter gets 2 and the Elf and Dwarf both get 1.  It would have been nice had the Dwarf's gone to the Wizard as a melee option - but perhaps in the future.
As to the faults of the game, yes it's not perfect.  The Bots are a new kind of stupid.  They make the L4D bots look like intellectuals.  There is no collision detection, so enemies can move through you, attacking as they do, and you have little recourse when you can't see them.  It is easy to get caught up on the smallest obstacle at times also and the game does crash probably more than i'd like - though this has been greatly improved in the last update.  The randomness of the Loot allocation can be frustrating at times, especially early on, though nowadays it's far easier to get good loot and lots of gems to improve them with a very basic "crafting" system, though it still takes some getting used too, and a lot of luck to get the exact item - especially trinkets, that you want.
Overall, it's a very fun game to play - especially with friends, and all the more challenging when you try to carry bots through the missions.

This review is from the standpoint of someone who hasn't played any other Warhammer game; and that is a compliment. Vermintide on the surface seems like a copy of Left 4 Dead zombie horde co-op, and you wouldn't be wrong. It has many of it's aspect inspired by L4D, but it takes it's aspects and improves on them and makes it a game of it's own. The lore and fantasy in Vermintide is canon with the Warhammer universe, while also keeping it understandable or simple so new player, like myself, arn't confused. Not to mention it does have it's loading screens tell you a little lore, such as the character backgrounds, Dwarven language, and info on setting and enemy. Gameplay is really unique, where melee weapons are good for cutting down and blocking is needed to survive hits. Most ranged weapons have finite ammo, and have a good fealing of fantasy weapons and old timey weapons. If since put in many hours to this game; for what L4D lacks is reason to come back and keep going. Vermintide has a level system to unlock some weapons, and a loot system helps you customize weapons, trinkets, and best of all: HATS! This is a must buy, and your friends should also get it too for a full group.

I wrote and earlier review for Ratz Instagib, but I felt it was too praising. This review is not gonna be purely about how utterly fantastic this game is.
Ratz Instagib is a simple FPS. You are a rat, with a railgun. The railgun fires shots with no travel time that insta-kill no matter where you hit. You also have a secondary fire that acts like a rocket jump and launches you away from whatever surface you fire it on. You can also unlock cosmetics and their is a rating system.
But Ratz Instagib isn't that simple. Other than rocket jumping, you can bunny hop for mobility and the main key to this game IS mobility. Trying to hit a fast moving Rat across the room with an extremely precise railgun is both hard and rewarding. The gameplay is simple, but it certainly ain't easy.
The rating system in Ratz Instagib is pretty much cosmetic. Matchmaking puts everyone in one big pool regardless of rating. This means as a new player, you will fail a lot and you will fail for a long time. As of the time of me writing this, I'm lucky to get 5 kills in a game where the limit is 30.
Not only is it hard to win, it can be hard to even find a match to play in. Since the game is in early acess, new players are rare especially considering the hefty price tag. And as mentioned above, even if you do find a match you have a good chance of finding someone twenty times better than you. This problem with a lack of games is likely due to the $9 price tag. Nine dollars is just too much for only a handful of maps and only a few unlockable cosmetics (tho the "wheel of hats" sure is addicting). I'm sure Ratz would be only greater with a lower price tag.
But despite the problems with Ratz Instagib, the game is awesome. And if you buy it, you'll be one more person in the queue and the developer will have 9 more dollars to make this awesome game just more awesome. And Ratz's huge issues will be steamrolled out over time as more players come in, hopefully enough to warrant better matchmaking. So yeah, I think you should buy Ratz Instagib (especially if you snag it for less) because of its simple yet totally skill based gameplay that is totally worth all nine dollars.

I really want to like this game but I just can't.
It's obvious the creators put a lot of time and effort into crafting the experience, but it's all so cliched it's impossible to play for very long without getting bored and rolling your eyes. Seriously, you could play "horror cliche Bingo" with this game. A haunted mansion, shadowy veiled crying women, creepy dolls, echoing children's laughter, the protagonist's "terrible secret" -- there's nothing in this game you haven't seen many times before.
And it's so SLOW that you find yourself mentally hurrying it along and groaning when it traps you in a room yet again only to open the door after yet another jump scare. The entire game basically boils down to trying doors and walking through the ones that open. You walk through a door, are shown some creepy but cliched things, the sequence ends, you try all the doors until one opens, rinse and repeat. Occasionally the game forces you to look for a key or solve a simple puzzle.
I liked the tricks they pull with perspective and the way things rearrange when you're not looking. It's cool how you can turn around and the room is suddenly totally different. But I found myself wishing it was in a more original setting rather than the same old haunted mansion we've seen a thousand times before, starring the same old crazy, guilt-ridden protagonist with memory problems.
If you liked horror walking simulators like Amnesia 2, you'll like this. If you want a bit more excitement and originality from your gaming experience, avoid this one.

I think most of us thought the PT demo looked pretty cool and were disappointed when the game was cancelled, so making a game based on that concept seems like a good idea. But imagine that what you got was just more of that thing, about 5 more hours of the same. That is not to say that this game is incomplete or barebones, but it does not stray far beyond its basic concept.
The main attraction is the art. The rooms you explore look really good and the crazy stuff is properly crazy looking. Sound effects are good too. The story itself is just ok. It is rather obvious right from the beginning. I suppose the game is about you exploring the layers of your character's insanity, but in essense you are just collecting items like in Gone Home and looking at vagely meanimngful weird stuff happening around you. The ending was a bit disappointing, though I am not sure what else they could have done with the material at hand. The "scary stuff" is what you have already accustomed to see in the modern horror movies: jump scares, sudden things moving, etc. After a while, your body gets accustomed and even the jump scares were not startling.
This game is about walking through dark eye candy and that makes it worth it.

Note, I didn't buy this at full price, I spent 10$ for it when it was in early access. But I have played the whole thing now after they released the full version
Layers of Fear tells a cliche story, but it tells it very well. Bear in mind however, this game is VERY dark, and I'm not talking about brightness settings. Some themes in this game can be very disturbing. Layers of Fear is incredibly unpredictable and because everything just comes together so nicely, you're constantly on alert; I have yet to come across a game that does that so smoothly and efficiently as this one. You're in for one hell of a ride if you get this game. I would definitely recommend this game to horror fans. It's a must play. The whole game plays like you are walking through a haunted house, and it is GREAT. Every time you walk into a new room, you never know what to expect.
10/10 I recommend this to all horror game collectors

My favorite game of 2014 and one of the best Survival/Action Horror games I've ever played! It's also a VERY contentious game, with people either loving it like myself or hating it like it's the plague. This makes it a tough game to recommend in the senes that I can cite games that I love: Resident Evil 4 and Dead Space for example. I can say, "if you like either or both of those games you will also likely love this game too!". The problem is that many of the people that hate this game will also cite those games and how Evil Within fails to live up to them. Instead I will try to list elements that I loved.
Pros:
-The game does not suffer fools gladly and it does not hold your hand. You learn by your mistakes, potentially dying over and over in a single location.
-Supplies are often very limited, and in my first playthrough it was common to have enough ammo that I could count it on a single hand.
-The story requires the player to pay close attention to figure out. It reminds me a bit of Lost in the sense the forums were flooded with fan theories and ideas. I also found the characters to be fairly likable. Sebastien is a bit of a blank slate but I actually like when the protagonist allows you to project a bit of yourself on them. This especially helps in a horror title to draw you in.
-The game has a great sense of tension. I found it to be a scarier/tenser experience than Resident Evil 4, but found it less scary than Dead Space.
-Wonderful gore. Perhaps a bit of a childish thing to point out, but this IS a horror title. I've never seen such glorious headshots in a game. Like hitting a ripe melon with a sledgehammer.
Negatives:
-At release the game had massive borders on the top and bottom, the framerate was locked at 30 FPS and the game had some severe performance issues. All of these issues were patched, but it gave a very bad first impression as a sloppy console port.
-The game can, at times, simply be janky. An example was when I was standing on one side of a fence. I took a melee swing at an enemy and my arm passed through his body. The enemy then swung at me and hit me through the fence. Either allow both of us to swing through the fence, game, or neither of us!
-The game has some RPG like mechanics for shooting. I actually don't mind this. If you've played Deus Ex or Alpha Protocol you know what I'm talking about. You can aim at an enemy, dead on and still miss. Not because of a glitch, but because until you rank up certain skills your character will be a terrible shot. This heightens the tension and encourages you to get up close and personal to nullify your poor accuracy but it may also enrage gamers who are more used to playing standard third or first person shooters where you can actually hit what you are aiming at from the very start.
-The early game is pretty slow and linear. It doesn't really pick up until chapter 3. Again, this gives poor first impressions.
As you can see, some of those negatives may be huge turn-offs... but I found the game absolutely thrilling and intriguing...  a flawed gem. Try the demo out to see how it runs on your computer, maybe watch some youtube reviews and give the game a chance!

So here in lies the rub. Management is a serious part of this game. Sure you can take over some of the people to do specific things and I like that, in as much as it is pretty neat. Having read more of the reviews I’ve realized something. This game doesn’t allow for more specific management of items. You can’t tell hunters to not gather furs or villagers where to and not to store things. I know A.I. hasn’t been perfected yet, but some of these features should be there. It hurts more now that Forest Village has been released out of Early Access. In playing I’ve not noticed this as much, but if I look at how I’ve been building, every little area is its own independent city just sitting next to each other because of the lack of better management A.I.. It makes the game a bit more of a challenge. “What do you mean there’s no flour? There’s 4k of it in that storage facility!” Sure you can carry over 16 or so at a time with taking over individual people, but let’s be honest: that’s ridiculous. More to the point, it is still a good and fun game that I’ll keep playing and building small cities right next to each other and pretending that it’s a thriving metropolis, but somethings could be better.
Full Review:
So here we have a “… blatant rip off of Banished. I can’t believe this is legal.” game that is currently getting mixed reviews on Steam. Is this accurate? Does that make the game any less of a thing? I’ll put this on the table for you readers: I haven’t played Banished. I’ve had it on my wish list for a while, but I haven’t got around to pushing the button. Life is Feudel: Forest Village does look similar and I got a chance to run around and make a village myself. I can’t say whether or not it’s a copy of Banished as much as WoW is ripping off Warhammer. It’s in a similar genre and setting and I’m going to review it on its own merits. There is a difference between clones and being in the same genre and I don’t really want to get into that argument. Did it stand up to my “is it fun to play” tests? Was it all just a shallow place to build or a survive fest and get boring soon after? Let me break it down for you.
The first thing that stands out the most about Forest Village is the difficulty. The crazy part is that the more I got used to it and was able to expand my village it got even more complicated and difficult as the variables increased. I think I had five or six villages that all fell apart and crashed before I even got one that was able to survive. One of those attempts lasted for quite a while until I made a mismanagement in how I allocated my resources and lost about ten plus people in a winter. I struggled with it for a while not willing to give up on what was a great looking village and in the end I had to give into the obvious: I had lost that village too. One mistake can literally spell your undoing. In addition to Forest Village being a city builder and resource management sim, I would also like to put it in the roguelike genre as well. My friend was put off by the comment, but I’ve had a few villages now that were done in by a single mistake. I should have started to farm quicker or a craft a specific item. All the choices seemed like the right choices at the time though… and that’s the worst part.
Forest Village, as a roguelike, has its challenges. It’s like a puzzle you’ve got to solve one step at a time lest you are forced to start over again. Build up to a certain size and then be able to maintain life at the current level and then expand from there. Slow and steady really does win the race here (although I always play at max speed). The times I’ve gotten the farthest are the times I took my time and was being very methodical about my choices. Right now my village is about 52 years old (which I think is pretty good). I’m fairly sure others could have made more progress in the same amount of time, but I’m still figuring out the balance and how the game mechanics work.
There are still bugs that I’ve dealt with. The most recent one wass crashing. Recently I couldn’t actively save my game. I had to wait for the game to do its autosave and then I could close it because if I tried to save it manually, the game crashed and I lost my progress. That’s been fixed. Closing crashed the game proper for a while and I had to log out of Windows just to get my desktop back. That has also been fixed. In the game, there is some weird stuff that will occur randomly and is frustrating because things will look fine, but not work properly. A few examples: I finished building a stone road around a home and then my villagers who lived in said home couldn’t find the door which means they won’t eat or get warm in the winter and die. By simply not connecting the road all around the house, that problem didn’t occur. Another time, the orientation of a building stopped people from being able to enter it and they were stuck in a “must get in this building through a wall and finish my job” mentality and wouldn’t go home to get warm and so they died of hypothermia. I destroyed the bakery and made it again facing a different direction and they were able to find the door this time and live.
One of the biggest hurdles in this game that will beat you mercilessly if you’re not paying attention are the seasons. More specifically winter. Make no mistake; winter is coming. When it officially hits, all of your non-harvested crops die. You’ll lose any extras you could have had if you don’t start picking.  It can happen sooner or later than last year and can last longer or shorter than the previous. It’s almost like… real life? Which is fine as long as you understand that. When spring hits, you need to be ready! You also need to be watching when fall is ending so you can tell your people to get on it and maybe even take over a few additional units to help with the gathering to speed it up a bit. I’ve lost a lot of food by not paying attention to the seasons and then I look over at the temperature and realize that it’s 1 degree Celsius. At that point you’ve already lost the non-harvested food. Pay attention!
To expand on the “take over a few additional units” bit, that’s one feature that I really like. Sometimes your villagers will go 50 miles out of their way just to get up a hill to terraform it when they could just walk up to the base and do the same job. Sometimes it’s necessary to do this in order to kill an animal trying to eat your chickens/pigs/cows. Before building a school I would take control of my three-year-olds and go about doing manual labor and killing bears because they can’t work yet and were able to perform all of the tasks well. I figured why not; they weren’t doing anything else anyways. I also used this mechanic to take control of harvesters and make them put freshly harvested eggs/milk/apples directly into the bakeries so the bakers could use them first. Villagers will take the ingredients and then the bakers have nothing to work with to make the more satisfying foods; it’s very frustrating. The A.I. is kind of goofy like that, as it is in most games. However in Forest Village, this feature is borderline necessary.

I'm giving this a positive feedback in full conviction this game is going to be finished.
The Ups:
- A beautiful atmosphere with good music and landscape.
- many buildings and a sense of developing your own village into something bigger
- decorative items and walls to make your city your actual city
- a use-proven UI design (though it's not scalable)
- easy to learn controlls
- villager posession to overrule AI decisions and boost up production!
The Downs:
- blunt copy of banished
- villagers eat foot only in their houses
- villageers put foot in their houses only from barns
- nonesensical food-production (farmers reluctant to harvest, bakers, fishers, farmers, and bakers can't provide for themselves when they are uneducated, even under best circumstances)
- bakers and fishers fall awefully behind in food production (two bakeries take several years to use up the grain harvested from one 15x15 sized field)
- herdsmen starving with food (meat units) at their coop!
- in comparision farms are 'overpowered'. 2 people on one 15x15 vegetable produce more food than 4 in bakeries, or six in fishers, or 9 in hunters)
- once starving starts, there is no way back. Suppose you got an infrastructure that sustained a total 35 people pretty nicely. The babies are born, and you reach the 40, your food supplies reach zero. You're people start to starve. And all the fishers and bakers and hunters and gatherers you have can't stop that until the next years harvest of a vegetable field comes in.
- some conter-intuitive controlls
- empty hints (like hunters won't protect your animals, you have to do that yourself)
- disabled difficulty selector
- foxes, bears and wolves give no food
- grain and oats don't count as food (your people'd rather starve)
- no documentation / wiki
All in all, it's a nice game and offers challenges which can be overcome, though it means in general to go through trial-and-error for a while until you get a feeling for the not-so-common-sensed designs. But all it needs is like the obviously missing contents and a serious balance patch. (Seriously, a villager fully comitted to food production should at the least be capable to sustain herself.)
~Cheers
Edit: Sadly it seems to have just one strategy. Vegetable fields. Don't try to buidl anything else of the food production houses, but a fisher for the first year. :(
