Binary Domain is a game set in the near future where Global Warming has made most of earth uninhabitable with most cities flooded and/or destroyed. Governments were forced to make new cities above the ones that were already destroyed. Robots were used to create the new cities and with the rise of demand for robots, the American-based Bergen company rose to dominate a large majority of the robotics industry.
The game starts with a hollow child ( a robot that could pass for humans) attacking Bergen's HQ in Detroit with no idea that he was a robot himself. Believing that the founder of Amada Corp created the hollow child, you play as Dan Marshall, a member of a team called the rust crew Sent to japan to question Amada.
Gameplay - The gameplay is average, with nothing interesting that you can't find in any other 3rd person action game. It isn't bad but it isn't amazing either. The AI is very poor and the robots feel like zombies. The larger robots are similar to the monsters in DMC where you have to shoot the weak spots.
Story - The game has a good story. It isn't the best but it was interesting enough to make me play through the whole game. The characters are well thought out and every single one of them is unique and different. It asks you to make tough choices and
Voice Acting - Voice Acting isn't good but that is to be expected from a Japanese developer and publisher
Overall, the game is worth it for the story alone. the combat is average but forgivable

Fun to play, few quibbles that shouldn't get in the way:
Pros:
First off, let me share the good news: If you're a Trekkie, this is a gem for the look and feel of the game. You can see spots from the movies and shows, with little details that show the developers really care. (Baseball on the desk in DS9, for example)
It's also interesting to be able to play a number of the races from all generations of the show/movies. Bajoran, Klingon, Nausican, Gorn. Oh yes, Gorn.
There are three storylines, you can choose Federation, Klingon or Romulan. Each character must choose one specialty: Engineering (support and mines), Tactical (both Tank and Stealth), Science (jamming/tractor beam/healing).
I do like the feel of the space interface, you don't exactly have 360 degree of motion, but you have a lot better than the ground-based games I've played online. I'm a relative newbie to MMOs with space environments, so check another review for better details there.
It does a good job of balancing Free to Play, you can grind to get in-game currency, and there are some things that you need to buy to use. Some of them are frivolous, like extra uniforms or a captain's yacht. Some are pretty cool, like being able to play Remans or get specific classes of ship, or different mission tracks.
Cons:
There are really only two quibbles (and you know the Trouble with Quibbles, they multiply) about the game, but they don't prevent me from enjoying it.
1) I'm playing on the PC, and the controls/interface is a little clumsy. Navigation with the keyboard leaves a little to be desired. This might be different on a console, I did have that experience with other MMOs. This includes navigating through the different character/status/game interfaces in the top right corner. Shortcuts for these are not intuitive, some practice is required to get the hang of them.
2) There are some software bugs around. Found an environment which placed you in a gray featureless fog if you stepped into certain sections of a room. Found a few places with invisible walls (though some of them were just rendering delays, where the obstacle hadn't displayed yet). Haven't encountered anything that would freeze the game entirely, and the bug reporting interface is simple enough. (There are occasional "patching files" messages in command line font that show up when mission sections are loading, but they go away rather quickly)
I'll be playing this for a little while at least.

One of my favorite games, but it has a ton of problems...
The gameplay is really good, and some could say it's even better than the first Hotline Miami's gameplay but I'd say that aside from polishing it a bit it's not really changed at all.
You get more weapons in the game for some characters and you get a few changes such as characters who can't pick up weapons or ones that come in with a weapon and never leave it.
I could also say that while in the first game you could try to be stealthy and less "guns blazing" you kinda can't do it here because the thing that makes this one harder is the fact the game developers put in a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of windows and you'll get detected pretty easily the first couple of times you play a level, and in some levels they just shove a bunch of armed guys infront of you and you can't duck or avoid bullets so you kinda have to try and lure them without dying.
I also have to mention Evan, who you can do a pacifist run with and not kill anybody which is a pretty neat idea that actually kinda sticks with the game unlike some other elements you'd expect to be better.
A Huge part of the first game was the masks which were almost fully dropped in this game for some odd reason, I guess it was to add to the story and feature "powerless" characters but that wasn't really an excuse because half the masks in the game have no powers.
Just like the first game's OST, this one rocks hard and adds to the atmosphere, featuring old composers from the first game like M.O.O.N, El Huevero, etc and I think they also feature some new ones like El Tigr3.
The level editor saves this game and is worth buying the game for alone (aside from the OST). If you didn't like the campaign you could just download a better one from the level editor, and trust me some of them are great, and actually somewhat well written ones like Miami Falls, Madness or Hunter: Snowfall just to name a few I enjoyed myself.
The game is pretty decent as it's own game, and doesn't fall too hard as a sequel, and it also has great new features worth checking out and if you love Hotline Miami and want much, much more you can grinf the game to it's core with hard mode or with the level editor, or you can try to get all the achievements.
It's a solid 7/10 and really fun game to waste your time and hard earned money on.

Cat Quest is an action rpg where you play as a cat who collects items and fights enemies on a world map and underground caves.
Cat Quest is charming. It's easy to like it. Controls are good, graphics are easy to look and well done, there are lots of quests and items to get. Though no usable items what so ever. The only usable you have are your spells.
Basically you level up, gain more hp, attack and spell power from levels and items. Also items level up when you find a same item you already had.
What ever Cat Quest has is fun and nice but it doesn't have too many different enemies and the sound track is pretty short.
The same formula repeats over and over where you get a quest, walk where you're supposed to and then back. Sometimes you clear an underground cave and open 1+ chests. This might or might not bother you. To me it's kind of a problem but not big enough of a problem that I'd stop playing.
Cat Quest plusses:
+ very charming world and characters
+ fun music and graphics
+ simple and fun to play
+ lots of quests and items
Cat Quest minuses:
- it does get repeating pretty fast, it repeats the same formula for all the quests with very little variation
- not too many different enemies, gets repeating
Final words:
Cat Quest isn't my favourite game at all but it might be one of my favourites. Right now I'm okay how it is but I can't recommend it to everyone. At this price you need to like the game genre and the style of the game.
Personally I'm on the edge if I regret buying the game at full price. I suppose I do not but I'd hesitate buying it again without a discount.
At full price:  8- / 10
At half price: 8½ / 10

Easy to pick up, hard to master, and overall really fun to play.
This whole review in two sentences: If you don't mind being fragged a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, you will really enjoy this game.  Listen to the in game music, your own music or a podcast, sit back, and instagib.
The movement system stays relatively simple while being pretty damn fun.  WASD to move, space to jump, and right click to boost yourself off a wall or the ground.  Repetitively jumping in a direction will gain speed faster than walking on the ground would.  Boosting off objects can be done consecutively to the point where you can climb walls or even quickly zip between walls to the point where you never touch the ground.
The shooting is extremely simple, but it brings in a major skill curve.  If you can click on someone, one shot from your instagib lazer will kill them.  The big contingency being if you click them.  The skill curve of this game quickly shifts from movement to aim.  Aim is what seperates the noobs and pros.  People with fps experience are at an extreme advantage.  I've been owned by people playing their first game Ratz Instagib because they are Global Elite in CS:GO or have a few thousand hours of competitive TF2 under their belt.
You WILL OWN the people worse than you, and you WILL GET OWNED by the people better than you.  If you can't realize that, this game isn't for you.  If you make the choice to drop the ego and enjoy the game, you WILL see yourself improving.  If you can't drop the ego, you won't have a very fun time with this game.  Because of these truths, this game has one of the chillest communities.  Everyone is really nice and ready to help.  That occassional raging noob will be gone in one or two games.
So... are you going to be the raging noob who quits after a few matches, the noob who enjoys seeing themself progress in a game with a large skill curve, or the ♥♥♥♥ing CS:GO Global Elite who owns us all?
See you in Ratz :-)

A well blended mix of Left 4 Dead style gameplay with the Warhammer Fantasy setting, this game sought to copy the game formula Left 4 Dead used almost down to the letter and from what i've seen that isn't a bad thing. Gameplay wise most of the formula is nearly the same as L4D, enemies consist of your run of the mill cannon fodder by the dozens, as well as a number of special snowflakes that mostly consist of expies of L4D's specials. While the specials are mostly the same from L4D there were a few I thought improved a little on the formula as well as one or two unique ones.The Gutter Runner, for instance, is essentially the Hunter from L4D, but with a few more brains than the merely brain hungry Hunter. Gutter Runners will, instead of merely approaching the group and pouncing on the best target of opportunity before stabbing away like Hunters, will actually hold off if your group is too close to make an attack feasible, and if he IS caught but survives he will dissapear and wait for another opportunity.
The classes I feel are a double edged sword. One one hand, this forces players to really think about how best to use their characters strengths and weaknesses and how to work with teamates to make up for those weaknesses. On the other hand, it also keeps you from playing as the mage if someone is already playing the mage, meaning you might have to make do with a character you either don't like or don't have practice with. As for the loot system, honestly, I feel there had to be a better way to do it than this. If you wan't any chance at something decent you have to play on the harder difficulties which means playing with friends or, if you are very brave and patient, solo with the A.I. (not recommended on anything more than hard.). You then have to play the whole mission through and if you really want to make sure to get the best, the whole party must work its butt off to find all the dice they can, pick up every tome (thereby sacrificing a healing item per person as each person can only carry one tome), and contemplate cursed tomes (which on top of the previously mentioned, also takes away some of your health bar). All of that and even then what loot is available is based on luck, as is any remaining dice you didn't get dice/tomes/cursed tomes for. Didn't get what you want? Congrats, you get to do the whole thing again. Die mid mission? Too bad, gotta start over. Some people may like that, but I know it'll annoy just as many.
For mission variety, again, heavily borrowed L4D affair. The objective usually consists of travelling from point A to point B, along the way completeing objectives such as fetch three things, destroy three things, fetch a whole mess of things, collect ALL the things, or protect four things (can't have people thinking there's something special involving the number 3 now can we?)
As for the story, as one might expect the overall story is rather slimly written. You play as a party of 5 misfits (gameplay involves 4 not including whomever presumebly drew the short straw and got stuck babysitting the nagging barkeep) all visiting the lovely cesspit of Ubersreik when the town goes to the vermin (vermintide, go-figure). It's up to our band of misfits to not skip town and instead find everybody food, protect the water, clear out the rats, sound the alarm, kill more rats, get more food, protect the water again (the resistance is useless in case its not clear yet.) If you're expecting plot hooks, best i can do is recommend you look up what "The End Times" are in this setting if you don't know already.
All in all, despite some things that could have used a little more polish, this is otherwise a solid game to play, especially with friends.

Descend into the protagonist's mental disorder as he completes his final masterpiece.
In a market completely inundated with half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥survival horror titles, Layers of Fear is a gorgeous, shining example of how it should be done.
The game unfolds like a haunted house. Navigate the mansion as it changes around you. Even as you look away, doors disappear, phones fall up stairs, paintings change. It's ... crazy. Casual puzzles (find the combination, find the key) keep the action interesting as the threat of tastefully-placed jump scares heighten the tension. The attention to detail in this game is very impressive. Every corner of the game is inhabited by props and hidden goodies abound. Completionists have their work cut out for them.
While Layers of Fear does indeed rely on jump scares to keep players on their toes, they are not overdone and are always appropriate.
The game takes place over six chapters, each more disturbing and gruesome than the last. By the end of the first chapter, I thought "this isn't that scary." But by the end of chapter six I was having dreams about this game. And they weren't of gumdrops and junk.
I finished Layers in about 4 hours, which I felt was well spent. The ending was subtle, but not anticlimactic. It was pretty good and it left me wanting more.
Despite the really top-notch graphics, my little laptop managed to run this just fine. Framerates weren't the best, but they weren't bad enough to spoil the experience.

I never played "Banished" so here is a non-biased review. I have 36 hours on record. The game is great. It needs some work for sure, but it is a great game. The biggest issue I have with the game is the lack of a guide. I would say, it needs a guide because it is very difficult and complicated. And I don't mean a guide of what to do and how to do it, I just mean a guide of how to do it. For example, in your barn and storage, you have a list of all of your items, but you don't have a list of how to make new items. You don't learn how to make those items until you get the required building and it tells you. For several builders, there isn't a description of what they do. The blacksmith, weaver, carpenter, and kiln don't have descriptions. For some strange reason, the carpenter builds tools, but the blacksmith builds high quality tools, but the weaver makes regular clothes and warm clothes. So for tools you need 2 buildings, but for clothes you need one. In one of my play throughs I ended up building a blacksmith because I didn't know it only made high quality tools, which need cast iron. You get cast iron from charcoal, which you get from the kiln. None of this is listed, which means there's even more that can only be learned through failure and guesswork. Which is the problem.
Other than that, I love this game. It's not what you would consider "exciting" and "thrilling", but it is a very beautiful game, and it gives new meaning to "real-time". This game is sloooooow. So sloooooow that they allow you to fast forward time x10. But then you get disasters, if you play with disasters. You don't have to play with disasters. I do because I like my games as hard and challenging as they come. Speaking of difficulty, it could do with a difficulty setting. I think it took me killing 3 villages to get things figured out. On my current village, i'm on year 11, and I think we can take this to the long haul. I save my game before making big decisions that cost a lot of time and resources, because those decisions can kill you 6 months later. So if you save during sustainable periods, you can go back to those times instead of starting all over again. And you don't have any save boundaries like some games, so you can always save your game.
For the people who call the game unbalanced, those people just may not be utilizing all of the games tools to their advantage. When I starting rationing certain foods during certain times of year, my villagers stopped dieing of starvation. The more patient you are with building houses, the less chance you have a being surprised by a baby boom, and everyone dieing because they ran out of resources. I don't think a game like this is supposed to be easy. It's already slow, with virtually no action. It doesn't need to be easy too. This game does hard "right".
The tutorial was ok, but unimpressive. As I mentioned, it still took several play throughs and village killing to learn the game without a guide.
All in all, I'm glad I decided to purchase this game. It's been fun, and I look to enjoying hundreds of hours on it. I hope you enjoy it too! Don't listen to all the negativity. If you enjoy a challenge, and you're mature enough to take a loss, and you look resource management and village building, you'll love this game. Just keep google in the background until you learn how to play.
Oh, one last thing. The terraforming does suck. But it just adds to the difficulty. Check the map after you start a new town to see if you like it. You DON"T want a map that'll end up putting all of your buildings too far apart and away from the barn and warehouse.

Some game about transhumanism or something plus robots. The writing is the strongest point, particularly for the numerous team members you'll encounter. It's a cavalcade of racial stereotypes, but who cares, they're pretty endearing.
What's not so great is their capacity for combat. Despite how much emphasis the game puts on you working with your team, customizing their weapons and skills, and improving relationships with each one, they're somewhat dim in combat. The worst offenses involve a lack of understanding of line-of-fire and staying out of it, not using cover properly to (repeatedly jumping between cover, not providing covering fire, no concept of vaulted cover maneuvers), and general lack of battlefield presence (a lot of the more hairy encounters could have been dealt with the teammate who specialized in deploying anti-armor, but refused to do it against lots of armor mysteriously).
It's fairly solid with regard to gunplay, although there isn't much creativity between weapons (pretty much automatic rifle, sniper's rifle, shotgun, pistol, RPG). Fighting robots is pretty fun, especially how blowing off their heads, arms, or legs can do different things to their combat capacities. Level design isn't particularly outstanding and very hallway-filled, not really giving many opportunities to fix, flank, and finish enemies.
Eh, it's a fun game. Seems to lose steam close to the end, and I personally disliked one of the pivotal characters, so maybe that didn't help...

Now for my thoughts.
The Evil Within is for fans of survival horror who are looking for a challenge.

A decent entry in the action/horror genre, with decent visuals, some genuinely scary looking enemies, and RE4-like combat mechanics. The atmosphere of this game is well set, although through a lot of the game you'll be wishing you could switch out of the tight third-person camera angle to get a better look at everything. I understand why that view is set, but when your looking for collectibles and the ever-easy to miss goddess keys you'll be wishing you could pull the view back a bit. The writing and plot are passible for this type of game, but it does feel like a bit of a missed opportunity from the creator of the original Resident Evil. The end boss and the final plot revelation to kind of take the wind out of this game's proverbial sails. I know it sounds like I'm dumping on this game a bit, but it is still worth a playthrough and if you need that action/horror itch scratched you won't be disappointed, ammo is scarce and enemies are relentless. Still, you may want to buy this when the price drops down.

This game is in my top 10 Third Person Shooter games of all time.  Most everything of this game is unique! When I played the game I got really attached to my comrades, especially the ones I always team up on.  And when they almost die, it is like a stab in the heart for me.  I never have been so attached to an NPC in my life, other than Mass Effect Series.  This game is amazing beyond compare, and I do not realize why it has such a low metascore it deserves at least an 80 or higher in my standards.  The one other thing that caught my eye is the mass number of different kind of robots that are in the game, sure there are the average Green Foot Soldiers but they account for the mass horde that attacks you!  It is just an amazing feeling to go up to an enemy Scrap Head and mash it to pieces with the butt of your rifle and watch it fall apart!  I must say the Graphics are amazing, and the physics are just as great!
Anyone looking for long, hard, and enjoyable story needs to check out this game!

This is a really fun game, brought down by terrible engineering.
I'm writing this right after losing yet another game to the horrific networking code in this game.  As soon as the "host" leaves a game -- for whatever reason! -- your entire play session is gone.  That nice successful run, with all the loot?  Gone.   Nothing you can do.  Who, in this day and age, would think a peer-to-peer networking model -- with 1 peer being "special" -- was a good idea?  A very dumb person, that is who.
Think back to Left 4 Dead -- really, the ancestor of this game -- and in 2008, they did it right:  if a player leaves -- any player -- no worry!  A bot fills in, the game resumes.   A server keeps things stable and consistent.  Maybe even the player who crashed can rejoin later.
There's various annoying other bugs in this game: the fullscreen mode sometimes flakes out putting you into a window mode.  Some crashes if you play a long time.  All of those forgivable, if you just didn't mess up the networking so bad.  So.  So.  Bad.
Now, the sad part.  If you could overlook these two glaring problems...
What a nice game.  What a story, what a setting!  What interesting characters!  It looks gorgeous and stylish.  The loot heavily RNG but who cares it's not a gear check.  What a good group dynamic of tanks & DPS and casters -- a new and exciting improvement from L4D.
That's the tragedy here:  a really nice game, with a rotting, corrupt heart of networking code.  The exact code that a L4D  type game must, must have working.
EDIT:
Ok -- I can't deny it, I'm still playing.  Are there some weird networking problems, sure.  Is it rare enough not to matter?  Yes.  Is the game fun?  Yes.  Yes it is.  It's worth it.  Make more of these games.  Buy it so people make more of these types of games.

The gunplay mechanics tend to make it so that whoever has the faster gun and the larger magazine will win the firefight. Personally I like sniping people from far off, unfortunately for me to aquire the gear I would need to even begin to do that would take weeks of boring, unsatisfying gameplay. Another aspect that I can't stand is tanks. In order to disable a tank you have to rely on the unimaginably low chance that a driver is stupid enough to run over and AT mine (which take up 1 of you 3 precious equipment slots), or to sacrafice any kin of practical gun for a rocket launcher for which you have just 4 shots. This makes an AT role very uneventful and boring, thus no-one plays it, however because of that, whenever a tank comes to the battlefield it pretty much seals the game's destiny. Given all of the bad things I've said, if you're looking for the LEAST BAD F2P WWII game, then look no further. After that I can give you no advice.

Star Trek Online is by far one of the best MMOs that I have played.
Personally, I'll try out an MMO for a couple hours, maybe play here and there later, and then uninstall because I've lost interest. But not this.
Cryptic has done a great job in developing this game. There are a few bugs here and there, but nothing too game-breaking. The story is very well done and is the part that keeps my attention. The leveling is also stellar, in most MMOs you'll sit there for hours and hours grinding to get to the next level. Or it sets you on a quest and the area is for level 20+ and you're level 10, you'll have to grind for days just to get to progress the story. Not with STO.
Each mission in STO does require you to be a certain level, BUT each mission also levels you up just enough to get to the next. And with the DOFF system (which is very easy to get the hang of) is an easy way of getting XP. I've known a few players who have gotten some of their characters to max level and not even leaving their faction's homeworld by using the DOFFs. The story is also interesting to say the least, it wasn't so good that I couldn't keep it off my mind, but it was good enough to keep coming back.
TL:DR The story is great, the developers are cool, and the leveling is stellar.

-Choose from 3 different classes: Engineering, Tactical, and Science. Each class has its own special attributes.
-Literally no way to greif
-Great stories, with multiple "episodes", or story arcs, and plenty of special episodes
-Huge community and fanbase
-Literally hundreds of ships to choose from, with a perfect one just for you
-Thousands of items, weapons, shields, and other in game objects to customize with
-A robust gaming server with few downs and frequent maintenance
Cons:
-Some ships and items cost real money
-A steep learning curve(I have still not mastered it!)
-Some features will not be avaliable to newcomers, such as Adventure Zones and other endgame location and activities.
Opinion:
Overall a good game and if you have enjoyed the Star Trek franchise, a definite yes. This game exemplifies what the Star Trek universe should represent, exploration and cooperation.

Hotline Miami 2 Wrong Number is the sequel to what else?  Hotline Miami.  Anyone who has ever played Hotline Miami knows how thrilling and exciting it is.  If you have played Hotline Miami you owe it to yourself to get the sequel.  Hotline Miami 2 Wrong Number is more than just more Hotline Miami (even if it was more Hotline Miami, why wouldn't you get it anyway?), it is a more difficult and brutal than the first.  Hotline Miami 2 Wrong Number doesn't just take place in Miami where you tackle the Russian mafia while wearing a rubber mask, it puts the player in swinging during not only a drug war between the Russians, Colombians, and random gangs who want in, but also during a real war between the United States and Russia where the player needs to employ a more tactical approach unlike the other levels.  In the end, Hotline Miami 2 Wrong Number is a fantastic game with an amazing story (I would recommend going into Hotline Miami and Hotline Miami 2 Wrong Number blind as it completely ruins the story and all its twists and turns as the story is meant to be put together by the player as they progress through the game).   Hotline Miami 2 Wrong Number is worth a buy in my book.
Great sequel. More difficult than the original and new variations on gameplay keep it fresh. If you enjoyed the first game but wanted more levels, you'll be happy with the second release.

The Evil Within is the spirital succesor of the famous Resident Evil series and is developed by Shinji Mikami. The illusion of the game is of a detective whom is stuck inside a machine that crosses multiple "subjects" minds together and has to physically and mentally push himself to leave his eternal hell of, and others', his mind. The game has an intense horror genre description, yet the game is made to be replayable which gives of feel of domination after 30 hours in game. The game is still horrifying and heart-stopping every run through for me. If one needs something new, there are 3 DLC and a Season Pass purchasable. The Evil within isnt made to be played as a Resident Evil game, however more as a Bestheda game with its explorability and many options of survival. All in all, I love this game and enjoy gunning down or stealthing my way through 15 chapters of horror filled FPS, survival, horror, and psychological traps embeded in that of whick is the ultimate evil within.
Great game, longer than I anticipated, worth every cent!

So why am I recommending this? Simple. At it's core, it's a weird, macabre "escape the room" game that's $2 regular price. Strictly as a puzzle game, it's entertaining. Some people think the puzzles are really obtuse or impossible to figure out. I would politely disagree with that. There are certainly some parts in each room that can leave you scratching your head, but all of the puzzles are DEFINITELY attainable without any sort of guide. Because of this, the game is worth the $2 price tag.
Also, don't let the hours played fool you. I left the game on for at least 3 hours while I went off to do something else. Depending on how much difficulty you have with the puzzles, I'd say the gameplay is 1-2 hours.
To sum up, it's a cheap bit of puzzle entertainment with a weird twist a lot of puzzle games don't have. The story is not really there and the ending feels more like what you might see on a Saturday morning serial cartoon rather than a fully fleshed out end. But it kept me entertained and I wasn't bored or frustrated, to its credit, so I would recommend this.

This review will contain mild spoilers for the premise of the game.
You work at the Rusty Lake Hotel. Presumably. Who you are or what your name is never gets established. Your only job, apparently, is killing off the guests one by one and serving them for dinner the next day. Why? Who knows.
Rusty Lake Hotel was the first commercial entry for a longrunning series of free games. This was my first foray into Rusty Lake's setting, so it's possible those who have prior experience with the games might better understand what's happening. Still, just the tiniest of hints about what's going on, to make the game more accessible to newcomers, would have been quite welcome.
The lack of guidance extends to the gameplay as well. The puzzles in Rusty Lake Hotel can be as surreal as its setting. Sometimes that works, forcing you to think outside the box in novel ways. Sometimes it really doesn't. I frequently had to use the built-in walkthrough to get through a chapter.
Let me give you an example how how obtuse the puzzles can get. In one chapter, I got stuck trying to find tabasco sauce so I could make an anthropomorphized deer his drink. (Yes, the entire game is that weird.) The solution? Click on the antlers of the deer skull mounted on the wall until tabasco sauce runs from its nose.
There's barely a plot to speak of, either. Not only do you not know why you're murdering all these guests, they themselves don't appear to care. Each morning, if you choose to click on the remaining characters, they recite the exact same line as they did on the first day. None of them ever comment on the way their numbers are dwindling. Killing them barely affected me, because they didn't feel the slightest bit like people, just cartoon props.
TL;DR: I'd advise those interested to skip straight to Rusty Lake Roots instead. You'll get similar puzzles with a better storyline.

I’d first like to say that I really did enjoy this game. It was a lot of fun and I can’t wait to see more support from the devs for this title.
On that note, I have issues.
My main issue is with the story. I understand this is about a mad artist going...well, mad. That’s all fine and good but it feels redundant. I understand that he is mad, I just do not know why. Is it because he’s focusing too much on his work and not enough on his family? It feels obvious there but I don’t feel like there is any real payoff. I would’ve like to see a bit more narrative and a bit more substance with the artist and his family. What really set him off the deep end?
That’s what I love most about these adventure games. Yes, people call them ‘walking simulators’ because you’re just walking from one bit to another bit until you get to the end. However, I hate to use those words to describe this type of game because you’re going through an interactive story. This isn’t just a game but a full-length fictional novel that you get to explore and interact with. When it comes to these types of experiences, you can do so much with world building and character development.
When you read a book, you get so much out of it. The Picture of Dorian Gray by Oscar Wilde is a grand example since that is what the game quotes in the beginning. There is so much depth and character development within that book as we watch Dorian transform from this handsome, polite individual into an unnerving monster. Also, ‘Dorian Gray’ is classified as a philosophical novel. That’s why I wanted more depth in this story. The game quotes ‘Dorian Gray’ but merely uses it as a placeholder for haunted house scares rather than as a foundation for an unnerving narrative about a struggling artist. I don’t feel like there was enough weight to the narrative to continue carrying on.
Let’s even take a look at Silent Hill 2. James Sunderland, when you first see him, is an innocent man who seeks out his wife in the resort town of Silent Hill. He doesn’t know why he was called to this place but came anyway due to a letter from his wife. He knew that his wife had died from disease three years ago yet, he still came. Why? Silent Hill 2 does a fantastic job exploring the why and how of James Sunderland as we watch him grow from this innocent bystander to the actual monster that he locked away. We believed him, believed that he was a good person through and through who went through unusual circumstances until we get the carpet thrown out from under us and find out that he was the actual monster in the first place. That is good storytelling, that is good psychological horror.
On the graphics standpoint, the game looks and feel wonderful. Some choppiness here and there but I’m pretty amazed at the results of the constantly-shifting mansion. It made me wonder if Unity can do this good of a job then I’d love to see Unreal 4 engine bust out its chops on this kind of experience. Another point to mention is that the puzzles feel a bit hollow. The puzzles do not feel like actual puzzles but more like ‘calm moments’ between the scary bits and that is disappointing as well. There were some moments when I felt more like I was walking around in circles trying to figure out where to push the next button for the next sequence rather than an actual puzzle. I understand that Layers of Fear was trying to go for a ‘haunted house version’ of Gone Home but at the same time, it needed a bit more structure.
To conclude, Layers of Fear can be much more than what it currently is. How it handles its narrative and story is great but feels a bit lifeless and hollow. There is good replay value, enough to warrant two or three playthroughs, since there are multiple endings to find and so on, but that’s all I can really say. The game does have heart and I give the devs more than enough credit for trying but this heart needs some fresh blood pumping through its veins.

I came in with no expectations. Over the course of the game, however, I formed exactly one expectation: to get to the ending and have that "ah-ha!" moment. I've chosen to do neither of those things to remind myself that I shouldn't need to.
This game could have easily divulged more information like any good story should. Everything in this game is scripted: where you go, what you see, etc. It's the perfect atmosphere for effectively telling a story because of how controlled the narrative could be. Unfortunately, the notes, documents, and audio you encounter are essentially garbage because they only serve as descriptions of the story they wanted to tell--instead of being the story itself.

Despite remaining nameless throughout the whole story, the main character still manages to exert an air of importance. Ultimately, you are tasked with the problem of completing a 'masterpiece', a
. In order to do so, the player must endure a series of "tasks" within a broken home. Explore the environment and manipulate it in order to discover unique scenarios and, overall, the morbid history behind the house. Fight the inner demons that plague this individual and seek the truth one winding hallway at a time.
In order to make a horror story seem believable and 'realistic' you require decent, vivid graphics.
delivers just that. You are able to switch between low, medium, and high settings in order to best cater to your computing needs. With my computer being at the lower end of the gaming spectrum, I was able to run the game on low with relatively decent FPS and enjoyable graphics.
Even playing on low graphics makes you feel immersed in the game. Despite all the head-bobbing, there was never really a time where I ended up feeling naseuous. Various FOV and similar settings helped alleviate such issues that usually crop up within horror games.
Another aspect of this game that really jumps out at me (no joke intended) is the music and sound effects. What starts off as a calm melody quickly crescendos in urgency and madness. The music compliments the game very well and jeez, the sound effects really chill me to the bone. It is terrifying when it needs to be and suspenseful all the same.
+ I don't like playing horror games at all, yet this one somehow manages to keep me engaged...
+ If you plan on getting all the achievements, then replayability value of this game is high, otherwise... (continued in Con)

+ Audio really enhances the game. The music and sound effects just deliver the right amount of "oompf!" required to make a horror game work. The narration is creepy yet captivating at the same time as well
+ The graphics are pretty stellar despite them being on low. The lowest FPS that I've experiencd so far was 6, and that was when things started getting a bit hectic. Other than that, I've maintained a decent 30 (based off of a Toshiba E45T (in other words, a crappy laptop))
+ Has a good number of jump scares that, in my opinion, didn't really seem unnecessary or ridiculous; wasnt overdone. You aren't just simply being chased by something like is already familiar in this genre, but you actually have to interact with the environment in order to initiate scares

An absolutely delightful romp. Quite a balm in a game industry overrun with grimdark gorefests. If the Gentlebros hope to be the next SpryFox, I wish them godspeed in that noble endeavor.
The cat theme is taken just far enough. The sound design is cute, and the music is just right, although not likely to be added to an audiophile playlist. Gameplay is smooth, and the art is fun to look at without looking cheap. It's an easy game, and death has no consequences besides sending you back to your last catnap location. Those seeking a challenge can choose to tackle higher level dangers or make use of nerfing equipment like the Crappy Set. No grinding is actually required except to get the Level 99 achievement, and even that took me only 15 minutes in the purpose-built leveling field. As for accessibility, the game lacks custom key bindings, but scores good marks on audio being unnecessary and color blind friendliness.
10/10 Would Catventure again.

I love Banished and so was quick to give this game a shot. Within 40 minutes I did something I've never done before, requested a Steam refund. Why? Terraforming. To say I disliked it would be a huge understatment. It's not really difficult to use but it makes the terrain ugly and unnatural looking (it's also an annoying step I just don't want to deal with in this type of game). Look at the official screenshots and you'll get an idea of what I mean. The second to last screenshot clearly shows the weird "bumps" underneath a few of the buildings at the bottom left corner of the image. To me this looks very weird, unnatural and ugly. Also, if you flatten a large area all the green goes away and is replaced with an ugly, grey, cobblestone looking ground that stands out as a stark contrast to the more natural looking terrain around it. Hence, this beautiful game is no longer beautiful. If an auto terrain leveler ever becomes a thing, and it doesn't make the ground hideous, I'd consider this game again.

Forest Village - great game overall. Still a work in progress, and that shows in some areas of the game. For example, some of the castle buildings don't do anything yet, they're basically just pretty buildings that cost a lot of resources to build. And the patches are....hit and miss. Sometimes they implement a patch and leave the game slightly worse off than it was before.
However, the villager management aspect of this game is excellent. It's really easy to get all your villagers doing exactly what you want them to do. The village and all the buildings look very cool. If you just slightly move a building before you place it you can get different variations of the building. It's not a huge thing but it's just one of the little things that help add to the game. And if you just want to enjoy how well designed your village is, you can go first person with a villager, which isn't necessarily very useful but it's a neat thing. Sometimes it's helpful if you have livestock being attacked you can just grab the nearest villager and shoot the animal that's attacking them.
I think the most enjoyable part of the game for me is that it's actually pretty challenging. Everything matters. There's really no way to just go hands off and let it blaze through the seasons, especially not at first. You always need to tweak here, tweak there. Compensate here, adjust there. Sometimes you get a good harvest of crops during the warm season and life is great. Other times, everything goes wrong and you don't bring in nearly enough to get through the winter. Things get interesting. If you're me, you just produce so much wool that you can take it to the market and buy some resources. But if you didn't have a guy taking your excess wool to the market over time, you may not have that option. Maybe slaughter a bunch of livestock for a short term meat surplus? But then your milk, wool, egg and consistent meat production goes in the tank for a while. Oh, by the way, you forgot to have your people make warm clothes for the winter. Or cut firewood. Now you don't have enough food, your villagers are freezing to death, and because they're dying off slowly you're losing the very workforce you need to recover.
I've seen some reviews saying you can't sustain large populations because of balancing issues. I've got a village of about 200 right now and some 75ish years, and we're still chugging along. It is difficult, but that's a positive, not a negative. It does probably need some rebalancing in some aspects but it's not broken by any means. I've also noticed people complaining about the terraforming. Personally, I think it works just fine for what you'll need it to do.
If I have complaints, most of them would actually revolve around the balance of food items. There really doesn't seem to be a huge benefit to using multiple ingredients to make baked goods. The population seems to use the baked foods at the same rate as the raw ingredients, and the problem with that is the baked food takes way more workers, time, resources and buildings to make. Take bread for example, almost the same calorie (or kcal in the game) output as raw vegetables. However, raw vegetables can be eaten right out of the field and bread actually requires a bakery and more workers to make. The payoff for making it is really non-existant.
Other issues I have are probably things that will be implemented at some point.  The "Keep" building says you can reasearch new technologies for your villagers, but right now it does nothing. One would expect something like carts for hauling large amounts of raw food to be one example of a technology you could research. That way, instead of harvesting a couple crops at a time and having to walk to the storage, the villagers could fill carts and then send the carts to the storage, vastly speeding up harvesting.
It's a fun game, looks good, and there's still more to come. Even as a partially completed game it's solid.

A really,
bizarre point & click/puzzle/adventure/horror game. I'd want to give it a mixed rating - the theme and atmosphere are really cool, but as a puzzle game it's way too impenetrable.
+ Creepy atmosphere
+ Nice visuals & sounds
- The puzzles are extremely opaque. I had to use the official walkthrough for parts of every single room. It's not that they are necessarily difficult puzzles, but it's often really hard to figure out what the game expects you to do to proceed. Your actions often have bizarre results, and you frequently have to repeat an action that at one random point gives a different result than at the previous repetitions.
- There is a secret correct order to do the rooms at, which is the only way to get 3 stars for all dinners (and it's not the order the game implies by the room numbers).
- Additionally to the previous one, some of the secret ingredients require completely unintuitive steps done at exactly the right occasion to acquire. And if you acquire them after you've already finished the room they belong to, too bad, you missed the opportunity to use them.
To sum it up, while it has an uniquely creepy atmosphere, the game does a
bad job of communicating with the player.

The macabre has ironically been beaten to death in the gaming world, what with blood and viscera having become a more common room decor than wallpaper. That makes it all the more refreshing when a game takes a more cerebral approach to murder, such as with a sophisticated murder mystery. If you’ve come to Rusty Lake Hotel looking for that, however, you’re not going to get much more than the appearance of sophistication. There are hints of something special here, but it’s obfuscated by a thin plot, awkward puzzles, and literal boar♥♥♥♥♥♥
You are introduced to the proprietor of the Rusty Lake Hotel, one Mr. Owl, as he guides a raft of five guests across the quiet waters to their lodgings. Each of the animal-faced visitors has their own reason for attending Mr. Owl’s gathering, and it’s your job to attend to their needs during their stay. Every evening the guests will set down to dinner, and then afterwards you will follow one of them to their room to assist them in some way. There is an ulterior motive to your service, of course, and it will see more and more vacancies open at the hotel as you progress.
Spoiler alert for the main plot which you will learn about maybe five minutes into the game: The hotel has no main dishes to serve the guests, and said guests happen to be comprised of delicious meats. Whatever you may have been imagining about mysteries and intrigue, you can dump it because what you are actually doing here is murdering guests to feed to other guests. Most of the game takes place in the five rooms of the visitors, where a complex series of puzzles and brain-teasers will allow you to engineer a fatal encounter with the occupant and harvest their flesh. The next day you serve it to whoever remains, and then roll on to the next unlucky critter.
That makes the meat (heh) of the game the puzzles, and this is where most people are going to stumble. Each room is four walls covered with shelves, portraits, tables, and other decor that will be clicked upon and used to eventually kill someone. Expect plenty of locked cabinets with hidden keys, letter and number substitution puzzles, classics like unlabeled weights and measuring water out, and using strange items on other items. About half the puzzles are pretty logical and easy to spot but the other half is the killer, requiring you to click on sprouts until they randomly blossom into keys, or click on toy monkeys in a specific order, or look out a window at the right time, or feed a boar♥♥♥♥♥♥sandwich to the boar who♥♥♥♥♥♥it out. And let me assure you, I do not possess the capacity to make that last one up.
Mr. Boar’s room was where I almost gave up on the game, between the fecal snack and the bleeding toilet and the insipid, confusing puzzle-locked cabinets. I stuck with it to see where the game went and I’m happy to report that the ending is interesting, even if the means of getting there were not. Rusty Lake Hotel feels like an excerpt or aside from a much longer tale, one that needs context that isn’t given anywhere. Things happens because they HAVE to happen to advance the plot, not because they make sense. There’s a dark aura to the proceedings but the ridiculous elements like animal heads and poop take the Lynchian edge off and make it all feel awkward and arbitrary.
This one rides the line between yea and nay moreso than any other game I’ve reviewed thus far. It’s mechanically thin, the puzzles are poorly designed, and what little story there is is tainted by absurdity. But once you understand what it expects of you and what it offers it becomes a much smoother ride, and honestly the ending was a very bright point of darkness that helped color the game in retrospect. It’s hard to recommend but I don’t regret playing it in the end, and I must admit I’m interested in seeing what the rest of the series can offer.

+ Combat in general, and melee combat in particular, is very polished and open for an older title; everything can be controlled, such as directional blocking, without overcomplicating the mechanics involved
+ Character creation is meticulously in-depth; initial backstory creation works seamlessly with selection of primary attributes in a way that makes the final product always feel refreshingly unique
+ 'Story' is about as open-ended as can be, to the point where the game essentially has no story, and is something of a thirteenth century sand-box title; the player has complete, unadulterated freedom
+ The game encourages the player to recruit and build a personal army as he/she progresses, and the mechanics put in place for doing so are well-rounded and complex
+ Extremely easy and satisfying to mod; highly recommended
+ Sorting and commanding one's troops is key, and the player would do well to benefit fromt he excellent command mechanics of the game; strategy is massively important and competently implemented
+ Economics of the game add another layer of challenge to the game; trade and balancing one's income against one's expenses are both crucial elements to consider
+ Multiplayer is fairly standard, run-of-the-mill stuff, but it's still densely populated and everything seems to connect well; the charm of the game, and its solid combat system, keep the players coming back in droves after more than five years
- Politics, which are interesting and engaging in scope, end up being a somewhat weaker feature in practice, as NPCs are largely static during negotiations; this does break the immersion slightly, as it seems that your successes are based purely on stats, and not on the actual implications of one's choices
- Quests often become tedious and repetitive
- Tutorial is underwheling and largely insufficient to introduce the more in-depth mechanics that will be used outside of combat
- Visuals are outdated and didn't stand well the test of time; even for the year of release, the textures and polygon counts are well below par

The first steam game I ever purchased, this game is my bread and butter. I love this game. If you enjoy a fast paced game, will plenty of content and a good (most of the time) community look here!
Classes; The 4 classes of the game, miner, sniper, engineer, and commando, all have their own advantages. The commando is the mid ranged destroyer, the sniper being the long-ranged dominator, the engineer being the tactical strategist,a dn the miner being the close-ranged troll. Whetever your strategy is, you'll probably find it in this game!

Modes; There are plenty of modes to choose from, from the classic TDM, destructive Multi Hill, and the awesome VIP. IN addition; if you want a slower game, there is classic CTF (Capture the Flag) which is a 90 minute game where teamwork matters.
Zombie; This mode, is possibly the most fun. You can either run around as a miner, blowing out zombie brains with a shotgun, or heaping up points as a sniper far away. In addition; who doesn't want to be a zombie, tearing the human's constructs down and feasting on their flesh?
Maps; The official maps, well some could use some work. Arctic base, the green team has a direct line of sight into the blue's at all times, and London is very open. However, most of the maps are decent, and there's the ability to make your own maps and share them with the community, so the world can know of your ingeniuty!
Community; The community in Ace of Spades is big (in my opinon) There are plenty of clans, some commpettitve, and some for just having fun. There are your friendly people, and there are the un-friendly people, but you can just ignore them. When people say "this game is dead" don't listen, they're just hating. (:
Verdict; All in all, this game is very good. I dont understand why people hate it so much, they're probably too upset about the beta. Now I'll put in some statistics, in case you were just too lazy to read my awesome knowledge about this game!
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-Maps;
Some maps need some work, but you can still just build your own (:
-Classes
The sniper class is too op (don't listen to those weirdos who say sniper is the hardest, that doesn't apply here!) it's just too easy to get headshots with their heads so huge and blocky!
Modes;
All the modes support every type of person, and are all fun.
Community;
Some people are jerks who can't take losing, but most are friendly!
Average; 8.8/10

Mais do que um jogo de tiro em terceira pessoa, esse daqui tem enredo interessante. O relacionamento entre os personagens, as diversas possibilidades de alterações do final e a ampla discussão sobre o quanto os robôs devem envolver-se no nosso dia-a-dia fazem valer a pena a trama. O sistema de upgrades é bom, mas poderia ser melhor, com mais armas, outros shock bursts e outras habilidades a partir das nanomachines. De qualquer forma, é uma aventura com começo lento, mas que vai ficando mais divertida com o passar do game. As piadinhas entre os companheiros, o romance, as gun fights e as action scenes vão melhorando a cada capítulo. Sugiro, sempre que possível, ignorar os metascores e experimentar os jogos por si mesmo, porque eles podem lhe surpreender.

Rather than focusing on nothing but action, Binary Domain creates a unique blend of RPG elements and third-person shooting. With an incredibly engrossing, philosophical story that will drastically change depending on how you treat and respond to your seven squadmates, perfect voice acting with many dialogue branches depending on which squad members you decide to accompany, and incredible diversity to the bosses you encounter and the strategies used to take them down, I find it hard to dislike this game, even though I usually despise third-person shooters. This is a truly unique experience, though it was sadly overlooked by the majority of gamers. If you find the chance, play this game. I wholeheartedly recommend it.

Mash every tired horror theme together and throw in Sebastian Castellanos, the 90 pound horror game protagonist who can run for about 15 feet before before he has to stop to catch his breath. This guy couldn't even bag groceries at a supermarket without having to constantly hold his knees to regain consciousness.
Remember how games in the 90s would make your blood boil because just getting touched by the boss once would make you have to replay the entire level? That's exactly what this is like, except games from the 90s were good.
If you've ever seen a bad slasher film, you've already played this game and can easily pass on it without missing anything.

Very fun and difficult game. One of my favorites. I would freak out whenever Laura would show up. A very difficult and scary boss. The ending's a bit stupid but most of the game is top notch. Definitly worth the money.

Edit: Thanks for telling me that hitting an enemy in the head with a bottle allows a sneak kill afterwards. In chapter 15!!!! The final chapter! Stupid "tips".
Edit 2: Ends on a ♥♥♥♥ing cliff hanger. Of course. Not sure if the DLC changes that.
"Pure Survival Horror Returns
Shinji Mikami, the father of survival horror, is back to direct a chilling new game wrapped in haunting narrative. Tension and anxiety heighten dramatically as you explore the game’s tortured world."
"The New Face of Horror
Experience a disturbing reality as you try to break free from warped machinations that could only exist in the most horrifying worlds. Defeat insurmountable terror and experience the ultimate thrill by discovering The Evil Within."
These are quotes from the game's store page...and that's why I have to give the game a "not recommended". It's not that The Evil Within is a bad game, it's just not a survival horror game.
The gameplay just contradicts these statements in every way. While the levels themselves have a haunting atmosphere, the gameplay is mostly "kill, kill, kill". There isn't any "big bad" in the game you can't kill (maybe initially). Heck, there are even boss monsters you have to off. To do so, you get pretty much every weapon in the 2nd or 3rd chapter. From hand gun to shot gun, sniper rifle or spear thrower or even melee weapons you can pick up, there's usually enough around to get you through a level. The biggest enemy here is not the enemy AI, but rather the terrible controller aiming (maybe you should play this with mouse and keyboard then), as well as the narrow view the game offers. The protagonist can also sneak around and 1 shot many of the normal enemies in melee if they don't see him. Yes, you feel REALLY powerful, especially since taking a few hits doesn't mean you're dead. You almost never feel powerless in this game. The few times you do are obnoxious boss fights you have to repeat until you realize what to do, then just follow the routine.
This is the antithesis of survival horror in my opinion. At no point in the game was I anxious or afraid to move forward. The game is gory and gruesome with good monster design, but those monsters are so "standard" to deal with. 1 example: Later on in the game you come into a room with a crank handle. You need to operate this to open a gate. By this time you know this won't work without enemies spawning (because the game does it almost every time and because there was another gate with a handle a few minutes earlier). So, you approach the handle and WOAH there are bodies falling through the ceiling. WHO would have thought. Now at this point that was actually new and I was thinking "huh, better get the ♥♥♥♥ out and grenade them to♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; (yes, you have grenades in this game -.-). Turns out that was a waste of a perfectly fine grenade since those enemies flop around helplessly like fish on land and can be "kicked" to death...*sigh*.
Like I said the most difficult aspect about EW is the camera and the aiming. The game's "artistic vision" means black bars that take over 1/3 or more of the screen estate, meaning you can't even see your own character properly and will get nauseated at worst. You can only shoot while aiming, which means the game will zoom incredibly far in and since you need head shots to dispose of enemies that could get problematic with a controller. My tip is to google how to get rid of the black bars and do so. I personally use r_forceaspectratio 2 to minimize black bars and still have a good aspect ratio that looks normal.
You should NOT unlock the frame rate. I learned that the hard way when I was stuck running away from a scripted mob. I checked online and all walkthroughs just said "yeah, just run away to complete the chapter". Turns out the ♥♥♥♥ing monster was running a lot faster thanks to the unlocked framerate...jesus christ. Reversed the change and completed it without issues.
The rest of the game constist of scavenging for ammo and some sort of "brain gel" or whatever to UPGRADE your character. Yes, you can get upgrades: more life, faster running, more damage, better accuracy, etc.
Another thing that doesn't fit a "survival horror" game imho.
The story is something I won't touch, since I still need to complete the game anyway, but it's "disjointed" to say the least. You better don't take too long to complete the game or you will have forgotten what is even going on. The characters also act completely unbaffled by the fact that they are now in some kind of hellish horror world...for whatever reason. It's a bit annoying that no one really acknowledges this. There is no sense of hopelessness...the protagonist, despite not looking the part, actually has the most positive attitude of all. Maybe he just loves mowing down hordes of mutants, because that is what you are doing in this game. Literally. There are chapters that just have constantly spawning enemies that you can shoot or hit or whatever.
If you want survival horror, play another game. EW is not it. If you just want to shoot mutants, you can buy this.

[I have far more than 5 hours in this game, I imagine because I played it offline it didn't count my numerous other hours spent here]
Nothing says TRUE Survival Horror like shooting up enemies with a turret and then running them over with a bus. This game lasts far too long, with an unengaging world that feels like the developers couldn't decide what setting they wanted as you are thrown from a mental hospital to an old village to pseudo-Silent Hill Otherworld corridors to catacombs, most of these being as much as a single level so you never have time to immerse yourself in any of these worlds before you're launched into a completely different one.
The story is absolute pants. It didn't interest me at all, and after the Big Twist (which I will spoil near the bottom, hidden behind spoiler text) it lost me even further. If changing my environment every 5 minutes wasn't immersion-breaking enough, the story twist was the final nail. The characters have absolutely no personalities whatsoever except for generic descriptions that could be applied to just about any character in the same area, in this case mostly detectives. Because of this, you can't help but not care for anybody in the story as there is nothing to care about.
As for the gameplay itself, it is incredibly repetitive, focusing heavily on generic zombie enemies that utilize a QTE grab attack 95% of the time. The stealth sections are tiresome as the AI isn't particularly smart or interesting, and you will find yourself waiting for far too long before having a window to progress. These stealth sections also only really cover the first chapter or two of the game. After that, ammo becomes fairly plentiful. You probably won't be breezing through things carefree, pockets lined with handgun bullets and shotgun shells, but you'll most likely have enough to get by without too much trouble. That is, until the game decides to throw all it can at you to completely starve you of ammo just to make the next area more obnoxious than it should be. Knocking enemies down also allows you to set them on fire, should you have matches, which kills them instantly and has a chance of setting other enemies close enough on fire, although this does not seem to work quite as often as you'd hope, and the game flat out forgets to give you matches through a big chunk of it iirc.
There are also far too many insta-kill situations, such as various traps and every boss being able to kill you just by coming into contact with you. This only adds a facade of difficulty and tension, and becomes incredibly tiresome after the third death. This, plus fairly infrequent and inconvenient checkpoints, creates a very frustrating experience.
Now let's talk designs. As far as the enemy designs go, it's fairly hit or miss here. Creatures such as Laura, the Shigyo and the Trauma, in my opinion, have very neat designs. However, the default enemy, the Haunted, are very generic looking, your standard Zombie with a bit of extra gore thrown in for good measure. These make up a very high percentage of what you will be fighting, and they're not particularly interesting in that regard either. There is a more dangerous common enemy introduced later in the game which are more interesting, looking like they would fit right into The Thing. I want to say I really do enjoy the Keeper's design, but it is held back by being a fairly blatant Pyramid Head knockoff. I don't hold that against the design too much, though, as despite lacking subtlety it looks cool and doesn't behave too much like Pyramid Head to be a total ripoff. Much later into the game, though, the enemy designs start to go a little overboard, with some of the creatures looking like incomprehensible piles of flesh and giving off a vibe of "trying too hard."
Personally I believe you can't really be frightened of something visually if you can't tell what it's supposed to even be.
The world design is inconsistent and most areas feel like a funhouse minus the fun, with traps everywhere and strange architecture that, while it might make sense in the story's context, continues to make the game feel completely unengaging. It's also nothing you haven't seen before with, as stated above, mental hospitals, old villages a la RE4 and destroyed cities.
Also at the start Sebastian can only sprint for about 2 seconds before he runs out of breath.
THE BIG TWIST:
TL;DR as I absolutely put way too much into this than it's worth:
+ Some interesting designs
+ Game feels a bit more solid when it sticks with a setting and environment for more than 5 minutes
+ Somewhat interesting boss fights. Maybe.
+ A li'l bonus from me for having a cool water monster even if it wasn't mechanically very interesting
- Unengaging world
- Uninspiring story and bland characters
- Lackluster enemy and world design overall
- Drags on far too long
- Frustrating stealth segments
- Numerous one-hit kill moments
- Repetitive
- The story gets more fleshed out and interesting, but only via DLC
- At one point you fight 2 keepers y'all ain't even tryin LOL
Unless you get this on sale for cheap or in a bundle, it´s not really worth buying, imo.

Played Rusty Lake Roots and very much enjoyed it.   Had similar hopes for Rusty Lakes Hotel but was to be sadly disappointed.
It has the same quirky artwork and surreal (macarbre) settings which is fine but the game suffers from a HUGE problem
That is, you can not SAVE the game and it's own AUTOSAVE funstion is totally f***ed up.
To explain . . .
Your task is to collect the cooking ingredients for a variety of meals (3 ingredients each)
There are essentially 2 location areas.  There's the downstairs lobby and the upstairs rooms.
For some of the menus, the ingredients you need are both in the lobby and in the bedrooms.
The way the game works is that once you enter a bedroom, it locks the door and YOU CAN NOT LEAVE THE ROOM until you have collected the "meat" element of the recipe for that room.  This is an immediate problem.  If you didn't realise that one of the ingredients was downstairs and you've entered the bedroom there is no NO WAY to complete the full recipe (for which you gain 3 stars).   It's insane.  You even get to go back downstairs after you leave the bedroom but the item you wanted can not then be acquired.
There's a similar problem with the order in which things MUST be done if you want to achieve the full list of 3 ingredients for each recipe.   For example in one room, you get a knife and you use it help you get into a box.  However it is also used to rip open a picture on the wall.  Guess what, if you open the box first then the knife stays there and can't be picked up again.  Result you can't complete the recipe.  WTF?!   There is literally no clue about this unspoken order that is required, you thus are forced to keep redoing the "level" (bedroom) until you get it right.  There is however a HUGE BUT . . . .
When you go to reload from the autosave it puts you back into the bedroom before you touched anything which seems great until you realise that your inventory is MISSING THE INGREDIENT  that you previously first picked up in the lobby !!!   So once again you now can not complete the full recipe to gain your 3 stars.   At this point you are totally stuffed.  Your only choice now is to restart the entire ****ing game !
Sorry but this is simply ridiculous.
Any player is going to want to at least be able to complete the game and do it properly to earn all the stars.   However it simply isn't possible due to that broken autosave problem.
After 3 bedrooms I had to abandon this.   I could put up with reloading specific bedrooms, if that actually worked, but having to restart the entire bloody game over and over to get a perfect score is just ludicrous.
A shame as Roots was a lovely game.  This is unplayable imo.

text:
People say that this game is bad as of the most recent updates, but as a new player I can honestly say I disagree.
The map-making mode is smooth and runs well no matter what I build, and there is a wealth of prefabs, very few of which are exclusive to the themed sets that can be chosen (mountain base, desert, ect). The easy to use UI made it easy for me to create, as of now, five small maps (which is what I intended to do, I was aiming for small maps) as well as a few unfinished projects.
The classes are your standard FPS-style units, with four of them to choose from. There's the commando, who is the classic, Quake-style class that has the ability to rocket-jump and chew up the map with his minigun. Then there's the marksman, who plays in the same way as a Counter-Strike player with the AWP - hit hard and keep moving. Third is the engineer, formerly the rocketeer, who has the largest pool of available blocks to build with and can reach great hights or avoid death with his jetpack. Finally, there is the miner (my perferred class), who can dig his own tunnels with the super shovel or drill gun, and can breach walls with TNT.
There is no way to comment all the maps, since anything is available to create. The stock maps, however, are vibrant and varied, from London to outer space. Most are too large for small teams, but that is why the map creation mode is there - to tailor the game to your liking.
Even though I got it for £1.99 in the sale, this game has already proved it worth after just over four hours of play time. 8/10.

This is a really fun game!  It's not pay to win, but does take some grind.  It's challenging enough on the grind, though, and so it doesn't get boring.  That said, it does take a while to learn how to play well.  Anyone can just pick it up, and get shot to death.  But, to survive, and get high scores, one needs to practice, and experiment.  It suits anyone's play style.  There's no right or wrong way to play.  Teamwork goes a long way, though.
No built-in voice communications.  Although, there's a vibrant community on Teamspeak.
The graphics are good, but can seem a bit dull, and jaggy.  I recommend disabling FXAA, and using SweetFX, but leave the DPX, and Cartoon off.  Looks great without them, and can see everything just fine.  Has flickering shadows on some Nvidia cards, which is because of Nvidia's drivers, and not the game engine.  Common problem those cards, and many game engines.  Also, for snipers, disable DoF, because it makes far away objects blurry, even through the scope.
Boosts can be bought through the store, but no amount of weaponry, or badges are going to make you a better player.  My advice, is only buy them, if you are getting good, and really need something.  Practice is more important, especially at lower levels.  Grinding for medals, ribbons, and upgrades will help improve your game, not buying upgrades.  Don't think of weapon upgrades as something to make the game easier.  They won't!  They offer an edge, but only to match a certain play style.  There are no ultimate weapons, and head shots are always one-hit kills, anyways.  Get better at head shots, and leading your targets, first.  And, don't spend any money upgrading low-level weapons.  Save your money for better guns, and upgrade those.  Again, upgrades only slightly tweak the weapon to suit your style, it won't make your play-style moot.  Also, all camo is ineffective.  Save your money, unless you just have a lot of it, and want the prestige.  Camo often makes you stand out more, and can get you killed.  Only rich players, or players who've grinded an awful lot of money wear it, and so it makes them prime targets.
Definately, add friends, and try to play together, as you can learn a lot from other players.  The people on Teamspeak are also very helpful.  Watch some YouTube vids, but expect your mileage to vary considerably.  You really have to find your personal taste.
Also, stay out of tanks, unless you're a very skilled player.  Tanks are just expensive explosives.  They're not in any way invincible, they move very slowly, and people love to blow them up.  ::raises hand::  You'll just go boom, and wish you hadn't.   They don't help that much in-game, either, because it's difficult, if not impossible to capture certain objectives from sitting inside them.  You will have to get out, and walk inside, and most likely get your head blown off.
Sniping also, takes practice.  So, get good with an unscoped rifle, and earn that scoped version the hard way.  You don't automatically get one for going Recon.  Recons, and all others carry less stuff, too.  Easier to figure out what you're good with, and prefer doing, if you can carry an assortment of armaments.
It's so enjoyable to get those epic kills.  Have fun, and don't give up!  You will die a lot!  Even experienced plyers die a lot.  Everybody dies.  Period.  There's just no way around it.  War is heck!
The biggest downside to this game is all of the whining and crybabies who don't even have the slightest clue what the point of the battle is. This is a capture the flag game, and practically nobody understands that fact very much, at all. They think it's like Counter Strike, and it's absolutely NOTHING like that game. There are only two kinds of enemies in Heroes & Generals: Obstacles, and distractions. Most players only focus on the latter, unfortunately. Nobody has any focus. Usually, it's up to one team member, or two, to carry the entire team. It's not uncommon for the player at the top of the score board to have double or tripple what the other players earn. And, usually, that guy is having what he considered a rough match, because he keeps getting killed, and can't make any meaningful progress. It's true, most team members are more of a hinderence than an asset. Of course, they all think they are the best. However, it's usually the case that the guy carrying the team has a score that is double, or tripple what the rest of the team has. He's not stealing kills, in fact, he usually has fewer kills than the guy in 4th place on the board. Kills are meaningless, in this game. Players will only respawn, and get sent back to the front line, where they are now in the way, again. They've just been converted from a distraction, and back into an obstacle for the lead team member to have to deal with. Killing them only helped the enemy. It's often better to let the enemy players live, and continue being where they shouldn't be, and doing what they shouldn't be doing. They aren't helping their team win, and are actually helping to lose the game for them. Killing them is doing the enemies a favor. LEAVE THEM ALONE, and simply sneak past them. By the time they figure out that they are not where they should be, it'll be too late, and they will be chasing after time, trying to make up for their mistake. This is a good thing for your team. So, I'll say again. Only kill people who are in your way, and hindering you from reaching your goal, and you should know, your goal is to capture the forward objective, and then MOVE ON to the next one. Stay focused on that, and try to control the pace of the battle. Don't let your enemy control where the front line is, or what pace the battle will be won (or lost) at. YOU need to be in control of the situation, and you do that by keeping your activities limited to capturing the next flag, and making sure the enemy is forced into constant retreat. They should be behind you; not in front of you. And, no player should be far away from that forward objective. Every tank, and every sniper should be where the team is at, and doing what the team is doing. Good luck with that, though. The theory never works out that way. So yes, you will have to do all of the team's dirty work. You have my condolences, but if I may mention, you'd best just get used to it. Don't try to herd the cats. You'll only succeed in driving yourself crazy. Besides, on the bright side, you're a hero! Our great savior! Praise you! And, peace be with you!

Like many early virtual pinball tables, Worms Pinball showed promise. All the classic pinball elements which you'd expect are there. An interesting table layout, a couple of multiballs, various modes with different objectives, nice ramp and orbit shots. Unfortunately, pinball emulation in 1998 was just not that sophisticated and that is ultimately what lets Worms Pinball down. The flippers are slow to respond, the physics are totally inaccurate and the visuals are just not very pretty. It's a shame because the theme is executed perfectly and if it were a real table it would be a blast to play. The callouts and sounds are great, the dot matrix animations are well done and the playfield design is cool. Disappointingly, that doesn't make up for the poor pinball simulation, which is what a game with pinball in the title should really be about.
P.S. Stern, please make this game.

Positives:
♦ Pinball (Who doesn't love Pinball?)
♦ Worms Theme with all the unique and classic sounds, sayings, animations and much much more (Who doesn't love Worms?)
♦ Highscores (Everytime you play you can try and beat your own highscore)
♦ Acts just like you were playing on an Arcade Pinball Machine at the bowling alley :P!
