Warhammer: End Times – Vermintide:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The empire fought bravely but there is no doubt mankind is on its last legs. An ancient, powerful and destructive enemy is rising again from deep underground. Half rat and half men, better known as the Skaven, will run at you as one massive wave over and over again!  Only five incredible people, no . . . heroes, are standing up to confront these packs of deadly vermin. Is it truly the end of time or is it possible to change the tide? Only YOU can find out the answer to this question by entering the fantasy world of Warhammer: End Times – Vermintide!
Warhammer: End Times – Vermintide is an Action/First Person shooter /Online Co-Op game where you take control of one of five characters; each has its own weapons and abilities to face the Skaven onslaught.

The action is taking place in the city of Ubersreik and its surroundings. Your first stop, like all good heroes, will be at a tavern. In this case, it will be the Red Moon Inn. Here, several options will be available to you. First, you can see the inventory of all your heroes which is located in the big chest near the table. You can change the melee and the range of weapons your character will be using in his/her next mission as well as his/her trinket or hat. At the forge, you can update or create new weapons or salvage material from weapons you collected.  At the Shrine of Solace, you can create your own trinket, but make sure you have enough stones (plentiful, common, rare or even exotic) to do so.  And of course the last one is the mission selection. In the original title, you have 13 missions available and they’re divided into three acts.
You can decide in which difficulty you want to play a mission. If it is the first time you have played this type of game, I strongly recommend that you start on the easy or normal level, especially if you’re playing your first couple of game with bots (AI is controlling the other three characters).  You have to win a mission on the difficulty you set to unlock the next difficulty. There are five in total, the two I mentioned above as well as hard, nightmare and cataclysm. For these last three, you need join a party of players to be able to win. Far too hard with the AI.
The gameplay is just incredible, no matter which character you play, and the fluidity of the animations is just marvellous! The missions vary from collecting items (barrels or supplies), to destroying specific landmarks, surviving and of course escaping in order to win it. Within the levels, you will find chests, sacks and boxes of ammunition. Chests have great goodies: health potions or kits, strength and fast potions. They might also contain special die or tomes; they will give you additional experience points at the end of the mission if you recover one or all of them.

Of the nine types of rat-men to fight against, four of them are soldiers. The Stormvermin unit will be the hardest of them to kill. The Ratling Gunner and the Poison Wind Globadier are a range units and can inflict severe damage to your character. Very deep world + gameplay allowing for an immersive medieval experience. Pretty hard to find a game that covers so many aspects of medieval times as well as this. Can't wait for Bannerlord to hopefully build upon such a solid foundation of a game.
Immersion: 8/10
You'll find yourself getting into the spirit of the game and creating your own storylines and narratives (in an otherwise sandboxy game) simply from the features offered. You'll rise from a wandering nobody to a fearsome ruler with his growing empire, all inside a fictional world that still captures various Euroasian cultures within the 6 in-game factions, and encounter just about every facet of what an actual journey like that would encompass. That so, there are some minor issues such as the occasional unexplained move from the AI, some UI inconsistencies, and some aspects of the game can become repetitive and even frustrating when they otherwise don't need to be.
Gameplay: 8.5/10
Lots to do, which makes for a fun game. For instance you can: Battle it out in a unique (and yet barebones) combat system in both land skirmishes and sieges on castles and cities, use the overworld map to move your party across the world making profitable trades and managing fiefdoms, train and arrange troops to help you in battle, and vie for power among the various in-game factions. Sometimes it can get repetitive though, and frustrating when some seemingly obvious features are left out for unexplained reasons.
Overall a very fun game easy to put many hours into, and with it's offering of tons of mods there's little reason you won't be playing this game over and over again.

About six years ago, Tom Clancy's 'End War' introduced  fully functional in-game voice commands.
Binary Doman introduces voice interactivity with the game's AI.   Your party members (the AI) will ask you questions and make small-talk with you based on the missions at hand, the decisions you make, and what you say back to them.  Why is that such a big deal? It adds another dimension of immersion based on the plot of the game (and not soley on idiots babbeling on about how good they are as they do in most party-reliant multiplayer games like Left4Dead, etc.).
Picture playing a mystery where the small talk you make, the freinds you choose, the questions you ask, and how you reply determine the information that you gather, and the outocme of the game.  Yeah, it has been done before without voice interactivity, but, with voice it, playing the role of the protagonist is that much more 'real.'
I hope this game going by unnoticed doesn't discourage its developers from the core concept.

This game is clearly pay to win.  While you can play through the game without spending anything purchased ships and items have clear advantages over the ships you aquire  through regular means.  Ground combat is hidiously designed and clunky as hell.  You'll find there are significant delays between ordering an attack and executing it.  The game offers a choice between "RPG mode" which does all the aiming for you and "FPS" mode which allows more action oriented combat, but there's almost never a reason to leave the aimbot mode.
Locations are generally uninteresting, and the game often doesn't reward exploration of any kind.  Puzzles in the game are often too easy to be considered interesting, and too long to be considered anything other than extremely annoying.  In fact, so much about away missions is annoying that you'll find yourself skipping as much text and dialog as possible just to get back in to space quicker.
The redeeming feature of this game is the space combat which is well executed and visually pleasing.  It's possibly the only interesting part of the entire game.
Like many other people, I figured this game would have a strong PvP element.  I chose to play as a klingon because the idea of engaging ships in raw comabt was appealing.  However as it turns out PvP queues are almost always empty and the likelihood you'll get to try PvP is almost nil.  I asked around about why PvP was so dead and .. SURPRISE: it's because the game balance is broken, and every experienced player knows it so they only play PvE.
Missions are mostly wooden and uninteresting.  Sometimes you spend a lot of time annoyingly running between two points.  90% of the items sold in the game require currency that you either have to pay for, or is difficult to figure out how to acquire.  The currency you get the most of (energy credits) is mostly worthless for anything other than buying items which won't be better than the drops you get or speeding up travel which can be very slow over long distances.
This game had the potential to be something special, particularly with the space combat which will suck you in - at least at first.  However it drops the ball in so many ways you'll wonder why you bothered to waste time with this dud.

Layers of Fear is an excellent narrative experience, successfully crafting an immersive story and rich, detailed world that captivates until its conclusion. Atmosphere is handled very well through beautiful music, detailed environments that felt lived in, and fairly good pacing. The game did have some downsides, however. Early on, scare chords clashed with the otherwise subtle use of suspense. I am hesitant to call the game scary, though "intense," "suspenseful," and "engaging" are apt descriptors. I was enthralled with the game and had to finish the base story in one sitting. I assume there are more endings, but after the first playthrough I had of the game once it left early access, I felt little reason to replay it. Overall, I think it's worth playing if you like immersive games with interesting stories, but I think if the term "walking simulator" makes you hesitate to pick it up, then go with your gut instinct. This probably isn't the game for you.

SIMPLE:
Enjoyed Left 4 Dead 2?
Love murderizing loads of enemies?
Enjoy Co-Op?
Dreaming about a variety of weapons ranged and melee?
Get dis muddafukin' game.
IN-DEPTH:
The game features similar ''special/specialized'' rat types like in Left 4 Dead, hordes of rat-men to slaughter, and a WIDE range of weapons (depending on your character) from shields/swords, 2-handed melee weapons, daggers, bows, crossbows, hammers, and flame/poison weapons! Gear also have a rarity/quality system which is neat. It's quite melee-based and thankfully, the main part of the game: melee combat, is very meaty/gory and feels satisfying. If you hit a rat-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, he's gonna feel it.
It also has a very entertaining loot system where exploring can either; be quite rewarding, or you'll eventually go back only to have a bowl filled with your tears. Basically, a risk vs reward situation. The entertaining part being the reward you get upon completing a mission. Depending on difficulty, and special, hidden ''books'' hidden around the map that you collect, you can acquire some of the best gear. The reward system is you rolling several dies into a metal pot, and whatever number you roll, a meter on the right will go up. The higher = the better in gear rarity/quality.
Only negatives I have with the game is, it CAN feel a bit grindy and/or repetitive if you're playing alone/trying to acquire the best gear/weapons. But I tell you, it can be very rewarding and worth it, and just try to not let that feel of grinding/repetitive get to you. There's also not alot of content, missions-wise, in the base-game, there's only about 8. The DLC's thankfully tho, are very nice.
Game is overall good, feels very nice and is quite fun, gives me Chivalry and Left 4 Dead vibes together which is cool, but I think shines the most in co-op with amigos.

So, I know a lot of people might hate me for this. But I'll just speak my mind.
I don't have a whole lot of hours in the game yet, but enough to tell my thoughts about it.
I have more than 100 hours in Banished too, so I can trully do a good comparison still.
People saying it's just like banished. They aren't wrong. That's true. I am aware that there IS a lot of stuff that does seem copied from banished, and I certainly can say, it is wrong. But honestly?
Life is Feudal still offers a lot more than Banished. And I do expect more from the game than Banished gave.
-In banished, You cannot upgrade your buildings. Life is feudal can.
-In banished, it is a very simplistic graphic and view model. In life is feudal, you get a massive look improvement compared to banished.
-In banished, you don't have sea explorers or anything. Life is feudal does.
-In banished, you have... Fish, meat, most crops and living stock, fruits and such. Alright. But in Life is feudal... The wheat you grow, you need to grind it into a flour to make bread. You get more kind of fruit, you get additional processing steps to make pies for exemple. In banished, no such things. Apparently they can eat the wheat directly.
-In banished. There is no ocean. Unless you mod it. Life is feudal, on the other hand, only has island, sadly. Could use more terrain type, hopefully later on, more will be added.
-In banished, you cannot control your citizen in a 1st person view, and do whatever you want with them. Life is feudal can. In fact, I would have loved that kind of ability in Banished because I've seen so many time my stupid people do other things than what should have been prioritized. In life is feudal, since I can control them, I can make sure that something imporant is done. In time.
-in Banished, you cannot build decoration, or castles, or walls. Life is feudal. You can. And I'm talking about vanilla game. No modding.
-in Banished. You only have stone wood and iron! which are mysteriously already ingots. in Life is feudal, you have clay and hay too! And the ore is ore! if you want iron ingot you got to smelt it first! Again NO MODDING!
I may miss more, but these are the one I can recall perfectly from playing Life is feudal.
I honestly love Life is feudal, and I expect to play it a lot more than banished. Because of what it offers more than banished in term of vanilla game.
Do not agree with me? Suit yourself.

The meowment Cat Quest loaded, I was pawsitive I was in for a grrreat time.
Okay, got that out of my system we can move along now. If there is anything that the internet doesn’t get bored of it’s cats. I can’t exactly explain it, but an obsession that goes back to Egyptian times can’t necessarily be overrated. Cats invading video games isn’t exactly new either, with games such as Cat Goes Fishing, Catlateral Damage, Fort Meow and many more. Maybe I have been fortunate, but I have enjoyed them all and never been left with a fishy taste in my mouth. When I heard about Cat Quest, an open world RPG, I knew I had to check it out.
Needless to say guys, its pretty pawsome.(I swear that’s the last one.)
Right off the bat, I do recommend Cat Quest. Not just because its adorable and over the top, akin to something like Slime Rancher. I recommend it because I genuinely had a blast and couldn’t stop playing the game until it was all over. If Cat Quest accomplishes anything, it is that it is super simple and fun to play. This game is going to attract a wide age group and its got something for all of them.
As soon as you start the game and get past some story tidbits, the first thing I noticed was this huge vivid over-world map. Felingard is the name of this huge continent and you will explore all of it. This map isn’t just a means of getting from place to place. This map is the game. Monsters, towns, and events play out on this screen or one of the fifty two dungeons. You begin your epic quest to defeat a mysterious figure named Drakosh and his dragons.
The combat itself is all real time from an isometric view. The beautiful part is that the combat is super simple but manages to stay complex enough to keep you on your toes. You can slash with your equipped weapon, dodge roll, or cast one of the many spells in the game. This is one game I highly recommend you play with a controller. The enemies telegraph their attacks with either a red circle or symbol to represent a spell they are about to cast. Some enemies are faster than others and using different spells/tactics to overcome them is required.
The problem I found with Cat Quest’s combat is that it tends to have extremes. The combat is either far too easy or you’re going to die very fast. It never quite hits that sweet spot in the middle. Cat Quest does however have a good pace as the dungeons themselves range from level 1 to 99. If you find it to be too easy then just hop into a dungeon five or six levels higher than you and feel the pain. The dungeons themselves are rather simplistic in design and more about combat and loot.
Loot in this game I felt a bit divided on. Cat Quest has a stat system with the usual suspects, e.g. health, magic, damage, armor. You can mix and match armor pieces to create your own play style. If you don’t like physical attacks, then wear magic armor. Some armors even go to extremes giving huge benefits to one stat and taking away from others. Also some armors just suck in general, guess they are there to keep the game challenging maybe? The problem lies in Golden Chests.
Sometime in the middle of the game you will get access to these beauties. Golden chests contain rare loot. These rare items can break the game quite easily. I stumbled upon an item called Courage that gave me vast amounts of health. This item made bosses seem like they were tickling me and I just stood there whacking away at them. Now I could’ve not used that item, true, but I didn’t know any better. Plus if it’s in the game, why not use it? Cat Quest respects your time as a player and for that I appreciate it. However, the game’s combat just loses some of its enjoyment once you gain access to these golden chests. It’s like the game gave up and handed me the win.
That isn’t to say I didn’t love the combat in Cat Quest, I just wanted the last boss to actually be a challenge instead of dead in five seconds. I think the combat system had great potential to keep things fresh and fun all the way until the end. Cat Quest didn’t need to hand me the keys to the kingdom, proverbially.
Side quests and story galore.
One of the main highlights of Cat Quest is by far is its dialogue/story. Side quests are filled to the brim with cat puns, and hilarity. There are times where I found myself genuinely laughing and that isn’t an easy task for a game when it comes to me. On top of that, there is actually a pretty intense lore here that I found myself being wrapped up in as the game progressed. Drakoth’s story and the birth of the Dragonbloods is very interesting and far from what I expected.
The story isn’t one dimensional, despite appearing that way. The reason behind dragons tearing up the place is rather sad. When I finally reached the end of my “Cat Quest” I was left with far more questions than answers. Which also left me with a bit of a gripe. The end feels like it’s baiting for a sequel or DLC. While I don’t want to give any spoilers, Cat Quest comes to a climax with a threat looming, but the game just ends abruptly. It felt odd. Queen’s Bay an area that has one quest and no follow ups, more or less confirms this suspicion. Then again, more Cat Quest is hardly a bad thing.
In all, the side-quests were fun and enjoyable. They brought a life and personality to the world that left me wanting more. I can’t wait to see the Mice Pirates and the Lupus Empire. There was one side quest though that annoyed me to no end. One which had you traveling back and forth from opposite ends of the continent. Silly Chef cats.
Another obvious statement is that Cat Quest is very family friendly and pleasing to the eyes. This game is candy wrapped up in kittens. One fear I had was that the huge over world map would be one tone but Cat Quest does manage to keep things varied. You will venture on islands, snow caps, plagued lands and more. The art is very well done and mixes seamlessly with the combat and magic effects.
The monsters, and sprites themselves are cute and I couldn’t help but chuckle when I put a big metal helmet on my cat. Item design is one area that I was also impressed with. It added plenty of personality on its own. An area that didn’t hit the mark for me was the menus. They were very bare-bones. Cat Quest is also available on mobile devices, and it shows in the menus especially.
The music and sound effects are as equally pleasing to the ears as the graphics are to the eyes. Every time I heard a meow when I got hit, it made me smile. There were times people nearby thought an actual cat was meowing, if that tells you anything. The music is as fun and adventurous as is required for this type of game. You can expect an orchestral soundtrack and if you keep moving in the game, no one track over stays its welcome.
I guess you could say I had a purrfect time.
Sorry I lied, I couldn’t help meowself.
I finished the game out at about nine hours and that was getting all the current Steam Achievements. Including all the outfits, and clearing all the dungeons. You’re looking at anywhere between six to ten hours total playtime. The game doesn’t have much in the way of replay. There is no new game+ and it’s basically a get done and go type of deal. Keep an eye out though for future DLC or an update. Aside from the achievements across all platforms, there are also Steam Cards. Obviously that’s computer only.
To wrap up, I found Cat Quest to be a highly enjoyable popcorn style game. You eat it, you love it, it’s bad for you chances are, but hey life is short and there is cats. It’s not going to rock the boat for innovation or expand your mind on new levels of philosophy. What it is going to do is give plenty of entertainment that you or your kid can enjoy together. I personally think it’s a good homage to the ARPG genre and worthy of your attention. Did I mention the cats?

I watched someone play a bit of Cat Quest and I thought to myself "would the novelty wear off and the cat-jokes fall flat after a while?". I decided to give it a try as a couch-relaxing game, and I loved it.
While the cat/purr/mew/paw jokes are repeated over and over again (maybe a bit too much, but as some say "so bad it's actually good") they actually help keeping the tone and atmosphere where it should be, never taking itself too seriously. It is a game, after all, and we already have plenty of "serious" games.
The gameplay felt fantastic and quite responsive, even though I played it from the couch with a steam controller while streaming the game off another PC. You can also tell the game is also pretty well crafted and balanced, with a touch of "dark souls" difficulty: the quest level is a mere indication, not a necessity, and while significantly harder nothing stops you from doing quests or engaging monsters 50-150 levels higher than you. For example I did one of the toughest side quests (level 99) around level 55-60. It proved VERY challenging, but significantly fun and engaging (and also rewarding, mind you).
While not an extremely long game, if you're just looking for something to play over a weekend, from the comfort of a couch, this game is terrific. The devs also hinted to possible future expansions, and given the fun I had with this game, I'll definitely look forward to it.
TL;DR: highly recommended.

The one good part about this game is that the controls are relatively tight.
Hit detection is a joke. The sound effects are either royalty free or literally the Mario 1 UP noise. It's impossible to tell the difference between a wall that can and cannot be wall jumped. (This is only mostly true. SOME walljumpable walls are marked, but not all of them.) The amount of damage enemies do is seemingly unrelated to what they are. Stationary spikes are a heart and a half. Moving smashy spike columns are half a heart.
Some enemies will hurt you when you jump on them, but also take damage. It's impossible in many cases to tell when a cliff will lead to more level or will instantly kill you. It has a lives system with coins, but the lives and coins don't carry over between levels. The final boss gives you 100 bullets, but those bullets don't refresh between lives, though the final boss's health -does-. This game takes less than an hour to beat. Pursuant: I have, in fact, beaten the game.
The background art is pretty good, but the other tilework is terrible. Enemies can have the same sprite, but vastly different mechanics and different health. You have to manually select the next level after you beat a previous one.
The 'beat the game' art is actually worse than the title screen graphic. Of the guns you can get, one of them is an actual upgrade, and one of them shoots three shots (which you will never need) for three times the ammunition, which is acceptably sparse to begin with except for when you get a million ammo in areas with like three enemies.
The box physics are horrendous. In one level, I pushed a box down a thin shaft, and it got stuck halfway. Boxes on moving platforms will skitter around like nervous squirrels, and none of the puzzles are interesting enough to merit there even being box-pushing in the first place.
There's an enemy that is basically a koopa troopa, but not a single level ever puts you in a situation to use this to your advantage, or against you. It's there just for the sake of being there.
TL;DR Quite literally everything in this game that is not 'controlling Super Mustache' is achingly bad.

The game is exactly what it says - you're a bunch of rats hopping around playing instagib. The music plays like a little radio in the corner and you can hit pause to change it at any time you want. The music kind of has that late 90's feel, reminds me of the Dreamcast days. It's awesome.
The game has a lot of maps for an Early Access game and is getting great support from it's lone developer who is active on the forums listening to suggestions and squashing new bugs rather fast, which is always great. I'm impressed with how far this game has gone and I can definitely suggest this game, especially to those who loved playing instagib mods back in the day.

Second, the standard stuff you get is...ehhh...ok.  I haven't played much, so I don't know the knitty gritty details about the gear. Common gear, in my experience.
Space battles are much more well done.  it actually feels like Star Trek, unlike ground combat.  Who doesn't want to fly around in a spaceship and blow everything up?
All in all, good game, but I would not recommend playing it.  Getting zen and trying to get a new ship is nearly impossible unless you pay for it, and that's a step too far for me.

Layers of Fear is a first person adventure horror game, developed by Blooper Team, and published by Aspyr Media. The game was released in February 2016 on PC, PS4 and Xbox One. This is probably the most notable title to come out of the Polish based development studio.
You take on the role of a 19th century painter, aiming to finish his masterpiece. You follow the harrowing tale of this man who struggles with mental illness which leads you down a troubled path into his mind along the way. The game is split into 6 chapters, each chapter’s aim is to find a key item that helps you complete your masterpiece. Whilst the main story is fairly linear, you do get chances to break off the main path to explore the dark and spooky manor in which the game takes place in. You will be able to find family heirlooms which contains snippets of extra plot for you to delve deeper into this ghostly plot. The exploration portion of Layers of Fear reminded me a lot of Outlast – the way you explore rooms and navigate around the world has many similarities. There isn’t a combat system in Layers of Fear, again like Outlast, but this is because you won’t really run into any combat facing scenarios. You will come up against your foes, but these will be part of scripted events which you cannot escape or bypass from.
As you would expect from any Adventure game, the puzzles are your standard “horror style”, that usually involve the use of candles, dead babies and dolls, blood written on walls to reveal codes for lock doors and many more. I really enjoyed working out the resolution to all of the puzzles throughout, and was pleasantly surprised with myself when I did it all unaided without a walkthrough.  Some of the puzzles were sadly marred with technical problems, which resulted in me needing to load from a previous check point, because simple things like objects that you need to move, suddenly stop being able to be moved. These small technical issues grew a little tiresome towards the latter chapters as game’s checkpoint system is not the best to say the least.
The graphics in Layers of Fear look spectacular – the game is built on the Unity 3D engine so the highly details character models and locations were brought to life. The scares use of lighting is used perfectly as it leads you down an even darker path throughout the game.  The manor you are exploring is filled with creepy art work on the walls, which are well worth the time just to check out.
The game took me just over four hours to complete, I managed this in on sitting which is something to be noted as I often find adventure games like this to be slow paced and I usually need to break it up into multiple sessions. The game’s pacing right from the start is slow, but you are able to take the game at your own speed. If you want to spend an extra fifteen minutes exploring the house, go right ahead, it’s not going to deter you the path, however if you choose not to, you won’t be missing key plot points by skipping over the extra lore items that can be found.
Layers of Fear does offer alternative endings; these are done by playing the game in certain ways, for instance not picking up the hidden secrets throughout a play through will unlock a special ending; this encourages players to do more than one run and will reward them rightly so at the end.
I would have to say Layers of Fear has been a brilliant adventure game that hit all the sweet spots for any horror story. The game is owned by over 100K players, so it has been accepted by the wider audience, and rightly so. It’s hard to find fault with many aspects of this game, and the price tag is fairly targeted for a game with plenty of replay value.

Finally, a narrative experience that utilises player identification and perspective to narrate a story through the medium of gaming itself! 'Layers of Fear' draws on art history, Lovecraft, Poe and others, synthesising them into a psychological exploration of an artist's fractured mind as he attempts to work through the loss of his family.
In terms of mood and mechanics, it feels somewhat like what I saw of the 'Silent Hills' demo; you explore and interact with the environment to move the story forward: the way you interact with the world will affect how things unfold. It falls somewhere between the uninteractive walking simulator and a full adventure game. However, the game's relative lack of mechanics never bothered me, as the art and sound design, the narrative, the environments, the use of visual effects to suggest feelings/mental state are all absolutely brilliant and compelling in their own right.
This is one of the very few games that have ever delivered on the promise of telling a story effectively through a game engine, while also using game mechanics effeciently and intelligently to enhance its storytelling. I look forward to seeing whatever this studio comes up with next.

This game will practically hit you over the head with how much of a big Japanese blockbuster it is. Tired of the whole "zombie scene"? Well, then maybe you should look into Binary Domain, the third person cover/squad-based shooter where you shoot ROBOTS. Pick your two teamates for your squad that you can change at designated moments, each with their own special skills and weapons, enhance their skills as well as your own, and command your team WITH YOUR VERY OWN VOICE. That's right, if you have a mic, you can set it up to use voice commands with your voice and Dan Marshall (the main character you play as) will repeat it and your allies will respond. But that's if they like you, if you shoot them or do things they don't like, they may not even obey direct orders! It's a fun game, shoot off an android's weapon arm, he'll just pick the gun up with his other arm and continue shooting. No legs? They crawl and grab you. Fast-paced, epic shooter action with a thrilling story, great voice-acting, epic writing, and uber-awesomeness.

The squad mechanics are poorly executed; your squad shoots (and kills) enemies just like you do, but I hardly even had to use the squad menu to command them, and when I did it seemed to make no difference at all. The idea behind it was good though.
Same goes for the loyalty system. It seemed to make no difference. At. All.
So... an average game.

Hard to recommend this game at the moment. It is so similar to Banished, and adds so little, with problems that are long fixed in Banished.
Firstly this does have better graphics, and the first person mode is useful to use.
Problems and Issues:
1) There is a woeful lack of decorations, placables, clutter objects, whatever you want to call them. No decorative trees, gardens, dock items like crates or nets, fountains. There is some walls, arches, signs and light posts, that's it.
2) There are no couples. People will move to the closest house to their job. This can mean houses full of only women or men or even only young children. Women seem to magically get pregnant, based on the house they live in.
3) The people are work units. They never get bored, which is good because there is literally only the tavern, which isn't that useful. No games or recreations or festivals or even idle chatter.
OK these three problems mean the game has a massive lack of personality. You get food, have houses, make tools and clothes. Grats you are done.
4) Farming is based on temerature. This forces the gameplay around a winter mechanic that drops temperature to stop farming. Longer winters = less farming time. Crops don't have a planting season, they have a planting temperature. You can usually do 2 harvests in a field. Game seems balanced for this. Breaks immersion a bit and also means the game is impossible to have a hot climate option, since it would be year round farming = too easy. Hot climate have it's own challenges. Australian here, want winter planting and early summer harvesting :(
5) Map generator makes janky maps. Needs a loooot of work. All maps are island that centre is high ground. No lakes, no rivers, no plains.
Unlike banished which had every food item be it's own item (gather collected mushrooms, onions, blueberries, etc, same for each field crop, etc, etc). This game simplifies those to fruit and vegetables.
To be honest everything the devs seem to have done is to have the game be mechanically functioning while making it easy to code. Having each crop have it's own growing time and storage icon is a lot of work, having people live as couples in the same house, that's more work. I want more work. This game could be great, but it needs the hard work to make it great. Right now it's Banished with better graphics and less personality or gameplay.

I've played banished as well and both of these very recently in order to compare so here we go:
Yes it clearly is a blatant rip off of banished, I'm very surprised if there isn't a legal issue going on here somewhere. That said banished is as far as I can see a finished game and this is still being updated. So what does it have that banished base game doesn't:
More buildings, different and better music (subjective), does not have irritating building, stonemining, cutting, farmyard noises which drown out everything else, houses are better and more varied with upgrade options, better UI more information is given in the base state of clicking on a house and menus provide clearer more detailed information overall, houses work better for family arrangements, no more old people causing the death of said village by hogging homesteads. Wildlife, which at the moment doesn't do a lot except add hunting options as the bears don't seem nearly hostile enough and there are too many of them, the ability to build walls and decorations. mines of which they have added a clay mine are more easily built and don't leave horrible huge holes, Vastly improved graphics.
Possibly balance issues: Farming is a little funny, you can't assign more people to efficiently harvest a field, (it gets done when it's done) which is a problem if you're nearing winter which will destroy all the crop. General laborers and builders are terrible about getting their work done and will often be assigned from the furthest away house only to tap once or twice at their job and then run home to sleep. Day and night cycle which doesn't make a lot of sense given it's fast seasonal. Trees make it very hard to see the village leading you to often clear large spaces around village even if you didn't need to.
Overall the game is more fun to play for me than banished and the fact that people are still working to improve/tweak it makes it worth recommending.

OK, a lot has changed since the last update and it is quite positive.  I have been playing this game for a while and I like it quite a lot.  First, the negative: you need some grinding (which is annoying) and you have to think of this like a shooter-RPG game, where your soldier "improves" as you rack up experience.  Of course, your experience as player counts even more: knowing where to run, where enemies usually lurk, etc.  It is fun to play, and it has very interesting concepts (airplanes, tanks, infantry, vehicles, all in one fight).
I have seen a lot of negative reviews from people, but I must say that these guys just didn't get it.  I will try to address a few of these concerns, so that you can enjoy the game and don't make the same mistakes:
#1 The game is pay to win: people enter the game for 10 hours, get rolled over, rage quit and scream: "pay to win!".  So, these guys expect to kill people like me who have been playing for months, knows the maps, understand each wepon's strengths and weaknesses... simply delusional.  I don't think I managed to kill more than 1 player when I started and god knows how many times I died.
#2: Tanks are OP: common sense tells you that, if you run in front of a tank's turret, the tank will blow you up... yes, they are annoying, but as infantry you got AT weapons that will make tank drivers cry (I know, I love to watch them blow up).  Just make sure to sneak behind them instead of running around like headless chickens.
#3: It is hard to level up: although it is somewhat true (you can't go to level 15 in one day as you would in any MMORG), you need to understand what gives you exp: defending objectives and capturing objectives.  Kill-to-Death ratio is just for bragging purposes.  If you have 30 kills, 0 death and only 300 points (points = experience given at the end of the match), you are doing things terribly wrong.  Capturing an objective (which can take as little as 30 seconds) grants you 50-200 xp.  And you get 60 XP for each enemy killed that is attempting to capture (i.e. defending).  Blowing up enemy tanks grants 40 xp... killing a random person who is not doing anything useful: 3 xp (good luck leveling up if you go duck hunting).
#4: Submachine guns are annoyingly inaccurate and suicidal to use (yes, hard to believe but I did read this one): Submachine guns are close quarter weapons.  Don't try to use it as sniper rifle...
#5: Bolt Action rifles and they can 1-hit kill... it is OP!! (After getting all the upgrades): yes, they are annoying, but you should not run around as moving targets in an open field... use cover, bend with the environment, use buildings...
And you can also hear where they are and go and hunt them down! Usually, players playing sniper can't detect your presence before you get too close.  And actually, the bold action rifle is quite difficult to "level up" to the point where it can 1-hit kill (and unless you are willing to pay like 1 000 EUR (without exaggerating, pay to win his difficult in this game), you can't really buy it with real money, so the player has gone through quite some pain to get this cool 1-hit kill weapon.  Oh, and the player who does pay the 1000 EUR to get it without grinding? well, if he is willing to dish out that much, he is the reason why the rest of us can play for free.  And this poor soul will figure out that bolt action rifles need skill to use (When I finally got my first sniper rifle, I found out the hard way that they are not that easy to use...)
#6 The credit reward system is broken: "credit" is the in-game currency.  It was broken until the last patch (you would sometimes have to repair more than you could earn if a game became too long, because they gave you a flat amount of credits per game).  Now, the credit system seems to be working quite well.
#7 Everything needs repairing and is too expensive: and again, the pay-to-win argument.  More powerful weapons are more expensive to repair, but unless you start shooting without thinking, I can't see a way to lose more money than you earn since the introduction of the new patch (they increased the amount of money earned depending on the playing time).
I think there are a few more complains out there, but I can't remember right now.
The game has some negative aspects as well, but I think it is doing overall pretty well for a beta.  Those issues are:
- The match making can be terrible: they can throw you into a game where all your enemies are experienced players while yours are newbies.  It can also throw you in a game that is 5 minutes from finishing.  I hope they fix that.
- We all like to whine: US players say that German and Russian weapons are OP, Germans say that US and Russian weapons are OP, Russians say that they have the worse weapons of all factions... so, the grass is always greener on the other side...
- Queues for the german faction can be long: everyone seems to want to play Germany, so the queues therecan be quite long (minutes, in contrast to seconds for the other factions).  The point is that German players seem to have a better team spirit than their US counterparts.  But this is changing rapidly as bad players join the German ranks , under the believe that the German weapons are OP, to the point that I am switching to the Russian side.  Russia is still a new faction, so they have less experienced characters (but have quite a bunch of experienced players).
I hope this review is helpful.  I think the game has its defects, but it is worth the try.  Just use your brain while you play instead of playing rambo.

In Zelda games, Link has a "Pushing" animation or "Pulling" animation, that doesn't exist in this game. Is that too much to ask??? I last played (or tried to) this game a couple of years ago and was disappointed to say the least. It had a weak introduction followed by the game promptly crashing after the space tutorial started. Needless to say I uninstalled it and thought no more of until now. I used to really like star trek and the new film reboots got my interest again. Anyway I thought I would give the game one more shot and glad I did. It seems to have improved a lot from my last experience. Its a lot more stable and with some tweaking here and there I have got it looking good. They have also changed the tutorials and added a lot more content along with the most recent expansion. You get an awful lot with the free to play side of the game. The game is still not perfect though as the odd bugs can surface. The UI can also be very confusing at first and you will probably want to customise it to suit your needs. That aside, you do have to devote quite a lot of time before you start to see everything the game has to offer. It is without a doubt probably the best star trek title there has been in its long history of jaded game releases. It also still has a very much active community keeping it alive. There are a huge amount of customisation options for your ships and characters. This is a great feature as it means not everyone has to go around with the same looking ship or characters. There are some cool features I like to. With the federation ships the name you give it will appear on the saucer section. That really makes it feel like your own ship. As you complete space and away team missions you earn skill points. These can be used to upgrade your own skills and that of your senior officers. The game offers both PVP and PVE environments. I haven't tried the Romulans yet, but have started a Klingon character. Although gameplay and layout is similar, the culture and storyline is very different from that of the federation. The ships are different, with the most obvious being the Klingons cloaking device. As in the films it seems the Klingon ships are more about offensive, as opposed to the federation's more defensive approach.
All the major locations are in the game including Kronos, Vulcan and Starfleet academy. All of the star trek's favourite villians are here including the ever popular Borg. Regardless of which of the three factions you join, you can choose from a range of different alien types depending on who they are allied with.
If you hate star trek then don't even bother installing this. If you are or have been interested in star trek then chances are you may already be playing this. If not then do yourself a favour and try it out. Its the only game out there now keeping the spirit of the series and films alive.

I play a lot of horror games, but few of them scare me as much as The Evil Within. There's a little bit of everything here: Texas Chainsaw Massacre, Silent Hill, zombie horror, Saw, and body/medical horror. Probably more I haven't even discovered yet, because the game keeps surprising me. The essence of horror is dreading what comes next, or fearing that you won't be able to survive it. The Evil Within makes me do both, because it's challenging enough that I'm constantly fearing death, and inventive enough that I'm not sure what I'll encounter and afraid that the rug can be pulled out from under me at any given time. It's a good feeling, when you're looking to get scared.  Although the comparison has been made already, it's very similar to Resident Evil 4, although much scarier. Many elements are there; the traps, the zombies, head parasites, an infection in the main character and his partner, giants, and freakishly mutated dogs. The longer the game goes on, the more its influence becomes clear, although it isn't really a problem. The story does wear as it gets to the final chapters, though. I think that maybe 2 chapters could have been cut to tighten up the game, and that maybe focusing on smaller enemies, chases, and stealth might have kept the tone scarier than when it shifts to House of the Dead-style giant bosses. Still, this game is great and I haven't felt this engaged with a horror game in a long time. I'd highly recommend it to any fan of the genre.

Ever run out of ammunition, and had to loot the dead for weapons? Check.
This game has it all. And if you're a fan of turn based tactics games, you owe it to yourself to check it out.

I like this game a lot - and I've found it very different from Banished. The graphics are great and have a properly medieval look. I love the eye-level view. Farmers seem much more important in this game and need to grow resources like flax and hay (for clothes and building) not just food. I like that you have to water fields and both feed and water livestock. I haven't got as far as a bakery yet, but I like the idea that baked goods are more nutritious than basic food. And I very much like the idea of moving goods from barn to barn. The best feature for me, though, is that the forest is itself a character in the game as it keeps trying to encroach on the village - I don't bother with a forester now as the trees grow back on the edge of the village quickly enough to keep it supplied with wood. And, of course, the animals. It's annoying to have your chickens eaten by foxes, wolves and bears (and, yes, I built a coop far too early in the game), but very realistic. It's a slow game as it takes years to build up to enough adults to expand much beyond food production, but maybe all the better for it. That said, it doesn't feel finished yet. The game crashes to the desktop everytime the screensaver comes on, and the main menu looks very basic. Still, I'm looking forward to many hours of play and more features as the developers have said they are continuing to develop the game.

-Pros-
-The Graphics in this game are very colorful and meld very well with the world. They seem to make every part of the world blend together in a painting, but the painting is a open world RPG.

Surprisingly good and fluent (although a little simplistic) combat in a world where cats rule - this time literally.
Puns are more hit than miss, stories make sense (usually) and are a blast to go through, very rarely outstaying their welcome. Main story is well thought out and you might want to have a second playthrough to see if you spot some stuff that will make more sense.
Inventory system is a little different -  duplicates level your existing items. This works well for the most part, although if you get a streak of 1 item dups, it gets a little too powerful.
From difficutly perspective, game is definitely on the easier side of things, at least if you use the dodge-roll correctly.
World is consistently built, with characters that just fit in it - from the random villager to main characters they feel a part of it.
Overall it was much better than I expected. While some of the time was just on pause (paws) screen, the ~8 hours of relaxing gameplay was definitely worth the price.
Becomes even more ameowzing if you play it with someone else, as the humour spreads rapidly.
Definite recommendation if you look for a relaxing, yet surprisingly fluent little game. Cats are a bonus ;)

This was simply a-meow-zing to play.
Chock full of cat puns and visuals, there is little to dislike about the game. A top down ARPG with everything centered around cats, what could possibly go wrong? Melee attacks are assigned to one button with a simple 3 hit combo, regardless of weapons. Magic however can get pretty interesting. There are 4 slots to equip different spells each being assigned to a trigger or shoulder button. In practice this a fun way to mix and match the spells to counter enemies.
The majority of the adventure has you on a map overworld searching for dungeons. The first few hours feel fresh, however this gameplay loot repeats for the remainder of the game. Quests are all fetch/kill quests which have you go to another dungeon. While the game pokes fun at this RPG trope, it also follows it to a T.
My only real gripe has to do with the nature of chests. There is only one or two chests available in each dungeon and they do not reset upon completion. Depending on your look you could get a great item that you want, or a useless one. Getting a repeat item from the chest simply upgrades it. When going for the achievement for obtaining all items I had to do quite a bit of extra grinding since each roll is against the entire set of equipment.
Definitely a fun little jaunt if you don't mind the repition.

Interested in a game where you can turn your brain off while enjoying cute visuals that have more polish then most indie titles in this genre? Then Cat Quest is for you. It's smooth and simplistic gameplay combined with low consequences for failure made this a fun game to play while catching up on podcasts.
If you're looking for story, you won't find it here. The end makes a half hearted attempt at causing feels, but mostly sticks to the breezy, no greater impact tone from the rest of the game. Your actions are less about helping the 'peasants' and more about getting that next guiding arrow to appear. Which was rewarding in it's own way.
Misc.
*While you can complete the main quest with minimal grinding, my current attempt to 100% the game involved me going to the two lv99 caves over and over again.
*The randomized leveling of equipment solved some of the problems RPGs have of never using a piece of armor again after finding something better, but there was still a bunch of stuff I never used.
*Only once did I change my build. The gameplay neither encourages or discourages trying different spells or proficiencies.

Extremely challenging game. So much so, I'm not surprised a lot of people quit after the first 5 levels.
But stick with it. This game was 20 hours of the most terrifying, unique, and brutal survival horror I've ever played. It's made by Shinji Mikami, the creator of Resident Evil, and it plays like Resident Evil 4 with a very Japanese Silent Hill-esque horror story with crazy bleeding, gore filled walls and enemies.
You will not get many bullets. Nor will upgrades make you OP, at least not in your first playthrough. They simply scale with the increasing difficulty as you progress. You will never feel like you have an advantage. And although it's immensely frustrating at times, it's never cheap. You learn from your mistakes and do something different next time. All of this helps to create a true feeling of terror and fear and really makes you think of your next move to deal with the next situation. The fear of the unknown and what is waiting for you in the next room never let's up, and it's a fantastic game because of it.
The production values are insane as well. I kept stopping the game every once in awhile just to admire the design of the levels and enviorments. Urban cities crumbling and shifting around you in real time, along with claustriphobic corridors bleeding and dripping, this is one of the best looking games I've ever seen.
If you don't like your games too hard and just want to easily walk through a spook house, move along.
But, if you want a true survival horror experience with a real challenge, pick it up.

This review is constructive criticism ONLY. I suggest that everyone try the game for themselves and form their own opinions.
-PROS-
Ratz maps
Instagib
Soundtrack

-CONS-
Movement feels absolutely terrible
Characters feel weightless (personal con, may not bother you)
Rails inconsistent with objects
Inconsistent boosts
No auto team balancing (in Team Deathmatch at least)
No way to see pings on players
Soundtrack (It becomes repetitive and annoying after hearing it for the 20th time)
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
I bought this game as a veteran of FPS games, growing up with the likes of Doom, Quake, Unreal Tournament, and Counter Strike when I saw this game I was instantly excited. From the videos here on steam and the reviews it appears to be a great nostalgia stimulating experience which will have you thinking back to "the old days" once again.
After watching the steam trailers and looking at the reviews I had somewhat expected it to be a standalone railgun type game on ratz maps.
What I got was a game where the movement feels awful, to the point where I'm not even sure if I'll ever touch it again for that main reason. Maybe I've become accustomed to other games styles of movement but something about Ratz Instagib's style of movement rubs me the wrong way. This is something that every player will have a difference in opinion on and has to experience it firsthand to fully understand what I truly mean when I describe it as awful.
You use your gun to boost in a similar manner to rocket jumping in Quake/UT, that's another huge mechanic that just feels really badly done and would benefit if it was made into a simple double jump/boost maneuver instead. Often times after boosting at an angle to propel myself forward and increase velocity I found myself slowing down instead, that's a huge problem in a game where it only takes 1 shot to kill you. I also at times found myself pressing the boost button only for it not to respond and end with me dead. Boosting is also the main way to get around the map, however there is a jump feature but after many attempts to string together more than a few jumps to gain speed and move around the map I found that it was largely ineffective.
Another issue would be the fact that rails are inconsistent with objects, quite a few times I was killed by rails that just seemed to magically go right through the object I was dodging my opponent around. I'm not sure if this an intended feature but I'm going to assume not since it couldn't be repeated on a consistent basis.
Looking past these HUGE issues there's tons of little ones that stuck out to me almost instantly. The lack of auto balancing teams in TDM leads to 2v1 situations on a consistent basis which honestly just amazes me that the developers didn't include a key feature like this before putting this up for early access. There is also no way to view current players pings to tell if someone is truly lagging or not, once again something that should be in the game before putting it up for early access.
Another small issue would be that players just generally feel weightless, this is something that may not bother everyone but I found it to be extremely disorienting after many years of enjoying other similar games.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
The entire game needs some real changes so that it will feel solid enough before this game comes out of early access. The boosting feature should also be re-evaluated to see if it can be made more consistent as well as experimenting with the possibility of removing it all together in favor of a better alternative. Adding additional music to cut down on the repetitiveness would be highly advised as well. Overall, the game would be fun to play if they could tighten up the movement and that's the real deal breaker as of right now for me.
I really want to like Ratz Instagib and I intend to try and continue to play it and keep up with the development but I cannot recommend that people purchase this game in it's current state. However that does not mean this game is bad what-so-ever, I'm finding myself enjoying the game a lot even with what I mentioned above. You need to play the game and try it for yourself, cause it's blast. It is currently on sale for $6.02 USD and usually sells for $8.99 USD, I feel that at this discounted price that I have gotten my full moneys worth and honestly would of purchased it at full retail.

is a 'class' based cooperative wave shooter based on the Warhammer fantasy lore. Expect comparisons with other games on the same genre like the Left 4 Dead and Killing Floor series to put things into context.
So how does Vermintide fare against other similar games? From start I can say that the developers created an intriguing atmosphere and environment which helps to create a nice immersion for the player. I'm not into Warhammer lore in general and playing the game actually motivated me to learn more about the franchise. When a game manages to invoke such a reaction from a player, I'd say that's a very good start. The graphics, textures and environment are quite decent on some of the 'larger' maps and the level design is pretty solid as a result. There's strict linearity of course due to the fact that is an objective driven game, as in you go from point A to point B while at the same time trying to accomplish your map objective.
At the same time you'll have to hack/slash/cleave/shoot/incinerate your way through the
. The enemy is the Skaven, rat-like people with a beef against anyone who isn't them, and sometimes as referred to the lore, even with their own kin. Killing your way through the enemies might seem like a simple task and while that is partly true, in higher difficulties proper cooperation is paramount to your success. While playing alone is sometimes fine or even part of the 'meta' (Killing Floor 2), in Vermintide being alone is a recipe for failure. Interesting to note that the characters themselves will comment during the aforementioned events with witty dialogue. "I hope I'm not talking to myself over here”; the developers cannot emphasize enough the need to work together as  a team in order to win.
The Skaven's greatest strength lies in sheer numbers but make no mistake, special enemies are present and at inopportune moments they
wipe your party of 4. Sneaky assassins, neck grabbin' packmasters, poison hurling rats, the aptly name Ratling gunners, Roman Legion Stormvermin and the mighty Rat Ogre are not to be taken lightly. But while in L4D/KF2  some of the specials require teamwork, in Vermintide you can easily take out most of these enemies with a well placed headshot. This seems counter intuitive to the cooperative nature of the game nevertheless good teamwork will ensure that the specials will cause minimal damage to the players and in higher difficulties that could make the difference between winning and wiping.
The are 5 'classes' in the game and I'm using the word classes here very loosely. While in KF2 classes exist with their own perks and weapons, in Vermintide the 5 heroes have no major differences between them, with the mighty exception of the weaponry they can use. Everyone has a melee weapon, a ranged weapon, a slot for a healing item, a slot for either a speed or strength potion and a bomb slot. Depending on what class you play, you'll get a variety of different weapons. Some might be two handed, slower and more on the knockback/stun mechanics, other might be one handed swords, less on the damage and more on the attack speed. Ranged weapons include pistols, repeaters, bows, crossbows and magical staves for the Bright Wizard hero. There is a plenty of variety betwen weapons and each weapon has a few traits you can unlock via the forge system in order to help you during your adventures. Traits as passively healing you on kills, increasing your knockback, chance to instantly kill enemies, refilling your ammunition for your ranged weapon, there are several ones which give
to the way you play. Furthermore there's an RPG quality system of weaponry, with white/green/blue/orange/red (ascending).
Now as with all cooperative shooter, repetition and replayability are key aspects which will determine the success of the game. And to be frank, the game is quite repetitive. You kill Skaven, move around the map, do your objective, move towards the escape point and you're done. Secondary objectives are thrown here and there during a mission but nothing fancy. For better or for worse, that is the nature of this genre. While KF2 is by definition more repetitive since it lacks any objective driven play, Vermintide is more in that regard with L4D which offers players something to do in between killing. There are plenty of missions, some longer than others and at the time of this reviews two
DLCs each with 3 missions. There's a XP leveling system but it's character only which is an interesting feature. While on KF2 each class has their own XP and bonuses, in Vermintide the XP level represent your account and each class will have their own weaponry.
The 5 heroes, Witch Hunter/Empire Soldier/Bright Wizard/Elver Waywatcher/Dwarven Ranger are all very colourful characters and interact with each other on various points during a match. Their dialogue is superb and I think is a nice titbit which makes the game more fun in my opinion. They will taunt, praise, joke and outright insult on occasion each other but their relationship seems to grow over the course of the game. They will be upset when one of them dies, they will compare kills, it certainly creates a very nice atmosphere when playing and I have nothing but praise for the voice actors and the developers for including lore in such a way. Truly fantastic.
The gameplay mechanics involve swinging/firing your weapon and killing the Skaven onslaught. However there's a very important core aspect of the swordplay which involves blocking and pushing the enemies away. I cannot stress how important that is. Blocking either with a shield or with your melee weapon is the one mechanic you'll have to master if you want to win. Failing that means you'll take damage and if you're swarmed that means you'll probably die.
While Vermintide is fun, it certainly has its drawbacks and you should be aware of them before getting it.
First and foremost in my opinion, NO DEDICATED SERVERS.
That's a huge negative. While KF2 and L4D featured dedicated servers, in Vermintide you connect to other people. That means you are the mercy of the host having a decent connection or you will lag to hell. And let me tell you, lagging in this game is a guaranteed fail. As I mentioned above, properly timed blocks will save your life and if you have bad ping that means you cannot play. Hits register when they shouldn't, Skaven evolve wing and fly through the map, bad ping means that you should play somewhere else. The questionable netcode of the game doesn't help either. A few dedicated servers will fix the problem for many people and will certainly make the game much more appealing to people with medium connections.
As a second offender the game is quite repetitive. This sort of got fixed with the recent quest/bounty system implemented a few months ago which allows players better ways to get loot but still it feels like a band-aid to a big trauma of the game. Objectives are fun but they tend to repeat over time.
The game feels unoptimized at times, there are a few visual glitches present, and while it looks pretty but I cannot help feel that it still needs a little bit polish.
To sum up, if you're into the cooperative shooter genre, if you enjoyed Killing Floor and Left 4 Dead, if you're a fan of the Warhammer fantasy or if you like killing rats, Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide is a pretty solid recommendation. You can even play solo with bots if coop is not your thing! There's occasional free updates, a couple of paid DLC with content (which you can play if one of your friends owns them even if you don't) and the game devs seem willingto provide more support for the game this year. It is reasonably priced and you can find it in deals/sales quite frequently if the price is not within your budget. Not without its flaws, but as a coop experience there's fun and reasonable challenge to be found.

This might be a game that slipped past everyone's radar earlier this year, and that's a real shame.
Story is really good and engaging, and the characters in it are interesting and relatable. The combat is very satisfying, where the robots respond depending on where you shoot them.
There are many boss fights, they are immense, intense and insane. A few QTEs here and there so be ready for that.
It uses a trust mechanic with your squad-mates, it'll rise or lower depending on your actions and responses to them. The higher it is, the better they'll do in combat and they will follow your orders. It'll also change the ending a bit.
You can issue squad orders and respond with your microphone, although I wouldn't recommend it, the tech isn't very responsive even though it's cool. You can use your keyboard instead.
Sleeper hit of the year, folks. Possibly a cult classic in the future, just like Alpha Protocol.

If you know your way around a shooter, this game will only take 8 hours. But it is an awesome action packed 8 hours! Filled with an amusing and interesting story, rock solid gameplay and interesting minigame like levels that break up the running and gunning.  Think Terminator and Battlestar Galactica met, then made sweet love and gave birth to an ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic gaming experience.  And you would have Binary Domain.

13+ hours of pure cinematic fun, at least the first playthrough, I'm going for the second since there is a new difficulty level and different endings! The gameplay is like Gears of War, the cover system and the movement, but the shootouts are with robots. Robots that not only react dinamically to your strategies but you can actually "handicap" them if you aim at certain spots, for example : if you take out the head, their aiming system goes nuts, if you aim for the legs, they crawl, if you aim for the arm... well they won't hold a weapon anymore. The shooting with petty robots is fun, and so are the big robot boss fights, kind of reminds me of Monster Hunter in the slightest. Finally, the great part is the RPG part, you build trust levels with your comrades, talk to them, get to know them, you split up, choose your team, you respond to them, I really like that. The only fault with this game is it's Voice Recognition system, turned off immediately. Definitely underrated, love it.

This has got to be the most poorly crafted game I have ever played in my entire life. The mechanics are clunky, aggravating, and inconvienient. The graphics are mediocre at best. The plot was an absolute drag to get through and highly uninteresting. None of the characters were even slightly memorable or captivating in any way. The Evil Within no doubt was a game first created over a decade ago and then was slapped on the same band wagon as all of its modern day peers.

The best thing to say about it is how absolutely gorgeous it is. But generally speaking if that's the best you've got to say about a game, then I think it speaks volumes.
So, yes. Aside from the stunning light, shadows and particle effects (truly some of the best if not THE best I have ever seen) I dd not enjoy the game.
Story - Extremely convuluted and falling into the trap of taking itself far too seriously, not knowing when to stop flipping things after the umpteenth time gets annoying in the end. The truly great games, never mind horror games, always find a way to keep you engaged narratively by actually keeping itself focused and by definiton, yourself the same. The Assignment and Consequence DLC help to an extent, but all in all it is just not an interesting enough story. Or, rather it is , but the way it was told was far too bloated.
Gameplay - Ultimately if a game isn't fun it doesn't succeed. And I can honestly sit here and say the only 'fun' I had was with The Executioner DLC. Perhaps because it kept things simpler and was, again, more focused. 'Safehead' as a character felt right, perfectly paced, well balanced, and every movement felt like it belonged to who you controlled. Compare that with the main game, where it couldn't decide whether it wanted you to be stealthy or all out action, and the 'Kidman' DLC that forces you to be stealthy but actually has nothing new to bring to the table other than making you wish you had a gun sooner - the stealth controls, sneaking and hiding are very badly executed thanks in part to the camera but just an overall 'unnatural' feel. Lots of jarring animations and the like.
It just goes to show how in actual fact The Evil Within was never really a survival horror game of sorts - it was always meant to be an action game but with 'somewhat' of an older inventory system and the need to be a bit more careful with ammo. That being said, even on a harder difficulty I could get away with killing nearly everyone I ever met and only once or twice in the entire adventure did I ever have to preserve what I had. Which links in to the truly awful boss fights this game has. Just put a load of bullets in them, very little strategy, and you always have plenty as there are rooms leading up to them that help you out. Feels totally artifical. Should be grateful there were no QTE's I suppose.
So I ask myself, having completed the game and all DLC, would I honestly recommend it? Ultmately no. I played it out of respect for Mikami but if I would never have played it I don't think I would have missed out on anything worthwhile.

So I basically dropped it for good after an hour of play.
, that is no longer an issue on the PC. Turns out this is one of the most visually stunning games I have ever played. All in smooth 60fps all the way.  (FYI, maxed out everything in 1920x1080 with an MSI GTX1080)
The game basically wants to be Resident Evil 4 in a bad way, and that is not a bad thing in this case. It pulls it off very vert well. And RE4 is the absolute king of this genre as far as I'm concerned. The game also delivers respectful nods towards Resident Evil at several points during the story. Hell, at some point you actually play in a spot-on recreation of the lobby and adjascent rooms in the mansion from Resident Evil 1 for gods sake. But it works.
Not going to ramble on much more, other than to say that I am really glad I gave this another shot. This is truly one of those "underated" and overlooked gems in the genre. Good story, insane production quality, some real tension, some real scares and a small lake of blood.
- Better than Resident Evil 5 and 6. Go play it.

Overall, there were too many points where I went "Lame!" to recommend the game. Get it cheap or not at all.

I only have 5.4 hours clocked on this game at the moment, but I am completely in love with it. The fast paced gameplay and small (but wonderful) community is extremely welcoming to all ages, and you can only get better. I played with the actual creator of the game this morning, and after playing for a while we found a chat bug. He immediately set off to fix the problem, and even stuck around to have some fun afterwards.
The community? Incredible. The gameplay? Even better. I recommend this game to people who enjoy other fast reaction-based games such as Quake Live or even TF2.

The game is surprisingly simplistic; move around and shoot, however a combination of rocket-jumping and the 1-hit-kill railgun create an intense, competitive environment where timing and precision is your key to success.
Not only does Ratz bring back great memories of Quake II railgun battles and Unreal Tournament's instagib mode, it has its own merits—primarily the level of customization which creates a very level playing field and a very personal experience—you are free to individualise almost all aspects of the game from the colour of your railgun beam to the colour of your name, team mates and enemies.
The newly introduced item drop system is purely based around cosmetics which maintains the balance and integrity of the game.
Game-modes include Team/One man army Deathmatch, Freeze Tag, CTF mode and most likely more to be introduced in future updates.
Updates seem to be introduced on a relatively frequent basis but at this point, the game looks very much like a finished product:
These features successfully disguise the fact that it is an early access game and are the reasons why I highly recommend Ratz Instagib!!

The Ship is a take on a first person shooter. You can either become a spectator or a hunter. If you choose to become a spectator you get to board the ship as a spectator and you can interact with other players but you can not loot or kill people but can yourself be killed as an innocent bystander. If you however choose to become a hunter you also board the ship but you can loot people and containers in order to get weapons, once you have some weapons you will be given a target; who if you have identified you will have a picture of; you will also be given a location where they where last identified by someone. If you have not identified them yourselves you will only be given the rough location. Once you track down your target it is your job to kill them in the most unique way with the weapons not used in a while giving you more money then those used recently. To increase the difficulty you must also kill them whilst not in view of any cameras or staff and depending on the settings other people in general or you will be sent to the onboard prison. Finally you also have to interact like a standard human being ensuring that you eat, drink, sleep, entertain yourself aswell as using the bathroom for the toilet and for cleaning purposes.
However the server list on steam is broken :( and you will have to look on the internet to find some of The Ship servers. I should also note that the graphics on this game serve it well but its not going to win any awards in anyones books. However this game is great fun and I would highly recommend it to people who want to have some fun.

Pretty soon even the story wasn't enough to make me start the next missions.  I found myself burning through repetiive missions simpy because there was a particular ship I really wanted to unlock.  "Just one more mission, and the Enterprise D or Voyager is mine!"  What also kept me grinding (besides that one ship I just had to have) was the occassional run in with a particular character or location that brought the nostalgia flooding back all over again.
Again, for someone who doesn't do PvP and hasn't dropped any money on this game yet, it's a decent binge here and there on a long weekend.  I don't know that I would invest much more in it than that, though.
