First of all I would like to say this is my first dating sim I've ever played.  This game was a complete impulse buy for me as I was interested in trying out an anime dating sim just for the hell of it. I have to say this was a great first experience in the genre. From the moment you start playing it hooks you with its simple and addictive puzzle gameplay and keeps you coming back to "conquer" the various girls. Each time you have a successful date you get a tantalizing text message/pic that really keeps you invested in the relationship you have with each of the girls. One big positive is the game is completely voiced in english which adds a TON of personalty to each girl. The writing is also a strong point, as there were few cringey lines in the game.
I will say on an negative side the girls hardly interact with each other. I have to imagine they had story lines involving each other at one point but were cut at some time in development because its really odd the game makes a point to show you how each person has a history with each other, only to mostly ignore it the rest of the game. Also the sex mini game is kinda boring and pointless since you can't fail it.
Overall this game took me about 13 hours to complete the first time though, but I imagine the typical person could finish it faster if they are good at the bejeweled style puzzle game. All in all I can recommend the game to about everyone over the age of 18, but especially to those who are new to dating sims, as this is a fun and simple entry into the genre.

In Binary Domain, global warming has taken its toll on earth, burying cities all over the world. With millions upon millions of people dead, the task of rebuilding falls upon robots. The game sees you take the role of Dan, a wise cracking American who is a part of a task force known as a "rust crew". The rust crew is on a mission to determine whether the Amada company has broken clause 21 of the Geneva Convention - building robots that can pass as human.
In terms of gameplay, the movement and cover system feels like it is taken straight out of Gears of War, however, the gunplay is much more satisfying than Gears. Robots fall to pieces as you shoot them. If they lose a leg for example, they will claw their way towards you, if they lose their head, they will shoot other robots.
There are a few questionable sequences in the game (turret sections, amongst other things) but the good far outweighs the bad. It is a strong addition to anyone's library.

Lots of spectacular boss fights, minimal ammount of QTEs (4-5 in total). Can't recommend enough.

I am not very versed into survival-horror. Following you guys recommendation, I played **The Evil Within**
. With Mikami at the helm (RE4) I was promised a great experience.





----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

First of all, I was scared more than once and had some stress induced moments. But it was more than that, it was not just jumpscare, you tend to be on guard at all times. I don't feel like waiting for something to happen, more than reacting to events and mostly, escaping from them.
Especially those moments when you are trapped in a very small room with one crazy opponent, your brain calculating the odds of success especially fast. Just to conclude that... you should run. The stressful music adding to that fact it is necessary to escape while keeping your distance from the enemy. You can use your surroundings to your advantage, using a multitude of traps to inflict damage.
The stress is here, growing in you the more you advance in the game. The game challenge yourself to keep your cool and analyzing the situation while it happens. **The Evil Within** is filled with moments like this and I believe they are very well made. Those elements are what makes the game great.
The graphics and the art is very well made and showcase a dark and gore environment. While always playing with the head of your characters and yours at the same time. The monsters you will encounter aren't simple zombies and will make you rethink how twisted some stuff can be.
Story-wise, it is very tough to grasp and isn't made for you to fully understand until the very end.. And even then. Lots of symbolic, very few explanations and it is thought that way. I believe this made the entire experience very good Characters are well developed, all with a tragic story.
You will always lack ammunitions. Enemies come in horde and are extremely tough to kill. Traps are also everywhere on the map and you need to learn how to use them against your enemies. I think the idea is great, too bad that the AI is extremely weird and will either never respond to your aggression, or just overreact.
The usage of weapons (or even punches) is strange, and there's a lot of bugs, clipping of textures. The problem is that it happens extremely frequently. I can't say the amount of time I missed a shot while the enemy was standing right in front of me, simply because the gun went through the enemy. There's multiple examples with almost all the traps and or weapons. Cumulated to bugs and bad AI, the usage of checkpoints is strange as well and makes the gameplay experience. I really hated the fighting and sneaking mechanic, I feel it was too clunky, especially the sneak part.
Checkpoints are placed at random spots in the maps making you question why they made some spots this way. Sometimes too close one another, most of the time forever away.
On the other hand, there's barely any repetition, always have different way to play the game, beat the maps and enemies.
I played the game on PS4 and PC, the same bugs and review would be made. The lifespan of the game is very reasonable and between 9 to 12 hours.
The Evil Within is one of the best games I've ever played. I loved every piece of it, especially its haunting, creepy atmosphere and so damn cool characters. The story was also excellent. 10/10

Gameplay :
Another masterpiece by Lord Mikami san. Must play title for survival horror fans. Its like Resident Evil 4 with stealth and ammo management playing a bigger role. You keep your ammo in check, make right upgrades, pick your shots carefully and use the crossbow to your advantage. The bolt crafting and stealth movement is like The Last of Us. Crossbow is going to be your best friend as different bolts helps in different situations, for ex: use freeze bolt to freeze a group of enemies and using shotgun blast or melee to kill them all. You can also use them bolts as proximity mine, which covers your back while you clear the enemies in front. Shoot an enemy in the leg, it will cripple down, burn it quickly turn 180 and take down another one. Lure enemies into water, get out quickly and fire electric bolt in the water to take them down all.Trust me it helps a lot as the game throws you again and again in overwhelming situations.
Game also has a match mechanic where you need to burn enemies to make sure they are dead. So its either headshot or burning the corpses to be totally sure that enemies dont get back up but tbh powerful blows also kills enemies permanently. The match mechanic was under utilized. It helps to conserve ammo as with right timing you could take down 3-4 enemies together. The levels are designed well with enviornmental traps for you to utilize and get rekt so be careful, giving room to enemy to ambush you and encircle you. The level and encounter variety is one of the strengths of evil within. There are full blown action levels like RE4 and god they are amazing, the regular encounters are combination of more uneasy, stealth and action approach. The encounters are clevery designed and are not hand holding at all. The gameplay is ace and when the man behind the title is Shinji Mikami then you can trust him eyes closed. Such a fantastic record of games and that too in diverse gameplay titles.

I really wish I could say I loved this game. I honestly do. As many have said, it does have a lot of similarities to Banished, though I would disagree with some reviewers who say it is being "copied". There are just a number of things about this game that personally make it not fun to play. (Mileage, of course, may vary) First, it takes FOREVER to do anything. Building a house, a farm, gathering a certain type of resource....expect to wait a LONG time for it to be done. Second, a few of the food sources are nearly impossible to keep going/problems with food. On multiple villages I've had the fishing just stop producing anything. I figured maybe that section of the waterfront had gotten fished out, though with the graphics it still looked like it was teeming with fish. I shut down that fishery and made another one much farther away. Still was getting next to no fish at all. I've had this happen with orchards, farms, and the other modes of food production as well. I've had multiple villagers, while in the town and no tasks before them, with food available at the storehouse starve to death. Third, you'll spend almost the whole game terraforming and the terraforming mechanic is frustrating to use. Unlike Banished, you are provided only with Islands and whatever terrain you choose will have hills of varying sizes. It's very difficult to find a map that won't need you to terraform within the first 15 min of gameplay. Trying to get everything flat so you can build on it also takes FOREVER and it's hard to eyeball it right to even get things flat. I'll freely admit that I'm a casual type of player of this game as I don't often have long swaths of time to devote to it. However, when on a rare occasion I /do/ have the time to play, playing for five hours and feeling I've accomplished NOTHING is off putting to me.  It does have some good points. The graphics are pretty nice, being able to control villagers is cool, but not enough to draw me back to this game. Having depth (though depends on the person if you feel terraforming for an hour to be able to place a house that will take another half an hour to build is depth) to a game is great, but not when the starting off point can be so frustrating you don't even care.

I approached this game not as a survival horror junkie looking for my next sleepless night fix like Amnesia or SOMA, but more about the main protagonist’s tragic story, along the lines of Dear Esther and Gone Home. And it’s brilliant. The game is an interactive story novel rather than a game with a challenge, and there’s no losing condition whatsoever. However finding more clues can alter which ending you receive.
On that note, finding clues throughout the game provides a cryptic non-direct story telling narrative that heavily suggests (however doesn’t directly imply) what happened to the painter’s family, the loss of his muse, his downfall from the peak of his career, the impact it had on his mental psyche, his marriage, the toll on his mental health, until its ultimate tragic conclusion and the painter’s failure to cope with it. The result of which being his extreme mental illness entailing hallucination, schizophrenia, masochism, etc. We as the player are invited to see his extremely warped mental mind as he strives to complete his Magnum Opus in hopes that will cure him of his insanity and the suffering he’s endured will be worth it. Or will it? The narrative leaves out just enough for us on purpose to fill in the pieces about what really happened.
As an artist myself I could sympathize with the loss of the painter’s muse and his absolute frustration on why he couldn’t seem to pull it back together. Something like that has got to be incredibly self-defeating, where one minute the painter is at the top of his career, and in the next it’s all taken away and he loses his creative drive to continue his work, winding up with lackluster paintings panned by critics, which set the tragic stage for everything else to follow.
The horror elements provided in the game are good, however they do get repetitive towards the end. However I think that’s the point. We the player begin to feel numb and desensitized from the horror presented in the game just like the painter, as that’s his and our way of coping through this new warped mental normality that he’s constructed. Despite all that’s happening around him, he presses onward determined to finish his painting.
An excellent tragic horror story worth anyone’s time to delve into the mind of a fallen artist.

20ish months ago PT appeared on the PS4 and was a runaway success and probably the most talked about demo/teaser of all time the project to make the next Silent Hill game was cancelled when Kojima left Konami last year in soap opera fashion.
Enter Layers of Fear a horrific gothic walking simulator that sees you explore the house of an insane painter that borrows a lot of its style from PT and a lot of its basis from “The Picture of Dorian Gray”.
As the game begins you wander the house with the idea of finishing your Bacon inspired painting but pretty soon the♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan and things start getting terrifying. Not sure if the bizarre goings on are supernatural or simply the protagonist losing his grip and perception of reality.
As you continue through the game a story is told through notes and findings in a similar vein to Gone Home albeit in a more linear fashion. There is a genuinely creepy atmosphere throughout backed up with some excellent jump scares that really get the heart racing.
Layers of Fear is a walking sim with some minimal puzzle elements that normally involve searching the room you are in, finding and interactive object or sifting through some draws. At no point do you get lost and the game is pretty much on rails but to be perfectly honest this is why the game shines. It is well crafted and a game with a more open playstyle would not have been paced as well.
There is no combat in the game just puzzles. One thing I was not keen on was the physics based opening and closing of doors. A minor quibble but I always dislike when games do this and this one does not improve the design.
The first hour of the game definitely shines with a little bit of repetitiveness setting in as you progress. While all of the jump scares are good after a while you begin to spot when they are coming. The artistic themes in the setting and design are outstanding but eventually the jump scares become samey and predictable.
The game is relatively short running at about 3 hours and while that may be a tough pill to swallow for some seeing the game’s £15 price tag it is definitely polished enough to warrant a play through if you are a horror fan. Not perfect but definitely one of the best true horror games in recent years.

*In the interest of transparency, I'd like to make it clear that I bought a life sub for this game. I wouldn't say that it was a waste of money, but there is no way in hell that I would get one now*
**************************************************************************************************
For this review, I'd like to do something different and talk about experiences.
What does Star Trek mean to you?
If you're like me, then you're a middle-aged Star Trek fan, who has seen every episode of every series. You didn't set out to make that happen, but you like the franchise and realised, one day, that you literally had run out of Star Trek, because nobody was making any more.
If you're not like me, then you don't care about what Star Trek represents, then you are essentially viewing Star Trek as Star Wars: a simple space opera. And as much as I hate this fact, both our viewpoints on the series are equally valid.
If you're like me, you won't just be disappointed in this game, it will actively depress you and make you mourn (Morn? Ha!) the loss of a great franchise, which is clearly well and truly dead by this stage. Oh, sorry, I mean "alive in name only" which is, of course, completely different and totally not the exact same thing.
If you're not like me, you might like this game.
If you're young, I don't think you can even 'get it', because there's nothing else like it in the modern age.
Dark Mirror, MAYBE. Yes, I just compared ST to DM. Because both are (or should be) at their core, a uncomfortable look at 'what humanity could be in the future' vs 'what we are now'.
While one may say that about any Science Fiction series, that's kind of the issue - Star Trek ISN'T SciFi, just llike Star Wars isn't. They're both Space Dramas with a SciFi flavour. Star Wars concentrates on conflict, and Star Trek concentrates on resolution.
Well, it DID. Once upon a time. A long time ago.
There's nothing else like it now, because everyone is all grimdark because idiots mistakenly think that darkness equals depth. That is certainly true of the oceans, or of holes in the ground. But not entertainment.
So, everyone reading this is probably thinking the same thing: "oh, boo hoo, we have one less talky game in the world."
If so, you've misunderstood completely.
Would you be happy if you downloaded a Batman game and got a My Little Pony one instead? Because that's my experience here.
(CAVEAT: Even Bronies must surely be like "Hey, this is great, but where is that other game that I thought I was getting?")
Free to play? No. NO games are f2p. They all cost something, either time or money. And STO is greedy with both.
*************************************************************************************************
I only wanted ONE thing from this game:
The ability to experience the Star Trek universe in the same manner as it is seen on TV or film. The ability to explore. The ability to affect the universe by my actions. TOUGH moral decisions which would teach me something about myself and/or the world around me.
This is what I got:
A shooter, where I sometimes talk to people but I can make literally no decisions about anything, because the text is all railroaded, a la Fallout 4, and also the space combat isn't in 2D or 3D, but some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ised version of both - there are no real manuevres you can do here. A loop-de-loop? Nope. Not even as a special ability. You CAN do a cvery small orkscrew roll, but it will literally take you about 40 hours to earn and can only activate once every few minutes.
Now, being a Star Trek shooter is no issue in itself. It was great when Elite Force did it, because it was a good game and marketed itself as a shooter. Same with Klingon Honour Guard.
But that was nearly 20 years ago now.
And STO doesn't market itself as a shooter.
***********************************************************************************
STO, in reality, is a poorly-made linear adventure game with all the trappings of mobile games. Proprietary resources limits, more powerful gear for real money (or stupid amounts of time), gambling in the form of lockboxes. Further, we still have bugs from launch - that's over 7 years ago.
In closing, I would like to state that this game is poor, even as a franchise money maker. They don't even want our money. Well, they don't want specific amounts of money from me.
I want to buy the Intrepid bridge, because I've started watching Voyager with my daughter, who has started showing an interest in the game.
She can buy one. I cannot. It doesn't even appear in my store.
And what is the reason for this?
Because I already own some of the ships.
Let's examine that.
Because I financially supported the game years before the Intrepid pack was released, I am ineligible to buy one of the most famous bridges in Star Trek history.
I'm going to say that again, because that really needs to sink in:
"Because I financially supported the game years before the Intrepid pack was released, I am ineligible to buy one of the most famous bridges in Star Trek history."
This is the level of greed and/or incompetence on display in this game. They don't even try to hide it.
I am utterly disgusted that this company is continually allowed to do their part to destroy the Star Trek franchise, one ♥♥♥♥♥♥ patch at a time.
*************************************************************************
VERDICT:
If you like Star Trek, play Star Trek Timelines instead. It doesn't lie about being a mobile game, and they let you buy what you want.

Far too much luck and repetition involved in order to get things you actually want and frankly the game's not -that- good that I'm wanting to repeat missions over and over in order to unlock gear that will allow me to repeat missions over and over in slightly different ways.
Compare to something like Payday 2 for example, which is quite similar, you grind, you get some random stuff, some predictable/fixed stuff, skills and whatnot, and then you progress and can do different things with different weapons and skills. With Vermintide you complete a mission, have a random chance to get a random item for a random character, which you can trade in for lesser, random items if you don't like it. There's no sense of progress, there's no sense that you can work towards a 'build', you either find the lucky item or you don't. While I'm sure plenty of folks out there do have all their dream items, I bet they require a hell of a lot of grinding to get, and I'm not sure I'm on board for tens or hundreds of hours of the same thing.
The game outside of this plays okay, I like it more than Left 4 Dead, but it's not good enough to warrant the sort of repeat play that you'd need to get all the shiny things and cool weapons.

The Evil Within is one of the best games I've ever played. I loved every piece of it, especially its haunting, creepy atmosphere and so damn cool characters. The story was also excellent. 10/10

Gameplay :
Another masterpiece by Lord Mikami san. Must play title for survival horror fans. Its like Resident Evil 4 with stealth and ammo management playing a bigger role. You keep your ammo in check, make right upgrades, pick your shots carefully and use the crossbow to your advantage. The bolt crafting and stealth movement is like The Last of Us. Crossbow is going to be your best friend as different bolts helps in different situations, for ex: use freeze bolt to freeze a group of enemies and using shotgun blast or melee to kill them all. You can also use them bolts as proximity mine, which covers your back while you clear the enemies in front. Shoot an enemy in the leg, it will cripple down, burn it quickly turn 180 and take down another one. Lure enemies into water, get out quickly and fire electric bolt in the water to take them down all.Trust me it helps a lot as the game throws you again and again in overwhelming situations.
Game also has a match mechanic where you need to burn enemies to make sure they are dead. So its either headshot or burning the corpses to be totally sure that enemies dont get back up but tbh powerful blows also kills enemies permanently. The match mechanic was under utilized. It helps to conserve ammo as with right timing you could take down 3-4 enemies together. The levels are designed well with enviornmental traps for you to utilize and get rekt so be careful, giving room to enemy to ambush you and encircle you. The level and encounter variety is one of the strengths of evil within. There are full blown action levels like RE4 and god they are amazing, the regular encounters are combination of more uneasy, stealth and action approach. The encounters are clevery designed and are not hand holding at all. The gameplay is ace and when the man behind the title is Shinji Mikami then you can trust him eyes closed. Such a fantastic record of games and that too in diverse gameplay titles.

"I PLAYED THE GAME FOR 30 MINUTES AND ITS BAD CAUSE BANISHED."
Let's dig a little deeper and actually talk about Forest Village for a minute.
Based on May 26th release:
It doesn't feel like a $25 game.
It feels like a $15 game.
The game is out of early access but Banished + CC mod brings more content and end game scenarios.
So why have I been playing this for the last 3 days straight....?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This game is fairly well balanced, the grind is slower and realistic, it's just hard enough to keep me challenged and interested in expanding my city. The immersive graphics/ambiance reminds of my early days of Skyrim.
I'm at ~150 people in my city, It's been going for about 12 hours now, I still haven't built 60% of the buildings in the game, I still only dream of sitting in my castle. That's 12 hours of gameplay! 12 hours in Banished and you should have like 800 people running around and access to every resource in the game.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
But is there lots to do in the game? I don't want to beat the game in 5 hours!
- You aren't getting many late game buildings in the first 5 hours.
- The grind is slow, you need to build up man-power and have a massive stack of resources to build anything.
- Life is feudal devs want you to work hard for your resources, look at their MMO its just one huge grind!
- When a building recommends using 5 builders, give it the 5 builders or you will be waiting a very long time for it to complete. This isn't like Banished where 3 people can assemble an entire city.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Grind grind grind, is it even worth it? Who wants to wait 5 hours and not have anything to show for it!?
- That's just for the end game resources like iron/quality tools or late game buildings like castles and accountants house.
- Building better houses and expanding food production/population production is easily accessible in the early game
- Getting over the initial 'not enough hands to work the jobs I need' was a lot of fun and didn't take very long.
- You get punished with slow expansion if you try to expand too quickly without enough workers. If the game is too slow for you, play on x5 speed and focus on getting more people.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
So the core gameplay is good, the resources seem balanced, the graphics are immersive and the Ai/Pathing is better and smarter than it was in Banished?
- Yes
- Warehouse/Barn placement is very important in this game
- Spread out your resource/food production around the town. If half your town makes all the food, the other half has to walk to that side just to eat everyday. It will damage your towns production!
- "My Ai keeps dying when I have tons of food, why?" - read the above points.
- "My buildings produce nothing!" - Workers run too far to get food/resurces, too far to get home, and have no time to do their job, organize your city so people have access to the goods they need!
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Then why does it feel like a $15 game?
One big reason, lots of little reasons.
- no Ai enemies, not even the wildlife will attack you (they will attack your chickens)
- castles are cool but again, whats the point of building a giant castle if nothing will raid you
- there is no way in the early game to check building statistics like seasonal production rates.
- buildings get hit by lightning way too often, its made of wood and hay what the heck is the lightning attracted to? (its really easy to put out fires and a building can burn for up to 5 minutes before getting destroyed)
- a tornado hit my town and ran over my apiary and a house but didn't even damage them, yo its made of wood and hay that should've decimated my town.
- Discovering new animals/crops is through the Port and and the Journey feature where you have to send fisherman away on a boat. Great idea but why do I need to make 3 different pies for them to eat just to start the journey? You really think 9 fisherman want to eat old stale fish pies when they could just you know...eat fresh fish they catch in the ocean?
- The rate trees are planted is a little too slow, the regrowth rate is fine, but the 'seeding' part of the game is a little broken, the only way I can get my foresters to replant trees is turning off cutting and waiting literally 10-15 minutes. I cycle my foresters so the north side of town is seeding and the south is cutting and I swap that back and forth.
- why is there no currency or bank?
- The Ai first person stuff is a nice touch but its very basic and basically just a walking simulator but it reminds me of the old days of those roller coster tycoon games where you get to play as the people on the ride.
- the fog is too much you cant see far at all when winter rolls around and snow starts to fall
- camera should zoom out more its hard to get a view of your entire town
- the bloom setting is absurd, the sand and snow is so bright its like staring into 1000 suns.
- needs more time for community mods to hit the steam workshop.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Can't you just download some mods off the steam workshop to fix like 80% of those issues?
- Steam Workshop just released, we need to wait for more mods to get created.
- Banished was a decent game in the vanilla, but an awesome game with the community made mods
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Banished drops to $5 for a reason, its abandonded, dated, broken ai, tons of bugs, and relies entirely on the modding community which is dying off too. It's a legendary game but lets support the new version that has an actual dev team and  planned upates.

This game is a well-paced descent into insanity and back. It's a short story that leads you through an ever-changing mansion by way of corridors, light puzzles, and jump scares. Note that this game is a psychological thriller, not survival-horror. You will not be running for your life or conserving ammunition. Just enjoy the atmosphere, story, and scares. Absolutely brilliant.

Seldom I come across a game with an atmosphere as good as in Layers of Fear. The execution of every part of the game is great, meaning the seamless exploration that at times seems to be neverending. The story, albeit simple, has many leads and references around the world in which the game takes place. Reasonable replay value there.
One thing I dislike about Layers of Fear, is how the only elements to thrill the player are jump scares. I can appreciate a good story and a good atmosphere, but I do think the team could have done a lot better by coming up with some mature, well-spun horror instead of childish scares. It's sad to see such a good effort on the development side go to waste on simple shock effects.
I recommend this to players who like to immerse themselves and experience a solid, albeit shallow, horror story.

The game is a massive time sink, it will take you many weeks of casual play to do any form of dent to the size of the island you inhabit.  Good luck and I hope you enjoy it as I have.

Rusty Lake Hotel
The Lake will be Grateful
Developer: Rusty Lake
Year:  2015
Genre: Horror, Puzzle, Point 'n' Click
Franchise: Rusty Lake/Cube Escape
Engine: IDK
TL;DR
Rusty Lake Hotel is an inexpensive, eerie point and click puzzler by the folks behind the excellent "Cube Escape" series, which can be found on Kongregate or through the devs at
. For under 5 NZ dollars you can pick up this game and the sequel, both of which fit into the larger narrative that started in the aforementioned flash games. Score, Visuals and Puzzles mesh to make something truly special.
REVIEW
Story:
I've seldom seen storytelling done like this. Characters speak directly very infrequently and intuitive pictoral hints tell you a ton about the characters you meet. The story seems minimal, but everything that happens means something, even if you can't tell what it is. This game is ideal if you want to sit back and revel in the weirdness of some incredibly creative indie devs. Deeper story elements are shown, but they are murky and obscured, masterfully working with the continued theme of the lake. Dark gods, esoteric spirits and twisted motives lurk below the seemingly innocuous children's book style and mundane puzzle tasks. The story is a delight to unveil, so I will tell you no more. 8.5/10
Graphics:
The art style is... Unique. Imagine a blend between 'American Gothic', 'Over the Garden Wall', old silent cartoons and creepy taxidermies, and you begin to get an idea of the excellent visuals presented in this game. Click through the screenshots if you can't be bothered googling those things. Everything is unsettling and surreal, but subtly. It feels like a dusty piece of American folk art, which really clicks with my particular sensibilities. With that said, I can see how the limited animation and somewhat simple graphics could be a putoff. For me, it's a real hit. 9/10
Gameplay:
Aside from a few irritating or samey puzzles, Rusty Lake Hotel is a sterling example of puzzle gaming. The game sets seemingly mundane tasks with esoteric twists and disturbing results. I won't discuss the intent of the puzzles, but they follow a shared, sinister theme. While the weakest element of the game, the puzzles are still excellent. 7/10
Overall:
I opened my steam wallet and found it was bare,
I thought to myself that there was something there
Just a moment before, but I remembered with shame,
That it a fever I had spent it on games.
I looked through my library for something new,

The visuals, the music, the tension thick as tar,

I soon bought the sequel, my thirst not yet slaked,
I'd become an addict of the studio Rusty Lake.
In short, RL:H is a game that I am proud to have in my Steam Library. It's Short but Satisfying, Unsettling but with no Jumpscares and Interesting without Exposition. 8.5/10

I won't discuss graphics and sound, as they can be observed without playing the game, except to say they are really good.
As many others have pointed out, this is similar to L4D. Some of the Skaven, like the rat ogre, have direct equivalents in that game, and all of the special Skaven serve the same roles as enemy classes in L4D - which is basically to divide the team or immobilize a player. (Except for the Stormvermin) It is 4 player co-op, and the final objective of several of the missions is to defend the area until a carriage or boat arrives to allow escape. Downed teammates can be revived and dead teammates can be rescued.
The common Skaven that attack as a horde are a bit different from the zombies in L4D. Like zombies, they attack as a group and are very weak individually, but the behavior of the Skaven is not mindless. If a Skaven is alone, it will cower from you and attack only if cornered. Additionally, they can be seen crawling across rooftops preparing to ambush. They feel like a more intelligent enemy. The Stormvermin that command them are formidable soldiers in their own right, with armor, blocking ability, and on higher difficulties, one hit kills. They are best avoided or sniped out from a distance.
The five characters have the same health capacity and each have a ranged and melee weapon. However each weapon in the game plays differently, and each weapon is exclusive to a specific character. While there are a variety of different ways to build each character, they remain distinct from other characters. You'll want your party to have a mix of crowd control and high damage weapons.
All of the weapons feel/sound/look amazing and distinct. The melee system is really the crowning achievement of the game, with strikes landing with a real sense of weight and causing different damage, dismemberment, rag doll physics, and blood splatter depending on where you land them. There's even a button to look at your weapon, which gets caked in blood as battles progress. It's just the most satisfying melee combat I've played by far. (Turn blood splatter up to 500 percent for maximum fun)
The weapons are mainly rewarded upon successful completion of a mission, and can be combined to form weapons of higher rarity. Which weapon is awarded is based on a dice roll, as inspired by the tabletop game, and the dice can be upgraded with certain mission items. This main loot system reminds me of Pokemon Go and feels a bit grindy, but it's more than made up for by the additions brought to the game by the free Sigmar's Blessing DLC.
This DLC adds 2 more ways to get weapons/trinkets, and 2 more ways to upgrade them. The bounty board allows you to select quests that give you certain rare items after completing a number of contracts. There's no time limit, but each day brings new quests and new contracts. Some contracts give you temporary stat buffs or rare gems instead/in addition to contract keys. The gems allow you to upgrade existing weapons or to buy semi-random weapons. I say semi-random because you can choose the character, the weapon rarity, and whether it is ranged or melee. You can also salvage duplicate weapons to acquire gems.
I can see why some people were unhappy with the loot system at launch, but I love it in its current state. It's really flexible, well balanced, and adds a lot of replayability.
The map design and aesthetic are fantastic, with tons of detail and variety. There are 13 maps/missions in total and each feels distinct with unique layouts and objectives.
The settings are very configurable, and indicate which ones cause more stress on the CPU vs the GPU. These scale well, as one player in our group plays just fine on a mid grade laptop.
Finally, the DLC system is quite generous. Only the host needs to own the DLC in order for everyone in the party to play it. There are still some benefits to everyone having a copy of the DLC, (you need to own a DLC to get the daily contracts for it) but you can experience all of the DLC missions without buying them.
It's currently my favorite multiplayer game, so this is a big thumbs up from me.

Fun game so far!!  After not having played an arena shooter in about 10 years, this game instantly brought me back to to my days with Unreal Tournament & UT2k4. If your like me and your aiming sucks.. I would recommend creating your own game and adding bots to practice getting your timing down a bit before jumping right into a multiplayer game.
If you were ever an instagib fan in any games like UT and Quake I would definatly advise you to give this game a try.

To begin with I'd like to start with saying that I'm giving this game an overall positive review, however I do think it could do with some improvements (that's what  Early Access is all about, right?) and polish.  I'm a huge fan of instagib (from Quake 2/3/Live, UT etc) and really want games like this to succeed!
- Colour scheme/art style/visuals:  I think it could really do with some work in this area.  Sometimes it's hard to pick out players amongst the various colourful effects, decals etc.  I don't think it's an impossible problem to solve, just some minor changes to the colour palette used for players versus what's used for effects could help, or possibly the use of a different outline shader (edit: I'll admit I haven't played around with the graphics options available here which might solve this, but if that's the case then perhaps the defaults could be improved).  In regards to the overall visuals, I think it could do with some polish... while I appreciate the oldschool style of the frontend/HUD some of it clashes quite badly and makes my head hurt!  The characters themselves also look quite rigid at the moment, again just polish needed there with the animations.
- Hit registration:  There appears to be a bug here, sometimes you'll hit someone, get the ding noise and they'll flash white but they won't die.  It isn't because their hit registered first, because you don't die either... it's simply some weird inconsistency between the client and the server it seems.  Upon mentioning it on the server chat other people all said they experienced the same thing in the same game.  I'm sure this will get fixed, but for the time being it's a little annoying when it happens as you feel robbed of a kill (though it's possible you simply didn't hit them on the server).
- Movement mechanics:  I'm in two minds about this one, to be honest I find it a little too floaty for my liking... though the boost mechanic (rocket-jumping with your gun essentially) is interesting and adds some depth to the movement (I'm terrible at using it though).
- Matchmaking/Servers:  Currently there isn't proper matchmaking, undoubtedly due to the small playerbase right now (as the game isn't Free to Play this isn't surprising).  That said, I've not had a problem finding a regular deathmatch game yet.  An issue this does introduce though is that you can get stomped by the players that have played the game for a while, however they all appear to be very friendly and happy to sit out of matches so others can have fun.  Don't let this put you off buying or playing this game, as there are plenty of noobs just like you and I.
Overall it's a nice idea, a game dedicated to instagib is definitely something I'm happy to back!  Whether it's worth the price of admission depends on how much of an instagib enthusiast you are and whether you're happy to support a developer making a game in a genre you love.  I look forward to seeing how this game evolves and I'm happy to update this review as it does.

Scrap Mechanic, one of my favorite games! This game really does have creativity at its core. There is already quite a lot you can do with the game. It is smooth, intuitive, easy to learn, has great gameplay in my opinion, and is overall one of the more unique games I have seen in a long time.
I am going make a PROS and CONS list.
PROS
-The gameplay is smooth and enjoyable. It is easy to figure out and get going!
-The audio is nice. When placing items down the sound is very pleasing. The audio in general is great.
-Graphics. The style of this game (kind of like a 3D cartoon, lots of vivid colors and a nicely styled environment) make this game very good looking. The overall graphics in general are very good.
-Replayability. I could play this game for hours and not get bored. There are so many things you can build and experiment with, not to mention the content being added each update.
-The building system is very simplistic and easy to grasp quickly.
-Lots and lots of customization for your builds. By that I mean that there are tons of things to build with, and you can even color things with a Paint tool!
-The mechanics of machinery and moving parts is easy to grasp as well. It's simple enough for the average gamer, but able to be used in the most complicated ways to create almost anything.
-It has multiplayer.
-The developers are very active with the community and are implementing requested features. They are really trying to be very close with their community.
-You can save your creations for later used and even share them to the workshop.
-The community is very friendly!
CONS
-There are some bugs.
-Every now and then (and this might only be me or something my computer is doing) my character's movement will be lagged. I will press W, and he/she will move forward after like a second or two later.
-No survival mode yet, but they are working on it.
BONUS PRO-CON (It's a pro and a con kind of)
-Development is kind of slow, but the up side is that each update brings great things!
So those are my PROS and CONS.
Overall, I would give this game a 10/10.
It is Early Access of course, so expect some bugs and things alike, but other than that the game is fun, replayable, and has great possibilities!
My final conclusion is this; If you don't mind waiting for update, you want to support the awesome developers, and you like building things, then I say go ahead! If you would rather have a much more finished game without bugs and other things, just wait a while. But I fully recommend this game!

At first, I wasn't sure I would enjoy this game. As a fan of survival horror, I thought I would only find true fear and enjoyment in being chased by something that could easily kill you. While Layers of Fear does not have this standard layout, its use of the atmosphere combined with truly creepy themes will keep you on your toes the entire time. You will be in a variety of areas resembling the painter's home with the landscape constantly changing. At times, you will reach a dead-end, you will turn around, and the hallway you came from will now be a small room. Turn around again, and you be surrounded by eerie, beckoning paintings. My only complaint with this game is that it was not longer. If anything, that's a compliment to the developers for sucking me in and leaving me wanting more!

The game is a design nightmare -- and certainly not the good kind of nightmare. From a technical standpoint, nearly every drawer and cabinet in the game is openable. What's in the drawers? Sunglasses. Books about pandas. Inkwells. War medals. A red herring is fine every once in a great while but sheesh. To open a drawer or a door you have to hold down the trigger on your controller and twist the thumbstick awkwardly. A useless mechanic that adds to the monotony. Save that stuff for Quicktime Events. The game is equally broken from a storytelling standpoint. The letters and drawings are full of tired attemps at dark humor and trite metaphors. The story isn't even especially interesting. There are no puzzles. "Gone Home" is a walking simulator done the best a walking simulator can be done. This is a walking simulator that epitomises the failure of the genre.

Right from the moment you roll your first character and give them the right race, hair, uniform, build and then give them a ship (again, customisable to look how you want it) and a crew you can make almost every aspect of them look how you want.
Ground combat is fairly standard (not great but not awful) but space combat is pretty good and where I spend most of my game when not actually running specific missions.  With scores of iconic ships to choose from (divided between the 3 main factions of Federation, Klingon and Romulan Republic), along with dozens of "alien" ships available to buy or earn in-game, you'll find a few favourites easily enough and have fun.
All-in-all I've stuck with this game since F2P and plan on sticking with it for a long time to come.

Binary Domain will be an aquired taste for some. Underneath the embarrassingly busted voice command system, the mediocre squadmate AI, and the oddities that come with Japanese games featuring a predominantly "Western" look and feel you'll discover a pretty solid shooter. Blasting off bits and pieces of hostile robots is surprisingly fun and at it's heart there's a deeper commentary on artifical intelligence and evolving technology (though nowhere near as discussed or explored as I would've liked). Simply put it's a fun shooter - worth a try if you can find cheap.

This is a really good game for people who like the action style of mass effect (but this has alot more Intense action) and the squad system but with a bit more of a JRPG feel to it, the action has a good flow to it, the characters are well designed and have unique personalities of their own and you can build trust with each one of them which in turn affects how they support you. a simple yet good story (about 8 to 10 hours but it has replayability), and I'd say some pretty decent graphics too. Platinum delivers again and this is definetily worth the price tag. also on another note, if you have a mic plugged in while playing you can use voice commands to issue different commands to team mates such as cover, rush, defend while playing and your team mates will judge your command performance based on battle results and the commands you gave. this can affect their trust levels which effects other aspects of the game. you can also use voice commands when they speak to you, asking things about your personality, thoughts, feelings and so on, which can again affect their trust in as well. All together this game is definitely worth getting, its unique, action packed and has an overall personal tone making you care about team mates and whats happening within the story.

Binary Domain doesn't really add anything new to the shooter genre, but it executes on established mechanics extremely well. The shooting is extremely satisfying with chunks of metal flying off your robotic foes with each bullet. Enemy behavior changes depending on where you shoot them. Shooting off a leg causes a robot to crawl at you for a close attack while shooting off a robot's head causes it to shoot at friend and foe alike.
Other features such as purchaseable upgrades for your guns, your character, and your allies help enhance the sense of progress through the game. There is trust system in the game that aims to add a sense of depth and connection to your NPC allies. Trust isn't very important to the core gameplay, but having a certain trust level with certain allies does affect your game ending, which adds some replayability.
Binary Domain is a strong 3rd person shooter with a great story, corny writing, and fun characters.

PLANETS OF WAR (ALLCAPSOMG) is a 10 minute long game about shooting the same borrowed asset over and over again. An on-rails shooter *kinda* you go through scripted events shooting ground units and ships that all use the same 3 assets. Running off Unreal of all things, this looks polished for a game ran through Unreal but what it offers in content falls very short.
4 stages I think, Fight on earth, fight above earth, kill a mothership and a boss back on earth. When I say boss, I mean click a lot on the person to win. Nothing of any actual threat can be thrown at the player, besides the hurling astroids section, that can be tedious, but with the option to enable auto-fire this aim and squeeze is a breeze. Same sounds for pretty much every action, same explosion used for small and large gets.
I think It had a story, but the crackling of the audio and poor voicework made me mute it. A lot of still or idled animations. Much waiting for the actual 6 minutes of scroll shooting.
No badges but a simple achievement pool. Its not good, but for the price and what you are getting from it, ive seen far worse. At least they tried the minimalistic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.

I went in the game expecting almost nothing: it's supposed to be a clicking adventure. Sounds okay'ish.
looks quite nice, and that's the only compliment I can give it. But making it in Unreal Engine 4 was clearly an overkill, because the only gameplay out there is clicking on "enemies" that go past the screen.
You can even make it auto-fire and just keep the cursor on them to kill everything.
After just half a minute of gameplay I was totally bored.
The story is traditionally unoriginal: somehow you are the only one with a spaceship to defend Earth against aliens. An okay premise. But then it's ruined: somehow, the whole alien armada dies when you look at it.
Enemies have cool guns and spaceships and they do damage to Earth if they miraculously get past you. I went my way to try and see what happens if you lose:
. I was sorely disappointed.
There's lots of achievements but it's clear they are there just to fill space: several of them are duplicates of each other. In that it's merely cashing on the recent trend, though thankfully (ooh, a second compliment!) it's not doing an overkill of it.
Even priced at $1, this game is overpriced. "Gameplay" lasts just short of 20 minutes. Created by just two people, their other stuff looks okay but this game is little more than a tech-demo, and Unreal Engine already has better ones at that. Save your buck
your time.

I usually like turn-based shooters, but this game is weak. It's no XCom. I wouldn't even have liked this in the 1990's, which I presume is when it came out based on the graphics.
I had a feeling things weren't going to work out when I was in the training mission, standing literally right next to an enemy... just standing there, and I shot at him twice with a rifle and missed both times, then he unloaded his pistol at me and missed all of his shots, too.
In the the campaign mission I attempted, I was outnumbered 4-1 and dropped in the middle of the woods. I was a sniper, so that is exactly what I'm not built to do. There isn't really any room for planning or strategy. You're just sort of there, and enemies start moving towards you. The board is really small, so you can't maneuver much.
Even in the training, I was outnumbered 4-1 and it looks like the game compensates for a weak AI by just spamming enemies at you.
I had to fight the camera. If you're among trees, you can't strip them away to really see what is going on. It's also easy to accidently start climbing over cover instead of moving around it.
I didn't have a very good time here, is what I'm saying.
I'm guessing this is a good game for nostalgia value if you played and enjoyed it when it was new. I absolutely can't recommend under any other circumstances.

A must play Turn Based Strategy game (TBS), which focuses on squad tactics, and has RPG elements. I pretty much forgot about this game, until finding it on a $team sale. Glad I re-discovered it!
Pros: [Partial list, just too much to include everything]
Elaborate critical-hit system, which plays well into tactical decisions.
Bodies as impromptu cover: May allow LOS, but block weapon targeting (reports as 0%).
Physics are fun; some kills are priceless.
Kill enemies by destroying terrain features, like guard-towers or even the usual tanks/barrels.
Muzzle & trajectory can be altered by aiming at particular crtical zones on target!
Long weapons extend muzzle beyond an adjacent friendly unit (less friendly fire).
Variance or "spread" of rounds enroute to target,along with minimum and maximum ranges.
Pathing indicator can be set as visible in settings, good for precise troop movements.
Dynamic destination indicator, which displays AP amount requried.
Double click for movement in real-time (in settings); priceless for simutaneous commands.
Pause command is also invaluable for simutaneous commands (even to synchronize attacks).
Enemies can suffer from morale issues and attempt to retreat, when appropriate.
Pathing and flanking abilities of AI.
Virtually every object and structure are destructible!
Shooting through ceilings, floors, and walls for kills... pure joy.
Enemies hiding in bushes? Throw a grenade to defoliate the area... lovely.
Weather and time of day affect accuracy; night decreases visual range.
Vision and detection can be decreased with foliage and even tall grass.
Enemy and friendly units are aware of sounds (player has sound and vision icons).
Limited LOS information, where direct LOS has red icons, while non direct have gray.
Enemy indicators can be used to aim and even jump to enemy location.
AP cost & chance to hit is reported dynamically, even upon mouse-over while unit is moving!
Grenade tosses are designed for units to lob them around corners.
Prone position is invaluable for decreased noise, decerase detection, and increased accuracy.
Rolling terrain, rather than just flat maps... one small hump can be incredibly useful.
The manual is comprehensive and really shows the detailed level of game's design.
A plethora of arms and ammuniton to choose from (only about 4 dozen are worthwhile).
6 character classes, but 3 are rarely desired (Show stealers: Sniper, Scout, Soldier).
Various characters, builds, loadouts, and random spawn locations to increase re-play factor.
Creative uses of grenades and mines: Chain reactions, path blockers, door removers....
XP is shared, so appropriate units and tactics may be used, rather than awkward ones.
Camera can spin 360 degrees, along with limited altitude and angle (KB and mouse).
Cons:
No grid overlay and toggle control, which can make planning precise movements awkward.
No toggle control for tree canopy, only in settings; this is not good for repeated quick looks.
No night vision appropriate to period, not even flares.
No equipment to break LOS or decrease accuracyl, like smoke grenades.
No range finder. Workaround: Save, shoot, check range in console (if activated), reload save.
No control for units to check LOS and cover on map.
No way to determine value of a unit's cover.
No overwatch feature for snipers, or supression fire commands for others.
No fire based weapons, or flammable environments.
Tech trees are generally too costly, with some pertinent skills separated.
No information regarding crtical results (activate console and check log if desired).
No AoE coverage indicator.
No way to speed up time, pass/eliminate ally turn, or know when all enemies are dead.
Ai is basic, either camp or assault. Bad news? Assaults die one by one in corner ambush.
No meter for magazine counts (unlike JA2), pop-up only, so set timer to zero in settings.
Supplies and ammuniton cannot be combined/consolidated.
No control over skill upgrades for reserve units at base.
No battle-scape inventory screen like JA2, which makes looting awkward.
Minor bugs, such as KB will issue mass commands, but not all mouse buttons do so.
Some KB commands omitted, like the sniper scope's extra aim commands (mouse only).
Note:
No strategic layer, other than adjusting loadouts and deciding on mission order.
Sci-Fi elements would be less bothersome to some players if it could be turned off.
Balancing is shot with sci-fi equipment, but a player could choose not to use them.
Manual training is tedious, units become overpowered, but a player could ignore training.
Facing changes cost full AP every time character sees an enemy, so get "Look for Free" skill.
Loot is not destroyed in AoE attacks. Which seems odd, but this design is so convenient.

A solid squad level, turn-based tactics game. This type of game seems to be missing in recent years. Released in the early 2000s; you control a 6-man squad from the top down in a WW2 setting. The weapons are concurrent to the setting, complete with corresponding range, accuracy and power; EXCEPT for the bits of science fiction thrown in...I'll just leave it at that. The environments are descructible with beautiful physics. Depending on the weapon, you can shoot through walls, ceiling, or floor...if you're sure of the target on the other side. If you were a fan of JA, the original XCom, or even SWAT 2 (remember that one?), you can't go wrong with this. It's a classic that might even beat those examples given. I only wish i'd discovered this when it came out. In fact, it made me go out and get a copy of Fallout: Tactics, for my library. This came on Steam through Greenlight; while lots of trash comes out of that program, diamonds like this exists.

If you want more specific detail: There are 6 "classes" to choose from, and each class have their own special skill tree, although I've noticed they pretty much overlap with each other. Each character has a class, attribute (strength, intelligence, dexterity) and "secondary attribute" (throwing, melee, sniping etc.) For example: a Sniper class character is likely going to be good at "Sniping"...but that doesn't mean you can't get your Medic to get up to speed at "Sniping" as well. Classes are as follows: Scout, Sniper, Medic, Grenadier, Soldier and Engineer. There's also a "weapons familiarity" modifier each char has with various weapons...as you can see, there's lots of customization that can go into this game.
I recommend this game because it's one of the best turn-based tactical squad games. For more info check out my quick review online:
A classic masterpiece in its genre. Not for those easily frustrated.

Silent Storm does what XCOM does, only better and more convincingly.
I've played HUNDREDS of hours of the GOG version of this game offline on my old laptop.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The difficulty isn't artificially bolstered by just throwing in men with more health.
Men are not bullet sponges, and a single headshot will kill ANYONE permanently.
Weapons have penetration and range values dependent on their loaded ammunition type,
and woe betide anyone firing a high-caliber weapon in a building containing fuel barrels.
Ricochets can and will kill your squad simply by causing the entire f&^%ing map to explode.
Speaking of explosions...if you can see it, it's destructible. It's the only strategy game I've ever played that has convincing levels of destruction modelled for EVERYTHING. Buildings crumble, floors splinter, that fire escape you were stood on fell into the street and killed half of your squad. Battlefield 4? HAH!
Squad injuries are dealt with in a convincing way, with most status ailments treatable only by a medic. None of this namby-pamby 'healing glue-gun' nonsense the new XCOM kiddies love, oh no. Bandages, painkillers, forceps, morphine; you name it, you'll need it. It's WAR, dammit!
Minor Spoilers(?):
About half to three-quarters of the way through the game, you'll find the oddity that is the PanzerKlein. I ADORED them, as they freshened up the gameplay in a way I wasn't expecting, but a lot of people despised them. You can mod them out easily enough, but personally I'd wait and see what you think of them.
BOTTOM LINE:
----------------
If you're a fan of turn based strategy games and like options for different tactical approaches,
then you probably already own Silent Storm and Sentinels, possibly even Hammer and Sickle.
If you don't usually go for turn based tactics, however, it'd be worth watching some YouTube vids of the game in action, as some sections can be slow. XCOM fans will probably adore it, though.

+Ability to aim at different body parts using the NumPad, including going for the headshot.
+If you're good, you can even shoot the enemy's weapon out of his hands.
+Several different weapon and equipment classifications with a HUGE variety.
+Amusing voice acting.
+Somewhat aged graphics that are still awesome.
+Ability to destroy the environment. Hear someone above you? Use your machinegun to completely take out the ceiling!!
+Turn-Based combat, but ability to do Realtime or Turn-Based when out of combat.
+Awesome character classes (Snipers for those who like popping skulls far away; Scouts for people who like to sneak and backstab; Grenadiers for people who like blowing stuff up; Medics because death sucks; etc.)
+The game seems very extensive and tremendously replayable.
+The mission progression isn't all linear.
-Relentless AI (think of X-Com: Terror from the Deep. Now slap yourself if you thought that was hard).
-The game doesn't ease you into things. It's like being a little kid and your dad gives you "swimming lessons" by picking you up and tossing you into a lake. Silent Storm doesn't have much mercy. Probably because its devs are Russian, and Russians are tough.
-The tutorial is simply the very first mission, in which you're surrounded without a squad and armed only with a pistol (for Allies, anyway. I don't remember Axis). The third mission you have to wipe out an enemy squad, but knock out the officer without killing him -- but it doesn't tell you how to do that. And it isn't easy to do in the beginning. :-P
-----
All in all, even though after all this time I still haven't gotten very far in the game despite trying hard, I still have to give it a solid
, simply because I don't recall playing a game that was almost too good. Nival and JoWood, you teams made awesome games!! Y U NO STIL AROUND?!?!?! :( Thanks Obama.

One of the humans is a wizard and has the most distinct playstyle of the 5 characters, though the Dwarf gets fire pistols that function on the same heat mechanic. Nightmare is where I feel the game is best enjoyed, though some out there claim that Cataclysm is too easy for them.  Cataclysm is hard enough to the point where the game slows down and you spend a lot more time dealing with each vermin.  At Nightmare with a good party you rarely have to slow down and a good player can make up for an inexperienced player.

Summary:  This game has come leagues since it's original release. I greatly enjoy this game now as compared to it's release. Well worth buying. Well worth playing. Well worth sinking time in to get good at.
If you need more than that from this review; Aside from good stability, major facets of the game have gotten overhauled. Particularly the melee feels far less unforgiving and mysterous a quantity than I remember from release. Attacks connect solidly when I feel they should have, and I don't need to be up a skaven's nose to hit it now. While the RNG reward system for completing levels is still present, several other methods have been added for gaining gear that can be induldged in at the same time. Meaning hard word in progressing is met with actual progress. Far more weapons feel worth using thanks to huge balance changes. The influx of new players, and returning vets, have brought the game to life again. Though I feel I would like more people to be adventurous about trying to complete the game in nightmare difficulty, you can likely find the map you want to play in progress at any given time. Though, as always with these games, having reliable friends to trick in to playing with you helps loads.
DLC thoughts specifically; I like the new weapons a lot, and the maps themselves bring some new interesting mechanics along with the map, rather than merely being a new level. Every new level feels very different from all the others. Brings new challenges to consider even for experienced people.

I reviewed this game roughly 2-3 years ago and my opinion of it still stands although it needs revising.
Star Trek Online is another example of free-2-play done WRONG! The developers of STO have put virtually everything worth interest behind paywalls, and not all of these paywalls can be dealt with by using real money either. You can complete the main storyline and participate in a fair amount of what the game has to offer without spending a single cent but everything worthwhile is just not accessible without paying.
You start out with one ship and then every 10 levels you gain a newer, better, ship unitl you reach level 40 and then from there to level 60 the only way to get new ships is one of a few ways: buying them through the exchange for upwards of 100 million credits, spending Dilithium crystals (which only lets you buy the basic ships from the different tiers), and buying ships through the Zen store or the Lobi Crystal Consortium. There's another way but I'll get to that later. The basic ships will only get you so far in PVP if that's what you're looking for. It'll quickly become a situation where the players who don't pay for anything are easily beaten by the 12 year olds with daddy's credit card.
There are 4 main currencies in STO: Energy Credits, Dilithium Crystals, Zen, and Lobi Crystals. Energy Credits are probably the most abundant but the least useful as anything worth while that can be bought with energy credits require millions of energy credits on the Exchange and free accounts are capped at the amount of energy credits they can carry, usually at or around 1-10 million. Dilithium Crystals are acquired in unrefined form through certain story missions, repeatable daily missions, duty officer assignments, and by completing reputation assignments. Dilithium Crystals can be sold on the Dilithum Exchange to acquire Zen, the paid currency in STO. Zen is not acquired naturally and can only be acquired through paying real money or by trading it on the Dilithium Exchange.
The problem with the Dilithium Exchange is that the price fluctuates. It usually costs upwards of around 220 dilithium to acquire 1 Zen. You only acquire Dilithium ore in bunches of around 960 or 1160 on average for some missions and you can only refine 8000 Dilithium Ore a day per character. Once you hit the limit for a day, you may as well quit because there's just going to be that extra dilithium sitting there that is worthless until you can refine it the next day. If the items in the Zen store were 1000 Zen at the most, it wouldn't be so bad but no, the really good stuff costs 2000 or 5000, with one or two things costing about 12000 Zen. You can sell Zen but trying to game the system where you sell for more than you bought it is likely not going to happen as the exchange always seems to sell Zen at one dilithium less than you bought it for.
Then there's Lobi Crystals. Lobi Crystals are only acquired by opening Lockboxes. The Lockboxes are somewhat common drops from killing enemies but the only way to unlock them is with a Master Key and Master Keys can be acquired from the Exchange for a million minimum on the exchange or for 125 Zen in the Zen Store. Then you get "a chance" at acquiring something really good like a new ship but most of the time its just ship consoles, weapons, or maybe even a duty officer of some kind. You always get a few Lobi Crystals for opening these lockboxes but again, everything worth buying on the Lobi Crystal Consortium is roughly 100-500 Lobi Crystals so you'd need to buy countless Master Keys and open just as many lockboxes to get them. This was that other way of getting ships.
The Klingons and Klingon aligned Romulan Characters seem to have a better time of getting Dilithium as a level 40 Klingon character has access to four repeatable daily missions that reward 1100 dilithium ore each so by the end of the day, you can earn as much as 4400 Dilithium for one character on those 4 alone. It might get you 20 Zen on the Exchange if you're lucky.
The only currency that fits in, lore wise, is Gold-Pressed Latinum. Sadly, Latinum is the most worthless currency in the game, only good for purchasing useless items like a disco-ball that makes everyone within a certain distance of it start dancing or holographic costumes for your character or ship that only last a short while. You can't buy anything decent with Latinum. A Ferengi playing this game would be disappointed by this.
The paywalls aside, if you're looking to roleplay in this game, don't bother. No one I've met roleplays in this game. And once you reach level 40, aside from trying to grind daily to earn enough Zen to get even the cheap things of value (like costumes and tier 1 ships) there's really nothing else to do in STO. If you're a fan of the JJ Abrams films and want to use the ships from that universe, forget it. They're not in the game. They may be added at a later date but for now its only ships from Enterprise, the Original Series, the Star Trek Movies, The Next Generation, Deep Space Nine, and Voyager. Don't get me wrong, they're all great but the Abrams verse has no presence here and even if those ships were here, you could bet that you'd have to drop a supreme bundle of cash just to get them.
Star Trek Online has potential. They tried staying true to Star Trek Lore, they've got the ships, the characters, the locations, even most of the original actors from the franchise to reprise their roles (or voice new ones in some cases). But the developers are clearly Ferengi in that they're trying to nickel-and-dime you for anything of value in the game. They clearly have forgotten that in the Star Trek Universe, the Federation has abandoned currency based economics.
To fix the game I recommend the following to the developers: Do away with the lockboxes, take it down to one currency that is semi-easily accrued (preferably latinum), go back to a subscription model or offer a single one-time-only payment with optional purchases for vanity items that are only cosmetic in nature, make ALL ships availible and attainable through gameplay, and then you might have a decent game worth my attention. But as it is, I cannot recommend any game that promotes a pay-2-win business model that is decidedly anti-consumer.

So right off the bat, I'm going to make the claim that if you're a Star Trek fan, you'll find something to love about this game.
Whether it's the episodic campaign that draws heavily upon the series and films. Or the vast overworld that allows you to beam down to many of the iconic locations you've come to know and love, such as Deep Space Nine, Starfleet Academy, Earth Stardock, Risa, and, taken directly from the most beloved film of the series, Paradise City from ST V. (Kidding.) Or just being able to run around your own ship or shuttle, most of which are inspired by, or are of the same class as, the ones from the show/films, and pilot it around the galaxy. There's something in this game for everyone.
Since most people here have already covered the big parts of the game, I'll point my own personal list of Pros and Cons:
The devs for STO are big time Trek fans, and you'll definitely discover this once you start making your way through the campaign of your choice: Starfleet, Romulan, or Klingon. Each episode is formatted like an episode of the show, most of which are heavily inspired by plotlines from the show and films. Some of the episodes even continue the stories of some ST characters. Some devolve into shoot-'em-ups, but most --
the recent ones -- are 100% Trek, on par with the show. There are also player-created missions available to play through by way of the Foundry, which is awesome and something I wish more MMOs would incorporate.
-
Cryptic update the game with major episodic content a few times a year, most of which have featured actors reprising their roles from the series, such as Michael Dorn (Worf), Tim Russ (Tuvok), and Denise Crosby (Tasha Yar). Leonard Nimoy also narrates many key parts of the game in-character as Spock. Each new episode has added new story content, dailies, and general updates -- and all of them have been free. We've had one full-fledged expansion,
, and another one on the way in October called
.
-
A lot went into making the game feel like a genuine Trek experience. The general atmosphere, the scale of the overworld, the missions, the visuals, locations, and characters. You take command of your own ship, and you can pretty much roll up any character you can imagine: from the stock races, such as Human, Vulcan, Romulan, Klingon, Betazoid, Trill, Orion, etc., to a custom alien race that you can define. There are also a lot of RP opportunites: Dabo(!), asteroid mining, ship interiors, and seasonal events. Just a lot of great stuff.
-
If I had to make a list of the most ethical F2P MMOs on the market... it would be a short list, but STO would be near the top. All of the story, PvE, and PvP content is free, as are all the updates. Most of the things Cryptic are making money off of are cosmetic items (uniforms, ship interiors/exteriors), ships (but the free ships are just as competitive), and services like inventory space, character slots, bank space, etc. The two things that I would count against it are the lockboxes, which can be easily ignored, and the two races locked behind a paywall, though with nearly infinite races available to you, it doesn't make much of a difference in my opinion. With a model like this, I've been happy to support it since I started playing.
Initially, it's no big deal, but after some time you start to realize how unintuitive Sector Space can be, sectioned off the way it is. Can you land here, orbit, or do nothing? Why are there invisible walls in space? There's an event here, but is anyone participating? What does the event even entail? Cryptic have stated in the past that they want to give Sector Space an overhaul, which would be awesome, but we still have it for now.
-
There are a lot of PvE and PvP instances to queue up for. People play a select few, but most have stagnated -- not from lack of players, just lack of interest. I'd much rather them not be there if no one's going to play them, so that Cryptic would be able to put more focus on the ones people still enjoy.
-
Do yourself a favor and find a good fleet that you can get along with, because the community in STO, at least the vocal part, might just drive you insane. This is nothing new to online games, but it seems abnormal in a Trek game. Part of the reason might be how fragmented chat is in STO, which makes moderation rather difficult. Making chat universal across individual sectors would make things better, I think, but for now reading ESD chat might just make you go blind.
I think that about covers it! Like I said, if you're a Star Trek fan, you owe it to yourself to give this a try, especially now that we're on the verge of a new expansion.
Live long and prosper!

I had risen to be one of the top men in the Nordic army, leading a glorious crusade against the evil savages to the north.  Me and my army of 200 stood again a combined for of 150 enemy soldier, our victory was almost assured.  Without hesitation, I headed the charge up hill, and my men ran along side me without question. We finally crested the tall hill, a wall of enemy arrows blotted out the sun, and my men fell in waves.  I, having been spared only by trusted heavy metal shield, gathered the remnants of our first wave of troops, and continued down the hill, hitting the enemy forces in a glorious clash of blood and steel.  The archers were the first to fall, their weak armor splitting under our heavy Nordic axes.
We fought until the last enemy man was dead, and having lost only 23 men continued on our rampage across their land unhindered. Finally, only the King's army of the foul Swadian kingdom remained, and I had them outnumbered 3 to 1, so I figured my newly recruited men would be able to pull the battle to victory.
I was wrong... I was so wrong. My first wave on highly trained Nord warriors ran to their demise in minutes, and I had to sit and watch wave after wave of fresh-faced farmer's sons rush to their deaths, and finally the enemy knights found and put me down in a matter of minutes, after being able to end only one of their lives, alongside a few horses. The unbreakable army had fallen, all due to my hubris.
Long story short, the Swadian king is a cool guy and tried to sell me as a sex slave after killing all my men. 10/10, I would definitely waste another 100 hours of my life as a strong independent Nord trying to make his way in a world full of suicidal thieves.

After playing this game for over 100 hours I can honestely say this game is GOOD.
First off, the Ship combat is extremely fun and makes you feel like a badass. The missions throughout the game require an even combination of Combat Skill and Puzzles which makes you concentrate on the missions instead of mindlessely killing 10 bats or other such reasons.
The ground combat is quite good, but not as good as the Ship Combat. Though it's still extremely enjoyable at times and has a huge amount of room for you to find a combat style that fits your skillset.
CUSTOMIZATION! This game offers a huge amount of customization for everything about you're character, ship and main crew. It really allows you to create someone unique every single time you play.
This game does feature a fair amount of micro transactions, but it's fairly easy to earn the Payer Currency in game through various tasks.
The crafting is something I never really got into, and it's been recentely updated and from briefely looking into it seems really in depth and fun.
You also don't have to just do the main missions, you can go to the Cardassian Sector and do mining, Fight the Borg and even do PVP along with many, many other side missions offered.
My final verdict and rating for this game is 8/10 and I STRONGLY RECOMMEND IT. It's worth a try and it's free so you're not losing anything. If you're a fan of Star Trek and even if you're new to Star Trek then this game is a must have.
