The Evil Within feels a lot like a successor to RE4, but it also differs from RE4 in many ways. For starters, TEW feels more like an actual horror game, due to the addition of stealth as a major gameplay element. Although both games have combat, TEW doesn't focus on it as much, and actively punishes you if you rely on it too much yourself.
Overall I have to say The Evil Within is definitely a must-play for any horror fan. It's not without its flaws, however. Off the top of my head... There are lots of forced walking moments. The main villain has an anime villain design that is hard to take seriously. The story is presented in a very disjointed manner and makes NO sense unless you play the Kidman DLCs (The Assignment and The Consequence). If story is very important to you don't bother buying this game unless you get those DLCs too. I personally still had fun with the main game regardless of how stupid the story was though.
Play this game for the gameplay. It's fun, and it's got some really memorable mind-blowing environments and set pieces. However, if you absolutely can't stand stealth gameplay and having to play hide-and-seek from enemies, stay very, very far away. You will spend a good chunk of time doing that in The Evil Within.

I bought this game expecting something highly cerebral and spooky, but just about every design choice detracted from the overall experience:
The notice at the beginning of the game informed me that the experience would be a creation of the player, which changes according to the players choices, but over the course of the four hours I spent playing, I don't really recall making
choices. There are no puzzles to solve, just codes for safes and doors painted very plainly on the walls. Keys to pick and use in the very same room, for no reason than to briefly distract the player. Lots of drawers to open, but rarely anything worthwhile to find.
The notion I was sold on of exploring a constantly shifting Victorian mansion was also a letdown. The game takes advantage of the 'changing environment' trope to the point of vulgarity, and it becomes tiresome very quickly. After acquainting myself with the opening setting, everything is thrown out the window in favor of a very linear corridor-after-corridor approach, every door locked firmly behind you as you proceed. Expect to bump into reused assets through the entire game. It would have been much more effective to familiarise yourself with a set environment, and then maybe have it deteriorate/mutate halfway through the game.
The nature of the protagonists' quest is revealed through a series of hamfisted cluedropping, which left me saying 'get on with it!' for the rest of the game. The ending reveals what is at that time practically an open secret, and is very underwhelming.
The most cardinal sin here is the lack of any real danger to the player. There's a creature that shows up here and there, but evading it is as simple as going back the other way. You don't even have a reason to do that. After a brief spook, you get back on your feet and be on your merry way.  The absence of any kind of fail-state fails to induce any kind of creative or intuitive play on behalf of the player; You can go through doors and corridors right up to the end after every encounter with the creature.
The multiple endings seem to be built around the notion of returning to previous chapters to collect more things and evade the nasty, but just finishing the game once proved a real chore. I can't recommend this game for anyone but the thirstiest horror fan. A poor man's Amnesia.

Silent Storm started out as an interesting tactical squad game that ended as a real disappointment for me. Initially, the character customization, range of classes, and diversity of weapons and equipment seemed to reveal a great deal of complexity in the game. Which to me looked like a lot of fun, or at least that’s what I thought…
Gameplay is pretty similar to the older XCOM or Jagged Alliance games so if you’re familiar with either of those you’ll pick up the basics really quickly. The voice acting is pretty silly and the overall story for why you are involved at all is pretty minimal.
After about 5-6 missions I realized that realistically, the only classes worth using were sniper, soldier, and scout (engineer and medic are both broken and useless as of patch 1.2) and anything except for single shot rifles and ‘secret’ weapons was totally useless in combat. The enemy AI has a habit of doing really weird things like crouching in high places and forcing you to start combat, but never leaving to engage you.
If that wasn’t bad enough, the way the game gets you to the next mission requires that you find special clues in each mission. So if you don’t find the right clues you’ll end up like I did, stuck at a mission where I was totally overwhelmed by a sudden special enemy (Panzerklein) against which _none_ of my weapons worked. After experimenting with different approaches over an hour or two, including stealing some special weapons mid-battle, I managed to defeat the enemies…except the game announced a self-destruct sequence that I had no chance of avoiding or overriding.
I decided to throw in the towel after that. I had already rerolled once before just to try out different classes and weapons and by this point the game was getting really tedious and unrewarding. It’s just not worth the self-punishment when there are better squad strategy games out there.

"Rusty Lake Hotel" is a point and click puzzle game that has a disturbing underlining plot laced into it. Join for 5 nights to solve puzzles in your guests' rooms and to cook them a dish each night that they will die for.
Each room is a whole puzzle to get what you ultamately came for
, and to ensure the player to complete, it halts you from leaving the room. This can be appealing, as you know the solution is somewhere in the room, not having to run between rooms to get clues or objects. With each puzzle, it gives you enough clues for you to figure it out, but not too much to make it too easy. Each room has its own theme with the puzzles designed to correspond with the theme and the music different with each room. Depending on your puzzle solving skills, each room varies between completion times.
Not only does every room act as a whole puzzle, there are two puzzles that are active throughout the whole game, making the meals and a key puzzle. While making the meals perfectly can be difficult, the game does help with guiding you through the most effective way to get the ingredients, some requiring you to look closely and some requiring you to remember if the guest was drinking something.
The negatives with Rusty Lake Hotel is the ending, especially to those not familiar with Rusty Lake's other works like I am. Another can be the length, but this game is very puzzle driven to progress, so the length may vary between person to person.
Overall, Rusty Lake Hotel is a charming and surreal puzzle game that makes the most out of the time it has.

Absolutely worth the price if you liked the other games.
I think they made a smart move in making a game moderately different from the others: I would have been disappointed if this had been "the lake," which was  a good game that just didn't suit my fancy.
Instead, this game features 5 rooms and an overarching puzzle, with most of the rooms being slightly more elaborate and much more visually complex than the online games.
Much like the original game, this game has some flaws. Some puzzles require solutions that are slightly nonsensical (especially the bonus puzzles), and some of the moments fail to make an emotional impact. On the balance, though, it is a great addition to the series.

If you liked their cube escape games, and want to learn more about what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on with all those creepy animals, this game holds the answers you desire. Just as creepy and strange as I've come to expect from Rusty Lake, and I was glad to know that by buying this game I was supporting their future projects.

I've played the other games made by the developer and this game still holds the eerie feel that the series has. As for gameplay, you still need a keen eye to spot the clues to solve each room. While the optional ingredients are quite unforgiving (if you miss it, you'll need to restart the entire game) you can sequence break a fair amount of the puzzles in the rooms to quickly amend your mistakes. I can recommend this game to any lovers of mysterious and a little gorey puzzle games.

This is a tough one for me... I'm a huge fan of this series, but I had to spend much of the day thinking about it.
If you're a huge fan of the Rusty Lake series, like myself, and you're more interested in the lore than in the gameplay - it's definitely worth it.  Otherwise, ultimately, I can't recommend it with a clear conscience, because the developer's made the error of selling a game with the same quality as the games they gave away.
1) The rendering engine: If you full-screen the game, it looks pretty awful.  Textures are blurry, lines aren't sharp, etc.
2) Progress: There are no checkpoints, and there is no way to reset to the start of a day in case you screw up.
3) Replay value: There is no accumulation of already-gathered optional ingredients from a previous playthrough - so, for every day you want to go back and "fix", you have to play it VERY carefully (unless you want to play the whole game over again because you got the one you missed, but missed the other one).
These are all forgiveable for free games, but the moment I've paid even a couple dollars for it - these are essential.

I got this because I am a big fan of the "Room" series of puzzle games and had just finished The Room 3 and was interested in playing another puzzle game. (I played this on Steam and also on my tablet as an Android app, so my gameplay time doesn't reflect how much time I actually spent with the game, which is closer to two hours). However, I didn't enjoy playing this. As other negative reviews have mentioned, the gameplay was not intuitive for me and I found myself looking at the walkthroughs more than I wanted to (I hardly ever have to look at walkthroughs with the "Room" series). I liked the graphics and the overall aesthetic of the game. But (spoiler alert) here's the thing I really didn't enjoy, and I am sure some people will say this is oversensitive: I did not like having to kill the animals and feed them to each other as an integral part of the game. I'm not that squeamish (nor am I a vegan/vegetarian), and I usually like things that are considered "macabre," but I just didn't like it. And I couldn't get past it. I was squicked out. Between that, and the nonintuitive gameplay (and I'm sorry, but not all the puzzles involve deduction and logic - I only got through the one with the beetle on the tabletop because I got lucky, after several tries, and MAN that got tedious) didn't make this a winner for me. I don't think I would buy another one from this publisher again. Playing this game felt too much like slogging through something I didn't really want to do. I get enough of that at work.

Summary:  This game has come leagues since it's original release. I greatly enjoy this game now as compared to it's release. Well worth buying. Well worth playing. Well worth sinking time in to get good at.
If you need more than that from this review; Aside from good stability, major facets of the game have gotten overhauled. Particularly the melee feels far less unforgiving and mysterous a quantity than I remember from release. Attacks connect solidly when I feel they should have, and I don't need to be up a skaven's nose to hit it now. While the RNG reward system for completing levels is still present, several other methods have been added for gaining gear that can be induldged in at the same time. Meaning hard word in progressing is met with actual progress. Far more weapons feel worth using thanks to huge balance changes. The influx of new players, and returning vets, have brought the game to life again. Though I feel I would like more people to be adventurous about trying to complete the game in nightmare difficulty, you can likely find the map you want to play in progress at any given time. Though, as always with these games, having reliable friends to trick in to playing with you helps loads.
DLC thoughts specifically; I like the new weapons a lot, and the maps themselves bring some new interesting mechanics along with the map, rather than merely being a new level. Every new level feels very different from all the others. Brings new challenges to consider even for experienced people.

Next, combat system is dull in my opinion and stealth gets repetitive and annoying to some degree. Ammo indeed is scarce but not to the point where you'll be extremely desperate. Environmental kills were supposed to play a huge role (at least in the trailers) but in reality they're almost useless and difficult to execute, may well use two precise pistol shots and end with everything quick.
The story is interesting, extense and mysterious. If you want a decent action-"horror" game, look forward to the base game.

The Evil Within is a criminally underrated and awesome stealth action-horror game that deserves way more love than it got. It's by no means a perfect game as some questionable design decisions and frustratingly tough sections can hamper what is a really fantastic and intense experience that's full of intense, challenging fights as well terrifying stealth and chase segments. It's a game I've found action-packed and terrifying on both an atmospheric and mechanical level. Word of warning; yes Shinji Mikami worked on this and Resident Evil 4 is amazing but don't bother trying to play this game like that because it's a VERY different game - no roundhouse kicks and uppercuts here. This is a Steam review so bullet points for days:
Pros:
*Awesome psychological story - mysterious, weird and creepy, not everything is told, you'll have to piece a good bit of it yourself.
*Fantastic gameplay - from fighting hordes of monstrosities with meaty gunplay to sneaking around insta-kill bosses looking to find the perfect strike to frightening, heart-pounding chase scenes against a handful of unkillable horrors.
*Well-rounded mechanics - Whether you prefer stealth, combat or being a coward, the game design around all aspects is nicely balanced, making all play styles possible (I like my shooty bang bang approach).
*Very challenging - from waves of powerful monsters to difficult stealth (the stealth really is that hard, I've never cleared a single section with pure stealth in both of my playthroughs - it's fun trying though), this game never pulls a single punch.
*Looks beautiful - this runs on idTech 5, the same engine as RAGE and that looked like♥♥♥♥♥♥ need I say more?
*Disgustingly beautiful art style - I love grotesque and macabre monsters and locations in my horror games a lot.
*Item management - you may have guns and other doohickeys but ammo and health items are severely limited, you're always running out of ammo which forces players to adapt to the situation via stealth, running away or hiding.
*Good level variety - It's not always from A to B, sometimes you'll have to survive waves of enemies or explore an area to solve puzzles or you'll be forced through a tough scenario against an enemy that cannot die; it's not afraid to throw player into new scenarios around the core gameplay and that makes each chapter distinct from each other. Chapter 9 even comes with a call back to Resident Evil 1 with its own miniature Spencer Mansion with a great deal to explore.
*Awesome soundtrack and sound design - very reminiscent of Silent Hill 1, tons of creepy industrial banging, horrific moans, lovely weapon sounds and all that jazz. You'll be surprised how much the music can do for those chase scenes.
*Great length - I'm not one of those gamers who believe every game has to be a whole saga but 15-20 hours on your first run is pretty great and necessary for fleshing out the world and characters, it took me about 16 on my first run and 13 on my second and I prefer a combat approach; it will definitely take much longer if you focus on stealth, fleeing and hiding.
*Highly replayable - new game+ is arguably better than the first run now that you have the necessary upgrades where you can just enjoy yourself the second time through. You will also unlock new weapons and difficulty modes.
*Fair price point - £15/$20 for this hidden gem is a steal and definitely worth the asking price, the DLC is very cheap too and I have heard it's good stuff.
Cons:
*Frustrating to begin with - with a mimumum damage output, flimsy health bar, tiny ammo pool, pathetic melee and the sprinting ability of a 100 year old disabled granny; starting out without the upgrades can be VERY rough indeed.
*Unavoidable grab attacks - a lot of enemies have grab attacks and they are completely unavoidable when you're right up in their face (it's very easy otherwise) as the attack frames are way to unforgiving and you are unable to break free from the Haunted that carry weapons, forcing you to suffer massive damage.
*One-hit kills - when done right with the proper amount of wind up and plenty of opportunity to dodge, they can make certain enemies and situations terrifying and they are for the most part; however there are parts of the game where they're way too hard to avoid.
*♥♥♥♥ing crossbow ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s are massive♥♥♥♥♥♥♥- probably the worst enemy design I've seen in a game for a very long time, certain Haunted can be tough with hard-to-deal with weaponry and armour but none of them beat the crossbow guys who can shoot sticky explosive bolts into you with terrifying accuracy and rate of fire and will effectively try to stun-lock you until you're dead. Utterly atrocious - thankfully you'll encounter roughly six or so in the entire game.
*Is this game Haunted? - There's a good number of fun and interesting such as The Keeper, AlterEgo, the invisible dudes and one particularly famous monster that all sadly gets hardly any game time at all as there's way too much of a focus on the common Haunted enemies, they're fun but it's like how Lost Planet 2 focused on dudes with guns rather than the awesome Akrid.
*Tricks And Traps - this game is FULL of traps and unlike Resident Evil 4, Tango Gameworks made them fiendishly difficult to see this time around - from explosive trip mines in a dark village at night to bear traps completely hidden in murky water full of poo. It gets really mean sometimes.
*Horror is subjective - different things scare us and The Evil Within is probably not going to scratch that itch if you're looking for a true horror game to scare the daylights out of you; it's called action horror for a reason.
*Performance - while the game runs at 60fps the vast majority of the time for me, there are points where it very rarely drops or suffers from microstutter; my rig is pretty beastly so expect plenty of hiccups on weaker hardware.
I totally recommend The Evil Within wholeheartedly - just know that it might be a rough ride on your first time through and you'll probably have even more fun in new game+. To me it nails the action and the horror the vast majority of the time and backed up with an engaging, crazy story makes it all the more entertaining and is definitely a go to for me whenever I feel up for a good ol' action horror. If you're into the more recent Resident Evil games including 4, Dead Space, Cold Fear and any other game in the action horror genre then The Evil Within is absolutely worth playing.

A good game with a lot of interesting mechanics. Feels very similar to Resident Evil 4 (done by the same guy). The shooting is solid, it has a decent upgrade system, and you never have to completely master one thing; you can always try different approaches. It has a few questionable designs (like a hub-world style checkpoint system), re-using some areas, and some very briefly touched on mechanics (there's a section where you have to keep a buddy alive) that are seen once and then never again.
My gripes are that the game doesn't seem to commit to either survival horror or action. It will shower you with items and supplies before bosses and wave-style fights, and other times completely skimp on stuff during regular fights. Don't go into it expecting a survival-horror game, and don't go into it expecting an action game.
Acting is kinda bad too, and while the story is supposed to be surreal and crazy, it feels like at the same time it's trying to remain rooted in reality. So this results in the game progressing things along 'just because'.

Binary Domain is a 3rd-person tactical shooter (like Gears of War) in a cyberpunk setting. Dan Marshall & his crew are to clean-up the mess a corporation made, creating robots that look & act like humans.
The action, shooting & destruction of robots is just pure bliss, as enemies can be destroyed to pieces & will keep coming at you 'til they're completely destroyed (like in Dead Space)! Boss fights are awesome - though, there are a few that are tough.
The characters, voice-acting, writing & dialogue are good. The premise & plot itself is pretty good, better than the writing. You give orders to your party members, via selecting dialogue options on your gamepad or keyboard/mouse - or even w/ the mic, since the game has voice-recognition & recognizes numerous phrases you say. Well, it tries to, at least. You're better off using dialogue options via KB/mouse or gamepad.
Simply put - BD is an awesome shooter & easy to reccommend.

Good: Looks lovely and spooky, and the endless, ever-changing house gave me a shiver of pleasure the first few times I experienced it.
Bad: But once that wears off, you realize that the entire game mechanic (quite literally) is just walking through doors.
Walk into a room. It's spooky. Walk out.
Walk into another room. The other door is locked. Now you have to wait around for something "spooky" to happen. Then you walk out.
Walk into another room. Turn around, the door is gone. Another door appears. Walk out.
Walk in. Walk out.
Walk in. Walk out.
Walk in, wait around for the animation, walk out.
Walk into a room. It's spooky. Walk out.
Walk into another room. The other door is locked. Now you have to wait around for something annoying and "spooky" to happen. Then you walk out.
Walk into another room. Turn around, the door is gone. Another door appears. Walk out.
Walk in. Walk out.
Walk in. Walk out.
I made it through to the end, but man was it a long, tedious slog. And this is coming from someone who generally loves both  "walking simulators" and horror games.
Updated tl;dr: This is an art concept in search of an actual game. The very cool design can't save it from its own lack of storytelling, puzzles, or danger. Still might be worth it on a good sale.

I don't endeavour to write reviews very often, and this is going to be EXTREMELY biased, but as a huge fan of the Rusty Lake escape series I just coudn't help myself, first up; what you get with this first premium title of theirs:
-Beautiful visuals that give off a calm and unsettling vibe
-Tricky puzzles that require you to think out of the cube (scuse the pun) and are definately satisfying to be solved.
-Bonus items to be found for people who like to dig deeper that provide a higher star rating with each part of the game
-If you are a fan of the series you get MORE GLORIOUS LORE, that can either make you think or make your head hurt.
-The characters are nicely articulated and presented, each with their own themes and stereotypes that make sense when considering humanoid versions of the animals portrayed, as well as mr.owl and mr.crow making another appearance.
-The music is fantastic and settling to the theme of the game, and not frustrating to listen to looped whilst busy solving puzzles.
Now onto what I didn't think was that great which is only a couple of things:
-The game is shorter than I would have liked for their first premium title (which is to be expected as it follows closely to the format of the previous titles) so not so much a complaint as something to watch out for if you're not sure what the previous games were like/about (and honestly for only costing pocket change, it's really a small price to pay for any delicious nugget of gold the developers of this series puts out)
-There is no option to go back specifically to certain days and acquire the stars you are missing, and in some cases whilst going through the game, you may realise you haven't got everything yet and are not allowed to go back.
-The scenarios (rooms) are a little more static than previous titles, as you move from left to right there isn't a smooth moving transition as was present in previous games but honestly this is a tiny issue as it doesn't diminish the atmosphere whatsoever.
So all in all, head over to
, play through some of the cube escape games free and see if the style of game is for you, and if you find yourself inclined to deep mystery and ingenious puzzling, then please please PLEASE consider supporting the developers by purchasing this title.

One of the few games that I would purchase again at what I consider to be an expensive price since the game is over a decade old.
I bought this when first released -- probably on discount, after gaming for such a long time and having suffered many disappointments, I resist trying to pay full price for something any more.  This is to protect my wallet from the effects of the "glitter and flash" that accompanies a game, particularly on its box (then) but (now) with multiple screenshots on Steam.
One thing likable about this game -- there is a ton of content here.  For those unfamiliar -- it is a squad-level based game that becomes tactical and turned based whenever you alert the enemy (or when you want it to become turn-based).  Stealth in this game is key, there are very few situations in which you can run in with guns blazing and escape without losing a team member.
And you want to keep your team members alive because they gain experience that can be spent on fairly elaborate skill trees.  So pretty quickly I learned (at least the way I play the game) that I needed to keep my doctor at the rear of the group.  I liked having a sniper (for obvious reasons) to cover my flank.  WIth a little patience you can position the sniper extremely well so that at a critical time in the battle his shots have a great impact.  After this, I liked having a scount and an enginer, a light infantryman and a heavy one.  THis is the combination that worked for me.
The player has the option to be either on the allied side or the axis.  The missions are different depending on which forces you play.  And, because of the nature of this game, no two session will be the same.
It's a difficult game and it can be frustrating.  You have to be patient.  Those bullets hurt your character, this isn't like a FPS when you can pick up a health pack in every room and boost your health.  I'd say the replay value here is medium, after you have played both sides, but the longer I waited the more I forgot and found it interesting again.
Easily one of my favorite games.  Would recommend to anyone who asked.

Let me get the first thing out of the way: The idea of and the initial execution of the game is really good. DOTA as a third person shooter with more direct abilities and a gamemode where towers can be rebuilt, themed as a gladitorial combat future sport in a strangely dystopic future. The gameplay and handling of it all is quite well done, and things handle very well, and the controls are simple and intuitive while still having the depth of a regular MOBA type game.
That said, there are some major issues. Between class balance needs work, and the overall game needs a bit of work. The matchmaker is not very good, and the tutorial amounts to a single map with voiceovers when you hit a button ans some bots wandering around for you to shoot. It doesn't really progress beyond that, test your skills, or try to teach you essential tricks to the game. The addition of new heros was fairly slow and seems to have ceased now, and each one requires quite a lot of in game grinding or a fee that is annoyingly large for how much gameplay there is. The game is frustrating to new players in ways DOTA isn't. The idea of bot matches and practice lobbies and private bot matches and unranked games are seemingly absent from SMNC in favor of a wave survival, a more DOTA like take on the game, and a mode with increased character lethality and rebuildable turrets, or the training arena with lines of bots marching onward and ignoring you completely. The way to learn the game is to jump straight into the game, which results in people getting destroyed by experienced players. See, the game has these other things called endorsements and products, which give you special abilities and boosts to speed, damage, accuracy, and various other stats. They take quite a long time to buy one, or less time if you get good victories constantly, and they give a notable advantage. As a new player, you get dropped into the game with the long time experts and the game becomes you being cannon fodder. That of course drives off the new players, leaving more and more experienced players who keep playing each other and pushing their own skills up, making entry even harder. The new players have been driven away so badly by the balance of products and endorsements and the poor matchmaking have reduced this game to nothing but a wait for hours, hoping one of the few rare people still playing it might be on and enough will join that a match can happen.
Oh sure, it can give a tf2 hat, but for me one of the achievements is completely broken, and for anyone who did not play this game at the peak, you will spend far more time than is worth it to get a single hat.
The audience has left and the game is functionally dead. The ideas it presented were new and unique and it handled them well enough, but the matchmaking and other things added to increase the various options and playstyles (go for super accuraccy and health at the expense of everything else, or speed above all, or...) ended up being the undoing of the game. I can recommend the ideas for someone else brave enough to try to remake DOTA as a shooter, but I can't recommend this game.

Yes the game play is pretty old school, but there is SO much to do, The value to this game is outstanding. There is a certain satisfaction that this game gives you that I have yet to see in other games (Watching a horse rider topple from his mount when you hit him vitally with an arrow or javelin, Or charging full speed and landing a mace blow straight to your enemy's face.) This series of games just does something for me I've never seen in a game before, it's pretty magical.
You can be a bandit and raid caravans, you can be a merchant and build quite a bit of wealth, you can become a vassal for a king and be granted lands, you can get married, you can turn the vassals of another kingdom to your cause with some fancy convincing, OR you can start your own kingdom and gather followers through positive influence, or you can take the land by force. I suggest checking a wiki, some of the routes you can take are not very intuitive.
On the downside, I kinda wish there were more options in the ways of diplomacy and resolution, once a territory decides to go to war with you, the only way to get them to give it up and leave you alone is by smashing their entire kingdom to bits, or by coaxing vassals to join your cause, which (depending on the kingdom) can be nearly impossible to do. I also don't like how often enemy vassals escape from a defeat in battle, since when you are defeated in battle you almost ALWAYS get captured... Very annoying. I also wish there was a way to garrison villages or dispatch patrols without using vassals.
Over all, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone with a bit of patience and bloodlust. If the looks of the game put you off, wait for the new game to come out, it looks gorgeous and they may even address some of the negatives I brought up. Definitely worth a good look for anyone who loves midieval style fighting.

GREAT GAME, read all this:
The story concept is something new.
The levels have variety, inside and outside as well.
The bad guys are different and have reason for their identity.
You will see things not in other games.
The gore is well done, the violence is well done. This can be tamed in settings.
The curiosity makes it hard to stop playing.
You will be experiencing some jump scares, and lots of panic. If you don't feel panic change the difficulty.
You will be sneaking, running for your life, hiding, and often saying "where is it, which way do I go".
You will learn what is happening, what happened, and realize what you thought is not so.
There is plenty of content, you will not get into it then say "thats it? done?"
Most important: This is not a shooter, not a stealth game, not a puzzle game, etc. It has shooting, stealth, puzzles, character customization, story following, collection, and achievments. You don't have to do a lot of anything if you don't like it. Best of all no level grinding, the game is always moving forwards.
Linear Yes: Not an issue with this game. You will find yourself leaving one world to another mid chapter and returning to places in a different year at times. There is no issue with linear. There are plenty of save points and auto saves inbetween as well so you don't feel like the game is in sections, it flows like one story in many places. It's really nice when you go to your save area and things are different and events even happen. Some times your safe place is not always safe! They did a damn good job with this game.
DLC:You can enjoy just the main game without it. I recommend getting it all. Main story flows right into the 1st DLC. 1st DLC makes the second DLC great and at the end of the second you are like "Yeah, time to end this evil!" Third DLC reminds you, it's all about the Evil. You experience the killings with purpose, you see places of the past, it all makes sense and still has story. Not as much story in the last DLC but it's a nice little horror icing on the meaty death cake.
I see some bad reviews saying the game is aweful. Maybe you want a shooter horror and not this. Maybe you want one character to focus on with a skill tree and endless stats and not this. Maybe you have expectations that won't be met. I told you how the game is and really I am impressed. I think this story is so deep because they plan to continue with the game. I imagine this is only the intro to a new story concept that we will see lots more of until they run out of ideas 6 games later. Is it worth the money? I see people spend $40 on pizza delivery and conplain about a decent game on sale for $20. Yeah it's worth the money. You want the most out of it stay of the internet, stay off the discussions, put that difficulty up and enjoy every minute.

The Evil Within is a must-have for people who love Survival Horror games. It feels heavily similar to Resident Evil 4 in terms of gameplay. The story is interesting, and you'll need to finish the game to truly comprehend it.

If you're into gore, horrific monsters, a humanly scary story and creepy places: this is a game for you.
This game in a nutshell:

Evil Within isn't sure if it's a stealth game or a shooter and gets stuck in an unpleasant limbo in between.  It encourages stealth but doesn't offer mechanics or controls to meaningfully support playing that way, but neither does it give enough resources to play it like an RE4 shooter.  It doesn't help that the game isn't very scary, not offering much more than cramped camera effects and chainsaw cliches.
There are hints of an interesting narrative and some good set pieces and ambience, but it's buried under a game that just isn't very much fun to play.

I haven't really entered the mid- to late game yet, so there might be a lot I've not put into consideration. But if you like Banished and can work with the graphics, then you'll like this game.

This game is the full package as a hybrid rts/rpg game.
The gameplay succeeds in fitting the turn-based combat into the context of both expansive and interior environments alike. I have experienced minor bugs, including 20-second lags inbetween when a soldier stops firing and when you can control their actions again. These aren't gamebreaking, just slightly annoying.
Gameplay also fits into how you use the character classes available, from snipers to grenadiers. A branching skill tree system makes you plan out what skills to take now in order to arrive at the skills you'll need later.
Personally, I didn't feel drawn into the story of Silent Storm. The story mission levels were not interesting to me, but the fact you can set up camp and walk around your virtual camp really sells the context of the game.
The game really sells you are this character, which you have the option to create or pick from available templates. Granted there isn't much you can change about character actions or motives, but you can create your own stories within Silent Storm just because of this focus on context as well as a randomized mission option.
I had a lot of fun, but there were just enough small details to irk me. The lag can get annoying when it happens more often with more participants in combat. You have to return to base to grab more ammo, and the little dot on the map has to physically move over to the 'base' button. I understand building context as a figure moving on an actual map, but the maps just aren't detailed enough to draw you in to the movement. See Mount & Blade: Warband in which they do movement on a map correctly. When you return to base to resupply, there's little interaction with the people who administrate your operation. You just stare at them while changing figures and items on a screen overlay. It breaks the game world interaction to the player, breaks the sense of realism and importance of your role in the war effort. Like no one cares what you do.
All things considered, I'm at a strong 7 of 10 for Silent Storm

For any of you that remember the boardgame 'Ambush!' (by Victory Games) or the PC title 'Soldiers at War' (by SSI), this game will probably seem familiar to you.  It's a full 3D, turn-based, World War II tactical combat game where you control individual members of your squad in special ops missions.
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
Pros:
* The AI (while not fantastic) is pretty good - or at least seems pretty good - definitely going to give you a better run for your money than most games
* Everything is destructible – walls, doors, chests, windows, and even trees and floors!  It's a game like no other
* It's very addicting.  I have over 200 hours playing it and have still not come close to being bored with ANY part of the game yet
* Game physics are amazing - easily beats out some triple-A games with how well they're implemented - nothing beats killing an enemy a level above you by blowing up the floor below him
* The array of weapons and ammunition types are awesome (most completely accurate, given the genre)
* The music is not bad... it'll either get on your nerves or grow on you - or both ;)
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
Cons: (in paragraph form with explanations)
Most complain about the dated graphics, but while I love the jazzy newer games like Diablo III, I found the visuals in Silent Storm (or S2) to be quite functional... even sort of impressive.
The voice acting sucks, but the cheesy quips the soldiers (both friendly and enemy) say are so funny, you wind up almost liking it better that way.
The missions are all based on this clandestine what-if slant on World War II (such as fully uniformed Germans operating with near impunity all throghout Britain, or Axis commandos striking targets they never even dreamed of having access to in real life).  This (IMHO) is really no issue – just simply pretend everything is happening somewhere in occupied France or something.
A really odd game decision made by the developers was to include (later in the game) such things as laser guns, PanzerKlien (near-impenetrable armor that makes soldiers look like space robots), and modern-day-esque weapons.  This has game-altering impact and is the source of many complaints regarding gameplay.  There is however an easily found and installed mod that removes all this wacky stuff from the game entirely (replacing it with better equipped enemy soldiers... which works).
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
All and all, I love this game and HIGHLY reccomend it to anyone who likes turn-based games and World War II tactical combat.  Hell, even people who play games like Jagged Alliance, X-Com or Fallout-Tactics will likely enjoy this as well.

Have been on this game since Beta, and quite honestly, I can not help but keep returning to it.  Although it does not follow ST cannon (being set after the god-awful 're-boot') it is very entertaining & quite immersive

First, the good. Star Trek Online has by far the most well-written stories I have ever come across. And with the new updates the story has become even more polished. I won't spoil anything, but by the time you have reached max level your captain will have done some cool stuff. With a custmizable character feature that can be used on both you and your major crew members, you can customize quite a bit.  There's lots of areas to explore in the galaxy, and the community is fairly nice, then again i have zone chat disabled most of the time.
Now the bad. Star Trek Online's space combat is an acquired taste. I personally like it, but people whom have played EVE Online may not. People have reported to me that the combat is slow (even though they were flying newbie Cruisers, which are notorious for being slow and slow-turning. My observation is that you will be perusing the cash shop alot, and while the game has one of the best ones I've found in any game (who doesn't like looking at new shiny ships!). Another observation is lockboxes. I'm not a fan of them. but this game has them. And this game will drop more than you could possibly hope to open.
And now the ugly. Cryptic and PWE work really hard on this game to be the best MMO out there, and it shows. Unfortunately, no game is without it's glitches and bugs and STO is no exception. Luckily, they maintain the game almost weekly to make sure they keep things in working order. Federation captains will find polished bugfree content galore but once you start playing as KDF or the Romulans, things change a bit. I once had to abandon a mission because I got stuck in the rafters of a KDF base.
Overall, though, I love this game. I'd love Champions Online even more if it were written as well as this. I can't wait for what new updates come out and the new adventures my character will have.

Rusty Lake Hotel was a game I bought instantly upon only viewing half of the trailer. I knew instantly that it was going to be a game that appeased my curious appetite. Food and Murder, I'm absolutely in! It was a jump into my recently found love of Point&Clicks. Unfortunately, this quick ordering left me a little hungry since it only feels like an appetizer. All the same...It was delicious.
Pros:
- The character designs are what made me buy the game so quickly. They're seemingly basedon Victorian/Edwardian taxidermy and photography. They are delightfully creepy and appealing to the eye. They fit into the atmosphere around them, and for me they help make the game feel like a dark picture book.
-Music wise the Rusty Lake Hotel is haunting. Each room has sounds unique to it, and they do distract from the puzzle solving process. Each piece sets the mood for each room, and it really adds to the game without being annoying.
-The Puzzles for this point and click adventure are interesting and properly themed to each Dinner Guest. Often they are macbre, fun, and not too frustrating. There are exceptions to this,however.
-Each room tells interesting hints about their occupants. They are all unique to their guests personalities/lives outside of The Rusty Lake Hotel.
Cons:
-Honestly, this game is incredibly short. You can work your way through the meal fairly quickly. In my excitement to order I didn't completely read up on the game. For the price, however, I likely should have known. Still...It really left me wanting more despite my enjoyment of the puzzles and death.
-Some of the puzzles for extra ingredients could be incredible frustrating. Often, I was unable to find optional ingredients because I was too soft hearted or it just didn't seem like something one would naturually do.
Overall, I really enjoyed Rusty Lake Hotel! I got more than enough entertainment out of it for what I paid...even if I'm not quite full yet. The good news is the next game Rusty Lake:Roots has been announced! So, it seems that we may be getting a second helping yet. Bon Appetit, my friends.

It has a great deal of potential, but it just was not well executed. Maybe I have been spoiled by games like Amnesia and Outlast, but the horror elements didn't affect me and it became more of a task to finish than an immersive experience. Half of the problem is the poor control and interaction system. You have to be in very precise locations and at specific angles to interact with the objects, which becomes even more frustrating when you have to open doors through holding a button and rotating/moving. This often became extremely frustrating, since much of the game is just opening doors or drawers.
If they worked out a better control system and fleshed out the game a bit more, it certainly would be a game to pick up, but right now I cannot recommend it at full or even half price.

This game is absolutely amazing. If you're a hardened FPS veteran, or even a newbie, you will definitely enjoy this game.
First off, I have never played any Quake or Unreal games so I'm very new to the FPS sub-genre that Ratz occupies, so this game was completely new to me. But boy, what a breath of fresh air it was!
Firstly, the graphics. Never have I seen a game with such simple, but at the same time, elegant graphics. Having such simplistic graphics not only makes the game look nice and modern, it also helps you spot the enemy rats that could be lurking around the corner, just waiting to shoot you.
Secondly, the level of customisation in this game is astounding. You can customise your FOV so you can either be like a Quake pro or have a Call of Duty-esque FOV (like me). But that's not all: you can also customise your laser colour, type, enemy colour, gibs, crosshair and team colour. You can also disable the ingame music, so you can add your own heart-pumping music to suit your playstyle.
Also, the gunplay is very barebones, but at the same time very fun and enjoyable. Everyone gets the same, beamshooter gun, which means that no one is every at an advantage over another player and therefore who gets the kills is determined purely by player skill rather than a weapon advantage. Also, if you're familiar with TF2 or other games where shooting rockets at your own feet is beneficial, you'll LOVE this game. The beam jumping in this game is so fluid (even at a high ping) that you'll be impressed by the mobility you can achieve with your beamshooter. WIth the jumping, you can constantly strafe around the map, but you can also reach strategic map positions that can help you gain an advantage over your enemies.
The maps in this game all have their own unique style and I've also noticed that they all seem to have a different colour palette. For example, one map may be predominantly green coloured, while another could have mostly red tones. All maps which I've played seem to have a good balance between stratergy and fun. Although some maps are definitely more enjoyable than others, in the end, no matter what map is chosen, you should have a blast playing.
Finally, the gamemodes. Due to a lack of players :(, I've only been able to play deathmatch so far, which is enjoyable even in its own right. The other gamemodes are classic staples: you have duel, capture the flag and survival. I can't really talk about these modes since I've never played them, but according to other people they are great fun to play.
Overall, this is an excellently-made game that excels in all aspects of its design. From the gunplay, to the customisation, you should have an excellent time playing Ratz!

This game freaked me out--I thought I was going to die because the design is so dull. Most linear game I've ever played, literally. This is no hyperbole, the game would shuffle you through a series of rooms and not even let you turn around because it would lock every door behind you and have the architecture change almost every time you turn around (so spooky). Bad lighting, too: I had to play in the dark not to increase the horror factor (of which there is none, and this comes from someone who cries when playing Silent Hill), but to be able to see anything. Finicky controls; closing the elevator door is really a ploy to give you carpal tunnel. It's unclear what items are interactive, forcing you to scroll randomly about the room.
Long story short, you've experienced the game's full repetoire of tricks after an hour's play. $20 is a joke for the reasons outlined above, and I never even broached the ridiculously basic design of the house through which you roam. It reminded me of something I would create absent-mindedly as a child while playing Sims: Livin' It Up. I do feel obliged to say in the game's defence, especially after so damning a comment, that there was the occasional visual trick that is impressive. Not enough to earn your dollar, though.

I bought this game during Early Acess and reviewed it then. I wasn't as detailed as I would have liked. Now that the game is fully released, I'd like to reassess my opinion of it... because while the game is amazing in a lot of ways, it also disappointed me in other areas. Layers of Fear really shines in the horror genre for stepping away from the survival action aspect and comes forward to being completely story-driven, but what it gains in storytelling, it lacks in horrifying me in the way I hoped.
I have played the game multiple times during Early Access, and completed the fully-released game once.
1) The story itself. It’s deliciously dark. I might be a little biased when it comes to enjoying the story, because like the protagonist, I'm also an artist, so it spoke to me in ways other horror games don't. The main story has a very cryptic nature to it, and it doesn't come right out and tell you what's going on-- you figure it out on your own by inspecting letters and items. I enjoy that kind of writing.
2) The "insane" feeling you get when wandering the house. My favorite kind of horror is psychological, as I don't believe in ghosts or demons, and therefore don't find them scary. So, as you might imagine, I'm very tired of games or movies involving demons or possessions or haunted houses. This game seems to be almost entirely a mind-trip, as it plays off of what you might consider common for a game to have or include, then changes it. It surprises you by throwing twists and angles you didn't expect, thus giving you the feeling you are "going insane". I loved that feeling, and it made me love the game.
3) The visuals and sound were done very well. That goes without saying when complimenting its nuanced style of psychologically-influenced gameplay, but they also look amazing in other areas. The lighting is perfect at times, as are the many paintings on the walls. The sound is haunting and creeps its way into your brain with eerie, low piano music, hums and static fizzles. Playing this game with headphones on seems almost necessary. That voice acting, though… it’s all right, but not the best.
1) I hate saying "such and such part of the game was easy!" because it insults anyone who got stuck on a particular part of the game, which I find to be tasteless. Some things are obvious to people in games, and for others, we overthink it, because we assume to be in a game that's more complicated than it is. I have fallen victim to this trap many times.
In my personal opinion, the “puzzles” weren’t challenging enough. I don't even think they should be considered "puzzles," because they required almost no solving. Usually the solution was something like "turn on light switch" or "light the candle" in order to see a certain number or letter on the wall. Maybe the game didn't intend to be heavy on the puzzles, so I can't blame it
much for this. It’s likely they didn’t want the game’s precious, though minimal three hours of time to be bogged down by “solving” things. I’ll give it a slight pass on this one, since the quick, simple feeling of the game might be my personal preference to be challenged by something.
2) The Silent Hills P.T. has influenced this game a
, and while that isn't really a negative... there were some things that felt directly ripped off of it.
. While I never played the P.T., I did watch playthroughs of it, and honestly, it was in a class all its own. Others can mimic it, but it felt like it did something right. And even just watching those playthroughs terrified me more than playing this game did.
3) Jump scares aren't scary. Maybe other people disagree with me on that, but I've never been afraid of them. Yeah, I jump when something goes "BWWWAAAH!" because that's an organic response. I don't feel "scared" afterward. I just feel annoyed. Layers of Fear uses
jump scares to deliver its horror to you. While I loved the "insanity" feeling mentioned above, I hate that it just used generic methods of scaring you rather than make something look and feel horrifying just by looking at it and feeling horrified. There are the occasional "Whoa, that's effed up" paintings that have creepy, grimacing faces that send chills down my spine, but those moments are rare, and honestly, there wasn’t nearly enough of that. I wanted more of the “good god, that painting is watching me” rather than the “BOO! GOTCHA!”
4) I've beaten the game and I still don't know any of the characters' names. Would be nice to feel as though I was part of an identity so that I could relate to them. If you
learn their names, and I just didn't manage do, forgive this note. However, I don't think finding out the name of the
should be a mystery.
5) There are multiple endings to the game (3 to be exact), but there's no way to know how to get them unless you look it up online and possibly spoil it for yourself. I hate games that do this. I already know the other endings, and I know how to get them-- but I had to look up what I was supposed to do (and thus spoiled them for myself, so I have no reason to replay the game). This is also an indication that to get the more "complete" of endings, you need walkthroughs to know where to pick up the items (because it isn't always very clear). I was as thorough as I could possibly be in my previous playthrough and I still somehow missed a lot of items.
6) Game length is shorter than what I'm used to. The fully-completed game took me about three hours. Twenty bucks… for three hours. Just no. Get it on sale.
While I do have a lot of nitpicks, I still recommend Layers of Fear to all horror fans. Why? Well, mostly because it's unique, and tries to do something new (well, new-ish). It's not an FPS, it's not an action game, it's not even a survival game (which seem to plague the market these days). It's a story-based game, and when all said and done, it is
at telling the story. I do wish, however, that the game had been more atmospheric, and less predictable in its execution. And I know this might sound stupid to some people… but I wish it was scarier.

Heroes and Generals is a Free 2 Play, Massively Multiplayer, World War II based, FPS game. I have about 40 hours into H&G and I have a great idea on the concept and function of this game. Now the real question: Is this game right for you? Well, continue to read and you will find out!
The game is very fun, allowing you to play as either a Soviet, German or American soilder, and switch between them whenever you want, but not during a war. The equipment, rank, weapons, and vehicles an American soilder can use is completely different than what a German, or Soviet soilder can use. In the beginning, you are usually playing skirmishes, as you capture the points. This is all that is availible to you in the beginning. After reaching Level 5 on any soilder, you can do other maps and gamemodes with that soilder and even choose a profession [Tanks Lvl 5, Planes Lvl 6, etc]. I find it extremely satisfying when I kill someone in a game where you need to find enemies, unlike other games where enemies are on a map and easy to find. So, pros and cons.
Pros/Great characteristics of Heroes and Generals
Extremely fun and satisfying game
Full of action for how large maps are
Good assortment of classes and personalization
Game UI is solid and functions well
Ambient sound is pleasing, as are the graphics
Hit markers while firing on the enemy are spot on. No 1 hit kills with regular small arms as seen in other games.
Good assortment of maps with modes [Larger amount of gamemodes and maps are found when you have played a decent amount]

Can be a game played serious or for fun. Like, what FPS allow you to ride a bike into battle?!
Graphics still look amazing in low xD [Good for players with not the best computers.
Cons/Bad Characteristics of Heroes and Generals
Could get bad FPS if you are not on a good computer
If you become a pilot or parachuter, it might be hard to play with your friends who are under leveled, but when there is a will, there is a way.
When a game finishes, players in that game already are dispursed. I would like if it we were put into a lobby, speak amongst eachother and maybe create more friends for a squad.
Pay 2 Win. Personally, I don't feel the pay 2 win aspect of H&G but many others do. The ingame currency can be used for everything. You either pay large amounts of ingame credits, which takes time but is simple and satisfying to get, or used a small amount of paid credits.
Matchmaking needs to be fixed.
Obviously, this game is in Early Access, meaning the game is not fully completed and may change in the near future. I do not know the specific date, but there is a huge update coming soon. Personally, I believe the Pros outweigh the Cons heavily for a Early Access, and these cons may not even exist in the near future. I would recommend this game to anyone who likes realistic FPS games that are based of something real, like history. Great Game.

Shinji Mikami, the creator of Resident Evil, the father of survival horror games, returns to give us Resident Evil 4.5 AKA The Evil Within (TEW). The only problem is that it’s 10 years too late and frankly feels outdated.
I was hoping for a return of an open central setting like Resident Evil’s mansion or police station, or Silent Hill 1 and 2’s towns. Instead, TEW is chapter based, simply moving from point A to point B for the progression of a vague storyline that could have been told in a much more impactful or engaging way. The story is actually fairly decent once you read up on it, but it’s just so poorly done as you’re playing the game.
Survival horror? I guess so, if you consider chase sequences, dark environments, clunky controls, jump scare attempts, random camera switches, and cheap deaths as survival horror.
You will also need the DLCs to fill in a ton of plot holes in the already Swiss cheese storyline. In the DLC you play as Juli Kidman, as she does the damsel in distress playthrough of the game. Seriously Juli, did you really wear high heels as you cosplay a detective? With almost no offensive capabilities, Juli’s playthrough is supposed to be “pure” survival horror, but it was just the longest and most annoying 4 chapters of the game.
Usually in RE games, there is a way to get unlimited ammo or a mercenary mode (for the ish and giggles), but in TEW there’s none of that. This severely cripples the replay value. Also, why can’t I play the game on Hard without unlocking it? I hate it when games do this. Akumu (1 hit death) mode should be locked, not Hard.
Overall, if you enjoy RE4, you’ll most likely tolerate this game as I did. By the way, RE4 is a masterpiece of a game when it came out and is still better than a lot of games out these days. However, TEW just fell a little flat.
Personally, the Evil Within bundle with the DLCs is worth maybe $10. I would say $7 would be more accurate, but I don’t think the bundle would be $7 anytime soon. (I paid more than $10)

EDIT: I think people are misunderstanding the review, so I will explain it a little better. There are lots of games that have borrowed from other games of the same genre, that is definitely true. However, this is a completely different situation.
When Banished was first released there was a ton of praise for one thing: Being Original. The fact that this game had such a different feel to it than other city builders, the UI, the way the world worked, everything about it was different made it feel fresh and unique. Ask anyone now who plays Forest Village and most people will say "it's like Banished".
So, when one game comes out and is praised to be original, and the next comes out as something so similar to that original idea that it is constantly compared, it means that they took that original thing (that didn't exist before) and copied it. So, it is no doubt that Banished was the inspiration to this game, but they, as some would say, "borrowed too heavily from the source material."
This game is exactly like Banished. The added features do not add any additional substance to the game.

Vermintide is a great co-op experience as long as you have some friends to play it with as the bots can be pretty awful. The mechanics are very similar to Left for Dead in the way that you carry similar consumables (throwable, health, and extra consumable), fight the same special enemies, and have to progress through hordes of enemies to finish the level. Where Vermintide really differs from Left for Dead however, is in its satisfying melee-focused combat and loot system. Each rat you chop through feels like a real threat that needs to be dealt with (especially on higher difficulties) and the gaining of new weapons and trinkets for any one of the five characters you can play as gives the game a feeling of progression that Left for Dead was missing. Had to adjust some graphics to get the game to keep a consistent framerate during large waves of enemies but besides that runs silky smooth.

A great entry into the field of first person melee combat. There is a balance between both melee and ranged combat that initiates a necessity for both, which is mostly unseen in other games. Overall, a must have for your steam library.

I have been playing this game since the private Beta when Atari still owned it.  This game has seen so much positive change since then, it is almost astounding.  I remember when there used to be 15 ships on that you could play as on the federation side, and the only diversity was the meager hull decals selects Captains could choose from.  Now, OMG! it has gotten to the point where I am seeing ships I don't know the name of, or even where in the Star Trek universe it came from! It's amazing!
The development team behind this game is churning out new content and upgrades, some good some bad, pretty consistently.  It may help that the weekly(?) dev blogs outline what’s new and what’s being worked on, so it keeps you in the loop.  STFs (Raids) have grown from, like 3, missions into 3 STFs per faction.  O yeah, there are factions now. So you can get your reputation up with a certain race of aliens in order to be able to craft rare item sets and unique weapon and console pieces.  There never used to be anything like that.
On the downside, they have taken out some content, such as Memory Alpha and huge exploration areas that used to yield special crafting materials.  While this deletion serves a purpose, it outraged many long time fans.  But, as I said, it served a purpose, and you will either appreciate it or or loathe it, it's up to you.  Graphics have never gone down, they have remastered almost every mission that has been in the game since the beta.  The missions regains replay-ability for some of us veterans, as the levels and story are now more coherent and look beautiful.  Character models stay true to Authentic Star Trek cannon, as does the political and physical map.  The new Star trek movies play a part in this universe as far as time line so, but it is not significant.  (Spoilers) Aside from the Romulan home world being sucked into a black hole the universe still contains TNG, DS9, and Voyager characters and past events laid forward in those series, including TOS are laced within this storyline and time arc.  So consistency will remain from all the old TV shows you grew up with. Which, for me, was very important.  Voice actors from all those series have or will participate in lending their voices into the game, so keep an ear out for your favorite TV show character.
The free to play system is one of the few games you can truly accomplish anything without paying a dime.  That is, if you don't mind a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of grinding.  Still, grinding the only way to truly earn something in a video game and that will remain true in any video game you don't have to pay for.  If you choose to pay, you can purchase points to use in an in-game store and get anything from ships, to crafting material, extra character slots, ect...  You can also purchase a lifetime membership that gives you an allowance of those points to use each month.  You can also purchase this membership on a monthly time table.
Overall, I would give this game a solid 8.5, and this is coming from a lifelong Star Trek fan and video game enthusiast.  While some would argue a 10 would be more fitting for a game that allows space and ground combat AND also follows very closely to the source material.  I have to agree but also point out that there are still things that need to be added and slightly polished.  At times, its a bit chaotic to know what the best build are for a specific armor set and ship combination, due to the sheer size of the available content in the game (google STO faction sets).   I feel they need to make some of the more rarer ships more easier/cheaper to obtain, as you could spend over $100 buying in game currency to open enough lockboxes to obtain enough Lobi Crystals to buy a special ship from a certain Ferengi vendor. It's insane when you think of how many steps, time and money that go into purchasing a ship, even when compared to EVE online's mining and refining process.
Hope this help any prospective player/Captain!

I've been playing a lot of turn-based squad tactics wargames in my life, every now and then. And of whole this genre (or sub-genre) I place Silent Storm in the top 5 of them all. Even after 12 years, with out-dated graphics (which is still looks quite decent, though), with some flaws in the late progress in the game (yeah, I guess you've already heard of Panzerkleins) - still it is a masterpiece.
Why do I praise this game so high? There are several reasons:
1) game's mechanics at first seems quite similar to Jagged Alliance. And that's not a flaw, because JA2 was one of the major swallowers of my time in the early 00's, compared only with Civilization 3 and TES Morrowind... More to it, Silent Storm is not trying to wear JA shoes, it walks its own path, and somewhat similar technical solutions only helps to get familiar with the game.
2) Game's setting puts us in the perils of WW2, but, despite the fact it was created by Russians (maybe because of it), it lacks many of typical unnatural cliche, WW2 games usually so full of. I can't say that a gameplot is a "War and Peace" in a new cover, but it is certainly a result of good thought. It is clever all the way through, it is not using dehumanization, so common in the late media (you know, "good guys - bad guys" pattern). Everybody are players in the plot, which makes it sound like a good spy story, with unexpected trivials and rivals along the way. And all of that still plays like Jagged Alliance! You get it now? Nival created a very distinct game, but was clever enough not to distress people with new gamedesign decisions. So it has a very comforting start, and then the tide catches you, and you swim into completely another world of alternative history, where Nazis was not a menace, but just one of parts of the long-going power struggle, with their own hopes to better future... I don't making excuses for Nazis doings in the WW2, mind it! Many of my relatives died because of them, and I hold that score with me. But then again. Axis warmachine was very far of those mindless Ubersoldiers from Castle Wolfenstein, and it is good that at least somewhere soldiers of Axis block shown as they were.
Oh, well, I'm skidded away a bit, talking about game's topic. Let's just say, game gives a very thorough dive into the WW2 reality... and then adding some spice with technologies-never-existed. Most of the players like the game more without that spicy part, but hey! All other stuff is great without any doubts!
3) And of all of the great stuff in that game, one of the most exciting features is the level of destruction you can add to anything around you. By that parameter, Silent Storm stands proudly above all other tactical games up to this moment! Battlefield Bad Company 2? Mercenaries 2? There are so little games where you can level literally everything to the pebble and dustl! But in the Silent Storm it is not only fun to do. You actually training your characters skills with every shot and explosives usage! So please, don't hold yourself! Shoot through walls and ceilings, blow everything apart! Become the weapon of mass destruction! Groovy!
Okay, let's finish all that praising: game has some minor flaws, but they are very little comparing to the amount of fun that game can bring to you. And it is on sale now! Go for it, right away!
Mark 9.1/10

The developer was kind enough to give out a bunch of keys when this game launched on steam, and a good friend got me a key even though I had missed the giveaway by 15 minutes. I was very excited to feel all the nostalgia of my instagibbing days. The experience was satisfying and great.
If you enjoy instagib (one hit kill) gameplay, boosting (shooting the ground to shoot yourself upwards), twitch shooting, and an intense, fast-paced FPS experience, then you will enjoy this game.
As a disclaimer, I always try to avoid mentioning the price of a game if I feel that its mechanics make up for any monetary value, however, for the current price ($9.99), the game is more than a finished product for an early-access game. Believe me, you will get your money's worth for this price if you are looking for a no-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t instagib experience.
The aesthetics are very good - the levels are nice and bright and colorful. You can customize everything from the color/type of your laser beam, to the type of explosions when you kill an opponent, to the color of your character model (and your opponents'). Personally, I prefer to have the environment in greyscale and the enemy in a bright, pop-out color (red). You can even change the color of your name in-game. When you shoot, it will leave a paintball-style mark in the color of your laser - by the end of the match, the area will look like a paintball battlefield. The music and sounds are very good, especially if you like electronic music.
The controls are typical of a traditional FPS, however, you will need to get used to the instagib style if you are a newcomer - boosting (shooting the ground to propel yourself) and constantly moving is a necessity to survival. Being able to shoot from a far is also essential (you can play around with the FOV, however, I feel that the max setting is a bit disorienting). Be warned, the instagib community for most games is relentless and unforgiving, so don't be surprised or disheartened if you have a hard time getting kills. From the servers I've played, the community seems very friendly. There is no tutorial, and the learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with FPS games - in particular, with the instagib game mode.
Gameplay is extremely fast-paced - you must constantly remain on the move. There are a variety of game modes, like deathmatch and team deathmatch. The online community is fairly small, but still decent - you might not always have a full server. Everyone dies with one hit, and you can shoot across the entire map. Staying mobile, timing your boost jumps, and maintaining battlefield awareness (this is where the high DPI players will get to flex their skills) is critical to doing well in this game.
Overall, the instagib game mode is represented very, very well in Ratz, and anyone interested in that style of FPS should definitely check this out.
Recommend!
Cheers,
DJSF

So, Binary Domain is actually kind of great. The action is entertaining enough, but the game may surprise you beyond that. Gameplay-wise it's got great pacing: throws just the right number of enemies at you at a time, gives you rests between firefights, has some rail shooter and vehicle segments for variety. Port quality is fine. Just use a 360 pad, which is something all PC gamers should have by now.  There's a glitch with water appearance, but otherwise the game is stable, runs at 60fps, and has FOV adjustment. It's definitely worth getting.

I have to admit, I purchased this because I'd seen the Let's Play videos of ths game and because the premise was just so ridiculous that you couldn't help but have your curiousity piqued. There are some reviews/coverage out there that paints this game as being an insult to women, but I didn't entirely see this. I suppose that to a point I could see where some are coming from with that, but any sexism was definitely not intended.
Your enjoyment of this game will ultimately boil down to how much you like games like Bejeweled since that's really the main thrust of the game (no pun intended). The dating sim aspects are somewhat weak and mostly there to string together the various game levels for each girl and give you power ups. The story is probably the weakest part of the game and probably why the charges of sexism are even being levied, since there really isn't a lot to these women other than their datability. While yes, this is an aspect of datings sims to a degree, the good dating sims give you a chance to become at least slightly emotionally invested in the characters. I didn't really get that feeling with this game's characters- not even the person we're supposed to be portraying.
Some of this I can handwave away by this being a "first game" that was funded via Kickstarter. The learning process is always a rough one and for this to be the developer's first official game and sorta dating sim (that I'm aware of) it's a pretty darn good one since there are no visible glitches or errors that interrupt gameplay. I'm aware that there wll be a second game and I hope that the developer brings in more character development since that was something that was sorely missing with this game. The dating sim aspect was no risk and while I didn't entirely mind that, I did want to see more interaction with the characters and more development. This game had a lot of potential and while it lives up to that on the matching game end, it was sorely lacking on the dating sim angle. I think that more character development, the ability to have some slight risk (like being caught with another girl means that you can't date one or both girls for a set period of time), and the ability to choose a Final Girl would have improved this greatly and would be great to have in the sequel.
Ultimately I'd recommend this, but not to anyone looking for a more involved dating sim or one with any true storyline.

I bought HuniePop because I heard interesting things about it's gameplay, and that it had decent writing. Of course, that's the best kind of cover-up story, isn't it?
In all seriousness, if you're looking for an dating sim that is first-and-foremost a game, then that is what you will get here. It's not about simulating the dating and getting a realistic relationship with a girl going, it's just not that type of game. It knows that, and plays to that strength. You use accumulated knowledge to impress/attract the girls and make them more interested in you, and while you're not punished for being honest, you're rewarded for giving them the 'right' answers. It lets you take the 'strategic' approach, while letting you play the game the way you want to, and not punishing you for taking whatever route you choose. The puzzle aspect, while simple in construct, does get progressively harder and it's not mindless.
The aesthetic is pretty well done, but, when I take a step back from it, a little disappointing. It's very faithful to what it's trying to recreate visually, and it succeeds with aplomb in both the interface (extremely easy to navigate, it could only be better if it had hotkeys) and the designs of the girls, and the backgrounds are also well done. There is a bit of a problem with the girls though, and it's a victim of its own goals. By trying to emulate the styles, I feel like they could have done their own style and made something truly unique designwise. Unfortunately, this probably wouldn't have been as catching, and maybe wouldn't have gotten funded or whatever. They're each distinct enough, and their designs fall under 'creatively stereotyped'. It's done well, but it's not groundbreaking in the slightest. The music, however, is INCREDIBLY catchy and good. Most of the tunes just fit the atmosphere perfectly and are really just pleasant to listen to. I wouldn't be exaggerating if I said the music was the best part of the game, and that's not a slight either. It's very fitting to the name of the game, so it's quite sugary, but again: it just works.
The writing is also pretty decent, but again, only plays to the stereotypes and makes them, if you're not into them, only slightly unique and if you are, more enjoyable. They're there for the typical visual novel reasons, as far as I know anyway. It caught me off guard a few times, and is mostly funny, though one of the secret characters did grate on my nerves quite a bit.
You'll know if HuniePop is the kind of game you want, but if you are on the fence, I'd say go for it. I was able to enjoy the other aspects of the game because the gameplay aspects were very strong. Maybe you'll have a similar experience. Just make sure to clean up afterward.
