I like the game. Truely, I do! I love the concept of it, and for someone who's probably spent 1,000 hours playing Banished, this is a nice new take on it. Don't get me wrong, it's basically the same thing, but this game cost an extra 10 dollars and has much better graphics than what Banished had. However....
There are major cons to this story. My favorite aspect of this game is what Banished sorely lacked the most [for me]: Predators! There are wolves and bears in this game who will attack your livestock and honey houses unless prepared with hunters and a mental map of your layout before placing buildings (otherwise your honey houses are too close to the woods and a bear will wreak it! But, the houses also need to be near trees and plants in order to produce honey faster...). I can see this concept going over really well once the AI is worked out some more. It's really odd-looking to have wolves and bears roaming around in the streets, and people walking past them like they were harmless pets or something...
A huge con for me is the progression. Workers are slow as molasses! Unlike Banished, where people would get sh*t done and take res. to the soon-to-be-buildings; no matter if they were lazy farmers, builders, etc., you HAVE to have laborers here. If you want trees chopped, stones picked, or buildings built - you have to have laborers to do it! Doesn't seem so bad, until you realise that you start each game off with only 6 working people... eh...
and even with laborers, it take a while...
Next major flaw and one I seriously hate and thought about returning this game because of it: Terraforming. A great concept, and one I still like, BUT if there's ANY form of a slope (be it a mountain or a litteral molehill), you can't place buildings there! Farms can go there, usually, but most buildings can't. A majority of the map it seems HAS to be flattened in order to even BUILD a wretched building in any spot past the spawn point!
THAT, my friend, is bullsh*t...
The main aspect of this game is building, I thought, but it turns out to be terraforming! And that isn't as simple as it sounds. You need workers, laborers, and a WHOLE lot of time on your hands. Time you usually don't have because - while your people don't eat nearly as much as they do in Banished - you still need homes and food sources in order to grow your population past 7 or 8 workers, and it'll take a year before any building can really be done (past the first few homes that you can place).
It hardly even looks natural when you're done flattening the place out. Imagine in the Sims 3 you lower an entire plot downwards a bit from the rest of the map outside of the plot itself: That's what it looks like! Maybe it'll look a bit more natural if you use the other terraforming tools available; but it takes such a long time that hardly anybody would have time for it!
*UPDATE*
Okay, the Devs are trying to make an a** of me, lol
Just days after I wrote this review, they release a major Part 1 update to the game (part 2 being released in about a couple weeks) that should fix some graphical errors, AI issues, as well as the whole building nonsense where we couldn't build on any form of slope: Apperently now we can and the ground will auto-flatten unleveled areas slightly so we won't have to terraform the hell out of the place.
I have tested out the new update and, honestly, I'm impressed. I like the fact we can build now without having to worry about slopes. The laborers are still slow when it comes to certain things, but it seems like they're working faster now too (usually). Maybe that has something to do with happiness, but I'm not sure...
I also found out that there is indeed a modding community out there. They're very small and, this game being early access, these mods are at risk of breaking when new updates release, but it's still nice to see that there's a beating heart here.
So, all and all, I think I can honestly recommend the game now. It still has issues (like when you have a chicken coop, it tends to store the eggs that are produced like squirrles store nuts), but it is still playable. Before, I couldn't get part 50 people. Now, I managed to get to exactly 110 people before I f*cked up and they all starved to death (fortunally, there's an auto save system where if you screw up, you can go back to one of the 5 or so saves and retry, but I gave up on that town after that).

People who like "Jagged Alliance"  would like this, that is if it had any of the details and depth of that game.   Instead they get repetitive combat with a flimsy story linking the battles.  JA had a significant economic aspect that could keep you on a fairly short leash, limiting advancement and forcing you to make do.   Good guns were in short supply, ammo was hard to find and expensive.  In Silent Storm,  your supplier gives you free weapons and ammo while every enemy drops weapons and ammo.  After a few battles you have virtually everything you will ever need for this game.   Character progression is broken and many specialty items are not really worth the time.  Why lockpick when you can simply machine gun open locked doors and crates?  Enemy AI is dumb enough that all battles feel exactly the same.    AI in this game simply means "move into visible range then move out if you have enough action points left".    Many missions degenerate from first contact into "lay all your guys into a line and snipe enemies as they come into your field of fire.   And almost all of them will, one after another like lemmings.   Huge piles of bodies do not deter them.  And conveniently they come one at a time so you never have to worry about being overhwelmed.
It's a shame because the game system has promise but it's far too simplified to make a memorable game.   Feel like blowing ten bucks?   Go ahead - it's good enough for a few hours distraction.   But I was not hooked enough to bother finishing the game.  At least it didn't cost that much unlike that horrible xcom remake where they stripped out all of the aspects that made the original game fun.

TL;DR:
PT revolutionized the walking simulator sub-genre of horror video games, for better or worse, and many games have followed suit. There have been plenty of crappy horror games that involve just walking from Point A to Point B. Layers of Fear, however, sets itself apart with clever scares and more realized effects. This was made by people who knew how to put the psychological aspects at play in their psychological horror game. I love survival horror games and was therefore excited when this game was available as early access on steam. After the first thirty minutes of gameplay my excitement turned into disappointment. To explain why, these are the factors which I believe makes not just a great horror game but also a great horror story.
1. A somewhat believeable starting point for the story.
2. A central mystery which the story slowly unravels.
3. Pacing & suspense.
Point number 3, that is pacing is the flaw here. Why oh why is there jumpscares all the time? It does nothing but ruin the suspense and I feel like I am in a spooky mansion attraction at a theme park and not an interesting horror story. Great horror titles such as Amnesia and Silent Hill understands that building and keeping a constant suspense is everything.
Point number 2 also fails because one can quite quickly figure out what is going on in the story, altough the central theme is disturbing it lacks punch due to the non-subtle and quick way it is delivered. After the central mystery is revealed so early in the game nothing remains but the shell, I.e. the game has been transformed into a spooky house with jumpscares.
This is not a bad game really, the graphics, sounds and story all hold up very well. The pacing of the story, the way the player is presented with the story and its environment ruins it. I would not recommend it at its current price, buy it on sale.

“Every portrait that is painted with feeling is a portrait of the artist, not of the sitter.” - Oscar Wilde.
'Layers of Fear' is not so much a 'game' as it is more of an 'experience' The player finds themselves in the tourted shoes of a freelance artist.
You will spend the majority of your time stumbling all around his mansion, as the world literally, falls apart around you. With the world constantly changing and the pace fluctuating akin to Bill Clinton taking a lie detector test, you hardly find time to appreciate the stunning graphics Layers of Fear has to offer. The experience itself is similar to paying twenty dollars to visit a haunted house attraction, albeit an absolutely spectacular one. This is, without any hint of doubt, the game 'Silent Hills' (May it rest in peace) would have been.
To elaborate on the semiotic conventions of this game, one would be forced to spoil the story. So to avoid any spoilers I shall say just this:
"There is a fine line between reality and one's subconscious. However, where that line is, you must play the game to find out"
In conclusion. If you have even a inkling of interest for psychological horrors, purchase his immediately and...Don't Look Back.

Despite the Cryptic Engine not being the most innovative graphics engine out there, the game has some of the most fun space combat I have tried out of the non "FPS" types.
Cryptic keeps pushing out content patches, new ships, and the class costumisation is one of the most in-depth I have ever found in any game. It's heaven for theorycrafters. Every so often however, Cryptic might release a new skill or item that makes one type of build the flavour of the month and in one case it can shadow all other builds, which are left in the dust.
That's always the risk in a game where every class can access virtually every skill.
The game merges two types of gameplays, the ground combat and the space combat. They work and feel different and you are able to concentrate only on one if you don't like the other. While levelling you might need to do a little bit of both, so depending on your tastes it might be either welcome variety or a minor annoyance, until you get to end game and are completely able to pick what kind of content you want to play.
The ability to walk around your ship and starbases also allows plenty of opportunities for RP if you are into that. Talking of which the character costumisation in this game is on par with games such as Aion, if not better. The graphic style is not Asian, but when you can pick things like the length of your fingers, you know you can do almost anything.
The game isn't necessarily pay to win, although items from the Zen store do have their advantages. If you have the time to grind, you can exchange in game currency for Zen (which you can buy with real cash) but the process is considerably slower.

Star Trek Online (STO) is a solid MMORPG with tons of customization option for those who are willing to work for it.  It is not, however, a good Star Trek game.
For me, the main draw of Star Trek isn't so much the science fiction, which let's face it, is on the silly side.  It is the characters, the dynamics between the crew that makes it interesting.  In-game, however, crew members are treated as little more than equipment, so that personal connection is gone.  You gain the ability to customize your officers however you want, true, but you lose what makes them characters.
Another problem of the game is the randomly generated sidequests.  Sure, it's fun to pretend that you are the star of your own Star Trek show, routinely investigating strange species, artifacts, and negative space wedgies, but the mad-lib style of quest generation means that after a while, all these quests seem to blur together.  So aside from the story quests - which are well done, by the way - none of the other content is memorable.
The saving grace for these sidequests is the Foundry, which allows users to create their own quests and stories.  Sturgeon's Law is in full effect here; 90% of the custom content is lackluster, but the other 10% makes it worthwhile.
While the game has problems that prevent it from being truly great, I would still recommend it for MMO gamers.  The universe feels big, the ship-to-ship combat is frantic but tactical (although sometimes you fight with the UI more than the enemy), and the amount of reference to the Star Trek shows can make Star Trek enthusiasts giddy.  If these sound exciting, that this is the game for you.

A truly stellar and criminally underrated Survival Horror masterpiece. Feels like a true spiritual successor to Resident Evil 4, carrying on the classic survival horror and Resident Evil staples with more modern gameplay design.
The story follows detective Sebastian Castellanos and his team. They get called to investigate a mass murder at Beacon mental hospital. What starts off as a rather routine crime scene investigation quickly turns into something more sinister, as all semblance of logic disappears and reality starts to literally break apart around them. The 15-20 hour long campaign will have you falling down a seemingly endless nightmarish rabbit hole, as you try to piece together exactly where you are and why. A special mention to the antagonist of the game, who manages to be one of the most interesting horror villains I've seen in a while.
Level and game design is a rather devisive topic with this game. It is fair to criticize the levels due to how they don't exactly flow into one another, leaving the impression that setpieces were made and then the rest of the game was added in to connect them. That said, the design also makes sense and very much makes you feel like you are in a nightmare with no concrete sense of progression or way out. That is one of the most fascinating aspects of the world of The Evil Within. As mentioned, the game carries on elements of classic survival horror with modern gameplay. It manages to create one of the most dangerous and deadly environments in a video game and not through old methods, such as fixed camera angles and tank controls, but rather by keeping the environment progression chaotic, leaving the player constantly guessing what's next. The environment is also littered with deadly traps and enemies, advising a much more cautious approach. A rushed playthrough will turn into a very frustrating one.
Gameplay feels very much built on the groundwork laid by RE4. It's third person survival horror, though unlike RE4, you can aim and move at the same time. The inventory seems to be kind of a half and half between RE4 and RE5, not exactly pausing the game, but slowing it down enough for you to be able to switch weapons and craft ammunition. The movement also feels a bit more sluggish than your normal third person shooter, though this may be to compensate for being able to aim and move. Weapon variety is rather standard with the exception of the Agony Crossbow. Each weapon carries different ammunition, which is distributed just enough so that you can make it through most fights with careful aiming and planning. The Agony crossbow and matches demonstrate a unique flexibility in the combat. As most enemies are vulnerable to fire, players can find creative and ammo efficient ways of killing them with just a match, such as shooting an enemy in the leg and lighting them on fire, while they are down.
As for the PC port, it seemed to have a very rocky launch, but seems to be quite good as of now, with some slight annoyances. Despite being able to switch off the letterboxes, they still appear occasionally in scenes, making transitions from cutscene to gameplay a bit more jarring than it needs to be. The 30 fps cap has also been lifted, though the game is now capped to 60. The game itself looks fantastic, despite being over 2 years old. Environment and enemy design is very well done, bringing to life some truly horrific locations and creatures. The gore effects are also very well done, featuring some of the most satisfying headshots I have experienced in a game.
Overall, while it may have some setbacks on a technical standpoint, it's a truly amazing return to form for third person survival horror games. With an amazingly paced lengthy campaign, multiple difficulty settings, ng+ as well as 3 DLCs with different gameplay elements, it's very easy to recommend. If you love RE4 and RE5 left you a bit cold, or if you just want a third person survival horror game with interesting level design and a very compelling villain, this game should be right up your alley.

So, to start off, everyone who is mentioning the performance issues, is completely right.
But keep in mind, that while the game does need a lot of optimization, yet...there will never come a point when its physics and such are not resource intensive in the extreme.  There is simply too much going on.  Optimization won't cut it, they'll either have to accept the problem at a certain point, or try a completely different way of handling the processes.
Now, that said, even as it is, this game is amazingly fun.  You can build almost anything you can imagine, and even a few things you might not be able to, yet.
Transformers, aircraft, all manner of vehicle or Rube Goldberg machines...the possibilities are very nearly limitless.
Most of all, unlike most building games/digital toys, it's FUN to build in Scrap Mechanic.  While very large and complex projects are bound to get a bit tedious at some point, the overwhelming majority of the time, building is simple and quick when it comes to even moderately complex builds.  The build system is actually quite intuitive, but that's such a radical departure from similar games, that it ends up taking a bit of getting used to.  But, once you get over that hurdle, you get spoiled on it in a hurry.  I like Space Engineers, but its build system is so clunky and unfun.  Scrap Mechanic is much, much more user friendly, and it's much more versatile, also.
If building and mechanization are your bread and butter, this is the one you want.

is the 7th game in
series, a series of mostly freeware room escape games with elegant yet disturbing undertone. All games in the series can be either reached via Kongregate, or can be purchased as a freeware for iOS or Android. I've played the first of these games,
in Kongregate some years ago, and found out that the developers continued to make new games in the series, revealing new clues to the spiritual, surreal yet eerie world of the Rusty Lake, connecting pieces of a morbid story with each new game. If you are curious and would like to appreciate the world of Rusty Lake appropriately, I strongly suggest you to play other games with the intended timeline to fully enjoy the experience that is Rusty Lake. Most of these games present you 15-20 minutes of gameplay with more anecdotes to speculate about the nature of the given world and its setting.
In this short yet morbid puzzle game, we take the role of a butler that serves in the Rusty Lake Hotel, a mysterious establishment settled upon a small island in the middle of the infamous Rusty Lake. The world of Rusty Lake is inhabited by odd andromorphic animals, including our hotel staff: all knowing and charismatic hotel manager Mr. Owl, silent attendant and receptionist Mr. Crow, bell boy Mr. Bat and chef extraordinaire Mr. Toad. In a fateful evening, our guests arrive: Mr. Deer, Mr. Boar, Miss Pheasant, Mr. Rabbit and Mrs. Pigeon. They will be staying with us for a short while, and it is our duty to attend their needs and arrange an excellent dinner party for our guests each night. Sounds simple enough, yet with each passing night our encounters grow a bit more disturbing, ending with a peculiar story revelation somewhat meaningful only if you've played previous games.
Here comes mild or speculative spoilers, so feel free to skip this paragraph if need be. As a personal interpretation, the Cube Escape series, aside from highly disturbing point and click adventures, serve as symbolic happenstances concerning memory, deed and afterlife. Various figures with their own vices - like vanity, gluttony, greed etc. are presented as andromorphic animals in this surreal habitat where they'll be lured with their own vices as bait and used to satisfy a supernatural demand by gruesome means. The hotel and its environment serves as a Limbo-like setting for their memories to be extracted and collected. It was mentioned in previous games that the lake feeds on memories and whence memories are extracted from guests, what is left would be unsettling creatures of nightmares - or rather our antagonists for the following games. Yet again, this is just a personal interpretation, so I highly suggest for you to try other games to present your own. It all is quite
-ish with a touch of John Keddie.
The game mostly consists of a basic point & click adventure, with some neatly arranged puzzles and a room escape concept for each night. If you manage to complete the game, you will be given a code to use in following Cube Escape games, revealing more information about the nature of this symbolic setting. This is a gruesome and short experience for your own contemplation considering all events and figures presented are highly symbolic and more so supernatural. It's more like surrealist art; completely open to interpretation and even to introspection. Enjoy!
Please also check out Lady Storyteller's Curator page

This game is a medieval city builder/suvival sim. For those aquanited with Banished this game almost certainly used that game as a base with the intention of building on it. The basic premise and gameplay is the same although time may progress a little more slowly. The majority of the buildings are also essentially the same.
How the game differs as of thise time it does include a few new buildings as well as upgrades for some others. It incoroprates things like different potenital birth rates for different dwellings. It also includes a few new features that are presumablely still in development. These include predators (bears/wolves) that at this time eat your livestock or birds that can eat your crops. Also in introduction of illnesses that can run thru a village desimating the population.
The graphics are upgraded and look very nice. The camera allows you to get right down into the village including inside the buildings which are more than empty shells. The game seems to play in sandbox only mood at this time but seems to run quite smoothly with only minor issues here and there I'll get to those below. Considering that this is still early access buying the game at this time is essentially for one of two reasons.
1. You want a city builder in this historical era never got banished and figure that the major graphics upgrade and promise of a more extensive experience is worth the extra $10.
2. You like banished and wished it was more extensive and wish to support development of this title and believe it will push the game in directions you find interesting enough to put up the funds.
pros
+Nice new graphic upgrade
+Some new and potentially interesting additions and features although most still require further development gives the game room to grow.
+mostly stable game few major bugs found thus far.
+maps are nice size allows for plenty of room to grow
Cons
- not really enough well developed new content seems more like a banished mod than a new title
- camera has some issues with the environment especially zoomed in it can be a bit hard to see paticularly in thick forested areas also doesn't really zoom out as far as most city builders do which means long term city planning can be a bit more difficult, the mini map is also pretty much useless for this or any other function at this time.
- Tutorial needs to be a bit better than it's current state new players won't really get a good handle on what they need to do to give them a chance to get a basic village up and running.
-Game seems to  currently only support windowed mode it seems can futher complicate camera control.

** This next one is not really a con as it's early access but it should be noted considering the asking price.
- Many supply chains and new features appear to still be in some phase or another of development creating some odd but non game breaking behaviors gives the game an unfinished/ rough feel IMO.
So what's the verdict. I would probably say yes as the game is certainly worth having in your library and it will doubtlessly get better before release. How much better well that depends on how you interpret the road map and what your looking to be added.
One thing makes me say no at this time the fact the game price will not change from early access to full release unless you meet one of the two criteria mentioned above. Your really not losing anything to wait and see what the final product will look like and even wait a little past that to see what the vision for the game is post release. It was pretty close call partly  because I already have banished but I have to give this a thumbs down for now I hope to update this review and my choice post release.

Oh wow! I just got done playing my first game...

Multiple game types; Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, Freeze Tag (thats a new one), and several others.
Statistics to keep track of you're K/D ratio as well as double, triple, quadruple kill and 2 more above that.

Bottom line, it's fun and a great way to kill some time... and rats.

A few days ago, I started to play Hotline Miami, it was an amazing experience and I was looking forward to the second game.
First impressions were pretty good. HM2 is more colorful, visually improved, added some weather effects, breakable objects and more gore + more variety in level design.
But then I encountered a "thing" that I didn't experience in the first game. This "thing" is called - f*cking game breaking bug. It's not a big deal if you get it on the first level, but when you are on a mission that takes 20-30 minutes to complete - it really leaves a bad taste. There is always a possibility to get teleported outside of the house when you use the stairs. Once I teleported into some kind of a fence and couldn't move my character anymore. Had to restart the mission.
Sometimes you can shoot enemies through walls, which should not be possible. Sometimes dogs get stuck and start to whirl like tornadoes. There are a lot of similar visual and pathfinding bugs throughout the game.
I really dislike that there is no indicator where to go when you complete a level. You mostly have to backtrack using your own memory.
HM2 has far less masks, but it has more unique characters with unique abilities, so it evens out a little bit.
I feel that the core gameplay has slightly regressed. Item variation has decreased. Mission maps got bigger and longer. Sometimes you need only 2-4 minutes to complete a level, other times it can take 20-30 minutes. I think that the first Hotline Miami did a better job with level design. It was visually less varied, but just felt better and was more fun to replay them.
HM2 has an unique storytelling. It feels inconsistent, disjointed and doesn't make sense up until the very last missions. Most of the time you are in a "WTF?" state. I kinda liked it and disliked it at the same time.
Overall, I think that the first HM game was more straightforward, more concentrated and more polished, but that doesn't mean that HM2 is a bad game. It's still very good, but could have been a little bit better.
Oh and you can create levels with the level editor! Pretty neat.

Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number has made me angrier than I have ever been in a very long time. With an overabundance of glass panels and eagle-eyed enemies with guns, this game takes Hotline Miami's difficulty and chaotic gameplay to sadistic levels of anger.
There have been many positive reviews of this game, and I can understand why it's so highly praised; but I hope having a different opinion doesn't bring angry mobs with pitchforks to the comment section of this review. For this reason, I'm going to focus on the negatives, because there's just so much that annoys me with this game, that I find it hard to overlook the positives.
As previously mentioned, the levels are filled with glass and holes in the walls that are very easily lost in this games pixel-style art, I can't count how many times I've been running around only to be obliterated by enemy fire because half the glass panels look like solid walls. The enemies can see you way before you can see them, I found myself holding shift during the entire game so I could maybe get the jump on them before they fill me with lead.
The levels are designed to make you feel vulnerable at every corner, and it worked. If you don't have a gun, you can consider it nearly unplayable, I've found myself strafing out of cover to lure enemies over to me and killing them one by one just so I'd have a chance at completing the level. Half the difficulty of this game isn't in the gameplay, but in the level design. Enemies blend in to the background, different lighting effects and filters hinder your vision and just get you killed. I had the hardest time completing the prison level, because the guys that charge you and bash your head on the ground just look like normal enemies; so you don't realize the threat until you get killed by them over and over and over.
This game's story was vastly longer than the first Hotline Miami, and although some might like it; I can't stand it. They try to introduce lots of characters with different abilities, but all they succeed in doing is confusing me and making me change my style of gameplay after every scene. For example: there's a character that refuses to kill enemies. He incapicitates them with melee weapons and if you pick a firearm; all he does is unload it and make it useless. For the first few times doing this, I thought it was cool. But all it does is make me wish I could actually kill them. It's Hotline Miami for crying out loud, why WOULDN'T you want to kill people?
Not to mention the boring dialogue between action sequences. What's the point? After finishing a level, you're so on edge and amped up that you just want more of the game, the whacky 80's pink and cyan font is NOT something you want to stare at, but they make you because that's how the story unfolds. I don't care about it. They bounce between time frames like some sort of Crime-Drama or Quentin Tarantino film, and it just gets disorienting.
I'm going to try and not spoil the overall story for anyone reading, but whenever something happens to the characters in the game, I feel nothing. A good game makes you feel connected to the antagonist you're playing as, but everytime something happens to them; I don't have a care in the world. In fact, I feel pleasure when anything goes awry for them because it just reminds me that I don't have to bother with them anymore.
The game's music is great, I have to mention. And I'm a little disapointed that you don't get to play as Jacket; the character of the first Hotline Miami again. But that's all this game is to me, a disapointment. Dennation Games took the difficulty of Hotline Miami and said "Yeah, let's make it harder and stretch the game out with pointless dialogue and useless cutscenes for characters that no one cares about".
Anyway, that's my review, I don't like it as much as the first Hotline Miami. And I uninstalled this game the moment I got done with it. There was zero satisfaction upon completing it and I have nothing but bad memories.
Sorry if I upset anyone, but that's how it is.

Hotline Miami 2 is a brutal top down shooter, and the sequel to Hotline Miami 1.  The two games have strong gameplay similarities, but the sequel expands on the themes introduced in the first game.  The game took me about 10 hours to beat, and has some replayability.
The core of the gameplay is the same as Hotline Miami 1. The potency of the adrenaline-packed gameplay is equaled only by the lifeless silence after a mission is completed.  Polished pixel graphics enhance the gameplay experience.  Although Hotline Miami 2 adds new weapons and masks, it seems that more of both were removed than added.  Some may not like this change, but I don't mind it.  The game also features a Map Editor, which I have not yet tried.
My only complaint with the game is the inability to change the crosshair color.  The white crosshair blends into some of the maps, and is easy to lose track of.
References to movie scenes, play acts, and VCR recordings intentionally make what is 'really' happening in the game difficult to follow.  The distinction between in-game acting and reality is blurry, and perhaps nonexistent.  The transience of the story's narrative framework helps form a commentary about the game's audience.  The lack of distinction between acting and reality within the game points to the fundamental uniformity between in-game characters and real life people.  Humans relish violence.  The developers contend that while we may be sympathetic towards a character that is forced to violence through their own internal instability or by external forces, the audience can give themselves no such mercy.  The audience does not only participate in the violence, but commands and enjoys it.
As alluded to above, the game explores the moral culpability of various motives to violence.  These motives include, but are not limited to, mental disease, coercion by other parties, revenge, vigilantism, enforcement of moral hazard, war, fame, and as the means to an end.  This theme deserves its own analysis.  But the core theme of the game is that while a variety of motives exist, intrinsic violence is the defining element of human nature.  Dialogue, especially later in the game, is used to speak directly to the audience about about this message.  Even seemingly normal characters are unable to resist their violent urges.  Such is the fate of the characters, and such is the fate of the audience.
As in the first game, events are not meant to be interpreted as part of plot formation.  This is clear in the transient narrative framework and dubious narrator.  We can be confident that none of the events in the game actually take place because characters don't actually behave like real humans.  For example, enemies are almost zombie-like in their exceptional reaction time, lethal alacrity, and total disregard for blood-splattered walls or the corpses of their comrades.  The game likely takes place in the unhinged mind of some anonymous narrator.
The events are instead taken as connected thematic episodes.  The introspective qualities of the game and the abandonment of a traditional event-based plot indicate the game is a meta-story.  But interestingly, the game does follow the format of a traditional narrative on the macro level.  A character is introduced within a setting, struggles to understand their world, and finds a kind of resolution.  But in Hotline Miami 2, the character is the player, the setting is the game, and we come to understand that morality exists only as a trivial buffer against our impending demise.  This enigmatic relationship between the traditional narrative macro framework but micro thematic focus is diametrically opposed to the structure of most storytelling media.
Hotline Miami 2 is a masterful sequel to the first game.  Gameplay is very similar, but the clarity and coherence of tone and mood are noticeably improved from the already high standards in Hotline Miami 1.  The game is so successful because of its transient narrative framework, abandonment of a traditional plot, and player-focused development.  Themes linked to nihilism and bloodshed are unmatched among any other video game that I have played.  Hotline Miami 2 is both philosophical and blunt, both harsh and precise, and both exhaustive and vacant.  I very highly recommend this game.

Layers of Fear is a must-have for fans of the genre. Although the game relies heavily on jump scares, the beautiful atmosphere and it's great graphics and sound kept me interested. The last part of the game is a bit dull and you really need to be a true explorer to finish the game with the 'true' ending (one of the three possible endings that the game has), but that doesn't stop me from recommending this twisted psychological horror piece.

Layers of Fear is the most immersing Horror game I’ve played in 2015. The protagonist you play as is this one time prominent artist, who sinks into alcoholism and dementia and becomes a mockery as a result. From the very beginning you’re searching for the answers to uncover just how it is he came to be like this, through everything that he’s done, and everyone he’s lost. The unnamed tormented artist is someone you can sympathize for as you tour through his haunted home, as well as his haunted memories that bleed into the present. You play as a man so out of touch with reality that you can never be certain if what’s happening is actually real, or part of his delusions. Only, is he really the poor wounded soul he appears to be?
Now, a couple of things. This is a story told through interacting with objects, so if you’re someone who doesn’t believe less is more when it comes to a game, this may not be for you. But as far as story-telling goes, it does offer some of the most believable, beautifully voice-acted monologuing ever composed for a video game. Both well written and performed, the actors breath life into the story and leave in just enough blanks for you to piece together the displaced and twisted narrative. It is terrifying and sometimes shocking, but it is also interesting and leaves you eagerly pulling at the plots thread to unravel each mystery of how things came to be.
One of my favourite aspects of the game is the art direction. It is deeply satisfying. There is such lifelike detail that you can even see the textures of the paint that you'll splattered around or framed. I'll be honest, this game had me sold on the psychadelic visuals alone. And the way rooms melt or paintings ooze down the walls is so visually striking, it’s like nothing i’ve ever seen in a video game before. It is very beautiful, and I think is a huge accomplishment in integrating artwork with gaming.
However the game is not without it’s fumbling, whether it’s literally limping through what some may call a “walking simulator game,” or it’s moments of predictability or even perhaps too much linearity. (I’ll say that there are a lot of closed spaces, so my message to those with claustrophobia: you are not crazy, those walls
closing in on you.) But those brave enough to look for them will find there are secret collectibles placed throughout, so that you can go back and fully appreciate the details of each chapter. There were certainly thing I missed my first time through, and you will want to play through again... and again... and again... to get the true ending. Which i’ll admit is a lacklustre way to make players invest more time in the game than they might like to, as you can only be scared by the same ghost story so many times before you want to move on to the next. But that’s not to say there isn’t any replay value, there absolutely is, I’m just disappointed in the way the developers sort of insist on it for the full experience, rather than inviting the player to explore. It feels almost as if they were afraid the story doesn’t stand up on it’s own enough to do that, which it bloody
So I completely one hundred percent recommend this game to anyone with a fondness for atmospheric horror games. You will not be disappointed.

This is. hands down, an immensely enjoyable experience.
Layers of Fear uses visual tricks and audio cues to invoke feelings of confusion and horror in the player, from turning a previously-trodden corner only to find that the environment has completely changed, to the more subtle things, such an object out of place or a lack of wind and traffic noise from the outside.
Visually speaking, the game is impossibly beautiful, and the level of detail on the level design and texture art gives triple-A "next-gen" games a run for their money. Each area of the game clearly had an immense amount of thought put into it, down to the last slightly-rotated bread knife surrounded by bump-mapped crumbs in the kitchen (seriously, look at some videos/screenshots online; the level design and detailing is amazing).
My PC was able to run it on a mixture of medium and high settings at a near-solid 60 FPS, with only occasional dips into the mid-fifties, so, even though it's a little demanding, it still is well worth it if you have a good rig.
For horror veterans and enthusiasts, such as myself, this game is, at once, terrifying and down-right enjoyable. I felt like there was never a dull moment, and I anticipated the coming parts with a most wondrously confusing combination of fearful apprehension and wide-eyed excitement. There's just something about the gameplay and the progression that leaves you genuinely wanting to play more, rather than just feeling the need to finish it so you can free up some hard drive space.
While I admit that the $20 price tag is a little steep for my frugal mindset (most of the games in my steam library are the result of giveaways, gift cards, sales, and birthday/christmas money, rather than the result of a 9-5 job), if you have a little extra cash to spend and are even remotely interested in horror games,
Otherwise, wait until it's on sale for even a slightly reduced amount; you
regret it.

Rusty Lake Hotel is a short yet unforgettable point and click adventure game, with a very strong emphasis on “thinking outside of the box” puzzle solving.
You’ll have to approach the puzzles with a completely different mindset compared to other point and click adventure games you may have played. Ridiculous, irrational things will happen. There’s not much of a story, nor is there engaging dialogue. If you’re willing to accept these facts, and ditch the sacrosanct rules of traditional point and click adventures, I think the game will be a delight for you.
I wouldn’t call Rusty Lake Hotel violent or anything, but some events do occur that are macabre and unsettling. It’s not a game for young children, but for any other gamer who wants to experience a mind-f*ck, surreal casual adventure, I would strongly recommend this game. The voice acting is quite amateurish (fortunately there’s not a lot of it) but everything else – the eerie atmosphere, puzzles, art style and music soundtrack – are top notch.
You can expect about 2 hours of gameplay without using a walkthrough.

Alright, listen up. You will either like this game or hate this game. If you enjoy trying to kill people at high speeds while jumping around a map while your enemies do the same YOU WILL LOVE THIS GAME! Otherwise, you will probably hate it.
Lets talk about the movement. It's fast and it's all over the place, tapping spacebar as you hit the ground will let you bunny hop and if you do that enough times in a row you will be going pretty fast. Add to that a rocket jump like boost by right clicking while looking at a wall or the ground and you will be a 2fast2quick machine. Think of the scout from tf2 and then just give him the rocket jumper. It's that amazing.
Secondly lets talk about the gunplay. You get one gun, a lazer, you can customize it to be whatever color you want and then you just shoot people, it's a one shot kill. This game will beat you up with it too. There are people who are really good at aiming that thing. But for the 100s of times you will die, that one kill you get will give you the best damn feeling ever.
Lastly lets talk about maps, there aren't a lot right now, but they are all very unique, my favorite currently being the office map and least favorite being the pool map. They all have ways to gain speed and things that will get in your way and stop you. With that being said though, I would like to see some kind of map creator or something in the future, could be fun.
Final thoughts: Just get the damn game. If you loved quake and other arena shooters like it, jthis brings in the best parts and just makes it its own game. Seriously though, once you get a taste of the speed and adrenaline of getting that first kill, it will be hard to switch back to games like Call of duty or Counter strike.

The past years have been a dark time for arena shooter fans. But now Ratz Instagib is here!
It is well.. Instagib at its finest. Meaning one shot kills with fast paced action and aerial controls.
The Controls are very responsive, which is absolutely necessary for arena shooters.
And it feels really good if you frag someone..
Especially with customisable frag types, beam types and colors.
And boy is this game colorful. Every map has its own color scheme which can also be costumized.
Ratz has a insane skill ceiling, unlike most modern shooters. If playing on an insane level against opponents of your caliber is something for you, then you'll like the anked mode.
The gamemodes include: duel (1vs1) deathmatch, team deathmatch, capture the flag, freeze tag and survival where you and your team shoot your way through waves of different monsters for a global highscore.

Ratz Instagib, a game I played really early on, and now that it's on Steam with noticeable improvements, prettier, more maps, more customization, unlockable cosmetics, more game modes, private matches, and more fun.
The game is for people who hunger for the 'Instagib' game mode, like me, because its hard to get really good ones nowadays, aside from the old ones that has it, but this game has a focus one that one game mode only, which is Instagib, meaning insta-kill, one shot one kill, and this one is a great one, and as far as I know, it's the best one.
All the game modes are great, duel mode, death match, team death match, capture the flag, freeze tag, and survival. I haven't tried freeze tag yet, but everything else is nice, fun, and competitive, the most competitive an FPS can be actually, and it's not just doing matches and winning, there's a skill progression in which the game monitors your skill and ranks you accordingly. There's also unlockables that you can set a goal for to unlock, these unlockables are only cosmetic and will not change the games simple fair and competitive nature.
The one thing I have an issue with is the same issue I have with any multiplayer game only, and that is it doesn't have bots to sustain the game if there are no players to play it at any given time, so keep that in mind, but it has a game mode in which you can play the game and shoot at things, and that is the survival game mode, it's a solo or coop game made where you (your self or with your friends) go up against a horde of unique (land and flying) enemies where you have to dodge their slow orb-like projectiles, and shoot their core at the center of their bodies, so it's not normal bots of the same type as you with the same weapons, but it's good, requires more precision, and good to play solo or with your friends as coop. It's better than nothing one would say.
For the asking price, for the fan that I am for Instagib, and for the content that it has and future content that it will have, it's worth it, even more so if they add normal insta-gibbing bots to play with.

This game is an absolute masterpiece.
Story: The game does not present the story to you perfectly chronologically. Instead, it jumps around from one period of time to another, where you play as different characters each time. For example, the first level takes place October 31st 1991. The second level takes place on October /25th/, 1991. Then, the third level goes back in time and takes place on April 25th, 1989. There are various jumps in the time period of the levels, but it's meant to be this way, so the player can piece the story together, like a puzzle. And either way, the game has an amazingly done storyline.
Graphics: The pixellated graphics and 80s aesthetic of Hotline Miami 2 are overwhelmingly nice to look at. It's just more proof that you don't need god tier graphics to make a game good. The facial expressions/face sprites that appear during cutscenes, or dialogue from the characters, may seem sort of...odd at first, but you get used to them.
Soundtrack: I can't praise the soundtrack of this game enough. There's so many unbelievably memorable tunes that I still can't get out of my head. Various amazing artists contributed to the game's OST, such as M|O|O|N, Carpenter Brut, Mega Drive, and many more. I can't say I disliked any of the tracks in the game, I legitimately enjoyed every single one. A few favorites of mine include Carpenter Brut's "Le Perv", or M|O|O|N's "Quixotic". I absolutely love Hotline Miami 2's soundtrack. I honestly think it's perfect.
Gameplay: Hotline Miami 2 is difficult. VERY difficult. To start off with, at least. I found the game extremely challenging at first, but gradually picked up the gameplay and found myself becoming more skilled the more I played. Once I got the hang of the controls, I found that the game controls very well. The vastly preferred method of playing Hotline Miami 2 is with a keyboard and mouse, which in my opinions makes the game much easier to play. Though, some people do choose to use an Xbox controller, or controller of some sort. I managed to get the hang of controller controls as well, and it's equally as fun, but takes more getting used to.
Overall: Please, PLEASE buy this game. You won't regret the decision to do so. With an amazing plot, beautiful graphics, god-tier soundtrack and challenging gameplay, I can honestly say Hotline Miami 2 deserves a 10/10 rating. If you're thinking about buying this game, by all means, go for it.

Then you throw dices, each having a random chance to count, and based on the amount of dices that count you get one of the 8 items. You go through 2 random checks to get an item. This is. hands down, an immensely enjoyable experience.
Layers of Fear uses visual tricks and audio cues to invoke feelings of confusion and horror in the player, from turning a previously-trodden corner only to find that the environment has completely changed, to the more subtle things, such an object out of place or a lack of wind and traffic noise from the outside.
Visually speaking, the game is impossibly beautiful, and the level of detail on the level design and texture art gives triple-A "next-gen" games a run for their money. Each area of the game clearly had an immense amount of thought put into it, down to the last slightly-rotated bread knife surrounded by bump-mapped crumbs in the kitchen (seriously, look at some videos/screenshots online; the level design and detailing is amazing).
My PC was able to run it on a mixture of medium and high settings at a near-solid 60 FPS, with only occasional dips into the mid-fifties, so, even though it's a little demanding, it still is well worth it if you have a good rig.
For horror veterans and enthusiasts, such as myself, this game is, at once, terrifying and down-right enjoyable. I felt like there was never a dull moment, and I anticipated the coming parts with a most wondrously confusing combination of fearful apprehension and wide-eyed excitement. There's just something about the gameplay and the progression that leaves you genuinely wanting to play more, rather than just feeling the need to finish it so you can free up some hard drive space.
While I admit that the $20 price tag is a little steep for my frugal mindset (most of the games in my steam library are the result of giveaways, gift cards, sales, and birthday/christmas money, rather than the result of a 9-5 job), if you have a little extra cash to spend and are even remotely interested in horror games,
Otherwise, wait until it's on sale for even a slightly reduced amount; you
regret it.

I'm fed up of horror games. The constant "something scary is gonna happen but you don't know when and then suddenly a scream" thing is getting real old real fast, and even when they try to add atmosphere and a cryptic story it just seems like they're trying too hard.
Layers of Fear doesn't do that though. In fact, it plays off that. This is one of the few games I've played where I don't get scared out of shock, I get scared because I genuinely don't know what is coming up. It seems to know the exact moment when players expect to be scared, and then they let nothing happen, and wait until you're at you're most vulnerable state before punishing you for thinking you knew what was coming.
This is how horror should be done.

I never had such mixed feelings for a game before I played Layers of Fear. The first hour of it was absolutely exhilarating, props to the devs for absolutely nailing the bone-chilling atmosphere. Jump scares were minimal and the ever-changing layout of the protagonist's mansion helped alleviate the theme of insanity. I honestly regarded the game as one of the best horror games ever made, making even the likes of Amnesia pale in comparison.
Then, I got bored. The repetitiveness of the game did not bring out a sense of fear as it initially did, but instead brought out one of boredom. 2 hours in, and I didn't give a crap about the obviously painstakingly crafted environment, the changing layouts of the house and even the jump scares, and that wasn't all because of the repetitive nature of the game, about halfway through the game, there was a scene involving a ghost baby running into a drawer, how anyone found that to be even the least bit scary is beyond me. From then on, I failed to take the game seriously, the "babyface" artwork that intentionally sent shivers down my spine for being disturbing soon descended to be nothing more than a funny face.
The thing which Outlast and Amnesia got right is that they never showed their hand too early on, they always had something new to offer. Granted, Layers of Fear had me more terrified than either game, but as I mentioned earlier, this fear faded away to boredom, whereas Outlast and Amnesia had in me a sense of dread, a sense of actual fear, from the beginning, all the way to the end, and that was probably due to the actual threat the enemies faced in both games. The antagonist in Layers of Fear was nothing more than a jump scare machine. With the realization that there is no actual threat to the player, Layers of Fear soon became nothing more than a walking simulator with jumpscares added for good measure.
All in all, I really wanted to like this game, and I did, at first. Unfortunately, Layers of Fear is nothing more than a sad case of wasted potential. The story is pretty decent but the gameplay really really gets boring after a while, and the "sanity"-like aspect of the game becomes a dumb gimmick at a certain point in the game. Also, I want to point out that this game has 3 endings. Sorry devs, but I think a single playthrough is enough for me.

I purchased this game last September shortly after it was released in Early Access. I have now played the game for well over 2000 hours including offline play. I have seen it develope from a buggy game to a real gem. The graphics are very good and I love the First Person mode something I have never found in any other city building game.
It is a game of balance, of figuring out how to make it possible for your villagers to survive in a wilderness. You start with six adultsk three en and three women and four children/teenagers. They grow up very quickly if you are playing the base game. The biggest mistake that beginning gamers make is to expand the village too quickly. Since the villagers need a house to eat and get warm the first thing you do is build a house. You can then demolish one shack. Keep your initial village small. You must collect food, build a gatherers hut, a fishing pier and a hunters' lodge. What I do is make two adults gathers and either one or two fishers. Once winter comes you can change the gathers to hunters and or fishers. You also need to build a Lumberjack yard so that your villagers have an ample supply of firewood.
Distance in this game kills. Send a villager too far to collect resources and he or she willeither starve or freeze to death. Build a house too far from the barn and the residents will not be able to get food and fuel for the stoves. Build houses too far from jobs and either laborers will again either freeze or starve or will have no time to do any work. Keeping the village in good balance is very important and there is no reason why any villager should die from starvation or freeze. Absolutely none.

Oh they will die in child bearing, accidents and of old age but if properly provided for they will NOT starve or freeze. I cannot repeat that too much and it seems to be the biggest problem new players have.
Bugs have been fixed I have played for well over 100 hours recently with no ctds or freezes. This is not however a game I would recommend to those who want to rush everything, who need their hands held and to be instructed every step of the way. There are also excellent Community Guides available for those who are seeking help and the experienced forum members are also very generous with their help.

Okay, right off the bat; this game is a laugh. But a really good laugh. It's one of those Japanese (inspired) anime/hentai games of which the primary objective is sex. Chat up girls so you can get into their pant(ie)s. We've come a long way since DOS's Lascivious Larry and Windows' strip poker.
The (perhaps) unexpectant side about it? It's actually good. Despite a small number of inconsistencies that really only bother perfectionists like myself, this game is a hoot(er)! And the gameplay is actually really nice.
Like undoubtedly a lot of others, I learned about this game via Youtube videos. And since I like Match-3 games, I figured; "What the heck, I'll give it a look." And I have to admit, I like it more than I thought I would. And not for the obvious reason. Get your minds out of the gutters, yeesh =P
So from the start; the gameplay is intuitive enough. You open with a start screen that has four Save File boxes, plus buttons where you can change all the usual settings such as audio levels, windowed/fullscreen mode, and those kind of things. As well as a few less usual settings; an audio setting to choose between voice-over or boops? I have no idea what that's supposed to mean; I haven't yet tried it. You can also set if you want to start out as a male or a female. You can change this setting in-game as well, but it really doesn't make much of a difference; it just sets the sexual preferences of the in-game girls to suit the gender you chose. Because there are only girls in the game; no boys. That's wasting about half a target audience, but who knows, perhaps there may be a future DLC for this game to add guys, or a sequel that has only guys.
So your settings are set. You start. You're an awkward, shy, possibly introvert person (M/F) who doesn't do that whole 'dating' thing because you couldn't get a girl if your life depended on it. It's Sunday night. You're in a bar/lounge place (first inconsistency for perfectionist whiners like me; WHY would you, as a shy, introvert, awkward person go into a public bar on your own? But never mind that, the game has to start somewhere after all). This girl in a sassy uniform dress type outfit steps up to you and says hi. You get three options for a response, and they range from "Uhhh..." to basically "OMGFLAILOVERREACT!". Quite humorous, actually. The ensuing conversation has subtle differences based on the responses you give (three options every time, with really quite humorous and also quite inappropriate responses), but it all boils down to the girl promising you'll see more of her. You go home, most likely leaving a trail of fear-sweat behind you and hoping that every crack in the sidewalk opens up into a fiery chasm to swallow you off the face off the earth. You are, after all, a very shy and insecure person, and that girl was really cute and hot and all those common denominators.
But, you make it home to your bedroom. It's quite Japanese-looking; a low double bed on no legs, a rug in front of it, candles in somesort of basket-like holder at the corners. A fireplace. Skateboards on the wall. Ooo-kay... I have questions already. First off; WHO would put their bed at that weird an angle to the wall? Secondly, why the candles at the corners? Sure it's romantic, and I like candles, but that just looks like a fire hazard and pain waiting to happen right there. Thirdly; skateboards on the wall. I'll say that again. Skateboards on the wall. The last time I can remember having a skateboard was when I was like 12 years old, and I sure as heck did not keep it in my bedroom, let alone hanging from the wall. This is already kinda weird.
And the magical sex fairy has yet to appear.
Ah, there she is! She wakes you gently ("I said GET UP!"). Just so you can faint at the sight of her. Not because of the pink hair. Not because of the butterfly-y wings (which really are gorgeous I have to say, the artwork is very well done). But mostly because the dress she is wearing is even more revealing than what that girl in the bar was wearing. And that was not easy to do (seriously, a public bar where waitresses wear uniform dresses that hardly come down over the hips? Why have I never found any places like that?). Anyways.
The fairy basically kicks you out of your bed. You have three response options again, quite comical ones. she threatens to pull the covers off. Now you only get a good look at her for the first time it seems, and you have three more response options. Ranging from "I must still be dreaming" to "There's a stranger in my house! Police!" Quite normal reactions.
So you talk to her. She reveals herself to be Kyu, from the bar, remember? Uhm, yeah, but... back there you... Yeah, she can disguise herself. And she is pretty full of herself, and quite the snarky one to boot. It makes her dialog pretty darn entertaining. Especially when you realize she is a 5'4", causacian love fairy... who talks ghetto. Oh yes, as you progress through the game, her opening lines when meeting up with her, and a lot of her dialog, not just gets laced with, but almost entirely consists of, expressions like "How's it hangin', playa?" (Or, once you get that far into the game so that you get to bed her, the next morning she can say things like... ah, no, I'm gonna let you find that out for yourself. It's just too funny)
Now, the whole review I typed up was waaaaaaaaaay way too long to fit here. so the rest of it can be found right here:
Beware. It's a long read. I'm a writer, so even when I type things that are supposed to be short, like reviews, they tend to get out of hand when I have a lot to say =~.^=
To end;
Is the game sexist? Yes, yes it is. Is it racist? To a degree, yes, it is, some of the stereotypes are wincingly sharp. Is this a problem? No. It's all done in good humor, the game even clearly points that out itself. Nothing is meant hurtful or derogatory, it's all in good fun and should be seen as that. Like I said; don't take it too serious, as the game doesn't either.
Do I recommend it? Yes, yes I certainly do. The Match-3 aspect of the game is very replayable due to the constantly increasing score objective and the 20-move starting point, making you constantly having to think, to strategize, about getting enough Sentiment points to use Date Gifts, and then about which Date Gifts to use (and you even have to get lucky with those too; in my first playthrough I got a gift that turned all broken hearts into joy bells, you know, the ones that give you extra moves when matched. In my second save file, I have gotten over twice as many Date Gifts, and not one of them has been that broken-heart-to-joy-bells one, while I have gotten ones that are, pretty much, useless, three to four times over)
So. In short; a solid Match-3'er with a fun date sim aspect mixed in, funny dialog, good art, good music, good voice acting. I wouldn't say a must-have, but definitely worth a look. Also; good luck explaining your reasons for having and playing this game to your family/friends/etc =~.^=

Hotline Miami 2 is a brutal top down shooter, and the sequel to Hotline Miami 1.  The two games have strong gameplay similarities, but the sequel expands on the themes introduced in the first game.  The game took me about 10 hours to beat, and has some replayability.
The core of the gameplay is the same as Hotline Miami 1. The potency of the adrenaline-packed gameplay is equaled only by the lifeless silence after a mission is completed.  Polished pixel graphics enhance the gameplay experience.  Although Hotline Miami 2 adds new weapons and masks, it seems that more of both were removed than added.  Some may not like this change, but I don't mind it.  The game also features a Map Editor, which I have not yet tried.
My only complaint with the game is the inability to change the crosshair color.  The white crosshair blends into some of the maps, and is easy to lose track of.
References to movie scenes, play acts, and VCR recordings intentionally make what is 'really' happening in the game difficult to follow.  The distinction between in-game acting and reality is blurry, and perhaps nonexistent.  The transience of the story's narrative framework helps form a commentary about the game's audience.  The lack of distinction between acting and reality within the game points to the fundamental uniformity between in-game characters and real life people.  Humans relish violence.  The developers contend that while we may be sympathetic towards a character that is forced to violence through their own internal instability or by external forces, the audience can give themselves no such mercy.  The audience does not only participate in the violence, but commands and enjoys it.
As alluded to above, the game explores the moral culpability of various motives to violence.  These motives include, but are not limited to, mental disease, coercion by other parties, revenge, vigilantism, enforcement of moral hazard, war, fame, and as the means to an end.  This theme deserves its own analysis.  But the core theme of the game is that while a variety of motives exist, intrinsic violence is the defining element of human nature.  Dialogue, especially later in the game, is used to speak directly to the audience about about this message.  Even seemingly normal characters are unable to resist their violent urges.  Such is the fate of the characters, and such is the fate of the audience.
As in the first game, events are not meant to be interpreted as part of plot formation.  This is clear in the transient narrative framework and dubious narrator.  We can be confident that none of the events in the game actually take place because characters don't actually behave like real humans.  For example, enemies are almost zombie-like in their exceptional reaction time, lethal alacrity, and total disregard for blood-splattered walls or the corpses of their comrades.  The game likely takes place in the unhinged mind of some anonymous narrator.
The events are instead taken as connected thematic episodes.  The introspective qualities of the game and the abandonment of a traditional event-based plot indicate the game is a meta-story.  But interestingly, the game does follow the format of a traditional narrative on the macro level.  A character is introduced within a setting, struggles to understand their world, and finds a kind of resolution.  But in Hotline Miami 2, the character is the player, the setting is the game, and we come to understand that morality exists only as a trivial buffer against our impending demise.  This enigmatic relationship between the traditional narrative macro framework but micro thematic focus is diametrically opposed to the structure of most storytelling media.
Hotline Miami 2 is a masterful sequel to the first game.  Gameplay is very similar, but the clarity and coherence of tone and mood are noticeably improved from the already high standards in Hotline Miami 1.  The game is so successful because of its transient narrative framework, abandonment of a traditional plot, and player-focused development.  Themes linked to nihilism and bloodshed are unmatched among any other video game that I have played.  Hotline Miami 2 is both philosophical and blunt, both harsh and precise, and both exhaustive and vacant.  I very highly recommend this game.

The itemization is something i actually was looking forward to, until i realized how random it is. At the end of the level you are presented with 8 random items. Then you throw dices, each having a random chance to count, and based on the amount of dices that count you get one of the 8 items. You go through 2 random checks to get an item. The higher the item is on the list the quality of it improves, but so does the required  dices you need to count. In the 32.9 hours i have played i have never gotten above the 6-th item and that is with the best dices.
Finally it's the dlc. Each dlc is just a few more maps, but the actual problem lies elsewhere. There are quests in the game that can award you with specific items. While the items are randomly chosen each day you can see what the items are, and if you like something you can get it. To get the items you need to complete other quests that award keys. When you get enough keys you can get the item. Each quest is map specific. Can you guess where this is going by now :). You cannot complete many of the quests because they are for the dlc maps. So you just skip a day and hope that next day the quests will be for maps you actually have. Now if they continue to make just more maps as dlc, eventually you are going to be waiting quite a while to actually complete the item quests.

I'm 1.7 hours in, according to Steam, & I've screamed maybe 3-4 times. These were not gasps; gasps don't break my apartments' "don't be loud & annoying after 10pm" rule. They were out loud & almost certainly annoyed my neighbors.
If I did not have +5 Constitution from being a survival horror veteran (read: I beat Fatal Frames II & III on Nightmare Mode, come at me bro), then I would probably nope out of this game, BUT I GOT THIS.
The graphics are beautiful; a lot of thought & attention went into making the setting feel both genuine & discomforting. I compare this to the Fatal Frame games because it has that same degree of immersiveness that I always felt when playing those (& didn't always feel playing other games in the genre). As you begin, it's not exactly clear whether YOU, the protagonist, did something wrong, or whether something wrong was done to you, & there's a much deeper sense of unease in that, I think.
There are jumpscares, yes, but it feels disingenuous to call them jumpscares because they're not gratuitous; they're actually sort of predictable. The game interacts with objects that are significant to the story, but they're still scary. You walk into a room, you see one of those objects, YOU KNOW SOME♥♥♥♥♥♥IS ABOUT TO HAPPEN, but it's still scary.
I'm anxious to find out how the story progresses & how it ends. The premise, that an artist is tormented by the work he didn't do, is a premise close to my heart (because "I should be writing right now" is a thing I tell myself maybe 800 times a day).
Play this game, though; it's loveable.

Layers of Fear is an epic horror story game, that guides the player on a twisted world, imagined by the artist. The world changes around you, much like a painter who is forever recreating and changing his art work. The never ending search for perfection!
The whole game fills the player with many different emotions, depending on the play style you take. Are you a selfish artist? Are you a regretful husband? Are you a loving parent? These questions and more, give the player a real sense of life and helps create an excellent atmosphere for each step you take.
For an indie developer, Bloober Team, have created a "master piece", not only in story but in the amazing world they built. The eye to detail makes you stop at every little item, just to see the work put into it. With great art, comes some magnificient sound. Music and sound effects sit perfectly with the tone of the game, whilst the amazing voice acting captures the heart.
With 3 distinct endings, based on every choice you do, every item you grab and read, it makes for lots of replayability. I spent almost 24 hours just to get all three endings and I tell you, it wasn't a walk in the park! The game challenges you on a deep psychological level, especially to get these different endings. Much time and patience is needed for all three.
Just like all great works of art, this will live on as a cult classic game for those who love something entirely different!

Cat Quest is a colorful breath of fresh air in the RPG genre. It pays homage to other classic titles, especially Zelda, and is filled with paw-some references. It's also filled - FILLED! - with cat-puns. Some of them are quite bad, like "catfrontation" (Clawfrontation was the obvious choice).
The game is stunningly well-made, it is perhaps the cutest game out there, but in terms of art direction it's bright, colorful and uplifting, the animations and character designs are great as well. You control the protagonist, who has his sister kidnapped at the sea by a magical white cat. You are then accompanied by a Na'Vi-like guiding spirit that is as annoying as her who will help you on your quest to rescue your sister.
Combat is in real-time, just like Zelda, in which you click to attack freely, and you must run around the map to dodge incoming attacks and spells. Some enemies can be quite challenging. While the game isn't linear, meaning you can go wherever you want to in any order you'd like to, areas are separated by level, which means you might need to get a few levels before advancing further. The world is pretty big and is filled with dozens of quests.
Overall, the game is really fun, it's super cute, very entertaining, but unfortunately too short. It can be completed in less than eight hours, which is feeble compared to the staple of the RPG genre. But in-game the developers have inserted many meta jokes, like the wolves of the Lupus Empire will only appear if Cat Quest becomes popular enough. My guessis this version of the game is testing the waters, because it growls for more content and it has the pawtential of being a good classic of the genre - if given enough attention.
You should definitely play this game if you love adventure, RPG and kittens.

Bought it because: unique concept.
A card game that looks like an old black & white movie, you against a skeleton dealer, with an old-timey piano soundtrack playing in the background. You're dealt 7 cards to start your turn, must discard two, and then play anywhere from 2-5. If you play fewer than 5, the dealer adds more from his hand, so it's in your best interest to play anything good you have.
You start as a baby; each hand is one year in your life. You have various stats (health, popularity with family, popularity with peers, etc). The basic cards you play are "have something happen to me" cards, such as having a bad dream as a baby, that force decisions, such as whether to cry for your parents. Outcomes from your decisions can be good or bad that affect your stats; some cards just apply effects with no decision possible. You also have cards in your hand that can force good outcomes for these events, or change the rules, change your card loadout, etc.
It's easily to learn, fairly basic and fun, and is the kind of game you play in short sessions.
There's a game shop where you can buy additional cards for your deck (using game money you earn as you age and start to earn a salary) to improve the virtual life you go through during the game.
Full price for this game is $9.99. It's fairly casual and I would recommend a lower price point, $4.99 or $2.99, to drive sales. I also think it would do much better in sales numbers as a tablet game, and recommend the devs port it to iOS or Android.

Earthtongue is a really simple, accessible game for those interested in the ways different creatures interact in an ecosystem - the graphic style is the familiar sort of minimalism common to indie games at this level of production, but I find the simplistic graphics helps you project your own image of the world you're tending to. The interactions between the different bugs and molds can be surprisingly deep - it can be a bit inscrutable at times, but once you start to get a feel for each organism's behavior, you can fairly reliably cultivate a very diverse ecosystem. What pushes Earthtongue over the top are the built-in hooks for mods, which are quite powerful and offer options for lots of variety, even behaviors and qualities not expressed in the base game, like the option for creature immortality and hard population caps. If any of this sounds appealing to you, it's worth picking up, especially for a game so cheap!
Full disclosure - the developer is a friend of mine, and I have provided some feedback here and there during its development, but I was not solicited to write this review at all - I just think it's neat!

Overall, I played the game for a few hours. Had a great time leveling. But the instant requirement for better gear without a fair, fun way of earning it was too much.
