I played this a lot now. I played the single player mode up to 200 days in so far. I will say that it is not perfect. It doesn't deserve 100%. It probably deserves more 80% which is still pretty good.
In many ways it is very much like Pirates! type gameplay. You travel the map from a top-down godlike view with parties represented by single units on the world map. Battles take your right into the action. Lots of menus and options to navigate as you enter cities and talk to NPCs. Individual quests, business, trade, warfare, joining factions, reputation, owning towns etc...
Pros:
-You are the master of your destiny. There is no real storyline you have to follow. Go do whatever you desire. But the game is really designed for you to conquer lands and become a king yourself. There are numerous ways to proceed.
- Large battles with wide variety of units putting you right in the middle of the action. You can command your troops in the battle and organize them into groups. My strategy for now has been to charge the enemy with cavalry, breaking their formation, then advancing my infantry. I am only playing on easy though. :P
- Really well done combat system allowing you to move your weapon about in different directions with the mouse for attack and defense.
- RPG style gameplay. You also get to hire, kit and lvl up companions/heros. Your regular troops also gain experience and upgrade and you can also find mercenaries.
- Own villages/cities/castles and manage their garisons and improvements.
- Trade on a large scale.
- Own businesses and incorporate their needs into your trade strategy.
- MULTIPLAYER
- Highly moddable
Cons:
- Grindy. Although there is a staggering amount of depth to the game, there is still a lot of tedious thnigs that you need to do over and over. The major thing to me seems to be upgrading favor with either villages or lords. Its a lot of the same quests over and over and a lot of the time they don't have any quests for you.  So its a lot of riding the same paths over and over to grind out the gold and favor. However. war time can be very lucrative.
- No real instructions that I've found to help you understand what the game is all about except for what is found through exploring in-game. If it wasn't for the wiki and forums to help me I would not have enjoyed the experience unless i had hundreds of more hours to spend playing it and my own self-made wiki! Kind of like minecraft in this regard.
I feel like it is a really great accomplishment however there is a ton of improvements that could be made.
That said, I would buy it again and I have bought the whole pack of m&b games!

A fantastic horror game. This game has some of the most disturbing, beautiful, and surreal imagery I've ever seen. It could easily be called a masterpiece if not for the following caveats:
1) I highly recommend you get this game with the DLC. It's a shady way to operate, but the developers basically cut half the story out of the game and decided to release it in the DLC, so it's really necessary to play through them to get the full story. Otherwise you'll be left scratching your head.
2)The first 1/3 of the game has serious pacing issues and is incredibly confusing. I really had to trudge through it. So much is left unexplained that you spend the first 6 chapters just asking yourself "What the everloving f**k is going on? How did I get here?" The story doesn't really get going until about chapter 7 or 8, because of this the beginning chapters really feel like filler. But I promise it's worth the agony.
3)I'm the kind of gamer who enjoys playing hardcore games like Dark Souls, and it literally pained me to switch the difficulty down to "Casual". But after hours of yelling at the screen, being constantly low on health, and getting one-shotted by every other enemy in the game, I finally relented and began enjoying the game SO MUCH MORE. The game is incredibly imbalanced on "Survival" difficulty and will do everything it can to convince you to NOT change the difficulty to "Casual". But I highly recommend you do.
The game is brought down by a series of really bizarre choices and game imbalances, some badly designed boss fights, and crappy clostrophobic camera controls. Overall, The Evil Within would've benefited from some more focused direction and a better writer.  But underneath these issues there's a really fantastic horror game waiting to be explored. There's clear talent at work here and they do a great job evoking fear in a variety of ways. The game has some of the creepiest, grossest enemies around and features some of the coolest horror set pieces I've ever seen. One level has you crawling through a city as the landscape collapses and shifts around you, while a boss fight has you run through a maze of body parts as you're chased by an incorporeal blood monster.
This gameis a must-have if you're a fan of horror games.

For people who don't want to sit through a long explanation of why this game is good and how more people should be playing and just want the TF2 hats I'll give you a few tips
*play blitz, it's the easiest game mode to get xp on, it only requires 5 players and is co-op, so you can find a game pretty quickly, just set up a game and invite everyone in public chat
*use these codes, they're for xp boosts and will help you burn through the levels quickly, however I reccomend using them once you've gotten through the easier levels so starting in the 5-10 level region:
2718-2818
4070-9098
Okay, now we're through that, is the game any good? Simply put, yes, yes it is. I find all the modes quite fun, blitz is good if you like TF2's MvM, but wish there was some sort of survival mode, turbocross and super crossfire are very similar, however it is a lot easier to get a game on turbocross. The pros have a good mix of roles, mainly focused on either attacking or defending, with even the support based classes having the ability to deal decent damage. The characters are also very entertaining with very distinct personalities.
Gamemodes:
*Blitz
Blitz is a 5 player co-op mode, where you defend your moneyball against increasing hordes of robots, a lot of fun to play with friends, also helps you to get a hang of difficult classes. A good tip for playing this mode is to keep turrets healed, so having either a support or combat girl is a must
*super crossfire and turbocross
Both very similar, basically each team is trying to take down either side's moneyball, to do this you must guide your robots through, killing enemy robots, players and turrets. The only real difference between these two gamemodes is that turbocross moves a lot faster, the differences can be read here:
Pros:
Pros are the name in this game of what heroes are to dota and what classes are to TF2. There is a very good selection and you'll almost certainly find at least one that fits your playstyle. Like sniping? Choose sniper or artemis. Like upclose and personal action? Veteran and captain spark will likely be your jam. Like going on the sneaky beaky? Then you'll likely love assassin.
Why is this game dead?
Well actually, it isn't. It's very small but far from dead. It's only really hard to get games on super crossfire, blitz and turbocross are played very much. What the game really suffered from is poor matchmaking, it's not possible to join a game half way through, and it also lacks any sort of server browser, making you rely on their strange party matchmaking system to get into games.
Final Verdict:
This game is fun, and good for those who are hesitant towards MOBAs but enjoy shooters. It mainly suffered from poor matchmaking and an audience that migrated towards DOTA and LoL, it could really benefit from having more players as it's only real problem is having too small of a community. (Also, if you like the game and are thinking of supporting it, don't buy the turbocross bundle, get the pro pack, it's the same price and comes with all pros, all their blitz gear and 2 taunts for each pro)
Edit:
These are some of my major gripes with SMNC, as I feel I should mention some of the negative along with the positive
*grapple
Dear god is grapple important in smnc, however, it feels to much like it was handed out between pros willy nilly. The biggest issue is every pro can grapple, however, whereas the commando pros (assassin, captain spark, and wascot) rely on grapple to do most of their damage,  other stronger classes can also grapple, the main ones that really make this a problem is megabeth and combat girl, they do a lot of damage from their weapons and are by no means reliant on it to do damage, however, they can easily knock off a third of your health by grappling you, and the effect of ping can sometimes cause them to grapple you first, quickly killing you, as they may not kill you with a grapple, but they can easily finish you off with ranged capability you don't have. This is perhaps the largest balance issue in the game, as it often feels unfair when a pro that you've expertly hunted can kill you due to a split second difference in grapple.
*communication
it is very hard, and has been poorly implemented. There is no real way to use proper voice communication, making you rely on text chat and voice commands, this is problematic as smnc, whilst not as reliant on communcation as something like Guns of Icarus, has the communication aspect as an important part of the gameplay.

I suddenly found myself in the care of a planet in some far reach of space.
The more time I spent with this planet, the more attached I grew to its inhabitants.
I remember an era of pure blue, the mushrooms and beetles spanning miles and miles. Few could dispute their claim to this world.
Little by little, the yellow slime took over... Then the spiders came. It barely resembled the world I once knew. With them, the world had taken a different shape.
I wanted all creatures to share this planet. I'll admit, I've interfered a lot. I just want to see them thrive. This is the task I've charged myself with. Whether I achieve it -- if the powers that be allow me to achieve it -- is a different story...
But I won't give up.

Earthtongue is a really relaxing terrarium game.  It's something nice to leave on in the background for a while.  If you've ever played The Sims or any small-scale simulation game, you'll know you get strangely attached to your little simulated world.  It's yours!  Nobody else will have quite the same interaction with their world, and that makes it really special.
If you're looking for a really deep, directly engaging game, this probably isn't going to scratch that itch.  Earthtongue is a game that's at its most fun when you check in on it every now and then, tweak a few things, poke at your mantises, cross-pollinate a few mushrooms, and then leave again.
There's an update coming out pretty soon that'll add user-made customizable gardens, which is a REALLY cool addition.  If you're on the fence right now, that update should probably push you over.
Also it's just five bucks.  C'mon.  Skip coffee tomorrow morning and grab a copy.

Earthtongue is a fun, mostly hands off ecosystem simulator. You start off knowing nothing about what you're doing and you slowly have to learn the rules of the different species through experience and research notes in game.
The players role in the ecosystem is two fold, in my experience. Firstly, the player has to introduce the species that will populate the world. Secondly, you will try to maintain the ecosystem. This is done by adding nutrients and water as well as moving bugs and spores to new areas. Most of the game is spent just watching the species cohabitate the once desolate planet.
I've had a lot of fun with it. I've had planet destroying swarms of locusts (a couple hundred in total) that I proceeded to exterminate and completely collapse the worlds ecosystem. I've built massive fungal forests occupied by only spiny slugs, spiders, and wasps. I've fixed a massive overpopulation of herbivores by dropping voracious mantises on them, leading to a massive overpopulation of mantis. Everytime I enjoyed myself and learned a bit more about how to balance the ecosystem.
I would recommend the game if you want something to waste away the time with. It really is a lot of fun to watch.

The main problem comes in progression; if you are not a member do not think about using a fancy gun, grenades, tanks, etc. Because you will not be able to repair it without a membership, as the credits(in game money) you gain in battle will not exceed the credits used at the end, but since you really can't enjoy the game without utilizing all the fun toys you can see the impasse.
Now a single month subscription costs you about 12 dollars through steam to buy the gold then to purchase the membership through the in game store. Though because a month membership costs 2400 gold and the only option is 2200 gold for $11.22 and 5100 gold for $22.5 you have to purchase the more expensive gold bundle. The main problem with this is cost vs. content, the core game is fine, the gunplay is fine, but in my opinion the content is lacking and the game is STILL IN BETA. Let us look at other subscription-based games, WoW which I have never played for lack of interest will cost you $15 dollars a month (for a monthly subscription, comparing apples to apples) and has a HUGE wealth of content. The Old Republic, which again has a wealth of content, will also cost you approximately $15 dollars a month for a reoccurring subscription (though you can play free for the entire main storyline). A daybreak membership which gives you benefits while playing games such as Planetside 2, DC online, Everquest 1&2, and I think h1z1 (though you still have to purchased h1z1) costs you again $15 dollars per month (most of these games are free to play). Now, you might think. “well it’s cheaper than the rest of the games mentioned” but in terms of content vs costs I’m afraid it just can’t hold up to the other contenders out there.
Now I have subscribed to several games in the past, and currently do subscribe to a few games but the idea of purchasing a membership for this game in its current incarnation leaves a bad taste in my mouth. I do not disagree that there should be benefits to subscribing but the pay wall in this game is way too steep for what I get from the game itself. The very fact that you will spend most/all (or go into deficit spending) of your resources gained during battle in repair and resupply if you so choose to use anything besides the base weaponry is ridiculous. A combined arms game should allow for combined arms, not combined arms if you throw your wallet at the Devs.
If the developers decide to stop choking off new players from nearly all the good content I will come back to play this game. However, at this moment I do not have the stamina to grind away for things I cannot use without a penalty. So therefore, I do not suggest you play this game until, if ever, the devs readjust how they approach new players.
Honestly I love combined arms games, I like the idea of having infantry, tanks and airpower all working together (or sometimes running around like insane chickens) towards victory. I really REALLY wanted to like this game, but sadly I just cannot.

As someone who desperately wants to love this game, it can go ♥♥♥♥ itself. It's a good game dragged down by three particular things that absolutely poison it and rob it of any possibility of fun for me.
First and least important, the hit detection is garbage. You will probably see a LOT of attacks harmlessly pass through your enemies. This might just be related to the game's performance on mine and other system rather than a universal one, though, so it's not as bad as the other 2 problems.
Second, the loot system is a giant "♥♥♥♥ you" to the player. The idea of it is good, but since they made it so that you receive no real rewards of any kind if you fail a mission, you can waste over an hour at a time playing and finding all 3 tomes and working through the level, but as you get to the end of a mission you get ♥♥♥♥ed when the game spawns 8 stormvermin, a globadier, a packmaster, and a gutter runner alongside a big horde and they all hit your party at once just before you complete the event that ends the level (as happened in a recent game for me in Castle Drachenfels -- we never even got to move before being taken down). Or it just streams stormvermin at you so fast that there's never fewer than 4 standing directly in front of you on a narrow path until you all die. And no, getting a handful of crappy raw materials is not a real reward or even a consolation -- it's an insult. And that's on easy.
Third, the AI is ♥♥♥♥ing unacceptable. It's just as awful now as it was at launch, and that simply boggles my mind. It has not been fixed *at all*. Bots are worse than useless and can be an active detriment to your progress, especially with how frequently they just. . . break. I'm talking stopping and standing in place until the game teleports them or they die, or cowering in a corner the instant a ratling gun shows up and refusing to move for anything so they get to die in that corner. And since the community is often incredibly toxic and likely to boot you for not being high enough level, it can get really difficult to find even a pick up group. And the bot AI isn't the only one that breaks a lot. Ratling gunners in particular will break all the time and just walk back and forth or simply stand still, and their presence seems to flip an idiot switch in the other Skaven and breaks them too.
All that said, I'd recommend this *if* you have people you know you can play with. Solo play is a broken pile of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that Fatshark has made no apparent effort to fix and the community is not one you can rely on to help you out.

This game is awesome. If you love squad-based action/strategy games as much as I do, you will undoubtedly agree. The character progression is great, the loot is bountiful and the gameplay is addictive. But what makes my heart skip a beat is the combination of believable physics with highly destructible levels... Enemies in the next room? Empty that machine gun into the door and catch them off guard. Goons in the basement? Detonate a charge and bring the floor/ceiling down on their head. Pesky fiend hiding in the library? Have your skilled sniper fire a high-caliber round through two walls and a bookcase and right between the ribs... Take all that, set it in an increasingly fantastical version of WW2 (mechs, anyone?) and you have a recipe for good times. If the visuals and presentation were better, even a little bit, this would be fighting for a spot in my 'top 10 favorite games of all time' list.

I've enjoyed all these games but this one by far takes the cake.  Not much to say here in terms of game mechanics, you walk, explore, and open doors and drawers, searching for clues and mementos although not required to progress or finish the game gives you a deeper understanding of the character and the events leading up to what's going on in the game.  Those of you looking for heavy game mechanics I'd say stay away from this game as it's not what you're looking for.  Graphics wise the game is amazing, though it is comparable to other triple A titles currently out.  The voice acting is also fantastic, the sound (effects and music) are quite good, and the nuances and different tactics the game throws at you are unique and refreshing.  Though quite simple in hindsight, progressing through a certain area in the game isn't straightforward, as to do so you might have to light some candles, continue prgressing through a seemingly endless loop, pick up an item tucked away somewhere or simply look in a certain direction.  But the main reason you play a game like this, is for ambience and mood which it is very heavy on and does quite well.  I have to say (and you can argue this all you want) but for me, for whatever reason, I always had that edge of your seat feeling, always a bit nervous as to what was around the next corner or through the next door.  There are some truly horrifying moments in this game and found myself jumping or jolting back from the seat I was sitting in.  It's the flurry of extra beats your heart makes at certain points that makes you want to take a break for 5 or 10 minutes just to remind yourself you're not really in this world and you can in fact go back to reality any time you'd like.  As you do learn more and more of the story however, the horror aspect is also anchored to real world (although unfortunate) realities and that pehaps is even more erie than the big bad beastie monster hiding under your bed.    Apparently this game was inspired by the P.T. trailer that was on the PlayStation store, and when I heard that I was very interested in purchasing this game and once it actually was finished being developed, it did not dissapoint.  If you like horror definitely buy this game, it pretty much does everything right.  Even if you don't generally like horror games, I'd say give this a shot.  This game might be the exception for you.  10/10 from me!

As a gamer who has been playing the game since the demo, I have to say that Layers of Fear has developed into a game that exceeded my expectations by far.
To truly draw a player into a horror game and fully immerse them in its enviornment involves many factors: timing, pacing, use of music, sound effects, visuals, and a realistic storyline. The right execution of each variable creates an experience that leaves you feeling connected to the game.
Surprisingly, this game left me feeling sad and empathetic for the characters. Perhaps Amnesia, Outlast, Slender, and other classic horror games made it harder for me to be filled with fear- but I was afriad. I just got rooted into the story so passionatley that emotions like love, regret, redemption, and hope were more powerful than my fear.
The best part was I had no clue if my actions to face scary situations for these positive emotions even made a difference- I didn't even care. Despite the outcome of the game, I could fall asleep knowing that I didn't succumb to my fear when faced with horror. I didn't run away from someone who deserved my compassion despite being scared of their monsterous appearence.
Amnesia and Outlast have been my favourite games because they nail the pacing, jump scares, and creepy atmousphere. I always felt hooked into the storyline- I had to know what happened. But in Layers of Fear, for the first time, I felt like my own morality was drawing me in. These characters did not bring themselves into the story, they were victims of circumstance; as most of us are to the situations we deal with in real life.
With other games I pushed through the fear for uncovering captivating storylines, but with Layers of Fear I pushed through it for the purpose of making things right (for my character). As a result, Layers of Fear does not feel like a game to me, it feels like a test of character. I found that under many layers of superficial fear lies what really matters. As much as I loved the jumpscares, the puzzles, and the random mapping, I truly loved the imprint this game left on my heart.
Everyone should play this game. Even if you hate the horror genre, this game might help you find the bravery to face your fears. Every person that worked on this game should feel proud of themselves, and I thank them for the opportunity to experience this.

What makes this different compared to other typical horror games is that danger isn't necessarily dangerous. While there are few instances where you will feel threatened with your life, death isn't the end. It's simply another choice. Every cause has an effect, and here you're urged to approach danger with curiosity, not run away in fear. Doing either will lead to a whole other story.
So don't fear the danger, but approach it cautious. Do you want to know what happened to
?
There's only one way to find out...
Game highly recommended, I don't regret buying it at full retail and will still say it's worth it. I've played for ten hours after the pre-release and have still not finished, because taking your time, observing your surroundings and searching for the past is the only way you're going to find out what the hell is going on in this place. Not to mention it has high replay value due to the amount of choices one can make to progress the story a little differently each time.

The game isn't bad, but I won't recommend this over the original when the first one was better.
I went back and forth playing HM1 and HM2:WN to figure out why I don't like the second one, so here's what I've decided.
Clearly the maps are worse in the sequel because of how open each level is. In the original you could run into a room and outmaneuver the baddies if you were quickwitted enough and had the reflexes. In this one, the rooms are so large that running straight into any room is certain death, so everytime you have to bait them out and wait at the doorway to kill most enemies. It's boring. My pinky finger was sore because I practically had it down one the look button for the entire game just so I could see who was shooting me.
Something I didn't realize until going back and forth is how stiff HM2 feels in comparison with HM1. I already knew that takedowns took longer, but attacking, moving, changing direction, etc, all feel more sluggish.
Some of the character abilities are boring/useless. Tony and Alex & Ash are the only fun characters for the vigilante crew, and Alex & Ash can be pretty buggy. Corey's roll causes more harm than good most of the time because you can't turn and can only change between 2 distances to roll for. Mark's ability to shoot in 2 directions is only useful in extremely specific situations where the developers want you to use him.
The story is a harder thing to discuss. The original was interesting because it was seen from Jacket's perspective, and the fact that he never spoke left a lot of his character to interpretation. That can be a good or a bad thing. There's more of an effort of a narrative in this game, but it's not great. Most of the characters' stories don't go anywhere or are just cut-off because story events come out of nowhere so often. The characters are hard to like because of how much they talk and how many there are and how the game has to divide attention among them (very unevenly at that).
Now it's not all bad. The most notable possitive aspect is the music, which saved the game for me. It's different from the original's, but in a good way that matches the tone.
TL:DR
+The music is bangin'
+/- More of a story(?)
-Too open maps where you get shot from a mile away
-Controls that are somehow worse (if subtly) from the original
-Bad character abilities
-Character stories go nowhere or are cut-off
Addendum:
It's not the worst thing ever, but it's inferior in almost everyway to the original. The onlyy saving grace (for me at least) is the soundtrack, and you can just purchase that separately.

Despite Manny always being two steps ahead of the rest of the force, the Miami Mutilator somehow manages to stay three ahead of him. When he starts to discover cryptic pleas for help written in the blood of the Mutilator's victims, Pardo discovers that things never turn out how you expect them to. Originally published in 1981.

Seeing as I have about 10x -30x  the hours of any other reviewer in playing this game, I guess it's time that I say something about it.
Lots of people have already described what it is. I'm going to say a little about getting the most out of the game.
First, think of it more as a 'Garden' that you just leave running in the background, and come back and tend to every so often. For me, that's about every 20mins or so.
At first, you need to unlock all of the descriptions for the different plant and bug types, so that yo know how they interact... what the feed on, how they reproduce. To do this, you need to keep that plant/bug alive for 5000s straight. I'd recommend focussing on the Moulds first (OK, some of them are Carnivirous, worry about them a bit later, then) and pretty well ignore bugs altogether early game. Why? because The wrong bug can easliy wipe out an entire species or 10 of Mould.
If you have a Mould or bug that keeps dying, for no reason, it's probably Carnivorous, and has no food. Try reintroducing it once you have a bigger eco system running.
I have yet to create a balanced, self sustaining system. It involves quite a lot more than you might think, actually. Right no I am in the middle of Terraforming to create separate Mini-Biomes, so that I can introduce several complementarty species that can rely on each other, and hopefully not wipe each other out.
This is the appeal of this game, it's preject with a view to the long term, kind of like making Bonsai.
It's always interesting when the planet decides to throw something random in the mix, though.

A fantastic game, with an outstanding storyline. There's a lot to get from this game, and you really get that "Star Trek" feel from the game. There's a large community, all on one server, with an instanced setup, allowing for you to group with all of your friends, without having to correlate with their server(s).shard(s).
The Dev team is active, and spend time in-game, and with the single-server setup, this means there's always the chance that YOU may run into a Dev.
The community is decent, as far as MMO's go, with fleets (the equivalent of a guild) all over the place, and with varying styles. From heavy RP Fleets, to Endgame Raid fleets, you can find everything, in one place.
Star Trek Online is my most logged MMO to date, and I hope to keep it that way.

STO as one sentence: DO NOT PLAY UNLESS YOU REALLY LOVE STAR TREK BECAUSE YOU'll BE SO LOST IT'LL PHYSICALLY HURT.
STO as a set of percentages:
- 25% decent single player campaign (of which 60% cool space combat, 30% passable ground combat, 10% dialogue)
- 15% references to Star Trek TV and films
- 5% references to books I doubt anyone's read
- 35% grindy end-game content (of which 40% Special Task Forces, 30% ground battlezone, 20% getting stuck in another GODDAMN UNDINE RIFT DAMNIT FULL POWER TO IMPULSE, 10% New Romulus)
- 5% scumming the exchange to put together your ship build
- 5% grindy holiday events
- 5% customising the look of your ship because it's never quite right
- 5% slightly-iffy-but-erring-on-the-side-of-acceptable real-world-money transactions (NOTE: optional, yes I'm talking to you, official forums)
In summation of the summation - I always claimed not to like the 'theme park' style MMO, and STO does have shades of that, but I thought the extremely competent single-player missions make up for most of the other shortcomings. If you're only  interested in that, there's probably somewhere in the region of 100-150 hours worth of decent Star Trek here that you won't have to pay a penny for.
If you want to go deeper, find a fleet. Worst case scenario - it's a place to dump all your excess resources in return for some shiny ships. Best case scenario - the above plus a group of cool people who do events and stuff. Overall - 7.5/10.

So, what can be said about the newest addition to the Rusty Lake/Cube Escape series?
As my first review on Steam, it's only fitting that I write something about my first purchased game (Terraria, being a gift, not counting). And while I could say a whole lot, I'll try and keep it brief.
Firstly, this is perhaps my favorite game from the Cube Escape series. It's hard to make that judgment considering how much I love every game in this series (as you might have noticed, my avatar is a screenshot from the recently-released Cube Escape: Birthday). But Rusty Lake Hotel does something special by bringing together elements - and characters, as you'll realize if you played the previous installments - from the games before it, and makes for a very intriguing, very eye-opening, very unnerving and unnatural experience.
What do I mean by that last part? Simply put (and without spoiling anything), things get weird, and some would say gut-wrenching. The gameplay is similar to all of the games before it, as it should be, with the goal being trying to find particular items to accomplish the main objective. In this game's case, the objective is to find ingredients each night which will allow you to cook a savory dish for your guests the next day. A new element not previous in past games is the ability to find bonus items, which will allow you to get higher scores each day and eventually unlock something special in the end. The gameplay is, as always, thought-provoking and unnerving; mildly puzzling in some cases, moderately challenging in others. I guarantee you moments where you'll be grinning, gasping, and subsequently staring in disbelief at your screen in the span of minutes. It's the kind of game that makes you want to know more with each passing moment, and it fully delivers in the uncanny department. There were also parts where I was simply hesitant to act, knowing what would come; other times I was laughing at the ridiculousness of the circumstances, particularly the happenings in the room of Mr. Rabbit (Rest In Peace, valiant hare). All around, it's a game both chilling and absurd, enjoyable and brain-racking. All around, it's a great experience. I could complain about the problems I had with some puzzles, and my inability to collect all of the bonus ingredients, but I'd really only be expressing personal issues at that point - I'm admittedly dense at times in games like these, and so there's really nothing wrong here but my own lack of sight (or so I'd think). That being said, beware the water jugs.
To summarize, Rusty Lake Hotel delivers excellently for the first premiere game from the series. It keeps in line with the previous (extremely bizarre and difficult to understand) storyline and general style, while also introducing more through some new elements and abilities. It's plot is strange to say the least, but makes you want more - much more, in my case. The game gave me a couple hours of fun and frustration, and in the end left me jaw open and wanting a sequel immediately. If you're a fan of the Cube Escape series, point-and-click games, and dark, eerie, and morbid storytelling, then this is the game for you. And if you're not a fan of any of these, buy the game anyway; Rusty Lake Hotel will make you a fan.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game, and it's fully worth the price.

At its core, Cat Quest is a game that ditches unnecessay frills and features and instead has a polished core gameplay that works exactly the way you want it to. Though combat is simplistic (with a button for attacking, one for spells, and another for rolling), there is a great amount of enjoyment to be had with this title. It's back to basics, the fundamentals that make other action RPGs so much fun: fighting, looting, and fashion.
Combat is boiled down to the bare essentials. You have one button for swinging your melee weapon, a selection of up to four spells to cast, and a dodge button. All of these are used with equal frequency. It's not enough to just whack an enemy, more often you will need to slow them with ice or weaken their defenses with fire. You can't just stand there and wail on the baddies, you will need to watch for their attack warning and roll out of danger. You're given a lot of warning when danger approaches, and in exchange you are punished greatly if you do get hit. Cat-like agility will be needed.
Loot is comprised of armor, helmets, and weapons. Every chainmail helm has the same stat distribution as the next. However, every time you get a new chainmail helm, the one you already have goes up in level, and thus in stats. This means you might be mixing and matching sets rather than sticking to one for the entirety of your playthrough.
Side quests are sadly tedious, all falling under the umbrella of Kill X or Fetch Y. There is some variety thrown in, in the form of tracking and chasing, but those moments are just a game of follow the dotted line. Avoiding side quests isn't really an option, either, as they're the best way to level up. Simply killing monsters won't be enough, unless you go after those of a much higher level than you.
Balancing is an issue, in terms of leveling. Starting off, you'll see a lot of quests above your paygrade, though you're free to attempt them. After awhile, you'll find yourself rocketing past the level recommendations for the main quest and going back to find side quests you're now 20 levels too big for. Eventually you'll want to tackle quests that are deemed too high a level for you, but with the right gear and magic, you will do just fine.
Heading straight for the end of the game, ignoring any side content you don't have to touch, you'll likely finish the game in 3~ hours. Factoring in all the side quests and dungeons, expect to get about ~6 hours out of this game. There's promise for future content, though it's hard to tell if it's hinting at a sequel or DLC.
If you're looking for a fun and simple (but not too simple) game to relax with, this would be a great fit for any veteran or newcomer to the gaming scene. It's accessible and charming, and while the content isn't as substantial as some may like, what is there is better polished than in most other games for its cost. Quality over quantity is the name of the game.
+ Charming art style and orchestral soundtrack blend for a simplistic but enjoyable gameworld.
+ Decently sized selection of gear, some original and some referential.
+ Simple combat, but more depth there to be found if you look.
- Very boring side quests that lead to mashing through dialogue just to get it over with.

The combat is very fluid, with intuitive controllers and a simple but efficient and enjoyable skill system. There are four basic stats – life, defense, melee power and magical power – that will improve as you level up. They are modified according to the gear you wear, which are varied enough to allow you to choose your own playstyle (spellcaster, melee, tank…).
There isn’t the usual buy / sell merchant system - you can’t sell the equipment you collect and can only buy “equipment chests” that contain a random item (you can’t buy specific gear). Despite that, you will find a good amount of gear inside dungeons. Equipment can also level up, usually by completing quests, even though you can’t choose which one will be upgraded – it’s random.
You can save at any time, which makes it easy to interrupt game sessions without losing progress. When you die, you don’t lose any gold, gear or experience – only your progress on the current quest is reset.
The graphics are great, sound effects are pleasant and the soundtrack is very nice, even changing “tone” to fit the atmosphere on different situations (humor, action, sadness, etc). This, added to the cute avatars that accompany the text pop ups, convey the character’s emotions very well, even without voice acting.
The game has lots of humor and funny references to pop culture, and at the same time manages to have a touching story.

+ Can save at any time

+ Good sound effects and soundtrack

O combate é bem fluido, com controles intuitivos e um sistema de habilidades simples, mas eficiente e agradável. Existem quatro atributos básicas - vida, defesa, ataque físico e ataque mágico –  que aumentam conforme você sobe de nível. Eles são modificados de acordo com os equipamentos que você usar, que são variados o suficiente para permitir que você escolha seu próprio estilo de jogo (mago, corpo a corpo, tanque, etc).
Não existe o sistema usual de compra / venda - você não pode vender os equipamentos que coletar e só pode comprar "baús de equipamentos" que contenham um item aleatório (você não pode comprar equipamentos específicos). Apesar disso, você encontrará uma boa quantidade de equipamentos dentro das masmorras. O equipamento também pode subir de nível, geralmente ao completar missões, apesar de você não escolher qual deles será melhorado - é aleatório.
Você pode salvar a qualquer momento, o que torna fácil interromper uma sessão de jogo sem perder seu progresso. Quando você morre, você não perde ouro, equipamento ou experiência - apenas o seu progresso na missão atual é resetado.
Os gráficos são ótimos, os efeitos sonoros são agradáveis e a trilha sonora é muito boa, até mesmo mudando de "tom" para combinar com a atmosfera em diferentes situações (humor, ação, tristeza, etc.). Isso, adicionado aos avatares fofinhos que acompanham as caixas de texto, transmitem as emoções do personagem muito bem, mesmo sem dublagem.
O jogo tem muito humor e referências engraçadas à cultura pop e, ao mesmo tempo, consegue ter uma história emocionante.

TL;DR
HM2 is very different from its predecessor, some changes make it better but some are also a bit detrimental. Level editor provides a huge amount of replayability and the story gets even more crazy. Play HM1 immediately before this game.
FULL, PROBABLY IN-DEPTH REVIEW:
Oh, Hotline Miami 2.
It's a game that got a bit more mixed reviews than the first game did, and for a number of reasons that make sense. But what do I think? Well, gather around, kids, it's time for a wall of text.
Story:
But anyway, Hotline Miami 2 serves as a prequel, sidequel, AND a sequel to the first game, having chapters in 1985, 1989, 1990, and 1991. The chapters aren't chronological though, but people pieced it together and there's videos on YouTube discussing it. This did wonders for the development of characters returning from HM1, though. I'd strongly advise playing the first game to have a good idea of most of what's going on in HM2.
The first things you'll probably notice are that HM2 has much more, better gore, the soundtrack is completely different (almost all of the artists who had songs in HM1 have songs in HM2 though), there are a ♥♥♥♥ ton of new characters, be them playable (12 new playable characters. T W E L V E.) or not.
Remember Richard the rooster head man from the first game? He's back and warns (very cryptically, might I add) of the ending. And by the way, the ending is bleak as all hell. It's like Dennaton didn't want the plot (which could've gone anywhere) to move forward. I think the main reason they didn't want to is because they didn't want Hotline Miami games pumped out every year or two like FNAF is, but then they dropped the level editor, which basically hands the direction of the story to the fans, which spawned the End Times campaigns, or to just make meme and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ levels, like the Jackt campaigns.
Weapons:
Just about every weapon from HM1 is back, with a few getting some tweaks, and a few additions. The beer can and bottle are gone, though, and the MP5 is only usable with the Mark mask or the Son's Bloodline skill. There's an unsilenced 9mm pistol now that isn't used by Jacket just for him to kill his last Russian. There's an AK rifle, the silenced pistol always kills in one hit, the drill is only usable in the level editor by Jacket with the Carl mask, you can get a katana as the Son, and the list continues.
Scoring:
Scoring in HM2 is a lot different from the first game. Knocking people down with your fists, doors, or throwing a weapon at them doesn't give points, the point awards from kills with weapons are different (400 with the flamethrower, 500 with the nail gun, 600 with any other gun, 800 with melees, 1000 with executions or unloading guns as Evan), and combos will give you points in the scoring screen like Mobility, Flexibility, and Boldness do instead of just after the combo window ends.
Characters:
The new playable characters are the five Fans (Corey, Tony, Alex and Ash, and Mark), Detective Manny Pardo, Jake (you can get his mask in HM1), Beard (the convenience store owner who gave Jacket free stuff in HM1), Evan Wright, Richter (the rat mask guy who Jacket actually didn't kill in HM1), the Son of the Russian mob boss in 1989, the Son's henchman, and Swedish singer H.M. Hammarin (only in the level editor). Their stories are pretty weird, and all of them meet a fate, be it for better or for worse. Find out for yourself. Hammarin isn't in the canon story at all so you can do whatever you want with him in the editor. Jacket and Biker are also playable in the level editor, but a lot of Jacket's masks have been changed because of the way the editor works. Biker is just as he was in HM1 though.
Soundtrack:
The soundtrack has a lot more variety to it. Sun Araw's music is completely gone, and the menu theme was done by the Green Kingdom. Combining the menu theme and the background of Hard Mode (more on that later) will make you wish this series got a third entry, though, so don't stare at it for too long. M|O|O|N, Scattle, El Huervo, Perturbator, and Jasper Byrne return with all new tracks, Carpenter Brut brings two new amazing tracks (three if you count the edited Escape from Midwich Valley in the Dial Tone trailer), Magic Sword, Life Companions, Dubmood, Prey Growl, Light Club, LipPi Sound..the list continues. I prefer HM2's soundtrack overall but I do miss Knock Knock and Paris from HM1.
Hard Mode:
After finishing the game, you unlock Hard Mode. You can replay the game, but the levels are mirrored, guns have half ammo on pickup (this also applies when you throw a gun and pick it back up, so beware), enemies have better reflexes but can be baited easier, and you can't lock-on to targets anymore. It's a hell of a lot harder, but it makes finishing levels even more satisfying. Since you unlocked all of the masks for the Fans and Jake, the Son's skills, and Beard's weapons, you can bring all of those into Hard Mode. Want to use Alex and Ash on Down Under, the sniper rifle on Stronghold, or Dallas on Hard News? Go ahead.
END:
In conclusion, Hotline Miami 2 is both different and similar to the first game. Its tone changes completely, as can be seen with its menu backgrounds and menu theme, it develops some characters from the first game while adding a lot of new ones, it offers new weapons to go on killing sprees with, and it gives you some new music to jam out to while, again, going on a killing spree. However, the game plays almost identically to its predecessor even with the new features some characters get, like Pardo's ability to execute with guns, and Evan's fighting style (non-lethal, melee only but you can still kill people if you R E A L L Y).
I love this game. $15 might be a bit much but when it's on sale, it's cheap as all hell. You can get a bundle of this and the first game for $5 when there's a big sale. If you get the special edition, you'll unlock Jacket as a playable character in Payday 2. Not a bad idea.
You can't go wrong with this game at all. Definitely a recommendation for any Steam user.

Game is very, very similar to Banished, but being early access, not nearly as polished. For me there were many issues. Game isn't all that stable. Put it back in the oven, its clearly not done.
Tooltips could be more informative, and the grading/leveling terrain system seems flawed to me. After I flattened terrain to build on it, it grided as all red, meaning i couldn't build anything on my newly flattened terrain. All the maps have same small level are to get a few minor buildings started, then you are extremely limited on placement due to the near perfectly flat requirement for most buildings. Forestry lodge will destroy all the surrounding forrest in no time with only 1 worker, with both plant and cut selected. You have to micromanage population depending on season to keep them working. At max speed(x10) its still pretty slow pacing.  Entire villages will freeze or starve very quickly, disasters are random as they should be, but also severe.  Since its not complete, there are no mods. Mods added alot of depth to banished. The build order is a little more deep than banished, for example you need charcoal to make ore into iron, then you can make tools. This is a 3 building progression to make something you will need fairly early. I can't overstate how much like Banished it is. At the very least Shining rock should be flattered if imitation is the sincerest form of flattery.
The game could be really good for what it is, if it were finished. For now I would suggest you hold off until its more developed. If I could i would get refund and put the game on my follow list. I will check back in this time next year and maybe it will feel more like a finished project. I'd give 4.5 of 10 at the moment.

Not so much a game as an experimental, observational lab where you can conduct various experiments with bugs and fungus and note how they all respond to the environment and each other. Minor tweaking is the order of the day. You subtly change the environment by introducing new lifeforms and controlling the weather. Then you sit back and observe. A meditative experience, perhaps.
Definitely not a game for everyone, given that it's rather slow, doesn't contain a lot of instructions or feedback, nor have any particular goals to work towards beyond those that you define for yourself, but I'm quite enjoying it so far and would recommend it if you're looking for a slow paced game that's something out of the ordinary.

I originally played this game on Itch.io and really loved it. The pixel art is lovely and the music is soothing :)
There aren't any tutorials or instructions, although there are journal entries with specific information on each fungus/insect that are unlocked after a species survives for a long enough time. This means that the player will need to observe the behaviours of the insects and fungi in order to determine how to properly care for them. Some are herbivores, some carnivores - some fungi even eat bugs.
Balancing the ecosystem is both challenging and rewarding. A species can easily die off if they over-consume their food source, for example. Some insects are bad at climbing terrain and may get stuck in an area with no food.
The player is given Intervention points which replenish over time, and allow them to add insects or fungi, change the weather, or alter the terrain. Choosing a random insect, fungi, or weather effect to add is significantly less expensive than choosing something specific, but of course the player receives less control over what will be added to the ecosystem when it is randomized.
Insects can be picked up and moved by the player, allowing them the option to manually balance the ecosystem. Fungi, however, cannot be moved.
Earthtongue can be addictive to play, but also fun to just leave running while I do other things. It's exciting to come back and see what has grown, which populations have survived, or which species have gone completely extinct ;)

Earthtongue is a fungal ecosystem simulator.
I bet you've never heard of that before. Well... unless you were a mycologist.
Earthtongue is unique in that it's less of a game and more of a simulator with limited interactions. It still has some minor goals (unlocking journal entries) but everything is largely freeform and open-ended for how you decide on what you want to do with your little fungus world. A fully diverse ecosystem is a thing of beauty and playing Earthtongue will teach you to appreciate the balance such an system requires. It'll show you just how fragile the ecosystem around you -- just like on this simulated planet -- really can be.
While its a great little simulator, and I can easily recommend Earthtongue, I wouldn't recommend it to everyone. Its for people who liked games similar to Mountain or watching Breve 3D Evolution simulations. Earthtongue is for people who like watching aquariums full of fish, or ant farms. People who want more interaction with their simulation games -- such as those who play Dwarf Fortress, or SimCity -- probably won't enjoy this nearly as much.

I never enjoyed any Horde-mode Left 4 Dead games, nor their rip offs, but this... this is something different and the realization why I like this game so much came with time.
Despite the title in question being developed by a very small studio, you can see they deliver standards of AAA industry in terms of design, craft, gameplay... Does that mean the game has no issue? Of course not, the bugs are still there, the netcode is still being worked on, BUT here's where Fat Shark differs from most AAA Industry. They listen. Whereas fixing their game, addressing jarring issues and just patching it all up would be a work long overdue and abandoned (just look at Assassins Creed or recent Batman game) those guys support their product and player base. Some weapons or mechanics were overpowered whereas others underpowered? We've recently seen a rebalance patch, fixing a lot of stuff! The Engine runs smoother, bugs are being gradually eliminated... people found the progression too grindy? The devs offered two solutions to the problem, first with forge and shrine, now with contracts and missions.
The new content patches are gradually being produced, while the core game is being improved and fixed to match expectations of the playerbase, while taking the criticism like grown men and improving their game.
And perhaps the most important is: the game just works. You can make a horde-mode out of everything, but where Left 4 Dead had to twist the idea of Zombies to make them more viable and exciting, Vermintide goes for obvious staple race of the Warhammer universe, which just FITS the premise perfectly, including all the special rats and challenges!
Where the game shines for me however, are the combinations of weapons and their traits. You don't know Vermintide untill you discover how a great-hammer, known for delivering devastating blows to just one or two targets in a sweap, can become a devastating weapon when matched with a trait, allowing it to instantly kill any target it hits in a sweaping-arch before, not only the ones damaged by the core model. Suddenly, you can transform a crowd control weapon into one of mass destruction. Double that with a trait which boosts the attack speed and watch the hefty soldier turn into tasman devil wielding a mace-of-death.
Some traits allow you to regain health, other stagger the enemies, causing them to take an increased damage, some allow you to gather reloads for your ranged weapons with each kill delivered, whereas others are more tanky. Those combinations are plenty and finding your build of choice, finding this perfect team synergy of talents, playstyles among the characters and their loadouts, is what makes this game so engaging. I'm having multiple weapon sets, just to test and fiddle with what suits my tastes best, some go well with special trinkets, others are reliant on my companions, but that very fact causes the gameplay in Vermintide to remain solid despite me investing so much time into it.
As for Warhammer? It's one of most atmospheric games a fan of the franchise could desire, getting you to the ground level of a unique character in this universe, and speaking of characters they are so delightfully spiteful bunch of misfits, who aren't your usual heroes. Far from it! They got themselves in a pickle, and got to work out some way of surviving the Skaven blight at hand. They are ugly, battered bunch of individuals who in any story could be just as well anti-heroes of the world, well maybe with exception of Sgt. Kruber, who seems genuinely good fellow. Their banter is sometimes hilarious, sometimes delightfully sarcastic and they make sure to throw in some snippets about the state of the world...
On the negative side... well, I wish there was more content. I'm saying that having just played through the new DLC expansion, after a huge patch, but still... this game needs more content. Perhaps additional characters. I know however that for a small studio like Fat Shark it's not an easy task, so I am willing to wait patiently and support this game as long as I can, since the very inception I see the game get better, improve, get more stuff to play with, meaning the devs are there, listening to us! Show them some love and aid in the creation of Vermintide.
PS. God I wish this game get's a mod support some day down the line. It would be so awesome to see custom maps, or even some alternative mode where we get to explore more of Ubbersreik.

2011 came and things were looking okay for the game, content was still coming but behind the scenes, the cryptic developers and atari were having issues, some of it was serious money issues. a new investor was found that wanted the game engine which cryptic devs had built, in a previous version it was used to power city of heroes that recently sank without a trace. the version 2 engine which champions online and star trek online runs from was of interest, cryptic were bought out in full from atari by perfect world entertainment, and the game developed on, to my way of thinking i thought it was a bad idea when it went f2p or free to play, but after the rest of the year came in a number of important changes were made to the game that effects everything these days, duty officers and one such example, more content. The old stf's were broken in half, a dark day indeed.
2012 rolled on and even more stuff had happened, more content and towards the end of 2012 there was efforts made towards the romulans. to be honest 2012 was the most unspectacular of all the years. Klingons got noticed at last and received a major upgrade to be on par with the federation.
2013 produced a 3rd faction to the game, the romulan republic, a splinter faction of the old star empire which was mired in it's own problems. and then the worst design choice in the games history was the dyson-voth season, i mean dinosaurs with freaking lasers on their heads! seriously?! The lead dev never once apologized for that choice either. So 2013 went out on fireworks.
2014 has produced some minor content but there is a crafting update on the table which is received negatively so far because exploration content will be cut as dead weight as an addition to apparently improving the game quality, and an expansion into the delta quadrant later on in the year. so 2014 looks to be just as explosive as 2013.
The game forum is always fun to be in, however the devs pay little attention beyond their designated zone, only one dev frequents the forum and its general topics on sto that i know of. Beyond that sto had picked up when pwe came mostly because of one nicknamed "branflakes" who really picked sto up off the floor and turned it into something really respectable. But recently he was promoted and then left the pwe group to focus on his own matters, ever since the game quality has dropped like a stone in deep water.
The overall impression from the people in charge is a negative one, as stated before it was good, now its just no one wants to know from pwe.
As far as the game goes thats a strange one, because of how limited the game engine is that sto runs from the devs can only do so much with what they got and because the engine is 4 years behind the times the graphical quality is not on the same level as other mmorpg's. the music is fine listening to it the first few times but then you ignore it and ask for more, there are some network issues that sometimes prop up, and sometimes the game server is not entirely bullet proof reliable. I mean there are lots of things with the game itself. The most recent design choice to sto was more grind based content, recent gotten more reputation based grind gated content that gives powerful kit pieces and weapons, both ground and space for example.
If you plan to play this game, please realize there is more to it then a simple surface read. If you read around on the game, you will find out that there is a lot of problems with this game and frankly i would not recommend it to anyone else. its in such a poor state as it is and still doing a downward spiral.

Why am I recommending this game then?  Well, there's two reasons. First is that it's a pretty fun Bejewelled clone with an interesting twist. Before each game of Bejewelled, you can choose up to 6 items to equip.  You can then spend mana to use their effects, which are extremely varied.  Afterwards, you can level up your character to increase his/her multipliers, 4-5 match bonuses, and just straight increased power.  This adds quite a bit of strategy to the game, when it clearly didn't need any to sell.  You can set up some pretty crazy combos with your loadout, if you plan correctly. Eventually, you actually will need to, because the difficulty does ramp up and if you don't pay attention, you'll eventually start getting rocked.
Second, the writing is exactly the level that it needs to be.  It doesn't take itself seriously at all; it's just self-aware enough to get some decent laughs going.  Take Kyu to the Ice Rink, you'll see what I mean.
Everything else in the game, from the music (except for awesome Ice Rink song), to the voices, to the... art is not bad at all.  Better than it has any right being, anyway.  It feels like the developers care quite a bit about their product.
So yeah, it's a mildly enjoyable game... Not really worth 10 dollars though.  At the end of the day, you can just play Bejewelled on one screen and browse porn on the other and get an extremely similar experience. I feel like they're charging double because of the "plot."  Wait for a sale to at least 6 dollars, then it's a good time even if you leave it censored.

This is micromanagement on another level.  I'm not talking about taking control of an individual sim, which is little more than a gimmick and doesn't really fit nor belong in the game.
If you like micromanagement, then this game might be for you.  For me, it's a bit much.  There are some things that just should be automated.  For instance, if you don't designate a sim as a farmer, he/she should do the next job that needs doing without me being required to designate that job to him.  Specifying specific jobs for a certain number of sims should be done when you want to ensure priority of work, not that the work will never get done.
In this game, the population is your true enemy.  There isn't a way to stop or slow down your birth rate, which causes the majority of the issues.  For instance, the larger house you build, the more efficient your sims are at just about everything, right down the chance of birth, which again, is your enemy.  To make this issue even more annoying, if you upgrade a house to fit more sims, that house is not usable by your sims, so they are now homeless until the construction is complete or there is free space in another house ... except that due to the rapid birth rate is not likely to happen unless you just finished another house build ... which is an issue because of the rapid birth rate and explosion of your population.  If they are left homeless for too long, they will die, meaning you lose productive members of your populace but still have babies and children to feed (but are not yet productive) which just leads to a major case of colony colapse disorder.  In the end, I feel this is a balance issue and hope they adjust this in some way.
It's really not that bad of a game, just be prepared for a level of micromanagement that you're not accustomed to in a top down city building sim.

Earthtongue is a great simulation game about gently guiding the ecosystem of a mysterious planet. You take the role of an observer, watching fungi and insects live and die. Occasionally you can intervene and bring in a new species of fungus or bug, changing the ecosystem. The art is very cute and minimalistic though still very colourful.
Earthtongue isn't your average game, and it does ask that you carefully balance some complex systems, but that's a fine thing. You're rewarded with a thriving world and intriguing research journals along the way.
The game was also made by one man, which is very impressive.
Update: This game is still good. Please play it.

Earthtongue is BASICALLY a terrarium simulator but it's so much more than that!  With the journal entries adding a deeper narrative and user-driven choices it's hard not to recommend it.
There's a very steep learning curve and that can be a major turn-off for a lot of people, but for gamers in this day and age I think it's very refreshing when a game doesn't hold your hand and tell you how to do everything off the bat.  Experimentation is key!  There's not much in the way of permanent consequences as you can simply start a new world if your current one is off to a shaky start.
GIVE EARTHTONGUE A TRY!  U GON LIKE IT!!!!

For First Impressions and Gameplay Footage:
+:
-Complex rule sets that if you can get to understand and exploit, may lead to a very circle of life kind of simulator.
-Components that work off of each other to get the ecosystem going.
-Experimentation section can work for those who don't want to be handed things.
-:
-Lack of tooltips and information to start the game really hampers the experience, especially when unlocks are tied to keeping the organisms alive....which may only happen if you get lucky considering the rules. Can be infurating.
-Too little detail in interventions as you basically experiment (wasting resources) to see what they do at first.
-Letting the game play out without your intervention seemingly has only a little bit difference then you playing with it: which makes you wonder why you are playing. This could lessen over time, but to stay around, you're going to want more then what the game gives you.
-Lack of tutorial and letting journal entries attempt to guide you doesn't do the job in terms of a tutorial. Wants you to experiment, you need to slightly nudge in the right direction.
-Would have like to have seen an evolution mechanism of some sort.
-Sound can get to you after a while.
While I appreciate the effort from the one man team on a game that has obvious complexity to it in a simulator nature, the fact is that I had major problems enjoying the game due to the lack of end user feedback or tools to truly understand what is happening in the game's environment. You'll sit there either touching or not touching the environment, and noticing that there's not a lot you can do to really create your own world seemingly, you're only slightly infleuncing what's going on. There's a lot of complex rules seemingly and someone who's willing to experiment with the game may have a lot of fun of it. But the lack of seemingly true tools to test things out really Killed the game in the end for me.

I never enjoyed any Horde-mode Left 4 Dead games, nor their rip offs, but this... this is something different and the realization why I like this game so much came with time.
Despite the title in question being developed by a very small studio, you can see they deliver standards of AAA industry in terms of design, craft, gameplay... Does that mean the game has no issue? Of course not, the bugs are still there, the netcode is still being worked on, BUT here's where Fat Shark differs from most AAA Industry. They listen. Whereas fixing their game, addressing jarring issues and just patching it all up would be a work long overdue and abandoned (just look at Assassins Creed or recent Batman game) those guys support their product and player base. Some weapons or mechanics were overpowered whereas others underpowered? We've recently seen a rebalance patch, fixing a lot of stuff! The Engine runs smoother, bugs are being gradually eliminated... people found the progression too grindy? The devs offered two solutions to the problem, first with forge and shrine, now with contracts and missions.
The new content patches are gradually being produced, while the core game is being improved and fixed to match expectations of the playerbase, while taking the criticism like grown men and improving their game.
And perhaps the most important is: the game just works. You can make a horde-mode out of everything, but where Left 4 Dead had to twist the idea of Zombies to make them more viable and exciting, Vermintide goes for obvious staple race of the Warhammer universe, which just FITS the premise perfectly, including all the special rats and challenges!
Where the game shines for me however, are the combinations of weapons and their traits. You don't know Vermintide untill you discover how a great-hammer, known for delivering devastating blows to just one or two targets in a sweap, can become a devastating weapon when matched with a trait, allowing it to instantly kill any target it hits in a sweaping-arch before, not only the ones damaged by the core model. Suddenly, you can transform a crowd control weapon into one of mass destruction. Double that with a trait which boosts the attack speed and watch the hefty soldier turn into tasman devil wielding a mace-of-death.
Some traits allow you to regain health, other stagger the enemies, causing them to take an increased damage, some allow you to gather reloads for your ranged weapons with each kill delivered, whereas others are more tanky. Those combinations are plenty and finding your build of choice, finding this perfect team synergy of talents, playstyles among the characters and their loadouts, is what makes this game so engaging. I'm having multiple weapon sets, just to test and fiddle with what suits my tastes best, some go well with special trinkets, others are reliant on my companions, but that very fact causes the gameplay in Vermintide to remain solid despite me investing so much time into it.
As for Warhammer? It's one of most atmospheric games a fan of the franchise could desire, getting you to the ground level of a unique character in this universe, and speaking of characters they are so delightfully spiteful bunch of misfits, who aren't your usual heroes. Far from it! They got themselves in a pickle, and got to work out some way of surviving the Skaven blight at hand. They are ugly, battered bunch of individuals who in any story could be just as well anti-heroes of the world, well maybe with exception of Sgt. Kruber, who seems genuinely good fellow. Their banter is sometimes hilarious, sometimes delightfully sarcastic and they make sure to throw in some snippets about the state of the world...
On the negative side... well, I wish there was more content. I'm saying that having just played through the new DLC expansion, after a huge patch, but still... this game needs more content. Perhaps additional characters. I know however that for a small studio like Fat Shark it's not an easy task, so I am willing to wait patiently and support this game as long as I can, since the very inception I see the game get better, improve, get more stuff to play with, meaning the devs are there, listening to us! Show them some love and aid in the creation of Vermintide.
PS. God I wish this game get's a mod support some day down the line. It would be so awesome to see custom maps, or even some alternative mode where we get to explore more of Ubbersreik.

No one was more excited to see this game come back to life than me.
Back when Metal Assault was being hosted by Aeria Games, I had a really crappy laptop from 1999 and it was the only game that was playable.
I played the crap out of Metal Assault. While I would not have considered myself a great player, I knew the game like the back of my hand. Unfortunately, when the servers got shut down, there was no other way to play the game unless going through a weird process to play it on an Asian server.
When I saw this game on the front page of Steam, I immediately told all of my friends about it and downloaded it.
For the first few hours, it was like a parent finding their child who had been lost for 5 years. After the nostalgia wore off, I had no more interest in playing the game.
The game has very limited graphics options (no 16:9 aspect ratio), you constantly have people with pings in the 200's, and overall, the game has not aged well.
For the newcomer, it is fairly hard to get into a server that doesn't have expert level people. Most of these people have bought weapons that are seriously broken (I'm talking flamethrowers that shoot through walls), and it is hard for anyone new to have legitimate fun. The PvP maps for TDM are only limited to 3 (I think), and are missing a lot of maps from years ago.
The pay-to-win issue was prevalent in the original game, though.
As for the Co-Op missions, I don't remember anything that was changed about them, especially the community. You better hope people don't start typing in the chat, "KICK!"
I really wanted to like this game again, but unfortunately it's not what I remembered it to be. For those who were fans of the original game, maybe you will have a better experience than me.

Well, It had to happen sooner or later and after the Fiasco that was Resident Evil Six Leon Kenedy has finally snapped.  Time has not been good to our Leon, unable to sustain his Clean Cut "All American Hero" image Leon, now in his Fifties and married with a young Daughter, has Turned In his Badge  with the Raccoon City P.D.   He is now a Gruff, Cynical "Gutter Detective" working in the district of Bedlam and Squallor, Beacon Town, Krimson City.  Leon has also changed his name to Sebastion (in honor of his fallen friend no doubt), He has Quit Bleaching his Hair and  has been hitting the Jack Daniels Hard for Years......OK so it's not exactly Cannon, but our Protagonist in this game looks identical and has the same Voice Actor so it's an entiely Plausable Hypothasis.
The Good -  In Many ways The Evil WIthin has delivered on it's Promises in that Strategy and Atmosfear (sic)  is much more important than action.  There is a very real sense of Danger that does not rely entirely on Jump Scares, on the contrary you will recognise many of your favorite Horror Tropes here.  The Evil Within is best described as a Melting Pot of all that you have been missing from "Real" Horror Games, you will see parts from Amnesia, you will See Parts from resident Evil (Before it went Full On Rambo), you will see Parts from Outlast, you will see parts from Alone in The Dark, you will even see the "Sneak Attack" from the reboot of TUROK which is used to exellent effect here I might add.   And Yes, you will see a measured amount of Combat as the Game Progresses.  Nothing is given to you easily here.  You will have to search and scrounge for every last bullet and every last upgrade and you will have to make every bullet count.  The Story is anyones guess but I'v seen enough to conclude that they are going for an Inception / Matrix - It's not really Happening - Virtual Reality type Plot here.  I have still to complete the DLC so I will Hang fire on that for now.  And OOOHHHH The Dialogue Oh Ho Ho ho it's BAAAAD, it goes way beyond "Jill Sandwitch" grade Bad all the way to Full On Scooby Doo grade Bad.  Clearly this is deliberate self parody and I would expect no less.
The Bad - Ironically the game's Construction is also it's weak point.  Yes there is Nostalgia Value and Yes it feels as though our wishes have been answered, but, in it's desire to please the fans by being a Portmanteau of all our "Memory Making" Horror Gaming Moments it has no identity of it's own.  I cannot imagine there will ever be an Evil Within Part 2 or Part 3, this is at best a stand alone game that is makng revinue on the dissapointment of Horror Gaming fans but it could not stand on it's own merits.
Secondly - (and this Drives me Nuts with modern games) Making it Damn Near Impossible to Play DOES NOT EQUAL ENTERTAINMENT!   Yep things are good for the first half and then it's Goodbye Scary Game and HELLOOOOO  QTE!   Thats QTE's and Instant Deaths........Lot's and lots and lots of them.  In it's attempt to recreate the survival element the Game often puts the player in No Win Situatons where progress can only be made by dying many, many,many, many, many, many, many, many, many, many, many, many, many, many, many, many Times. Instant Death after Instant Death after Instant Death after Instant Death after Instant Death after Instant Death after Instant Death after Instant Death after Instant Death......it just goes on and on and on.  The Thrill of Survival gives way to Boredom and Tedium very quickly after the Half way Point and the final Stage is completely ruined by being almost exclusivly QTE.  RE6 has got Nothing on this for the sheer amount of instant death situations and QTE here.  I won't give the ending away but I found it to be a complete mess of Instant Kills and QTE's that were Visually Incomprehensable and I was glad when it was all over.  Such a shame that This Game left me with such a bad taste in my proverbial mouth.
Regretabbly The Evil Within is also PLAGUED with Technical Issues that have never been resolved. The optimisation is, well, not very good.  Even with the latest and best components overclecked to the max The Evil Within proves to often be a Stuttery, Glitchy mess.  Even with the settings at medium to low there is a Significant Reduction in Frame Rate and animation that seams entirely inexplicable.
Equally the Controle System is also plagued with issues, particularly in the combat sections, the controles, whether Keyboard or Joystick, are often a Glitchy, Buggy and Unresponsive mess.  This seems to have been a problem from the Get Go and I do hope they release a patch to deal with it because it could so easily be taken care of with a little tweaking.
I give it a Thumbs up because of the Enjoyable First Half and I'm hoping that the DLC will improve my opinion of the Second half somewhat.
