Most people I know think I am talking about the adventure game "Syberia" when I talk about Cyberia. This one is much older and is a real retro game. When I first got this game back in 1995 I wasn´t really into PC games. At that time the only games I played were DOOM and a motorcycle game called "Cyclemania" aaand well Rebel Assault!
Then I read an article about Cyberia a new Sci-Fi action adventure with amazing graphics action sequences like Rebel Assault and adventure gaming like Creature Shock. Playing the Demo get me hooked because it was just awesome at that time.  This is a real blast from the past I would say.
The Steam version of the game runs pretty good and the DosBox is properly configured. To write a review is a bit hard because the game reminds me of my childhood and people who never played this game before may have a different opinion about it.
This game is not about graphics it´s the story and Cyberia tells a cool one. To keep things short. You are a criminal but you have a chance to run free if you do a job for the FWA - the Free World Alliance. Mission objective is to enter a research complex codenamed "Cyberia" and find a weapon. Sounds pretty easy but somehow most people you meet on your way want to see you in a body bag...
When arriving near the complex you are told that something isn´t right within the Cyberia complex something about an infection! And this part of the game is where the♥♥♥♥♥♥really hits the fan. I died thousand of times because Cyberia complex is heavily secured with traps, code panels that electrocute you, many guards who aim and shoot as fast as robots (There is a room with 4 guards in it and this room really sucks and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off!) and an action sequence that is nearly impossible if you do not know the "special key"  that fires a shockwave to kill all enemies on screen.
But the camera angles are so damn cool! The sound is amazing it reminds me of DOOM3 this kind of sound is used here. This is what get me hooked! It is like no other game back in the day was.
So if you like retro games that offer

- rail shooting
- a research complex with circle like corridors.
- lots and lots of traps
- a story about an infection because of a "gone wrong experiment"
- a slimy contaminated sealed off area with slimy enemies called "Nanites"
- a little decontamination robot called Charlie!
- a Rebel Assault like final action sequence
Then go ahead and buy this game immediately you won´t regret it. I am glad I got it back in the day as a boxed version but even if I didn´t have this game I would give it a try because it is a fair price for a game that takes several hours to complete if you haven´t played it before.

Rusty Lake Hotel is an eerie Victorian fever dream that asks "What if Hannible Lecter was a character in the Wind in the Willows?"
This game seems to draw from many great cultural influences. It is Lewis Carroll's disturbed children's book characters meets David Lynch's sense of the mundane transformed to horror. In Alice in Wonderland the Walrus and the Carpenter trick the Oysters and eat them. In the Agatha Christie mystery novel/film 'And Then There Were None' a group are lured to an island and picked off one-by-one in bizarre killings. In Rusty Lake Hotel these influences combine. It is cerainly worth the very small price of admission to see this morbidly fascinating story explored
Pros
+ Mysterious setting
+ Murder mystery seen from the opposite perspective
+ Surprising concept if done blind
+ Interesting Victorian-storybook-like art
+ Good soundtrack
+ Eerie atmosphere
+ Room escape puzzles are reasonably challenging, got stuck a while a couple times
+ Surprise drug trip
+ Creative murders
Cons
- Minimal animation
- Minimal voice acting
- Plays in an Adobe Flash window with problems with Steam overlay
- Adobe caused some freezing issues
- Requires replay for all the hidden ingredients if you didn't use a guide
- No cards
- No achievements

Wonderfully charming little point and click game! It has just the right amout of gruesome macabre action to fit with the atmosphere of the game! It is also very surreal which was very interesting to think about. The puzzles are a little brainracking which is rather enjoyable, however there is an occasional need for a walkthrough to get 100%.
Short, morbid, surreal. It's a fine little point-and-click Flash game with some glitches and several pretty weird puzzle solutions.

Tags: Adventure, Indie, Puzzle, Horror, Point & Click.
You are tasked with welcoming the newest guests to arrive at Rusty Lake Hotel. Every night you have to make a new dinner for the guests, collecting ingredients from their rooms. There are 6 guest rooms, each filled with puzzles that you have to solve in order to…
Each of these rooms has a different soundtrack and puzzles, pertaining to the residing guest. The ways of killing are brutally creative. Sometimes it takes 20 minutes or more to solve the puzzles. You have to complete the whole puzzle in order to leave the room.
The guests start disappearing one by one; accompanied by a most delicious meal (a very delicious meal). Each time, the remaining guests enjoy the food without having a clue where it came from and not bothering to ask about the missing guest(s)… Unnerving if you think about it.
+Immersive soundtrack, varying from room to room
+Simple but appealing graphics
+Price is right
+Fun puzzles that can be very challenging
+Brutally creative ways of killing
-Short: only around 2 hours
-Nothing else bad to say: I was really impressed by the quality of the game and its difficult puzzles
There is almost no reason why you shouldn’t buy this game, it’s only $2 and even cheaper on sale. Even with only a few hours of content, the surreal story and mind boggling puzzles make up for it. A must have for point & click fans.

The game is full of sinister scenes, a sinister and yet a deep, sad story and that 'strange presence' (wife?) that will keep haunting you throughout the constantly twisting and maddening corridors and rooms of the old mansion. You feel as if you're being constantly watched from some dark corner; never knowing what is behind that door or in the next room, this 'walking simulator' will keep even the most fearless of individuals at a total discomfort and unease. Its overall outlook is so horrifying that you won't be able to watch it approach you in a dark corridor. Of course, if your curious enough, then you can simply go and say a 'Hi' to it and have a look at its 'fine features' to suffice yourself.

Alone, you are a helpless bystander to the Skaven apocalypse - together, you just might survive.
And to top it all off, the loot system is brilliant.  Different types and grades of loot for the five individual character classes drastically change how each class plays.  Aquiring loot is done by diceroll, and only after the SUCCESS of a mission.  Which means that if you fail, you will not earn a chance to aquire loot.  And there are certain items inside the levels that you can collect that will essentially make the level incrementally harder, but also give a better chance of better loot.  Unwanted loot can be grinded down to upgrade or alter preferred loot.  It is in this particular system where the game really shines.  Because it gives tangible weight to the success of the mission.  You WANT to win so so can earn loot.  And you WANT to challenge yourself so that the loot has a chance of being better.  Couple this with a loot centric character modification system and a foundation of rocksolid gameplay, and you've got yourself a recipe for a game that is more addictive than...  Like... cheese.  God, I ♥♥♥♥ing love cheese.
A bustling online community means that you'll never have a shortage of players.  At least, that's what it seems like right now.  (12/23/2016)

This is a delightfully macabre point-and-click that should be a good way to kill a few hours. You can tell right from the introduction what you're going to be getting yourself into, but it's still rather delicious fun and a recipe for some brain teasing. The vast majority of the puzzles are self-contained in their own areas, so you don't have to worry about getting part A from room B after unlocking the door for room C with the key that you found in room D.
If I have any complaint it's that you essentially need a walkthrough to get everything because some of the requirements for 100% completion and even a few of the required solutions are bizarre and by no means obvious.
Still, it's worth a few hours of your time for some wonderfully dark humor and simple yet charming art direction.
Interesting story, eerie and charming soundtrack, great aesthetic, simple yet elegant art, moderately challenging puzzles, some replayablility.

The game is set on a isolated mansion-on-the-lake and is headed by Mr. Owl, a probably sadistic owl hell bent on having meals made out of the meat of his guests. His guests are each a different animal. We have Ms. Pheasant, Mr. Boar, Mrs. Pigeon, Mr. Deer, Mr. Rabbit – a fine meal indeed.
4.8/5
Full review:

I do recommend buying this game, even if it is only to support the developers who made the fantastic cube escape series (and provided it for free on various browser game sites). That being said and since others already wrote enough about the content (point and click, surreal setting, a bit gorey, setting at a lake with anthropomorphic creatures that run that hotel and have tasks for you, solve riddles to proceed), here are my points of critique regarding the gameplay.
First, the pros:
- the game is entertaining. If you like point and click games, especially those leaning to the dark and surreal side
- most* of the puzzles are logical and therefore, solvable by using your brain
- the music is fitting and atmospheric
- no pixel hunt
- if you played the cube escape series, THIS game is where all open questions seem to start to fit together. Expect some cameos.
- the game has some additional, optional puzzles that are a bit more difficult to solve (yay, extra challenges!)
- you will get a reward if you solve those as well (yay, rewards for going the extra mile!)
- for not even 2€, you get at least about 1 to 2 hours of entertainment, which is a good value!
Now the neutral things (aka: things I'd like to see improved in further versions that catched my eye but didn't bother me that much):
- the language needs some improvement to avoid involuntarily comical situations. The sentences spoken are very minimalistic (which is a good thing, since it fits the atmosphere nicely), but sometimes the grammar seems off or very simplified (I'm looking at you, evening initiating sequence)
- there is one point where you are reminded where you currently are (the lobby) via a UI notification that pops up, states that areas name and has to be clicked to close. I found this a tad annoying since the area is not disorientating at all and it felt tedious to always close the notification without any benefit.
Of course, that are only very minor issues. I did not find anything too negative about this game, except from maybe being a bit short.
Other features:
The graphics are simple, but beautiful and very well fitting to the cube escape series. The sounds were fitting and subtle as well and provided to the atmosphere. Still suffering from deer-man related flashbacks (would recommend playing the cube series alone for this! Go and get your dose of trauma today! It's free!), I expected to be startled more often. In comparison to the other games from this developers, I found the Rusty Lake one literally placid, harmless even. There was a bit of gore, but sparsely (it's up to you if that's a pro or con).
There was an * to the notion of "most riddles are solvable by brainpower". Some few are not. Regarding the games of this developer, "logical" has to be a term to be stretched a bit. First, let's say: the WAYS to obtain or interact with something are logical - what exactly you will get from this interaction, needs not be. For example, you might spot a puzzle, do what you think you are supposed to do and solve it without much strain, but what you get out of this might be leaving you thinking "wtf". This is one thing that I enjoy about these games. And in this sense, most are logical and solvable. There were only about two riddles that were not exactly solvable by deduction but more by "doing things randomly and having something happen" - and this is what I meant. You can solve them anyway,  just more in the "I wonder what happens if..."-way.
To sum up: if you like point and click and a bit of a dark twist, go and play it, you probably won't regret it. But don't expect to be busy more than 1 or 2 hours with that game. If you want to maximize your experience, go and play all of the cube escape series games first. This should take several hours and a few minor emotional scarrings. Then come back, buy that game and feel like you just got about 8 to 10 hours of gameplay for a bit short of 2€.

The reviews that say this is Banished with nicer graphics are pretty spot on. I was surprised to see the similarity even to the point that the UI and icons used are often very similar. Imitation is the sincerest form of flattery? If you liked Banished then you should give this a try.
The frame rate was all over the place. When I first loaded the game at fullscreen 1080p with high settings I was looking at 15 fps. I turned all the settings to low got 85 fps then turned them back up (trying to figure out what was causing the low fps) and was sitting at 35-45 fps. Turning the SSAO and Bloom off then back on again seemed to be connected to the jump in frame rate. I'm running a Core i7 with a GTX 760.
I found the terraforming to be more frustrating than interesting. Auto terraforming would speed up development and make the game play smoother - by that I mean flattening the ground under a building as part of the construction process. I found that if I flattened a patch of ground I seemly couldn't expand that patch if it was too small for what I wanted to build. Maybe I missed something.  Also showing a grid of where an object can be build over the entire visible area rather than just under the building would also ease building. Searching for a spot to build is like trying to find your phone in the dark... You can do it but its not fun.
Much like Banished the pace of the game is fairly slow at least at the early stages. You have very few workers and seemly lots of products to produce. I quickly ran out of wood and labors and had to wait a while to complete buildings so that I could advance the settlement. Again like Banished, much of the game play is seemly in micro managing the workers.
It's good that the developer released this as Early Access. It's good, playable, but could use some tweaks and polish.

Pros:

Cons:
It goes far too dark at night, but work still gets done, creatinga a lot of wasted time in a game that needs excessive micro-management.
Chickens are candy to the wildlife, even with more than adequate hunters. When they get eaten one by one over a short period of time, you have no alternative but to tear down the coop and build again.
There is no trade system, you can only advance by expeditions which may, or may not, succeed, but you never see them in action.
Terraforming is crap. Stretched scenery, ugly results and the risk of destroying navigation make it just plain stupid as a technique for construction.
I believe you tried to make Banished what you thought it should have been, but FV is missing the simple fun of just watching a balanced game play itself without the need of constant oversight.

If you want a finished game, this isn't it. However, if you liked Banished, enjoy testing, and providing feedback, then you might like Forrest Village's EA. I do. There's still a lot of work to do on the game, but the developers have been fixing bugs and adjusting/adding content per player feedback. Everyone here writes a review and makes it negative, due to the fact that "they can't level up enough" "it's completely pay to win" "it's too hard". These statements are absurd and make me sad about the gaming community, but let's get on to my main point, I just thought I'd give this game some defense. Anyway, my main point is, I lost interest, before I even reached level 5. The level requirments used to be much smaller, and given that this game is early access, this may change. But for now, I have to disagree with the dev's choice to limit your actions before you reach level 5. The one thing that kept me interested for as long as I was, was my friend, who brought me into the larger maps because he was a high enough level. When I decided to play the game without him, I was faced with absolute boredome. There are only 3 beginning maps, smaller than half the size of the larger maps, and you cannot play the larger maps until you are level 5. I'm a decent player, and I got about 200-300 xp each round I played. I can't give exact numbers, but I think starting from level 4 and on to level 5, you needed 18,000 xp? I may be completely wrong, but that seems to be how I remember it. Now I can agree with some of the other reviews to a certain degree, yes, it does take a while to level up, and these matches normally last half an hour, if not more. The amount of time required to make it to level 5 (if you don't have a friend pulling you into the larger maps) is more than a week (also given that you play 4 hours a day or more). Until this game changes, the career opportunities and the maps are too far out of reach for people playing alone. This is my only complaint, if you can get past this, this game is absolutely great.

My friend and I played this game through twice together and coming from both of us, this game is pretty darn good. I see a lot of people on here whinging about how nothing really happens in the game action-wise, but there's a reason this game shows up on the 'walking simulator' tab –
This may sound like a re-hash of what other people are saying about this game, but it's all true. I was actually more unnerved on my second play-through of the game than the first; so unnerved, in fact, that I had to mute the sound at one point and blast pop music so I could continue through to the end.
Layers of Fear is more of an immersive experience than a game where the goal is simply to outrun or hide from enemies. On our first run-through my friend and I breezed through the story with no regard for mementos or those little rat drawings that pop up occasionally, and we found that we took away so little from the game that we had to play it a second time to at least uncover more of the story. And if you
rush through the game, you come away with a very different impression than you would glean if you merely brushed the surface of the story –
. This is a game that invites you to savour it; to play it through over and over again to ensure that you've squeezed every last bit of information out of it to get to the true story behind the artist and his unfortunate family. And I'm not just saying this because of how devilishly hard it is to get those other two endings.
Also, the Furboy really really made my day. That achievement was so worth just staring at it for five straight minutes and nearly laughing my way to a hernia.

This game is awesome. I was kind of confused when I beat the game for the first time and got a normal ending. Not until then did I realize that there are actually three different endings. The drawings and documents in the game contain tons of secrets. In order to get the other two endings, these items are necessary. I finally got to understand what the protagonist was doing and why he was doing it. In this game, you will go through the painter's madness and explore the context of his wife's and daughter's deaths.
In conclusion, the only thing you need to keep in mind while playing this game is to EXPLORE. The game has a great story that awaits the players. If you don't read anything you find in the game, you will definitely be confused and very likely to dislike the game. IGN's rating on this game was 5.8, simply giving the comment "A paint-by-numbers horror game that can't capitalize on its concept." I strongly disagree with this statement and would like to condemn IGN for being so irresponsible by posting this bad review without collecting everything and playing through all three endings thoroughly.
If you like horror games and story-rich games. YOU SHOULD BUY IT.

Layers of Fear is a first person horror experience that relies heavily on creating a creepy atmosphere rather than resorting to cheap jump-scares. It's an approach that works well, complimented by the game's story revolving around a once-renowned painter's slow descent into insanity. Over the course of a playthrough, Layers of Fear will have the player exploring and navigating through a constantly changing Victorian-era mansion, encountering ghostly visions as well as haunting flashbacks that offer some insight to the events leading up to the artist's breaking point. The princial focus on art and the supernatural carries over to the game's level design as well, making for some abstract and often nightmare-ish environments whilst exploring the mansion. More often than not I would find myself feeling more uneasy with my surroundings more than anything else, this is thanks in part to the game's incredible soundtrack. While there's not much substance to the music past some white-keys piano playing for ambiance, there's a certain beauty to the music that goes hand in hand with the game's overall tortured artist motif. Layers of Fear is a great pickup for fans of the horror genre, while the game's ending can leave a bad taste in the mouths of some, rest assured that Layers of Fear paints a portrait worth going insane over.

I just picked up the PC version of The Evil Within and it is still a great game. I should let you know I have over 100+ hours in this game on the PS4 version, and got all the achievements in the game twice on separate accounts. I love this game.
The PC version seems to have more technical issues than the PS4 version, such as small graphical bugs and stuttering at times. The increased framerate at 60fps dramatically improves the game though and makes the game more smooth and responsive. The game looks similar to the PS4 version, and I recommend getting a graphics mod to have the game look its best.
Now into the gameplay. This is honestly one of the most satisfying games you can play. It's mainly a stealth game and you should conserve ammo whenever possible. The great thing about the game is that even though it's linear, each level is big enough to explore and you can find collectibles, extra ammo and gear, and green gel to aid you in surviving the nightmare. Green gel is basically the currency for a very thoughtful and well executed upgrade system. You can upgrade weapons, your crossbow bolts, how much ammo you can carry, and main character attributes like sprinting stamina and how much health you have. I could go into more detail, but my point is it is a very good and rewarding system. There is also a very neat system where you can burn bodies. Once you shoot a zombie, they won't stay dead. You either have to pop their heads off with a bullet, or stagger them and light them on fire otherwise they get back up and fight until the bitter end. There is also traps. It adds a lot more depth to the gameplay, as you can either use traps to lure zombies to death, or take them a apart and use them to craft very useful crossbow bolts. These arrows significantly help you in combat, as they serve many purposes. You can freeze, stun, burn, harpoon, and explode the zombies into bits. It's an addictive gameplay. The AI in the game is also top-notch. Difficult and unforgiving, they will actually work together to kill you. Honestly, the only flaw with the gameplay is sometimes Sebastian doesn't go where you want him to, or the camera angle is in a strange position, but it doesn't happen very often.
Gameplay 9.5/10
The story is actually good, but executed so poorly in the game with it's cringe worthy cutscenes and writing. I have never seen such boring, undeveloped characters in my life. Sebastian will keep saying, "What the hell is going on here?" "I must be losing it" to the point of comedy. If you watch youtube videos or read the wiki on the game, there is an intriguing story behind the mess that was shown in the game.
Story 7/10
The game isn't scary, but it sure as hell is creepy. The Evil Within has some of the creepiest and atmospheric environments in a horror game to date. There is an amazing use of lighting and sound that will give you a sense of insecurity. The way the story is told, you will be visiting many memorable locations and bosses that are top-notch. The enemies are also very well designed. You will encounter masked humans that look like the are ready to go out on Purge night, to squid-like enemies that turn can invisible, The threat is even greater on AKUMU difficulty, where you die in one hit from anything that touches you. There are more enemies, more traps, and less ammo.
Environment/enemies: 9.5/10
SHORT CONCLUSION:
I could go on talking about this game and make the review way longer and in depth. Despite the many flaws, the total experience is a masterpiece and my GOTY game of 2014. The games pacing is excellent, and the level diversity is great. That along with the smart AI and addictive gameplay loop and mechanics, it is definitely a game worth picking up, Even though the story was lacking and the writing and cutscenes were cringe-worthy, the excellent gameplay and level/sound design saved this game.
9/10

Rusty Lake Hotel probably won't last you more than two hours unless you make a mistake or two in the process of getting full completion, but it's also priced to reflect that. The game is essentially a series of 5 puzzle rooms similar to Escape the Room-type flash games (which is what this developer is mostly known for), and while it isn't amazingly complex it's still relatively fun, and the interesting concept of the game helps keep it going. The only problem I have with it is that the story just leads up to a To Be Continued message, making this the sort of game that I wouldn't recommend unless you're more interested in the puzzle solving than the story. It's hard to deny the fact that this is a game that probably would've been free on a flash site a few years ago, but at least it has the courtesy to only charge $2, unlike plenty of other indie games of the same length.

I've played both Banished and Forest Village. Also a big fan of Li:YO. I love the asset carryover from LiF. Very authentic midieval feel. My biggest town is about 35 people.
I have just gotten my first successful town in FV, and I"m really enjoying the game overall. Definitely worth it, but there are just a few gripes I have which could and should easily be taken care of with a patch/update.
1. Ran into a bug where flax harvested as grain. This meant I didn't get to make clothes for my villagers one year. It was not a good year. This is the only bug I've encountered in my weekend of play.
2. The day/night transition is awful. It's just foggy and you can't see♥♥♥♥♥♥ There are NO nightlights. Playing during night sucks because of this.
3. need some way to prevent townsfolk from using up materials I want to use in higher tier stuff. Charcoal, and some food items, for example. I need to be able to route my materials to where they need to go better.
4. Seems many things in game dont' make any sound. The soundtrack is alright but my village seems awfully quiet.
5. It rains too much. The thunder is too loud. I'd like to turn off weather effects.
6. There are very few options for settings. I am hoping this is just an early release thing.
7 the FONTS ARE TOO DAMN SMALL. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I'm old.
8. The terraforming controls seem a bit wonky when adjusting up and down. I like the terraforming being realistic (no, you can't build a hill without actually having the dirt to do it.)
Things I love:
1. Starvation is a REAL threat. Managing your people's jobs is a big deal. Having good tools and good clothes MATTERS in terms of productivity, happiness and health. Starvation is, however, just about the only threat besides old age. I think a couple people died of hypothermia one year and a tornado came near my town once ( I didn't see it, but the message popped).
2. There is enough building variety and reasons to build different things (people say you only need 1 food source, but you quickly realize that it's a bit more complicated than that if you want a town over 30 people).
3. Control carryover from banished = no need for tutorials for seasoned players. New players will probably have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ time trying to figure out how to get off the ground and not starve (I starved out probably 10 towns myself now)>
4. The ambience is great. The game is engrossing to me and I feel I got my money's worth. It's not a fancy game, but there's enough to keep you busy that feels necessary and not like some artificial roadblock in progression.

*Quick note - I see a lot of reviews on here with like 0.3 hours played or less. My teammate clocked in 146 hours and I'm over 50 so perhaps ignore the positive reviews that show the person installed it and ran the title screen over people like me that actually put some time in. Sadly the fact this game is even still listed on Steam reenforces the feeling that over the last 2 years Steam has gone from a solid platform for good games into an unchecked and uncontrolled shovelware factory for novice made indie garbage.
Funny a friend introduced me to this game maybe two years back because he was friends with one of the devs. Comically over time said unnamed dev grew tired of some of the BS going on with the leads decision making which becomes a large part of this review.
When I first played the game it was actually fun. There was a lot of potential despite being extremely rough. I was part of one of the first teams to play the game for cash as competitive eSports players, something I hadn't done in a long time. However despite the potential the net code alone made even simple practice with teammates brutal if not impossible.
We gave feed back, the team ignored it. Each release the game got worse and worse with a clear focus on skins, visuals and other garbage they planned to monetize rather than making the game work. Believe it or not the net code got worse as it became clear the team really had no idea what they were doing when it came to networking. So rather than fix the match making and network issues they changed the menus, added new sounds and other pointless crap that didn't matter because you rarely could join a game and when you did you'd probably get disconnected at some point anyhow.
There were so many problems and I wrote about them on my teams website and various other places for the devs to review but jump ahead it looks like they gave up much like the majority of the player base who they alienated during feed back sessions and the tournaments they put on.
All in all it's quite sad to have seen the potential and then to watch them flush it. More so it's incomprehensible they would charge you $208.96 even if the game was complete and rock solid. That's like three or four triple A games or a crappy beater car for an unfinished no name game!

I feel bad, but I am giving this game a mild "Not recommended" rating.  I feel bad because it is such an original concept and really is a good puzzle game... but it is so hard and very, very frustrating especially on the last 2-3 chapters.
In the game, you control an amobea / blob like creature.  You move by erasing part of yourself, which causes the remaining leftovers to grow in a somewhat random fashion.  Your creature can take on almost any shape, but getting how you want is not always so easy.  The goal of the game is to just reach the end of each chapter, of which there are 7.  Each level also ends with a boss, he being just another puzzle but where you need to somehow destroy him.  Things start out simple with you just needing to reach up to grab things and cross empty spaces.  By the end you will be pushing buttons, riding rockets, pushing balls and racing to make a bridge for them and many other complicated things.
This is all great but the levels are simply too long and many of the puzzles are too fiddly.  Since you grow in a somewhat random fashion, you can know what you want to do and still fail miserably at making your creature do it.  A few of the puzzles in particular will take the average player 10 to 20 attempts to complete them (you riding a rocket across a pool of acid for example).  If these difficult puzzles would have been reduced and the chapters been reduced in length, the game would have been fun and I would have recommended this.  Most players simply won't have the patience to get through to the end of the game, I almost gave up on it myself.  Those with lots of patience might want to try it out though if the concept looks intriguing, others should pass.

Mushroom 11 has a really unique central mechanic that is fun to play. I really liked the subtle storytelling that comes through in the background.

Weird and enjoyable physics-based puzzle game.  The challenge is essentially to get a blob of cells from point A to point B without direct control over its movement.  Instead, you have control over a cursor which can delete cells from the blob, which will cause the blob to randomly grow cells elsewhere, as long as it is in contact with a surface.  In the simplest case, you are killing cells on one side of the blob in order to force it to move the other way.
But it gets a lot more challenging than that, and a lot of the fun comes from inferring the rules that govern the re-growth of the blob, and then mastering those rules to overcome obstacles.  Sometimes, the obstacles require too much luck for my liking (one boss fight in particular was a huge pain), but in general, the game is not too difficult and checkpoints are frequent.  In fact, the difficulty balance is a real strong point.  The most difficult challenge lies in reaching some of the entirely optional collectibles peppered throughout the levels.  The best of them were satisfying to
reach AND they forced me to learn something that made me better at the game.  The worst of them, I gratefully skipped.

Mushroom 11 revolves around a unique mechanic that is best explained by just watching the trailer. I'll call it scrubbing. It's a really fun way to navigate around, and the game does a decent job at exploring what you can do with it. One complaint is that the later levels add mechanics that take away from scrubbing (rockets, specifically). Overall, it's a fun mechanic to use and master, so I'd recommend the game.

The Evil Within is not a terrible game and there are certainly good parts about it. It's well made, looks fantastic, has great sound, and some genuinely creepy atmosphere. However be warned that this is nowhere near a classic survival horror game. There are levels that invoke this yes but a good 2/3 of the game has you fighting or sneaking through various battle arenas instead of actually exploring environments.
Health and resources are indeed scarce but that aspect of the game seems at odds with how action and boss fight heavy the rest of it is. I genuinely enjoyed the weird safe room hub world and the upgrade system but it seems like you can easily screw yourself over investing in the wrong things. Hey cool there's a magnum in this game with its own upgrade path! Oh no I dumped my valuable points into it but there's maybe a dozen rounds of ammunition for it in the entire game. Sorry!
By far the worst part of Evil Within are the one-hit kills. They're cheap as hell and absolutely everywhere. I think maybe 40 of my 50 or so deaths were due to getting offed instantly due to a trap, special boss attack, or environmental puzzle. It absolutely sucks and drags the game way, way down.
Also if the model viewer is any indication you find maybe a third of the weapons in the game on your first playthrough. Why hide so much behind unlocks and new game plus for game this long and plodding?
Lastly I wanted to touch on the story: it's nonsense. Yes I've heard it makes more sense if you play the DLC but I'm sorry, no. There's no sense of place to this game because you're constantly teleported around chapter to chapter. Yes it's on purpose but it doesn't help ground anything that happens. This just happen for the sake of it and I could barely tell you what any of the characters did at the end of the game. Do not play this for plot.
If you like the idea of a game controlling like Resident Evil 4 but want something more action heavy then Evil Within is right up your alley. If you're looking for classic survival horror look elsewhere.

Difficulty in this game is ridiculous at times, especially on Nightmare (I don't even want to try Akumu) But even on Survival (Normal) you're going to have trouble on your first playthrough.
In short and no spoilers, You are a detective that gets a case about a hospital, you go inside and you are strangely transported into another "world". You go through the game hoping to find a way out, fighting undead, bosses, and someone watching you.
Third person shooter, you find ammo on the ground and off dead bodies, the higher the difficulty, the more scarce ammo is. (Also harder enemies obviously). The boss fights WILL aggravate you at times, but you eventually get past it. You might have to look up internet guides, I know I had to. You can craft crossbow ammo which you get from traps. The rest you can see for yourself.
As far as the horror elements go, yes they are definietly there. Very creepy game, however at times it loses those elements in some chapters but they always come back. If you're an experienced horror gamer, then it might come easy on you. There are definetly more horror games that will scare you even more. The DLCs however, are definietly nightmare fuel.
As far as bugs, I haven't experienced anything major. Some people say it's buggy, I say it's not. It could use better optimization I'll admit but don't judge the game's optimization off of the demo because people are saying that the demo has never been patched like the main game.
As one of my favorite games of all time, I say go ahead and buy it if you're a fan of horror games, if you're not, don't bother. But if you are, definietly pick it up and play it, amazing story, amazing combat, good characters, very hard game. (Please make a sequel <3 ) 10/10.

HuniePop starts up with a coloful screen showing the girls in the game, then takes you to a save file screen, where you can chose to be either a guy or a girl. Regardless of the choice, you can only date girls in the game. I honestly didn't have high expectations from a dating game, but right from the start there is plenty of humor in the interaction with the love fairy, the players guide to dating.
The girls come with a great variation in looks and personality, the only thing they all have in common, is being hungrier then starving wolves. In order to talk with them, you need to give them food and lots of it. Though they have a lot to say, and even after having reached the final stretch of the game, they sometimes say things I haven't heard before.
The dates evolve around a puzzle game, it is similar to bejeweled, but demands a lot more strategy. Checking what a date wants from you before the date is the key to success, as well as in the interaction, where it's good to refresh what you know before being put on the spot with a question. The strategy factor and the puzzle game is most the game, the girls are just a bonus. I'm sure this game could have been just as good with a different theme. Perhaps meeting fluffy animals and making friends with them? It wouldn't affect the puzzle factor at all.
Positive aspects of the game:
Every location has its own music.
The characters come with great variation.
A lot of comedy, this game isn't in any way serious.
The difficulty is balanced, and increases over time.
Negative aspects of the game:
The full screen mode glitched for me, though that could be a result of my screen resolution. Otherwise I don't have many bad things to say about the game. I should note that there is a strong chance someone on your friendslist have a thing or two to say about dating games. It is a game that comes with a douchbag stamp, but that is okay, the game hardly tries to make you think that seducing 12 girls makes you any better then that.
I recommend this game to anyone who likes strategy/puzzle games, but would prefer to look at sexy girls while playing them. To quote Kyu; "Come on! Seduce me with your sexy puzzle skills."

Okay, elephant in the room: This game has porn. Softcore porn but porn nonetheless. That said I don’t feel that takes away from the gameplay at all. I’ve seen comments where people act as if it’s less of a game and more of a guilty pleasure. Frankly I’d play it regardless.
The core gameplay is the classic match-three puzzle mechanic. You can drag your tokens anywhere along the X or Y axis to make matches and of course getting four, five or multiple tokens to line up gets you combos and a better score.
The tokens include:
Pink hearts: Passion - the higher this is the better your combo scores become
Teardrops: Sentiment - Sentiment points allow you to use date gifts to give yourself a strategy boost.
Gold Bells: Extra turns
Broken Hearts: Reduce your overall match progress
Each girl has a favored and least favorite token that will grant you a better score when you match them.
Red - Sexuality
Orange - Romance
Blue - Talent
Green - Flirtation
One of the nicest things I like is that you can set your character to either be male or female and the characters will respond in dialogue accordingly making the game just as accessible to bi/lesbian women or guys just wanting some yuri RPing. (Your character doesn’t actually have a physical presence in the game so just consider it a POV thing.)
In between matches you meet with the various girls, give them presents bought with money you earn from matches, talk to them to learn about them and answer their questions, sometimes quizzing you on their personal stats and sometimes general personality questions. Answering correctly earns you “Hunie” which allows you to upgrade your own stats for matches and in post game straight-up order favored presents for them. Giving a girl her favorite things unlocks “date gifts” you can use in matches to give yourself an advantage or unlocks new hairstyles/clothing for the girls.
As you progress with each girl she’ll send you photos, generally a safe pic, an ecchi pic and a dirty pic. The final pic you get when you actually score with her. In-game is just bare breasts and panty shots but you can buy the digital art collection from the official site
and it comes with uncensored versions of the final pics both with and without creampies/♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. (The version available on Stream is apparently censored BTW.)  It’s only $3.99 and I went ahead and got it as well partially to support the game and well, porn. My only complaint is that it doesn’t also have the topless versions of the girl’s sprites from the getting lucky matches. It also has profiles for eight of the twelve girls’ stats for quick reference if she asks you a question and you completely blank on the answer. The other four I suppose weren’t included as two are hidden characters and two are end-game spoilers.
The girls themselves are varied enough that no two are too similar and on a personal note there was only one that IRL I would have avoided socially and another that I just wouldn’t have gotten physically involved with as our personalities just wouldn’t mesh well. The other ten range all the way from friends with benefits to waifu material.
The dialogue is all fully-voiced, though you can turn them off if you want and the soundtrack is catchy instrumental stuff. I don’t think there was a single bad song on it. (You can also purchase the soundtrack from the site as well.)
All in all I’d highly recommend this game.

An effective blend of elements from both the match-three puzzle and dating simulator genres, combined with a unique flair and focus on style that results in a very memorable experience.
Everything in this game is well executed mechanically. The match-three puzzles are addictive in their precise implementation, perhaps the single best I have played in this genre. Menus feel responsive and are easy to navigate, the UI is clear and simple to understand.
All round excellent art direction, from the backgrounds to the character designs, to the colourful menus, the production values are akin to a high profile platform exclusive. The uncensored patch is recommended for the full version, but the censored art still holds its own.
Very memorable use of spoken dialogue, each character exuding personality and catch-phrases that make them instant classics. The sounds are high quality and satisfyingly produced. The music is excellent, at once catchy and memorable, and captures the up-beat mood perfectly.
If you enjoy match-three puzzle games, I highly recommend this game. If you enjoy dating simulators with memorable dialogue and characters, with memorable visuals and music, this game is a must-buy.

Rarely have I been so sure of the power and quality of a small indie game as quickly as I have with “Rusty Lake Hotel”. I’ve played less than an hour and a half so far, so there will likely be more to be said, and this may be uncommonly brief.
The premise of “Rusty Lake Hotel” is you are Mr. Owl, and you have invited 5 creature friends to your hotel for a visit, including a special meal each day. Not to give too much away, but each day there is one less guest to entertain. This is a humorous game, but which also contains some pretty graphic cartoony violence and gore.
During the day you explore the hotel, talk to the guests and employees, and look for objects needed later. This phase is generally quite brief, as it’s basically just a preamble to the nighttime puzzle work. Only at night are you able to visit the guests in their rooms, and that’s where the fun begins. Each guest’s room has a theme. Mr. Rabbit is a magician, and his room, and the puzzles to be solved, involve magic. Mr. Deer involves finding the ingredients to fix a drink, including puzzles involving volume (as well as others, all closely inter-related.) Ms. Pidgeon, who has asked you to run her bath, has puzzles involving electricity and math. Most of the puzzles are simple, and provide some small item to lead to a quite possibly bigger puzzle to be solved. But (so far at least), each room’s puzzles must be completely solved, and the meat needed for the next day’s “special meal” must be found, before each room can be exited. Some items for the meal are optional, but the more you find, the more stars you receive for the quality of the meal when served. Presumably, the number of stars unlocks some feature(s) later on.
And that’s something new, in my humble experience. Rarely have I encountered a puzzle game where each area MUST be solved completely for game continuation. As such, it will most likely need to be restarted FROM THE BEGINNING, including all the dialog involved, repeatedly. The good news is that once each room is solved, repeating is simple, if you’ve kept your notes and have a decent memory. (Yes, you will need to solve some puzzles with the help of paper and pencil.)
But more good news: the game includes some form of Walkthrough, yet to be investigated.
Each day, having solved to puzzles in one room, you will take the ingredients you have found to prepare a meal….for one less guest. Presumably a larger puzzle opens as more guests are………served.
I don’t doubt the repetition in “Rusty Lake Hotel” will prove a bit tedious, but quite likely there’s a good reason, yet to be determined. For full price, non-discounted, of $1.99US, I would give this game my NEXT TO HIGHEST RECOMMENDATION – 4/5.

And btw why do you need to level up your Driver Ribbon before you can drive a jeep or why do you need to level up your Anti-Tank ribbon before you get some decent AT explosives against tanks? An effective blend of elements from both the match-three puzzle and dating simulator genres, combined with a unique flair and focus on style that results in a very memorable experience.
Everything in this game is well executed mechanically. The match-three puzzles are addictive in their precise implementation, perhaps the single best I have played in this genre. Menus feel responsive and are easy to navigate, the UI is clear and simple to understand.
All round excellent art direction, from the backgrounds to the character designs, to the colourful menus, the production values are akin to a high profile platform exclusive. The uncensored patch is recommended for the full version, but the censored art still holds its own.
Very memorable use of spoken dialogue, each character exuding personality and catch-phrases that make them instant classics. The sounds are high quality and satisfyingly produced. The music is excellent, at once catchy and memorable, and captures the up-beat mood perfectly.
If you enjoy match-three puzzle games, I highly recommend this game. If you enjoy dating simulators with memorable dialogue and characters, with memorable visuals and music, this game is a must-buy.

I was kind of dubious about this one.  Real-time card-based tactical battles sound like they could be fun, or a disaster.  In reality, it's kind of in between.  You only have a window of a couple seconds to play stuff, and if you're trying to do multiple things, it's easy to click in the wrong spot and screw up your whole plan.  It also sounded like it was based on the old Bureau of Steam Engineering browser game, which I played only a minute of and found incomprehensible.  Luckily, there's no connection except theme.
The game also has the problem that you're drawing at random from a 20-card deck, so even with a lot of redundancy, you can get starting hands and continued draws that are exactly not what you need.  If one side gets a good draw and is running right out of the gate, while the other has to wait around for a few turns to get anywhere, the game could be effectively over already.  That's because board presence is vital, and there aren't that many ways to catch up once you're behind.
The other thing about the game is that it lives or dies based on card variety and interactions (like most card games).  The cards are divided into factions, and you can only have 2 different factions in your deck at a time.  Some of these factions feel more fleshed out than others.  You unlock cards by completing missions in the single-player campaign, but even 100%ing the 2nd playthrough doesn't get everything.  One faction's cards wait on the first expansion campaign, which is good, but has to be purchased.  Once you've done the campaign, there's not much else to do but try multiplayer.  Each match you win here gets you a card unlock from a new, distinct faction.  The trouble is, there hardly ever seems to be anyone on.  So, it's a catch-22.  You want to get more cards, but can't get them until you win, but have only MP battles to use them on once you do, but can't even get those battles in the first place.
Still, I enjoyed it quite a bit.  These potential difficulties mostly fade away when you get into the game.  The interface, the look and sounds of the units all feel right.  Evan LE NY returns to do the soundtrack, which once again fits the style well.

After a full year and I still heavily enjoy this game.
Have had a lot of friends let down by the recent Space Hulk: Deathwing, and my thoughts are that for all the things that Space Hulk got wrong, Vermintide got right. And the few things Space Hulk got right, Vermintide got right a year ago anyway.
+ stable
+ very, very satisfying combat. Mowing down a row of ratmen with a giant two-handed hammer strike has such a satisfying crunch.
+ actual equipment progression outside of one play session
+ gorgeous level design
+ good voice acting, just like cousin Okri used to do, with enjoyable exchanges between the characters. My dwarf was singing old dwarven drinking songs as he descended into besieged courtyards so we could drop powderkeg bombs in rat holes.
+ overwhelming, difficult enemies. I won't say that they're brilliant fighters, because they ain't, but they come from EVERYWHERE and if you're not in top form then you're going to get overwhelmed very, very quickly. And even if you are in top form you might get overwhelmed anyway because of a random Rat Ogre.
The only major complaints that people generally have for this game are lack of content and difficulty scaling up their weapons.
To the former I can only say that 1) it still has double the levels of Space Hulk and 2) DLC has been coming out routinely that adds another 3 levels, and those levels have in some instances blown the original ones out of the water in terms of detail. The latest Karak Azgaraz dwarven halls missions were fantastic. Best of all, ONLY THE HOST needs to own the DLC.
To the latter, I think that the fairly recent Quests and Contracts system has sped up getting good gear significantly. Took me a month to get a really good hammer for my soldier. After Q&C, I got really good melee AND ranged weapons for THREE of my characters, after less than two weeks. Only downside to Q&C is that apparently you only unlock it after completing all of the Ubersreik (read: doesn't include DLC) missions, but you can do that on any difficulty anyway.

The Evil Within is not a terrible game and there are certainly good parts about it. It's well made, looks fantastic, has great sound, and some genuinely creepy atmosphere. However be warned that this is nowhere near a classic survival horror game. There are levels that invoke this yes but a good 2/3 of the game has you fighting or sneaking through various battle arenas instead of actually exploring environments.
Health and resources are indeed scarce but that aspect of the game seems at odds with how action and boss fight heavy the rest of it is. I genuinely enjoyed the weird safe room hub world and the upgrade system but it seems like you can easily screw yourself over investing in the wrong things. Hey cool there's a magnum in this game with its own upgrade path! Oh no I dumped my valuable points into it but there's maybe a dozen rounds of ammunition for it in the entire game. Sorry!
By far the worst part of Evil Within are the one-hit kills. They're cheap as hell and absolutely everywhere. I think maybe 40 of my 50 or so deaths were due to getting offed instantly due to a trap, special boss attack, or environmental puzzle. It absolutely sucks and drags the game way, way down.
Also if the model viewer is any indication you find maybe a third of the weapons in the game on your first playthrough. Why hide so much behind unlocks and new game plus for game this long and plodding?
Lastly I wanted to touch on the story: it's nonsense. Yes I've heard it makes more sense if you play the DLC but I'm sorry, no. There's no sense of place to this game because you're constantly teleported around chapter to chapter. Yes it's on purpose but it doesn't help ground anything that happens. This just happen for the sake of it and I could barely tell you what any of the characters did at the end of the game. Do not play this for plot.
If you like the idea of a game controlling like Resident Evil 4 but want something more action heavy then Evil Within is right up your alley. If you're looking for classic survival horror look elsewhere.

Easily one of my favorite games of all time. Holds one of my favorite antagonists (Ruvik) in any game ever. Story is amazing as well as the combat (third person). Difficulty in this game is ridiculous at times, especially on Nightmare (I don't even want to try Akumu) But even on Survival (Normal) you're going to have trouble on your first playthrough.
In short and no spoilers, You are a detective that gets a case about a hospital, you go inside and you are strangely transported into another "world". You go through the game hoping to find a way out, fighting undead, bosses, and someone watching you.
Third person shooter, you find ammo on the ground and off dead bodies, the higher the difficulty, the more scarce ammo is. (Also harder enemies obviously). The boss fights WILL aggravate you at times, but you eventually get past it. You might have to look up internet guides, I know I had to. You can craft crossbow ammo which you get from traps. The rest you can see for yourself.
As far as the horror elements go, yes they are definietly there. Very creepy game, however at times it loses those elements in some chapters but they always come back. If you're an experienced horror gamer, then it might come easy on you. There are definetly more horror games that will scare you even more. The DLCs however, are definietly nightmare fuel.
As far as bugs, I haven't experienced anything major. Some people say it's buggy, I say it's not. It could use better optimization I'll admit but don't judge the game's optimization off of the demo because people are saying that the demo has never been patched like the main game.
As one of my favorite games of all time, I say go ahead and buy it if you're a fan of horror games, if you're not, don't bother. But if you are, definietly pick it up and play it, amazing story, amazing combat, good characters, very hard game. (Please make a sequel <3 ) 10/10.

The Evil Within is an over-the-shoulder shooter starring Sebastian Castellanos, a detective with a troubled past investigating a violent outbreak at a mental asylum when he is suddenly pulled into a horrifying distortion of reality by a creature known only as Ruvik, and must do whatever he can to escape it.
Gameplay in TEW is very similar to more recent games in the Resident Evil and Silent Hill series (this isn’t surprising as it has the same director as Resident Evil 4). So if you’re used to playing those games you will be able to learn and adjust to this one very quickly. For everyone else: It’s an over the shoulder stealth-action hybrid that features an upgrade system with various weapons and statistics that can be upgraded via a single currency (green gel).
Another neat addition to the game is the burn system where the common enemy, known as “the haunted”, can be set on fire with matches you find throughout the game. The main purpose for this seems to be ammo conservation, as on regular difficulty the bullets and bolts will be few and far in between. So, rather than spend 4 shotgun rounds on a haunted, you could shoot him in the legs and then run over and toss a match on him. If there are other haunted close enough to touch him, they will also catch fire. Clever players can exploit this by baiting enemies into groups and burning the first one to fall down to start a chain reaction, spending very little ammunition in the process.
The game features a few stealth sequences where our hero will be hopelessly outmatched either via numbers of enemies, lack of ammo, or certain special mini-bosses, like the keeper (a nod to pyramid head from Silent Hill 2) that hit like a truck. During these, you can use noises as distractions to help sneak up on haunted from behind for an instant kill or to draw more dangerous foes away so you can make your escape.
By the time I got to the end of The Evil Within I started asking myself how I got there so fast, mostly because the first half of the game up until the mansion part was pretty fun and frantic, and the remaining 5-6 chapters were a bit of a drag. I feel like this game could have been a bit shorter chapter-wise but with bigger areas per chapter wrapping up the same number of events, if that makes sense. It’s not like the story was bad per-se but the game could have ended several times before the actual end and there really wasn’t a reason for Sebastian to be where he was other than “oops, guess I have to be the hero now” so I wasn’t personally invested in the story either.
Thankfully, the gameplay is actually really good and some of the areas are downright clever and fun with how they handle the various traps and surprises. I also have to give praise for the director, Shinji Mikami, for trying something new instead of clinging to a previous IP (we really need to see more of that in gaming). I would recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a game that has the gameplay of Resident Evil 4, but with more horror included a la Silent Hill 2.

Mushroom 11 is a game with a wonderful aesthethic, but is heavily flawed in every other area. You travel throughout the levels in the game by erasing part of your mushroom, making it grow in the opposite direction. The problem is you have no real control over where exactly the growth comes from. Erasing a section on the left could add to the right, yes, but it can also add to the top. While this isn't a problem with the early levels, this lack of control makes most of the later puzzles frustrating and unenjoyable. That being said, the game has a beautiful look and sound to it, nailing that post-apocalyptic feel. Each level ends with a boss that looks fantasic and surreal, and the level design and music adds to this as well. But does this justify having to slog through an unfairly difficult game? No, it does not.

At about 4 hours of play, I recommend this as it's a good example of a successful experiment in game design.
The controls are entirely unique, erasing part of your blob so it can grow out of another part of the remaining blob.
This is enough to traverse terrain, climb walls, operate machinery, and battle bosses.
Although there are a few moments of frustration due to the precision sometimes necessary, most of the game is relaxing and fun.

An imaginative game, but frustrating.
Instead of jumping or moving like a normal puzzle platformer, in Mushroom 11 you erase parts of your "body" which will cause growth in other sections. This leads to some fascinating puzzles where you have to stretch out to reach ledges through erasing parts that are not useful, but it leads to frustration when you can't get formations to go where you want.
It is worth a try for the creativity and design alone, just don't expect a smooth ride.

Disclaimer: I paid for the game, but I was also a beta tester, and I'm friends with the developers.
You've already seen, and probably likewise heard, how Mushroom 11 isn't your typical platformer. And it isn't. But platforming isn't what it feels like you're doing most of the time. It's more like you're accompanying this interesting little organism on a tour of a post-human world ravaged years ago by those who once inhabited it, full of environmental puzzles and other creatures just trying to stay alive.
With the most limited of abilities in your corner, the game still provides enough variety to keep you engaged the whole way through, with variations in environment, enemies, hazards, and boss battles. It gets a little more difficult than I would have preferred toward the end, and slightly tedious in a couple short parts, but finishing the game is entirely possible, and rewarding.

Although I wouldn't recommend this game, I must admit that it starts out rather fun, and is full of interesting mechanics. Particularly enjoyable are the "upgradeable" cards, where doing certain things with a card gave you a new related card (i.e. the cavalry sword is a melee weapon, and using it enough gives you the officers sword, which does higher damage but has restricted use. Enough uses of an ally-buffing trumpet will give you a flamethrower "trumpet" weapon). And while early levels teach you some of the mechanics, they quickly become puzzles that test your understanding.
However, both of these only extend so far into the game. After a few near the beginning, upgradeable cards become few and far between, and while early levels provide a variety of cards, later levels may require multiple playthroughs (including NG+) to simply get a full set of one card.
And while the game starts off fairly forgiving, at certain points the difficulty signifigantly ramps up. At first this is just a change to requiring some planning for a level (which may require playing through and failing a level just so you know what is happening), but at a certain point the game starts increasing difficulty by making things increasingly unfair against the player, with some levels requiring a near-perfect deck and/or being the unholy union between a puzzle and a slots machine.
Or maybe I'm just bad at the game.
Either way, I've definitely had fun with this game, but its far from perfect and is becoming decidedly less fun as I progress further into the game.

When I first saw the trailers for Layers of Fear, I expected a mucher bigger and more intense expierence in playing it. I was quite disappointed with how the game actually plays, as there's not really any story except for light hints found in notes, but even they don't really draw you in enough to feel curious about the character(s). Layers of Fear is an overwhelmingly linear game and only really has one answer to anything, which left me feeling a bit bored by the end. It's a very short game (2-3hours max) albeit the way you progress in the game is very impressive, for example, one second you're looking at an item on a shelf, then you turn around to see the whole room has completely transformed, or even more subtle changes such as a painting transforming into something more sinister. The name Layers of Fear did convince me (and I'm guessing most people) that this was a horror game with tense and unsettling characters and setpieces, but I can only really think of 2 or 3 outright "scary moments", but even then, these moments were much less poignant and unsettling than many other horror games around, such as Soma or Amnesia. This game is creepy and unsettling at times but never really seems to build to anything significant. I wouldn't recommend this game to people expecting a horror experience, but if you're into games such as 'Gone Home' and other setting-based exploration games, then you will probably enjoy this much more than I did.

This is my first review, but i just finished the game for the first time and i thought i have to make a review on this.
Now let me start of with a short explenation of the genre, because this game falls into a specific horror genre that a lot of people might not like.
This game is purely psychological horror, it is not a survival horror like Amnesia or Outlast, it is not an Action Horror like Alien: Isolation, it is a psychological thing. Just like hypnosis you have to accept the game and let yourself fall into the world of Layers of Fear.
If you like this type of horror, then buy it, wait for night time, grab your headphones and play it. I guarantee you will have a unique trip that you wont forget.
This game does not help you at all, the story is out there, if you want to know it you just have to explore and find every bit of the puzzle. It has a main story, but many many little side stories that you might not get, if you dont explore everything. The game has three endings, depending on your actions throughout the game.
The game is really detailed, there are so many collectibles, secrets and eastereggs, so it is worth to take your time.
The biggest plus however is the sound. I have never experienced such acoustics in any other game so far. Starting with the beautiful soundtrack and going into the smallest details like the sound of footsteps, closing doors, thunder and even the creaking of the wooden floor. It just feels like really high quality and thats why it is so important to play this game with headphones.
It even ♥♥♥♥s a bit with your mind, because sometimes there is a really deep bass - just like a roaring - barely noticeable, but its there and when its not there you still keep it hearing in your head, its just indescribably.
The only thing that i could possibly criticize is that it ended so fast.
So if you like this really specific type of horror, even if you liked amnesia and penumbra or soma, if you like art and a bit of philosophy and you wouldnt mind playing story driven walking simulators, then buy this game. It works perfectly. I streamed it for my friends and even they got scared.
In my opinion the best, scariest and highest quality horror game ever being produced by an indiependent developer team. A masterpiece.
Ps.: There is an easteregg artbook you can find in the end with drawn pictures of the dev team, that just looks so amazing !

"Layers of Fear" is a pretty unique horror game with a very strong focus on lore and lore-exploration.
You'll play an unnamed painter who's struggeling to finish his final painting...
Doesn't sound that scary, right? Well, as you can imagine, the games story gets  deeper that that - You'll have to collect certain mementos (which I cannot name due to them being spoilers) to finish named painting... I can tell you, that those aren't your typical souvenirs but way more sinister objects... During your search for those you'll stumble upon more objects to pick up and collect which will involve you more with the games (by the way very well made) lore! You'll slowly uncover the secrets and make connections - eventually comming to a uncanny conclusion! The explorartion and search for those items, along with mutliple endings are a good reason to play through "Layers of Fear" multiple times, the game is variable and there will most certainly be new paths to discover upon making different (walking-) choices... The only negative aspect I found here is, that you will not take that long to play through the game (only up to 6 hours on my first playthrough, and those due to me playing really slow and careful)...
The games graphics are fairly beautiful - even at lower settings! And to me it preformed quite well, despite having a pretty old graphics card! The soundtrack stresses the atmosphere REALLY well!
Now for the horror-aspects: Aside of the games brilliant and unsetteling story, the overall horror setting is well-implemented! The atmosphere on my first playthrough was so thick, strange and tense that it took me long to finish the game, being afraid to stumble into the unnamed horrors of the protagonists past... The mansion is littered with uncanny notes and (mostly!) paintings, and there ARE enemies that will haunt you at times, resulting in sudden jumpscares if you're not careful... This creates a constant feel of dread, especially on the first playthrough, making Layers of Fear a genuinely good horror game with a strong touch of "mystery"...
tl;dnr?: Layers of Fear is a good horror/mystery-game with multiple endings, but it's very short if you're not frightend easily it might get repetetive if you intend to get all the archievements!

Teamplay is at the heart of the game, and you need to work together with your team mates when teams are about evenly matched. The game may seem pretty dead, but most days of the week there are streams where the active players tune in and have mini tournements, casual games, and the 2 weekly "main" tournements on saturday and sunday. EDIT: I decided to change my review and my opinion on the game. It has flaws, but you cannot get this type of awesome gameplay anywhere else, so I HIGHLY suggest any fan of Metal Slug or skill-based 2D shooter games check it out.
This game is a prime example of gameplay trumphs graphics. It's very skill-based. It has a questionable Item Mall (more on that below). But hot dang, is it ever a good time!
The core game breaks down into 3 parts: PvP, Mission, and Coop.
PvP is what the game was built around: the PvP in this game is awesome. The skill ceiling is super high, and I've seen some extremely good players do some phenominal stuff. The community is still very new, but mostly filled with players that have played MetalAssault when Aeria Games owned it, meaning these guys know what they're doing. The community is quite nice though, and if you're fast to learn and willing, they WILL teach you how to get better! You're going to get your butt kicked at first, but with some practice, you will get better for sure.
Mission mode is the "storyline" of the game. I say it with quotation marks, because the story is very bad and really is just there to have some dialogue talking to the user. This mode is very difficult until you have good gear. However it is quite fun, and it feels very satisfying to beat a level after trying it many times. When you get to the later maps, this mode becomes quite profitable as well, but at the time of writing, very little people have gotten to those maps (the game is new, and the best gear has not been acquired yet).
Coop is what drives the economy in this game. This is the mode where you make your money, and this is the mode that you MUST play if you're going to want to get anywhere in this game without paying real life dollars.
It's basically "zombie mode". There's many variations of maps, but the requirements are always the same: complete 10 rounds and get a bunch of EXP and Credits. If you successfully complete the map, depending on how many players you have at the time, you randomly roll for a chance to win one of 1, 3, or 5 box(es). This mode is also quite fun to play, but it is not for everyone, so if you do not enjoy Coop mode, you will likely not enjoy this game (more on that below).
ABOUT THE ITEM MALL:
I have been trying to play as a COMPLETELY free-to-play player and now have ~30 hours logged.
Yes, it is completely possible to play for free, BUT you have to enjoy Coop mode.
At the time of writing, the Item Mall has some 7-day weapons that make your life 10x easier in Coop and Mission modes (THEY DO NOT BREAK THE BALANCE IN PVP, WHICH IS WHY THIS GAME IS WORTH YOUR TIME!).
These 7-day weapons can be bought from other players for Credits! How do you make Credits? You must spam Coop mode for a chance to win a box, then sell whatever you got from the box for profits. Then, once you buy those weapons (specifically the Flamethrower is the best possible purchase), you can do the harder Coop maps for BETTER LOOT!
This is how you get rich, and this is how you get better gear.
I plan to make a free-to-play player guide eventually, once I get better at the game.
For now, if you have any questions, contact me in-game.
IGN: EggsDee

Mushroom 11 has some really interesting physics-based puzzle solving action revolving around erasing the cells of a constantly regenerating mold creature, but ultimately, it's a frustrating and tiring experience.
You can expect to run into a decent art style with some interesting backgrounds, but nothing looks as good as the creature you're solving puzzles with except for the bosses. The ones I ran into looked good with a touch of the slightly disturbing. I suppose the entire art direction goes for that post-apocalyptic, slightly creepy look.
What holds the game back the most is how the organism regenerates. You can use a large eraser or a fine erase to shape the creature and it'll grow itself back across however many pieces of it are in play. The way is grows back can either work against you or with you. There's no way to control that aspect beyond some very quick or patient erasing depending on the speed the situation calls for. It's genuinely annoying due to how it makes the game more trial and error than it has to be. I wouldn't have minded a way to draw the creature while depleting cells from its main body or something else in addition to the erasing.
The growing aspect and boss pacing were at their worst with the fourth boss which just killed any desire I had to continue. The boss would fire a spike drill at the body which creates an opening for an attack if you can guide the organism onto the exposed weak spot, but touching it isn't enough, you can have envelope the whole thing. The boss then just wastes your time by rolling its spiky self back and forth several times until it fires again. You need to destroy multiple weak spots in order to reach the creature inside to eat it. Trial and error at its worst.
Finally, the collectibles didn't seem to do much. I couldn't tell if they made me bigger or were just there for score. There isn't that much of an incentive to collect them within the game.
I can't recommend Mushroom 11 due to the frustrating gameplay. It's still a neat concept that they have that some curious people might want to see during a sale, but I need additional controls over the creature in order to have a better time with the game.

A quite unique puzzle game that plays a bit like platformer but due to its mechanics is nothing like you ever played.
in the game you are as the title would suggest a mushroom. But not any old mushroom - rather a radioactive mushroom blob thing. The way you control the thing is by cutting away parts of it with a rather thick brush - your mouse. The blob tries to keep its volume so once you cut away from one side the second one expands. And this is how you move, by cutting opposite to the way you want to move, forming different shapes and tackling obstacles.
The graphics are pretty decent and work well with what one might assume is a post apocalyptic environment. The sound accompanying you along your journey is quite satisfying an fitting.
The story is non existent as far as I can tell. You are in this place now and you need to go. That's about it. But it doesn't hurt the game as its all about the puzzle.
There are 7 levels in the game. The first six feel a bit on the easy side with some harder parts. The last one has a really big difficulty spike and I really struggled at parts but after finishing felt really good about myself.
Overall a very good and unique game I can safely recommend.
