Before I write this, I gotta say: I LOVED Hotline Miami 1. The flow of the game was so much fun. The music was hypnotic as you went around slashing people up in your ultimate badass character.
This game.....is just so frusterating. First of all, the people you play with are all over the place. You play as 5 different masked murderers just like the first game but you also play as a Detective, an author, a Russian Mobster, a russian Mob Boss, an actor and a soldier. The soundtrack is good but they really nailed it in the first game. It's much less exciting in this one and I don't leave the game with it stuck in my head like the first game.
It hot line Miami 1 the story was mostly hidden within the game. Honestly you could ignore it pretty easily if you wanted to. Some people just want to focus on the gameplay and wack people up to some sick tunes. However, in Hotline Miami 2, the story is basically shoved down your throat. Switching characters constantly and changeing play style between levels drasically just takes me out of the game. There isn't any rhythm to the game anymore. One minute you're playing a normal match as a Zebra man and the next you're forced to be a soldier who HAS to wield only 1 gun and a knife.
Which leads me to my next point, guns are much much more prevalent. I never liked useing guns and I always opted for something funny like a sword or hammer in the first game. Now, you pretty much have to use guns. Part of what i loved in the first game was the violence from wacking people until their head pops. Now its just a very repetitive shoot out.
This also slows the pace of the game down. More opponents are wielding guns and you're forced to use a dumbass trick to bait them into a door way to melee them....Over and over you have to use this trick. Also they took out a lot of the cool melee and throwing weapons from the first game for some reason.
There's a new enemy type in the game and it just makes no sense. He's a big buff guy who relentlessly charges you at incredible speed and can only be meleed to death. He dodges bullets. Combine that with the bouncers that HAVE to be shot....you're in for a very very annoying level.
The new levels in general are just frusterating. There's a level that is extremely dark and changes color. It makes it sooo difficult  to notice dogs, bouncers and what gun the enemy has. Many levels have you fighting off multiple areas at once while shooting and meleeing. This becomes overwhelming and there is little you can do to avoid it. These levels also through off the rhythm of the game because you have to stop and bait enemies A LOT. Towards the end of this game I was just wanting it to be over. It dragged on for me.
The main character in Hotline Miami 1 was a BADASS. Taking on and murdering houses full of mobsters single handedly. However, every shred of his badassness was torn away when you're given a WHOLE CAST of characters who can do the exact same thing! Really makes the first character less of a badass.
In short:
Music is worse
Gameplay is less rhythmic
Story is forced upon the player with long cut scenes and abrupt character changes
level design is worse, harsher enemies with some levels being overwhelming
Use of guns is heavily encouraged and required at some points
Baiting enemies becomes very common and repetitive
Other characters doing exactly what Jacket did just makes him seem like less of a badass
Smaller amount of weapons in general. Less melee weapons and far fewer throwing weapons such as the brick.
If you're really into the story, like REALLY into it, get this game. There's so much story here it's rediculus.

Don't let the lack of players stop you from playing this game. Yes it is true, the community is mostly dead and those who are still here are way better than you are. Play it anyway. I'll explain why, and then I will explain how.
Why should you play SMNC even though it has no population and you will get spanked:
The SuperCrossfire mode came out in spring of 2012 and there is still nothing like it. SuperCrossfire is intense, and will make you incredibly angry, but it is the most satisfying game I have ever player. Don't play SuperCrossfire, PLAY TURBOCROSS. When you see these reviews saying that they can't get into matches, or get into them infrequently, they are talking about SuperCrossfire which requires a full team before the match begins. In a perfect world, we could play that mode, but the world sucks so we have to play TurboCross.
Even though TurboCross is watered down SuperCrossfire, it still has no equivalent. Believe me, if I could find a third-person shooter MOBA with jumping, dodging, grapples, and class-synergy, then I would be playing it instead (assuming that more people played it). Here is the low-down, Uber spent millions on this game and it shows. Unfortunately, they didn't make money from it so it has been abandoned. But again, there just isn't anything like it and what it does is amazing.
The basic idea is that you and your team are supposed to help your bots advance in two lanes in order to take down the shields of enemy turrets and eventually take down the money-ball. There are two lanes, so even though you may be pushing one really hard, you have to worry about how the other is doing. All of the maps are symetrical. Now, a lot of players just don't understand how important it is to kill bots. Killing bots is the most effective method of winning the game. Of course the other team will try to kill you while you do it, and you don't want that to happen. Why don't you want that to happen? because while you are dead, you kill less bots. Kill bots, push your lane, take out their turrets once the shield is down, do the same to the money ball. If you see that the other lane is having the same done to it by the other team, switch lanes and push it back to atleast the middle.
Oh I forgot to explain why this is fun. It's amazing. When you and 1-3 other teammates are pushing a lane together and you make progress even though the other team is trying to kill you, you feel like you are making something happen. This is a different feeling than coming in first in a race or having a high kill-to-death ratio. Pushing a lane is slow and must me sustained. When I die, I worry about how far back my lane is going to get pushed and whether or not we will be able to push it back to where it was. It's different than k/d, it just is.
Other third-person shooters just don't offer this.
How to play with a low population:
Play a Pickup game of Turbocross on the North American server after 5pm EST preferably on the weekend. Yes, I know that this is limiting, but it's what you have to do to play this game that no one else has made yet and is ahead of its time.
It will take maybe 10 minutes to find your first game, but after that you are in rhythm, so most of the players of your last game will show up for the next. You will see the same names on different days, there are not many of us. Be nice because you will see them again. They will not be nice to you, I am sorry. Stay near your team and kill-bots. Stay on one lane until you know the maps. Eventually you should ask someone what the annihilator is. Good luck.

I really wanted to like L4D2, and to an extent I did. But that game made me nauseous; I'd be dizzy and dry heave after an hour of playing.
Enter Vermintide, the perfect game for me! Surviving hordes of man-sized rats with some colorful characters, satisfying melee combat, and in the gloriously rendered Warhammer universe. And best of all I don't get nausea at all!
This game is all about your interactions with what it throws at you, and the people (or bots) beside you. I've met good players, good people, bad players, bad people, and combinations of these. I've laughed at hilarious situations where 3 Gutter Runners would jump our group simultaneously, or double packmasters would drag 2 players in opposite directions during a spawning horde, or 2 Rat Ogres spawned in the pitch black of the Dungeons map 5 minutes apart (and we still had to fight the 3rd one that spawns in the big room at the end). It's all a lot of fun.
I'd like to address some of the most prominent criticisms of the game below:
It's true what people say that it's peer-to-peer and if the host disconnects or leaves, the level ends. That's kind of unavoidable unless they have a dedicated server. For me, it's fine the way it is. It doesn't take hours to reach the point where we left off, much less than that.
People talk about the loot system a lot. How it's a gamble and a dice roll; that's true. I also think it's not a big deal at all. Some crazy good people have beat this game on the hardest difficulty using starter gear before. The gear is a crutch, a really shiny nice-looking crutch, for you to recover from your mistakes while you play. Beyond that effect, I see it as people wanting their shiny things immediately. And with the Sigmar's Blessing addition they added a few months after release, you can make your own endgame weaponry from scratch.
All that's really lacking is more adventure missions. Fatshark take my money!

This game is complex, calculating, and difficult. Although you will go through many hurdles, the end result, is highly rewarding. If you can beat Banished in the hardest difficulty, think twice about beating this game that easily. This game will keep you thinking constantly throughout, and there is no point in time when you feel absolutely secure in one or more of your resources, because there is always a scarcity of something. Food acquisition is the biggest hurdle at start, but it becomes less of a problem later on. Expect alot of terraforming, which requires time and laborers. You will need to calculate mentally how much time it takes your people to do one thing to the next, where building placements and distance from one building to another can either result in food on their table or mass starvation. You will deal with various elements, including, but not limited to, hypothermia, avitaminosis, and plague. In order to succeed early in the game, you will need to frequently move around people in their profession. Depending on the season, time, temperature, and needs, you will be expected to assign your people to work for a season or two, and then reassign to another profession, repeating this back and forth. Early into the game, there are very little sit back and relax moments because you will have to tackle many issues and execute your plan, but late into the game, you will be able to have more sit back and relax moments, enjoying the sun fall down on your town while you sip on some lemon iced tea after a hard days of macromanagement and micromanagement, and with the beautiful graphics this game comes in, it proves that postcard images can come from games like Life is Feudal: Forest Village. To alleviate some of the stress from failing, I would suggest you read some of the guides in the guide section of the community hub. I highly recommend this game.
*There are bugs and occasional crashes, but the dev and his team are highly involved and active in eliminating them. They are adding additional contents at a gradual pace.

Well, I never really thought I'd ever play a game quite like this, Nor did I think I'd find it so fun. But, here I am, writing a review for the new game called "HuniePop", a combination of every Hentai dating sim and Bejeweled style puzzles games. So, without further ado, let's give you the story.
Story: You are a guy/girl who is unlucky in love. However, one day, a Love Fairy named Kyu approaches you with the offer of a lifetime, the chance to teach you how to seduce girls. Now, armed with your trusty HunieBee, plenty of gifts and pick up lines, AND one hell of a libido, you are off to win the hearts of 8 lucky ladies, plus a few secret girls~
Pros: Now, let's just start off by saying that the premise of a dating sim mixed with Bejeweled is very interesting, and handled well here. It is quite challenging, even on easy mode, so don't exactly plan to breeze through this. The tutorial for the game is also good and gets you a full idea on how the mechanics work. It also has some very great voice work that will likely make you decide you actually WANT to hear the women talk (though it DOES leave the option to turn off their voices). Furthermore, the women are each unique and fun to watch (though some aren't AS likeable, you will qucikly find). The HunieBee menu is also pretty easy to go through, besides some minor difficulties (which I'll explain later). The artwork is really lovely, with some of it being cute while a large portion is nice and sexy. Also, for those who are more hardcore when it comes to games, worry not. Because this game also has an "Alpha Mode" which you can get once you successfully seduce all the girls, including that "final boss" whom I won't reveal. In this mode, all dates you go in will be in Hard Mode AND increase in difficulty with every date. And finally for what it arguably lacks in story it makes up for with a rather off the wall, inappropriate humor that manages to come off as surprisingly charming despite itself. From having your Love Fairy mention having a taste for chocolate (she's talking about a black woman) to one of the girls, Audrey, asking another girl if she "hurt [her] ♥♥♥♥♥ feelings, the funny moments can be too many to count and honestly come off as hilarious, whether because it sounds surprisingly natural, or because it's much too corny to take seriously.
Cons: Now, while I did mention quite a few pros, a few of them could actually count as cons for other people. First of all, there's the fact that this game really has no real story or even character development, besides your guy/girl going from a shy, simple virgin to the town's biggest sleeparound. Oh yeah, did I mention that you sleep with every girl in the entire game and yet still go on dates with each one, INCLUDING a mother and her own college age daughter (granted, they're enstranged from one another, but still)? Because yeah, that's exactly what happens. And combine that with all the drug & alcohol references, inappropriate humor, some of the less likable characters (Audrey and her excessive swearing can feel quite grating when she isn't funny) and the mere fact that you end up collecting the panties of the girls you sleep with can easily make this a conservative's worst nightmare. Oh yeah, and if you aren't into the game's humor (which you can easily get a feel for early on), then trust me when I say it doesn't get any better. As a final, but minor note, I find that the HunieBee menu for the info on the different girls can be a bit of a pain to go through since you have to rely on the arrows to get you through it rather than tabs going to what you want to look at. Not big, but still annoying.
All in all, I was honestly happy with my experience playing this game, and NOT just because of the hentai elements. To put it simply, I managed to find that I actually enjoyed the puzzles and found winning the hearts of all the women to feel rewarding, expecially when I made them happy. While it can easily be argued that it stoops pretty low in terms of both the premise and humor, you may just find that to be a part of the charm. So if you can at least get a demo of it, try it out first and if you like it, go ahead and buy it. I honestly feel happy that I gave it a try.

2. This game is a soulless rip-off of all my favorite survival horror games and I hate it.
I fall into the latter category.
Imitation may be the sincerest form of flattery, but it helps if you actually put together something that is good...or at least written well...or voice acted well...or that has a coherent narrative...or consistent gameplay...or a protagonist with an actual personality, or, or something.

This game is unfairly difficult and frustratingly random. Enemies never follow a pattern so good luck trying to plan anything ahead of time. On restart of the level, a foe may come through the door, or it may not; it may run right out into the hall and hide near a corner, or it may not. There's a reason that normal stealth and shooter games have enemy patterns, because it allows the player to learn and plan with each failure. I get that the game is trying to recreate the tension of real firefights but the bottom line is, it KILLS the pacing and the feeling of player growth, and when those things are sacrificed, any victories feel more stumbled into than achieved. At least the first game eases you into the action more, but in the sequel Level 4, the Police Station is just a ♥♥♥♥♥ily designed, unwarranted difficulty spike. After 40 tries I still cannot pass it. There's just too much crap going on around the player with enemies circling the center and officers peeking out of doors at will. Add to this the convulted controls which constantly have the lock-on switching targets and the fact that the game views never feels like it is showing enough to be fair, and you've got one very haphazard experiment here. This is a huge mis-step after the first game and I just cannot reccomend it. I wish I had given up on it sooner to get my money back. The soundtrack is great, though; hopefully you can buy that separately.

Let's call it “space goo”. You use left and right click as more of an eraser to remove parts of the space goo and wherever you are not erasing it recollects or perhaps more accurately, it reproduces itself. This is not entirely intuitive. It's deceptively easy to grasp but very difficult to gain any amount of adept skill in quick succession.
There are numerous obstacles to overcome. Gears, lava pits-- even simple platforms afford some challenge; Plumes of smoke rise from factory pits and your ability to shoot the goo further becomes dependent on your current weight or inertia to be more precise-- Less mass, easier to move but less potential energy and so forth. The left click is a large eraser while the right click is a much smaller one usually reserved for cutting the goo into pieces lest you need to depress a button or lever while the rest of the goo presses forward. The larger eraser also affords you some level of creating your own platforms pushing the goo onward. Being that the goo regenerates upon collision with a solid surface you can sort of push it around by erasing what's behind it.
The art is really nice, it's got a sort of vaguely cartoonish--post apocalyptic aesthetic.
The puzzles are not expressly frustrating but for what seems like a relatively casual experience, some of the puzzles and boss creatures/scenarios can be overly specific and rely too much on luck of getting a teeny tiny piece of goo into a certain region. For most people this won't be a huge issue but if you're the kind of person that doesn't enjoy attempting something over and over when you already understand what is needed to get done and simply not being able to accomplish it because the goo tends to reproduce itself randomly when erasing rather than say.. on the opposite side of where you erased-- it can be needlessly frustrating when you just want to move on. It just feels a little out of place for the type of game it is but it's really not a big deal. You may just have to play around a bit until it something clicks.

Layers of Fear is a psychedelic horror story where you play as a deranged artist who can't quite seem to remember the layout of his house.
+excellent graphics
+excellent art direction
+excellent sound direction
+excellent atmosphere
- very short
- shock value wears off in the 2nd half
Layers of Fear starts off with a slow self narrated doublespeak exclaiming a hopelessness in his situation, with only one way to bring it all back...'Finish it' he mutters to himself as you hear rain and lightning droning in the background. Keys clanking onto metal, you hear sounds of a door opening, you are brought to attention from the pitch black screen to a scene of a mansion. You are now in control of the main character, whom you know absolutely nothing about until you explore the depths of the mansion, rummaging through every single drawer and cabinet looking for notes scattered about to give you an inkling of an idea of who the main character may be.
Early on you find out that the character is an artist, or at least was an artist sometime in the 19th century. You have the freedom to explore the mansion and it's room which are heavily Victorian in nature. A creepy piano piece plays in the background, that perfectly captures the mood of the set piece. You're alone in a giant mansion during a thunderstorm, the place feels eerily perfect, not a speck of dust can be found. You come across an easel covered by cloth. As you slowly reveal the unfinished painting, the room subtly changes. A message is sprawled on the exit that wasn't there before, 'GET IT RIGHT THIS TIME'. You go through the door, and suddenly the mansion has transformed itself. A mist of fog rises from the floor, doors lock behind you never to reopen again. The ambient tones of the soundtrack slowly haunting you as you hesitantly move forward through the rooms.
Layers of Fear introduction perfectly encapsulates a mysteriousness that had me paralyzed. Enraptured by the setting and the fear of what was to come next, it all felt vividly real. Especially with how beautiful the set pieces were room to room. On ultra settings, it's very easy to marvel at your surroundings with it's soft shadows reflecting off the dim lighted halls throughout. It's as pretty as a picture, as if it were carefully sculpted by the artist himself. The artist seems to have an obsession with perfection as when you listen to an auditory flashback of when he finds his muse, his proposal comes off eerily strange in retrospect. He wanted to put his name on the most beautiful woman in the world, just like the rest of his paintings . His object of affection was beauty at it's core, but what happens when the beauty fades?
As you find out, one way or another the beauty has faded from his life. And once it does, so does his inspiration for painting. He hits a giant roadblock which is expressed visually within the game. You the player, has to help the painter find just the right items to help him finish his masterpiece. But the house isn't what it once seemed, closed off walls will appear where they were once open hallways. You will go in circles and circles while the game will openly remind you through scrawled writings on the wall. The artist's inner narrative uses his house's walls as the canvas, giving you insight as to how he feels on his deranged journey to reclaiming his lost inspiration. They seem like ramblings of a madman at first but subtly aid you to progress in the game.
The mansion's are like the inner frameworks of his mind, cluttered and confusing. Neverending, yet constantly closing the paths behind you. What was once a simple mansion is now an endless mind palace that transforms at his whims, with his deepest fears manifesting , clouding the golden years where he was once hailed as a genius. The mansion from Layers of Fears strikingly resembles a similar theme from a book called House of Leaves by Mark Z. Danielewski. In the novel, the house initially has larger internal measurements than external. Over time, the interior of the house seems to slowly expand until a hallway appears that should lead outside to where the yard is but does not. The interesting aspect is that the book also has an unusual page layout and style, making it visually surrealist in it's own way.
Layers of Fears feels like it's takes this surrealist form one step further and perfects the execution using it's strong visual tricks and audial cues. Walls will shift, hallways will reverse, invert, making each room feel slightly familiar yet alien to both the player and the painter. Misdirection is key here, something Layers of Fears pulls of meticulously. The game will consistently find new ways to surprise you visually with it's metamorphic atmosphere, and this is only accomplished by the player being a witness to the painter's madness.
This is the majority of what you'll be doing all game, exploring dark dreary rooms for notes and items that will help you on your quest to finish a painting. Although it would be categorized as a exploration game, it feels more like an on rails horror set. Once you're finished with a room, you can never go back making you feel like a puppet being dragged from A to B with very little to interact with except a couple drawers or shelves to find notes about past events in no real chronological order. It's mainly up to the player to decide how badly he wants to find out what's really happening in the game by opening 100s of drawers in hopes of finding more notes. You never truly feel like a player in the game interacting with the world, more like another set piece that the artist has created for you to be a witness into his madness. It's when the game does take complete control away from you, does it feel truly unique. Helpless to the panorama of horrors slowly settling closer and closer, claustrophobia settling in to the point helplessness. Your control is truly gone, you are no longer a player but a set piece just as much the painter is and it feels wonderfully surreal.
The second and final act of the game delves heavily into psychedelic hallucinatory levels, where set pieces transform before you into sublimely grotesque imaginations of the painter. The problem is that the shock value of the similar jump scares have worn off at this point, and that I have absolutely nothing to fear. The first time I encounter a monster roaming the hallways, I'm terrified by the games brilliant usage of the lighting system. But you soon quickly realize that there's nothing to be done about them. The hallways are always narrow and small and the doors lock behind you so you have no choice but to either wait and see or just walk towards them and brave the brunt of their psychological attack. Once you realize that it almost feels like your 'death' is a plot progressor. This removes probably the most vital 'layer of fear' within the game. Once the element of fear is taken away, and replaced with plot progress you're no longer traumatized by their appearance but considering a quick death to move on. While you continue to march forward to find the final piece of puzzle to put the story all together, the ambiguous and surrealist nature never quite grants you that clear resolution rather leaving it up to the player's interpretation by how many notes he found throughout the short three hour game.
Overall Layers of Fear is a technical marvel that is both hauntingly beautiful and surreptitiously ambiguous in nature. While the ambiguity drives the narrative forward through the character's interpretation of the artist's evocative imaginings of his mansion, the game slowly loses it's pulse of mysteriousness through the over use of jump scare tropes and identical monster encounters but never it's beauty. I recommend Layers of Fear to players who want an exploration based game who don't mind letting their imagination run wild and want to enjoy a fresh surrealist take on the genre.

Ever wonder how it feels like being seriously mentally ill? Schizophrenic? Delirious? Combined with heavy alcoholism, hallucinating the hell out of this world? Not knowing where you are? whether what you see is real? Are you remembering or experiencing the present? Whether you are dwelling in one of the dark corners of your desillusioned broken brain? Are you dead?
This game is what nightmares are made of. Beautiful, crippling, disturbing, hellish, tragic nightmares. I understand that these descriptions may make the game sound chaotic and without sense, but it's really well made, consistent and a true gaming experience that no other form of medium could deliver.
Layers of Fear is incredibly smart. I want to praise the developers for following their ideas to the end and doing something different. The game is really beautiful, the dark ambience soundtrack is one hell of a mood setter, the effects and physics are also truly convincing (especially when things stop behaving as they should).
My advice is to play this game slowly, when it's dark and with headphones. Observe your surroundings. Listen to the sounds. Ingest every location. Don't rush it. Turn slowly. And when you find a god-damn writing on the wall that says "don't look back", seriously, don't look back. And the last tip: don't play this before you go to sleep. Also avoid mirrors and paintings in real life for at least 1 hour.
Don't look back.

The achievements in a game play many functions, they can be a roadmap for the interesting twists and turns the story could take, they can be a litany of what humiliations a human will endure, but all of them illustrate what the development team values in the player base.

Early Access Watcher Reviews Life is Feudal: Forest Village
Update Version: 0.9.4221
Disclosure: This game copy was bought by the reviewer.
Gameplay Footage:
I will not be comparing this title to Banished or to the previous game in the series, but I will point out that the user interface, game mechanics and overall feel share a striking similarity to the previously mentioned titles.
Before beginning each session, the player can establish what type of map they wish to settle. Map size ranges from small to medium, terrain varies from mountainous to the plains, and decide if you want harsher climate or the chance to deal with disasters. It is surprisingly limited and results in every game (at least the ten or so I created to test this) with the same amount of supplies, same population amount and always positioned along the coast. Every session also provides enough basic buildings to house the starting population and the required storage buildings to manage resources. It ensures the proper tools are available to at least get started, which gives the player a chance to absorb the gorgeous scenery.
The medieval aesthetic is the game's best feature with a wonderful visual appeal complemented by great weather effects (fog and rain for instance) and lighting. Texture quality for foliage and trees are pleasing with flowers, grass and even moss looking quite presentable. Trees give off proper shadows, move in response to a breeze and water flows with current. Character models share the same generic model type for their respective gender and age group, but they look good. Models do have a tendency to clip through trees, rocks and walls, especially the wildlife. Regardless, it is a beautiful game to walk around in or to zoom in on.
Unfortunately, the music does not have the same flair as the visuals and can become stale very quickly. There is an extremely limited amount of very somber, mellow instrumental pieces that are great to listen too a couple of times, but not for the length required to establish a thriving city. The ambient noise does not add much to the overall product, mostly devolving into dull wood cutting and clinks. Given the massive amount of time it takes for things to progress, an outside music source became a requirement to continue pressing forward.
Time is something Forest Village falls victim too with most actions requiring half a year at times to complete. Thankfully, there is a way to enhance the speed of the game up to x10, but even then I found things to be moving incredible slow. Similar to the music of the game, I was finding it hard to manage the city without a secondary game keeping me interested as I glanced over to see if something I requested ten minutes ago was finally done. This is mainly the case earlier on before the population reaches higher numbers and you are able to utilize more citizens. Things still move extremely slow, especially construction, infant to adult growth, and terraforming.
Terraforming allows the player to manipulate the landscape to help alter the terrain to better serve the community. It provides more flat land to build on and is essential for expanding a settlement further inland. It takes a great deal of time for the process to complete with the results requiring further adjustments. When matching the level marker to the same level as the ground I wish to be even with, the terrain would lower itself just enough to be uneven, forcing a second job to raise it a smidgen higher. There were multiple times I couldn't finish from what appeared to be an issue preventing the villagers from being able to enter the area being changed. This was also apparent when I was attempting to build a hostel on some flattened land, only to result in the construction teams going idle and two further jobs to raise the land up once, then back down to fix the issue. The idea is great on paper, but is unreliable in practice.
Building placement is hassle free as long as you have the terrain to place it down on. The area does not need to be free of debris, thanks to a feature that automatically marks all resources in the respected area for removal. Once a building is done a settler can be assigned to the building's respective task and a random person will begin work. Upgrading is also available, but only the housing variants and a couple of workstations have the function at this time.
AI is a mixed bag with most of the problems steaming from an issues I have seen other settler management games suffer. Settlers can be assigned to a job as long as the building for that job is available, but settlers also have survival needs such as eating, moving food and firewood to their home and acquiring materials from storage. This creates a dilemma factor that can have settlers stop a job half way to rush back to eat, go back to the workstation and once against leave it to move supplies to the home. This issue is why terraforming can take almost a year in some cases and buildings can be left unbuilt for months.
As with any Early Access game, there are technical issues. When a home is upgraded, I found certain cases where settlers would fail to register with an available home or with the upgraded home, resulting in them starving to death. Auto-saving has a common issue with locking, becoming unresponsive and sometimes forcing me to quit the game entirely. I noticed frame loss occurring during later segments of the game, possibly due to the size of the settlement. These are very annoying issues that are common with the Early Access territory, but that doesn't excuse it either.
Several other features in the game have very little impact on the overall product or do not seem to perform as intended. Disease was something I have yet to experience in a town that has sustained a death rate of 12 people in twenty years. I have purposely left them in the open (have not built a pyre) to see if anything would come of it and have yet to see anything. Illnesses also seem to have little impact, with a separate game having a town full of rabid settlers with nothing to show for it in the four years I tested Patient Zero. First person view felt more like a gimmick than a viable mode, restricting the actions of the settler being controlled and reducing time to x1 speed. Disasters have not shown up during my playtime outside mentions of tornados nearby. Advancement is also underutilized with the only discoveries possible revolving around new crops and animals. A port is required for this and the new benefit impacts one or two new items at best. Every building is available at the beginning (outside pastures) and every important item can be crafted from these buildings (except warm clothing made with wool by discovering sheep). These are very interesting aspects that could increase the quality of the game.
It is hard for me to really pinpoint my disdain for this game. I lost my first six villagers to old age, three more to mining accidents and ended up losing the other 30 to freezing temperatures when I forgot to pause my game. It was at this point I realized I had just been biding my time after building everything available. I created two more villages after this for testing purposes, but the real issue I had was with the lack of things to build and the lack of progression. There is no real end to these settlements outside the inevitable destruction to nature and no goals to strive for outside general survival. It needs more to do to eliminate the massive downtime. I just cannot recommend a game this light on content, especially at the price. I will return to port for now and set off toward a new settlement once this game leaves Early Access.
Pros
- Gorgeous scenery
- Building and layouts function properly
Cons
- Terraforming needs an overhaul
- General pacing is too slow
- Crashes, lockups and frame rate
- AI issues
- Content lite

HuniePop is a game of overt sexual objectification and casual racism wrapped around a solid puzzle game core.
The gameplay focuses on two play types; a "match 3 slider" style puzzle similar to Puzzle Quest and the "dating sim" style conversations.  In the puzzle sections, different matches score different levels of affection and special tiles earn "passion" multipliers or "sentiment" to be spent on power ups. This is simple at first, but the difficulty increases steadily. The player must perform well in the conversation portion of the game to level up skills and unlock power ups in order to keep up with the rising dificulty of the puzzle game. The mechanics at work are well crafted and kept me playing for hours dispite my distaste for the narrative.
As I said, the game is rife with sexual objectification and casual racism. The clear objective from the start of the game is to do and say whatever it takes to get a selection of women to have sex with you and then to never speak to them again.    You ply them with gifts and alcohol to gain their affection while memorizing trivial facts about them like their weight and bra size. Your mentor, a love fairy named Kyu, makes racially insensitive remarks along the way.  The game does this with accute self awareness; so much so that it seems like a satire of dating sims rather than a serious one, though nothing in the game description or in game content indicates it.  This is compounded by the fact that, while there is porn in this game, there is nowhere near enough of it to classify this as a "porn game".  If this was the developers' intent, then they did it well. The mark of good satire is verisimilitude.  Still, the conversations frequently made me uncomfortable and the lack of depth left little to make it worth it.
All things considered, I can't recommend this game.  The puzzle game was fun and very well crafted, but the time you get to play it is short compared to the dreadful slog through stilted, unnatural conversations.

Update: 7 February 2016;
It's a fun game to play for a while, especially for fans of the series. There are plenty of different ships, including the main ships from each series;
James T. Kirk's Constitution-class Cruiser,
Jean-Luc Picard's Galaxy-class Cruiser,
Benjamin Sisko's Defiant-class Escort,
Kathryn Janeway's Intrepid-class Long-range Science Vessel,
Jonathan Archer's NX-class Escort.
You can also find some movie-specific ships in the game, such as the Excelsior-class.
You could also go for a Klingon or Romulan Republic character, which opens up other ships and options, as well as unique story routes for these characters.
Endgame is a lot of PvE/PvP grinding, but what MMO does not have that? STO at least offers a variety of ways in which one can 'grind'. Such as research and development, special missions for duty officers or admiralty ships, and a reputation system with its own special rewards.
There is also room for daytrading on the exchange, although item prices seem regulated by a few dozen players who have large stocks of special items laying around on alt-characters and alt-accounts. Not too infrequently I have come across items which are no longer obtainable in the game, bought one or two to see if the price would rise, only to see five more of the same item put up on the marketplace within minutes, as if the sales triggered them to be posted.
PvE missions are all doable with items obtainable through in-game currency, but if you are looking to do PvP, it is more of a pay-to-win situation. The more competitive ships require ZEN to buy them or items for them, and while you can trade Dilithium for ZEN, at a cost of 316:1 it's simply not worth it.
The community is decent, and the new armada system allows fleets to work together more, so it's definitely worth looking at playing it with some friends.

Mushroom 11 is a somewhat physics-based puzzle-type game.
You're given control over a slime-mold like organism that is able to rapidly reform itself, either if damaged or if the player manually removes parts of the organism. This is the core mechanic of the game, and while it it easy to learn, it's hard to master.
Sadly, it might be too hard for some people and I personally have found myself frustrated to the point of just giving up, as the way the blob reforms itself is fairly unpredictable, making mastery somewhat of an impossible feat - at least to me personally.
At first, this problem is trivial, but as you move through the levels it gets increasingly hard to make the blob do what you want it to do. The puzzles in this game are easy to figure out, but the unwieldy controls of the 'mushroom' makes them very hard to execute, and not in a good or rewarding way. This is especially true from level 5 and up.
I must begrudgingly (as I applaud the developers for their willingness to explore new game concepts,) say that it is not what I had expected from this game, and unless you are forgiving in regards to bad controlschemes and frustratingly punishing trial and error puzzles, this game might not be for you.
In other words, the basic idea is good, but the execution is lacking. Therefore I do not recommend this game.

This game lives and dies by the uniqueness of its main mechanic. The movement of the character is unlike any other game I personally have ever played, and it is worked into the game very well. The level design includes places where you need to go quickly, and places where you need to take your time and work out how to reach a ledge or solve a puzzle. The randomness of the movement can be frustrating at times, but it adds a decent challenge to the game and is a part of figuring out the game. It's not a game that you can rush through and brute force to the end, at least not in your first playthrough.
Overall I'd say you should play this game if you're someone who likes unique and interesting mechanics, but if you're someone who wants a lot of depth in your game, this might not be for you.

I want to start by saying I like this game. I like it a lot. The setting is good and the gameplay is fun. It's a lot like Monster Monopiece, which I loved, but without the embarrising rub mechanics. Which is good.
So why don't I recommend it? Simply put, the single player campaign is cheap. Really, really cheap. After the first few missions you're almost always started off at a huge disadvantage.
The enemy has powerful cards that you don't have access to yet. The enemy starts with more AP than you. The enemy can field four ironclads at a time. The enemy has squares that provide and advantage much closer to their side. The enemy has a deck tailored exactly to take advantage of the battlefield.
The only way to finish a mission is to have the exact cards the game wants you to. Want to build a deck around certain cards, certian factions or a certain strategy? Too bad. You don't get to choose your strategy. What you do get to do is play a mission several times to see what cards the enemy has and where he tends to play them. Then you get to build a deck specifically to counter the enemy's deck.
Even then, there's a good chance you'll still end up playing the same mission several times. Like every card game, luck plays a large role. In this game it plays a very, very large role. Don't draw a single ironclad in the first six turns? Have four ironclads but no weapons? Have only powerful cards you don't have the AP for?
Too bad.
The worst part of this is that it's very hard to rebound from a bad initial hand. You'll run into situations where the enemy has four ironclads on the battlefield, while you have none. Even if you draw a few ironclads, chances are that the enemy's have better gear by this point and are already halfway to your side.
So yeah, this game is a lot of fun. It's also a good way to see how much patience you have.

I just removed everything I wrote in my last review.
Major Gripes:
-Going back to "homebase" during matches takes WAY too long to regain health and ammo. Why did you slow recovery to such a crawl? What could possibly be good and fair about this? Spoiler: Nothing. Nothing is good about this.
-No more weapon rank-up system. I used to be proud of my weapon rank because I actually took the time to get good with an actual weapon. That's one feature that used to be there but for reasons unknown isn't anymore. You're bringing back a new game but removing key features.
-Oh hey, that sniper can't possibly nail me while we're both moving around so frantically. Oh, wait it seems I'm dead. *Fart Noise.* Seriously, I get that sniper rifles are powerful and all that, but there HAS to be a disadvantage to using them while moving around. It seems there's none. Fantastic.
-No more new items in the shop while ranking up!? That's ridiculous. That's TWO features now that were actually removed from the original.
-Item shop stuff (including cosmetics) are now temporary? Temporary cosmetic items? Why bother? This is a side-scroller, and I'm seeing my toon every time I play. I'd like to actually like looking at them. If I was at any point inclined to put actual money into the game (overlooking the already big problems it suffers,) I'm certainly not anymore.
-When picking up items in Co-Op or Missions, why do I still get Korean letters on my screen? I'm playing on a US server.
-When signing up for a PvP match, at random intervals the game crashes. Seriously, I understand the oversight during launch but it's been a few weeks. I think this is the sort of problem that would have been addressed pretty quickly.
-Lagging players. They teleport and are suddenly somewhere else. What?
Minor Gripe:
-Remember the old style of helecopters, vehicles, robots and tanks? This could be just personal preference, but I really liked them. They were more ARTFUL and gave the game a more fun feel to it. Now with "realistic" looking tanks, and artillery graphics. Why not just play something that already is set in a modern real-lifeish setting?
-You know, you're re-releasing an old title. Perhaps add a new character or two? I'm sure it won't kill the balance of the game. Wouldn't even be hard to make them as a game like this isn't graphically intensive and wouldn't take long to make a new set of animations. This is a minor complaint only because it's not really a problem. Woulda been nice is all.
-Why the hell do I have so many quests? Not only that, but I really don't care what the NPC's are saying and just talking to them is like pulling teeth. Now I have a bajillion pending quests and I really don't care about a single one of them. Maybe NPC's that were at least mildly interesting.
-No character skill progression. Yeah. Remember when you had to buy that jump skill? Choose between dash or shooting while on a ladder early on (you get them all maxed eventually ofcourse.) What? Why? Why was any sort of progress besides rank (Rookie-SGT-etc) removed?
Non-Gripes:
-I do like the variety of co-op, with ability to choose difficult.
-For the most part (besides the things mentioned above) I actually dig the artstyle. It's fun and sorta whimsical.
-Not for nothing, this could actually be a good game. It's a sidescrolling shooter. It's pretty fast-paced and it has its fun moments. These moments could be more fun, and last longer if a lot of the problems were fixed.

MAGA The Trump Presidency is a pro-Trump/republican simulation game that puts you in command of Trump as he fulfills his long list of campaign promises.
Pros:
+Decent art style and sprites
+Clever integration of Trump related memes
+Use of Trump voice clips makes the game feel both more authentic and more amusing

Cons:
-A largely incompetent tutorial does a fine job of explaining several game mechanics, but not all of them. I felt lost trying to figure out the controls for each of the game's many menus, how to make money, and the best way to raise countries' trust in you.
-The controls for the fighting terrorist minigame are pretty terrible, making the minigame much harder than it needs to be

Everything I did felt meaningless, as it didn't so much as make a dent in terms of making other countries trust Trump, repay even a fraction of the national debt, or fulfill any of Trump's campaign promises. If you buy it on sale and are willing to rely heavily on the game's community to help you out, you'll get some joy out of it. But ask yourself, is it really worth all that effort for a cheap production value game you can buy for 70 cents? In my opinion, no, it isn't.

Warhammer: End times: Vermintide gets compared to Left 4 Dead a lot, and for good reasons – both are solid team based games with varying objectives. I played Vermintide with this comparison in mind but after my first game it dawned on me that L4D and Vermintide are more different than they are similar.
Unlike L4D, Vermintide has a WGBPOS loot system (White, Green, Blue, Purple, Orange and Superior (in this game expressed as red) which rewards you based on difficulty, luck and overall thoroughness when playing. At the end of the game you have a dice roll (more dice can be obtained via side areas and side objectives – which I will talk about later) which determines what item you will get, as you play on harder difficulties the quality ceiling is lowered, meaning you have more of a chance of getting an orange (exotic) or even a superior (red) item.
Alas, you can get what statisticians like to call “completely ♥♥♥♥ed” In the sense that you need 40% of the dice on the roll to get at least an orange item (which is about 3-4) but instead you roll just a 1.
I see a lot of people complain about this but honestly if you are playing for the loot then you are missing the point of the game somewhat. This is RNG. It happens.No one is going to get every roll they want.
In addition there are ways to re-roll stats, salvage weapons for in-game currency (which is used for upgrades and such) or combine several items together to make a rarer item. I really like this system because it takes the sting out of getting a horrible roll as you can put that orange you don’t want to use as either upgrade points or to make a better item later.
It seems I’m in the minority of the people who like the loot system – but what speaks volumes to me is how the game is so primed for a micro transaction store and there is none. This is a very nice change.
Within each level is a set of side objectives known as Tomes and Grimoires, both of which give XP when taken to the end of the level (Like Gnome Chompski but he fills your medkit/pills slot) as well as a free die (more dice = better chances of better loot).
Tomes take up your healing item slot but offer a lower but still slightly better than average quality of die when carried to the level exit, as well as some xp.
Grimoires are for the daredevils in the game that like to live life on the edge. Grimoires give a 6 sided dice with all sides lit up (i.e, a guaranteed roll every time) as well as xp but they restrict the health bars of everyone in the party by 33% as well as take up your buff slot (pills/adrenaline), if you die with a Grimoire in your possession you lose it forever. There are 3 tomes and 2 Grimoires most levels to obtain.
This feature gives a lot more risk/reward to the game and encourages players to explore and let the game judge them for their own greed. Extra dice can also be found in chests littered throughout the map randomly, which further gives more incentives to explore every area.
Some of the banter between the characters ranges from funny to grim and further on to world building and backstory, some of this is dispensed randomly or at particular events. What is best about this system is that characters will call out dead ends and things players should do to improve their survival (such as back off from taking heavy damage or raising a shield against a horde).
There are 5 characters in total, each with different equipment, play styles and voice lines. Some characters are handicapped by having strong ranged weapons but weak melee weapons or better defensive weapons for that class.
There are also trinkets which improve subtle elements of gameplay such as using healing items on yourself or consumables such as bombs, many of these trinkets effect team play and how the game plays out.
One thing I noticed very early on is how much more difficult Vermintide is compared to L4D as many of the ranged weapons in Vermintide are situational and mixed; meaning melee is a primary fall-back. When it comes to special enemies this means that the group needs to stay tighter together as ranged weapons can be unreliable – meaning the group needs to fight their way to their pinned team mate rather than spray a hail of bullets in their general direction when they are pinned. This leads to much tighter team play and more reliance on your team mates to block enemies or take out the heavy hitters you are weak against.
Swings, attack contact and overall weight and power is made very satisfying in Vermintide, it reminds me a lot of Chivalry or War of the Roses which revolved around slow planned attacks and outwitting your opponent using timing and strategy rather than swinging blindly. Shields and other weapons make fantastic crushing and slicing noises, the combat is a real joy to feel and watch.
I would also like to point out that Vermintide is very faithful to the lore.
In L4D the infected run blindly at you and attempt to swarm you, for Vermintide this is only half true as the enemies will attempt to get behind you to backstab you, which deals a whole lot more damage than a normal attack.
The Skaven (your rat enemies) are also stealthy but cowardly by nature, meaning they will often freeze or stall when encountered alone but will fight more furiously in large groups. They can also be very quiet and backstab you if you are not looking behind you.
Another feature that I noticed is how players are either on par or slower than the enemies attacking them – this means no one can speed run a level and effectively cheese it like you could in L4D, almost all the characters wear heavy armour and as such move slowly in comparison to their enemies. This tactical decision to make the players like this is really smart in my opinion, you don’t feel like an unbeatable chain-bashing god – without your team you WILL die horribly in multiple ways.
As much as I enjoy Vermintide I do have some issues with it.
Firstly I have a concern when it comes to replayability. The main storyline is over in around 9 hours or so and the only form of replayabiltiy is a pretty dry wave based arena or redoing the same levels multiple times or harder difficulties. (There is a bounty board system which allows you to earn currency as well as rare items in exchange for completing daily missions, but that is about it)
Remember those Tomes and Grimoires I told you about? They are also fixed spawns – meaning that searching for them after the first time yields no benefit as they will always be in the same place. There really needs to be a random spawn setting for them.
Levels can be quite long, which can be frustrating if you fail them at the end and need to restart the entire stage again.
Player handholding is quite low; the game throws you into the game with no instructions on how to play and therefore it can be jarring for new players to adjust.
There can only be 1 class per player per game, which means some more contested (okay, they are really just broken, semantics.) characters tend to be taken, meaning you could get forced to play a character you don’t agree with.
Overall would say that the asking price of £22.99 (or your regional equivalent) is a bit too much to pay unless you get a bunch of friends to play it with you, but at a discount of 33% or more I would say it’s a very good deal.

"You must really like hurting people, huh?"
If "Hotline Miami" simply didn't like you, "Wrong Number" ACTIVELY HATES YOU.
The original was a drug filled dive into pure madness and murder. Its sequel shows the world without the goggles of drugs and bloodlust, and reveals a darker, sinister plot. Jumping between characters and points of time, you're left confused as to what's really going on until a finale that destroys everything leading up to it in a way that feels like a dark punchline towards those trying to follow along with the madman telling this tale.
Playing through these games within days of each other (and spending more time with this one, due to more levels and being ((somehow)) even harder (((♥♥♥♥ THAT SHIP LEVEL!))) ) was an experience unlike any other. Confusion, rage, and satisfaction, all blending together amongst a backdrop of neon, synth, and pixels.
Bigger levels means harder to focus and grasp upon the much larger picture at hand, as you're too busy shaking in fear out of being sidelined across the map. Only through trial and error, may you find the way to outsmart those who dare get in your way.
Little do you know, the game is always two steps ahead of you. Throwing more and more stuff at you and handy cabbing for the sake of it's own pleasure. You could simply walk away, never play the game again, but you don't. You keep coming back.
As you keep coming back for that kick of adrenaline and release of satisfaction once it ends, the game brings your hopeful, monstrous spirit back, crushing you down spirit into a miserable puddle of blood.
Through Prison, War, and Writing, may you see the game taking its biggest jabs at its players. Constantly crushing, destroying, caving in each skull and putting holes into each body, until you finally break away and learn that it's simply not worth it...
We don't deserve two games like these, and they both know it.
As hard (and down right unfair at points) as this game can get, it's all your choice to continue onwards, and by that point, its already got you, hook, line, and sinker.
Part of me prefers the simplicity of the original, while another can't help but have the highest or respects for this genuine, ambitious, thought-provoking, and absolutely brutal dive down the rabbit hole.

The Evil Within is a masterful horror game from the master of horror himself, Shinji Mikami, the creator of Resident Evil series. The Evil Within has tense and horrifying atmosphere, gruesome enemies and bosses, heart pounding horror elements and satisfying combat. You'll be immersed into the world of this game as you try to survive through one terrifying encounter to the next. But the pacing is well thought out. It'll give you some breathing room before throwing you out to an unexpected and tough situation.
The gunplay is crunchy and satisfying but you'll have to manage your ammo carefully as it is not that abundant as you'd like...which is a good thing considering this is a survival horror game. The upgrade system is a fun. You use a currency called "Green Gel" to upgrade yourself and your weapons. It's a joy to explore the game's world as you get rewarded with stuff like green gel and other cool items.
The monsters themselves are terrifying and if you're not careful, even the most basic enemy will get the better of you. It's not always wise to approach every battle with guns blazing since ammo is limited. You can approach most of the scenarios with stealth to save ammo or when you're low on ammo. The game's stealth mechanic is functional and you're the kind of person who likes a stealthy approach to situations, you'll like it here.
The game is pretty lengthy. With the DLCs, it took me 30 hours to beat the game barring the new game+ more and harder difficulty modes which I'll get to at a later date. So the game is highly replay-able and you'll get your money's worth.
A word of warning: This game is not for the faint of heart. There's plenty of blood, gore and brutal violence in this game. So if you're squeamish of those, avoid this game. Otherwise, The Evil Within is an excellent survival horror game that is a must play and worth the money. This is a one of a kind horror experience that no survival horror fans should miss. Let's hope there will be a sequel for this game.

I haven't played very many survival horror games, so take this review with a grain of salt.
While the Evil Within has numerous problems from both a technical and game design perspective, the enjoyable core combat and memorably oppressive aesthetic make it worth a try anyway.
I don't feel like I need to give you any background to the story, since the story makes no sense at all. It's mostly just an excuse to push you through a variety of traditional horror settings (asylum, barn, church, ruined city) and have you deal with the monsters you encounter there.
The core combat is excellent - guns have significant weight and facing multiple enemies can result in a panicked frenzy. Enemies feel powerful and it takes more than a few hits from the starter weapons to take them down. Even on casual mode, you can easily be overwhelmed if you don't pay attention (though admittedly I am a noob at this genre). Crafting bolts for the crossbow is simple but does give item collection a bit of extra incentive. That said, the combat UI is clearly consolized and poorly developed for mouse + keyboard. I struggled through it because I vastly prefer shooting with the mouse, but many people may wish to use a controller.
Similarly, the stealth - when you are allowed to be stealthy, at least - feels tense but fair. The game takes into account noise, the amount of light you cast, and several other factors when calculating enemy awareness. When the game gives you a choice between stealth and open fighting, stealth is usually the better option.
That leads to discussing the game's biggest problem - there's not enough stealth. The game follows up the tutorial section with a pair of incredible non-linear levels that showcase the robust stealth system really well. Both levels are small open areas that you can approach in a variety of ways - basically little stealth sandboxes. Most enemies can be confronted directly, stealth-killed, or avoided. Both areas only contain one save point, so every venture away becomes an exercise in measured risk - do you check the next building for extra loot after recovering that shotgun, or do you head back to save your progress?
Unfortunately, after these two brilliant open levels, the game suddenly takes a hard right turn into stifling linearity. There are occasional sections that do return to non-linearity, like the haunted mansion lifted directly from Resident Evil, but they're usually just collections of hallways so stealth is much less of an option. The brilliant sandbox experience from the third and forth levels never truly returns. Despite its failure to live up to its early promise, the rest of the game is still fun, since the combat is pretty good, but it's a bit disappointing that the latter 2/3 is just decent after the masterful first third.
Aesthetically and technically, it's a mixed bag. The game contains a number of memorable visuals, such as the upgrade chair searing chemicals into your brain. The dynamic lighting casts spooky shadows that help add to the tension. However, the presentation is hampered by the awful textures and texture streaming characteristic of the Id Tech 5 engine. Some textures are fine, but some wall textures look like they were copied from Ultima Underworld. The poor textures are especially jarring considering that the game also contains some effects that look amazing, such as the police lights in the opening area.
Similarly, in CPU-bound situations (like when a heavy dynamic lighting effect is present) the engine tends to falter and drop frames regardless of settings, at least on my aging i5-3470 and GTX 970. I imagine a more recent 8-thread CPU may have less trouble with this. Taken together the frame rate/frame pacing issues and frequently subpar textures make the game sometimes unpleasant to view in motion. However, they aren't so terrible that they put me off the game entirely.
Overall, despite the less-than-perfect presentation and the significant drop-off in gameplay quality after the first third, this is still a reasonable purchase when on sale. I wouldn't pay more than $10 for it, though.

This is a game where you make decisions based on how much ammo you may have (or not have) and want to risk using that precious bullet.  Also, it's gory.  Very gory.  Not for children under the age of 30.  The end.

Would I recommend this game? That's very hard to say. There's promise, great graphics (compared to Banished) and some interesting ideas. But it's not complete - definitely Early Access, and if you are expecting a fully playable game this is not for you. Personally, I'll most likely put the game on the shelves for a few more months now that I've had a few hours of play time.
Here's my general observations - others have said it, and I'll chime in too. This is a better graphical implementation of Banished. Same idea, same concept but things look better. That said, Banished as a game is a lot more complete and consistent. Time lines in Feudal doesn't work out at all. Things move very slowly, and the peeps are dumb as hell when it comes to movement and actions. Literatelly, you're forced to take over a peep to get something done in a year. Like getting a field built, a builder will go there, do a few "builds" that may not even increase the build score, and then go back to eat or pick up resources for his house or something. And then maybe come back later and it starts over. Walking to/from a location is strange too - peeps will walk into trees and rocks and slow down to a crawn and easily get stuck. There are definitely some challenges in the general world design. I've lost peeps because they "build themselves into a corner" and cannot move away.
In Banished you need workshop items to change the landscape allowing you to build in more areas. A great feature with Feudal is that you have that as part of the standard game play - but man, it's slow and it takes a lot of practice to get things right. Just knowing how large to make an area to build on it is hard. And even small slopes and bumps in the landscape will prevent you from building on it. You would think that flatting out the ground for a building would just be a building build task, but no.
AI wise I found that once I got to about 40 peeps things went down hill. Hunters would just stay at the hunting lodge, gathers would not pick up anything, fishers wouldn't fish (and the feature to see production stats isn't working). You really need a general stats page to identity areas where you need to focus peeps on, but with 42 peeps, I had 12 fishermen and still no fish accumulation what so ever. Most likely due to the fishermen spending more time gathering food for their houses than they do fishing.
Storage is another game area that at this point needs work. I don't care that one barn is going full. I care that I have no barn capacity at all, so when I have more than one thing don't start warning me etc. and so far I haven't seen real good AI walks when there are choices for storage. It would be interesting to see if the closeth barn is full if that just means things are left to rot ... unfortunately at that point, the farmers and fishers just started spending less time working and production went down.
Finally, a big different from banished is the build chains required. To just make high quality tools, you'll need mines, wood cutter, furnance and a kiln. Then you can get materials and put someone in your blacksmith position. To get there takes time, and there's no real help when you start out to understand these connections. You have to find boards/pages or just make a few games where you learn how these things relate, and then start a new one where you can set the proper strategy. It just feels very strange that you need 5-6 workers to just make a tool. Of course there are wooden tools which are a bit easier to make, but the game will say you're out of tools unless you have high quality tools. Part of the game challenge is finding the right optimal way to place and assign job positions - and compared to banished you sure have to move your peeps around to different professions all the time. You need way too many peeps that a small town can have people just do one thing.  This is why the game is slow - getting enough peeps to just have a mine is hours worth of game play - I've found I run out of stones and other "found" items much earlier than I have enough capacity to build a mine (you need a lot of materials to do that). So you start by sending peeps on long walks at winter, taking extra time to collect things - and that just adds to the game time. That makes the game at this stage a bit borring.
The last item is the wild-life. That seems to still be a great work in progress. The hunters are supposed to keep a chicken-coup free from foxes but since they're more re-occupied "at home" good luck with that strategy. Instead, the offical guide says to take over a peep and have them kill the fox. But that means you have to constantly watch your life stock and _hope_ a peep is close enough to do something (you cannot run your peep when you have control of them).
All in all, I find it promising. Definitely a huge graphical improvement over Banished. But it lacks lots of features that Banished has, and your growth options are very slow. At this point I haven't seen "immigration" options, which in Banished allows you to jump up in population i sprints as long as you have enough resources to cope. I miss the trade posts, "mood" options like the churches and just being able to see real stats on a peep. You cannot see how hungry or cold they are. Just if they have enough clothes on. Again - Early Access so I don't expect it to be there yet. There's promise here, but I think Feudal should also be careful not just duplicate Banished. Even with better graphics, it seems Banish has a much better game engine and AI. And I for one will gladly overlook the cruder grpahics for better game play.

HuniePop is a game of overt sexual objectification and casual racism wrapped around a solid puzzle game core.
The gameplay focuses on two play types; a "match 3 slider" style puzzle similar to Puzzle Quest and the "dating sim" style conversations.  In the puzzle sections, different matches score different levels of affection and special tiles earn "passion" multipliers or "sentiment" to be spent on power ups. This is simple at first, but the difficulty increases steadily. The player must perform well in the conversation portion of the game to level up skills and unlock power ups in order to keep up with the rising dificulty of the puzzle game. The mechanics at work are well crafted and kept me playing for hours dispite my distaste for the narrative.
As I said, the game is rife with sexual objectification and casual racism. The clear objective from the start of the game is to do and say whatever it takes to get a selection of women to have sex with you and then to never speak to them again.    You ply them with gifts and alcohol to gain their affection while memorizing trivial facts about them like their weight and bra size. Your mentor, a love fairy named Kyu, makes racially insensitive remarks along the way.  The game does this with accute self awareness; so much so that it seems like a satire of dating sims rather than a serious one, though nothing in the game description or in game content indicates it.  This is compounded by the fact that, while there is porn in this game, there is nowhere near enough of it to classify this as a "porn game".  If this was the developers' intent, then they did it well. The mark of good satire is verisimilitude.  Still, the conversations frequently made me uncomfortable and the lack of depth left little to make it worth it.
All things considered, I can't recommend this game.  The puzzle game was fun and very well crafted, but the time you get to play it is short compared to the dreadful slog through stilted, unnatural conversations.

This game is what can be described as a "Magnum Opus" that has succeeded and at the same time fell short of it's expectations. I recommend the game but there are a few points to note:
- The game is incredibly detailed with numerous models and eye-viewing graphic and very "art"-fully designed to the point that it makes the game interesting.
- The OST and sound designed for the game is breath-taking, including the own main theme of the game which is gritty, melancholic and very emotional.
-  The game is incredible even on low-end devices, which is a bonus.
- Although at first it would seem the game isn't very story-driven, i can object to that since the game features numerous  texts ranging from documents of the residence and scribblings on the walls to the brief narrations when investigating objects which flesh small details of the painter, his wife, their daughter and the issues that surround them. Piecing it bit to bit, it makes things interesting as it fleshs out.
- The Jump Scares in this game are fairly light and shouldn't be too much for those not accostumed to horror games and they are well made to try and release itself from the cliche, although it's execution is not done well when in comparison with other games that have experimented them, which makes Layers of Fear's creepy factor pale (Example: P.T.). With a little bit more thought (and a few gameplay changes) the game could go miles.
- The gameplay is executed through exploration of numerous rooms to acquire items for your "magnum opus" while the painters suffers from his "delusions". The objective is clear and intriguing in how the painter will progress thorugh his painting.
- The game has three endings in which they are affected by certain actions taken during the gameplay, but as they are minor actions that are executed and the game would need to be played form the start, tends to make it repetitive. This is worsen due to the fact that it takes about 3 hours to complete the game.
- The game is what the community has annouced as a "Walking Simulator" (i prefer it to be named in this case as "Nightmare Simulator with a few annoying puzzles") and each "death" does not give a game over nor well affect much (except the ending) of the rest of the game, this makes Layers Of Fear lose part of it's appeal as a horror game and lessens the effect of the scares.
Layers of Fear had everything to become a dignifed game for the Horror genre and although it falls short on a few aspects, overall it has been made with (obssesive) love and care just like the "masterpiece" it is. The price is worth it and it makes a great add for the collection of any horror fan, although be warned that you might end up leaving it your library right after the first playthrough.
