I was looking forward to trying this game a while back, although I had no clue it came from Zachtronics, developer of the infamous SpaceChem. I haven't played much of SpaceChem yet. It intimidates me, and I'd like to devote my full attention to it, when the time comes -- soon, I'd say.
So, when I knew this came from the same people, I wasn't sure if I wanted to play yet. I did anyway.
Well, Ironclad Tactics is a different take on the lane strategy "genre", with the added complexity layer of deck-building.
This game is really, if you don't know what you're expected to do. This is mostly a deck-building game, as other reviewers have stated. Each level has a different challenge for your to overcome, and you overcome it with a different deck, mostly. Certainly, tactics are also very important, but a good tactic will do very little if you don't have the correct deck.
While the concept is interesting, and I did enjoy the game, I can't say that it's perfect. At all. It has several design points that I heartily disagree with, and make it simply a "good" game. Which isn't bad, mind you. Just not quite what I expected after trying SpaceChem.
I've completed the game (without the DLC). Done all the optional objectives as well as game plus. It was a challenging task, for sure, but also very rewarding!
Each level has a main objective. There are several different types of levels: there's the common level, in which you try to get victory points by moving your units into the end of the map, there's an "hold position" level, in which you try to survive for x number of turns, and there's the Boss levels. Each of them play very different. Level variation is also pretty good, which is surprising. It seems very limited with the 3-5 lane maps, but there is a surprising number of subtle changes that make all the different.
Then, there are optional objectives. Some are puzzle levels -- these were easy, but really great! Basically, they teach you a certain mechanic with that: limited deck with 3 or 4 cards, and you have to make the best out of it. Unfortunately, there were only 3 or 4 of these levels.
Then, there are some that make you gain VP by other means than moving units to the end of the lane. There are some that make you play with a completely different deck: don't use Y faction, for example.
All of these provide interesting challenges.
Now, what's wrong with it, exactly?
Well, you unlock cards by completing levels and secondary objectives. However, since this is such a deck-oriented game, you'll often be missing the cards you need for a given deck. And so, you have to push through some challenges, until you can go back and complete the secondary objectives.
It has a very awkward pacing, like that. Some game encourage you to play previous levels better, but this one does that weirdly, since you can only play
of the previous levels better, since you're missing cards.
You'll have to go back and forth a few times, but it's doable. Just not as
as I would have liked.
Then, there's the random elements. Argh, the randomness...!
So, you build a deck. Great. Then, you have to hope that you draw the correct cards at the right moments. One bad draw can screw you over and make you restart a level. Oh, but wait: there's no restart button! I'll talk about it later.
Yeah, lots of restarting, until you get the right draws. It's... not to my liking. Maybe it works in multiplayer. It certainly works in most card game. But here, it's just a matter of restarting... Tactics play a lesser role than the actual cards used, and that's why the randomness doesn't work as well.
Also, the decks are very limited -- maximum of 2 factions, exactly 20 cards. So, you can't really create as much variety, or even guarantee to get a certain card, since there are at most 4 or 5 of each.
It's an interesting limitation, and it requires some creativity to beat levels. But then again, the randomness is frustating, since it's a matter of trying over and over until you get the right draws that you envisioned all along.
Now, about the lack of a restart button. I don't know why it is. It makes little sense. Perhaps it's simply a question of the designer saying "create the right deck and you won't have to restart". Maybe...
The game came off as a bit too random for that, but I don't know. Just a minor gripe made bigger with the amount of restarting...
Honestly, this is a very frustrating game, at times. Especially when you first start, not exactly sure how it works, it will be daunting. But if you keep trying, you'll learn how the game works, how the AI works, and how certain levels can be easily beat with the right decks.
NewGame+ is almost a whole different game, also! Don't just complete the main campaign, thinking that's everything. It's definitely not.
Well, not a perfect game, but certainly a very rewarding experience, if you feel like a challenge!

Ironclad Tactics is set during a ‘weird’ version of the American civil war that sees foot troops fighting alongside gigantic iron automatons that command the battlefield with classically inspired weapons including cavalry sabres, cannons and even morale boosting trumpets, welded to their massive frames.
Once you’ve assembled a deck consisting of ironclads, soldiers and various weapons and actions, you need to gain a preset number of points in order to win the round. Points are usually gained by getting your ironclads through the opponent’s defences and off their side of the screen, but certain scenarios can also include the need to hold fortified positions or destroy certain boss enemies.
What makes Ironclad Tactics very different is its unique spin on realtime gameplay. Each card you play from your hand summons a particular unit to the battlefield and as the game ticks over in realtime, those units will then move, attack or perform some other unique action. At first the game can feel overwhelming as you have mere seconds after drawing a new card to decide whether to play it now or wait until your action points increase for the more expensive (not to mention powerful) alternatives already in your hand.
The game has a very satisfying tactile feel to it and the rate at which you earn new cards (usually by accomplishing bonus challenges during missions) is judged perfectly with plenty of new and exciting additions to make to your deck as the game goes on.
Where the game really shines is its cooperative mode. Whether online or over LAN, this game doesn’t present any confusing lobbies or account systems; just a very simple click of a button and you’re in and ready to play.
It’s fast, clean and simple, and the game plays well with two players each taking their own personalized deck into an encounter.
All in all, I really appreciate this game and I hope that developer Zachtronics hasn’t been perturbed by a few tepid review scores because their effort here is worth a whole lot more than all that.

Playing as a faceless, money-loving monster hunter, you work through a 6x6 grid of tiles to find an exit from the dungeon. Practically everything is handled through dice rolls. The start and exit are determined by your rolls, as are the contents of rooms. Tables are provided for what each roll gives you, so you learn what to expect from what you roll on the dice. Most monsters, except for the vampire, have specific damage values that hit you each turn. You have to learn when to stick to a fight and when to run. Despite all the dice rolling, the RNG doesn't feel unfair. You're not really set back if you have a failed run. The pixely art doesn't strain the eyes, though the music isn't anything to write home about.
What you're really paying for is the ability to play on your computer and ditching the ads. Honestly, it's not a bad trade-off.

This Sim draws you in with its beutiful landscapes, better than desccent animations, and its great choice in music. There have been some bumps in the road with crashes but, the Develepors have quickly patched these issues for the most part.
Pros:
Seasonal changes in landscape and lighting
Choices in Map sizes and types from small to large with plains, hills, and mountains
Attention to detail in animations
Standard and first person view with direct control over a sim to complete a task
No Easy mode, you have to think about what goal your are trying to reach. You have to consider each choice you make. Make the wrong choice and everyone could die. This is not a launch and forget Sim. It takes careful planing to achieve each goal you will choose to meet.
Many choices to obtain sources of food.
The soundtrack carries you off to your distant land as it draws you in and time slips away.
Geat looking buildings and some even have upgrades.
Cons
BALANCE - Although I do not want easy mode, I also do not want to have to pay attention to every second of the game.
Step away on 10x speed for 10 minutes and you are likely to find half of your population has expired. There has to be an adjustedment in consumption for all things.
I have a list of saved games where I have tried and failed. Sometimes miserably and other times I try a different approach and gain one step just to go three steps backwards.
The element of intrigue to want to keep playing for hours on end is certainly here. However, in the end the BALANCE is just completely OFF of its mark where it needs to be. This makes for a very tedious gameplay and thus I keep finding a reason to exit the game.
I have reached 17 years but that isnt really meeting any real goal being just to get there was a constant and meticulous ever changing of man power. A sim doesnt need to be that draining just to end up with a dead village.
At its current state in balance. It is a constant back and forth of Constant fishing which works well in the begining to the feeling of I am not sure why anyone is fishing at this consumption rate everyone is starving, to I have an ample amount of food and now not only am i just about out of firewood but I have no more logs to make into firewood.
If the Devs would lower the consumption of all things considerably, I could see myself being wrapped up for an entire weekend of play. I hope they are listening.
I love this Sim. But, until there is some balance, and not to make it easy mode, just reasonable. I can not reccomend this Sim at this time. Once there is balance, I will highly reccommend it.

Hi guys this is Vladimir’s Justice and this is my review of the LIF: Forest Village.

Straight away lets jump right into it comrades. This game is a medieval village simulator that is still in alpha version, which means there are lot of things that will get better. As to the relation with the Banished I have to say that after playing both games (I owned Banished for a while) one could tell that FV is heavily borrowed from Banished. However I can’t say if that was intentional or subconscious. One can argue that both games were influenced and inspired by Settlers games.

In terms of gameplay FV has quite a nice flow. First couple of years tend to be the most difficult and then once a player completes building all the structures it turns into a baby sitting game which is fine with me. So if you are a fan of those kind of games, then I would recommend it.

The artistic style is similar to the LIF and it is kind of a cool thing if you are a fan of the game. The graphics are pretty nice and the world feels solid. However the first person view feels like a gimmick and didn’t give me any incentive to use it.

There are few variables in the starting menu that could be tweaked to raise the level of challenge but it is nothing like the Rimwold for example. Tutorial is informative and gives a player good foundation knowledge of how the game works. The content is still limited and I feel like it definitely needs more filling. Hopefully that at the time of the release it will have more guts to it.

There are few features that require more work, mainly stability ( it didn’t crush every 30 min though) and the way terraforming is implemented (personally I think we could have done without it) can throw spanner into the works of a player who like symmetrical planning).

My recommendation is that if you don’t mind paying the price, it will pay off in the future. It is a lot of money for an alpha game, and my recommended price would be around 15$ US.

Summary:
This soccer-style game is obviously still in the early stages. The gameplay is fun, hold left mouse button down to hold the disk, and release to shoot. The cut-scene and runner artwork is very well done, the "runners" look cool and the heavily outlined style (similar to Borderlands) gives the game a cool comic book feel. The biggest downfall of this game has to be the home screen UI. It is bloated, outdated, and makes you feel like you're playing a pay-to-play game on facebook. All-in-all, the gameplay of Arena: Cyber Evolution is genuinely fun, though they need to focus on sharpening their UI, Increasing their player base, and balancing the runners. I'm going to give it a 2 stars (out of 5) with definite potential.
Pros:
-Gameplay is very fun. Moving with WASD and shooting the disk with the mouse feels good and fluid.
-Intro stage is well done. The "Entry Test" is a good way to immerse the player while also teaching them to play.
-Lines come off of your character to show where your allies and current aim are, giving the game a very cool geometric feel.
-A lot of the artwork is really good, though the UI work is absolutely abhorrent.
-The leveling system is clear and easy to understand
Cons:
-Players move very slow. A small speed bost would help the flow of the game.
-General character balance. There is a goalie ability that can pull the disk to them (even if the disk is already inside the goal) way too frequently. I suggest replacing this with a dive move or increasing the cooldown time to somewhere around a minute.
-Bloated home screen UI. This is the first impression of the game and what people have to stare at while waiting for matches. Put some effort in to it.
Things that need to happen before this game is good:
-Update the awful UI. It looks bloated like a facebook game.
-ENFORCE THE GOAL LINE. If the disk goes past the goal line it should be a point.
-Show a quick replay of the goal after it is made.

Brilliant card deck strategy game.
Use your Ironclads and soldiers to beat a civil war in the USA.
For each move you have action and move points. The game field is quite limited (mostly 5x8 squares) So you have to figure out the right tactic. After every mission your success is awarded with an extra story comic strip. Later you can build your own card decks or beat missions with infinite card dropping. Tip: Use pause button on your Ironclads to stand them. Tip2: You can repair your Ironclads.
This is a combination between turn based card games, real time strategy games, and graphic novels.

Ironclad Tactics presents an entertaining alternate take on historical events, and gameplay elements of a deck-building game combined with sort-of tactical aspects on a grid. Building the decks with new card unlocks is interesting, but only delves so deeply, and, in the end, the game suffers dramatically from poor randomization; I spent more than a few matches constantly drawing only the least useful cards in my deck, which is an even larger hinderance when it's clear that the computer has very plain advantages over the player in terms of deck power and how often the computer seems to get exactly the card it needs to stop my already weak advance. All in all, the game is fun for a few hours, and then frustrating for the rest.

This is one of the most unique puzzle/"platformer" games you'll ever see. The unique control concept is intuitive and drives all the puzzles. It also has a great progression of difficulty in both the puzzles and the need for speed and precision, and hits all the right notes for this type of game.
Being a puzzle game at heart it's on the short side, but between the secret collectibles, no death runs, and just generally seeing how much you've improved, it has better replayability than the average puzzle game. And in any case you're getting a unique experience you won't find anywhere else.
One caveat: You will need a lot of patience to enjoy this game. Approached from the wrong mindset, the game is quite slow. You can spend a long time shaving off little bits to force yourself in the desired direction, and it doesn't really force you to learn how to go fast until halfway through the game. Also, each level is extremely long (the last 3 levels each took me just over an hour to beat), so by the end of each one I found myself praying for the boss to show up so I could do something else.

STO is fun. I've been playing it off and on since it came out in 2009 and it's consistently gotten better with every update. I like how it mixes things up, letting you shoot stuff in space, and then letting you shoot stuff on the ground. Don't get your hopes up too much, though, this is not a faithful recreation of Star Trek at all. It has the races, the ships, and a lot of the characters (or their descendents) which you might be familiar with. However, the game is set in a time of war, and it's 90% combat focused with only a little bit of diplomacy, exploration, and solving mysteries (time loops, anomalies, mistaken identity, etc).
However, some of the storylines are really quite clever, and with the Foundry system, you'll run into some even more clever storylines created by players.
The customization options are fantastic. You can play around a dozen or so different races, both genders, and you can deck out your character and crew into whatever kinds of uniforms you want. What's more, it also has multiple costume slots, so you can mix things up. There are 30 or so different hairstyles, plus various accessories, tattoos, and multiple head and body sliders.
The class (role) system takes a little getting used to. You can do the typical tank/healer/damage trinity, but those roles aren't always obvious. You have to think about what skills you choose for yourself and your crew. On the other hand, there's a ton of flexibility there, so almost every character can be unique.
The game also has level scaling and mission difficulty sliders, so it's very accessible for casual players, or you can crank it up for a challenge. Missions also scale to group size. It's a great game with loads of content and really shows what you can do if you think outside the MMO box a little.
Monetization? Most people consider it to be fair. Personally, I'll typically subscribe to a game if it has the option and I like it. That's just me. There are some really nice items you can purchase from the cash shop, but it's perfectly viable to play this game for dozens, even hundreds of hours, and still have a great time without ever spending a dime. I wouldn't recommend it though. If you like something, support it! Vote with your wallet!

A pretty solid package overall, but one with some significant issues.
Good:
-gameplay is excellent, controls feel good and natural
-closer to classic survival horror, not an all out action game- has many elements of Resident Evil and The Last of Us, though characters and story are not as interesting
-great atmosphere and graphics, grossly/disturbingly gory, gruesome- maybe moreso than any game I've ever played.
-DLC really changes up the gameplay
Bad:
-technically pretty poor- I have frame drops that make no sense on my GTX 980Ti even though Steam frame counter says I rarely go under around 80fps during gameplay. Just poorly optimized.
-Not enough save points and no auto save- sometimes you will have to play for up to a half hour without being able to save, and the checkpoints are very spaced apart.
-Many cheap one hit kills- the worst thing about the game for me are the numerous sequences where you can be killed with one hit, which are often extremely hard to avoid- I seriously hated those parts. I think it was Chapter 9 that was just an awful example of this.
-matches never seemed to work consistently- some enemies seemed to walk over burning bodies and wouldn't catch on fire.
-Juli Kidman's in game model doesn't match the picture on her ID card very well- whoever did the 3D model didn't do a very good job on her face
-Even on casual this game can be unforgivingly tough and frustrating- it's not like Dark Souls tough, where you usually feel you died because it was your faullt- oftentimes in this game you'll die and if feels completely unfair- I got really angry several times.
I know that looks like a lot of negatives, but if you can look past the cheap one hit kills especially, this is pretty good game- overall I'd give the main game a B+.
The first 2 DLCs are interesting, featuring much more stealth based gameplay from Juli's pov, although you'll be going through a lot of the more visually uninteresting/generic looking environments ripped from the main game, but I enoyed it enough. Probably a B- overall.
The 3rd DLC is a first person combat mode- I found it kind of fun at first, but it quicky gets frustrating due to difficulty spikes and sluggish feeling fps controls, and I admit giving up on it around halfway. I'd probably give it a C-, others may get more enjoyment with it than I did.
Overall, including the DLC, this is a very solid package and I can certainly recommend it, keeping in mind it is absolutely not for kids.
One last note- the game and DLC total is almost 60GB, so make sure you have plenty of space on your hard drive. I for one am getting kind of sick of these monstrously sized games- developers need to do more to make these games take us less space.

So the thing why this game is better your average psychological horror/walking simulator is not because the psychology itself, rather the way it shows it. It's not scary and it's barely a game, but in exchange you get great symbolism and gorgeous art style, that's the least from a game having art as the main subject. The themes are dark and personal, although we can't be entirely sure what exactly happened, but that probably adds to the game. Why? Because we know one thing for sure: the character we control is a maniac and has basically zero sense of reality, I doubt he knows exactly what he had done, therefore we don't know either.
What sucks is that it's a walking simulator and it's ridiculously short. It wasn't an overwhelming experience, but it was a good one. I'd just be glad if developers making psychological horrors stopped making their games this short. It's not artsy or anything to not leave room for character development. It's just not complete, just for example look at Silent Hill 2 or Cat Lady, those games are longer, therefore they can show more, more character development (can) brings more symphathy for the characters, more complexity and depth. Just because you fill your game with notes, even if they are interesting, it won't bring the same satisfaction.
So, I don't know. I liked it, but if not on sale, I can't recommend. Objectively it's a good game, so whatever.

This is a very different kind of puzzle platformer. You control a green mass of what I'm assuming is fungus (given the title of the game) by pushing and erasing its edges by swiping the mouse, clicking over it. These erased bits are pushed out of all sides of the blob, and it's your job to use this strange movement mechanic to latch onto bolts, spurt through tunnels, and jump over death pits. It's unlike anything I've ever played.
The artwork for the different worlds is excellent. You obviously traverse some sort of post-apocalyptic wasteland with only bugs (that you consume for points) and mutant bosses as survivors. The boss fights are complex, but doable.
I completed the first five (out of seven) stages. I enjoyed the first three or four worlds, but the last couple I tried--worlds five and six--didn't make the game more challenging, just frustrating. This exasperation stems from the lack of control you have over how your blob forms itself. You cannot force it to grow the way you want, and this will cause you to take damage and die for little fault of your own in the later levels. When it's my fault for screwing up a platforming puzzle, I have no trouble repeating the task ad naseum until I get it right. When it's part of the game's design mechanics, and whelp, too bad, get over it... I'm less motivated to play.
This is mostly a positive review. I find unbalanced game design killing you to be one of gaming's cardinal sins, but I understand that's probably not the case for everyone.

Mushroom 11 has some interesting concepts and is generally fun for the first 45 minutes to an hour (up through chapter 3 I would say). From there on out it starts feeling far too luck based. As you progress in the game you don't gain any more control over the blob so the challenge in puzzles starts feeling more like getting lucky with how the blob grew at a specific point in time as opposed to simply being about your skill. Due to that fact and the general feeling of frustration I can't recommend this game. It doesn't feel satisfying to complete the puzzles, it simply feels like you happened to get lucky doing the exact same thing you did the last 10 times.
Interesting for a few minutes, but I can't recommend it.

If you've ever played a collectible card game, do you enjoy constructing a deck as much as actually playing the game? If so, then you'll probably enjoy Ironclad Tactics.
It's possible to slog your way through missions with sub-optimal builds/tactics, and granted, it is incredibly frustrating when played in that manner. The core missions are tolerant of bad play, so you can get pretty far into the game before realizing what you're doing wrong. After unwittingly playing badly throughout the main campaign, I eventually hit a wall in the additional content.
The final mission of New Game Plus was particularly brutal, and I barely beat it after a couple hours of reckless attempts. As I moved onto the DLC missions, I found myself frequently devastated by the enemy having 1.5-2 times the resources that I do. Slogging through these missions was becoming increasingly unlikely, and I was questioning whether these missions were fairly balanced. Did I have to rely on the AI screwing up to stand a chance, or was there another way?
At that point, I approached the game from a different angle. First play a mission noncommitally with a simple deck, just to grasp what's being thrown my way. Then go to the drawing board and construct a deck particularly for that mission. With that mindset, I was crushing missions on the first "serious attempt" and feeling accomplished in my decision making.
Playing in this manner is a bit artificial. In what other game do you play a level for the first time solely to analyze it, with no intent of winning? I wonder if Ironclad Tactics could have been more forthcoming with its mission content, rather than have players flail through the motions with an uncatered deck.
I recommend trying Ironclad Tactics with the "study first, succeed later" approach. That's what tipped me into the "recommended" camp. This is certainly a game for analysts/tinkerers.

Are you a social outcast who has no friends?  Do you wish to indulge in the fantasy of interacting with
but through the safety of a virtual medium? Then look no further, this game is for you poor, poor, lonely soul.
Now I realize this sounds like every

on Steam ever but trust me on this one, this ain't nothin' like that. Why
you are going around, hunting down people like their Pokemon tossing all sorts of sh*t to befriend them, but the game takes a fairly "realistic" approach to this. Sure, while you do end up actually befriending some people, (whatever that is.) such is not always the case. Some characters begrudgingly add you to your friend list just to stop you from bothering them anymore. Not to mention they still act like total assh*les to you even after befriending them. Considering how many supposedly "anti-social" VN protagonists are actually charismatic gods, this MC is a weird fellow and acts like the part. So yeah, if you're concerned that this is yet another game where everyone worships the MC at the end, fear not, there will be people who are either merely putting up with him or outright dislike him even though they're supposedly "friends."
While the subplots are good, the process of unlocking them can be a tad tedious. Not too much to be a major flaw  but still annoying. For one, you need to buy items that specific character likes (Though if you're lazy you can totally brute force it by just using the cheapest item on everyone.) which costs bits. These can only be earned by
playing either Puyo Puyo or Tetris. While these minigames are fun (No sh*t it's f*cking Tetris/Puyo Puyo.) it does disrupt the flow of narrative quite drastically. Running out of bits means the player has to stop whatever they were doing and spend time playing minigames they might not actually enjoy. Or perhaps enjoy but dislike due to the fact they are forced to play it to make any further progress. Now of course, the devs were wise enough to consider this and gives the player an option to get 999999 bits right from the start. Unfortunately, this option is hidden away (in the bottom right corner of the room where you buy stuff.) without any hints to it's existence...at least none I'm aware of. This could be chalked up to me just being dumb and not noticing it and if so, then I'll drop this point completely. Another quality of life issue would be being able to buy items directly from the inventory screen instead of having to backtrack constantly.
But all the above is mere nitpicking, the game overall is an excellent experience well worth your time. Interesting character designs, endearing characters, a nice soundtrack (Ah one last nitpick: I would recommend not having a vocal track during sequences that require deep thought e.g: the discussion/talking segment. While nice, the lyrics end up being a distraction to the player. Though perhaps it's just me...) and an intriguing story all make up for a great game.
I highly recommend this game!

Ah, 1bitheart, my favourite of the three miwashiba games.
Anyway, short in short, this is, in my opinion, a well made and visually appealing game. The low price tag certainly nets you more than you can buy, and then some.
First off, the story: Nanase Yoshi, a fourteen-year-old boy who goes by the moniker "Nanashi", is a reclusive, yet outwardly cheerful shut-in during a time period where technology has advanced rapidly. One day, he discovers a girl fast asleep in his bed who, when woken up, proclaims she has lost her memories.
Sound familiar?
Despite the use of cliches, the game doesn't feel stale. The story itself is, admittedly, not the most complex or thought-provoking story of all time, and there are certainly better ones out there, but it doesn't make any glaring flaws that turn someone off from playing the game entirely, unless you're a temporal scientist, theorist or fanatic. The characters, both main and side, are all certainly quirky and enjoyable to watch as your cast stumbles through a rather slipshod plot, and there are some genuinely funny moments that you'll grin at, as well as some surprisingly philosophical rhetoric that you wouldn't expect.
However, know that, in my opinion, the story and plot is perhaps the weakest portion of this game, and not something you should be expecting a whole lot out of. (Though that's not to discount the entire writing at all; there are certainly some better parts than others and it's still worth reading.)
Next, the gameplay; the game plays out like Danganronpa; using information you've received from the story to find holes in someone else's story and progress forwards afterwards. As a big danganronpa fan myself, this was a very welcomed way to progress, and it, for the most part, was smooth and intuitive, though admittedly sometimes it wasn't very mentally stimulating due to either A: being too easy to deduce, or B: being too *hard* to deduce. There were definitely a few kinks in the system (particularly the discrepancy between "present a topic" and "hold a sec!"), but those are fairly easy to pick around and ignore afterwards.
Now, that isn't the only part of the game. The second portion of the game is Making Friends. Surprisingly uncommon and inane, but nevertheless decently executed. The friend system works like Danganronpa as well: give a character a gift and, if enough gifts are received, a scenario will play out between Nanashi and whichever Side Character you've chosen to befriend. Eventually, at the end of a short side-story, Nanashi befriends the character and goes on his merry way.
Admittedly, this portion of the game could've been done better and had more effort put into it. The characters, while quirky and all (okay, maybe mostly depending on how you enjoy characters) lovable and appealing, lack a major impact on the plot, and, if it weren't for some factors affected by your friend count, could very well be erased from the game entirely. The sidequest storylines were rather unfulfilling, and it certainly made me wish that these side characters received more screen time, writing and character depth (though with an impressive number of side characters, that may be a feat in and of itself). However, the characters are still, for the most part, fun to interact with (for the limited amount of conversation they have with Nanashi)
(and a bonus nitpick from me: You buy the gifts on Nanashi's computer in his bedroom, and you get "bits" (the currency) from playing the games on the console in the middle. I either missed this explanation or the game lacked it entirely, and I didn't learn of this until the final chapter)
Finally, the visual presentation of this game. One of the best parts of the game without a doubt, and where miwashiba shines. The artwork is, simply put, stunning to look at. The colour palettes are extremely easy and enticing to the eyes, the sprite work is very well made, and the character designs are all extremely appealing, all of which are very typical of miwashiba. Admittedly, some of the backgrounds can be a bit simple, but the minimalistic feel doesn't necessarily detract from the overall presentation, and it feels complete. On a plus, the voice lines (while in japanese) are pleasant to hear, though admittedly you won't hear much of it.
Oh, and did I ever mention the music? The music in this game is amazing.
All in all, 1bitheart is definitely a game that's worth picking up for the amount of money that it costs (especially when it goes on sale), and I wholeheartedly recommend it.
++PROS++
Stellar visual presentation
Smooth, simple and intuitive gameplay
Amazing music.
Likable characters.
More content than expected for the price tag
--CONS--
Slipshod storyline
Lack of side-character interaction/depth
Slightly unintuitive game choices

Unfortunately, it struggles to reach a status any higher than this. It had great potential when i first played it before it was on steam. I occasionally returned just to see that all the basic flaws did not get fixed or were made even worse over a period of over 2 years.
Biggest drawbacks for me (besides clunky interfaces, bugs and other technical issues that could be forgiven for a game in BETA) are: 1. The horrible grind (it takes very long to unlock troop classes, weapons, equipment, ranks), 2. The insanely messed up economy. You pay for everything-  used bullets, used grenades, vehicle repairs (only if you spent 100 hours to unlock them in the first playce lol), even if you use a scope you have to repair it for credits or gold after battle! The prices are also out of sanity. You have to pay nearly 100k credts for a bolt action rifle (and get like 5k max as a beginner per battle). Depending on your view it makes this game either a pay2win or pay2play. 3. The online game with the most unstable servers i've ever played. 4. It also has a very unbalanced faction population (get ready to get stomped by german faction a lot).
It's also very beginner unfriendly. You start with crappy equipment and get matched against people who play the game for a long time and have unlocked all the good stuff. And it is expensive and takes a long time to get on a somewhat even level. Until that point you basically get slaughtered a lot.
Also, the devs seem to like to annoy you and take stuff away from you. For example, a few updates ago everyone was able to take part in the RTS part of the game, buy som assault teams and send them into battle. Then they decided you have to grind out a general (which basically takes some 300 hours playtime or 50€ worth of gold) to be able to do that. Suddenly half of the game was locked away.
Or you grind to unlock a tank, you use that tank a lot, and they decide to put in a special ribbon for that tank that makes you have to unlock ammo types before you can effectively use it in war etc...
TL DR: The game can be fun if you don't expect anything good from it. If that's not your attitude, i don't recommend it

Another one of the games that I would rather rate with mixed than positive or negative. In the end I go with positive here, since the fantastic design and atmosphere outweigh the many frustrations that you have to fight along the way.
The Evil Within is the logical continuation of the resident evil franchise, it plays a lot like Resident Evil 4 and resource management not unlike the original trilogy is an important factor. The game really brings the original Resident Evil formula to new life by giving you a weak underpowered protagonist going against relatively strong monstrous enemies in very very creepy and blood-soaked environments, constantly counting the number of remaining bullets. The game works greatly when it sticks to this formula, when it tries to ramp up into hectic bigger fights it gets frustrating fast unfortunately.
The game sometimes throws in horde-mode encounters, some where you need to kill all enemies, survive a certain amount of time against endless spawns or achieve a certain objective to end the encounter. The game mechanics simply are not build for those scenarios, protagonist Sebastian is much less agile as Leon Kennedy, he runs and turns relatively slow, is out of breath after 2 seconds of sprinting and can only jump through windows after shooting or smashing them. You might survive a hectic assault, low on health and out of ammo, and what does the game do, throw a boss fight at you right after the next door. Or you early one you could navigate a village full of enemies stealthily to reach an objective instead of engaging the enemies and what is your reward, you will have to deal with all the enemies that you avoided on top of the boss that you need to kill (and pray you updated your run-stamina for the first boss, or you can better restart the chapter). There is one resource that you use to upgrade weapons, skills, ammo capacity and use to buy ammunition. There is never enough of it! Dead Space balanced that pretty well, Evil Within is overly tight with it.
I like hard games, I played all the Souls games and more often than not play horror games on higher difficulty settings. The Evil Within is not hard because it requires skill and great reaction. It feels artificially hard because I constantly felt like the game is not giving me the tools and mechanics I would need to stand a fighting chance. Stealth, while encouraged, falls flat when enemies randomly turn around when you approach sneaking up behind them or spot you around a corner.
The story might not be for everyone, the game is structured like a nightmare, where dream logic applies and worldly rules are irrelevant. The narrative is confusing at first, but things come together nicely in the end. Enemy and Sound design are spectacular, the weapons feel great (if you happen to have ammo for it) and search for collectables might motivate for another run. The game is also fairly long (might be inflated, since you will die a lot).
I recommend this to horror fans. And I would really like to see a sequel, either direct or spiritual. However the designers really should do a better job of mapping the mechanics to the challenges, a bit more fine-tuning on the balance would have made this a great horror game. What we have is a good horror game with too many frustrating stumbling on its journey.
Pros:
- enemy and sound design
- dream-like weird but captivating story
- constantly tense, scary or disgusting
Cons:
- horde encounters feel unfair
- resource limitations more stressful than necessary

I (still) really want to like this better. Truthfully, its not bad,and while it's gotten better, its still not not great yet either.
Be forewarned....this is not your typical city builder/management sim. In fact, after I finished playing for several hours today, I realized just how little it actually has to do with city building. It has more to do with management than it does city building, but even that is more time management than anything. If I were to break it down, I would say that this game is 60% time management, 30% resource management, and 10% city building.
When you first start out. you really want to NOT grow. In fact you dont really want to grow until late into your second year, or better yet, your third. You will grow anyways, because you have to build a hut right off the bat, but dont build any other houses until, like I said, your 2nd or 3rd year preferablly. Your going to have to have a lot of patience.
In fact, I would say that is the main goal of the game, is "wait". For everything. For the entire durationof the game.
So expect, especially in the early years, do a lot of watching, and very little playing.
Having said that, going slow does NOT make the game uninteresting, just slow.
At this point, I have managed to get my village to last a whopping 21 years. It is still alive, but I just lost almost half my citizens, (9 of them),to starvation. We'll see what happens.
I've only had a few glitches. This bout of starvation was due to a glitch. In part, due to my not paying full attention. Usually, the game warns you if your food reserves are low. I dont know when it stopped doing that, but I received no messages informing me that I was running low, so I didn't focus on the numbers under the food icons in the barn......my bad.
Right now, to me, the biggest issues are with balance, and/or a lack of options.
One of the things that I miss about Banished, is that in LiF:FV, you can send your worked out to look for trees, rocks, ore, and hay. But NOT food. In Banished, I could look at my food stocks and go, "Hmmm, those aren't great, and winter is almost here.....I should send all my villagers out to look for food while I still have time. Try that in LiF:FV and you'll be sitting there in late winter going, I guess I had better put 3 people, (the max) into my gathering hut and hope they get more than 60 Kcal's in food before snowfall. Thats about 1 days worth of food for 10 people. Kcal's, btw, are LiF:FV's nutritional value system.
Anyways........
It very greatly irritates me that I cannot chose my starting location. I can pick the starting seed, but not where on that seed I will be placed. Once the game put me on this little strand of land that could barely hold the initial housing, barn, and warehouse they pre-place for you. Also the preview of the seed they show you is so small, I am not sure why they bother to show you at all.
The game is not always intuative either.
Many of the buildings in the game are upgradable. But until you have, "unlocked" that upgrade. It doesnt tell you what you'll be upgrading too, or even what you have to do to be able to unlock the upgrade.
Playing in 1st person (1PV) seems kinda cruel. I would probablly enjoy doing it more, if my character didn't walk slower than dead men crawl. And there is no way to speed up your movement while in first person view. You can blow a horn and watch all your other "settle-mates" move faster.....doesn't help you though. Nothing like walking down a wolf thats heading towards your chickens, wondering if you have time to read Moby♥♥♥♥♥♥while you walk there.
I would say that on a scale of 1-5 stars, Banished would be ahead, getting 4.5 stars, while LIF:FV would get only 3.5.
Comparing the two, I found that LIF:FV's UI was bulkier, but contained less info than that of its counterpart.
Also the mouse movement in 1PV are about 100% too sensitive. Barely moving the mouse almost turns your character all the way around. If the the caracter moved as fast as the mouse, It might make sense.....Right now I would be happy if my character moved 1/4 the speed of the mouse.
Hunter's and shepherds do crappy jobs of protecting your livestock. I've been trying to raise pigs for 3 seasons now. Just when I am about 3/4 of the way to getting a second pig, a wolf comes waltzing up and makes that piggie go "weee!!!!!"......all the way to his doom.
Yes, I know i can go into 1PV and kill the wolf. Unfortunately, everytime I have not been there to see it, (I'm on another part of the map trying to do something else), or I get there just as its happening.
The bakery makes about 3-5 loaves of bread/day. I could presonally make 8-9 per/day irl. And thats if I was only making 1 load at a time. Given that this is supposed to be an, "industrial bakery" that will feed all your people....the numbers seem a bit off to me.
These are just a few of the gripes I have while playing LiF:FV. I still enjoy the game, but it still needs a lot more work.

What is a good game? A question posed by the great scholars of not only our generation, but the generations that preceeded us. Up there with the likes of 'Why are we here', 'Is there a god' and 'Why do kids love Cinnamon Toast Crunch?'. Up until this day, this question has never been answered. Which is why I'm here.
A good game invokes emotion. A good game tells a story. A good game, is a good game.
ACE checks all but one of these boxes. ACE gets you to jump out of your seat, fist pumping in the air as you score that game-winning post goal. ACE gets you, head in hands, groaning at the incompotency of your goalie. ACE gets you to do all of this, and more. But what ACE doesn't do, is tell a story. What ACE does, is give the player, the oppurtunity to craft their OWN story. Their OWN legend. A game rich with replayability, a game rich with no glass ceiling, a game rich with a budding, growing e-sports scene. ACE let's you tell your own tale, your tale of bounce shots, your tale of overtime stress-fests, your tale of that one time where you scored a goal by bouncing the puck off their goalie. No other game does this, because no other game can. ACE acheives what very many dream of, but even more will never ever achieve.
Outside of the game, you find the company. The team behind, and pardon the rhyme, the dream. Spearhead Games. Responsible for such successes as Tiny Brains, as Stories. As ACE. With a community manager that cares, and a team of streamers dedicated to bringing you the best content they can at
or
ACE is constantly changing. ACE isn't just a game. Spearhead Games isn't just a company. These two things, brought together, are a fire. A fire that we, the players. We, the viewers. We, the dreamers, stoke. Fuelling that desire to reach for the stars then bring them back. Flames licking at heros. Smoke billowing into the endless sky, the endless possibilites.
I can only tell you so much about ACE. I can only put into words, how great this game is, if you just give it a chance. It's up to you to decide if you like the game. But take it from someone whose not being to paid to say this, but will lose his job if he doesn't.

Summary: This game is fantastic. Well worth full price, a steal when on sale; if you like first-person action co-op games you can't go wrong with this title. It's also playable by yourself with bots.
+Awesome melee combat with great ragdoll physics. Hacking and smashing vermin never gets old.
+Huge, beautiful, dark fantasy maps: rain slicked cobblestone streets of the city of Ubersreik, dark shadowy forests, creepy gothic cemetaries, a sprawling dwarven fortress atop ice-swept mountains... Every map looks hand-crafted and enhances the dark atmosphere of the game. Aspiring game designers should study these levels. They are near perfect.
+Easy to fine-tune the difficulty through the map settings as well as with Grimoires (tomes that limit your max health but offer a greater chance for better loot.
+Excellent voice-acting, every character feels unique and is brimming with personality.
+Each weapon has a very different feel. Two-handers swing slow but hit hard, some weapons are better at killing groups of lesser enemies, etc. The balance isn't 100% perfect, but it's solid and the developer is still tweaking them in patches which is always nice to see.
+Bots will use the weapons the host equips them with. If you get a new weapon for a character you're not playing; you can still use it for a bot when you host.
-Only 5 characters to choose from. They're all different, but it would be fun to have a few more to choose from. I'd love to see an orc added to the mix.
-Bot AI can be quirky, although the recent patch has improved this a bit.
-Failing long missions can be frustrating. You get virtually nothing for failing, even if you made it through most of the map.
-No witchhunter bot. It would be nice if the game randomized (or let you choose) which bots accompany you on a map.

Unique physics gameplay, beautiful hand-drawn like graphics. Can be slightly frustrating at times, but nothing major. Recommended.
EDIT:
I managed to get to the final boss, but could not beat it. Way too difficult for my patience.
Now that I've seen most of the content I also think that the game is a bit overrated. It's good, but not that great. My biggest complaint is the "puzzle" aspect of the game. In general I like when puzzles in games take a bit effort to figure out, and once you do get it, they offer reasonable challenge to solve them. There are few worst case scenarios: a) puzzles that are very easy to figure out and incredibly tedious to solve, b) puzzles that are tedious to figure out and also tedious to solve and c) puzzles that you manage to solve without figuring them out (by luck, by persistence etc).
Unfortunately a lot of the puzzles in this game fall in the category A, and some in B. Many times I figured out the "puzzle" immediately but solving it was so frustrating and lot of retries were needed.
The controls are bit arbitrary and bit frustrating by design as you can only cull the mushroom and not say where it should grow. But this is ok, it's the thing in the game. The game also has quite good camera work in principle, but unfortunately together with the controls this creates a huge source of frustration.
Even if you keep your mouse still, the moving camera affects the area where the mouse is culling the mushroom, and there's also a feedback loop where changing mushroom shape affects the movement of the camera. This was not bad as it propably sounds, but at times it was infuriating. Sometimes I was wanting for the mouse to move in WORLDSPACE, not in screenspace. That might have solved some of the issues...
Anyway, I do recommend this game. It's one of its kind, and really interesting take on the physics puzzle platformers. Despite all the frustration.

After finally beating the game after a few hours, I feel I need to write a review.
I got this game as part of the freedom humble bundle. This game is like nothing I have ever played before. The first level is pretty easy, but as you progress, it gets extremely hard, to the point of almost giving up. For some obstacles you need the slime to be in a certain shape in order to get past them. However, the slime regenerates randomly, meaning you have to carefully thin out the slime and pray it grows in the directions you want. When you need the slime to split into pieces, the camera also seems to wonk out bases on how close to the end each chunk is. I eventually started callining the slime "RNG slime". I used the name to yell at it or praise it when things worked, the thing drove me crazy. The second hardest thing with the RNG is when you have to fly missiles in one of the chapters. However, the obstacle that took the longest was when I had to pick a lock with the slime in the last chapter. It was very rewarding to fianlly beat the game.
Pros:
Beautiful art and music, gives off a cool dystopian apocalypse feel
Tons of checkpoints
Interesting mechanics
Cute slime mold creature
Fun boss levels (excluding the rocket one :P )
Difficult but rewarding levels
Cons:
Not for the faint of heart or low of patience
Difficulty spikes randomly, several obstacles will be easy, with an obstacle that takes an hour in the middle of them
Sometime obstacles depend on how lucky you are with RNG growth
Did I mention how difficult some parts are?
Overall, I enjoyed the experience. If they ever do update the game, I think a boss rush level would be nice for those who beat all the chapters.
Hopefully you will give it a try!

"When Ironclad Tactics was pitched to me as a ‘fast-paced, card-based tactics game’ set during the American Civil War, I have to admit, I was skeptical. Little did I know that it featured ROBOTS!"

Ironclad Tactics is a fast paced real time strategy card game set in a fictitious civil war era featuring steam powered robot warriors. The game features lovely artwork offering charming and funny comic strip style cut scenes. The core gameplay is centered on constricting your deck of 20 cards consisting of various human and machine warriors along with weapons and perks you can apply in combat.  You start the game with three randomly drawn cards and earn more cards upon one full cycle of the brief timer that counts as each turn, upon the completion of the turn you are also awarded an Action Point that you use to activate the cards from your hand. The main objective of each mission is to earn a set number of victory points that are obtained by one of your ironclad warrior robot troops successfully getting from one end of the battlefield to the other.
The fast paced nature of the game is both what makes the game shine and at the same time is its biggest hindrance, the fact that you have to make decisions so quickly eliminates the ability to really thoroughly strategize and plan out your next move as would a turn based strategy card game would, however this little bit of hectic fast paced chaos is what makes the game different from other card lane strategy games.  Upon completion of the mission you are awarded with a new set of cards that have some unique twist or element that was the featured gimmick of the level.
The game does offer a fairly steep difficulty curve that can become frustrating at times but adds to the overall length and replay-ability of the game when you have to go back and rework a new deck to try to conquer your highly competent AI foe. The game perfectly combines the good of both a Trading card game and a card lane strategy game; it offers a lovely art style, interesting setting, and a very challenging level of difficulty

Great for Star Trek fans...a typical MMO for others.
The game combines third person shooter with space sim to produce a fairly unique game overall.
Players are asked to choose a faction, which affects the look of the ships you have access to, as well as the initial plot and storyline. Players are then asked to choose a player class (usual rpg mechanics of tank, dps or support) and then a ship class (again from tank, dps or support). Your player class is fixed (unless you pay real money to change it), but your ship class can change as you see fit. This allows for different combinations and playstyles. There are multiple ships per class with slightly different stats and better ships and equipment is unlocked as you level up.
The ship combat is definitely a highlight of the game. It is real time combat and moving your ship whilst using abilities and blasting your enemy with your weapons is satisfying. The ground third person shooter aspect feels less enjoyable and ground sections can feel dull and boring.
As well as equipment, you can obtain bridge crew - other characters who will fight in ground combat with you and provide abilities for use in space combat. Like the player's character, they can be fully customised
In terms of content, there is plenty to do. The main storyline is interesting enough and can take a long time to complete, not to mention that it is constantly being added to. There are also plenty of side missions, seasonal events and also player created missions, the best of which are regularly put into the game. There are also the regular group pve and pvp missions.
As usual for an MMO, expect to do a large amount of grinding. Leveling up actually is not too bad, as you can reach the level cap fairly quickly. Grinding for equipment and reputation to gain better equipment will take up A LOT of time though.
Overall, it is a fairly decent MMO and worth looking into if you're a Star Trek fan or into space sims.

This game is great.
The game is free to play, and from what I've seen, the free version is good enough. I wouldn't know, because the beta had me hooked, and I signed up for a lifetime subscription before they went free to play. Even though they went free to play, I don't regret the lifetime subscription. This game is great.
There are two things that are awesome about this game:
1. Episodes. They have a bunch of quests in the game that are built together into an episode. Which mimics what you might see on the show. Usually they have some space battles, and some ground battles, and they always have great stories. The rest of the quests in the game are meh. Holidays can be fun, but I've never put tons of hours into those. Story missions bring me back. Not much else.
2. Space Combat. I love the style of space combat. Having to worry about shield strength, and positioning is a lot of fun. And because of the game's difficulty system, you can make it easy or difficult. Great thinking.
Things that are great, but not awesome:
1. Duty Rosters. It's basically giving everyone on your crew something to do. It's kinda like a minigame, and it can be tons of fun, but it doesn't have the epic feel of the Episodes or the Space combat, because it's just a quest.
Things that are not great:
1. Ground combat. It's not amazing, but it's fine.
2. Daily / repeatable quests. Boring. I thought I would really like the exploration system, but it wasn't really exploration the way I wanted it. It was grinding. Some of the storyline missions are repeatable, and that's not what I'm talking about, I'm talking about the quests that just keep coming back, like patrol missions and such. Meh. I just skip them. I can never even bring myself to clean more than one out of my mission log in any given month, so the few I've collected mostly just sit there.
Things I've got mixed feelings on:
1. "Guild" system. I'm in a guild, but I don't really feel like I do much with it. There's fun things to do with a group, but I can do most of the stuff I want to do without a group. I'd like to do some of the content that's multiplayer exclusive, but I want an easier way to do it.
2. Reputation.  The Reputation systems are kinda interesting but pretty grindy. I haven't committed months of my life to this game, but there's stuff to do if this is where you want to spend your time.

From a Gameplay perspective LiF:FV is extremely similar to Banished, however in my opinion this is NOT a bad thing in the slightest. I enjoyed Banished, but LiF:FV is graphically beautiful, and the ability to zoom in and watch your town grow and move, as well as the ability to hop into your peasants brain is amazing to me. One of my favorite experiences was learning the hard way about growing too fast(this game is slow paced for a reason) and almost lost my entire village in Y6 due to a food shortage, but with quick thinking and a little bit of forced homelessness I was able to salvage my people and grow beyond where I was when it fell apart.

"In a post-nuclear wasteland, you're controlling a radioactive mushroom that can regenerate itself from a single molecule. Therefore, you're able to shape your own form to progress forward and solve puzzles." This is the premise of Mushroom 11, a puzzle platformer.
Having such an original mechanic in a game, although it could be fun and interesting, would usually require some adaptation time from the player. But there is nothing out of the sort in Mushroom 11. It's instinctive, it makes sense, it feels great to play right from the get go. It's such a joy to twist your mushroom around that you barely even notice you're solving physics based puzzle.
The game is generous with checkpoints, basically give you one after each obstacle, so you will never have to replay a serie of puzzles already solved. That makes for a pleasant pace, and you feel like you're constantly moving forward with a difficulty that ramps up progressively.
However, i do think the game falters a bit on its 7th and last chapter as this level is way more difficult and longer than the rest, introducing new mechanics constantly with trial and error the only way to understand how theses new physical objects work. I think it would have been nicer to split the level in 2, and maybe introduce things with less deadly puzzles, as it took me about as much to complete this chapter as it took me to finish the 6 previous levels.
Nevertheless, the short length and the low starting difficulty should make this game acccessible to a large public.
If you wish for more gameplay and/or more challenge, the game keep tracks of your collectibles and will reward with achievements to complete a level while getting them all or without dying.

I've been playing Ironclad Tactics off and on for a big time Only now, after earning lot's card, I realize that I forgot to write a review.
The pace is realtime, but it moves slow enough to allow some thinking time for your next moves. Most of the challenge comes from building specialized decks to solve the puzzle that each level presents. Your AI opponent will have the upper hand with some new attack or defense and you’ll have to come up with a counter. Most of the time this results in a tense battle of planning, wits, and fortune. When you tweak a deck combo into working just right it feels great! Each new card opens up lots of tactical options and completing challenges for cards feels rewarding.
The civil war theme and story are awesome. I love the characters and animated comics that set up you journey across America. The in-game art and animation is beautiful. It’s easy to tell every unit apart and their abilities match the visuals. A robot with a jetpack files, dude with a shotgun has spread attack, and a flame thrower hits multiple targets. .
Each level starts by showing you 5 random cards from your deck of 20, so sometimes it feels like a lucky/unlucky start can make or break a win. If cards come out in just the wrong order it can kill a plan, but managing this problem is also part of the art of deck building. It improved a bit with the release of the first DLC where you can now spend 1 action point to ‘save’ a critical card for later.
The first DLC uses an army with a completely different and fun style of play. It’s satisfying playing as the boss enemies that were beating you down in the final levels and to understanding the logic behind how their robots transform. It also fills in missing parts of the story with more comics.
Not every ability or tactic is perfectly balanced, but there’s lots of viable strategies to solve each problem. That said, I haven’t played multiplayer which would be a much better gauge of balance. There’s not enough players to support random matchmaking and I don’t feel like it would be that fun against friends (even if they unlocked all the cards). I also haven’t tried the co-op mode, which is supported throughout the entire game but I think it would be pretty fun!

So, I loved this game. Keep that in mind while I review it, because I'm going to say some things that might seem negative. Layers of Fear is a wholly atmospheric game with very little in the way of gameplay, a 'haunted house simulator' along the vein of Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs. Very much inspired by P.T., it uses its environment to scare and unnerve you instead of relying on jump scares or forced stealth gameplay. The story is quite obvious, and the game uses numerous cliches, but for me, it simply worked. The 'paint' and 'painting' theming was well used, and it had some very good set pieces to it.
I do, however, have one major complaint. The game (apparently) has multiple endings based on some of the choices you made during play. This, and how well some of the mementos, drawings and letters were hidden made me feel like the developers were trying to force replayability into a game that, since it's akin to a walk-through haunted house, will never have any.
If you don't mind a few playthroughs to see absolutely everything, and you don't mind an experience that's low on gameplay(like A Machine for Pigs, Dear Esther, or Gone Home) then this is an excellent horror game.

This game expects you to play it over again until you get the "good" ending. I don't have the patience to go through the same crap doing differently subtle things in order to witness an ending that I can easily find on YouTube if my curiousity strikes hard enough. If you get this game for maybe 10 dollars, I recommend it but at full price.... no. Overall this game is gorgeous but it lacks game play. Its puzzles are plentiful and the environment constantly changes around you but its....a walking simulator type game. You can't really die. You don't get chased by anything, you just run into them and then you progress further indicating you didn't really die, rather you went through the motions.
The game is too short for 20 dollars is mainly why I don't recommend it. Took me 3.3 hours according to my Steam hour counter to complete the bad ending. It does have a cool and more unique kind of plot to it that I haven't seen before in other horror games. Its a psychological horror game and you are in the mind of a painter trying to make the perfect painting in his eyes. Throughout the game you are collecting materials (sort of) and then putting a painting together using those materials. As you progress further into the game, so does the painting and overtime, you see it form into what he's trying to paint. Alas, you get the bad ending, they tell you the painting sucks. Spoiler Alert. Oops.
So you can't die and the game is a puzzle fest. Yet, even for puzzles, they were rather easy for me. No puzzle had me there for a half hour. It was like maybe 10 minutes max that I was stuck on one puzzle.
This game copies the Penumbra/Amnesia style of game play where you can manually open things like doors or drawers and that's about it. You can't really pick up things and move them around.
This game disappointed me. Once you figure out that you're not really in harms way, you might as well stop caring like I did. I was not scared of the game anymore and I just went through the rest of the journey until I was told that my painting sucks. Spoiler Alert again. Yeah, if its 10 dollars or less, pick it up unless you don't own Outlast. Then buy Outlast and play that instead.

Your trigger finger will have to be disciplined so that you will have enough firepower to defeat or slow down larger enemies, such as bosses.
The Evil Within has a upgrade system that allows you to power up guns, character traits (sprinting, health), item storage, and the effects of bolts. Throughout the game, you will have to collect the goo-like remains from defeated foes in order to improve your weapons and yourself.
The soundtrack is great but not for all tracks. There are only several levels that the instrumental sounds were perfectly utilized and left a feeling of dread and despair.
The story starts the player off with a plethora of quesitons. especially in the beginning. It can't be helped but be dragged into the life of the game. How did it all happen? What do the manifsted buildings and levels mean?  Questions are enlightned with files. flashbacks, and recordings.
Get the game when you get the chance.

The number of insta-deaths starts racking up and makes it frustrating/annoying, which when you're annoyed, you're not scared. I loved the scarce-ammo dynamic early on, yes if you used a guide I'm sure there's plenty of ammo but it certainly feels stingy for most of the game (in a good way, ammo wouldn't just be laying around everywhere). The insta-deaths really start to ruin the gameplay though, since some of the parts are basically trial and error (die and try again), like you're supposed to know at certain points Ruvik will kill you with a single touch or things like that. On top of that, there's plenty of what I consider poor world coding. Like, certain shrubs are giant blocks you can't walk through, things that seem climable aren't, etc. Those sorts of things that really kill the immersion factor.
The story was, well, whatever at first. At points it seems interesting, but it's basically a big ol' inception BS plotline that really doesn't make much sense and while DLC may explain some of it, I'm not going to play no-ammo DLC, that sounds tedious.
I'd recommend this to those who are fine with all of the above. It certainly has its moments where it was enjoyable and left you wanting to play more when you'd stop, but there are just too many issues to say its a fully recommended game.

Layers of Fear follows the struggles of a painter as works to complete one final painting after his life has fallen into ruin. Piecing together layers of fear's story through letters and images is surprisingly fun due to good writing and interesting, well paced plot development. I found myself looking forward to reading each new story fragment. The story is suitably dark, greatly adding to the overall tension of the experience.
Layers of Fear is often terrifying, making good use of well paced and foreshadowed jump scares and thick tension. However, Layers of Fear truly excels when it is most surreal. No frightening moments were quite as memorable as watching furniture swirl around a room to the sound of classical music.
Layers of Fear also bears a strikingly distinct visual style. Hallways are littered with beautiful and bizarre paintings, many of which serve as nice motifs throughout the game. Many of these paintings carry unique and unsettling looks which make them instantly recognizable. Apart from the visual style, Layers of Fear is also one of the best looking games I have ever seen on the Unity engine, and serves as a testament to the power and flexibility of Unity's tool set. Sound design is also good, although it does make use of some fairly familiar noises. They are all well implemented, but be prepared to hear some high pitch screeches and other common horror sounds. One area of the sound design that does not suffer is the music, which always comes on at just the right time. It is peaceful and provides great contrast to the dark atmosphere.
Layers of Fear is a beautiful, surreal, and frightening trip into the mind of a broken man. What it lacks in traditional game-play mechanics it makes up for with a thick atmosphere and a great story.  Any fans of horror games will certainly find a lot to enjoy within Layers of Fear's winding halls.

The attention to detail, music and sound effects are truly awesome, a pure labyrinth of nightmares which I thoroughly enjoyed.
Big thanks to the game creators.

They do give you the option to play with additional hints, which I opted out of, but they may be necessary. Additionally, while befriending all the characters is fun, I was at a loss with how to figure out which gifts they might like the most. Maybe for some there were clues in talking to them, but I honestly had to look up a guide, which I feel takes a little bit out of the genuine experience of talking to a character and being able to discover things about them before initiating friendship events. Those issues I would say are just a rough design, not really anything that makes it unplayable or unsatisfying. My smallest complaint is the music ... some tracks were fitting, others were really odd and ruined the tone of the dialogue with certain characters - but that's just a personal issue, some may enjoy the music. That aside, I enjoyed the plot - it runs like a visual novel with just enough interactive portions to keep the player engaged, which can be difficult to do. The characters are memorable and well-written, and the art style is adorable - coming from their previous releases, which were pixels with the occasional full art slide, it's an interesting change and one that is much appreciated.

I want to like this game. I truly do.  While I could see myself recommending it on the cheap (20 dollars including all the DLC content) to shooter fans/Warhammer fans, the title simply isn't worth its 30 dollar price tag at all.  A cooperative/singleplayer L4D 2 campaign mod with various classes, the game uses the carrot of ever-increasing loot drops as an impetus to keep playing.  The premise isn't to survive and make your way through the map but, instead, to complete some rote objective (destroy xyz, exfiltrate abc items in a wagon/boat/caravan). Think Dead Center Map 4 over and over and over and over.  Consequently, despite the fact that the game is wonderfully atmospheric, graphically impressive, reasonably well-assembled and has moments of fun, the game can also feel suffocatingly repetitious and grindy.
To be honest, if I'm going to be playing a grindy title like this one, I'd much rather concentrate my focus on a more open, massive title like Diablo 3.  While the first person elements somtimes feel reasonably good (combat), often these self-same first person paradigms impair the feel of the legitimately diverse character classes.  Character movement is the most clear and egregious offender.  The trailers show characters moving around, bounding, acrobatically and colorfully but this information is completely obscured in first person and perhaps a third person view would be much more effective at conveying such class variation.  Additionally, the community is quite vacant, with only about 30 or so server instances populated by approximately 45 players at any given time.
With the dearth of players using microphones and a lack of clear procedural map-strategy, players mostly do their own thing and only help each other when it becomes absolutely necessary.  In this way, Vermintide feels terribly lonely (and dark...holy crap, give me a flashlight!).  You play alone, you level alone, you forge gear alone and only on brief crescendo events do you ever work together, with the exception of an occasional cap clear.  Unlike a title like Left 4 Dead 2, where each campaign is divided into maps with clear and differentiated events that mandate specific responses/strategies, Vermintide's mapping, while pretty, is simply an uninspired, maze-like mess of constant scurrying/front-running towards the next crate full of potions.
The inclusion of treacherous terrain where specific Skaven types would have improved efficiency is just one minor suggestion that could add significant variation to the title.  In light that Vermintide lacks vs multiplayer, the need for dynamic, reaction-inducing maps is oh so vital.  While I only have a scant few hours in the game, the title update erased all my progress and bugs seem to be crawling in this title.  The title runs reasonably well but crashes on occasion and somtimes demonstrates issues during combat, like clipping, animation glitches or the like.  While blatant animation problems never occur, being unable to hit a Skaven in front of you because you've already missed twice, and needing to change your position completely to actually connect a blow, can sometimes dull the intoxication that this game purports to elicit during combat.
It's not that Vermintide is a bad game or that it's badly made.  Vermintide, with the right group of friends can be good fun.  The issue is that the game has deep paradigm flaws in its core gameplay that render it less than what it could be and allow so many other titles to be so much better value for the money.
In light of those flaws.
6/10.  Not recommended. This game can be lonely, boring grind without the right group of people and even then...the game has limits.

+ Great rhythm. In some puzzles you through an area like a crazed psychopath hacking away at yourself with a chainsaw, and other times you are slicing tiny bits off with the precision of a surgeon. Both were satisfying.
+ Difficult puzzles towards the end, sometimes this was frustrating, and sometimes I had to rethink my entire approach to the game, and gravity, and life, in order to solve them. One of these puzzles I swear made me a better person.
- I'm a fan of post-apocalypic art styles, but this one was a bit... unpolished and overdone.
- Some aspects of the game design are also not quite polished, eg. in one of the later puzzles (surgical, not chainsaw), the camera kept moving inappropriately, causing me to cut myself in half and have to start again.

tl;dr - I stole a unicycle from a giant shrimp, rode on a rocket, and got jiggy with a mushroom. 9/10 would ooze again.
Overall, this is a fantastic puzzle-platformer! In all, You play as an oozy mushroom (the 11th of its kind? One of 11 siblings? No idea what the 11 of the game means) in a post-apocalyptic world where humans are clearly gone and only the fungi and lichen remain. The mechanic is easy to learn but has infinite complexity: You have an "eraser" that erases part of your mushroom, and it regrows in the opposite direction. So you don't so much as move as delete part of yourself in one location and transfer it to another. You can also split yourself into multiple pieces for various uses, and regrow from any of them until the very moment they are completely erased. Good way to give yourself a lifeline in case you mess up!
It only took me about 4 hours, but it seemed like the perfect length. Music is great, very atmospheric. Art is also great! Several different areas, all with a different "feel", like an abandoned hospital, spooky jungle, the obligatory lava level. Puzzles are challenging but never impossible. A lot of them take patience to ooze yourself into just the right shape to reach a high platform, and others require you to rush through so that you have the momentum you need to proceed. I think my only complaint is that the bosses have very little indication of how you can beat them, so it just takes a lot of trial and error, but that's just me being picky. If you're looking for an ultra-challenging puzzler, this may not be for you, but its frustration level is low enough for us regular puzzlers.
