I feel attention is due to this unique puzzle game I've come across. My verdict is:

But if you are looking for something more in depth then read away...
Ever since I saw the first teaser for this in 2013 I was ecstatic for something this strange and intriguing for a physics-puzzle title set in some strange overgrown apocalyptic world. The artist who did the music created an eerie atmosphere with each world, 7 in total that had there own characteristics and enemy types that add to a DNA based score system when you have the 'bacteria' you control consume it.
Within moments of it starting the game tells you everything that is needed, You don't control the green entity yourself you mearly control its growth with the two mouse buttons(I stritckly use a keyboard and mouse when playing so I don't know the specifics for controllers) by erasing parts letting it grow outwards whichever way works. The two buttons have a different size based on whether or not you want to finely erase with the right mouse button or take out a decent chunk with the left. Many mechanics are introduced throughout the levels with wildly varying types sometimes only shown once other times in many formats through the game.
each level is roughly the same in execution: Go through the level introduced to new mechanics that progressively become more complex the further in, come across some alter form of ultra bacteria killer, learn a thing or two about what went wrong with civilizatoin and where things began to sway from what we're used to, and fight a particular boss that may pertain to some relative history of that place.
Now for the gritty part, this game has an EXTREME escallation in it's difficulty probably somewhere between Chapter 5 and the start of six I ended up spending more and more time on single puzzles than I do the entire game. Certain physics are introduced that require precision and timing with erasing the bacteria and by the time I got to the final chapter I was taking long breaks because of how long I spent on it. This was mostly due to having a hard time figuring out the way it was supposed to be solved because occasionally I would spend more time solving it one way that ends up taking longer than the desired approach since the game doesn't exactly tell you HOW it gets done just that it can be done in any way desirable.
Now you don't need to play them all the way through as you can exit at any time and come back to the same puzzle though in doing so it will stop tracking the time at which you played.
Now all these issues could easily have been fixed by now since I played it before they added the cloud saving which is something I am grateful for since it is important to be able to save that progress to other systems or when something happens that erases your data. Another thing that might've been fixed since playing were some of the puzzles so any serious gripes I may have had with the difficulty spike may have been fixed although it is hard to say without going all the way through that stuff again.
I think I've said my piece on how I feel about this whole thing so what's the verdict on MY reccomendation and pricing? I will say YES, if a unique physics based puzzle platformer is what you are looking for then by all means try it out. I will say the price may be a bit much as I originally was able to beat the whole thing within 8 hours so you might want to wait for a slight sale before paying top dollar.

HuniePop will continuously surprise you with its depth and complexity. I haven't played a lot of match-3 games in my time (because they were too simple and boring), but HuniePop revolutionizes the genre through the simple innovation of allowing you to move a token as far as you want, provided at the end of the movement, 3 tokens somewhere on the board are in a line. The full importance of this won't strike you until most of the way through your first playthrough, but when it does, you'll be blown away.
I recommend people play this once on NORMAL then again on HARD. This will give an extremely satisfying learning curve, and if you are like me, you'll be amazed at how fluidly you adapt your strategies, as the game forces you to get better and better. The second playthrough also allows you to see how perfectly the dating sim part of the game merges with the puzzle part of the game. It has its own set of strategies for minimizing the number of days until game completion (which you must learn to get the Pickup Legend achievement).
Anyways, the game is really, really good. I give it a 9.75/10 (which may rise to a 10/10 if they fix a couple of bugs that affect the puzzle gameplay). Definitely the best puzzle game I've ever played.
Note: Make sure you patch the game so you get the uncensored versions of the pictures (it's easy, look it up on the web).
BUGS:
1. When two matching tokens (one on top of the other) fall farther than 1 spot and land on two other matching tokens (one on top of the other), only the bottom 3 tokens match, instead of the whole column of four.
2. Occasionally when matching 3 passion tokens, you'll get an extra turn. The game won't announce it, the turn counter just won't go down.
-----------------------------------
(STRATEGY SPOILERS BELOW) Notes on the game's design (STRATEGY SPOILERS BELOW)
1. I recommend that the developers remove the 10% and 20% chance of forming a power token from a 3-match from the top two levels of the Luck Trait. This chance is too small for me to use up three tokens of the girl's favorite trait in hopes of getting a power token. In the later levels of the game, the advanced player will save the favorite trait tokens for the big finale with the Tulip/Orchid/Pansy/Cosmos, and they will only be making 3-matches of non-favorite traits (which simply don't give that many affection points) to set up for a 4-match of the favorite trait for a near-guaranteed power token of the favorite trait. If a power token forms from the 3-match on the way to the 4-match, it can get in the way of the 4-match and screw everything up.
2. The best gift loadout in the game consists of Stuffed Penguin, Sunflower, Pink Mary Janes, and Tulip/Orchid/Pansy/Cosmos. The last two gifts can be anything, but I recommend Leopard Print Pumps and Stuffed bear/Shiny Lipstick. I'm perfectly fine with one loadout being superior to all others, and actually prefer it that way, but if the developers intended to allow different styles of loadouts to be viable in the game, a lot more hard work would have to be done to balance the gifts (for instance, the ones that clear a row, column, or square of tokens should be tossed as soon as better ones are available).
3. I recommend that the developers allow the player to start a new game in ALPHA mode once it's unlocked, and incorporate the 18 days requirement for the Pickup Legend achievement into this new ALPHA mode. This would have the effect of creating a 4th difficulty level that requires true mastery of both the puzzle and dating sim aspects of the game.

Very solid take on well-known and established survival horror (particularly RE4) mechanics. This is a game by Shinji Mikami, the father of Resident Evil series.
Buying The Evil Within, you get a mindf***ing-kind of plot, great level design (including awesome old-school boss design), well-paced gameplay and difficulty increase, all kinds of creepiness, and lots of satisfaction upon beating consecutive chapters. Definitely worth the 20€. Some people bash it's graphics, which I can understand, since it's nothing we haven't seen for the past 1-2 years (since premiere), but when I played, it wasn't a big deal. I barely paid any attention whatsoever to that. Good voice acting and also good music done with safe, old-school approach are worth mentioning too.
BUY IT IF: you enjoyed RE4, like well done old-school mechanics of a survival horror, and are a fan of the genre in it's entirety.
DONT BUY IT IF: you're a fan of a newer, more realistic approach to the genre, put the plot above everything else (TEW's is pretty satisfying, but as the player starts digging deeper into the game, it loses the initial freshness and traps itself in easily distinguished worn-out screenplay tricks/schemes).

I want to start this review off by saying that I'm someone that appreciates well fleshed out gameplay.  That said, I had a lot of issues with the gameplay of this game.  Don't get me wrong, the story and design overall of this game is actually very nice.  But gameplay wise, I'll be honest and say that there's more I dislike than I like.  Because of this, concluding whether or not I could recommend the game was tough for me, so here I try to talk about what bothered me most.
The very beginnings of my frustrations come from the hype that surrounded this game when it was going to come out.  It even exists in the game's summary at the top of the page - "The Evil Within embodies the meaning of pure survival horror. Highly-crafted environments, horrifying anxiety, and an intricate story".  This isn't 100% true.  This is
pure survival horror.  The environments look great though, I'll give them that.
The way this game starts out, you'd go to think it was teaching you that you're in for a survival horror where you have to sneak around and be wary of enemies.  This is not the case.  The game likes to decide whether or not you can sneak around enemies, or if it's going to require you to kill every enemy in the area in order to procede.  There are some segments where stealth is actually an option, but it's too inconsistent for me to say it's done right.
Here is one of the points that disappointed me most: A powerful enemy I'd rather try not to fight is trying to find me.  I'm sticking to the shadows, avoiding it as swiftly as I can.  I see an exit door, sealed shut.  I'm looking for any way I can to maybe trip the fire alarm, or fix a generator, to open the door to my freedom.  But, you can't do that.  I looked everywhere for a stealthy solution before I came to the conclusion that the game was forcing me to fight my way out.  So that begs the question, why give me the idea that sneaking past enemies is a possibilty when that's only true some of the time?  Why set that up in the first levels?
Other people seem to praise this game for taking multiple elements from other horror games.  Personally, I think this makes the game suffer somewhat, because the game just can't decide what direction it wants to take.  A little Resident Evil horror action here, a little Dead space gore there, some Outlast sneaking thrown in the mix, and a pitcher of Silent Hill.  I can't really understand what kind of horror game The Evil Within wants to be.  However, that makes the game special in its own right.  It's an interesting concoction, because I don't think it's a problem for horror games to include all of these elements.  But if you play The Evil Within I hope that you'll see what I mean;  at times the game feels like gameplay elements of multiple game series have just been smushed together rather than meshed together, if that makes sense.
A nitpick - the main character's jogging animation makes me cringe - something about the way his upper torso/arms move just doesn't sit right with me.
I had a few adrenaline rushes hiding from enemies, and I really do think the story got interesting at times.  But I never experienced the "horrifying anxiety" as advertised.  A few good moments are outweighed by multiple gameplay flaws, causing a fair share of headaches.
Overall - It wasn't what I expected, but it was still a great experience.  There were some parts I really enjoyed and things that made me smile.  The DLC made it overall an experience worth getting into, which gives me hope that if there is an Evil Within 2, it will combine the best elements of both the main game and the DLC.
8/10.
DLC:
Steam isn't letting me review the DLC on their actual pages, so here's some short thoughts:
The Assignment: Great!  I enjoyed this DLC more than the actual game.  Stealth actually works and I felt like I could control outcomes.  The way the flashlight is implemented is awesome and would have worked well in the main game.
The Consequence: Absolutely great.  I thought the enemies and pacing were awesome.  It's a great blend of the main game's style and the first DLC's.  Puzzles are also more interesting.  I'm hoping The Evil Within 2 is a lot like this. The ending still kinda confused me but oh well, haha.
The Executioner:  This DLC is so much fun!  It's basically a reward for going through all the challenge of the main game and DLC.  It changes up the gameplay drastically and still manages to tie into the overall story.  It could honestly be its own spinoff game (though it probably won't).
Final thoughts: Yes, the overall experience was worth it.  I recommend this game :)

TL,DR:
It's plagued by black bars on screen and a REALLY narrow FOV.
I've been playing 3d games since the N64 and have never lost my orientation so easily. I also never experienced motion sickness in a third person game before this.
Full-ish review:
A maybe great game with an issue.
The Evil Within is an interesting game, at least for what I saw of it. But, I only saw a small slice of it - literally.
The story had me interested, a nice, pretty gritty horror story. It's somewhere between Allan Wake's action, Resident Evil's pacing and, though only slightly, Silent Hill's creature design. Not a bad start.
It's gameplay feels is akin to The Last Of Us or the newer Tombraider games. Third person shooting and stealth. No big suprises here.
But, and regretably, the presentation suffers from a fatal flaw. There are black bars on the top and bottom of the screen. Constantly. You can't get rid of them. They're intentional.
This severly limits the player's vertical field of view. Adding to that, the horizontal FOV is pretty narrow too. And even worse, you don't have absolute control over the camera. It switches from side to side based on the players movement but there is no way to "fix" it to one shoulder of the avatar nor to switch it manually. And, adding yet more insult to injury, it often decides that, well, maybe the thing that should be the focus of your attention right now is the player character, not the environment.
A practical example:
You move up, through high grass, to an enemy in a village. As you come closer he walks away into a house and you follow for a stealthy kill. You crouch up to the building, leaning against the wall and want to peak through the open door inside.
There is no solid cover mechanic, so, trying to be careful you move up to the door along the wall. The camera sways forward so that the right half of the screen is occupied by your character and the wall, the left half of the screen shows the enemy who you followed move just a bit deeper into the room, slowly moving out of sight.
Whatever you do next, you are not only losing sight of the enemy, you will in all likelyhood be disoriented.
Option 1, do nothing: the enemy moves out of sight completely leaving you guessing and in a rather awkward spot. You could wait for him to maybe reemerge, but that's neither interesing nor does it leave you protected from other enemies around.
Option 2, rotate the camera to follow the enemy: as you do this, the view not only rotates but also moves just slighty to the right centering on your character. As you oogle the detailed figure that is your avatar, the already limited window into the room grows smaller. You may, if you're lucky have a small vertical line through which you can still see into the room. Since the viewing angle is getting steeper, this line has only a small chance of still showing the (still moving) enemy.
Option 3, go in after the enemy: since you have no way of tracking the enemy further, you decide to head in after him. While your character moves into the doorway he nearly completely blocks your view into the room. The screen is now filled with your character, left and right of him are the outside walls. Only a few steps into the building the camera move in after him and you can make out your surroundings.
No matter what you do, you're either going in blind or are left outside not knowing what to do next. All this, while your FOV, both vertically and horizontically, is so limited as to only show your character (and even him being cut of at the bottom).

Pros:
- Brilliant concept. The game presents itself as a future sport like The Running Man or Rollerball, leaning heavily towards the aesthetic of Smash TV.
- Beautiful game in every way. A bit light on art assets, but what's there is gorgeous to look at and listen to.
- Compelling Gameplay. The 3PS/DotA mix works much better here than the original Monday Night Combat. Metagame and strategy are equally important to shooter skills and teamwork.
Balance: (not really a pro or a con)
- The game is "fun". It's not really set up for competitive play. There are lots of random elements, such as bacon drops. Damage is slightly randomized. For most things this can be forgiven, but when your Jackbots can spit Bacon right into the enemy base, things get extremely crazy.
- The cash shop. This is why the game is free to play, and also why the game never made money. The ecomony, while robust on paper, is infinitely exploitable via Steam Trading. The game needs to retain players to sustain the cash flow and - for the reasons listed below - that never happened.
- Super Blitz mode is a decent way to farm Combat Credits and work on your PvE skills, but it will MELT YOUR FACE. It's impossible to win by design. The "goal" is to keep your Moneyball alive for as many waves as you can. You will fail eventually. You can buy tokens to repair your Moneyball and turrets during the round, but that's sort of cheating.
Cons:
- Matchmaking is completely broken. There is no "ranked queue". Everybody above level 20 gets thrown into one gigantic free-for-all and it sucks for new players. Newbs don't have flexible product loadouts or any endorsements (runes) worth mentioning. Combined with being generally unskilled at either the shooter or DotA elements or (god help you) both, newbs consistently get rekt every game until they can scrape together a decent understanding of the game mechanics and unlock most of the pros and products.
- The Practice Game mode doesn't work. At all.
- The tutorial is terrible, to the point of being arguably non-existent. The Training Camp is essentially a museum that showcases the various gameplay-related objects and lets you practice interacting with them to an extent. The ability to practice against Jackbots and Chickey Cantor in nice, but there isn't any particularly useful information to be found here, apart from what everything looks like and what each thing supposedly does.
What I would suggest after touring the Training Camp is running a few solo Custom Games so you can at least figure out how lane bots spawn and why killing them is important. Then close SMNC and watch a few gameplay videos. Perhaps uninstall entirely. Your call, really.
Turbocross is the only mode with decent queue times at the moment, and that's due to the drop-in/drop-out nature of the mode. Turbocross is rebalanced to play like old MNC, minimizing the importance of the DotA elements. If you're REALLY DESPERATE for Overwatch, you might enjoy killing time here.

____Original Review____
Vermintide is 4 player co-op, very much like Left 4 Dead 1&2 but in the Warhammer universe when the world is ending and the Ratlings are rising to destroy everything. It takes every positive aspect of the L4D series and expands on it with a decent story, some RPG elements and MUCH better melee. It even has some very cool homages to L4D.
It is an excellent game. At the time of this writing, It's been out for almost 1.5 years and the devs are still very active in updating it and adding content. All  of the paid DLC only requires the "host" to own it, anyone joing a game can join it and get the weapons from it, even if they don't own the DLC.
If you like L4D or the Warhammer uninverse or Co-Op games it's simply a "Must own".

Ironclad Tactics is a lane defense game with cards.  It is a top down style
tactical game that relays its story in a comic book fashion.  You gain cards
by completing missions, challenges, and increasing difficulty.
The cards are organized a bit haphazardly, making it difficult to build
a deck.  There are filters, but the way they are laid out makes it a
bit confusing
as you build your collection.
The missions aren't too complicated, but the game has increasing
difficulty and challenges that promote replayability.  The object is to get
your cards (or players) accross the board, on a turn by turn basis, and to
defeat the enemy cards.  There is a luck element into what kind of enemy will
appear and in what lane, and what cards you will have availble from your
collection.  This randomization may appeal to some players, but the way the
cards interact does slow the lane defense experience.  In the same vein, those
who are used to card games may be disillusioned by the tactical strategy that
is necessary to the more quicker paced lane defense mechanic.
I can recommend this game, but I strongly recommend that you are aware
of the hybrid card/lane defense elements so as not to expect all of one element
or too much of the other.

My first ever review, so be kind :D
This game is everything Banished should have been. And before anyone complains, i am a huge fan of Banished, i just think that this game is a step up from Banished.
The graphics are beautiful. Buildings, people, wildlife, livestock all look great, very detailed.
The game is easy to learn, but for complete beginners i think the tutorial needs a bit of work.
I haven't come across any bugs or crashes yet, i've only been playing for 3 hours.
The fact you can possess the body of a villager and take full control of them is great! You see through their eyes in first person view. You can take supplies to the warehouse, or kill a wolf that's eating your chickens!! Or just take a walk around the village you created.
I like the fact that the weather has a huge impact on what crops you can grow, and how they grow. How the weather affects your villagers and their performance when doing their jobs.
The fact that even when you make clothing for your villagers they actually change their clothing, so it alters the look of them.
The game makes the micromanagement of your villagers important. How your villagers feel and act has an impact on your entire village and it's productivity.
My only negative so far is the fact i can't use edge scrolling with the mouse. I hate using keys to move left or right in game. And the camera control needs calming down a little as it's super fast. But these are minor things that can be fixed as the game progresses.
The fact is, this is a Banished style game with everything Banished didn't include. It's fully working in Early Access, and it looks stunning.
Well worth getting if you like Banished, or if you're looking for a new city builder type game that isn't too easy or so simple it's built and finished in 5 minutes.

Win 7 64-bit.
8Gb memory.
Intel Core CPU i7-4700MQ @ 2.40GHz
Nvidia GeForce GTX 765M
(i also have second card Intel HD Graphics 4600 that i ran it on by mistake and it worked fine with that too).

This game is a short movie like experience in which you wander around an old mansion
from the victorian era as a painter. It's raining outside, you can see the water running down
the windows and sometimes you hear a faint thunder sound. With the moody lamps lit the house
looks somewhat cozy in some areas.
Overall however the games is "unsettling". While you are wandering around you find stuff that give hints
about who you are and what happened. You hear flashbacks. More than once you hear your wife crying from another room. You walk to the door when it suddenly slams shut. When you turn around to take another door you see the wall with the door has been replaced by a portrait with the paint dripping down. You turn 90 degrees to find that, that wall also has been replaced with an empty wall containing the same portrait. Same goes for the other 2 walls. When you finally look to the wall with the first portrait you see a long hallway instead. You follow the hallway, open the door at the end to find a brick wall behind the opening. When you turn around you see that you are now in a small room with 4 doors all hiding brick walls behind them. When you open the first door again the brick wall has made place for a childrens room with a sof lullaby playing and light from the device crawling around the wall. When you look at the small childrens bed the image of child sized doll suddenly appears and dissapears for around half a second...

I think 19.99 is a little expensive for such a short game so I recommend buying it in a sale or on a cheap key website (that's what I did), but if you are buying an exploration or horror game and you don't mind that's it's a little short than this is perfect. I've been playing Ironclad Tactics off and on for over a year. Only now, after earning every card, I realize that I forgot to write a review. It’s sort of a Plants VS Zombies game except that it’s Zombies VS Zombies, and the zombies are steampunk mechs.
The pace is realtime, but it moves slow enough to allow some thinking time for your next moves. Most of the challenge comes from building specialized decks to solve the puzzle that each level presents. Your AI opponent will have the upper hand with some new attack or defense and you’ll have to come up with a counter. Most of the time this results in a tense battle of planning, wits, and fortune. When you tweak a deck combo into working just right it feels great! Each new card opens up lots of tactical options and completing challenges for cards feels rewarding.
The civil war theme and story are awesome. I love the characters and animated comics that set up you journey across America. The in-game art and animation is beautiful. It’s easy to tell every unit apart and their abilities match the visuals. A robot with a jetpack files, dude with a shotgun has spread attack, and a flame thrower hits multiple targets. The music fits and is serviceable, but for me it’s one of the weakest points of the game. Something less traditional and more gutsy could have really helped some of the longer play sessions.
Each level starts by showing you 5 random cards from your deck of 20, so sometimes it feels like a lucky/unlucky start can make or break a win. If cards come out in just the wrong order it can kill a plan, but managing this problem is also part of the art of deck building. It improved a bit with the release of the first DLC where you can now spend 1 action point to ‘save’ a critical card for later.
The first DLC uses an army with a completely different and fun style of play. It’s satisfying playing as the boss enemies that were beating you down in the final levels and to understanding the logic behind how their robots transform. It also fills in missing parts of the story with more comics. The second DLC is very stripped down, but still provides new interesting abilities. Playing the ‘War’ mode, where you’re stuck with either French or Germany armies, varies the play styles just enough to keep things fresh.
After completing everything it feels like every inch of the design space has been explored. Not every ability or tactic is perfectly balanced, but there’s lots of viable strategies to solve each problem. That said, I haven’t played multiplayer which would be a much better gauge of balance. There’s not enough players to support random matchmaking and I don’t feel like it would be that fun against friends (even if they unlocked all the cards). I also haven’t tried the co-op mode, which is supported throughout the entire game.
If you liked Spacechem, you might like this. It’s about building machines, but stochastic machines rather than logical ones. If you loved Spacechem then definitely play this to support the awesome developers!

First things first: there is no "dying". There is no ammunition and virtually no inventory beyond a few specific items you have to pick up. This is essentially a story told through an interactive, but mostly linear, experience.
You're thrust into the world of an artist attempting to finish a painting of something. Initially, the experience is slow as you get your bearings and learn a few things about who you are and your life. It quickly changes, though, and by changing, I mean changing! Rooms vanish as you turn, doors close and disappear, and nothing, absolutely nothing, can be trusted. The puzzles are pretty simple but do change per reload/playthrough, so it's not always identical.
There are six chapters that take about 20 - 30 minutes each to complete. At the conclusion of the final piece, there is a short jump back to reality before the game ends, tying the story together.
If you're fond of psychological horror movies or really enjoyed the shifting environment of movies like Rose Red, this game will tickle your fancy.

Phew...how to classify this game? It's both a puzzler and a race game. It's a parkour for the thinking gamer. You have to trim out the parts of your blob you don't want so the remainder will grow in directions you DO want it to go to. So it's mouse driven, and most likely mouse only (perhaps with a touchscreen exception?). Everything in the game is fluid and strangely intuitive. But that doesn't mean it's easy. I've just passed level 5 and if other reviews are to be believed, things'll get harder quickly now. And yes, some 'open the door'-puzzles are already were quite hard (borderline frustrating). But the overall experience itself was almost worth the price of admission. So I'm confident enough to thumbs up this game no matter what future levels may bring. :-)

This is a somewhat hesitant recommendation. A handful of the later puzzles require extremely precise, methodical work, which is great until you realize the factors that combine into my 1 major issue with the game:
1. The delete cursor exerts slight force on the blob.
2. The random regrowth of the blob adds slight mass to a random edge of the blob and can unpredictably alter its balance.
3. The camera moves based on the position of the blob (and other factors sometimes) even during these puzzles, and cannot be locked.
Situations arise where these factors combine to ruin minutes of work on a puzzle and force you to reset. The worst part is that resetting these puzzles requires you to painstakingly remold the blob to the perfect, specific configuration by deleting randomly regrowing spots until they happen into the spaces you actually need them. When you need to utilize almost every single piece of the blob in precisely the right configuration, this can be pretty damn annoying to reset, work on for minutes, and then have ruined by the camera AGAIN.
Now that the bad is out of the way, Mushroom 11 is otherwise a standout puzzle game. It has an innovative, cool mechanic as its foundation. The physics are tight. Guiding the blob quickly comes to feel very fluid, natural, and intuitive as you build a skill unique to this game. Best of all, with few exceptions the level design teaches you how to use this core mechanic in new ways; it rarely adds a new "gimmick of the level" to shake up the gameplay as mediocre puzzle games do - the progression feels quite organic.
If a Camera Lock toggle was added to this game, its only significant weakness would be much improved. As is, Mushroom 11 becomes pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t at times. An otherwise singularly smooth, innovative puzzle game is worth that (significant) frustration.

Genre - Strategy lane game with cards
This is one of those games where you have to throw your units against your enemies on the other side of the screen hoping they get through, whilst they do the same to you. This is done by activating cards at varying cost that you collect as you play the game. Some units are better suited against others and you can get some cards to move units, heal and damage. On paper this sounds quite fun. However, I am not a big fan of these lane games as I find them quite boring. True the cards add a new element but just throwing units at the enemy hoping hey get through whilst they do the same doesn't keep my interest. Also I don't know if I am just crap at this game but I tend to lose quite a few games on a level before I get the win and this seems mainly down to luck. The idea of the American civil war with steam powered Mechs is a cool concept though. Basically if you like lane fighting games, you will like this. If you don't, you will think it is a good example of the genre but still won't like it.

Ironclad tatics is a turn based cards strategy game based on a alternate version of the Civil war (no doubt you can already guess that due to the look of the game). I've seen alot of negative reviews for the game and to be honest, even though I would recommend this game, I don't think it's as good as some people think it is.
First thing first, the good aspects of the game:
+ Incredible music, I'm still listening to the music and hell even the dlc music are actually better than the main music. Thankfully the soundtrack is free if you google it and is actually from the musician himself.
+ Artwork, while cartoony, it's pretty great. I enjoy the designs for the characters and landscape and the movement is pretty smooth.
+ Diversity, the game offers alot of cards and a total of 5 (+3 if you have the 2 dlc) that have different types of weapons, troops and tactics.
So those are some of the good aspects, what is it that I don't like?
-Luck, Despite being a turned based strategy game with cards, the game is 100% dependent on getting luck. There will be times that you will have to reconsider which deck you use but even if you have the right deck, the starting hand, timing and chances your opponent won't try to destroy you early in the match is pretty harsh and can put off alot of people.
-Story, I don't really hate the story much but to be honest, the characters could have been better. Often times I kinda felt the main character should have been another character, some characters don't feel like we know them too well or changes too quick.
- Limitation, Knowing this is on pc, the game still feels limited to being a mobile game. You can only have max of 4 decks  and can only have max of 20 cards and 2 factions per deck. This can be very frustrating if you want to get your favorite cards together only to either exceeded the limits. (I know how I felt about not getting my army of native flamethrowing/Drilling/tomahawk army)
-Challanges (Mission challange), um yea, I'm not gonna be able to beat that one level without breaking the walls........
Overall, why am I recommending the game? 3 reasons: the music is fantastic, it's a alternate historical game that acutally doesn't suck and it's actually makes you feel like you want to really win battles.

Mouse in game simply doesn't work in stable way, except Mouse1 and Mouse2 buttons
Game controllers that require remapper software do not work either. Apparently if you're not XBox aim-aid drone, you can't play.
Game assumes that PC  uses 4:3 aspect ratio, in result it   squeezes picture into what must be "Wide" screen. Of course, on wide monitor that creates ridiculous aspect ratio ( 2.5:1 ?), with picture distorted and a risk of motion sickness for player present.
There is debug console hidden. It can be activated by this:
1. In Steam, right click on The Evil Within and select "properties," then under the General tab hit "set launch options."
2. Put this in to unlock the console: +com_allowconsole 1
3. Once the game has launched, hit the Insert key to bring down the developer console
***How to remove black bars***
-"r_forceaspectratio 0" (without quotes) if you want to completely disable the black bars. This zooms  picture a little though, but on wide screen distortion is gone. on W screen picture still will have distorted proportions (i.e, a cube will look like a parallelepiped)
-"r_forceaspectratio 2.5" if you want to get the black bars again with the default size.
***How to remove the 30fps cap***
-Select the game from Steam library, right click on it and select properties.
-Add "+com_allowconsole 1" (without quotes) to Launch Options from General tab.
-Run the game and open the console with "insert" key.
-"r_swapinterval 0" (without quotes) for fully unlock the fps.
-"r_swapinterval -1" (without quotes) for 60fps cap.
-"r_swapinterval -2" (without quotes) for 30fps cap, this is the default value.

Hello everyone,
Szone is a different game, unlike most MMO's or Survival games out there, Szone has taken whats great about a MMO and whats great about a Survival game and they have put it together. If you die, you lose items in your inventory depending what you are carrying, any items equipt will not be dropped, this allows players to have a purpose when killing others, it is not your average tab target MMO where you die, run out, die again, repeat, no.. This mmorpg is about fighting or befriending who you want for whatever reason you want, the purpose can be to take their loot or mabye you have some unresolved conflict with them earlier? Mabye you want to be their friend but you decide you dont like them and want to part ways with their belongings?
What you do is only limited by your creativity, this game has a completely player driven economy, clans take bases which allows them to acquire rare devices such as land mines and then that clan has the power to decide who can and cant have these devices, this is what starts alliances and wars, clans will either decide they want to help the clan in control of the rare resources/devices so that they can get some too eventually or they will decide to wage war to take what they want.
The PVP combat can be compared to counterstrike, rust and dayz, there is bleeding, illness and medicine to heal like dayz but turn the wrong corner and you will die in a heartbeat from a fully automatic AK which will fire similar to counterstrike, the reason i say counterstrike is because the recoil and spray resembles counterstrike more than it does dayz or rust. The Political/RP aspect to PVP could be compared to Darkfall: Unholy Wars or Arche Age, you fight for bases / fortifications, you control the resources, the goal is to control the game.
Now when you start the game you will probably be put off by the mid 2000 style graphics or the unexplaining UI/controls   but if you can see past the early game difficulties, this will become a game almost any mmo/survival game enthusiast will enjoy and about those mid 2000 style graphics i mentioned, this game is going to go to the Unreal 4 Engine eventually, it has already been announced, the game is released but still has alot of plans for the future.
I could go on for ages about this game, i have not even scratched the surface about everything i would love to say about this game, all i will say is just try the game, see for yourself, give it a few hours, you wont regret it.

I loved the first Hotline Miami, but after playing for some time I feel that this game truly lacks something, that made the first one so extraordinary.
First of all – the controls seem like they haven’t changed, but they feel much more clunky then they used to be. Trying to take a dropped weapon feels unresponsive. Want to knock down the enemy and them kill him with your bare hands? Good luck standing at just the right place to try to kill him. In later levels you start out in a location outside your screen and then you have to play around every retry to find where you are and where the crosshair is.
Next, enemies can see you and shoot you when you don’t see them. What this leads to? Rushing in like an idiot for five or more times in a row just to pinpoint the exact location of your enemies. Let’s not forget how unpredictable they are – you can be shooting around with a shotgun and one time the same enemies come at you, sometimes not. This especially frustrates when you’re a few meters away from the enemy and you never know what is he going to do next.
Also, level design got worse. Sometimes the only option is to open the door or come out of a corner, expose yourself for a second or two and hope that somebody comes looking for you. Occasionally no one sees you and you have to repeat the same thing again. This sometimes happens on every level. Doing the same thing gets pretty boring after a while.

LiF: Forest Village V Banished (Answered)
So So many people are comparing this to a game called Banished (and rightly so they are both in the same catogory of games.) This however is everything Banished should of been but wasnt. So why is this better ? Well the first major thing is the AI - while still ropey in places - they are no where near the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ level of Banished (no villager will walk out into the middle of the map then freeze to death...). The buildings look better and more authentic. Resourses and comsumption of them actually matters as weather actually has effect on crops, growth and happines of villagers. Speaking of which - the villageres them selfs have a proper needs system in stead of a calculated prediction like banished. Each person has a Clothing/ Tool/ And happines bar as well as visual representations an example of this is the cloths you make actually visually change your villagers appearance.
If that wasnt enough. The gathering of materials is a constant struggle - really adding end game hardships. In banished after you got past a certain point it was VERY easy to manage as materials would be come so abundant ( i had a 1000 pop city in banished that laster over 100 years). In this game when winter hits, you feel it, food consumption is increased, as well as the consumption of wood. Villagers work less crops die (and unlike banished even gathering huts and herbs stop growing) so stockpiling resources and planning for winters ahead is essential.
If that wasnt enough of a difference well here is some other reasons why this is better:
- In its curent state its more indepth than and complete than Banished and is early acess - that means only more content to come
- First person View (while not fully incorpetrated yet) offers some amazing view of the towns you create (as well as you actually being able to help out and construct in that view)
- There is an indepth crafting system for chain buildings ( some even requiring as many as 4 different materials to produce matrials, for instance - Fish Pie.... To make Fish pie You first need a field that gows wheat - the wheat is then ground up in a mill and the flour is then taken to a bakery, at this point th baker will need to get Fish from the Fishing huy and water from the well ect) This is alot more in depth than Banished system as well as more fleshed out.
All in all this is VERY promising poduct and havent had this much fun since the original Settleres Series. In its current state it is worth the price tag as it already has more content than Banished.

I normally don't like horror games, or this type of gameplay. But just seeing someone else play this, I felt drawn to it. I took a chance. It was well worth it.
There are things I could nitpick about the graphics, the length, and the replay value, but I don't want to. The game's faults are tiny. The important thing is, there are moments in this game that feel like the nightmares I had after seeing The Shining for the first time. There are gorgeous, mind-warping, Escher-esque moments that are as effective as any bit of visual storytelling I've ever seen. Not just jump scares, but subtle moments that will make you doubt your perceptions and sanity.
I could gripe about how Layers Of Fear can be extremely linear, to the point where the moments of actual gameplay and choice can be few and far between. But it works. It creates a sense of helplessness that adds to the the dread. And it makes you pay special attention to the few choices you do have.
I think this is less of a game than an experience. A halfway point between 'game' and 'movie'. It's like the developers looked at Gone Home and P.T., saw two unfinished concepts, and squeezed them together into one. I love the result.
Plus, it's just so damn luscious to look at.

Let me be clear: I enjoy this game. I didn’t enjoy this game for the first 6 or 8 hours, and only kept playing because my friends did. But now, I think it’s fun, challenging, and exciting, but I can't possibly recommend a game that takes so long to really make any sense. If I was playing alone, I would’ve quit an hour in.

The learning curve is just too steep. And that’s not to say it’s an incredibly complex game. The objectives are simples. There aren’t complex, challenging puzzles to solve; for the most part you move barrels or destroy pillars. The gameplay is simple; you have a melee weapon and ranged weapon, each of which typically have a basic attack and charged attack. What makes this game difficult to learn and play, is the developers refusal to give basic gameplay information to the players.

Some examples off the top of my head –

There are almost no actual numbers. Your health is just a bar. Damage, speed, targets, knockback on your weapon are all each a bar (which from what I’ve read, bars that only give an approximation of relative strength and aren’t actually indicative of strength. Which makes no sense, but is perfectly in line with the rest of this game, so I assume it is true) Buff potions give speed or strength. How much? For how long? Who knows, no indication. Medkits heal you, so do healing draughts. For how much? Who knows, no indication. How much health do enemies have? How much damage do bombs do? How much more damage do headshots do? All of this is information that could either be displayed on the HUD, or maybe put into tooltips. But instead, the tooltips are filled with lore.

The wizard character overheats using her ranged attack and needs to cool down before casting more. You can manually vent to cool down quicker (this much is explained). I noticed I would take damage when seemingly no enemies were near me. I thought maybe I had been hit by a ranged enemy, or a melee enemy behind me had hit me but been killed already. Then I realized it was when I overheated a certain amount. Was I taking damage periodically for being overheated? Was I taking damage from heating up initially? Was I taking damage from passively cooling down? Was I taking damage from actively cooling down? None of this is explained at all (Hint: You take damage from actively cooling down)

The wizard character’s charged ranged spell is a large fireball. You right click to begin casting and left click to release. As you hold right click, she gathers more and more fire into her hand and you slowly overheat. It would appear as if she is charging up the fireball to make it more powerful. Does this make the fireball do more damage? Does this make the fireball have a larger splash radius? Does this make the fireball burn longer? Does this make the fireball stronger against armored enemies? Does this make the fireball fly faster or further? None of this is explained at all (Hint: I still have no idea, but I don’t think it does anything)

And I’m not saying this information isn’t out there. If you want it, it’s been datamined so you can actually see numbers of how the game works. But a game should have information plainly presenting to you and intuitive gameplay so you can gradually learn. You shouldn’t have to search online to find very basic gameplay information that should be readily available in game.

tl;dr: The gameplay is a fun; but the learning the game is too frustrating and difficult because the game doesn’t explain what 90% of things actually do.

I wasn't expecting to enjoy this game so much. I never liked Left 4 Dead, but from what I remember of it this is basically a cleaned-up, reskinned version of the gameplay. Or maybe comparing it to Left 4 Dead is unjust, because I know there's a whole genre of games like this. Whatever, I was never interested in them.
I got this because I've always loved the Warhammer Fantasy world, and I've never seen it translated well into a computer game. And while this isn't my dream game (basically, if someone invented an Elder Scrolls-style open world CRPG set in the Old World I'd never leave my room again) it does the Warhammer Fantasy world well. It's all in the details. The graphics are beautiful and well-optimized. The characters are all just twisted and deviant enough to fit the setting (except for the soldier, and he's a perfect foil for the others) and the exchanges of dialogue they have can, at their best, make the game feel alive. The skaven are foul and chittering. The mechanics (from the steady supply of ambushes to the claustrophobic corridors to the uncounterable disables from the Gutter Runners and Packmasters) give gameplay a real sense of paranoia and urgency.
It's enough to make me enjoy what is ultimately a grind-based game where every mission is basically a rearrangement of the same enemies and challenges as every other. I have enjoyed it for more than 30 hours already. QUALITY STUFF.
My only real complaints:
1. The AI is terrible, to the point of making games with fewer than three real players on any of the higher difficulty settings almost unplayable.  This makes mid-game disconnects way more frustrating than they need to be.
2. I'm not a huge fan of the difficulty settings.  Hard isn't all that challenging when you've got a good group, while Nightmare is insane.  Or maybe I'm just not good enough.  But I'd love to see a level beyond High but without friendly fire, because friendly fire is a super bad idea in pickup games (which are all I play; I don't have any friends who are into this game).
3. The characters don't seem super well balanced?  Or maybe it's just that the Bright Wizard is much more my playstyle than the others.  In any case, she rules, with the atmospheric Winds of Magic mechanic and her unlimited ranged attacks, while the other four all seem a good bit less effective.

To summarize my experience with this game: I should advise that this is not a game for a mature audience. I think it is game for teenagers and not adults. Fans of Siren, Silent Hill, Clock Tower and other stealth horror games should probably avoid this one. First Person lovers should avoid it also. Most of the puzzles are way to obvious and you don´t even need to look for clues to solve them. Ammo is not a problem. You can run with a certain type but you will always have some, even on hard difficulties. Unfortunately you have no option to chose a less blunt and dull character in the first run and you are stuck with the stereotypical cop. That kind that acts-first and thinks-after with a very obvious backstory. The DLC's are not a big deal so buy only when its cheap. The game is enjoyable and I could recommend simply because it might be a fun time for people, but you should check some gameplay on youtube preferably without commentary, because most youtubers will praise the game too much almost looking like they are merchandising it (and they probably are). This game will not make your jaws drop, cry or scream about anything, but it has some enjoyable things and nice graphics. Don't buy the Season Pass, you will pay for new DLC's that will not come at all. Bathesda did not announce The Evil Within 2 in its conference and I have reasons to believe that they will touch it for some time. Buy when its cheap so you won't regret if it sucks for you. I hope this helps people making a good purchasing choice.

I wanted to like this game, but the controls are among the worst I've ever seen.
Basically, you have to click the left mouse to grab the "disc". And hold it to keep hold of the disk. Your opponent can immediately grab it back, leading to a series of back and forth snatches until one of you screws up or magically rotates your player. Timing needs to be perfect or close to it to actually catch the disc. Opponents can magically scoop the disc from behind you, even if this is how the tutorial tells you to avoid getting it stolen.
Holding the disc drains stamina, which is a nearly-invisible circle that appears in front of you. LITERALLY UNDER THE DISC if you're holding it. Basically the worst possible visual choice the game could have made for a necessary mechanic.
This is a pre-release review, so it's entirely possible that some of these things get worked out, particularly the visual issue. However, I would be extremely surprised if the controls are fixed, since I think that's the whole design concept, so this game may as well be radioactive. Great idea, among the worst execution I've seen.

In later levels you start out in a location outside your screen and then you have to play around every retry to find where you are and where the crosshair is.
Next, enemies can see you and shoot you when you don’t see them. What this leads to? Rushing in like an idiot for five or more times in a row just to pinpoint the exact location of your enemies. Let’s not forget how unpredictable they are – you can be shooting around with a shotgun and one time the same enemies come at you, sometimes not. This especially frustrates when you’re a few meters away from the enemy and you never know what is he going to do next.
Also, level design got worse. Sometimes the only option is to open the door or come out of a corner, expose yourself for a second or two and hope that somebody comes looking for you. Occasionally no one sees you and you have to repeat the same thing again. This sometimes happens on every level. Doing the same thing gets pretty boring after a while.
In conclusion, I really wanted to like this game and was looking forward to it, but, unfortunately, devs did not deliver.

The original Hotline Miami is a great game, filled with blood, fast gameplay and a surreal vibe all over the plot. Dennaton Games decided to finish the story with the second installment, Wrong Number, and while I would prefer a trilogy, I can't complain at the duo, because HM 2 is the best indie game I've played so far.
The gameplay is the same of the last one, fast and brutal, but Dennaton ups the ante by including a "pulp fiction" like plot following several characters and their gore filled adventures. Not only that, but the pixelated graphics are more polished than the previous game, and the soundtrack is just amazing.
Some might play this just to kill russians and colombians, but it's very clear that there's a deeper meaning behind all this madness, and it'll provide the more observant players with some tought provoking questions.
Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is everything it needs to be and more. And I loved it!

I got this game only a few short months ago, and I must say, this game is one of the most emmersive, realistic (not that much), and fun games I've played in a while. The graphics in the game are a superior upgrade to its predecessor, (Mount and Blade), the colour labels for each faction are realistic, (e.g., Blue for the water-filled lands in the kingdom of Nords, yellow for the deserts in the Sarranid Sultanate, white for the tundra in the Kingdom of Vaegirs, etc.) I haven't downloaded any mods for the game yet, so I have yet to see what  mod devs have to offer. This game (that is if you are new to it) is very unforgiving, because say, if you lose a fight with a lord, then you can a) get the entirety of your army stripped away, and b) have to start all over again. Or, if you accidentially click the 'Besiege Castle' button, you can mess up any chance for being on good terms with a Kingdom. Unless you are loaded as s**t. Sadly, now to the cons about the game. Keep in mind that these are mostly just me nitpicking, so if you lose your s**t about it because you are a long-time fan of this game, calm down. Even though this game is in a medieval setting, there isn't much of an emphasis on religion. For those of you who don't know, religion was a crucial role in everyday life. For instance, let's say the Kingdom of Swadia declared war on the Kingdom of Nords because Swadians were Christian, and the Nords were pagan. This is what Viking Conquest did right. It put an emphasis on weither you were christian or pagan, and that slightly dictated if you got along with someone. Also, I would have liked a bit more troop variety. You have your skirmishers, crossbows and knights, but where was the bowmen for the Swadians, and Cavalry for the Nords. Now, I do realise that cavalry wasn't impelmented for the Rhodoks for, well, mountains, and that there were no high-level infantry for the Khergits, because they were there to reflect the Mongols, or was it the Khazars? I digress. Also, I wish the land of Calradia was bigger. I know that somewhere, someone will say, "What are you talking about? Calradia is HUGE!!!" No, it isn't. In fact, with no army, you can go from Durquaba to Chalbeck Castle in approximatley 10 DAYS! Hopefully Bannerlord will fix some of these issues. Overall, the game is solid, it's immersive, and is one of the best games I've played, and I would give it an 8/10. Great game.

I wasn't expecting to enjoy this game so much. I never liked Left 4 Dead, but from what I remember of it this is basically a cleaned-up, reskinned version of the gameplay. Or maybe comparing it to Left 4 Dead is unjust, because I know there's a whole genre of games like this. Whatever, I was never interested in them.
I got this because I've always loved the Warhammer Fantasy world, and I've never seen it translated well into a computer game. And while this isn't my dream game (basically, if someone invented an Elder Scrolls-style open world CRPG set in the Old World I'd never leave my room again) it does the Warhammer Fantasy world well. It's all in the details. The graphics are beautiful and well-optimized. The characters are all just twisted and deviant enough to fit the setting (except for the soldier, and he's a perfect foil for the others) and the exchanges of dialogue they have can, at their best, make the game feel alive. The skaven are foul and chittering. The mechanics (from the steady supply of ambushes to the claustrophobic corridors to the uncounterable disables from the Gutter Runners and Packmasters) give gameplay a real sense of paranoia and urgency.
It's enough to make me enjoy what is ultimately a grind-based game where every mission is basically a rearrangement of the same enemies and challenges as every other. I have enjoyed it for more than 30 hours already. QUALITY STUFF.
My only real complaints:
1. The AI is terrible, to the point of making games with fewer than three real players on any of the higher difficulty settings almost unplayable.  This makes mid-game disconnects way more frustrating than they need to be.
2. I'm not a huge fan of the difficulty settings.  Hard isn't all that challenging when you've got a good group, while Nightmare is insane.  Or maybe I'm just not good enough.  But I'd love to see a level beyond High but without friendly fire, because friendly fire is a super bad idea in pickup games (which are all I play; I don't have any friends who are into this game).
3. The characters don't seem super well balanced?  Or maybe it's just that the Bright Wizard is much more my playstyle than the others.  In any case, she rules, with the atmospheric Winds of Magic mechanic and her unlimited ranged attacks, while the other four all seem a good bit less effective.

Layers of Fear is a good example of how scares should be implemented in a predictable setting. With a broad range of traditional scares, it strives to terrorize the player with as many different tricks as possible. For some, it will be overwhelming, and perhaps the game could have provided more downtime—or at least something more substantial than searching through empty drawers for notes. Replaying the adventure results in a severe decrease in terror because the story plays out nearly identically. However, that does not change the fact that Layers of Fear will send shivers down your spine during its first attempt, thanks to many careful jump scares. With a steady increase in terror, Layers of Fear is a horror game that succeeds through its variety.

Okay so I just finally finished the final build of this game.
A few observations for your consideration.
Do not buy this game if it is only because you seek to play a scary game. In that way I think the game does a so-so job of finding ways to overcome your expectations. (Certainly it would be an even scarier game with future VR support. I saw someone say on one of the update comment sections something to this effect and the team that put this interesting  game together would be foolish not to pursue this line of thought someday.)
Now who I recommend this game to has a lot to do with who you are as a person. It's a very cathartic experience playing a game *slight spoilers ahead* about a man who has lost everything including his capacity to make art that still sells. It's a fear that I think many people will relate to whom they themselves (myself included) work in for a living. The late but always amazing Robin Williams was unable to generate the kind of income he use to when younger. He made a serious of flops box office wise. So eventually he returned to where he started by making a new television show. In the end, it did not fare well.
Throughout my time with this game it hurt me to see a fellow human being hurt himself, in some cases literally for his art. But for a lot of people this is something that can if not to this narrative extreme, relate to. It's in this way that I think it will be quite likely one of the most unique things you will ever play via Steam.
Now as far as my complaints go, the story was not as developed as I was hoping it would be, which is a shame because the pieces that are here make for a heart wrenching melodrama. Which is why I think in the end, for me at least this was more of a sad story then a genuinely scary one. I say this as someone who eats up paranormal psychological horror films as a film maker, mind you.
Should you buy it?
I would say that for the same price you could buy a film or you could try something that is an experimental new way to share psychological mental deterioration with you the participate. Either way it’s not something I feel like I’ve ever really played before, even if it is at best a haunted house with a refined sense of self. Finally unlocked all the achievements, so hey, why not write a review.
This game is really well-made. Graphics, level design, everything is top-notch. Any bad thing I may have to say about the game is due to my disagreement with the devs' decisions, not due to the devs failing to execute their decisions well enough.
The core mechanics is really innovative and different. For that alone the game deserves a recommendation.
Simply completing the game is moderately hard. Unlocking all the achievements is really very very hard. Think Super Meat Boy level of hard. If you don't intend to attempt to unlock all of them, the game may appear too short for its price. This game is really targeted at the masochistic kind of people who will replay the same level again and again until they finally manage to do it perfectly.
The biggest disappointment for me was that all the puzzles only test reflexes and manual dexterity. I wish the puzzles were more similar to Portal or Braid, clever riddles that you have to strain your brains to solve, and once you solve them you'd get a new broader understanding of the game's mechanics, and the puzzle will appear obvious in retrospect. Alas, the devs decided to go another route.
Connected to the previous point, I wish the core mechanics would change in later levels. Something like reagents that temporarily change your cohesion or make you smaller/faster/sticker. There are new elements that appear in later levels, but they're all in levels themselves - new objects to interact with, new liquids and traps. The mushroom itself stays exactly the same during the course of the entire game. Which is a shame.

Mushroom 11 is a puzzle platformer where you move your amorphous blob around the level by shaving or destroying parts of it forcing it to regrow in the direction you are trying to move. Thankfully it regrows almost as fast as you can destroy it , I assume it's powered by photosynthesis, nuclear fallout or just magic.
The game contains seven large levels set in a post-apocalyptic world and in a twist you move right to left on screen which takes a little getting used to! Each levels contains multiple puzzles like climbing stairs, riding rotating metal bars, an Indiana Jones cart sequence to running ahead of rolling balls creating bridges with your blob so it can pass by. There is plenty of inventiveness here and many of the puzzles in the last two levels are quite demanding.
The control system couldn't be simpler, left click to destroy a large part of the blob, right click a small part. Sadly here is the only weakness in the game, as the blob randomly respawns when you eat away at it some of the tougher puzzles are more trial and error and just plain frustration instead of fun.
Beautifully presented, Mushroom 11 is a very good game only let down by a control system that can't quite keep up with it's demands at times.

NOTE: This game was a large factor in me purchasing it with 5 other games in the BTA Humble Bundle for cheap.
This game has a very annoying concept, but very good level design. Controlling the character with the mouse was unique. It had a learning curve to it. The game explain how to do it somewhat, but i feel some more instructions could help here. Its possible to move through most sections fast, but it isn't intuitive how to do it. This made the game annoying. However, the game made interesting use of its mechanics with interesting physics "puzzles". I especially liked the rocket riding challenges in Chapter 6. As someone who played a lot of Portal 2. If you like spending hours trying to make stacks of cubes or wall portal climb to try and break a chamber, this game feels like a good fit for you.
One thing that often felt unfair about this game is that your body can often get split into pieces and the camera follows the wrong one. Then when you try to get back together by erasing the other side and the side you wanted to stay is already going off the screen which destroys it, so you die. Another problem with the camera was that it would sometimes shake erratically causing lots of lag, while your trying to make a precise move. This doesn't happen too often, but I would propose to fix it by giving an option in the options menu for the player to control the camera. This couldn't be used to look ahead because the player will still get killed if they move the camera away from the character.
One great feature of this game is that all levels save individually, so if your trying to get 100% on one, and there's a tricky one you can't get, and you want to try a different level no deaths, then you don't have to lose progress on that level. This is something I didn't realise at first thats a really smart feature most games don't have.
Don't expect to get all the acheivements from this one. The last chapter (level 7) is extremely hard to get no deaths. I don't think it's worth it. There is also a extremely well hidden "Strand" in each level. If you have lots of extra time and are looking for a challenging search this is a great part of the game, and adds replay value. If you don't have other games to get on to they're fun just to get. Check where they are on an online walkthrough video. Some acheivements are vague, and I can't find any information online about them.

It's a pretty good game.  Feels a lot like modern Resident Evils (which makes sense, given the same guy who designed RE4 did this one).
It's got problems, though, namely in the form of cheap deaths.  Case in point, during the prologue you're locked in a room with a butcher.  While his back is turned, you acquire a knife.  A tutorial tells you how to sneak.  You're supposed to sneak up behind the butcher and grab the keys nearby him.  But when you get behind the butcher, a prompt appears telling you to do a sneak kill.  This is your very first encounter with this prompt, so you have no way of knowing it's not part of the tutorial.  But if you attempt the sneak kill, you'll just make the butcher mad, and he'll 1-hit kill you.  The game is riddled with cheap 1-hit deaths you'll never see coming the first time through.
Another problem is items are scarce and without upgrades, you can't hold much ammunition.  That's fine, since the game is a stealth game..... Except for several chapters where it's not a stealth game and you're expected to be an action hero.  Kind of hard to fight off an infinite horde of monsters with just 15 bullets.
But if you can get past its (many, many) flaws, the game is actually pretty fun.  I'd still recommend checking it out.  I'd give it a 7/10.

It's obvious now that from the beginning, Rebellion had planned to make the Sniper Elite: Nazi Zombie Army spin-off series a trilogy. This second installment came just mere months after the first, and as such it doesn't offer up much that the first game didn't already have, save for new landscape visuals and a couple new demonic creatures. For a larger grasp of the core of the game, I'll direct you to my review of the first Nazi Zombie Army here.
Somehow this title manages to come bearing more blood and gore than its predecessor, not to mention a new fiery landscape that wasn't present previously. All of the maps have at least one area that's completely on fire, while others convey the sense of burning in surrounding areas due to thick plumes of smoke highlighted by an orange-yellow backdrop. There's also a bigger horror element to this second entry, one that is equal parts psychological, disturbing, and grisly. The amount of blood-drenched bodies, pentagrams, swastikas, gore spurts, spatters, and smears have increased dramatically, it's definitely not a game for the weak of stomach.
New enemies include a Fire Demon, who bursts with uncontrollable rage and sets any surrounding grunts on fire; turning them into speedy little bags of ignited charcoal. The other new "big" enemy is the Summoner, and you can pretty well understand his role by his name. Also included are a new skeleton model with a little bit of added armor, and remodeled grunt soldiers. The rest of the foes are ones that return from the prior title; snipers, gun-toting warriors, occultists, and regular skeletons. The story is also still split up into 5 chapters, all of which last about half an hour to an hour each. There's not a whole lot that's been added, as you can clearly tell.
All of the same gameplay elements that were present in the original title are still included here, Sniper Elite: Nazi Zombie Army 2 also comes with all of the annoying little quirks of its sophomore adventure as well; leaving it blatantly obvious that this game was either finished, or nearly so, long before Rebellion released it. Enemies still hit a little further than their model can reach, you still kick a little further than your model can reach, you still have to stop and press E to loot a body for ammo, and grenades are still difficult to control. There are a couple things that I ran out of room to discuss within my prior review, but I'm glad that it gives me something to talk about here.
While this spin-off series is indeed challenging, especially on higher difficulties, many of the confrontations can be completely sidestepped by backing yourself into a room with a narrow corridor; many of which are stockpiled with ammunition. In almost every instance when you're faced with a "siege" or "assault" moment where large hoards of undead Nazi's come spilling your way, there's a perfect alcove for you to funnel the enemy through, making it nearly impossible for you to get hurt. Though it can be ignored, having it there takes away a large portion of the core game mechanics, and not to mention the proposed threat. The aforementioned also negates the need for the cover system, which I personally never used in either title.
Even though Sniper Elite: Nazi Zombie Army 2 is clearly its predecessor dressed up with some new clothes it bought from the thrift store, it's still a fun wave-based zombie annihilation game. The new maps really help to keep the experience fresh, since they're so visually stunning and different than what came before. As for the story arc, it's lackluster at best but it serves an important purpose to what appears in Zombie Army Trilogy. As usual, the online portion of this game is dead, so if you're thinking about picking it up be prepared to play either solo or with friends. Recommended at a 75% discount, only if you want to play the original, otherwise pick up Zombie Army Trilogy instead.

Three-on-three ice hockey with a roster of robot players who are like MOBA heroes: Each with different strengths, weaknesses, and special moves.
Like a MOBA, you acquire new heroes (called "runners" in this game) with real money, or in-game currency you have to farm. Everyone starts with two runners: A forward (the player that tries to score goals) and a keeper (the player that tries to prevent the other team from scoring goals).
Matches are only three minutes long and the matchmaker puts you in with bots if it can't find other players (which is often).
Figuring out how to pass and remembering to keep your opponents covered is actually harder than figuring out the controls. After the unavoidable first impression that the game would be easier with a dual-analog controller, you'll quickly become an ace with the mouse-and-keyboard setup.
Beautiful graphics, cool heroes, catchy music, easy to learn.
All it really needs is a bigger player base.

I loved the first Hotline Miami, but after playing for some time I feel that this game truly lacks something, that made the first one so extraordinary.
First of all – the controls seem like they haven’t changed, but they feel much more clunky then they used to be. Trying to take a dropped weapon feels unresponsive. Want to knock down the enemy and them kill him with your bare hands? Good luck standing at just the right place to try to kill him. In later levels you start out in a location outside your screen and then you have to play around every retry to find where you are and where the crosshair is.
Next, enemies can see you and shoot you when you don’t see them. What this leads to? Rushing in like an idiot for five or more times in a row just to pinpoint the exact location of your enemies. Let’s not forget how unpredictable they are – you can be shooting around with a shotgun and one time the same enemies come at you, sometimes not. This especially frustrates when you’re a few meters away from the enemy and you never know what is he going to do next.
Also, level design got worse. Sometimes the only option is to open the door or come out of a corner, expose yourself for a second or two and hope that somebody comes looking for you. Occasionally no one sees you and you have to repeat the same thing again. This sometimes happens on every level. Doing the same thing gets pretty boring after a while.

The original Hotline Miami is a great game, filled with blood, fast gameplay and a surreal vibe all over the plot. First Impressions: Graphical style is solid, albeit, not amazing, but - good. Fits the theme, and makes me think very much of Penny Arcade in the drawing style, which is a positve.
Then, oh my, the game itself. It's a little... weird. I've never really played these kind of things online, but having been a huge M:TG fan way way back when, it's definately got a good spin on the idea. I dislike the idea of having such a limited pool of cards to play with. I can totally understand limiting the selection of cards so you have to have at least 20, but so far (and I don't know if this changes during the game later on) you're stuck with just twenty, and that's not a positive. We've all these wonderful combinations that we just can't do due to limited deck size. That's one major downside to the deck building aspect, but such is life - and it's not terrible, just would have preferred more wiggle room in that department.
In terms of strategy, seems quite simple, until you try and achieve some of the challenges - which make luck/rush a bit more of a factor, but they're fun to go for. Although there are times I wish I could freeze my cards from cycling, again, because of rng. But I do enjoy the timed aspects of the turn based system, making it simulataneous makes a huge difference to how it feels, and makes it much more actiony.
I can definately see me letting my boy play this, as he loves Pokemon et all, and this seems a little more grown-up in terms of game, but he's starting to get into them.
Cons:- It's random past your deckbuilding. If you're not a player of those type of games, this might frustrate you.
- Some of the starts you get, where you're outmatched immediately are frustrating, especially with random luck.
- It's a little simplistic. Doesn't have some of the same depth you may be used to if you're familiar to the format.
- While I've not played the game to death yet, although I can see myself enjoying this later on, I suspect it will feel very samey aftera while.
Pros:- It's cheap and while there's DLC, it doesn't have the spend spend spend attitude of many of the trading card style of games.
- If you enjoy tcg's, then you'll find the game quite intuitive, apart from the turns flying by if you're a "muller over of things".
- Graphics are nice, and the story so far seems interesting and for what few words there are, well written.
- Easy to get into, just from a short play time, I can see myself getting into this a lot more.
