Number one I am not an uber pvp master.  But I have played allot of games over many years and never felt I had to vent about any other game as strongly before I entered the S Zone.
I usually believe that most of the sniveling and whining about balance and cheating in pvp games are usually caused by younger people used to getting trophies for participation, the same ones who have  RTFM/L2P issues,  or who don't want to put in any effort in order to get the cool stuff.  And effort is a big thing in this game,  nothing comes from the zone without a struggle.  The one thing I first got hooked on was having to figure it all out myself,  from navigating a largly unmarked map to what the NPC's words really meant before they were translated to english. It was really fun,  I have always  enjoyed a challenging game.

About RTFM, forget about it. The manual is composed largly of myth,  like the zone itself. Even the devs themselves reach mythic proportions in S Zone,  some say that they even play on the PVP server,  racking up extraordinary kill ratios while observing and assuring balance. I cannot say myself that cheating or the devs padding stats does exist in this game, and would like to believe otherwise. But whether it does or not,  the PVP aspect is broken to the point me losing interest fast.

I particularly find it annoying that my rifle (cost $4.00 for 30 days) can dispatch charging boar with ease from 50-100 meters,  but trying to hit certain other  players  at half that range results in 25% hits or less.  Even the damage difference is painfully confusing,  I can hit an enemy with 6-8 times fairly regular with 7.62X51,  sometimes even up to 10 making the mark,  and in turn be killed by 4 rounds from same enemy. WTF?  Granted I am probably more easy to kill than most due to the fact that every weapon I have used seems to have a substantial  accuracy penalty when not stationary and/or in crouch,  as well as my reluctance to flit around like some sort of harlequin ninja doing a twitchy representation of Swan Lake.  While I am on the subject of ninja ballerinas,  they also seem to be able to hit me unerringly while running,  jumping,  doing pirouettes,  sometimes causing their bullets to bend around corners.  The stuff of legends indeed. FPS games where an advantage,  as opposed to a penalty,  is given to those who spam the space bar seem rather dated and silly,  to me anyway.

Now granted,  I am only lvl 18 as opposed to the cap of 30,  and no doubt several million experience points allocated to armor,  weapon, health/stamina recovery etc behind most players. But come on,  give a guy a break once in awhile,  I mean three 7.62 nato to the head should at least slow a man down one would think,  no matter what helmet he has on.  At least blur his vision a bit.

The kill ratio of some of these "oober" players is the stuff of legend.  Maybe it is because they have spent too much time in the zone,  allocating mass quantities of exp to their stats,  carrying around beneficial artifacts,  using gold weapons and armor,  fine,  understandable.  But 10-12 clan members being prevented from taking a base by 1 or 2 enemies with all the guards down is kind of difficult to swallow.  Since I play a medic,  I do try to avoid unwanted attention sneaking around  in order to revive my teammates,  so I probably don't die nearly as much as someone assaulting the flags,  but even then some of these players  have amassed 25-30 or more kills on me,  fine I suck and am underequipped. But since I have started watching gameplay replays,  some of these same players seem to get pretty regular 15 or 20 to one K/D. While being outnumbered 6 to 1.  Or more. I have spent almost 300hrs on my main character,  if at just over half level cap all I can expect is getting a 1:30 K/D  what is the point. I heard a wise man once say "the  sun shines on even an ugly dog's♥♥♥♥♥once in awhile".

There is lag.  Lots of it. More lag when certain players are close to you. Still more when they shoot at you. You get two or three of these particular un-named enemies shooting at you and it stacks, what a great buff. Some enemies even make me lag when it is me shooting at them,  turning my screen to a slideshow,  while being riddled by laser guided bullets.
Yeah I think it is almost over for me.  I really wanted it to work,  but it has almost reached the point of continued playtime equaling insanity.  Good Luck fellow Stalkers.

I mainly play in stereoscopic 3D so this rating is largely based on that aspect:
The environment and effects render perfectly and overall game runs/plays very smooth, this alone makes it a must try in my book. I know these factors can vary by PC build, so they have a demo available if you want to test your setup.
From a gameplay point of view, I would honestly consider the game more of an action genre than a suspense. For example; I would compare it to a creepier version of resident evil than to something like Silent Hill. I also like the fact that it has simple enough controls, accurate aiming is dam-near-impossible in 3D so the auto-lock feature makes the game actually playable.
As for the actual story, it’s not too bad this far in but honestly the 3D immersion adds to a lot of it, I tend to get sucked into the story easier and can play for hours at a time before the wife gets mad.
Overall 10-10 for a stereoscopic 3D experience!

Before this game got insanely popular I loved this game, one of my absolute favorites. I stopped playing for a bit and moved on to different games. When I came back (a few months later) I checked to see how my German character was doing. I was focusing on getting the Kar 98. You would need to level up your assault ribbon to a two star ribbon instead of one. Turns out that the price of it (credit wise) skyrocketed from about only 20k creds to 91k. As other reviews say that a bunch of people run around with insanely over powered one shot kill weapons, that's true. You take one step into a Pay To Win lobby and you'll be lucky to get over 10 kills and below 15 deaths. The starting weapons are usually a three shot kill, that I have no problem with besides for the lack of firing rate. If you go up against a sub machinegun close quarters there is zero chance you'll win. At a range you'll have a slighter chance of winning but you'll most likely lose. When you go into staged battles you'll notice that it "Attempts" to match you with people around your skill group. What that means is if you're a good player you'll be matched with a ton of P2W people. If you're a bit new to FPS's or just not very fond of them you'll still be matched with the same people. All in all I would not reccomend this game for the amount of time you need to farm to actually rank up and or get a new gun.

Imagine if you cross the quirky graphics  of  Team Fortress 2 with the freedom of building of Gary's Mod...
Whilst still in development, SM provides more than enough fun in it's Creative mode; esp since you can invite Steam friends to play along!
Speaking of Steam- It's via Steam Workshop ( the connection of which is built into the game; no need to minimize) that one can not only play around with other player's creations but can upload your own to be shared!
Basically, in it's current form, SM is a physics-based building tool. The player gets a Handbook at start that teaches, in very basic instruction, how to create truly remarkable creations.
The most popular creation ( as far as I can tell) is vehicles. However you can even find pre-built houses, workshops, garages, and a host of others via the Steam Workshop.
If you download another's creation and tire of it, simply put said creation on the work-jack and delete. The "blueprint" stays with you unless you delete it as well.
I have had two crashes thus far, once whilst loading another's creation and the other whilst using the paint tool. Overall it seems a remarkably stable game.
At this stage I give it a Rivscore of  89 /100

Ironclad tactics is a fast paced turn-based tactics game based on card deck building. Since this description doesn't help, here is a slightly better one: the player chooses various soldiers and weapons from a consequent number of available ones. A card deck comprises 20 of these picks. Each deck has to be chosen carefully according to the needs of each mission. The battles consist of playing the cards (appearing in a random order) to send troops and give them equipment. They move automatically forward on the lanes they are deployed on, but the tactical possibilities are numerous with the ability to stop a unit, sometimes switch lanes, use weapons that target specific lanes, add a specific customization to a mecha and so on. The game seems like real time to the player, but the actions are conducted by the computer in quick, seamless turns.
This might seem complicated on paper, but in-game it works very intuitively so that the player can fully focus on choices and tactical decisions. And the fast speed allows for the battles not to drag on, they even trigger a lot of adrenaline as the player has to think fast and is always kept on the edge. The gameplay is really good and works well in these half fast-paced half-slowed down conditions.
However, where this game also really shines is in the level design. Usually strategy games can be repetitive as the players figure out their favorite strategy and repeat it to go through every mission. In Ironcland Tactics, each mission is different with the levels having a specific gimmick and the enemy deploying specific troops. While at first it can seem overwhelming if using the deck that was tailored for the previous level, this actually relates more to a puzzle game where the player has to figure out a well suited tactic to win. Card decks thus have to be customized specifically for every mission. So even if some might consider this very challenging when they don't know yet which strategy to use, I find it brilliant. It completely prevents the game from feeling repetitive with a single formula repeated ad nauseam, and keeps me thinking on how to tackle each new battle and makes me feel great for figuring out new strategies. Although, even if I mentioned a puzzle game inspiration, this game is not as static and mind taxing as a puzzle game, it remains very dynamic.
The story missions are linked through nicely made comics, reinforcing the feeling that overall this game has been carefully crafted. Additionally, the story can be played in online Coop as the players fight together and have to coordinate their strategy (forget it if you are not on voice communication, good communication seems pretty much required to succeed without making stupid mistakes - well these mistakes still happen on voice communication and can be hilarious, such as when one player decides to give a speed boost to a unit from the second player who decided that it should strategically hold position). And if you want to get revenge on your teammate for a mistake, there is always the possibility for 1 vs 1 to settle things non peacefully. Also of note, some missions can add a nice twist to the 1 vs 1 multiplayer such as the possibility for one of the two players to use a boss deck.

It's always risky to try some radically new base mechanic in a platformer game, so I tend to hail anyone who attempts to do so. Enter Mushroom 11, where you can't control your character directly - all you can do is erase a part of it. What you delete will regrow in a few seconds, randomly across the bulk of the fungus. Result: if you persistently delete the right side, the entire bulk will move to the left. And basically that's all.
For such an odd mechanic to work, the puzzle design needs to be ultra careful, and this is one area where the game shines - most of the tasks ahead of our hero are well thought-out, rarely very difficult, and the checkpoints are thankfully frequent.
The other aspect worth mentioning is the incredible background art and atmosphere.
Mushroom 11 is not without faults, either. One is a direct consequence of the base mechanic - whenever you need to do something with accuracy, you need a lot of luck or a lot of patience. The latter can run out easily when you're shaping your fungus into something elaborate for the umpteenth time, and still end up eg. falling down.
The other is more strange - at some points, the game seems to interfere with the physics, forcing a certain solution path. I met this only 2-3 times - one example is the cart ride in level 5 where I found it impossible to keep the fungus in the cart at a certain jump.
Based on the above, there's a little secret to enjoying Musroom 11 - take breaks, even frequent breaks, depending on your skill. There are not many very difficult puzzles in the game (levels 5-7 are more difficult than 1-4, but not dramatically so), but the randomness tends to wear you down after a while, and you'll feel the game is unfair while it's only doing its thing relentlessly. Quit and come back tomorrow, it will feel fresh again.
Untame has done a great job with Mushroom 11 - made a very brave move with the base mechanics, and designed an interesting and visually superb world around it. Definitely recommended.

This is a challenging platform/timing game with mouse and alternative keyboard controls for the mouse buttons that I found more comfortable since you hold down the buttons a lot. The puzzles are logical if difficult. If you are observant you will see what you have to do, even if it seems unlikely to be able to do it. Experimentation is better than walkthroughs for this game, The epilogue is a neat final puzzle that could be read different ways. Sometimes momentum works in your favor - though I wouldn't call it luck - the flow of physics in the game is sometimes unexpected, forcing you to alter your strategy.
The game is neither easy, nor arbitrary. The difficulty often is related to the fact that earlier puzzles have many different ways to solve them. As you progress, it is clear that the designers have 2 or maybe even one solution in mind, and you have to try to figure out what that is.
Dexterity and precision with the mouse is required.

I got this game only a few short months ago, and I must say, this game is one of the most emmersive, realistic (not that much), and fun games I've played in a while. The graphics in the game are a superior upgrade to its predecessor, (Mount and Blade), the colour labels for each faction are realistic, (e.g., Blue for the water-filled lands in the kingdom of Nords, yellow for the deserts in the Sarranid Sultanate, white for the tundra in the Kingdom of Vaegirs, etc.) I haven't downloaded any mods for the game yet, so I have yet to see what  mod devs have to offer. This game (that is if you are new to it) is very unforgiving, because say, if you lose a fight with a lord, then you can a) get the entirety of your army stripped away, and b) have to start all over again. Or, if you accidentially click the 'Besiege Castle' button, you can mess up any chance for being on good terms with a Kingdom. Unless you are loaded as s**t. Sadly, now to the cons about the game. Keep in mind that these are mostly just me nitpicking, so if you lose your s**t about it because you are a long-time fan of this game, calm down. Even though this game is in a medieval setting, there isn't much of an emphasis on religion. For those of you who don't know, religion was a crucial role in everyday life. For instance, let's say the Kingdom of Swadia declared war on the Kingdom of Nords because Swadians were Christian, and the Nords were pagan. This is what Viking Conquest did right. It put an emphasis on weither you were christian or pagan, and that slightly dictated if you got along with someone. Also, I would have liked a bit more troop variety. You have your skirmishers, crossbows and knights, but where was the bowmen for the Swadians, and Cavalry for the Nords. Now, I do realise that cavalry wasn't impelmented for the Rhodoks for, well, mountains, and that there were no high-level infantry for the Khergits, because they were there to reflect the Mongols, or was it the Khazars? I digress. Also, I wish the land of Calradia was bigger. I know that somewhere, someone will say, "What are you talking about? Calradia is HUGE!!!" No, it isn't. In fact, with no army, you can go from Durquaba to Chalbeck Castle in approximatley 10 DAYS! Hopefully Bannerlord will fix some of these issues. Overall, the game is solid, it's immersive, and is one of the best games I've played, and I would give it an 8/10. Great game.

I went into this one with no expectations and having no idea what the point of the game was at all. I think that made the experience better. That being said, it’s an early access game with definite room for improvement, but it gets a few things right. Let’s begin.
TLDR: Not Recommended
The Good
ACE – Arena: Cyber Evolution is like futuristic air hockey, only it’s played at a life-size scale. You can select from a few characters to play as (others you have to unlock through in-game currency). Each character has special abilities he or she can use to aid you and your team on the path to victory. I’m sure most of us (if not all of us) have played air hockey before. It’s fun and it’s a fairly acceptable way to kill some time. As the game stands now in it’s current state, that’s the highest praise I’ll be giving it. A dressed up game of air hockey.
The Bad
As I mentioned above, some characters need to be unlocked through in-game currency. The same holds for character customization options (skins and the like). Most of it you’d be forking over actual currency to get and that, to me, is an utter waste for a game like this.
The game has only two resolution settings, neither of which fit my monitor. Sad day.
The only other real complaint I had had to do with the controls. Well, one specific control. Holding down the left mouse button allows you to grab and hold onto the disc (puck). Releasing the left mouse button (in theory) allows you to shoot the disc in the direction your cursor is facing. 70% of the time when I tried to shoot the disc, it floated in front of me in a pathetic manner and this often resulted in the enemy team taking control of it.
The Meh
Initially, I thought the artwork for the game looked like it was going to be my kind of thing. It has a sort of Borderlands-esque feel to it, right? Not so much. Actual in game graphics didn’t really do it for me. They just seemed lacking.
This game is very much an online game. However, I played for a good long while and only ever had matches with bots. the community is, for all intents and purposes, much like a cemetery. You don’t need other players to play, luckily. As I said, you can play with bots.
Verdict: Nay
While part of me feels this is a bit harsh for a free-to-play game, I just can’t bring myself to recommend it as it is now. Maybe once it hits it’s final release I will revisit it and give it another go. Until then, I think I’ll stick to real air hockey and I would advise all of you to do the same. As always, thanks for reading.

Whether you're a Resident Evil veteran or a Silent Hill fan; an Amnesia lover or an Outlast player, it doesn't matter, this game is not for you, do NOT play this game, this game isn't for anyone. Even if you're an absolute die-hard fan of Horror genre, it still doesn't jusify wasting your precious time on the horrible mess that's The Evil Within. Now, I came to this with very low expectations but was still disappointed. Even buying this title on a sale would be a mistake and I will explain why in this review.
First off, let me start by the nonsensical story and blunt characters, out of all the characters (and there aren't many to begin with) I couldn't find a single person that I could relate to or even like a little bit. Character design is utterly terrible, you can't feel anything for the characters because they're so undeveloped and plain weak. Story isn't any better, it doesn't many any sense and the ending is one of the worst I've seen in horror movies/games so far. Until the very end of the game, you literally have no idea what the hell is going on and the nonsense tapes and journals wouldn't help much at all. Overall, the story is just so bad that you'd completely lose any interest in the game in the beginning few hours. The nonsense story with its uninteresting characters is coupled with subpar voice acting and bad animations. If you're looking for a thrilling adventure, you won't find that here.
So hopefully gameplay would make up for it, right? Wrong. Gameplay is an unpolished broken mess. The mind-blowing difficulty of the game stems only from imbalances and cheap deaths. Half the time you have no idea WTF killed you, the other half it was an enemy you couldn't see because the camera just sucks. There's no adjustment option for FOV (Field of View) and if the default settings (whatever the hell it is) doesn't give you motion sickness, you will get headaches and/or nausea. Controls are extremely difficult and the main character is very sloppy. This game will make you wish you could have the tank controls of Resident Evil 4 back, this is MUCH worse than that. The level design is so poor that even though the game is pretty linear, navigation is difficult because there are traps LITERALLY everywhere. You would blow yourself up by traps or get eaten by invisible enemies A LOT. That's right, completely invisible enemies! As if the frustration mess of traps wasn't enough already...
Normal enemies can kill you in very few hits, and if they grab you, you're screwed. Because either the broken camera will disorient you or you get teleported through the ground then gang-banged by all of the enemies at once. Basically, in group fights if you're grabbed you're dead. There are many bugs and glitches and the technical side isn't any better. The only redeeming factor would be the somewhat appealing graphics which would take a high-end gaming rig to even run properly because the optimization is♥♥♥♥♥♥poor. NPCs have no hit detection, you can literally move through them. And the game will crash A LOT for no reason.
Overall, I wouldn't recommend playing this game even if you get it for free somehow. It's simply not worth your time, it could've been a great game but ended up utterly terrible because of poor development. Technical side is an absolute mess which by itself could make the game completely unplayable. On the other hand we've got imbalanced gameplay and frustrating level design which kills you over and over again just for the sake of extending play time through retries.
So let me make myself very clear now, this game isn't just bad it's utterly terrible. It's plain awful and a complete waste of time and 60GB.

I played this game for free and enjoyed myself. The game is a card game in which you need to win a certain amount of victory points by having key units exit the map on the enemies side.. of course the enemy tries to do the same with his  key unit exiting of your side of the map. Next to the units which you summon with the appropiate cards, you have cards that enhance them or allow them to do special moves. Some cards are tied in with a special units.
You can design your own deck with the cards so that you can play the game the way you want, although sometimes you are forced to play with a certain deck.. especially when you want to win bonus cards or solve puzzles.
I followed the story mode until I got stuck and discovered that next to the story mode there are other options to win additional cards and units. The end battle I found particular hard to win.
The game is a kind of a mixed bag. On the one hand it is fun game with a nice visual style and mood. The art design is cartoony which is well chosen as it fits well the mood of the game.  The story mode is told via cartoons, which I found captivating at first, but near to the end I started to click through to get to the battle. The makers made a wise choice not to force players to sit through a story every time they are defeated  and have to replay it again and I think I even gained cards when I was defeated.
The  other hand, the down side, is that the game remains a random card game and it isn't easy to build a tactic around it.  In addition you get often thrown into a unknown situation with no clue about what you are up against, so that you might find yourself losing because you simple have the wrong cards and units to defeat the challenge. Especially the end battle is heavily dependent on luck.. if you luck out you lose, if you luck holds you win.
In addition I don't quite understand why the makers chose to split the cards up in groups of which you can only have two at the same time. At least one group has no units and another consists mostly of units that are into sneaking and have no use in a regular fight. Why this limitation has been introduced remains a mystery as you are limited to 20 cards and I can't think of a combination of cards that would make someone invincible.. but maybe you can..
Anyway.. would I recommend it..

At a first glance this game seems like a very good one. It has a novel twist on the platformer genre, adding physics puzzles to a biological blob. Initially, the levels are fun and the puzzles are challenging, but by the time you reach the final levels you realise things stop being fun, and just become frustrating.
The game excells in the art department however, from the nice detailed backgrounds, to the feel of the diverse biology, the post-apocalyptic atmosphere, and the ambient background music.
The control scheme of using a mouse to click and grow a tol that burns away the blob work well initally, but when you need more precise control later on it becomes difficult to use. Mostly because you have either a very small brush, or a big one that changes in size. This, plus the mechanic seems more geared towards a touch device where you can touch directly on what you want to change, rather than dragging a cursor around.
The puzzles themselves are initially simple, and soon become challenging, but solvable. But eventually they require very precise movements to complete, which in my mind are simply too difficult for the control scheme provided.
The game idea is great but the automatic camera movement makes gameplay way more difficult than it should.

Okay That was ridiculous, I know. But the very least I could do was give Vermintide a romantic backstory because I friggin love this game. I am not sure what initially drew my attention to it. I have barely any notion of what the Warhammer universe is about. All I knew at the time was Warhammer games generally receive high praise. This title was no different. After spending some good ol' fashion quality time with Vermintide I can honestly say this has been the best purchase I have made on steam in ages.
During my first few moments lurking the dark streets and alleys I felt entirely uncertain and impotent with my weapons. And my character pane at the bottom of the screen came emblazoned with a big fat ZERO beneath my character portrait and steam name. That number representing my player level within the Vermintide universe. And so I did as all noobs do when in team-based gameplay where each players contributions matter and your ineptitude shines bright as the new dawn; I floundered miserably. You need me to bandage you? Here I'll throw this grenade instead. Need me to throw a grenade? How about I just hold this tome in front of my face and do absolutely nothing. Fortunately for my fragile ego, the community has not only been kind, but they have gone out of their way to teach strategy and educate me on some of the less obvious mechanics. In no time I had sunk hours into the game: dismantling and upgrading items, seeking tomes and grimoires, and even tackling my first few maps on Nightmare difficulty. My pistols breathed fire into the lungs of my foes. My axe was the bane of our enemies while my shield became a bastion for my friends. It seemed as if every time I logged in, I was in store for some epic encounters. Hell, even our defeats were glorious!
Overall, here's what matters.
It looks phenomenal. The controls are responsive. The content is engaging. The community, from what I have encountered, is helpful.

This game is a story of wasted opertunity!
Pro:
Cool gameplay.
Pretty desent enemy AI for a horde mode focused game.
Nice graphics and ambiance.
Really good sound design.
For the most parts - a good level design.
So what's wrong here? This game should be 9 out of 10 right? Well ... Sadly no...
Cons:
HORRIBLE companion AI. The game has a limited player base, which means you sometimes have to play with "BOTS" as the game calls them... Well... Let me explain how bad this is with an example. I'm plowing through a level with 3 BOTs ... nothing is really phasing me - I even picked up an item which helps get better loot in the end instead of a healthpack cause I had it under control... Weeeellll then I met a rat with a machinegun in a narrow hallway. I killed the rat, but 2 small minions which are normally no threat got me... and hacked away at me while I was laying on the floor. What was my AI companions doing? They where LITTERALLY just looking at it... doing nothing... And once you die while in single player "mode", there is no "save the captured" function which is normally there.... PUFF ... 20-30 min gone.... due to poor AI... F that... Seriously!
The loot is horrible... No really what you do during the mission is you can get random "dice" as loot in chests, and pick up up to 3 tomes, which also "boost" your dice. At the end of the round you get one throw with your dice which is LITTLERALLY limited to "how many dice have symbols vs how many dice have blank sides showing"... on the side there is a random loot table with white, then green, then... you get the point... The more symbols, the better loot. What is my issue with this? You spent a LONG time doing a mission, and there is basically no reason to be "good". You don't get anything from chests in the game, you can't pick up any items even though there are tons dropped (Even LARGE miniguns ala the Heavy from TF2) ... all you get is one throw on a RANDOM loot table (so you risk NEVER getting ANY upgrades for your favorite toon)... so you can be the worst player in history running into a wall while your team fights... and get the best loot... while the top contributer who has spend the whole time on the front line ...... gets shaftet with a white item he can't even use... Really LAME! Compared to how long a round takes, that's NO WHERE NEAR a good enough reward!
And oh yeah ... let's not even talk about the crafting/enchanting system... It reminds me of how mobile games and old MMO's does it... Boring and antique!
"Modern military shooter" system... Seriously you can only carry one healing item at a time... Why?... It makes no logical sense - especially seeing how one of the items is bandages. Bandages takes up litterally no space... soooohhh... why? Oh and why can't I carry a few bandages, but I can carry another potion for a temporary boost... why can't that potion be a healing potion instead? It's stupid... AND ... It get's worse... as I talked about previously, the "better loot" items - some of them takes up the spot where your healing item goes... which makes even less sense............ seeing how I can carry it all + a sack of food or a barrel of gunpowder no problem... Just... Poorly designed!
BORING character "costumizations" ... if you can even call it that... Basically you can pick a different melee and ranged weapon... and that's about it... No really... A fantasy game based on the WH universe with no stats of any kind other than some bars for your weapons.......
And now - about the worst... The monsters... This game is basically Left 4 Dead... No really - it's a carbon copy! Here is the "special" mobs:
A Plague Rat... Throws an area effect poison cloud which blurrs your vision and damages......... Ok that isn't damning right?
A Pack Rat... Throw a line and pulls a player away while draining life from them unless someone helps them................ erhm.......
An assassin... Which jumps a player and stabs them till they die unless someone helps them......... Really.... I mean... Really???
Rat ogre... A big hunk of meat who charges and knocks bac.... screw it I'm even gonna continue here... It's Left 4 Dead ... EOD!
I Liked Left 4 Dead A LOT - so I actually wouldn't have an issue if that was the only critisism I had here... But this game COULD have been SUCH a good game - Like - INSANELY good - if only they had put a bit more effort into the characters and the reward system. Games like this DIE so fast because there it has no lasting appeal - which is PRETTY DAMN BAD in a multiplayer focused game! And god help you if you deside to play with the AI BOTs... God help you!! How does a man reclaim his family? How does he return to the present-day future? How does he avenge his fallen partner? But more importantly, why does this Asian schoolgirl want to kill you? Answers to these questions, and all of life’s most philosophical quandaries in The Showdown Effect.
The Showdown Effect is a side-scrolling action game from Arrowhead Game Studios, creators of Magicka. This time around, the studio is focusing more on a competitive eSports approach. Combining parkour-style platforming and precision aiming, The Showdown Effect creates a menagerie of chaotic bullet fury, slick moves, great hair, and ostentatious blood sport. It has all the flair and witty humor one would expect from an Arrowhead game.
Controlled on a flat 2-D plane much like many games from yesteryear, Showdown’s unique feature is its precision aiming, requiring you to actually keep your mouse cursor over your targets to inflict damage. Most side scrollers only need you to aim in a general direction to hit targets, but Showdown‘s finely tuned aim separates the good players from the truly great players. It’s a mechanic like this that could have allowed the game to be a legitimate eSport. Some weapons can be spammed, such as the grenade launcher and throwing knives–this is when the platforming elements come into play. Skilled players are able to avoid such attacks while maintaining the dexterity to mow down their foes. The skill required to pull off such feats is what separates the game from other somewhat-competitive side-scrolling games like Smash Bros. Without these finely tuned features, the experience would be generic and bland. Like Smash but more skilled and less trash can button mashing.
There are many melee weapons like the katana that can be picked up throughout the maps. Each one has its own unique animation, damage, and timing. There are also many elevators and doors to allow for many sneaky tactics. Sometimes you just want to pick up a sack of flour and beat someone into a bloody mess. Or put all your weapons away and go straight kung fu on their♥♥♥♥♥ This is the app for that.
As usual, Arrowhead is up to its old tricks, parodying pop culture with a clever-ish sense of humor. For instance, take the game’s best character, Dutch McClone. Dutch is basically every single Arnold Schwarzenegger character in history. Sent back in time after having his identity stolen, he now fights to recover his stolen identity and discover just exactly who did this to him and why. On top of all that, he has an Austrian accent and constantly declares that he’s just a kindergarten teacher.
Each character has their own unique ability that they can use in combat. Dutch’s ability renders him invincible for a few seconds or until he takes a certain amount of damage. This causes him to be the most picked character, which is fine, since there can be multiples of the same character in each match. It’s unfortunate, however, that the other characters’ special abilities aren’t as competitively appealing.
With four unique game modes, Showdown offers everything from free-for-all to team deathmatch. Right now free-for-all seems to be the primary focus. Every time a character dies, they respawn in a second or two, keeping a constant flow of action going. Before the match ends, the Showdown round begins, where everyone has one life to live in a last-man-standing climax. The winner of the Showdown round gets a score point bounty based on the amount of players in the match. The person with the highest score after the Showdown round is  the match winner.
With so much replay value and charm, this is a game that’s almost impossible not to recommend. The marriage between humor and skilled gameplay makes it one of the most innovative games of the last decade. If you’re looking for a video game where a giant Megazord fights Godzilla in the background accompanied by an epic heavy metal song blaring at eleven, you might enjoy this.

Simplified strategy game surprisingly rich on content. In the role of President Donald Trump you start the game with three goals: Defeat ISIS, clear the national debt and maximize US production, all to Make America Great Again.
To maximize US-production you have to buy and sell products from different countries and continents, the simple but addicting strategy is to follow the global economy and buy cheap to sell expensive. Every country has fluctuating prices on the three resources (oil, supplies, food) and it's up to the player to either wait for the prices to drop and increase, or simply threaten or negotiate with the countries to make the prices go one way or another. With enough resources the national production can be upgraded in six levels, max out the updrages to clear the goal. The mechanics of this goal is tied to clearing the national debt and you simply continue buying cheap, selling expensive until the debt is cleared.
To defeat ISIS you enter a mini-game in the style of a 2D shooter in which you control President Trump flying a chopper shooting down ISIS-forces. This spans over five levels of increasing difficulty and ends in a boss-fight. To clear these levels you have to upgrade your chopper with armor and weapons, this is done by unlocking achievements connected to trading with the different countries on the world map; Upgrade the chopper to handle the more difficult enemies. The mini-game is not only well made but offers some well-needed variety to the game as a whole. It's a nice nostalgic throwback to the Megadrvie/Genesis-days.
I took my time trying to unlock as many trading achievements as possible in my first run and the game lasted just over four hours. Based on the entertainment provided during these hours I have to consider this game fantastic, especially for the price. I highly recommend this game for those looking for a simplified strategy game with a healthy dose of comedy, for €0.74/2.99 it doesn't get much better than this.

The Evil Within is a mixed bag, depending on what you expect.
The story, while interesting, tries a tad too hard to stay complex and mysterious. Several hours in, I have a broad view of what is going on, but in the overall sense, I don't have the foggiest of what my goal is, or what is going on. Characters abound, but most have brief appearances and outside of some minor dialogue, they contribute little to the story.
From the graphic standpoint, the game is beautiful looking. Locales are varied and go from oppresive linear corridors, and derelict buildings, to open ruined towns. The ambience, fog, darkness, all contrbute to create a somber, and tense atmosphere. The creature design is well done. Common enemies have varied designs, and minor changes to keep them from looking repetitive. And "bosses" are impressive on their own right.
The gameplay is primarily a stealth survival game. As a result, stealth kills are included, and for the most part, areas offer several paths to approach enemies and get the best angle. In addition, noise can be used to lure them to specific areas, and even into traps. Traps however (more specifically explosive ones), while they can dishout a ridiculous amount of damage to the player, seem to not do the same for mobs. Common enemies are tough. And can dish a lot of damage alone, and take the same amount of punishment. Bars, spears, and floor traps, on the other hand can insta kill lesser mobs. There are also areas where the player needs to fight swarms of enemies, and a wide array of weapons help the process.
There is also an upgrade system, that while I am not a big fan of, was added in a clever way. This will allow the player to boost health, stamina, melee damage, gun damage, explosives, stock, etc etc.
All these, contribute to make the game good.
What keeps it from being great, (at least so far) is the "hero" himself. Sebastian Castellanos is an unremarkable tool. He has the level of expression of a 2 by 4. He falls into a poll of blood, and expresses the same amount of distress as if getting a stain of mustard on his least liked shirt. And how he made it to detective is beyond me, because this a-hole does not question squat. In a segment a character than seems to have a deep insight of what is going on (as the NPC keeps talking to himself about recognizing many of the clues given by the story), Castellanos stands looking blankly wondering why Turkey's waddles hang to the left rather than the right.
From a gameplay point, he is the epitome of being a weakass. Initially he can barely keep up a sprinting speed for over 3 seconds. His aiming is awful. I have played numerous FPS, and over the shoulder view games, and by far, Castellanos is the worse offender of all. His aiming is slow, and somehow feels like waddling. Even at higher sensitivities, the aiming speed does not change greatly. Which is frustrating to keep from being mobbed in the areas where you need to shoot swarms of enemies. Enemies are an oddity in firefight segments. While charging speeds tend to make their movement erratic (preventing from scoring a headshot) sometimes, they will simply stand doing nothing UNTIL aimed at. At that point in time, they become active and bullets will fly hitting nothing. I just got to an area where I have been given a rifle with a scope, I can only wonder how that is going to work with Castellanos mental retardation when it comes to fine aiming.
So, do I recommend The Evil Within?. Yeah, it is a good game. It does the job. Jump scares are minimal and relies strongly in its ambience to create an oppressive feeling. That it nails. So, if you can see past Castellanos many failings then you will have, a mostly, frustration free experience.
A little nitpick at the game, is the random FPS drops that occur from time to time, without rhyme or reason.

Patience is the name of this game and when the art and music are as beautiful as they are in Mushroom 11, patience definitely pays off.
Mushroom 11 is the most inventive puzzle platformer I've ever played. You have to evolve and adapt by 'erasing' or destroying parts of your own organism, which then grow back - but not in an order you'd expect.
This allegory carries through to the game's post-nuclear plot. An organism that evolved to survive nuclear fallout would definitely have to be a highly adaptable and quickly-regenerating one.
Beyond that though, my own interpretation of this game is that it also has personal and political implications. When facing a tough challenge (and believe me, the challenges in this game are tough), be flexible and adaptable enough to erase your own outmoded ideologies. You will regenerate and in the process adapt around even the most daunting challenges.
This game is a work of art.

I´m kinda conflicted with Mushroom 11. On one hand looking back the experience was reasonable enough, but on the other this game manages to capture a lot of what is wrong with indie puzzle platformers. I think the polish and details elevate the experience somewhat, so keep that in mind as I list off the flaws.
Firstly the gameplay pretty unique, and it´s unique because it´s bad and other devs haven´t gone with it for a good reason. Every moment feels like you are just abusing the mechanics as everything is heavily physics/RNG based and moving through the game is a constant struggle for that next save point. Moving around is enjoyable enough as long as it remains novel.
Difficulty-wise first 2/3s of the game flows past nicely, but at a point the level of challenge and the physics-based gameplay come to a head and just unleash a torrent of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ obstacle after ♥♥♥♥♥♥ obstacle at the player.
The length of the game is good but it does say something about the game when after about 2.5 hours one is done with it. Short game is short and for a very good reason.
Audiovisual design is what benefits most of the polish and tons of custom visuals, but the only actually good looking screen in the game is the main menu. The rest has a lot of effort put into it but it doesn´t translate into anything that I would consider beautiful or memorable. It is one great main menu though.
On the whole Mushroom 11 is a very forgettable experience that couldn´t really be fixed without replacing it entirely. Slightly smoother difficulty would make it painless but that wouldn´t actually make it good, and the mechanics are IMO flawed from the start. The visuals are good but would require so much more than tweaking to make actually interesting. Experiencing this game mechanic for the first time was fun enough on the whole but past novelty there isn´t much here.

Hotline Miami 2 has its moments, but it is definitely something I can't recommend to absolutely everyone. Due to some players not playing the first one, they might perceive the game differently than I do.
The Right:
- Some Gameplay elements
Dennaton took a gamble with this character, and I feel like it was an interesting play style. Evan Wright, the journalist, takes the violent and carnage-filled gameplay in a different manner. Evan dismantles guns, melees enemies, but makes sure not to kill them. You are in fact rewarded points for not killing. Though the more available kills for other characters, such as the shotgun butt smash, are a nice addition to the game's nasty finishers.
- Of course, those incredible tracks
If there's one distinct thing that people praise Hotline Miami for, it's the powerful, bass-thumping synth/electronic soundtrack. This time around, they took the soundtrack to an entirely different level. This game locks in about 50 (I believe) foot-stomping and atmospheric tracks for you to enjoy.
- The Level Editor
This is a nice idea for the game, despite it being unfinished and broken as sin.
- The Looks
Even though a lot of the textures and objects have been recycled, there are plenty of new things to engulf you in HM2's locations. New assets such as: environment animations, rain effects, new textures, object destruction, more enemy animations, more gore (what hotline player doesn't like that?), hazy screen effects, and other things to give your eyes a gasm. Also, the pause menu is the most perfect rendition I've ever seen of a VHS style menu. It's perfect and pleasing to look at.
The Wrong (number):
- Level Design
Hotline Miami was a tightly-knitted, close-cornered rush of a game. Combos and the adrenaline had players, including myself, returning and wanting more of that sweet hotline carnage. In Hotline Miami 2, the levels were tripled in size. This resulted in a decent amount of frustrating issues. In both hotline games, there are issues with off-screen enemies killing you. It is far more prominent in the sequel due to awkward level design and abrasive level sizes. Due to this issue, it induces hide and seek and picking off enemies (an overwhelming amount) one by one. HM2 has far more gunplay involved. Though this issue resides, there are sections of the game where you're able to pull off using melee weapons and getting combos. Also, in this sequel, the enemy placement is randomly changed each time you spawn. So, strategy and planning is a bit deterred here. Trust me, you'll be pressing R twice as much as you were before. This game is difficult for the wrong reasons.
Also, did I mention there are windows everywhere?
- Glitches / Inconsistent AI
Dennaton, you had months to fix these issues. You delayed the game for bug testing. Why would you let these problems slip into release? Hotline Miami 2 contains: enemies with Parkinson's, doors that are actually airplane propellers, occasional game-breaking spawn bugs, occasional crashes, dogs that chase their own tales, indecisive enemies (recurring), getting stuck in walls and the screen edge, awful pathfinding with Alex/Ash, enemies with random and inconsistent attention spans, and some other distrustful things that slew around in this game.
Hotline Miami 2 has some purely enjoyable moments, but it lacks the charisma, charm, and flow that Hotline Miami had for itself. I feel that the sequel was trying to be too much, and it resulted in the recurring flaws sprouting out more noticeably. Overall, it's a good game. It just has issues that are stopping it from being more enjoyable than it already is.
7.8/10

This game is much more difficult than the first Hotline Miami. There are several reasons: wonky door physics, extremely fast AI reactions, and level design.
Doors will often continually open and slam shut if you are standing in a doorway, making it very difficult to use the door to control whether or not the AI can see you. Unlike the first game, where the levels were smaller, in this game there are almost always enemies offscreen that can shoot you, and you must know where they all are (by dying several times) and sneak around in order to not get it.
The enemy reactions are so fast, they can literally dodge bullets. Enemies can change their path at the sound of a gunshot so fast that the bullet misses them. Very strange design decision. Additionally, bullets travel so slow that you must shoot slightly ahead of them even if they are only a dozen strides away.
The level design is very different. I don't like it. Some levels are fun, but most I have found rather tedius. Often, after beating a level, I have found myself feeling "wow, that was terrible." Especially the Hawaii levels. It's almost like an entirely different person designed some of the levels, with the goal of eliminating all of the fun aspects of the previous game. Most of the fast paced meelee action has been eliminated in exchange for sneaking around and luring enemies.
I think that hardcore gamers might like this game a little more, but I am finding it tedious and unrewarding. I'm so disappointed that it's not more like the first game. That being said, I'll probably finish it anyways for the sake of completeness.

The primary draw of this game is the teamwork and combat.  It is a lot of fun to team up with some friends and tackle some difficult levels.  There are definitely drawbacks which make the game frustrating, however.
Pros:
-Fun gameplay with friends
-Satisfaction of slaughtering legions of rats
-Good combat mechanics
Cons:
-Loot  *see below
-Solo play is difficult with some enemy mechanics (assassins, packmasters)

* I like the idea of being able to increase the potency of my weapons and trinkets, but the system is infuriating.  For starters, there is very little to strive for in terms of rare, powerful items.  Items progressions is White, Green, Blue, Orange, Red.  Red items are extremely difficult to get your hands on, and  more often than not they are not worth the effort.  Once you get some decent Orange level items all that seems to be left is collecting and min/maxing, and you'll get good orange level items by level 30.  Red items don't seem to offer any more damage than orange items, but their asthetic is unique and their bonus mods are unchangeable.  I'm level 35 and I see no goal to strive for anymore since my gear is generally pretty solid.
I'd recommend picking up this game during a sale, but for most people there's a fairly short lifespan of actually having things to accomplish.  Also have friends to play with.  If an assassin or packmaster grabs you while you're solo, it's often game over.

ENGLISH REVIEW
Years ago work began on the MMORPS “Stalker-Online”, which – heavily inspired by the world created in GSC Game World’s cult classic “S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl” – sought to recreate that world in a multiplayer environment. For reasons unknown to me, a dispute broke out between two groups in the studio which worked on Stalker-Online. It was divided into two teams and both of them retained the rights for the project, but only one holds ownership of its name. Hence we now have two productions: Stalker-Online and “sZone-Online”, which are almost identical and to this day remain very similar to the closed beta of the first project from 2010.
Their graphics resemble an early alpha version of Shadow of Chernobyl, which by today’s standards is even more dated and stings the eyes with its ugliness. Nevertheless, the Eastern European style is accurately portrayed through the abandoned housing estates and other such Chernobylesque locations in-game, which should please fans of the original Stalker, though some more music and sounds would be nice. Unfortunately the performance of sZone-Online is awful even on good computers – with a GTX 770, an i5-3350P and 8 GB of RAM, the frame rate on my PC was swinging from 20 to 80 frames per second in the most random of situations, which sometimes caused slight nausea and hampered fighting. There are also crashes and lag, even when you have a good connection.
The gameplay is painful. Combat is exceptionally unfair and unrealistically designed; using firearms feels unsatisfying, enemies function like so-called “mobs” from MMO games (meaning they can sometimes notice you out of nowhere and attack you in swarms), and when you die you must wait 30 seconds before your character can get up again – of course with a minimal amount of health points – in the same dangerous area… The waiting time increases with each death. Alternatively you can respawn at the nearest stalker base (and the maps are large), but by choosing this option you risk losing precious items from your inventory.
Normally I don’t complain about rare ammo in games (quite the opposite), but in sZone – where it’s possible to die so easily, in such unforeseen circumstances and lose so much – it really is irritating. This is not S.T.A.L.K.E.R. or Metro 2033, where you can triumph over numerous enemies without wasting mass quantities of ammunition thanks to your own skill. In sZone-Online your character moves like a tank with the durability of a piece of toilet paper and all your efforts are liable to incongruous MMORPG gameplay elements, many bugs and the aforementioned terrible frame rate. Improving character skills and acquiring useful gear also takes an annoying amount of time.
However, when you do find yourself alone after nightfall in the wilderness, far from any NPC camps and hours past the starting areas of the game… then you’ll start to feel that atmosphere. You feel vulnerable and endangered. When interaction between players comes into play, who may be stalkers in a similar situation and become your comrades or turn out to be simple bandits, sZone becomes much more interesting.
In conclusion: sZone draws too much from traditional MMORPGs – boring quests, no engaging story, microtransactions and gameplay that rewards “grinding” as opposed to skill (which is at odds with the first-person shooter combat model). Furthermore, the game is barely evolving and has very shady roots… This whole project is based on plagiarism. Cybertime System is not the first developer to try to capitalise on fans of GSC Game World’s works. Even though in sZone you can experience a few amazing moments, overall it is a badly created game that will never reach its potential due to deep contradictions in its design.
---
POLSKA RECENZJA
Lata temu zaczęto pracę nad MMORPS „Stalker-Online”, która – mocno zainspirowana światem stworzonym przez GSC Game World w kultowej grze „S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Cień Czarnobyla” – miała na celu odtworzenie tegoż świata w trybie wieloosobowym. Z niewiadomych mi powodów doszło do sporu między dwoma grupami w studiu, które zajmowało się tworzeniem Stalker-Online. Podzieliło się ono na dwa zespoły i oba z nich zatrzymały prawo do projektu, ale tylko jeden do jego nazwy. W taki sposób mamy teraz dwie produkcje: Stalker-Online i „sZone-Online”, które do dziś są niemalże identyczne i wciąż bardzo podobne do zamkniętej bety pierwszego projektu z 2010 roku.
Grafika przypomina wczesną wersję alfa Cienia Czarnobyla, co na dzisiejsze standardy jest jeszcze bardziej przestarzałe i kłuje w oczy brzydotą. Niemniej jednak, ten wschodnioeuropejski styl jest trafnie odzwierciedlony przez opuszczone blokowiska i inne czarnobylskie lokacje w grze, co powinno spodobać się fanom oryginalnego Stalkera, chociaż przydałoby się trochę więcej muzyki i dźwięków. Niestety wydajność sZone-Online jest okropna nawet na dobrych komputerach – z GTX 770, i5-3350P i 8 GB RAMu, częstotliwość klatek huśtała się na moim pececie od 20 do 80 klatek na sekundę i to w kompletnie losowych sytuacjach, co momentami powodowało lekkie mdłości i mocno utrudniało bój. Są także krasze i lagi nawet, gdy ma się dobre połączenie.
Rozgrywka jest bolesna. Walka jest niezwykle podła i nierealistycznie zaprojektowana; strzelanie z broni palnej czuje się niesatysfakcjonujące, wrogowie funkcjonują jak tzw. „moby” z gier MMO (czyli czasem potrafią ciebie dostrzec znikąd i rzucić się na ciebie całym mrowiem), a gdy zginiesz musisz czekać 30 sekund zanim twoja postać będzie mogła znów wstać – oczywiście z minimalną ilością punktów życia – w tym samym niebezpiecznym miejscu… Czas czekania powiększa się z każdą śmiercią. Alternatywnie możesz odrodzić się od razu w najbliższej bazie stalkerów (a mapy są wielkie), ale wybierając tę opcję ryzykujesz utratę cennych przedmiotów ze swojego ekwipunku.
Normalnie nie narzekam na rzadkość amunicji w grach (wręcz przeciwnie), lecz w sZone – gdzie można zginąć tak łatwo, w tak nieoczekiwanych okolicznościach i stracić tak wiele – jest to naprawdę irytujące. To nie S.T.A.L.K.E.R. czy Metro 2033, gdzie można zwyciężyć z licznymi wrogami bez marnowania masowych ilości amunicji dzięki własnym umiejętnościom. W sZone-Online twoja postać porusza się jak czołg z wytrzymałością kawałka papieru toaletowego a wszystkie twoje starania podlegają niepasującym elementom rozgrywki MMORPG, liczebnym błędom gry i wcześniej wspomnianej marnej wydajności. Polepszanie umiejętności postaci i zdobywanie przydatnego sprzętu także zajmuje denerwująco dużo czasu.
Natomiast, gdy już znajdziesz się sam w dziczy po zmroku, daleko od najbliższego obozu NPCów i już kilka godzin po zwiedzeniu początkowych miejsc w grze… wtedy naprawdę zaczniesz czuć ten klimat. Czujesz się wrażliwy i zagrożony. Gdy w grę wchodzi interakcja między graczami, którzy mogą być stalkerami w podobnej sytuacji i stać się twoimi towarzyszami lub okazać się zwykłymi bandytami, sZone staje się dużo bardziej interesujące.
Podsumowując: sZone za dużo czerpie z tradycyjnych MMORPGów – m.in. nudne zadania, brak wciągającej fabuły, mikropłatności i rozgrywkę, która nagradza za „grinding” a nie zręczność (co jest sprzeczne z modelem walki strzelanki pierwszoosobowej). Co więcej, gra prawie wcale się nie rozwija i ma bardzo podejrzane korzenie… Cały ten projekt jest oparty na plagiacie. Cybertime Studios to nie jedyny producent, który próbuje skapitalizować niedosyt fanów twórczości GSC Game World. Mimo że w sZone-Online można doświadczyć kilka niesamowitych chwil, ogólnie jest to źle stworzona gra, która nigdy nie osiągnie swojego potencjału ze względu na głębokie sprzeczności w tym, jak jest zaprojektowana.

The Evil Within is a mixed bag, depending on what you expect.
The story, while interesting, tries a tad too hard to stay complex and mysterious. Several hours in, I have a broad view of what is going on, but in the overall sense, I don't have the foggiest of what my goal is, or what is going on. Characters abound, but most have brief appearances and outside of some minor dialogue, they contribute little to the story.
From the graphic standpoint, the game is beautiful looking. Locales are varied and go from oppresive linear corridors, and derelict buildings, to open ruined towns. The ambience, fog, darkness, all contrbute to create a somber, and tense atmosphere. The creature design is well done. Common enemies have varied designs, and minor changes to keep them from looking repetitive. And "bosses" are impressive on their own right.
The gameplay is primarily a stealth survival game. As a result, stealth kills are included, and for the most part, areas offer several paths to approach enemies and get the best angle. In addition, noise can be used to lure them to specific areas, and even into traps. Traps however (more specifically explosive ones), while they can dishout a ridiculous amount of damage to the player, seem to not do the same for mobs. Common enemies are tough. And can dish a lot of damage alone, and take the same amount of punishment. Bars, spears, and floor traps, on the other hand can insta kill lesser mobs. There are also areas where the player needs to fight swarms of enemies, and a wide array of weapons help the process.
There is also an upgrade system, that while I am not a big fan of, was added in a clever way. This will allow the player to boost health, stamina, melee damage, gun damage, explosives, stock, etc etc.
All these, contribute to make the game good.
What keeps it from being great, (at least so far) is the "hero" himself. Sebastian Castellanos is an unremarkable tool. He has the level of expression of a 2 by 4. He falls into a poll of blood, and expresses the same amount of distress as if getting a stain of mustard on his least liked shirt. And how he made it to detective is beyond me, because this a-hole does not question squat. In a segment a character than seems to have a deep insight of what is going on (as the NPC keeps talking to himself about recognizing many of the clues given by the story), Castellanos stands looking blankly wondering why Turkey's waddles hang to the left rather than the right.
From a gameplay point, he is the epitome of being a weakass. Initially he can barely keep up a sprinting speed for over 3 seconds. His aiming is awful. I have played numerous FPS, and over the shoulder view games, and by far, Castellanos is the worse offender of all. His aiming is slow, and somehow feels like waddling. Even at higher sensitivities, the aiming speed does not change greatly. Which is frustrating to keep from being mobbed in the areas where you need to shoot swarms of enemies. Enemies are an oddity in firefight segments. While charging speeds tend to make their movement erratic (preventing from scoring a headshot) sometimes, they will simply stand doing nothing UNTIL aimed at. At that point in time, they become active and bullets will fly hitting nothing. I just got to an area where I have been given a rifle with a scope, I can only wonder how that is going to work with Castellanos mental retardation when it comes to fine aiming.
So, do I recommend The Evil Within?. Yeah, it is a good game. It does the job. Jump scares are minimal and relies strongly in its ambience to create an oppressive feeling. That it nails. So, if you can see past Castellanos many failings then you will have, a mostly, frustration free experience.
A little nitpick at the game, is the random FPS drops that occur from time to time, without rhyme or reason.

The game uses these awful run a bit sections where you run from enemies in terrible run sections where it is hard to see due to the horrible camera which gets stuck on things easily. So, ive played some of this game before buying it, and wanted to give a basic review before playing it, that way, if I play it and love it, ill know to mention that the problems shown here shouldnt turn you away.
That being said, ill get down to brass tax. The game itself is designed by the bigwig who had his hand in the development of resident evil 4
Why do you care? Simple, resident evil 4 was originally a game with almost the same plot as the evil within, a "Silent hill resident evil hybrid" this can be seen here for those who need proof or just want to read up
So yea, this designers ideas got shot down for not staying true to resident evil, so what does he do? copies everything from resident evil and makes the game anyway under a different name.
The evil within features a police detective (With a stupid amount of similarities to leon kennedy) a bad guy who can move at the speed of light and looks just like Wesker, a weapons upgrade system and money collection system from resident evil, and even series tropes like finishing off bosses with a rocket launcher.
This rubs me slightly the wrong way, but for many of you it wont matter, so ill get onto the other points.
Aside from playing just like a resident evil game, this game does have some of its own perks and not so perky perks.
PERKY PERKS
-Much better feel to it than resident evil, more eerie and creepy and the noir dress code of this cities police department fits the horror genre better
-A stealth system that is really pretty good and contributes heavily to the creepiness of the game versus being a tank in resident evil that kills everything.
-DLC isnt bad, and enhances the story
Now onto the things i consider to be bad compared to other games of this style
NOT PERKY PERKS
-Slasher film horror, very rarely will you be scared as much as youll just be grossed out, the game is the kind that drops you in a pool of blood and guts and claims that is horror.
-Despite being a "silent hill resident evil hybrid" the enemies have very little symbolism on par with what you would expect from silent hills amazing "Artistic renditions of reality via horror" but the game isnt entirely devoid of symbolism
-Story is lacking entirely, no intros for characters, the game drops you into a butchers room in the first 5 minutes, and overall the story has a feel of "You didnt get it, that means its really deep and mysterious!" when in actuality alot of it just makes not a single bit of sense.
So why do i recommend this game? after all that? For one, i havent played it to completion yet, so this is slightly unfair to review badly without that, and for two, its not a bad game per se, its just a weird amalgamation of two series that never needed to come together, and the fact that its basically a unfulfilled dream from a dev who got shot down is just a weird thing in itself. Resident evil 4.1 kinda thing.
At its core, the gameplay is good, and despite mostly being stupid gore everywhere horror, the game does have some scary as heck moments, so if you shave off all the things I know about the background of the game and what it really is, you have an 8/10 decent horror game here with an OK story.
Ill tell more as i beat it and try the DLC's!

There is no exposition, but the setting and title give away this much: You play as a fungal biomass, with the goal to survive and evolve by devouring whatever you encounter.
All actions take place in the ruins of humanity, where you crawl through what is left after the apocalypse that wiped out all life, with the exception of mutated plants and beings.
Mushroom 11 is a puzzle platformer, you play (as I mentioned) as a fungal biomass, which you control by deleting it's cells. Whenever you do so, cells grow on the biomass you have left. The controls require quite a lot of getting used to, but with the necessary experience, the game both feels very smooth and rewarding.
Now, whilst overcoming the challenge of mastering these unique controls, you have to overcome the obstacles and puzzles of the environment. One can get stuck at certain puzzles for a longer while, which often comes with frustration, but actually finishing it feels all that more rewarding.
The levels themselves are designed quite nicely, with interesting backdrops and a variety of threats on your way, but the  game is not all that long, featuring only 7 chapters, where each ends with a bossfight (basically a puzzle), and only took me (with my not too outstanding skills) ~5 hours.
A level editor/workshop support would certainly have been a valuable addition.
+Unique concept
+Diverse level design
+Challenging Puzzles
-Quite short
With a fresh idea and a well implemented concept, Mushroom 11 shines as a puzzle platformer, with it's only downside being it's shortness.

Please note: playtime is inaccurate, at time of post I have already put in a few hours offline.
PROS:
-- Beautiful Graphics
-- Runs smoothly for an Early Access game
-- The First Person View is a really neat concept. It's fun to see your village from the perspective of a villager.
-- Pretty easy to pick up and learn to play
-- The amount of features that this game already has available in Early Access is definitely adequate enough for hours of play.
-- I've not experienced any of the crashes that the other reviewers have been experiencing as of yet but I've not sat down and played it for more than a couple hours at once. These crashes are still a possible issue.
CONS:
-- Not much diversity in island types. Once youve seen one island there is really not much variance with the others.
-- It can use some balancing in build costs. Some of the buildings are just too hefty in resources to make constructing them when you need them possible.
-- Terraforming is a little buggy at the moment so expanding your village out can be quite a task trying to get the land all flattened out.
-- Villagers are slow as all get out. It makes walking in first person mode a little tedious and frustrating. If you plan on using a villager to go out and explore the island in first person be prepared for the long journey at a sloth-like pace.
-- There are some little bugs such as
+ Bears/wolves getting stuck in houses and villagers not even minding that there is a giant bear in their house.
+ Woman villagers are self-reproducing. They don't need no man.
+ Sometimes orders placed for villagers to carry out won't go through.
--My last Con ismore of just a note again that it is an Early Access game so there is a lot of missing details such as very little difference in the villager models. Again, the islands look very similar to each other. Not too many building types (still a good amount for an EA game).
Thoughts:
If you really enjoy city management and like supporting devs with their projects then totally go for it. This game really takes me back to a game I used to play called, "Anno 1503", it is also similar to Banished, a tad more forgiving though and much more aesthetically beautiful. I really enjoy playing it an hour here and an hour when I have time to sit down and play. I'd love to see some more building types, disasters, and possibly in the distant future more role playing features when controlling individual villagers and other islands to colonize and set up trade routes with. I would just love to see more done for that first person view point because for me it is quite a unique, interesting, and entertaining twist in the city management genre.

Why the game has "Tactics" in the title is a mystery to all.
It certainly gives the wrong impression which is a huge shame because I went in expecting a deep tactical role playing game and what I got instead was Megaman Battle Network.
Now those were a good series of games! Following in their footsteps this game should at least be decent, right?
Well yeah, it is decent actually but for some reason they decided to make a hybrid between 'Megaman Battle Network' and 'Plants VS Zombies' so what you end up with is a not very good 'lane' game ala PvZ and a watered down MBN game which just leaves you disoriented. Battle network was good! If you are going to emulate an already good game then try to copy the parts that actually made it good, switching my robots from lane to lane using cards is unnatural in a fast paced game and also i have to click twice to switch lanes and sometimes it just doesn't register that I want it to move out the way.
The PvZ element is a little overdone in clone games but what do you expect, that game sold very well so I wouldn't mind the hybridization the developer attempted here if they didn't try to make you move robots up & down the lanes/battlefield when most victories are about out spamming your foe in PvZ and thinking on your feet. This game is just too fast paced to be able to keep up with everything that is expected of you.
Ultimately we have a good game here but it is very much NOT for everyone. You can play the story mode with a friend, the art direction is simple but good, the story telling is decent and the depth comes from learning to juggle the megaman aspects against the PvZ aspects, knowing which units are worth your concentration and effort versus which ones to just leave as cannon fodder and the music, the sound it is all really good and I haven't even mentioned the deck building either which lets you create dynamic tactics and builds.
Ultimately if you are expecting a tactical game in the vein of Final Fantasy Tactics or Tactics Ogre then no, this is NOT that kind of game but if you were a fan of the Megaman Battle Network games or the Plants VS Zombies then this game might be for you.
Personally I didn't enjoy this game hence why I didn't recommend it but I apprechiate that not only is the game itself well done and polished but also that it was very ambitious to attempt to combine two great franchaises.

Hotline Miami 2 has its moments, but it is definitely something I can't recommend to absolutely everyone. Due to some players not playing the first one, they might perceive the game differently than I do.
The Right:
- Some Gameplay elements
Dennaton took a gamble with this character, and I feel like it was an interesting play style. Evan Wright, the journalist, takes the violent and carnage-filled gameplay in a different manner. Evan dismantles guns, melees enemies, but makes sure not to kill them. You are in fact rewarded points for not killing. Though the more available kills for other characters, such as the shotgun butt smash, are a nice addition to the game's nasty finishers.
- Of course, those incredible tracks
If there's one distinct thing that people praise Hotline Miami for, it's the powerful, bass-thumping synth/electronic soundtrack. This time around, they took the soundtrack to an entirely different level. This game locks in about 50 (I believe) foot-stomping and atmospheric tracks for you to enjoy.
- The Level Editor
This is a nice idea for the game, despite it being unfinished and broken as sin.
- The Looks
Even though a lot of the textures and objects have been recycled, there are plenty of new things to engulf you in HM2's locations. New assets such as: environment animations, rain effects, new textures, object destruction, more enemy animations, more gore (what hotline player doesn't like that?), hazy screen effects, and other things to give your eyes a gasm. Also, the pause menu is the most perfect rendition I've ever seen of a VHS style menu. It's perfect and pleasing to look at.
The Wrong (number):
- Level Design
Hotline Miami was a tightly-knitted, close-cornered rush of a game. Combos and the adrenaline had players, including myself, returning and wanting more of that sweet hotline carnage. In Hotline Miami 2, the levels were tripled in size. This resulted in a decent amount of frustrating issues. In both hotline games, there are issues with off-screen enemies killing you. It is far more prominent in the sequel due to awkward level design and abrasive level sizes. Due to this issue, it induces hide and seek and picking off enemies (an overwhelming amount) one by one. HM2 has far more gunplay involved. Though this issue resides, there are sections of the game where you're able to pull off using melee weapons and getting combos. Also, in this sequel, the enemy placement is randomly changed each time you spawn. So, strategy and planning is a bit deterred here. Trust me, you'll be pressing R twice as much as you were before. This game is difficult for the wrong reasons.
Also, did I mention there are windows everywhere?
- Glitches / Inconsistent AI
Dennaton, you had months to fix these issues. You delayed the game for bug testing. Why would you let these problems slip into release? Hotline Miami 2 contains: enemies with Parkinson's, doors that are actually airplane propellers, occasional game-breaking spawn bugs, occasional crashes, dogs that chase their own tales, indecisive enemies (recurring), getting stuck in walls and the screen edge, awful pathfinding with Alex/Ash, enemies with random and inconsistent attention spans, and some other distrustful things that slew around in this game.
Hotline Miami 2 has some purely enjoyable moments, but it lacks the charisma, charm, and flow that Hotline Miami had for itself. I feel that the sequel was trying to be too much, and it resulted in the recurring flaws sprouting out more noticeably. Overall, it's a good game. It just has issues that are stopping it from being more enjoyable than it already is.
7.8/10

This game is much more difficult than the first Hotline Miami. There are several reasons: wonky door physics, extremely fast AI reactions, and level design.
Doors will often continually open and slam shut if you are standing in a doorway, making it very difficult to use the door to control whether or not the AI can see you. Unlike the first game, where the levels were smaller, in this game there are almost always enemies offscreen that can shoot you, and you must know where they all are (by dying several times) and sneak around in order to not get it.
The enemy reactions are so fast, they can literally dodge bullets. Enemies can change their path at the sound of a gunshot so fast that the bullet misses them. Very strange design decision. Additionally, bullets travel so slow that you must shoot slightly ahead of them even if they are only a dozen strides away.
The level design is very different. I don't like it. Some levels are fun, but most I have found rather tedius. Often, after beating a level, I have found myself feeling "wow, that was terrible." Especially the Hawaii levels. It's almost like an entirely different person designed some of the levels, with the goal of eliminating all of the fun aspects of the previous game. Most of the fast paced meelee action has been eliminated in exchange for sneaking around and luring enemies.
I think that hardcore gamers might like this game a little more, but I am finding it tedious and unrewarding. I'm so disappointed that it's not more like the first game. That being said, I'll probably finish it anyways for the sake of completeness.

Pros:
-Easy to get the hang of

-First person view allows you to control, play, and act as one of your villagers including doing their jobs and tasks
