Every once in a while a game feels entirely self contained and 'perfect'. The last one I can think of is Frozen Synapse and now there's this. It's been frustrating seeing it unreleased for so long, but now seeing the final product I understand the long delays. The visual polish is absolutely amazing. Slowly navigating through its post-apocalyptic wasteland reveals an infinite set of painted vistas. There's just enough visual storytelling to make you wonder of the purpose of the strange blob creature, but no more.
The closes comparison for gameplay is World of Goo with it's analog manipulation of complex physics systems. But otherwise it's entirely original. Nothing out there is quite like it and anything similar that follows will be branded as derivative. It encompasses every inch of the good ideas in this design space and nothing more. No filler.
Some of the later puzzles are a little difficult, but mostly they demand patience. Take a break and come back to it when you're ready to play with physics.

Oh man, am I looking forward to writing this review. Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is, to date, in my list of favourite games. I can never choose my favourite game, so I have a few games that I love. And up there with Kid Icarus: Uprising, Team Fortress 2 and Half-Life is Hotline Miami 2.
This review is going to be a little different to my usual reviews. As I already reviewed Hotline Miami 1
, there is no need to discuss gameplay mechanics that aren't new to this game. So, if you're new to Hotline Miami, I suggest reading my previous review on the first game to get an idea of what the game is like, as this review is assuming you know about how the game works. Anyway, without further adue, my review on Hotline Miami 2.
Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is the bloody, hard hitting, thrilling sequel to one of 2012's best indie titles, Hotline Miami. This game expands on everything the last game established; gameplay, story, gore, music. The game is built in a different engine to the last, making the game smoother, the AI better (although I wouldn't call it amazing) and adding a few other helpful little tweaks. In my opinion, HM2: WN is a perfect example on how to make a perfect game better.
Hotline Miami's gameplay was something I thought could not get any better. I thought the way it was set and the way it was played was perfect. Boy was I wrong. Hotline Miami 2 changes the scene with:
- New characters to play as (Jake, Manny Pardo, Tony, Alex & Ash, Corey, Mark, Beard, Richter, The Son, and that is to only name a few),
- New weapons, some even exclusive to certain characters, for example The Son's katana.
- New gameplay mechanics, for example Evan Wright will not kill enemies. He will only use melee weapons, if he picks up a gun he just unloads it and drops it, and hitting an enemy will simply knock them out instead of killing them.
- New enemies. It's not just Russians anymore. Although there is only one new type of enemy, they are reskinned depending on the situation.
One of the things that made Hotline Miami such an amazing game was the soundtrack. And this game does that justice, bringing back some of the previous game's musicians, such as my favourite of the bunch, M|O|O|N, while also bringing in new artists to create a soundtrack worth the £11.99. If you buy the digital special edition, however, you get six extra tracks from various artists. And that too, is worth the extra £3. Hotline Miami's soundtrack fits the game perfectly, with the music switching at perfect times seamlessly. It is truely one of the best parts of the game. Whether it is the eerie title song 'Untitled' by The Green Kingdom, the calming and saddening piece 'Dust' by M|O|O|N, or the upbeat track 'New Wave Hookers' by Vestron Vulture, no matter what you know you're in for some of the best music you've heard in a long time.
Hotline Miami's story was pretty darn good, I can say that much. However its problem was that it didn't give us much. Hotline Miami 2 throws that out the window and says 'HELL NO! HAVE SOME PLOT!', which I am forever thankful for. HM2 gives us new characters, new places, new times and ties up loose ends in the first game. Not only this, however, it gives us mystery to work out, and leaves some questions unanswered (ready for Hotline Miami 3: Right Number... Right guys?) which I like. I want to work out a mysterious plot using clues uncovered in the game, not just be handed a simple story and made to work with it. Hotline Miami's story is a lot of things: interesting, sad, funny, gripping, and just generally outstanding. The game somehow makes you feel so many emotions at certain times. I promise I didn't cry when
(GAME SPOILERS)
All in all, Hotline Miami 2's story is probably one of the best I've seen and had the pleasure of playing through in a long time. Everything fits together so well, and is made to tell a story perfectly. I've spent a long time on the Hotline Miami Wiki just reading about characters and thinking up headcanons. I truely love the story told in this game.
Earlier this year, the creators of the game released a level editor for the game. This means you can create your own levels. While it is occasionally annoying and frustrating to use, it can crash for seemingly no reason sometimes and there are some things you just can't do, I quite enjoy the level editor. The editor includes every playable character from the second game, along with the two playable characters of the first, Jacket and Biker. One can also create cutscenes, meaning someone could create their own story through their levels (as I'm slowly doing myself.) While I do believe the editor needs a lot of updating and changing to make it perfect, I do love the addition, it is pretty fun with all the customization, despite the nasty bugs.
Do I recommend this game? Hell. Yes. This game is
without a doubt. Everything about it comes together so nicely I don't even know how to explain how much I love it. So, if you have enough money at this exact moment, spend  £30 on grabbing the special edition of the game along with the soundtrack. If not, add it to your wishlist and when you have the money come back and get it. I promise, if you're into story rich, beautiful soundtrack, Godly hard games, get this game. You will not regret it.

There are 9 characters that you play as in Hotline Miami 2
(You can only select one of the fans at a time so each one functions like a mask for a single character)
but there are only 2 characters that can use different abilities depending on their mask.
With 9 different characters, this wouldn't be so bad if each one was bringing something different to the table but for most of them there are no differences except for 2 characters that have their own cripple which makes it harder. Beard can't pick up enemy weapons so he has to rely on ammo crates that only give him a small fraction of the bullets he was holding before, and Evan is unable to use guns. You can't choose which character you will play as so the game is constantly shifting you between different characters and sometimes you will have to play the characters with handicaps.
The lack of being able to use different masks or abilities for each level means that replaying levels isn't as fun, and it's frustrating to play the levels that require you to play with a handicap so those are even worse.

Most of them might as well just be reskinned versions of the guns in Hotline Miami 1. There were two weapons that I actually thought were pretty cool though and that was the chainsaw and the 9mm.
In the original Hotline Miami most of the levels were rooms that usually didn't have more than 4 enemies. Hotline Miami 2 levels are mostly big open areas with little cover. The shift+mouse look function still doesn't allow you to see as far as you need to when an enemy is far away. Not all of the levels are absolutely horrible but when they are it can REALLY suck. Nothing is more frustrating than getting killed by enemies you can't even see.
There are windows EVERYWHERE in this game. There has to be at least 20 times the amount of windows in HM2 as there are in HM1. This further adds to the problem of not being able to see what is killing you. Enemies have hawk vision but you can only see so far and with windows thrown into the mix many of the levels become a nightmare.
There is an obnoxious amount of fat enemies that require a gun to be killed and wont die instantly without a shotgun. I swear there must be 2 or 3 per level for every level.

Vermintide is an excellent representation of the Warhammer Fantasy world! Warhammer Fantasy is my absolute favourite fictional universe. Its dark, gritty and full of non-relenting conflict. Vemintide provides a gateway of insight into a particularly turbulent time period known as the ‘End Times’. The majority of the game is centred around the city of Ubersreik where 5 heroes (4 players) endeavour to defend it against the Skaven invasion. The game contains a good solid combat system with smooth, flowing animations. The visuals are superb, and the humorous banter between the characters really adds value to the game’s atmosphere. The co-op experience is great and even better when playing with friends! Support regarding updates and further content has been very good with issues being addressed and new content being of high quality. I really can’t express just how great this game as a Warhammer fan. Would I recommend this game? If you like the Warhammer Fantasy universe then look no further because this is on the absolute pinnacle of WHF games.

The characters are diverse, they all play differently. With the wizard you must balance the magic and close combat. With the waywatcher you strike very fast, but weak, and you always have to be on the move. The shield of the empire soldier makes it effective to jump to the middle of the fight and smash everything, but the "sniper like" gun makes it also possible to stay back and take down the most powerfull enemies with one headshot. And every weapon feels powerful because of the physics simulation.
The loot system and the random encounters (random generated enemies, loot dice) are fun.
Graphics and performance is great, can't complain.

A really fun real-time card-based tatics game.  Card unlocks are based on in-game progress - no micro-transactions to be found here.  Can sometimes depend on the luck of the draw, but if you have a solid deck put together that shouldn't matter as much.  Haven't tried the multiplayer yet, but the single player's gold.

This game was very fascinating for me, being completely unfamiliar with CCGs, limited interest in turn based strategies and none at all in computerised boardgames - this game is basically all three, and it's easy to see this as a tabletop game. However, it sucks you in quickly and, it must be said, sneakily. The tutorials flow seamlessly into the main campaign, from missions where you have just a handful of cards and playing them is so simple you don't even grasp what the challenge could possibly be, and yet soon every missions presents a new and fresh challenge. This may be the best learning curve I have ever encountered, and the tutorialising is very gentle. You encounter more and more challenging units to defeat, and the game encourages out-of-the-box thinking. Beating the game is a healthy challenge, and 100% completion is Herculean, which is how it should be.
The story, meanwhile, is absolute nonsense but very enjoyable. That is to say, it's steampunk.

The concept was excellent and the execution is fantastic. Buy this game.

It's great in a ton of ways, and maddeningly bad in another, separate ton of ways.
Combat's great and the system is logical yet fun. Horseback takes it further, letting you skirt around the enemy whittling them down until there's just you with one extremely bloody sword arm.
BUT... the AI is subpar at best and suicidally stupid at worst. Unless told otherwise, your soldier's battle strategy is "I'll run forward and die on them". As a result, the enemy can use archers and cavalry to devastating effect while using them on your side for anything other than siege defense and scouting teams respectively feels like wasted gold. Also nobody knows what strafing is except you, so skirmishing tactics are almost worthless (unless you tell all your men to retreat and 1v50 dem noobs). To my understanding the auto-battle function is somthing to fear and loathe, guaranteeing you a new Battle of Thermopylae at best or total loss against mediocre troops at worst.
BUT...the world is expansive and the little quests you do bring life to the area. You can carry shipments across the continent or deliver letters between lords, eventually participating in castle sieges to curry favor and rising up in power to become a lord, or even king. Enemies you fail to slay might organise a hit against you. You can usurp positions of power, or help someone else take the mantle (for a price, of course). You could become a famous prize fighter or a legendary mercenary.
BUT... quests are randomly generated, so many of them are impossible to do without a huge amount of luck. Chase some deserters on horseback! Where are they? Well, one guy saw them near Narra 16 days ago, and they left far away from the trade routes so nobody's seen them since then. It's like searching a haystack for a moving needle, disguised as hay. Or participate in a siege! It's entirely random how many of your own men are in the front of the attack party (and thus get wholly, without exception, pulped) so I hope you like training and recruitment!
if TL;DR: If you're into high strategy and RPGs, I'd suggest playing this at least once. Probably with mods. Especially if there's a sale. There's a bunch of small things that can ruin the game, but if you avoid them this is a unique and fun medieval RPG where commanding an army can naturally flow from 5v5 to 100v100 with a few hours' play.

While the game shows its age (hell it's got a DirectX7 mode too), it remains quite enjoyable.
So do not expect shiny beautiful landscapes everywhere, the game is a bit old, and it shows.
However, you'll have the satisfaction of building yourself a sizable army...
The combat can take a bit to get used to, I strongly suggest you get yourself 5 or 10 members in your party at the start, no more, and then, visit the training grounds, and explore ALL options. This will familiarize yourself with all combat options, and it'll give you some xp to start with.
While your army grows, until you get a decent trainer in your party, you can boost new troops by sparring with them in the training grounds (any of them). This is great to fairly quickly train your low level troops to be a bit more usable.
There are guides on companions, and which ones go together, and which ones hates each others. It'll make your life easier :).
You can be a man, or a woman. A woman will have a slightly tougher time, especially at the beginning. Finding a husband for a woman is also a bit harder, since most men are scared to death of you :).
It is said you can have your own faction, and become the Queen/king. However, I would not suggest trying that until you are familiar with the game.
Save OFTEN. Not because the game is unstable, if anything, the game is a prime example of stability, but because you can die very quickly in any fight, regardless of your advantage... make a mistake or two, or simply get pulled in battle after a tough one, when you and your army are still weak, and you're going to loose a LOT of things :).
All in all, even though the game is getting old, it remains one of my favorite. The wars can be tough, especially if you are on the loosing side, however if you do not mind killing innocents, raiding villages can be a pretty good source of income during wars.
One thing I'd recommend, is not to join a faction for a while, and try to get a healthy production going in every single towns. By then, you'll be rolling in cash. Once you have a steady cash flow, increase your army size, and pick a faction. You'll only have a couple of towns being in enemy hands while at war, so usually, your cash flow will remain high, even if you are loosing the war.
For the more challenging call, you can either go on your own, and capture your own city, or pledge yourself to a claimant. If you have a high charisma and invested some points in persuasion, you can bring down a faction extremely quickly, with little to no fights.

TIME FOR A PENGO GAME REVIEW OF A HORROR GAME YOU PROBABLY WON'T PLAY BECAUSE OF IT'S CONTENT!!! *game show bells*  First off, i've played through the first Amnesia game enough times to do it asleep and hands tied, so i'm not new to intensive fear games, but this one opens up a new jar of whoop♥♥♥♥♥on you I can ASSURE YOU , you are NOT ready for no matter who you are. Graphically it's stunning.  I had it maxed out and my R9 280x wasn't even sweating it, they do an amazing job with the lighting and coloring. But seriously, the gameplay was very smooth, no lag, you could go start to finish and it's smooth sailing, it never struggled, there's no load screens its all one big movement, one big stage. The game is split into chapters (DONT WORRY NO SPOILERINOS KIDS),  so it takes each thing to pay attention to a step at a time and no further than that.  So it gives you a lot to think about, but in chunks, right?  I'd say job well done there.  It just means you can easily pick up the game at any chapter and not so much not miss anything, but experience a certain part of the story without needing to much prior knowledge.  You still need SOME just because that's how it is, but it's not CRITICAL persay for entertainments sake, get what i'm saying?  Good.
Alright to wrap up this bull♥♥♥♥♥♥  i've been paying attention to this game since i saw a video playthrough of a demo roughly a year ago, and was excited to see a final version come out, I just had to play it, had to do it.  All-in-all its a game that will seriously (and I MEAN it) test your mental stability in your decisions.  It's also a game that comes right up and says, "hello!  I hate you!  So take this!! *scare*"  The scares are a good split of about 30% just pure jump scares to 70% of them actually being YOUR fault for bringing them upon your self.  It challenges you to play the game in such a way that makes you connect with the main character a bit more as it goes on, and you kind of understand what they are trying to tell you in the story.  I may be cryptic in all this but i'd still rather be vague in my review of actual content and more clear on its gameplay and structure that way I can tell you that it's a well-made game, go check it out yourself or watch a playthrough of someone who is very thorough if you can't manage to play it yourself.
The final verdict on Layers of Fear (bearing in mind after one full playthrough) --- A very solid 8/10.  Bravo, minor improvements in small places but nonetheless,  well worth the cost of admission.

Mushroom 11 is a game about flow, and it's biggest flaw is when it looses it.  This is an extremely unique and smart game which is a joy to play until approximately 70-80% of the way through the puzzles take a sharp turn from ones demanding thought and innovation in order to succeed to utterly finicky nightmares where the solution is obvious but hitting microscopic timing windows while getting the janky physics to play along required me to repeat some sections close to 100 times.
Still a reccomend, as it is still worth the asking price, but with some game design consultation and broader playtesting this could have been so much more.  As it is, only a very small fraction of players will have the skill and patience to finish the game - and that number will dwindle to zero for the less skilled casual audience.

THE BAD:  Honestly, this is not a solid MMO. The gameplay is uncreative and highly repetitive:  once you've done one investigative mission that devolves from a space encounter to an away party mission and back to a space battle again, you've done them all.  The various end game zones are endless rep grinds, again of highly repetitive (and boring) quests.  Familiar places are not built at all to scale, making DS9 the most disappointing place in the galaxy to visit.  F2P sets such a low cap on your credits that you can't compete with subbed players on the AH, although credits are worthless anyway.  The costumes are buggy and frequently ugly.  You can't fly your ship upside down.  Need I say more?
THE GOOD: The game does have one of the strongest senses of community of any MMO I've played.  The players are there because they love the franchise, which also results in some of the most hilarious barrens chat.  The set up of Fleets (guilds) actually encourages player participation in cooperative group projects that help you build up your space station and unlock personal gear.  I spent most of my hours playing the Duty Officer Missions, which is like a card game that lets you have multiple quests running in the background for rewards and XP. I don't think it's for everyone, but it's great to do in the background while working on real life.  Leonard Nimoy voices some small parts.  Oh, and it's F2P.

This game is near perfect, it's addicting, it's tough, it's responsive, it's satisfying, and the list goes on.
Geometry Wars is an arcade game, so obviously it's all about getting your next PB. As suggested in the title, you're a shape shooting other shapes. Graphics wise the game looks nice, you can tell each enemy from the other, and they don't blend in with each other. There's a LOT of fireworks, if you have problems with epilepsy, or anything that makes it hard to see "noisy" things, that might be a problem for you. the sound effects are useful. Each enemy makes a different sound when they spawn, making you aware at almost all times when and what enemies are going to come at you.
The difficulty curves perfectly, it starts pretty simple spawning 2 or 3 enemies at a time, and then ends up that you just hear infinite spawning noises where there's very little room to move and you're always shooting ( it gets like this around 200-300K points and on, getting harder and harder the longer you survive. Luckily because of the enemy spam, there's bombs that clear the screen ( but don't give you the points of the enemies it clears ) making impossible situations possible.
GW is rewarding, every 100k or so points you get an extra life or bomb, which helps a lot, while still keeping the game difficult.
I recommend this to casual players and hardcore player alike, it's very fun and has just the right amount of difficulty while still being fair ( mostly ).
the one bad thing about this game, is the controls are sometimes wonky. on keyboard, sometimes when you click the shoot key while holding down a movement direction, it doesn't shoot, or vice versa. And on controller sometimes it shoots on it's own or it moves on it's own. Luckily both are fixed by changing direction or letting go of the button, but it's still a minor problem
Overall 9.8/10 amazing game, cheap buy!

Fantastic game that is highly dependant on sticking together and co-operating. Despite it's high similarity to Left 4 Dead, Vermintide brings refreshing new things to the table such as a setting that is more melee based than ranged and a loot system. The higher difficulties and extra objectives in the game can really make it a challenge for even the most seasoned of players. The gametime you will get out of this game is highly dependant on you as a player, as just like Left 4 Dead it has a limited amount of maps so after a while you will be doing re-runs of the maps. However with the new "Quest" feature it will reward you for doing so. So far the DLC released for this game has been very statisfactory for the pricetag aswell, adding new weapons, maps and modes and i hope they will continue doing so in the future!
All in all i would highly recommend Vermintide especially for people who really liked Left 4 Dead and other very co-operation based games.

AI is pretty good, if you shoot something the rest of the rats will hear and rush to you. Combat against specific Rats are pretty interesting and difficult from time to time. There are some MINOR glitches from time to time but it isn't really bad, if anything they are very humorous.
A lot of replay value and a TON of content. So give it a shot! Really enjoyable game.

It is easy to join another game and play with other people BUT I would highly recommend finding friends and playing it together with some form of voice chat. By no means this is a bad game, but 2,5h of game-play for 20 euros ? I did pay a lot less because i bought it when it was in "early access" state so my opinion is based on playing both the beta version and the final one.
This isn't really a "game" by definition, it's more like an interactive story / walking simulator. And that shouldn’t be a problem, the graphics are great, there are some WTF moments when the DEVs do some crazy stuff with the game engine (hint: turn back and the room is not what it used to be) and unfolding the story of a crazy painter is done quite well.
The problem is that there is no tension in this "game". You'll soon realize that you are never ever in any danger. There are a few ways to die, most of them based on encounters with your lovely wife. And there are something like 3 such events in the entire game.
So the tension is kept by jump scares. A lot of them. And you'll start to expect them, like you enter a new room and try to guess what will happen. Will i crash through the floor ? will a knife fly by my head ? will that chair move it's position behind my back ?
Can you be scared when you know that nothing can hurt you ? I do remember playing Amnesia the dark descent...the graphics quality was wayy lower but damn, i was scared. You knew that if you did a wrong move, you were screwed. Here, you cannot go wrong, just open the new door and so on till the end of the game.
There are a few puzzles, all of them very easy. Special mention for the last one in the game for being quite annoying, searching some for small pieces in a dark room wasn't funny.
I was tired at the end of the game. And annoyed by the fact that in the last scene you find in plain sight a book with sketches of the DEVs faces. Really ?? The game wasn't even over yet, you had to remove me from the story and make me see your mug shots ? I do remember something very similar in Quake 2 (hey, I’m old) but that was a secret area. It was not thrown in your face.  I was perplexed. Was the game over and those were the credits? Nope, the game ended a few minutes later, with the usual rolling credits.

The game boasts some incredible visuals and offers impressive optical illusions. It does not lack atmosphere, but it does use way too many jumpscares. To the point of exhaustion, due to the fact that they lose their scarefactor. The game was doing incredibly well the first few minutes of me playing it, it used a few jumpscares here and there, together with the optical illusions and terrific atmosphere. But the jumpscares became too much, making the atmosphere the only thing drawing me in, and the scares were just a nuisance.
It was a short and sweet experience, but too heavy on the jumpscares, but other than that, it boasts great visuals, impressive optical illusions.
I would not recommend it at a full price though.

First off let me say that this game is one of the best games I have ever played.
If you're looking for an medivel simulator where it's just mindless killing, go somewhere else; because this game is so much more than that.
When you first start playing, you are immediatly thrust into an extremely diverse world where events are based off of your choices, not just code. You choose what you are most talented in, and what weapons you are best at. After that, you choose what your backround is, where you start your adventure, and most importantly, your destiny, whether it be a ruthless bandit or noble king.  During the rest of the adventure you are battling (and also playing a little bit of politics) in a fairly well made map, full of cities that each have their own unique design. One of my favorite parts about it is forming your army, because you choose what types of soldiers you have in it. Each faction also has its own unique troop tree. Towards the end of the game, if you have played it right, all of the pieces start falling into place, and you become more powerful, or you meet your demise.
Time for the mods.
This game is very good by itself, but if you put mods into the equation, it is limitless. There are hundreds of mods to choose from, but here are my 5 favorites you should check out:
1. Prophecy of Pendor 3.611
2. Warsword Conquest
3. RaW 2.5
4. Native Expansion (BETA)
5. Blood in the West
In conclusion, this game is a must buy. Definetly the best medivel simulator on the market in its time.

This is an early review, I'll update as I play more.
So far, I'm loving this game. In a marketplace full of rigid game genres, annualized franchises, and me-too clones, It's a very rare occurance when I can say that a game is 100% unique. If novelty is your thing, look no further than Mushroom 11.
I truly have never played or even seen a game like this one before. Mushroom 11 is based on the surprisingly simple mechanic of forcing your "mushroom" (it looks more like a green mass) to grow by destroying parts of it. Basically, it grows opposite of where you prune so if you want it to grow left, you cut the right side of it and vice-versa. Using this mechanic, you must navigate the desolate wasteland of a post-appocalyptic Earth. If this is difficult to understand, you're probably better off watching a video of this game in motion.
Where you are takeing your mushroom, I don't know. What the overall goal is, I don't know that either, but so far I have played the first chapter and I'm having a blast.
Pros:
+ Genuinely100% unique.
+ Long, intersting level design
+ Fantastic artwork
+ Challenging, especially if you try for 100% and absorb everything
+ The Mushroom is a treat to control
+ I have no idea what to expect next
+ Uniquely suited to the PC
+ Fun boss fights
Cons:
- Can't use a controller (probably for the better, I don't even know how this would work, but some may see this as a con)
Games as special as Mushroom 11 come along only every so often. This game will be remembered as a salient moment in the history of puzzle platformers. Don't miss it.

Geometry Wars is a great in-between game; meaning that, if you have 10 - 30 minutes it can be a great way to spend that time. Playing with friends and passing the controller is another great use of this game; but as one could expect, it loses its luster over time fairly quick. You move your ship with the left analog, and shoot with the right. There are plenty of mechanics and changes in theme to keep one's interest piqued for a decent time.
Still, I do recommend the game, provided you understand the sort of game you're purchasing.

So many taglines floating out there regarding this unique and enjoyable title. Are they all correct? Pretty much. There is nothing out there like Mushroom 11. Its unique take on platforming is refreshing and fun. Did I mention the art and musical direction? Well it's fantastic. It sets up the atmosphere very well, it surrounds the unique platforming concepts admirably. Are there any flaws? Some, I think replayability can come into question, I honestly didn't feel compelled to play levels again. Some stretches of the game were "the same" in a way, just slightly altered. Overall though this is an extremely fun ride I would enthusiastically recommend to platform genre fans, casual fans, and definitely anyone looking for something "different" (but good) to try.

When I read the game description, my first thought was that it would probably be something like Giana Sisters, as in a medium-paced platformer with the occasional puzzle. As I read further and realized the emphasis would be more about puzzles, I supposed it might be a little more like Nihilumbra, meaning slow-paced + puzzles. After actually playing for a little more than an hour, I can say for sure that Mushroom 11 is much more a puzzle game than a platformer.
Is that good or bad? I don't know, depends on which of those genres you like better. Personally, I'm usually not into complex puzzle games. I often find them tedious and generally uninteresting. This one, however, just like Nihilumbra, has a unique feel to it, that got me curious enough to keep going.
When I first launched the game, I picked up my Xbox controller and was expecting to play with it. When the game wasn't responding to the controller, I checked the options menu, expecting to find there an option to activate it... except there was no such option. I imagined Grumpy Cat look at me and say "No controller for you, dumbass! Deal with it!". So I went on and started playing with the mouse. The control felt really awkward for me at first. It took me a while to figure it out, but I have been learning along the way. Also, the game is quite challenging. Most of the puzzles got me thinking for a while before I could find the solution. Same for the bosses, and I'm only at chapter 3 (out of 7).
The game looks and sounds well, the level designs are really cool, and maybe most importantly, it runs smoothly and quickly. Nothing too fancy about it - no extra weight.
Ugh... what now? Oh, right - the bottom line!
Well, the bottom line is, that this game is mainly about patience, creativity and solving problems. You don't need fast reflexes or a good eye-hand coordination to play, but you do need to be patient and think. If you think that's for you - Mushroom 11 will definitely be a lot of fun for you. Otherwise, it might get tedious and frustrating very quickly.

Mushroom 11 is a unique puzzle-platformer. The objective is to traverse a post-apocalyptic world with your green blob. The gameplay is extremely simple but works well. You delete cells in your blob with an eraser and immidiately new cells will grown in another place on the blob. You move around this way and can split up the blob and make it grow in different directions and sizes. My First Impressions:
If you like puzzle games then you'll enjoy this one I think. The concept is very original.

While it probably won't be for everyone, Mushroom 11 is one of the most interesting/original puzzle platformers that I have played in a while.
In Mushroom 11 you play as a creature that can almost instantly re-grow its' cells. This means that damaged or "erased" cells will re-grow to the creature. The main mechanic in the game involves erasing part of the creature which makes that part of the creature re-grow somewhere else which you use to move the creature and solve the game's puzzles.
The game does a great job using this mechanic to create some interesting puzzles and boss fights. For the most part the mechanic works really well but the game does occasionally run into situations where the game keeps adding the new cells to an area of the creature where you didn't  want them to be moved to. This means that you sometimes have to waste time erasing the same part of the creature.
While I haven't finished the game yet I am through four of the seven levels and I have played the game for a little over three hours. I am guessing that the game is around six hours long.
If you think the game's concept sounds interesting I think you will enjoy Mushroom 11. If you are a little more unsure about the game, I think you should at least consider purchasing the game during a sale since it is a really unique experience that I think most people should enjoy.
Note: I received a free review copy of the game from the developer.

You do three things in this game:
1. Walk
2. Turn Lights on and Off
3. Pick Up Things that Tell You Things
4* Poop
And yet, this game is 100% absolutely worth playing.
Mechanically, the game performs magic tricks. Walk into a room through a door. Turn around. Now there's no door there. Turn around again. Now, the room's a different room. Turn around again, there's new writing on the wall behind you. These magic tricks are what make it fantastic to play on the surface.
The story is what will truly delight you. It's disturbing in a heart-breaking way. Sadness and trepidation are the two feelings that will consume you throughout. You're a painter who's insane. But, you're also the husband-half of a marriage that was truly Hell toward its end. I'm not talking about Ray-Donovan-style, "My husband's an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, my wife's a ♥♥♥♥♥" Hell. I'm talking about a state of marriage that closely approximates the Christian vision of Hell. This game's story is an extremely convincing portrayal of that kind of Hell.
Play it. Seriously.

Essentially, the gameplay is just 3 on 3 hockey like matches, set in the future. There are a number of different runners designed to fill certain roles on a team, each with different speeds and abilities. Even though there is currently not a massive amount of runners, I am yet to get bored of the intense and exciting matches. There is no story/campaign mode, and the entire thing is a multiplayer game. If a player ques and finds no people or only a few (as happens often) then bots will fill in for the missing slots. Most players like to focus on a single runner to excel at, but once in the character selection nothing is holding you back from choosing any of the characters you have unlocked (all characters can be unlocked with in game currency, or real money, but please, do not get the impression that this is a pay to win game. Certain runners are stronger than others but every single one can be played well, and no runner is too far unbalanced.) The matches are a short 5 minutes long in an arena with each team trying to shoot the puck into the other teams goal.
The community for this game is awesome. Its very friendly, and alot of the members have almost the entire community on their friends list at this point. The community isn't very large at all, and alot of the players in it have been playing since the start, but you get to know everybody this way, making it really great despite the size
Honestly, this game has so many flaws currently, despite so many already being fixed. Lack of players, bad bot AI, bugs, balancing issues, and various other things all pull this game back. But i think it says something that even amidst all these problems that on other games would be enough to make me quit, this game has kept me coming back for more.
Seriously, check out this game, and remember, don't feel discouraged when at first you can't find anyone.

That haiku basically sums up the whole game. Although I wouldn't say thats a bad thing. The game has four main goals:
But the games length and the way it's handled makes these goals fun. You max out the economy by buying upgrades with commodities such as food, product, and oil. This is one of my favorite parts of the game. Commodities can be bought from and sold to other countries, but prices are constantly changing. Occassionally prices will plummet or skyrocket for brief periods of time, which makes buying low and selling high more dynamic. Money and commodities can also be gained by invading other countries.
In contrast, defeating ISIS consists of defeating hordes of enemies in a survival mini game. While the free market trade mechanics are engaging, fighting ISIS is repetitive. There are commodities and money to be won by finishing a game, but since there are upgrades that are required to finish some of the "Fight ISIS"mini games, you won't always be able to finish what you start.
Upgrades can be unlocked through international relations. Goods can be bought and sold from other countries, but you can also send relief to countries, invade other countries, threaten other countries (to lower prices), schmooze other countries (to charge higher prices), and drill for oil in alaska. These actions will often raise or lower individual countries fear (lowers prices ) and love(raises selling values), or the overall world tension. If world tension rises to much World War III will begin, which acts as a gameover. But more specific actions (e.g buy x amount of y in country z) will unlock upgrades that can be used in Fight ISIS minigames or the main game. Some are optional, but a few are required to complete the game.

It's great in a ton of ways, and maddeningly bad in another, separate ton of ways.
Combat's great and the system is logical yet fun. Horseback takes it further, letting you skirt around the enemy whittling them down until there's just you with one extremely bloody sword arm.
BUT... the AI is subpar at best and suicidally stupid at worst. Unless told otherwise, your soldier's battle strategy is "I'll run forward and die on them". As a result, the enemy can use archers and cavalry to devastating effect while using them on your side for anything other than siege defense and scouting teams respectively feels like wasted gold. Also nobody knows what strafing is except you, so skirmishing tactics are almost worthless (unless you tell all your men to retreat and 1v50 dem noobs). To my understanding the auto-battle function is somthing to fear and loathe, guaranteeing you a new Battle of Thermopylae at best or total loss against mediocre troops at worst.
BUT...the world is expansive and the little quests you do bring life to the area. You can carry shipments across the continent or deliver letters between lords, eventually participating in castle sieges to curry favor and rising up in power to become a lord, or even king. Enemies you fail to slay might organise a hit against you. You can usurp positions of power, or help someone else take the mantle (for a price, of course). You could become a famous prize fighter or a legendary mercenary.
BUT... quests are randomly generated, so many of them are impossible to do without a huge amount of luck. Chase some deserters on horseback! Where are they? Well, one guy saw them near Narra 16 days ago, and they left far away from the trade routes so nobody's seen them since then. It's like searching a haystack for a moving needle, disguised as hay. Or participate in a siege! It's entirely random how many of your own men are in the front of the attack party (and thus get wholly, without exception, pulped) so I hope you like training and recruitment!
if TL;DR: If you're into high strategy and RPGs, I'd suggest playing this at least once. Probably with mods. Especially if there's a sale. There's a bunch of small things that can ruin the game, but if you avoid them this is a unique and fun medieval RPG where commanding an army can naturally flow from 5v5 to 100v100 with a few hours' play.

While the game shows its age (hell it's got a DirectX7 mode too), it remains quite enjoyable.
So do not expect shiny beautiful landscapes everywhere, the game is a bit old, and it shows.
However, you'll have the satisfaction of building yourself a sizable army...
The combat can take a bit to get used to, I strongly suggest you get yourself 5 or 10 members in your party at the start, no more, and then, visit the training grounds, and explore ALL options. This will familiarize yourself with all combat options, and it'll give you some xp to start with.
While your army grows, until you get a decent trainer in your party, you can boost new troops by sparring with them in the training grounds (any of them). This is great to fairly quickly train your low level troops to be a bit more usable.
There are guides on companions, and which ones go together, and which ones hates each others. It'll make your life easier :).
You can be a man, or a woman. A woman will have a slightly tougher time, especially at the beginning. Finding a husband for a woman is also a bit harder, since most men are scared to death of you :).
It is said you can have your own faction, and become the Queen/king. However, I would not suggest trying that until you are familiar with the game.
Save OFTEN. Not because the game is unstable, if anything, the game is a prime example of stability, but because you can die very quickly in any fight, regardless of your advantage... make a mistake or two, or simply get pulled in battle after a tough one, when you and your army are still weak, and you're going to loose a LOT of things :).
All in all, even though the game is getting old, it remains one of my favorite. The wars can be tough, especially if you are on the loosing side, however if you do not mind killing innocents, raiding villages can be a pretty good source of income during wars.
One thing I'd recommend, is not to join a faction for a while, and try to get a healthy production going in every single towns. By then, you'll be rolling in cash. Once you have a steady cash flow, increase your army size, and pick a faction. You'll only have a couple of towns being in enemy hands while at war, so usually, your cash flow will remain high, even if you are loosing the war.
For the more challenging call, you can either go on your own, and capture your own city, or pledge yourself to a claimant. If you have a high charisma and invested some points in persuasion, you can bring down a faction extremely quickly, with little to no fights.

Though there are a lot of good things about the game (the shooting mechanics are enjoyable, for instance), there are enough things wrong with the game that it's hard to imagine it being popular in the near future. There's no quick fix or simple tweak here; it needs a substantial overhaul. The content comes at you so fast that it can be overwhelming and there's very little information available on the game in English. It took me several hours just to figure out how you get more ammo or how to sell my loot. (btw DEVS, an open auction house in the starter area could really help with the new player experience). There are a lot of different sandbox-type activities (metal detectors for mining, animal skinning, "artifact" treasure hunting, etc), but they're limited by annoying in-game mechanics. For example, you need a hunting knife to, say, turn a stick into a useful tool, but you're limited to 1 or 2 knives per day. If you're very patient and you really enjoy figuring things out on your own in a wasteland/fallout type setting, you might enjoy it, but overall the quests are often frustrating and unclear, the business model makes no sense (you buy items from the cash shop which last only for a limited time), and it quickly becomes clear that the game hasn't yet been able to foster any sort of English-speaking player base, so you're going to be going it alone.

I have stumbled upon on Niche about 3 months ago, and I must say, I immediatly fell in love with it. The graphic style of it is very unique and colorful, and it gives you a vibe of happy and cheerful game, which I think fits this very well. But, of course you can change that. You can make a tribe full of gothic-like creatures, that live in the swamp. You can make a tribe where everyone lives in the water. You can basically do anything. You can shape your story however you like.
These are just a few examples of how many options there are.
There is no goal in this game, only to survive. You can do many challenges in this game, which makes it even more interesting. Talking about challenges, the game is not going to be easy all way.  Sometimes it can get hard trying to unlock the genes, to make a specific tribe, but thats part of th fun! There are also rouge males, predators, nicheling-eating plant, you need to keep an eye on, and many more obstacles. And then of course there are genes. Probably the most important part of all.
Now, I have a few cons about this game. First, sometimes it can get repetetive. When you have raised species you wanted, and they are healthy, there is not much to do then. I tried unlocking all genes, exploring, raising a new species....it still makes it broing after time.
Second, when a female is pregnant, you can put her onto a nest, and she will give birth over night, just like that. When she gives birth, she can just go away from the baby and breed again or do something else. I know not many games are realistic, but when I first played the full release version, I hoped they would make the mom stay with her baby and maybe somehow feed it with milk, as a maternity instinct to protect it, and care for it.
Third and final con is that you cant see the whole family tree. When you move to the next island, there are only the creatures that you brought to the next island, and their parents/kids. It is then very hard to remember who had who, if he
is related to her, especially for story-tellers like me.
Thats all I have to say. Overall, the game is beatyfuly made, and it lags very rarely, I dont see any bugs at all.
I sure recommend you to try it you. :)

TLDR: This is an arcade-esque twin stick shooter. It's worth the $4, but you'll need a controller to play it right.
This game was a launch title for the Xbox 360 when it first launched in 2005. Yet due to its simplicity still holds up today. Take control of a shape as you shoot other shapes in hopes to get as high of a score as possible. But beware as the waves of enemies get bigger and faster the longer you stay alive. It's a test not only of dexterity, but also of endurance. While this version lacks the retro mode the 360 version had, it's not really that much of an oversight as the Evolved mode will still have you hooked. You may play in small doses, but it's a game you'll be coming back to again and again and again and again and again and again and again.
Should you buy this: Yes, but ONLY if you have a controller. It's a twin stick shooter, so that should go without saying. You could theoretically play this with a mouse and keyboard, but just because you can doesn't mean you should. If you have Windows 8/10 you can hook up an Xbox One controller and it instantly hooks up.
Worth: $4 is a fair price, although you can usually get about a dollar off if you wait until it goes on sale (it doesn't happen often though)

I've finished the game on Survival (normal difficulty) after 29 hours. Here are my thoughts:
Difficulty: The game's difficulty is average to difficult, but never unfair (the game gives you enough resources and messing up does not mean you'll have to restart from an earlier save).
Graphics: playing this on Ultra, I was impressed and took many pictures of some really nice things I saw in the game. The game has many high points, with very nice light and dark scenes. The only con is the "cut and paste" of some models, which break the immersion.
Sound: I've played many of this game's quieter moments with my earphone, and I was really impressed. Amazing sound design, which makes you feel like you are playing a horror movie in the game's more stealth-oriented sections.
Gameplay: RE4 with some limitations, so you cannot fight like a soldier. You can use melee, but it is not effective for killing the enemies. You get some upgrades that, when used well, really make the difference, but running and using the environment is the key to survival, as the enemies are a lot more aggressive than in other games of the genre.
Story: Not too original, you'll feel like you are riding in a nightmare, but the pieces will make sense in time, especially if you play the DLC (I'm still playing the second DLC, but I can tell they really add meaning to the story).
Some complaints: copied assets (as mentioned above), dying fast because of powerful enemies, action sequences are a bit overused so you lose a bit the horror vibe to get a more action-oriented feeling.
Overall: 10/10, Essential game in any true gamer's library, especially if you enjoy survival horror games!

While it probably won't be for everyone, Mushroom 11 is one of the most interesting/original puzzle platformers that I have played in a while.
In Mushroom 11 you play as a creature that can almost instantly re-grow its' cells. This means that damaged or "erased" cells will re-grow to the creature. The main mechanic in the game involves erasing part of the creature which makes that part of the creature re-grow somewhere else which you use to move the creature and solve the game's puzzles.
The game does a great job using this mechanic to create some interesting puzzles and boss fights. For the most part the mechanic works really well but the game does occasionally run into situations where the game keeps adding the new cells to an area of the creature where you didn't  want them to be moved to. This means that you sometimes have to waste time erasing the same part of the creature.
While I haven't finished the game yet I am through four of the seven levels and I have played the game for a little over three hours. I am guessing that the game is around six hours long.
If you think the game's concept sounds interesting I think you will enjoy Mushroom 11. If you are a little more unsure about the game, I think you should at least consider purchasing the game during a sale since it is a really unique experience that I think most people should enjoy.
Note: I received a free review copy of the game from the developer.

Mushroom 11 is a challenging puzzle/obstacle course game from Untame. In Mushroom 11 you ‘take control’ of an amorphous organism and guide it through increasingly difficult obstacle course style chapters. The apocalyptic world you find yourself in is full of strange mutated creatures which either act as collectibles or bosses.
The game’s presentation is easily its strongest aspect. The organism itself looks great and fits well with the rest of the game. The backgrounds are incredibly well designed, each chapter having a different one, they really give the game the ‘destroyed world’ feel that the devs seem to be going for. There’s not really any UI during gameplay but it’s not necessary to have one so that’s fine. The menus are nice and simple but I did have one problem with the menus, no confirmation dialogue when quitting to menu. I misclicked during boss fights a couple of times which resets the bosses, a simple confirmation would have meant this didn’t happen. It’s not a major issue but I found it bothersome.
So you’ve got yourself a giant blob of an amorphous organism and an obstacle course, how exactly do you get through this obstacle course? Movement is pretty much just erasing parts of your organism so that it can grow back on a different part of your blob. It’s difficult to properly describe how this movement is achieved but the game’s simple tutorial explains it rather well. Movement is only possible while your organism is in contact with the ground though so when you’re in the air you just have to hope you make it across to whatever you’re trying to reach. As for the actual erasing you simply use the LMB or RMB. The LMB is a large eraser generally used for movement while the RMB is a small eraser that’s generally used to cut off certain parts of the organism or to make more precise changes to the organism’s shape. The simple control scheme for the game definitely works well.
The puzzles/obstacles you encounter vary but for quite a few of the obstacles in each chapter they’re just more elaborate versions of what you see in the first couple of chapters which leads to little variety, apart from difficulty, over the course of the game. That said new obstacle types are introduced from time to time and some of them are a lot of fun, such as slides and cranes.
From time to time you’ll find you’ve either managed to erase too much of your organism or you’ll find yourself up close and personal to a trap which kills the organism, such as a lava pit. In these situations you’ll find yourself at the last of the regular checkpoints that you passed.
As well as these puzzles/obstacles you’ll face a boss fight at the end of each chapter. There’s good variety between the different bosses and they all provide a decent challenge, the later ones more so than the early ones as would be expected. The bosses also introduce interesting mechanics such as bombs which, if they go off close to you, will burn through your organism.
Not too much to say about this one, the sound track and sound effects are both good quality and fit well with the game.
Mushroom 11 is a challenging puzzle game with a great look, good world design and fun gameplay which is let down by its high price. If you’re a complete puzzle game nut you might get your money’s worth but if you like a puzzle game every once in a while I’d suggest waiting for a better sale.

Mushroom 11 is what you get if you mix up a platform game, a puzzle game and Photoshop's eraser tool. And it's great!
The underlying movement mechanism - where you destroy some of your cells to force it to grow back in a different shape - is very simple, but the beautiful design, endlessly changing landscapes and inventive puzzles means that it never gets old.
It's so beautifully slick, too. Your organism gloops, squeezes and squirms around with a fluidity that is by turns graceful and hilarious.
Progression through the level is fairly A-B, with a few optional side-roads to find collectibles. You generally take on one puzzle (or speedy action sequence) at a time, with plenty of checkpoints between.
There's only the occasional bit of needless frustration - you finish off an end of chapter boss, only to have to perform some slow, painstaking final climb up a difficult chain just to finish the level, for instance.
My impressions so far of chapters 1 to 3 is that the game is quite gentle introducing itself to you - the puzzles don't get tricky for a while (variations on button pressing, simple see-saw physics puzzles etc), with the trickier bits coming more from when you need to somehow squeeze across a pool of lava without falling in. But I'm itching to get back to it - I can't wait to be challenged more.
Great soundtrack, too. It's exactly what you'd want to hear while being a giant, slimy mushroom.

DISCLAIMER: I was given a press copy of this game by the developers. If you feel that makes my opinions invalid that is your right. Though, for what it’s worth, this has never affected, and will never affect, the content of my reviews.
I like the way the game looks, but I’d say it really depends on your tastes. The aesthetic fits the world that is presented to us; one that is, seemingly, post apocalyptic. There’s a lot browns and greys, and maybe it’s just me, but even the bright colours, like the goo itself and lava, feel kind of toned down, again, fitting with the theme. I feel that there wasn’t a whole lot of contrast between the colours, which isn’t my favourite look, but again, fits what the developers were going for. I think the highlight of the presentation is the way the goo grows, and the sound effects that come with it. It’s really well designed, and feels satisfying when you get the goo to go the way you want.
Speaking of the way the goo works, it’s really difficult to explain. Even if it looks like it at first glance, you don’t actually play as the goo. You play as a sort of god-like guide for the goo, who’s only power is to erase the goo. That sounds really weird, and it kind of is, but basically you have to imagine it as though there is a certain amount of goo that has to be on the screen at all times. If you erase a section of the goo, it will grow back the same amount you erased only from different parts of the goo. This allows you to shape the goo in whatever way you please; you even have a much smaller “brush” that can make relatively fine modifications to the goo. The game continually presents new challenges to the player, and many times, like portal, it’s about thinking outside the box or approaching the situation differently.
The thing that was disappointing for me i terms of the story, is that it isn’t well contextualized, and that’s why I compare it to the first portal. Though, even then the first portal had more of a heart to it than this game. Because, really, it feels like a tech demo, and that the whole game is just a stage to show of this one mechanic and not really much more than that. Another game that comes to mind is the first Assassin’s Creed. It pretty much totally lacks a story, and while it does have the post-apocalyptic world, it felt like you could have re-skinned it with anything. Would this game be different if the goo was instead cotton candy in a cotton candy factory? Not really. Not in any big way.
So this is what I mean. Portal 1 didn’t have the character and charm required to really be a masterpiece although it was still a great game. Portal 2 built upon the foundations that Portal 1 laid, and made a truly ground-breaking game that got, and deserved, universal acclaim. This game feels like an even more bare-bones version of Portal 1 -- so it shows so much promise, and was fun to play and is an all round really good game, but it was also an empty vessel. It doesn’t really have a soul to it.
So as I mentioned before the game has 7 chapters and each will last, give or take 20 - 30 minutes. I think my longest was about 45 minutes, and my shortest was 13 minutes. So you’ll get about 3-4 hours out of this game, and maybe more if you go after the collectables which I didn’t do. $15 is reasonable for that amount of gameplay, and it’s pretty worthwhile gameplay too. It’s certainly fun, and becomes very challenging in the last few chapters so be aware of that. I’m recommending it, but if you’re only “kind of” interested in this game then wait for a sale. $5-10 for this game would be a steal.

If you don't want to read the whole thing, here's a quick summary:
PROS
Little to no bugs, doesn't crash

I'll go over some of the basics of Niche. First off, as far as I've seen, there are almost no bugs and the game has never crashed for me. It's also very rarely laggy.
The graphics are clean, simple, and colorful, which is a plus, but sometimes they're too simple. Like another review I read, I believe adding small animations to the nichelings would be endearing, whether they're idle animations or even just paw movements when actions are done.
You start off with five empty save slots that you can create worlds in. There are two modes, Story and Sandbox, with Story mode having more of a preset endgame goal and Sandbox being for more experienced players to make their own goals, while they can choose their own islands.
If you've never played before, definitely start off in story because sandbox doesn't have a tutorial. While Story does have one, it's rather lacking and I'd recommend reading the community guides to help you out because the game has many unexplained aspects. The tutorial is getting an update, though.
You start off with 1/2 nichelings, depending on your mode. In Story, the main goal they give you is to reach the main character (Adam)'s home island and meet the other nichelings that live there, his family. Once again, for a better explanatioin look for a community guide. In Sandbox people create their own goals- there are many challenges you can make and give yourself, along with trying to obtain certain genes. Genes are one of the defining factors of Niche, with a wide selection that can give you completely different nichelings if you carry the right genetics. However, the genes and breeding are not explained very well so if you don't understand it, find a community guide.
The game itself is not packed with action or tension. There is combat against predators, but it's mostly swiping against the enemy, breeding for higher strength, and then swiping again. Some are way tougher than others, but the combat process is the same. Don't buy the game if you're expecting a fast-paced combat simulator.
It can also be rather bland at times, and repetitive, but there are many biomes and islands to explore and every new world is different.
However, the game has high potential for storytelling, and is like it states: a genetics survival game. You collect food, breed, and fight to survive, all the while trying to breed out bad genes and keep the good, helpful genes. There are a wide  variety of nichelings possible, and you can tell stories and give each nicheling their own character and personality. Want your leader to be strict, cruel, and harsh? You can have them banish the rogue children, or even feed them to the birds. Want an ultimate fighter with genes of a predator? Go ahead, but it'll take quite some time. It all pays off when you see that 12 strength, though (haha). Over half the genes are locked when you start off, but there are different ways to unlock them all and different islands you have to explore. There's a whole system of dominant/recessive and each gene benefits/harms your nicheling's chance of survival.
There are also many things that can harm your tribe- freezing, overheating, starvation, predators, and leeches are only a few. A part of the game is based on luck, since you could begin the game and run into a predator immediately, while others might find a whole bunch of healthy wanderers with great genes. The cores and basics of the game are very solid, however there are many small things that could be added that would improve a player's experience. The in-game messages don't tell you much- for example, some genes simply say "Travel to new islands" to unlock them, which can be confusing.

Not a bad game but it has a little less to offer than a 18 dollar price tag would suggest. I was not suprised to learn it was Kickstarted and made by a small team. I think they did well with their means.
The gameplay feels more like a board game than a simulation, with action points, hex-grid movement, and sightlines. Reproduction is key as the longest lived animal only lasts 2 dozen turns, which naturally introduces the dilemma of who do you breed? Which traits do you want? Which don’t you want? Do you want to risk the chance of inbreeding to propagate a good trait? Do you cast out those with bad traits you want to weed out? The system is natural and intuitive and is even better that it well mimics the natural processes it’s based on.
Overall however, I feel this game could have used more effort put into it, not that I’m saying that that they didn’t put in enough. What is there is clearly put into the most important areas. The creatures are adorable and diverse, the genetics system is extensive and well designed. Those two things are the most important parts of the game and are well done.
My biggest problems with the game are the simplistic graphics, the lack of animations, and the clunky user interface.
I really expected more based upon the screen shots and the price tag but most of the environments felt bland, uniform, and tame from a graphical perspective. I got used to it but it was still a bit jarring. I’m not expecting physics and total realism, but a little more detail would have gone a long way towards making me feel like I’m exploring a wild and uncharted archipelago.
The animals lack nearly all animation which makes them feel more like board game pieces than animals, which is a real missed opportunity to further endear these cute animals to the player.
The interface was another missed opportunity which would truly benefit from some extra spit and polish. I found myself misclicking during actions in attempt to unselect or select different creatures but it wasn’t terrible. The notifications were not as helpful as they could be and should have taken a page from other games. Mousing over them should display their text and each’s text should have (where appropriate) the name of the creature, cause of death, damage values, etc, instead of showing a generic ‘a creature has died’ message. Clicking it should center on the area of interest and/or highlight the area/individual instead of opening a pop-up which must then be clicked.
Also with the interface, the thing I wanted the most was help managing my creatures’ genetics. While I like how the family tree graph and gene layout is displayed I want more. It is easy to forget who is related to who, who has too similar genes, which pups I wanted to ‘betroth’, which animals have and haven’t been bread. Since they have such short life spans it’s a lot of work to keep everything organized. I’d kill to be able to look and see
or
without having to write down his letters and compare them against all the other animals I have individually. Being able to tell who was male and female at a glance would have made mating a lot easier. At the very least a risk indicator of inbreeding chance before mating would help. If there is one aspect of the game to improve (in my opinion) it would be this. It would make things so much more enjoyable.
All that being said while I hope they update the game to make it better I would totally buy a $10 or more expansion that remedies these issues. This game has all it’s core mechanics nailed down and would really shine with more TLC with improvements and elaborations.

HuniePop is either the single worst or single greatest impulse buy I have ever done. Going into the game all
I knew was it was a dating sim with puzzle game elements…. what the real selling point was for me was when I saw all the incredibly ridiculous steam reviews:
“Well, I didn't expect her to ♥♥♥♥ on the first date let alone squirt. And when Tiffany refuses anything other than Anal, I almost choked one out right there and then”
That was when I knew I had to see what the heck this game was about.
The game focuses on you playing as a guy who is an absolutely hopeless virgin who is utterly horrible in the dating scene. That all changes the day that you get visited by the sexy, scantily clad dating fairy who vows to teach you how to play the field and promises that with her help you’ll go on dates and get laid. From there the “Yukki”-esque fairy teaches you the core gameplay mechanics which aren’t that too different from other puzzle games in the vein of Bejeweled. You go on dates that consist of the puzzles where you connect three or more of the various colored balls and earn “Affection” points, and you can earn bonus “Affection” points by paying attention to the girls personality and focusing heavily on the color balls that she desires most. You are tasked with reaching a set level of Affection points to pass the level and have a successful date, however with every successful date you have, the level of Affection points required for the next date becomes significantly higher which certainly adds to the difficulty considering you are limited to 20 moves per date. In addition to the colored ball tokens, there are also bell tokens which give you an extra turn, heart tokens which increase your passion level that increases the affection points you get when you connect the colored balls, sentiment tear drops that allow you to use various items, and purple broken heart tokens that sap affection points from your date and can be truly devastating to a date. At the conclusion of each date both successful and failure dates, you are awarded “Munies” that you can use to spend on food, drinks, and gifts for your dates.
As you talk to the girls and successfully choose the right dialog branch you are awarded “Hunie” which is used to upgrade your traits that give you bonuses and allow you to perform better in the puzzle dates. It’s sad, because one of the games both strongest and weakest points are the dialog, for both the cut scenes and dialog trees. The dialog is really what makes this game worth playing…It will make you laugh, cringe, and blush, however it becomes repetitive very quickly, and spending time with any one girl for too long will cause the dialog to loop back around and start recycling itself.
With each successfully date; you earn a “heart” in the girls love progression bar. Once you reach either 4 or 5 hearts depending on how into you the girl is, if you successfully pass a date puzzle at night then things will get disappointingly hot and heavy. You’ll finally get laid and the sex mini-game puzzle is just merely a puzzle similar to the ones you’re used to only with no limit on your number of turns, you have to rapidly connect the colored ball tokens to combat the decreasing Affection points bar all the while your date is moaning and egging you on. Upon completion of the mini-game you are awarded a semi-nude sexual photo of your date that gets added to your photo album. The fact that that’s as far as the game is willing to push the envelope is a little disappointing, If you are going to make a game that focuses on this type of subject matter and the entire goal of the game is to have sex…then there should have been more of a payoff than there was.
Besides the puzzles and dialog, the game also features a very large amount of “Plot”. The Plot is very well animated and the various image stills you receive in the game are all very well illustrated. The only issues some may run into with the “plot” is that the steam version is censored, but this can be easily remedied if you so desired with a patch released by the devs.
The game successfully delivers a fairly solid puzzle dating sim that is delivered with the look and feel of a visual novel. The game is held back however by its sub-par voice acting, repetitive dialog, and less than climactic climax scenes.

I'd give this game a 10/10. Honestly I've played quite the bit of horror games, from Resident Evil, which may or may not be considered a horror experience as of so far, all the way to SOMA and Amnesia: Dark Descent and Machine for Pigs. The amount of horror you get from games like that don't always appear genuine. In fact, while playing Amnesia, I don't think I got the feels I did from a game like Layers of Fear.
This game seduces me into the story. While I'm looking at notes and hunting rat pictures, I end up turning around to find that what I thought would be behind me was actually not there, instead a wonderful jump scare or two would greet me. That was wonderful, but when you think about that it seems like the jump scares would quickly get to be stale. Wrong. They end up getting creative with things and set up scares where you'd never expect them, and then switch right back to where you would expect them.
Developers of Layers of Fear knew exactly what kind of community they were trying to hit. Those who enjoy story and those who enjoy horror. They definately matched what they were going for. And this is coming from someone who had never heard of the game before I found it on Steam.
Again 10/10. I will most likely be playing this over and over again just to delve farther into the very pleasing story and horror environment. Well done.
